# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr — The Age of Strangers (An Aois Choigreach)

# Part One: Of the Opening of the Sea

# Chapter One: Of the Gauze on the Water


*AE 1 – 2*

> *A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.*
> Manannan, keep the sea shut.

## I. Of the Four Witnesses

This telling is set down in Seilear Muileann chaol, in the winter the rolls came down to it, by the copyists of Na Trì Teaghlaichean, who have kept the custodians' copies there through the last years of this age and now have more paper than shelf. The chests came in by cart over the frozen ruts from the west, some with their lids nailed and some with a rope round them, and some still smelling of the lamp-soot of the rooms they had lain in. There are four witnesses in them, and the telling leans on each in turn.

The first witness is the rolls of the custodians: the rolls of each town, and above them the roll of Comhairle a' Chùraim at Cathair dhearg, in the hands of a hundred and fifty years of clerks, a few fine and most of them hurried. The second is the letter-books of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, which were found on the shelves of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir when its last master went down to the water and left them behind. They are written in the humans' tongue and the humans' letters, and three of the copyists have learned to read them. The third is the daybooks of the beacon-keepers, who wrote down every sail they saw and every night the flame was lit, and had nothing to gain by lying about a ship that was not there. The fourth is the songs of the camps. They were forbidden, and for that reason somebody always wrote them down.

Where the four agree, the telling goes on without stopping. Where they quarrel, each is heard. When they fall silent, the telling says so once and goes on to the next thing it knows.

The age they speak of began in a winter like other winters. The crown had stood empty since the close of An Aois Scaraidh, and the council sat in its place at Cathair dhearg, which had worked well enough for long enough that nobody asked any more whether it should. Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was kept: the coal of the vein was burned in the measured handful at the shrines and nowhere else, and the island's hearths burned peat and driftwood and the wood of their own hedges. Clann Choinnich's petition to smelt silver with the coal lay unanswered in Taigh na Fèithe. The north-west was nearly empty, its fields gone back to rush and its harbours to the gulls. At Seann Skell of the west eleven people had kept Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh on Cidhe an Diosail the last time the harbour scribe troubled to count them, and the priests of Manannan went down to the river-mouth at every tide, morning and evening and in the dark between, to say their prayer:

> *A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.*

They said it because Ceò Mhanannain was thinning. For eighteen centuries it had stood on the eastern sea, where Cabhlach an Scaraidh had sailed into it and not come out, and on the north it had stood too, a grey wall a few oar-lengths off the capes, so that the sea ran into it and nothing came back. In the last winters of the old age the priests wrote that it lay thinner each year. On still mornings the fishers of the north-west could see through it to a dark line ruled across the edge of the world, which was the open sea going on. They saw it, and turned for home as the rule of sight-of-land told them, and said nothing about it in the alehouse, because there was nothing to say.

## II. Of the Gauze off the Cape

Lachlann Odhar was steersman of the larger of the two boats of Achadh àrsaidh that went out after the winter cod in the month of am Faoilleach, in the first year of this age. He was a thick, sallow man of near forty with a broken nose and a habit of talking to the tiller. Achadh àrsaidh was a small place then, a few households on the rise behind the north-west cape who farmed a little and fished more, and it kept two boats because it could not man three.

They went out in the dark with the lines baited and the lanterns shuttered, and by first light they were off the cape in the long swell, where the water shelves down from the rocks and the cod lie in the cold. The other boat worked a cable's length to the west, Lachlann's brother-in-law at her steering-oar. The wind was light out of the north and the sky clear. Behind them the land stood up black. Ahead of them, where the grey had always stood, there was no wall.

Lachlann saw it before any of his crew did, because he was the only one of them not looking at his line. The grey was there, but it had gone to gauze: a thin, hanging, shifting stuff that the light came through, and through it he could see the sea going on, and on, farther than any man of Achadh àrsaidh had been told the sea went. He watched it a long while. Old men said that Uilebheist na Mara rose in that water when it pleased, and Lachlann had half a mind that the paleness moving in the gauze was the beast's back.

Then the paleness took a shape, and the shape was sail.

It was one sail, high up, heaped on a mast taller than any tree Lachlann had ever cut or seen cut; then a second behind it and a third, and under them black hulls, wet and shining, riding higher out of the water than a hall stands on its hill. They came down out of the north slowly, with the grey tearing off their bows in rags and hanging a moment in their rigging before the wind took it. There were men along their sides. He could see the white of their faces.

Nobody in the boat spoke. One of the young men let his line run out through his fingers until it burned him, and swore, and let it go.

The first ship came near enough that Lachlann could hear her: the groan of her timbers, a block squealing somewhere up in the rigging, and then a man's voice from high on the stern, calling down.

"Ahoy the boat! What land is this? What land?"

It was no tongue that Lachlann had ever heard, or anyone at Achadh àrsaidh. He stood up at the tiller, set his feet wide against the roll, cupped his hands, and gave back the old hail of the north-west boats, which was the hail his father had given and his father before him, and which asks the stranger's harbour and his kin:

"Cò às a thàinig sibh?"

The voice on the ship called again, louder, as men do when they are not understood, and then another voice joined it, and a third, all saying something different. Lachlann hailed again. The ship's people pointed at the land, and at their mouths, and at the land again. One of them held up a wooden cask by its rope-handle and swung it so that it banged on the ship's side, and even at that distance Lachlann could hear that it was empty.

He sat down.

"Well," said his brother-in-law, who had brought the other boat in close. "What do we do?"

Nothing in all the customs of Dia-thìr told a fisherman what to do when the sea opened. There was the rule of sight-of-land, which said turn back, and there was the old law of the shore, which said that a man who asks for water is given water. The one told him to go home and the other told him to stay, and neither told him what to do with ships out of the north and a tongue that meant nothing.

"You go home," said Lachlann at last. "Tell them at Achadh àrsaidh what you saw. Tell them I've gone south to Cuan shean, and I've taken these with me, if they'll come."

"Why Cuan shean?"

"Because there are custodians there whose business it is to know. I don't know. You don't know."

His brother-in-law looked at the ships a while longer, spat over the side for luck, and put about for the cape. The boat went off into the light with her crew all turned round on the thwarts, looking back.

Lachlann put his tiller over and bore away south along the coast. When he looked back, the ships were following him.

That was the longest day of his life, by his own telling, and he told it often afterward. They ran south with the north wind on the quarter, past the headlands of the empty coast one after another, the black ships a mile astern and never nearer, shortening sail to keep behind a fishing boat as a man shortens his stride to walk with a child. Past the cape of Baile chrom, where no fire had burned for a generation. Past the mouths of small rivers where nobody lived. His crew rowed when the wind dropped and sat with their hands between their knees when it rose again. They ate the bread they had brought for the fishing and drank the water, and toward evening one of them asked whether they should give some to the ships, and Lachlann said the ships would have to wait for the custodians like everyone else.

The fishers of Achadh àrsaidh gave the place of that meeting a name, Coinneachadh nan Long (13 am Faoilleach, AE 1), and their boats slow there still when they pass it, as if something might come out of the north again.

It was full dark when Lachlann brought his boat round the last point and saw the lights of Cuan shean along the water, the long low rope-walks black against the town. He ran her up the shingle, and the first man who came down to see who was landing at that hour found him sitting on the gunwale with his head in his hands, and three lanterns hanging out on the sea behind him where no lanterns had ever been.

## III. Of the Empty Cask

Oighrig nic Leòid had been custodian of Cuan shean for eleven years, and in that time the hardest thing she had been asked to decide was the line of a boundary between two rope-walks. She was near fifty, tall and big-handed, a widow whose sons had gone inland to the salt-pans and the capital, and she lived in the custodian's house above the harbour with a servant and a grey cat and a roll that had nothing much written in it.

They woke her that night. She went down to the shingle in her cloak and looked at the lanterns, and at Lachlann Odhar, and heard him out. Then she said that nobody was to put off to the ships in the dark, nor light any fire on the strand that could be taken for a sign, and that she would see them in the morning; and she went home and did not sleep.

In the morning there was no seeing them. The wind went round into the west in the night and blew hard, and when the light came Na Trì Longan were standing off and on beyond the bar, well out, with their topsails reefed, the sea breaking white along the reef between them and the harbour. They kept off like that for days, through a run of westerly weather such as the west coast gets in the back end of winter, and the whole town of Cuan shean stood on the dunes in the wind and watched them. Children made up names for them. The rope-makers laid bets on whether they would come in or go. Old women said they were the ships of Cabhlach an Scaraidh come home at last, and other old women told them not to talk nonsense, and they went on saying it. At Seann Skell, half a day's walk up the coast, the priests of Manannan heard of the ships from a carter the second morning, and from that tide on they kept the prayer at every turn of the water without once missing, and a boy ran down the coast each evening to see whether the ships were still there, and ran back to tell them.

Lachlann Odhar stayed in Cuan shean. He said his boat was damaged, which was not true, and slept in a net-loft, and each morning he stood with the rest on the dunes.

The roll of Cuan shean sets the ships down first on 5 an Gearran, AE 1. On that morning the wind fell and the swell lay down, and the strangers' ships came in over the bar on the flood, one behind the other, feeling their way with a lead-line that a man swung and called from the bows, and let go their anchors off the town in water where no hull of their size had lain since Cabhlach an Scaraidh went out sunwise from Seann Skell and did not come back. The roar of the cables running out came over the water, and every gull on the strand went up at once.

Then a boat came off the nearest ship, with a man standing in the stern.

Oighrig went down to the shingle. She had her two fellow custodians with her, both older than she was and neither of them willing to be first, and behind them half the town, and behind the town the dunes with more people on them. She had put on her good cloak, and then thought better of it and put on her old one, and then gone back for the good one, and she was angry with herself about that all the way down the hill.

The boat grounded in the surf a stone's throw out, and the man in the stern jumped over the side into the water. It was up to his thighs and it was the cold sea of the back end of winter, and he gasped with it, and came on wading with a cask held up against his chest in both arms. Eleven men followed him out of the boat. She looked for weapons among them, and saw none, though one had a long knife at his belt such as a fisherman carries. They were thin, all of them. Two of them had to hold each other up in the surf. The one in front was a man of about thirty-five with a short brown beard gone salt at the edges, a coat that had been good once, and eyes that went quickly over everything on the beach and came back to her, because she was the one standing a step in front.

The roll calls him Edmund Harrow. He came up out of the water onto the shingle, and stopped, and set the cask down at her feet, and knocked on it with his knuckles so that she could hear it was empty.

"Water," he said. "We need water, ma'am. We've been on short allowance a fortnight and the men are sick. Water. Do you understand me?"

She heard it as sounds. He heard her silence and tried again, slower, as men do, and then gave it up and did what any child of any shore would have done: he pointed at the cask and tipped his hand to his mouth, and made a little tilting motion with it, and swallowed.

There is a law of the shore on Dia-thìr older than the custodians, older than Taigh na Fèithe and the crown, and every fisher's child knows it before she knows her letters. A man who comes up out of the sea and asks for water is given water. It asks nothing about who he is.

"Bring it," said Oighrig nic Leòid.

They brought it from the town well in two buckets, and she dipped the ladle herself and gave it into his hands, and he drank, and gave the ladle to the man behind him, and did not drink again until all eleven had drunk. She noticed that. The roll is silent on it; she said it afterward to the council in her letter, and the letter survives.

Then he pointed at the ships, and at the well, and made a gesture that took in the whole town and its wells and its fields behind, and looked at her with his eyebrows up.

She shook her head.

It was not hers to give. Water was given under the law of the shore. Anything more, a stay of a night on the strand, a sack of meal, a place for a sick man to lie, was a thing no custodian of Cuan shean had ever been asked in eighteen hundred years, and she knew it was not hers, and she knew that if she gave it the giving would be written in the roll and be a thing that had been done. She had them fill the cask. She had them fill six more that the boat went back to fetch. Then she went up the hill to the custodian's house and wrote to Cathair dhearg.

The rider left within the hour. He was a rope-maker's son who kept a good horse, and she told him not to spare it. It is some twenty-six miles from Cuan shean up the valley road to the capital, and he was at the council's door by nightfall with the horse lathered and blown, and he gave the letter into the hand of the clerk of the council, who read it standing up, then sat down and read it again.

## IV. Of the Forty Days below the Dunes

The council's first answer came back two days later. It said: feed them; keep them apart; decide nothing; the council will sit on it.

So Cuan shean fed them. The custodians would not let the strangers into the town, and would not let them stay aboard their ships and starve, and between the two they settled on the strand below the dunes, where the shingle gives way to hard sand and the marram grass holds the slope, a long stretch of beach with the town above it on one side and the sea on the other. The strangers came ashore there and put up shelters out of their spare sails and spars, and the town carried food down to them morning and evening. The roll gives it as forty days of feeding below the dunes. The roll counts the days and not the meal, which the custodians paid out of the town's own store and afterward put in the account to the council, where it was never repaid.

They were not easy days. The strangers were sick, most of them, with a sickness of the gums and the joints that comes to men who have lived too long on ship's food, and three of them died on the beach in the first weeks and were buried by their own people above the tide-line with a strange rite: a man read from a book, the rest stood bareheaded, and then all of them knelt on the sand. The children of Cuan shean watched that from the top of the dunes and could not be driven off. Afterward they played at it in the lanes, one reading out of a flat stone and the rest kneeling, until their mothers stopped them.

The fresh meat and the greens mended the rest. By the time the spring had come in, the strangers were walking about the strand like men and not like ghosts, and it was then that the town began to know them.

They could not be kept from working. That was the first thing Cuan shean learned about them. They had come down half starved and sick in a strange country, penned on a beach by people whose tongue they had not one word of, and as soon as they could stand they wanted something to do with their hands. They mended their own sails and caulked their boats. And then, because the fishers of Cuan shean spread their nets to dry along that same strand, the strangers began to mend the fishers' nets.

Nobody had asked them to. A fisher came down one morning and found a stranger sitting on the shingle with her torn net across his knees, knotting it up, and she stood over him with her mouth open until he looked up and grinned at her and held out his hand for more twine. He tied a knot the fishers had never seen, a flat hard knot that did not slip. By the end of the week half the strangers were at it. The fishers watched and learned the knot, and it is tied at Cuan shean to this day and called the strangers' knot.

Trade began the same way, out of nothing, with nobody deciding it. A stranger held out a button off his coat, a round thing of bright yellow metal with a device stamped on it, to a boy carrying a string of fish up the beach. The boy took the button and gave him a fish. By the next morning there were fishwives on the strand with baskets, and strangers with buttons, and the strangers' coats began to hang open. The custodians forbade it, and it went on, and they forbade it again, and it went on behind the dunes where they could not see. Oighrig let it be in the end. The roll notes that a good many buttons of yellow metal went into the town that spring and that the fishwives wore them on cords round their necks, and nothing more is said of it.

Word of the ships had reached Baile fhiadhaich, up the western coast, in two days, as word goes along a coast. Its custodian did not come at once, for the roads were bad and his knees were worse, but when the roads dried he rode south with two of his people to see for himself. He was an old man, a fisher's son who had held his town for thirty years and had opinions about everything, and he spent three days on the dunes and one on the strand among the strangers, feeling their ropes, looking at their blocks and their tackle, walking round their boats with his hands behind him. He asked Oighrig to take him out to the ships and she would not. Then he went home, and wrote to the council that the strangers' ropes were better than ours and their manners worse. The council kept the letter. The rope-makers of Cuan shean heard what he had said about the ropes before the ink was dry, and they took it hard, and three of them went down to the strand the next day to look at the strangers' cordage for themselves. They came back and said nothing, which in a rope-maker is a great deal.

Harrow came to Oighrig's door many times in those weeks. He learned her name, or the sound of it, and he learned the word for water and the word for bread and the word for no, which he heard more than the other two. She learned his. He brought her things: a little glass that made small writing large, which she put away in a drawer and took out at night when nobody was looking; a length of fine cloth; a knife. She sent the knife back and kept the glass. He tried to tell her, with his hands and a stick in the sand and a great deal of talk she did not follow, where he had come from, and she understood from his drawing that it was north, and then east, round some great corner of sea, and she did not like the drawing and rubbed it out with her foot when he had gone.

She was never sure afterward whether she had liked him. She said in her letter that he was a man who asked for one thing at a time and was glad of it, and who always had the next thing ready.

Through all those days the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell kept the tide-prayer. When the boy told them the strangers were on the strand below Cuan shean, eating the town's bread, the eldest of the priests said that it made no difference, and they did not miss a tide in the forty days, nor in the days after. The harbour scribe wrote down their number each week, which was nine, and the state of Ceò Mhanannain, which was thin.

## V. Of the Leave and the Margin

The council sat on it through the summer and into the autumn, and then, because nothing had been decided, sat on it through the winter. Custodians came in to Cathair dhearg from all over the island, from the hill towns and the eastern shore and the silver country and the far southern ports, some of them riding for a week, to sit in the council hall with the rain coming in off the lake and argue about ships that most of them had never seen. Ceann a' Chùraim in those years was Tormod mac Ailein, a heavy, careful man of forty-five with a lawyer's memory and a smith's hands, and he let them argue, and wrote down what they said, and said very little himself.

The strangers waited. They had long since come off the beach; the custodians had let them into the net-lofts along the harbour when the autumn gales began, since they could not in conscience leave men under sailcloth through a west-coast winter, and it was put in the roll that this was a shelter, and gave no leave. The ships lay in the harbour with skeleton crews aboard and their yards sent down. Harrow went twice to Cathair dhearg under the council's safe-conduct and stood in the hall and was looked at, and came back, and said nothing to anyone in Cuan shean about what he had seen there.

Oighrig nic Leòid fell ill at Samhain.

It began as a cough and went into her chest, and by the month of an Dùbhlachd she could not get out of her bed. The physician of Cuan shean sat with her, and her servant, and a sister of hers who came from inland; and Lachlann Odhar, who had never gone home, came up the hill one evening with a fish wrapped in a cloth, and stood in her doorway turning his cap in his hands, and she laughed at him and it made her cough for a quarter of an hour.

She knew the council was near to deciding. The custodians who passed through Cuan shean on their way up to Cathair dhearg came to her bedside, one after another, and told her so, each in the tone of a man who thinks he has brought news. She knew the way the hall was leaning. She knew that the iron the strangers carried in their ships was better than any iron on the island, that their carpenters had raised a boat-shed on the strand in four days that the carpenters of Cuan shean would have taken a month over, that their ships were the first ships in eighteen centuries, and that the ships that had brought them could come again. Every custodian who came to her bed told her one of those things. None of them told her anything else.

So she wrote to the council from her bed. The letter is in the roll of Cuan shean, copied fair by her clerk, with her own mark at the foot of it in a hand that shakes. It is short. She wrote that it was she who had given the strangers water, on the shore, under the old law of the shore, and that she had given them nothing more on her own word, because nothing more was hers to give. She wrote that she had fed them since because the council told her to, and that she had done it gladly. Last, she set down that the council should know, before it gave them anything else, that a leave given in the roll is given, and cannot be ungiven by the next roll, and that the strangers would know that better than the council did, since it was they who would be holding it.

She asked that it be read out before the vote. The clerk's note on the copy says that it was received, and does not say that it was read.

On 11 am Faoilleach, AE 2, Comhairle a' Chùraim, sitting at Cathair dhearg in the crown's place, gave the strangers leave to stay, with Tormod mac Ailein in the chair. The clerk entered the vote in the roll as given with one voice. Tormod signed below it.

Later, in another ink and another hand, somebody wrote in the margin beside the entry that three custodians had been absent that day. It does not say who they were. Oighrig nic Leòid was one of them, lying in her bed at Cuan shean with the window shut against the wind. The other two are not named anywhere.

The copyists of Seilear Muileann chaol have kept that margin as they found it, with the note beside the vote. It is the first place in the record of An Aois Choigreach where what was written and what was so do not quite meet.

The news came back down the valley road to Cuan shean two days after. The rope-maker's son who had ridden up with the first letter rode down with the last, and went up the hill to Oighrig's house to tell her before he told the town, because he thought she ought to hear it first. She was asleep. Her sister told her when she woke, and she lay a while looking at the ceiling, and then asked for the cat.

She lived through the winter. She kept the custody of Cuan shean for many years yet, and never spoke of the vote to anyone, so far as the roll knows, except once, to Lachlann Odhar, and what she said to him he did not repeat.

## VI. Of the Quarter of the Sea

The leave was read out on the strand at Cuan shean by one of Oighrig's fellow custodians, standing on an upturned boat, with a stranger beside him who had learned a little of the island's tongue in the net-lofts over the winter and put it into his own as well as he could. The strangers cheered, three times, in the way they had. The townspeople did not know what cheering was, and some of them thought it was a threat, and went indoors. Harrow shook the custodian's hand, and then the hands of everyone near him, and then went out to his ship in the boat, and that afternoon the strangers began to send the ships' yards back up.

It was in those weeks, at the back end of that second winter, that the saying began to go round the harbour.

It was the old sailors who said it first, the men who sat on the bench at the foot of the rope-walks in any weather and had done so since before most of the town was born. None of them had ever been out of sight of land, since the rule forbade it, but they had fished the western water all their lives, and their fathers before them, and they knew the set of every current and the lie of every sea-mark from the north-west capes to the mouth of the capital's river. They had watched the ships come in over the bar. They had watched the strangers' lead-line, and the way the ships stood off in the westerly blow and where they stood to. Over the winter they had talked with Lachlann Odhar about the gauze off the cape and the course the ships had come down on, and they had put it all together over a good many evenings on the bench.

What they said was this: that the strangers had come in from the same quarter of the sea into which Cabhlach an Scaraidh had sailed.

That was all they said. They did not say what it meant. But it went up the valley road with the carters in a week, and it was said in the capital, and in the council hall, where at last a custodian of the hill country stood up and said it out loud before Tormod mac Ailein and the whole council. The council forbade the saying in its hall (9 an Gearran, AE 2). The clerk was told to strike it from the roll. He struck it, and then, being a careful man, wrote below the striking what it was he had been told to strike, so that the next clerk should know. It is there still, and it was never answered.

Lachlann Odhar went home to Achadh àrsaidh at last in the month of an Gearran, more than a year after he had left it for a morning's fishing. On the day he went he walked down to the harbour at Cuan shean early, with his bag over his shoulder, and stood on the harbour wall to look at the ships. They lay at anchor off the town with their yards crossed and their sails loosed to dry, and there were strangers going up and down their sides and in and out of the town now as if it were their own. Three of the old sailors were on the bench below the wall, and a fishwife with a yellow button on a cord, and a boy mending a net with the strangers' knot, and a stranger with him, showing him how to draw it tight.

Lachlann stood up on the wall. He was a man who had brought Na Trì Longan down the coast behind him in a day, and he had heard that the saying was forbidden in the council hall, and he was not in the council hall.

"They came out of the quarter Cabhlach an Scaraidh went into," he said, loudly, so that the whole harbour could hear it. "I saw them come. The grey was gauze, and they came down out of it from the north, the way the old men say the old ships went. There's nobody here who doesn't know it."

The old sailors on the bench looked at him and then looked away at the water. The fishwife picked up her basket. The boy went on with the net. The stranger beside him looked up at Lachlann, hearing a man shouting from a wall, and smiled uncertainly, and went back to showing the boy the knot.

Nobody answered him. Lachlann stood a while longer on the wall with the wind pulling at his coat. Then he climbed down, and went along the strand to his boat, and put out for the north, and was a long way up the coast before the harbour lost sight of him.

# Chapter Two: Of Forty Words for the Colours of Coal

*AE 2 – 3*

## I. Of an Tìr Thall

By the back end of that second winter Comhairle a' Chùraim had given leave to a people it had no name for, and the clerks of the roll were the first to feel the want of one.

In the forty days below the dunes the clerks had called the newcomers the men of the ships, and Harrow's men, and once, in a hand afterwards scored through, the wet men. That did well enough while they were a wonder on a beach. Leave to stay is another matter. It is given to people who come from somewhere, and the clerk who entered the leave on 11 am Faoilleach, AE 2, left a gap after the words *the people of*, meaning to fill it when he knew what to put there. He never filled it.

The strangers had told their country's name to the custodians of Cuan shean many times over, slowly and loudly, as men talk to the deaf, and nobody on the island ever learned to say it so that its owners knew it for theirs. No scribe tried to write it down. What the island called the place in the end came up the valley road from the harbour with the carters, and it was the fishers' way of naming a thing they could not reach: *an Tìr Thall*. On 26 an Gearran, AE 2, the clerk of the council wrote it into the roll for the first time, and after that he wrote nothing else, and neither did any clerk after him. The people of it the rolls called the humans, as if the island had never had any of its own, and so they are called in this telling.

Gormshuil nic Fhearchair read that entry in the fair copy the morning after it was made. She sat on the council for Clann Fhearchair, as her father had before her, and she was in her forty-second year that winter, a tall woman with a long plain face and grey coming in at her temples, who wrote a better hand than any clerk in the hall and was known for it. When the leave was put she had given her voice for it, thinking of the cask Harrow had held out on the shingle at Cuan shean, empty and turned upside down, and of what it must be to be so far from home that you have to ask a stranger for water with your hands. Beyond that she had not thought much. Few had.

The news that came up from Cuan shean in those weeks was mostly of small things: sails mended on the strand, fish bought with buttons, singing on the ships in the evenings that carried over the water and set the dogs howling. On the day they kept for their god, which came round every seventh morning whatever the moon was doing, the strangers did no work at all, and when the rain came on they asked the town, by signs, for a roof to pray under.

A sailmaker of Cuan shean lent them his loft. The custodians of the town set down what they saw there, and theirs is the first entry on the island to tell of the humans at prayer under a roof. The strangers knelt on the sailcloth among the bolts of canvas, the captain with the rest. One of their priests stood before them with a book. They lit no fire and burned nothing. They sang, and the priest read, and at the end they all said a word together that sounded like a door shutting. Two of Manannan's priests of the harbour went and stood on the loft stair to watch, the roll says, and came down again without a word, and went to the water's edge to say their own prayer at the turn of the tide.

The strangers had one god, and no other, and they called him by a name the island heard as *Crìosd*. Their faith they called by a word their priests used of the whole company of their believers, and the Dia-thìrich made of it *an Eaglais*. Those two words went into the roll that season, the first of the humans' tongue that the island took and kept.

It was in the month after, when the carts were back on the roads and the rain had turned soft, that Tormod mac Ailein sent for her.

Ceann a' Chùraim was a heavy, slow man with a beard that had gone white before his hair, and he kept a room at the top of the council hall with a window on the lake. On the table before him lay a letter in the humans' hand, which he could not read, and one from the custodians of Cuan shean, which he had read twice.

"They want words," he said. "Their priests do. They cannot teach their god to people who cannot understand them, nor trade with them either, and they would like to do both. They have asked Cuan shean for somebody to sit with them at a table and trade words as a man trades fish, one for one, until each side has enough to buy bread with."

"And Cuan shean sends to us."

"Cuan shean has sent to us for everything since the first ship," said Tormod. "Oighrig nic Leòid is still in her bed. The priests will come up to the capital, and the council wants a custodian to sit across the table from them and keep our side of the list."

"The council wants a clerk."

"The council wants somebody who will not give away more than she is paid for." He moved one hand. "You have the best hand in the hall. You have more patience than I have. And you are not afraid of them."

"I have never been near them."

"That is what I mean," said Tormod mac Ailein.

So the council gave the keeping of the word-list to Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, and the roll enters it in a line, between a dispute over a mill-lade and the price of lamp-oil for the temple. She went home that evening and told her brother's daughter Muireall, who had been copying the roll for her since the autumn and had ink worked into the skin of her wrists that no washing would lift. Muireall was thirteen. She wanted to know at once whether she might come to the table, and whether the strangers really had hair on their faces as the carters said.

"You may come to the table," said Gormshuil. "You will sit at the end of it and make the fair copy, and you will not speak unless I tell you."

## II. Of Cup and Bread

They came up from Cuan shean at the beginning of the seed-time moon, which the old folk call Sìolach: two priests and a boy, on three ponies of the town, with a custodian's man walking at the head to show them the road. It is a long day's ride from the harbour to Cathair dhearg, and the priests were no horsemen. They came over the bridge at dusk soaked through, the older of the two sitting his pony like a sack of meal, and the younger coughing.

The younger was Samuel Wren. He was a thin man of about thirty, with long hands and a narrow face and a courteous way of bending his head when he was spoken to, as if to bring his ear nearer the words. The damp of the lake country did not agree with him. He coughed that first night in the house the council had lent them below the temple, and through most of the spring after, a dry catching cough that he would turn away from the table to finish, with a hand up, as if apologising to the room. The older priest was a broad red-faced man with the sea still in his walk, who slept a great deal.

The council gave them a long room on the east side of the hall, with a table under a window of thin-scraped horn, a shutter that could be taken down on fine days, and a peat fire at the far end. On the first morning Gormshuil was there before them. She had set her pens and her ink on her side of the table, and a stack of the grey rag paper they made at Muileann chaol, and Muireall sat at the end with the same.

Wren came in and bowed to her from the door. She inclined her head. He sat down opposite and took out of a leather case a quire of paper so white that Muireall gasped aloud and was frowned at; it was more paper than the council used in a moon. Then he looked across at Gormshuil, and she looked at him, and for a long while nobody said anything at all, because there was nothing either of them knew how to say.

In the end he picked up the cup at his elbow, which had water in it, and held it up between them, and said a word.

She dipped her pen and wrote the word in the stag-letters of the island, as near to the sound as the letters would go. Then she reached for the loaf that the hall's kitchen had sent up, and broke a piece off, and held it up in her turn.

"*Aran*," she said.

He wrote it in his own letters, slowly, with his lips moving, and said it back to her. He said it badly. She said it again. He said it better. And so it went, all through that morning and the mornings after: cup and bread, and water, and table, and hand, and knife, and window, and door; the one holding up a thing and giving its name, the other writing and saying it back; and the older priest asleep in his chair by the fire with his chin on his chest, and Muireall at the end of the table, copying every word fair, in both hands, as best she could manage the strangers' letters by the shape of them.

The things that could be held up were the easy part.

For three days Wren had her word for *finger* written down as the word for *that*, because she had pointed with her finger when she said it, and nobody could find the mistake until Muireall, copying, saw the same word against two things that were not the same. A whole morning went on *go* and *come*, with Wren walking to the door and back a dozen times while Gormshuil watched him. He pointed at the rain running off the sill and she said *uisce*, and he wrote it; then he pointed at the jug and she said *uisce* again, and he looked from one to the other, and laughed out loud, the first time she had heard him laugh, and wrote something long in the margin. Afterwards she learned that his people had one word for the water in the jug and another for the water that falls from the sky, and could not think how a people managed with only the one. She could not think how a people could need two.

He learned quickly. She learned more quickly than he did, though she was careful not to let him see it. By the end of Sìolach he could ask *Dè seo?*, what is this, with his head on one side, and she could ask him the same in his own tongue, and the table went faster.

There was one morning in that spring that the copyists set down because Wren's list still keeps what came of it. He had drawn a great wheel cut into twelve like a cake, with a word in each piece, and he tapped the pieces one after another and pointed out of the window at the sky. It took her most of the morning to understand that these were the months of his year, fixed to the sun, and that he wished to know what the island called them.

The island had no months of that kind. It had the moons. She drew them for him: twelve moons of thirty nights and twenty-nine in turn, each begun on the night of the full and turning at the dark, from Samhnas at the year's beginning, through Dubhlas and Faolach and Gearras, through the seed-time and the gap and the bright fire, round to the stags' moon at the year's end. He set his months against her moons one by one, as near as they would go, and wrote the moon's name beside each piece of his wheel. It went well enough until she drew the thirteenth.

She told him its name, *Eadrach*, the between-moon, and showed him with her hands how the keepers of the reckoning put it in at the year's end every thirtieth moon or so, so that Samhain should not come round before the summer was over. He understood at last what it was for, and could find nowhere on his wheel to put it. In the end he wrote it in the margin outside the wheel altogether, with a mark after it that Muireall copied without knowing what it meant, and which Gormshuil learned afterwards was the humans' sign for a question.

One morning in seven he did not come. The first time, Gormshuil thought him ill and sent Muireall down with a crock of broth, and the girl came back with the broth and said the priests were kneeling on the floor of the front room with the shutters closed, and the boy had shut the door on her. After that Gormshuil counted the mornings on her fingers. The island reckoned its time by nights, from dusk to dusk; the humans counted by days, and by these sevens of days, and nobody on the island had ever divided time by seven for any reason at all. She wrote the seven into the list with their names as he gave them, and beside each the thing she knew of it, which for six of them was nothing.

The peat fire at the end of the room smoked when the wind was in the east. On the worst of those mornings Wren's cough came on so hard that he had to get up from the table and go to the window, and Gormshuil had Muireall bring a brazier of the fire's embers up to his end of the table. He held his long hands over it. Then he pointed at the embers and raised his eyebrows.

"*Mòine*," said Gormshuil.

His face lit up. He said his own word for it and made a digging motion with both hands; then he made the motion again, deeper, and said a different word, and pointed away east over the lake towards his own country. This we have too, he meant, tapping the brazier; and this other, which we burn at home, the stone that is dug from under the ground. It was black, he showed her, holding up the ink-pot, and it burned hot and long, and his people burned it in every house.

Gormshuil wrote the word down as he said it, and beside it, in the Dia-thìris column, she wrote what he had told her: *the black stone the humans dig in their own country and burn on their hearths*. It was one line among two hundred, and she thought nothing of it.

By the dark of the year there were some hundreds of words on each side of the table. On 13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 2, the council's clerk came in with his own ink to enter in the roll how far the work had come, and found both lists lying side by side, Wren's in his white quire and Gormshuil's on the grey paper of Muileann chaol, and counted the leaves of each, and wrote that they were near enough even. The roll puts it no more warmly than that. For a season's work between two people who had begun it with a cup and a loaf, it was a good deal.

## III. Of the Basket of Coal

It was in the wolf-moon, when the island's hearths burn their hottest and the high passes are shut, that she did the thing the age remembers her for.

She had been thinking of it since before the dark of the year. Some hundreds of words lay between them now: cup and bread, rain and knife, a boat and its sail and every line that works a sail, and the moons and his months. They had peat, and the black stone of his own country. And in all those moons of pointing and naming, Wren had never once pointed at the coal of the vein, nor asked what it was called, nor seemed to know there was anything there to ask about.

He could not have lived three months in the capital and missed it. The shrine at the temple door kept the measured handful burning under its hood day and night, as Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig allowed, and the carriers came down from Taigh na Fèithe with their sealed baskets on the white road, and every child in the town knew to stand aside for them. He had watched them go by, she knew, because she had watched him watching. He had never asked.

So on a still morning of thin winter sun she went up to the hall early, before the priests were out of bed, and had the shutter taken down from the window so that the light came in clear. She took from the council's store the basket that the carriers had brought down for the shrines of the capital, broken fresh from the vein that autumn, and she chose from it with her own hands a double handful, the best-broken pieces she could find. It broke no law. A custodian may carry the coal and hold it and show it; it is the burning that is measured. She set the basket on the table under the window and sat down behind it and waited.

Wren came in coughing, with the older priest behind him and the boy with the ink. He bowed. She inclined her head. Then she stood up, took the basket in both hands, and tipped it out on the table where the sun lay, and the coal ran out across the boards and came to rest in the light.

It was black as a wet crow, and bright all over with a sheen like oil on water. Where the pieces had split, the colours lay along the edges.

Gormshuil began to name them.

There was the green that lies under the black like deep water under weed, and she laid her finger on it and said *uaine*, and then the word for that green and no other, which is not the green of grass nor of the sea. There was the red at a fresh break that deepens if you breathe on it, and she breathed on it and showed him, and gave its word. She gave the grey-violet of the old cuttings, that no dyer has ever matched; and the brown that shows the piece came from near the surface; and the blue that runs along a split edge like the light on a mackerel's back. She gave a colour like the heather in Lùnastal, and one like the dark of a blackberry, and one like rust on a nail left out in the rain. There was the colour of an ember just before it goes grey, and there was the colour of the ember after. There was a hair-line of something like gold that ran through one piece and out the other side, and a sheen on another like a pigeon's neck, which changes as you turn it; and she turned it in the sun and gave him the two words for the two colours it showed, and then the third word, for the piece that shows both.

She laid her finger on each piece as she came to it and gave each colour its own word, plainly and without hurry, as any child of the hills could have done, and as her mother had done for her with a double handful on the kitchen table when she was four years old. Muireall at the end of the table wrote them as fast as her pen would go. Wren wrote too, at first. He wrote the green, and the red at the break, and the grey-violet, and several more, and said them back to her with his head bent in the way he had.

She gave forty. There were more. She stopped because Wren had stopped writing.

He had put down his pen. He reached out and picked up one of the pieces, a large one with the green deep in it and the red at one end, and held it up to the window and turned it in the light, with his eyes narrowed, the way a man looks at a coin he suspects. Then he looked at her across the table. There was nothing unkind in the look at all. It was puzzled, and gentle, and a little sorry for her, as a grown man is sorry for a child who has told him a long story about the faces in the fire.

He laid the piece down with the rest and said one word. Then he took up his pen and wrote one word, and tapped the whole heap with the end of the pen, lightly, once, to show her that his word stood for all of it.

It took her a breath or two to know the word. When she did she sat without moving.

It was the word he had given her in the spring over the brazier, with the digging motion and the finger pointing east. It was the black stone of his own country, that his people dug out of the ground and burned in every house.

The sun had moved a little along the table. She could hear the older priest breathing by the fire, and a cart going down the hill outside, and Muireall's pen, which had stopped. She waited for him to ask for her word. There is an old courtesy on the island, when one has given the name of a thing and had the other's name back: *Agus thu fhèin?* And yours? It was in her mouth to say, if he would only ask the question to which it was the answer. She waited for him to ask what the island called the whole heap, the one word for all of it, since he had given her his.

He smiled at her. He moved the coal aside with the flat of his hand, gently, to make room on the table, and he reached behind him to the shelf and took down a candle, and held it up.

"*Coinneal*," said Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, after a moment.

He wrote it down. The morning went on.

When the priests had gone at noon she gathered the coal up a piece at a time and carried the basket down to the store herself, and saw it counted back in against the carriers' tally, not a crumb short; and it went up the hill to the shrine at the temple door with the rest of the capital's measure, and burned there under the hood in its turn, as it was meant to.

Muireall walked home with her that evening and did not say anything until they were over the bridge.

"He could not see them," she said then.

"No."

"Not any of them. Not the green. I watched his face. He looked and looked."

"He looked," said Gormshuil.

"Then how do they know what it is?" said Muireall. "When they burn it. How do they know what they are burning?"

Her aunt had no answer to give her, and gave none.

## IV. Of the Note under the First Leaf

The list was bound in the gap-moon, when the stores run low and the first green has not yet come. Gormshuil had kept it through the year on loose sheets in a box, as the words came, and now that the season of words was plainly done she gave the sheets to Muireall to copy fair into a book for the keeping of Clann Fhearchair, and to be copied again after that for whoever else might want it.

She gave one order about the copying. The colours were to go first.

Muireall looked at her. The sheets began with cup and bread, as the work had. That was the order of the table, and it was the order the council's clerk had counted.

"The colours first," said her aunt. "Before the cup. Put them on the first leaf by themselves, and leave room at the foot."

So the first leaf of the fair copy holds forty words for the colours of broken coal, in Muireall's hand, which was young and careful and larger than it later grew, and nothing else on it but the room at the foot. The copyists of this cellar know that leaf well. It has been handled more than any other leaf in the loft where it lies, and the corners have gone soft as cloth.

The list had two columns, the island's word on the left and Wren's on the right. For the forty colours Muireall came to the right-hand column and stopped with her pen in the air. There was one word she might have written in it forty times over. There was no other.

She went to her aunt with the leaf and asked her what she ought to put.

"Put what happened," said Gormshuil.

"All of it?"

"As much as goes at the foot of the leaf."

Muireall took it back to the table by the window and sat over it most of an afternoon. What she wrote at the foot of the leaf, on 23 an Giblean, AE 3, is short, and it is in the girl's hand and the girl's words, and it runs like this. The humans have one word for the coal of the vein. It is their word for the black fuel they burn on the hearths of their own country. No Dia-thìris word, in either list, answers to it. And they did not ask.

She brought it to her aunt, and stood while it was read.

"Should I have written that he was kind?" she said. "He was. He was kind about it."

"You have written what happened," said Gormshuil. "Leave it."

It was about that time, perhaps the same week, that Gormshuil went across the table to Wren with a request of her own.

She had been turning it over since the morning of the basket. He would not learn her colours, and she had given up waiting for the question; the word he had written for the heap was all his eyes could give him, and no patience across a table would put another in its place. Then she would learn his letters. There would be more of these people, and more paper, a great deal more paper, she thought; and a custodian who could not read what was written about the island in its own capital would be a poor sort of custodian.

She put her finger on a line of his writing, and then on her own breast, and then made the motion of a pen.

Wren understood her before she had finished, and was delighted. Since his god's book was written in those letters, he had been looking for a year for somebody on the island who would learn them, and here was the council's own custodian asking. From his white quire he took a clean sheet there and then, and wrote across the top of it the letters of his tongue, all of them, in their order, large and plain; and under them he wrote them small; and then, underneath, as a gift, he wrote her name the way he heard it.

She looked at it a long time. It was a long name in his letters, with more of them in it than it had sounds, and it looked to her like somebody else's. She let it stand. She copied it out underneath, stroke by stroke, the first thing she ever wrote in the humans' letters, and he clapped his long hands together, and the older priest woke up and asked what had happened.

After that there were two lessons at the table. In the mornings they went on with words, more slowly now, for the easy ones were done; in the afternoons Wren taught her his letters, and she learned them as she did everything, without fuss and faster than he expected. By the end of that spring she could spell out a line of his list with her finger under it, and she did.

She found the page of the coal. It was in his white quire with the rest, and she read it through with Muireall at her shoulder. He had written the green at the top of the page, as near to her word as his letters would go, and the red at the break under it, and the grey-violet, and a few more down the page in his careful hand. Then there was a line drawn under them. Under the line was his one word, and a stroke of the pen that joined it to all the others above it, and then nothing more on that page at all.

## V. Of the Chest for Muileann chaol

The fair trade began that summer, at the moon of the bright fire, and for the first time Gormshuil saw from her own window what the season of words had been for.

The strangers' goods came up from Cuan shean on the carts, iron knives and pots, window glass packed in straw, lamp-oil and white paper; wool and hides and salt fish and dyed cloth went down the other way; and in the market below the hill men of both peoples stood over the same bales and haggled with the words that had come out of the long room on the east side of the hall, and got them wrong, and laughed more often than they quarrelled. Gormshuil went down one morning on purpose, and stood among the stalls, and watched a hill shepherd give a fleece for a knife, and the stranger who took the fleece weigh it in his hands and nod, and the shepherd test the knife's edge on his thumbnail and nod. She could find nothing unfair in it anywhere. She looked.

The council entered the first of those bargains in its roll, fleece for knife, cloth for glass, with both prices in the island's reckoning, so that anyone who came after could see that the strangers had given good measure. It was good measure. The copyists set that down plainly, since much of what they must set down later is otherwise. The island had been alone for eighteen centuries and lacked a great deal that the strangers had, and it was glad of what it got.

Wren bought wool too. Gormshuil's sister knitted him a pair of stockings from the fleece of the hill ewes, grey and thick, for the damp; and he gave Gormshuil in return a quire of his white paper and a steel pen, the first she had held, which never needed cutting. She wrote with it for twenty years.

It was the paper that decided her.

Through that spring she had watched him use it as if there were no end to it. A word he did not like cost a fresh sheet. A page spoiled with a blot was crumpled in his long hands and, when the brazier was lit, dropped on the embers to burn. Paper came in his ship's hold by the bale, and he meant nothing by it, any more than a baker means something when he throws a burnt loaf to the gulls. But she saw him do it, again and again, and she thought of the fair copy of her list, and of Clann Fhearchair's book-chest, which stood against the wall of a timber house in a town full of timber houses, and of how the strangers' ships had come down out of a sea that had been shut for eighteen centuries, and what else might come down out of it now that it was open.

There was one place on the island where nothing was burned.

Muileann chaol is a narrow mill town in the eastern hills, where they made the first paper on Dia-thìr from rags, and in it stands the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais. Beathag had been a mill-owner's widow in An Aois Scaraidh who bought up the old copies of Leabhar a' Chùraim and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them, and stacked them in the loft over her mill; and when she died she left the loft and all that was in it to the town, on the one condition that nothing in it should ever be burned. The town had kept that condition since, and the custodian houses sent copies there when they had a thing they wished to be sure of.

So Gormshuil had Muireall make a second fair copy of the list, the whole of it, the colours first and the note at the foot of the first leaf, word for word as in the first. It took the girl the rest of that moon. When it was done Gormshuil read it through against the first and found two mistakes and had them put right. Then she wrapped it in oilcloth, and laid it in a small chest of oak with straw about it, and sealed the chest with the seal of Clann Fhearchair, and wrote on the lid in the stag-letters where it was to go.

The carriers going east to the hills left the capital two days after, with the chest in the bottom of a cart under a load of the strangers' iron pots. It is some three days' road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann chaol, and longer with a laden cart.

Gormshuil and Muireall walked down with the cart as far as the bridge on a bright morning with a wind off the lake. At the far end of Drochaid Cathair dhearg the cart went on up the eastern road, and they watched it out of sight between the hedges, and Muireall asked her aunt whether anybody at Muileann chaol would ever read it.

"Somebody will," said Gormshuil. "It is a long time, in a loft."

Then they went back up the hill, because Wren would be waiting at the table, and it was the afternoon, and the afternoons were for his letters.

The copy came safe to the loft, and the loft keeps it still. Gormshuil's own list, the one she kept at the table, is lost; Wren's lies in the humans' letter-books in his own hand, in a good black ink that has not faded. The copyists of Seilear Muileann chaol have the two before them as they set down this age, side by side as they lay on the table in the long room. They have set the first leaf of the copy, and the note at its foot in the careful hand of a girl of fourteen, at the head of the whole age.

# Chapter Three: Of the Post at Ros dhomhain

*AE 3 – 5*

## I. Of the Counter

The humans' post at Ros dhomhain opened its door on 22 an t-Ògmhios, AE 3, in a net-loft on the lake shore that the fishers of the town let to Thomas Pike for a bolt of blue cloth a season. The loft had a floor of tarred planks and a smell of old rope that never left it. Pike had a counter built across it from wall to wall, waist-high, of ship's timber, and on the counter he laid a book bound in calf, a pen, a pot of ink, and a steelyard from the ship's stores with its hook and its sliding pea. Behind the counter, on shelves his own men put up, stood what Na Trì Longan had carried over the sea for trading: iron tools in bundles tied with tarred twine, crates of window glass packed in straw, casks of lamp-oil, and reams of paper wrapped in oilcloth.

He was a man of some thirty years, short and square, with ink in the grain of his fingers and a habit of setting his hat down on the counter crown-first. The custodians of the capital shore who came to look him over on the first morning wrote that he stood up when they came in, which the strangers' sailors did not do, and that he looked at each thing that was set down before him as if it might be worth more than he had been told. Of all who wrote in those years he counted best, and his tally-book survives, in his own small upright hand.

The first thing across the counter was a bale of wool from a farm above the lake. The farmer had come in on a borrowed cart with two sons and a dog, and stood a long time in the doorway before he would come in. Pike weighed the bale on the steelyard and wrote the figure. Then he laid out, one at a time, the things he would give for it: a spade-blade, a hand-axe, a box of nails. The farmer looked at the nails for a long while. He took one out, turned it over, tried its point on his thumb, and at last put it in his mouth and bit it. Then he nodded, and Pike wrote a line in the book, and ruled it off.

That was how the post was kept for its first season: one thing set against another, each weighed or counted, each line ruled off. Wool came in, and salt fish in creels, and hides, and cloth dyed in the island's own madder and woad; iron went out, and glass, and oil, and paper. Pike had forty words of the island's tongue from Harrow's winter on the dunes, and he learned more at the counter, where a word is worth what it buys. He learned the words for hand and half-hand, for a creel and a fleece and a bundle, and the word for *enough*, which the farmers said sharply, as if it closed a door.

The custodians sent a clerk to sit on a stool by the door. He was a young man with ink to his wrists, and he kept a tally of his own on a long slate, marked in the old way with strokes and crosses, and at the end of each day he and Pike laid the two counts side by side. The clerk could not read the humans' figures and Pike could not read the strokes, and so each read his own aloud, item by item, in a speech that grew between them out of both tongues. On the evening they first found a difference, a single hide, they went through the day's goods again together by lamplight, and found the hide under a creel of fish where a boy had set it down. Pike wrote beside the line, in his own tongue, *found*, and the clerk made a mark on the slate that he said meant the same.

"Your book and his slate," Harrow said, when he came up from Cuan shean at the end of an t-Ògmhios and heard of it. "Two books for one trade."

"Two books that agree," said Pike. "I would sooner have that than one."

At the end of the first month the book balanced to the last line. Pike showed it to the custodians' clerk, turning the pages for him, and the clerk, who could read none of it, looked at the ruled lines for a long time, and then laid his slate beside it and showed him that the strokes balanced also.

## II. Of the Hull in the Shallows

In the first weeks everything that came to the counter had come twenty miles and more by cart from Cuan shean, where Harrow's hulls lay in the roads below the dunes, and everything the post took in went back the same way. It was slow and dear. The carts went over the moor road in two days with the axles shrieking, and Pike's men walked beside them in the rain, and the carters of Cuan shean charged for every creel. So Harrow went down to the strait of Caol leathan to ask the pilots there whether a ship of his could be brought up the Abhainn gheal into Loch chrom.

The pilots of Caol leathan had taken toll of every boat bound for the capital's waters since An Aois Naomh, and they knew the river as a ploughman knows his furrow. They came up the coast in their own boats and went over the smallest of Harrow's hulls from her keel to her masthead, and argued among themselves a whole afternoon in their own speech, and at last named a price. It was twice the toll they took from any boat of Dia-thìr. Harrow was angry, and Pike, who had come down to see it done, wrote the price in his book and wrote beside it in his own tongue: *fair, for they know the shallows and we do not.*

On 21 an t-Iuchar, AE 3, they brought her up. Pike rode on her deck. The pilots took her in over the bar at the flood with six of their boats ahead of her on tow-lines, the oarsmen singing a slow count that kept the oars together, and the hull came on behind them, a great dark thing among the reeds with her sails furled and her yards cockbilled to clear the alders. Below Baile ghlas the river spreads out over gravel, and there she touched. Pike felt the deck lift under him and settle. The pilots did not shout. They let her lie on the gravel a while, and put two boats to her stern and two to each bow, and waited for a gust off the lake that came when they had said it would, and she slid off and swam again. The people of Baile ghlas had come down to the bank to watch, the rope-makers with their hands still hooked from the walk, and some of them cheered and some said nothing at all.

She anchored that evening off Ros dhomhain, in the lake, with the capital's roofs red in the low sun behind her. Thereafter the humans' goods came to the capital shore by water.

A month after, on 19 an Lùnastal, AE 3, a coasting boat came in from the northern coast with wool from Cathair naomh, the city above Seann Toll, the first goods that came to the post from so far. Her master had brought her round the western capes and up the river behind a pilot of his own. He carried a letter from the custodians of Cathair naomh, which the clerk by the door read aloud to Pike slowly, and which asked to be paid for the wool in paper and in ink, and in nothing else.

"Paper," said Pike. "All of it?"

"All of it," said the clerk, and read on. Their roll was old and full, the custodians wrote, and written on skins that were cracking; they would begin it again on the humans' paper, fair from the first page.

Pike gave them a ream for every bale and two bottles of ink besides, and put a quire of his own writing-paper in with the rest, uncounted. It is the only line in the whole book that he did not balance. He wrote beside it: *gift.*

Harrow sailed for home at the end of an Lùnastal. All three hulls went with him, north-about, with hides and dyed cloth in their holds, and he left Pike four men, the loft, the book, and the half of the goods not yet traded. Pike stood on the shingle at Cuan shean and watched the sails go north along the coast until the grey of the sea took them. Then he rode back to the counter, and was there the next morning when the door opened.

## III. Of the Bar-Iron

Gilleasbuig Gobha was twenty-three years old in the year the post opened, and a smith of Cathair dhearg, as his father had been and his grandfather. He had a forge in the smiths' lane below the bridge, where the lane runs down to the Abhainn dhomhain, and he worked bronze there as his fathers had: he cast hoes and sickles, pins and pot-legs and bells, and mended what broke. He was a tall young man, long in the arm, and when he stood at the anvil he stooped like a heron over a pool.

The humans' bar-iron came to the smiths' lane on 17 an t-Sultain, AE 3, on a cart from the lake shore, twenty bars of it tied with wet rope, and the smiths of the lane came out of their doors to look. They had seen the strangers' iron since the spring, as axes and spades and nails in the hands of farmers who had traded wool for them, and they had tried to mend it when it broke and could not. Here it was raw, grey and scaled, each bar as long as a man's forearm. Gilleasbuig bought two bars with a bronze pot and a pair of shears, and carried them home on his shoulder.

He put the first in his fire as he would have put in bronze, and it did nothing. When he blew up the charcoal it glowed a dull red and would not move under the hammer. So he blew the fire white, and the bar came out spitting sparks like a green log, and when he struck it, it broke across in a spray of crumbs, and the broken ends were grey and grainy like stale bread. He had burnt it. That night he sat on the doorstep with the two halves in his lap and said to his wife Sìne that the strangers had sold him a thing made of ash.

It was a smith off Harrow's ships who taught him. The ships' smith was a short man and thick through the body, who had stayed ashore at the post with Pike's four men, and who could say nothing at all in the island's tongue and talked with his hands and his hammer. He came up to the lane in an t-Sultain, sent by Pike, with a bag of his own tools, and he stood at Gilleasbuig's fire and watched the colour of the bar in it with his head on one side, and took the bellows-handle out of Sìne's hand and slowed it. At an orange that had some yellow in it he drew the bar out and struck, and it moved under the hammer like cold butter. Then the man laughed, and gave Gilleasbuig the hammer.

All that autumn they worked together, the smith of the ships and the smith of the lane, with no word between them that both knew. Gilleasbuig learned to draw a bar and to fold it and to weld it in the fire with a pinch of sand. He learned to make a nail in eleven blows. The ships' smith had a word for each thing he did, and said it every time, and Gilleasbuig learned the words by the doing and forgot most of them, and kept the doing.

The tempering was last, and hardest. The ships' smith took a blade that Gilleasbuig had forged and ground, and heated it until it glowed, and plunged it hissing into a bucket of brine. When it came out it was hard as flint and would cut a hair, and it would also break like flint if it were dropped on the stones; he showed that with a spoiled one, and the pieces rang on the floor. Then he polished the hard blade bright and held it over a bed of coals, a hand's breadth above, and they watched it together.

The colours came up out of the bright steel like breath on glass. First a pale straw, then a darker straw, then a brown like a beech leaf in autumn, then a purple, then a blue like the sea in the lee of a headland. The ships' smith said a word at the straw and a word at the blue, and at the blue he took the blade away and let it cool. Now it would bend a little, and spring back, and hold its edge.

Gilleasbuig saw more in the steel than two words. Between the straw and the brown there was a colour like new rushes, and between the brown and the purple there was one like a hen's egg held to a lamp, and he had the island's words for both of them, and for the others as they came. He said them aloud as the steel went through them. The ships' smith listened, and looked, and nodded at each; and when Gilleasbuig named the last colour before the blue, the man held up a finger and said his own word for it, which was a different word, and they both looked at the steel and agreed that it was the same colour.

So it was that the two peoples first agreed on a colour, in a smithy below Drochaid Cathair dhearg, and the thing that they agreed on was the colour of hot iron.

Gilleasbuig tempered his first blade alone in the last days of an Dùbhlachd, when the rain came off the lake in sheets and the lane ran with water. It was a knife with a blade the length of a hand. He took it to the straw that is next to the brown and no further, as he judged a knife should be, and quenched it, and ground it, and cut a strip of hide with it that his old bronze knife would only have bruised. He gave the knife to Sìne, who kept it by her board and would let no one else touch it. The ships' smith was down at the post that day, and did not see it done.

## IV. Of the Hoes and the Bells

By the spring of the next year there were iron hoes on the capital's fields.

Gilleasbuig made the first of them in am Faoilleach, when the ground was too wet to work, and by am Màrt all the smiths of the lane were making them, each a little differently and each saying his own was best. An iron hoe was lighter than a bronze one and cut deeper, and it did not bend when it met a stone. The farmers who came down from the fields above the lake to buy them brought their bronze hoes with them in sacks, since bronze was what they had to pay with, and they laid them on the smiths' floors and went home with iron.

So the smiths of the lane had more bronze than they had ever had, heaped in their corners, green and worn. Some of the hoes had belonged to grandmothers; some had marks cut in the socket, a cross or a circle or a notch, that told whose field they were used in. Gilleasbuig kept these apart at first. Then there were too many to keep apart.

The custodians of Cathair dhearg asked the lane for bells. The town had had bells before, small ones, cast in An Aois Naomh and cracked since, and a bell of the old kind had hung in the arch of the market gate as long as anyone remembered, rung for a death, a fire, or a ship. Now there was bronze enough in the lane to cast bells such as the capital had never had. Gilleasbuig and two other smiths of the lane dug the mould-pit in the yard behind his forge in an Cèitean, and made the moulds of clay and dung and chopped straw as their fathers had taught them, and on a dry morning in an t-Ògmhios they melted down the hoes.

It took a day to melt them. The bronze ran into the pit with a noise like a river at night, and smoked and spat, and the smell of it filled the lane. Gilleasbuig stood at the lip of the pit in a leather apron with his face wrapped, and when the bronze had gone in he said the words that his father said at a pour, which ask the metal to settle. Then they let it cool three days.

There were four bells. They were hung in the town that summer, one in the arch of the market gate, one at the bridge, and two at the temple, and they were rung together for the first time at Lùnastal. The farmers who had brought their hoes to the lane stood in the market and listened. An old woman who had carried her mother's hoe down from the fields in a sack told Gilleasbuig afterwards that she could hear it in the bell at the bridge, and he did not tell her that the bronze of all the hoes had run together in the pit and could not be told apart. It may be she was right. Bronze remembers its fire, the smiths of the lane say, and so do bells.

In the same year the weavers of Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast came to the post for the humans' dyes. The word of them had gone north with the Cathair naomh boat. On 4 an Dàmhair, AE 4, they traded their cloth at Pike's counter for jars of a red and a blue brighter than any the island had made, and Pike set down in his book what the jars had cost him over the sea and what the cloth would fetch there, and found the bargain fair on both sides. The weavers opened one jar at the counter and put a finger in it, and held up the finger to the light from the door, and one of them laughed aloud.

## V. Of the Letter from over the Sea

Harrow came back on 16 an Dàmhair, AE 4, down from the north on a grey morning, with four ships in place of three. The fishers of Cuan shean who saw them first counted them twice. The fourth was a new hull, broader than the others and deep-laden, and she carried carpenters with their chests of tools, and a surgeon named Jonas Tull, and a stock of goods for the post twice the size of the first, and a letter.

The letter came up to Ros dhomhain by the river, in a sealed packet in the master's own coat, and Pike opened it at the counter on a wet afternoon toward the end of an Dàmhair. It was from the trading house over the sea whose goods he had been trading, and it had been written, by its date, in the spring. Pike read it through once to himself. Then, because the clerk by the door asked him what news had come from over the sea, and because there was no one in the loft but the clerk and Harrow's master and a smith from Cathair dhearg who had come down to buy bars, he read it again aloud, in his own tongue first and then, as well as he could, in the island's.

The smith was Gilleasbuig. He had come in out of the rain with his sack of bronze and his coat steaming, and he stood at the end of the counter with his arms folded while the letter was read.

It was a short letter and a civil one. The house thanked Pike for the hides and the cloth, which had sold well; it would send more iron and more glass; it named a price for salt. Then it came to what it had written for. The house asked what else the island had. It asked whether there was timber, and what kind; whether there was tin, or copper, or lead; whether the rocks of the island had been looked into, and by whom, and what had been found in them. It asked Pike to keep his eyes open, and to write.

When Pike came to the question he read it twice, once in each tongue, as he had read the rest, and did not stop over it. The clerk wrote it down on his slate. Gilleasbuig said nothing. He bought his bars and paid for them with his bronze, and put them on his shoulder, and went out into the rain.

He thought about the question all the way home along the lake road, and by the fire that night. It seemed to him a strange thing to ask. A smith knows what the hills have, since he works what comes out of them; and what they have is theirs, and a smith takes what the custodians allow him, and says the words. He told Sìne the question, and she asked him who in the world would answer it, and he said the stranger with the book would. Then he said that the stranger was an honest man, which was true, and she said that had not been the question.

A month after, on 14 an t-Samhain, AE 4, the shipwrights of Inis mhòr came the length of the island to look at the new hulls. Two of Harrow's four lay in the lake off Ros dhomhain that winter, and the shipwrights came to them in a hired boat, seven old men and one young one, carrying coils of cord knotted at every hand's breadth. They asked leave of Harrow's master, who gave it, laughing. Then they went over the hulls from keel to rail, running their cords along every plank and rib and hanging them from the yards, and the young one wrote down each count on a board with a stick of charcoal. They were three days about it. Pike went out to watch on the second day and sat in the stern of the boat with his hands in his sleeves.
