He asked the eldest of them, through the clerk, what they meant to do with the counts. The old man looked at him a while before he answered. Their guild had built nothing greater than a coaster since Cabhlach an Scaraidh sailed, he said, and the craft of building for deep water had been half forgotten, since there had been no deep water that anyone of the island wished to sail. Now it seemed there was. So they would learn it again from these hulls, and the cords would keep what they learned.

Pike wrote to the house that night that the island's shipwrights measured by hand's breadths on a knotted cord, and that their joinery was very good.

## VI. Of the First Debt

Pike went down to Cuan shean in an Dùbhlachd to make up the season's account with Harrow, and was lodged in the house of a fisherman below the dunes. It was a low house of turf and stone with its door to the lee, and the fisherman's brother lay in the box-bed by the fire with a leg that had been broken in the autumn under a boat hauled up the shingle.

The leg had been set by the town's bonesetter, and had knitted crooked. By the dark of the year the man could not stand on it. The bonesetter came and looked at it and said it would be so; there was a way to break and set a bone again, and he had seen it done once in his youth, and the man it was done to had died. The town had given the man up for lame. He was young, and he had a wife and a boat, and he lay in the box-bed with his face to the wall.

It was the fisherman's wife who asked Pike whether the strangers had a healer. Pike said they had a surgeon, lately come, and that he would ask.

Jonas Tull came down from the ships on 13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 4, in the afternoon, with his bag and two men from the ships to hold. He was a grey man near fifty with thick wrists and a patient, heavy way of talking, and he spoke no word of the island's tongue. He looked at the leg a long time, and felt along it with his thumbs, and asked through Pike how long since it was set. Then he said what he meant to do, and Pike said it in the island's tongue as well as he could, and the fisherman's brother turned from the wall to listen.

The custodian of Cuan shean was there. Oighrig nic Leòid was old, and not well, and had been fetched from her house in a chair. She had given the strangers' master water on the shingle the winter of their coming, and she sat now by the fire with a shawl over her head and her roll on her knees, and watched the surgeon unpack his bag. When the knives came out of it she asked Pike whether the man had done this before. Pike asked Tull. Tull said he had done it eleven times. Pike asked how many had walked. Tull said nine.

Oighrig said that nine of eleven was more than the island had.

They gave the man spirits from the ships and a strap of leather to bite. Tull broke the leg again at the old break with a stroke of a mallet that everyone in the house heard, and drew it straight with the two men pulling, and set it in splints of ash bound with linen. It was done before the fire had burned down. The man had fainted early and woke up after, grey and wet, with his leg straight under the blanket.

By the turn of the year he could sit up with the leg straight before him, and before the spring was out he was walking on the shingle with a stick.

That night, by the fire, Oighrig opened the roll of Cuan shean on her knees and asked Pike for the stranger's name, and wrote it, spelling it as it sounded. Then she wrote a line under it that Pike asked her to read to him. It said that a man of Cuan shean had been given back his leg by a stranger, and that the town owed the stranger a debt, and that it was the first such debt.

"He will not want paying," said Pike. "He has his wage from the ships."

Oighrig said that was the stranger's affair. The debt was the town's, and the roll would keep it until it was paid. She blotted the line with sand and closed the roll, and asked to be carried home.

## VII. Of the Middling Coal

In the spring of the post's third year the salt-pans of Seann Warr began to sell to Pike's counter by the barrel, on 30 am Màrt, AE 5. Seann Warr lies on the western shore of the lake, three miles from Ros dhomhain, and its salt is boiled from brine springs that rise in the reed marsh behind the town. It is grey salt, coarse and damp, and the strangers' cooks would have none of it at first. Then the ships' masters found that fish packed in it kept the whole of a crossing, and the first barrels that went over the sea came back as a letter asking for more. They were the first goods of Dia-thìr that the humans came back asking for twice. The salt-boilers of Seann Warr heard of it, and put up their price, and Pike paid it.

In the first days of an Giblean Pike closed the book on the post's second year. He sat up two nights over it by the lamp, with the clerk by the door on his stool and the slate on his knees, and they went through every line of both years together. Wool, fish, hides, cloth, salt; iron, glass, oil, paper, dyes. The pilots' tolls, the carters' hire, the rent of the loft in blue cloth. The quire of paper marked *gift*. When they came to the end the two counts stood level, and Pike ruled a double line under the last figure, and the clerk made a mark on the slate. Then they sat a while in the loft with the lamp between them and did not say anything, and the lake knocked at the piles under the floor.

A fortnight later, on 14 an Giblean, AE 5, the walled harbour of Caol leathan sent its first wool-ship up the river to the post. Her master was a broad, grey-bearded man of the pilots' kin, and he came up to the counter with three of his merchants behind him. Tools he would not take, nor glass nor oil nor paper nor dyes. He wanted iron in bars, and he wanted it weighed on his own beam, which he had brought with him in a canvas bag, and on Pike's steelyard after, and he wanted the lesser of the two figures. They were at the counter from the morning until the lamps were lit. When they were done Pike wrote in his book that the merchants of Caol leathan were the hardest bargainers on the island, and he wrote it with some admiration.

That evening he sat down to answer the letter from over the sea.

He had kept his eyes open, as the house had asked. He wrote of the timber: oak in the south and pine on the moors, little of either near the coast. Then the salt and the wool and the hides went down on the page, and the smiths at Cathair dhearg who had learned in one winter what his own country's smiths took seven years to learn. He wrote that the island had copper and tin, since it had bronze, but that he did not know where; and that there was silver somewhere to the east, from the pins the women wore. Last he wrote that the island had coal.

That he had seen for himself. There was a basket of it by the custodians' hearth in Ros dhomhain, where the clerk lodged, and a single handful burned on that hearth at each feast of the year and at no other time. He had asked the clerk why so little. The clerk told him it was the law, and had been the law since An Aois Naomh, and that no household burned more than a measured handful in a season. Pike had asked him how much of it there was, and the clerk had laughed and said the hills were full of it. And Gilleasbuig, when Pike asked him in the lane why the smiths burned charcoal when there was coal in the hills, had said *Tha an cnoc làn dheth*, which was the same answer, and had looked at him as if the question were a strange one.

Pike had taken a piece from the basket once, with the clerk's leave, and held it to the window. It was black, with a dull sheen at the break. It seemed to him much like the coal of home, a little harder. He had put it back.

So he wrote that the island had coal of a middling sort, and much of it. He read the line over, and let it stand, and signed the letter, and sealed it.

The letter went into a small iron-bound chest that stood under the counter, where Pike kept what was to go over the sea. The chest had a lid that sagged on its old hinge, and the next morning he took it up the lake road to the smiths' lane below the bridge.

Gilleasbuig looked at the lid and at the hinge, and put the chest on his bench. He could not read the humans' letters, and he did not ask what the chest held. He made a new hinge that morning from a strip of the strangers' bar-iron, drawn out and folded round a pin, and tempered it to the blue that is next to the grey, as the ships' smith had shown him, and set it with three nails on either leaf. The lid he worked until it swung true. Then he gave the chest back to Pike, and would take nothing for the work.

Pike thanked him in the island's tongue, and carried the chest back down the lake road to the post, with his letter inside it and the new hinge bright at its back.

# Chapter Four: Of the Council of Six

*AE 5 – 6*

## I. Of the Straight Town

Of all the towns of the west in the first years of the strangers, the copyists of the cellar found only one that kept two books. They were a pair of plain calf-bound ledgers, one written in Dia-thìris and dated by the moon, the other in the humans' tongue and dated by the humans' day, and they stood side by side on a shelf in the net-loft of Baile dhìreach. The pages match one for one. Where a hand in one book has struck a line through a word, a hand in the other has struck the line through the word that answers it. The rolls of the custodians are full of things done to the island by strangers. These two books hold a thing the island and the strangers did together, in a town of some fifty souls at the end of a long straight street that ran down to a quay.

Baile dhìreach lay on the south-west coast, a day's walk from the capital and a morning's sail below Cuan shean. Traders of Òrd Mhanannain had built it in the long quiet centuries, and it had kept its one street and its one quay ever since, with Òrd na Cloiche at the temple city of Inis thais a few miles east along the shore and the weather coming in off the open sea from the west. The people were fishers and net-makers and salters of herring. They had a well at the head of the street, a salt-house at its foot, a loft over the salt-house where the nets were hung to mend, and a strip of grey shingle north of the quay where no house stood, because the shingle above the wrack-line had been held in keeping for the whole town since before anyone's grandmother could remember, and nobody might build on it.

Eilidh nic Ruairidh was twenty-three that spring, and she mended nets on the shingle, as her mother had done before her and her mother's mother. The copyists knew her from both books. She was a broad, quick woman with scarred fingers who could work a needle blind. She was at her frames on a grey morning of Bearnach, the gap-moon between the last of the stores and the first of the green, when the humans' boat came round the point from the north.

## II. Of the Rule of the Shingle

It was a broad heavy boat, rowed by six men and deep in the water, and it carried timber: sawn plank, which nobody at Baile dhìreach had seen in such a quantity, stacked to the gunwales and lashed down, with tools laid on top in sacking. The humans had come ashore at Cuan shean four winters before, and every soul on the coast had seen them by now, or said so. Harrow had lately come back from over the sea with four ships where he had taken three, and carpenters in them. The carpenters had been looking up and down the coast for a beach with good shelving and good shelter, where they might mend the small craft of the post and build new ones; for the anchorage at Cuan shean was crowded, and the townsfolk there had begun to count the humans' fires.

Eilidh stood up from the frame with the needle still in her hand. The boat came in on the tide and grounded on the shingle, on the town's shingle, above the wrack. A man jumped out into the shallows and walked up to her, dripping to the knee.

"Dia dhut," he said. He said it badly, with all the sounds in the wrong places, but she knew it.

He was a big man with a carpenter's shoulders and a sunburnt head going bald at the crown, and he held his hat in both hands. Behind him the others were already handing out plank. One of them, a younger man with long arms and black hair tied back with a thong, had found a split cask in the wrack and was turning it over and looking at the staves, as a man looks at a horse he has been offered.

"Iain mac Chaluim," said Eilidh, and pointed up the street. That was all the answer she had, and it was the right one, for Iain mac Chaluim was the best fisherman on that stretch of the coast and the man the town sent to talk when talking had to be done. He was already coming down the street with half the town behind him.

So they met on the shingle, the town and the strangers, with the plank between them. The big man was William Rook, carpenter, lately of Harrow's ships. He had some forty words of Dia-thìris and the tall young man by the cask had perhaps twenty, and between them, with the help of a Cuan shean boy they had brought as far as the point and who then lost his courage and would not come further, they made the town understand what they wanted. They wanted the shingle north of the quay, for a slip and a yard, and would pay for it in iron and nails and tools, and build their own houses.

The shingle was the town's in keeping. It was nobody's to sell. Iain mac Chaluim said so, and Rook frowned, and said a word in his own tongue to the others, and they all frowned. Eilidh saw that they had no word for it. To them a piece of ground belonged to somebody or it belonged to nobody, and if it belonged to nobody a man might take it.

It was old Seonag nic Aoidh of the salt-house who settled it, on the second day of talking. The shingle could not be sold, she said. A man could be let work on it all the same, as the herring-curers of Inis thais had once been let work on it in a year when their own beach silted. The curers had kept the town's rule while they were there, and gone home when they were done, and nobody had thought the worse of them. If the strangers would keep the town's rule, then they might stay under it. And she said the rule over, the whole of it, standing on the shingle with her shawl pulled up against the wind: the well was drawn from in turn; no fire was lit on the shingle after dark in the herring season, when the boats were steering home by the lamps at the quay-head; no net was set and no hammer lifted on the night of the full moon or the night of the dark, which were the rest-nights; the dead of the sea were remembered in the black moon; the shingle above the wrack was held for the town and built on by no one.

Rook heard it through twice. He asked about the houses. They could not live in the boat.

There was a long argument then about whether a house of plank on a sill of stones was a house built on the shingle or only a tent that stood up by itself. The town decided in the end, on no grounds anyone afterwards could give, that it was a tent. Rook said that his men would keep the rule. He said it in his own tongue first, and then in his forty words, and then he put out his hand, and after a while Iain mac Chaluim took it.

The roll of Inis thais, to which Baile dhìreach sent its news, set down on 22 an Giblean, AE 5, that the strangers had been taken in at Baile dhìreach under the town's one rule. They were seven men. There were Rook and two other carpenters, a sawyer and his boy, a sailmaker who stayed only the summer, and the young man with long arms, who was a cooper, and whose name was Samuel Hale.

## III. Of Rope and Knot

They built through Bealltach and Ògach, under a sky that stayed high and grey and let the work go on. The slip went down first, of split logs bedded in the shingle; then a long shed with one end open to the sea; then the house, which was not a house, of sawn plank set on a sill of beach stones, with a door in the middle and a window of real glass that the whole town came to look through. It stood a little crooked on the shingle, with its back to the west wind, and the gulls liked its roof. The town called it the tent, and went on calling it the tent after it had a hearth and a chimney. The copyists found it in the Dia-thìris book as *am pùball* and in the humans' as "the first house", and nobody in either book seems to have thought the other name wrong.

Samuel Hale was the first of them to be any use to the town. The herring barrels of Baile dhìreach were old, and half of them wept brine at every seam. Eilidh's father, Ruairidh, who salted herring for his living and had done since he was a boy, had a whole row of them standing idle behind the salt-house because the staves had shrunk and the hoops rusted through. One evening in Ògach he found the cooper among them with his sleeves rolled up. Samuel had taken one down to its staves and laid them out on the shingle in order, like the bones of a fish.

Ruairidh stood over him for a long time, saying nothing, and then went and got the next one.

By the turn of the summer every barrel in the town was tight. Samuel took no iron for it and no fish. He took, when he took anything, a bowl of whatever was in the pot, and he ate it sitting on the salt-house step with the barrels drying round him, and then he would take out a scrap of paper and a stub of lead and ask for words.

Most of all he asked Eilidh, because she was on the shingle most. He would come down in the evening when the light was going long and yellow over the water and sit on an upturned boat by her frames and point. *Ròp*, she told him, and he said it back and wrote it. Then he showed her his word for it. She said his word back and he laughed at the way she said it, and then he wrote hers again under his own, very carefully, with a line between.

They came to knots in the third week, and there they stayed a long time. She had a word for every knot she tied, and there were many: the knot that joins two ropes of different thickness, the knot that holds on a wet spar and will not slip, the knot that a child learns first and the knot that only the old net-makers could still throw one-handed. He had a word for every one of his, and he tied them for her in a length of line from the boat, and she found that most of his were hers under other names, and some were not. There was one of his she had never seen, a knot for hanging a weight that tightened as the weight pulled; and one of hers he had never seen, the net-maker's mesh knot of the south-west, which she could tie faster than he could follow with his eyes. He made her do it slowly, eleven times, and on the twelfth he tied it himself and held it up, and she said *snaidhm*, which is only the word for any knot at all, and he wrote that down too.

Word had come along the coast by then of what had happened at Cathair dhearg in the season of words, three years before: how the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair had laid broken coal on a table and named forty colours in it, and the cleric of the humans had written one word for them all and put the coal aside to make room. The carters told it at the well. Eilidh had not thought much about it. It had seemed to her a thing that might happen between great people in a great hall.

She thought about it one evening at the end of Teasach, in her father's house, when Samuel had come up for his bowl and the rain had driven him in from the step. By the old law of the burning the house had its measured handful of coal for the hearth, and her father had laid a lump of it on the peat to catch, as he did on wet nights. It split in the heat and the colours came up at the break, the deep green under the black, and the red that grows if you breathe on it. Eilidh looked at it, as anyone would. Samuel saw her look, and looked where she was looking, and asked her what it was.

She told him. She gave him the green and the red and the grey that the old lumps have at the edge. He leaned forward with his elbows on his knees and stared into the fire until his eyes watered.

"It's black," he said, in his own tongue, and then in hers, which he could manage by then: "Dubh."

"It is not black."

"I see black. I'm sorry." He took out his paper. "Say them again."

She said them again, and he wrote them, all three, in her spelling as near as he could come to it. He had no word of his own to put above them, and so he left the space above them empty, and drew his line under it just the same. Her father watched the whole business from the other side of the hearth with his pipe gone out.

That Lùghnas the humans' slip sent down its first boat. She was a small one, a coaster of the humans' pattern with a deeper keel than the boats of the south-west, and she was built for Iain mac Chaluim, who paid for her in fish and labour and in his own time on the saw-pit. The town gave her their rope. They launched her on the first evening of the Lùnastal gathering, with the fires going up on the headland behind the town, and the humans stood on the slip with their hats off while Iain's wife poured sea water over her bow and asked Manannan to keep her. Rook asked afterwards what the words meant. Iain told him, and Rook nodded and said that his own people would have said much the same to their own God, and there the matter rested.

## IV. Of the Compact Written Twice

The trouble that made the council came from the dues.

By the time of Pailteach there were three boats of the post lying off the shingle for mending and a fourth hauled up on the slip, and the town's quay had never seen so much traffic. From of old the harbour dues of Baile dhìreach had gone to the custodians at Cathair dhearg, a few coppers' worth a year in fish and salt, carried up the road by whoever was going that way. Now the post's boats paid dues too, and the post at Ros dhomhain, which kept its books to the last line, wrote to ask where its money was going, and why a harbour its own men had half rebuilt should pay the whole of it to a council that had never sent anyone to see it. At the same time the custodians of Inis thais, to whom Baile dhìreach had always sent its news, wrote to ask by what rule seven strangers were keeping a yard on a shingle held in keeping, and for how long.

Iain mac Chaluim sat on the salt-house step with both letters, one of which he could not read, and said that the town would have to write down its rule.

"Write it how?" said Seonag.

"Twice," said Rook, who had the other letter. "Once in each."

That was in the last days of Pailteach. The writing took until the middle of Damhrach, and the copyists, who knew something of the labour of putting one tongue beside another, reckoned it the hardest writing of its length in the whole age. The custodian of Inis thais sent over his clerk, a young man with ink to the wrist and a portable desk on a strap, to write the Dia-thìris book. Rook wrote the humans' book himself, in a round slow hand, with his tongue between his teeth. They sat at the long mending-table in the net-loft over the salt-house, among the hung nets and the smell of tar and old fish, with a lamp at each end of the table and the sea going on below the window. Six sat to make the compact, three of the town and three of the strangers: Iain mac Chaluim, Seonag nic Aoidh, and the pilot Murchadh mac Iain for the town, and for the strangers Rook, the carpenter Nathan Cobb, and the sawyer Peter Lusk. They did not intend to be the council. They became it by sitting.

Eilidh was fetched on the third evening, because the harbour clauses had come to moorings and nobody at the table could agree what the humans' words for them meant. The humans had one word for a rope that holds a boat to a quay and another for a rope that holds her to an anchor, and a third for the ring the rope goes through, and the town had words for all of these and for four more besides, and the clerk from Inis thais knew none of them, having been bred in a temple city where the boats belonged to other people. Samuel was fetched for the same reason from the other side. The two of them sat at the foot of the table with his papers between them, the papers that had her words written under his with a line between, and turned them over until they found what was wanted. Then Eilidh said it in Dia-thìris and the clerk wrote it, and Samuel said it in the humans' tongue and Rook wrote it, and the line down the middle, which nobody wrote, lay between them all the same.

Not everything could be found so. There was a night-long quarrel over the shingle. The humans' book wanted to say who owned it. The town's book could only say who kept it. In the end the humans' book said that the shingle was the town's and the town's book said it was kept for the town, and both of them said that no one would build on it, and Rook said that his tent would be taken down when the council told him, and wrote that in too.

There was a quarrel over the rest-nights, which the humans agreed to keep, and a matching quarrel over the humans' day of rest, which the town had never heard of. The humans kept one day in seven for their God, whose name was Crìosd, and on it they would do no work and wished that no one would hammer near them while they prayed. The town agreed not to hammer on the slip on that day. Nobody at Baile dhìreach had ever hammered on the slip at all before the humans came, and Murchadh said so, and the clerk from Inis thais wrote it into the Dia-thìris book before anyone could stop him, and it is there still, in the margin.

The dues were shared. Half went up the road to the custodians at Cathair dhearg as before, and half went to the humans' post at Ros dhomhain, and the council kept the harbour in repair out of what the town took for mooring, and nobody in either book was to pay twice.

Last of all they came to the chair. There were six at the table, three and three, and some one of them had to speak first and speak last. They agreed that the chair should go between Iain mac Chaluim and William Rook, a year apiece. Then they found that they did not agree what a year was. The town's year turned at Samhain, with the dark half, and was counted by moons; the humans' year turned in the dead of winter on a day that stood still in their calendar and wandered in the moon's. If the chair turned at Samhain, Iain would hold it for a fortnight. Iain said that a fortnight was as long as he had ever wanted to hold anything. Rook laughed, and said that a year was a year, and that the chair should turn at the humans' new year, since that at least could be written down and would be in the same place next time. So it was agreed, and so it was written in both books: that Iain mac Chaluim should hold the chair until the humans' year turned, and William Rook for the year after, and so on in turn for as long as they lived or the town kept them.

On 10 an Dàmhair, AE 5, the compact of Baile dhìreach was read in both tongues on the quay, in a west wind with rain in it. The clerk read the Dia-thìris and Rook the humans'. The whole town stood and listened to both, the humans to the one they could not follow and the town to the one it could not follow, and then everyone who could write put a name in both books, and those who could not made a mark. The Dia-thìris book is dated by the island's count of years and the moon, and the humans' book by their day and month and year; neither gives the other's date, and each has a blank at the foot of its page where the other's might have gone.

The council of six sat for the first time eight days later, on 18 an Dàmhair, AE 5, in the net-loft, with Iain in the chair. They settled a quarrel over a mooring ring, sent the first half of the dues up the road to Cathair dhearg in a sack with a boy to carry it, and sent the second half round by boat to Ros dhomhain. Then they drank to the harbour, with the humans' spirit and the town's heather ale, and the clerk from Inis thais drank more of both than he should, and was put to bed in the tent.

## V. Of Her Father's No

Samuel came to Ruairidh's door on the night of Samhain.

It was the worst night of the year for it, and Eilidh told him so afterwards, and he said that he had not known. The whole town was on the headland above the quay. The fire was going up against a sky full of wet wind, and the sparks were driving inland, and the young men were running the embers along the street, sunwise about the well and down to the water. The old year was going out into the dark half and the dead were near. The humans had come up the path as far as the last cairn and stood there in a knot together, watching, with the firelight on their faces, the way men stand at the door of a house where a wake is going on and they are not sure they are bidden. Rook had taken his hat off again. Nobody had told them to, and nobody told them to put it on.

Eilidh had gone down to the house for more peat. When she came out with her creel her father was standing in the door, and Samuel was on the step below him in the rain, and neither of them was saying anything.

She knew at once what had been said, because the cooper had his hat in his hands the way Rook had held his on the shingle in Bearnach, and because her father's face had gone the colour it went when a barrel he had packed himself was opened and found spoiled.

"No," said her father, in Dia-thìris, and then in the few words of the humans' tongue he had got from the salt-house, which were mostly the names of fish: "No. Go."

Samuel looked at her past her father's shoulder. Then he put his hat on and went back down the street towards the shingle, walking carefully on the wet stones, and he did not go back up to the fire.

Her father would not talk to her that night. In the morning, when the headland was black and smoking and the gulls were at the scraps, he talked a great deal.

He had nothing against the cooper, who was a good cooper. A council, he said, was one thing and a hearth another, and he had put his mark in both books on the quay like everyone else and had meant it; the humans were welcome to the shingle and the slip and the well in its turn and the half of the dues, and none of that had anything to do with his daughter. He said that Samuel Hale had a country somewhere over the eastern water, behind Ceò Mhanannain, that nobody in Baile dhìreach had ever seen and nobody ever would, and that any man with a country might go back to it. He said that her children would be neither one thing nor the other. And then he said the thing he was really afraid of, standing at the salt-house door with his arms folded, as though it had only just occurred to him.

"When the chair goes over to the carpenter," he said, "they will have the town. You watch. A year of him, and they will have it."

"There are three of us and three of them," said Eilidh. "They will have it the way Iain has it now."

"Iain is one of us."

"Rook put his mark in our book," said Eilidh. "He wrote that he would take his house down if we told him."

"He wrote it in his book," said her father. "Who reads his book?"

She said that she did, a little. Samuel had taught her some of the letters over the summer, in the evenings on the upturned boat, and she could make out her own name in his hand and some of the words for rope. Her father looked at her as if she had told him she could fly, and went into the salt-house and banged the door.

For the rest of Samhnas she mended nets on the shingle and the cooper worked in the shed, a hundred paces off, and they did not speak. The whole town knew why. The two books, which had nothing to say about it, lay on the shelf in the net-loft.

In the black moon the council sent its bidding to Inis thais. The compact had a clause, put in at the clerk's asking, that any town of the coast might sit with them on the same terms; and Iain mac Chaluim, who had begun to enjoy the chair more than he admitted, wanted the temple city to know it was asked. Murchadh took the letter along the shore in his boat, the two books' worth of it, both tongues, and brought back word that the custodian had read it through twice and had said that he would write.

On the last night of Dubhlas the town remembered its drowned, as every harbour of the west did at the dark of the year, and set lamps along the quay for them. The humans came down from the tent and stood with the townsfolk. Samuel stood at the end of the line, and when the lamps were lit he took off his hat and said a prayer to Crìosd in his own tongue for the men he had known who had gone over the side in the northern sea on the voyage out, before ever they saw the island. Eilidh did not know the words. She set a lamp for them at the end of the quay, and her father saw her do it, and said nothing.

## VI. Of the Turning of the Humans' Year

The humans' year turned in the middle of Faolach, the wolf-moon, the storm-time at the year's dead end, when the nets were ashore for mending and the boats hauled high and the days were hardly worth the name.

The council met that morning in the net-loft with the rain drumming on the slates. Iain mac Chaluim stood up from the head of the table and moved down one place, and William Rook moved up one, and sat, and looked for a long time at the table in front of him, as if he had not expected it to be the same table. That was the whole of it. Both books enter it in a line. The humans' book gives the day and the year; the town's gives the moon and says only that the carpenter took the chair as the compact bade him, and that the fisherman gave it.

Before they had done anything else a boy came up the ladder, wet through, with a letter from Inis thais.

It was short, and it was courteous, and it was written in Dia-thìris only. The custodian of Inis thais thanked the council of Baile dhìreach for its bidding and declined it. He wished the town well of its compact. But, he wrote, one town may be a trial, and two would be a rule; and the city of Lia Fàil would not make a rule of a thing that had been tried for three moons, and would watch, and would write again if there was cause.

Rook had the letter read to him twice, once in each tongue, and at the end of the second reading he said, "That's fair," and had it laid in the Dia-thìris book, between the page of the handing-over and the page of the next matter; and the council went on to the next matter, which was a boat of the post that had dragged her anchor in the night and fouled the town's moorings, and whose master had refused to pay for the damage.

Eilidh's father was waiting at the foot of the ladder for that one, because it was his mooring.

She saw it all from the salt-house door. Rook came down the ladder with the other five behind him and walked out along the quay in the rain to look at the ring and the torn rope. He looked for a long time. He sent for the post's master, who was one of his own people, a man of Harrow's ships, and told him in the humans' tongue that he would pay the town's rate for the rope and the town's rate for the ring, and pay it in iron by weight, and pay it that day. The master argued. Rook heard him out and said the same again, louder. Then he turned to Ruairidh and told him in his forty words of Dia-thìris, most of them wrong, that he would have his rope, and asked him whether the town's rate was fair, because he had written it into the book from Seonag's saying and did not know it for himself.

Ruairidh said that it was fair.

That night the great storm of that winter came in off the west, three days of it, the worst in years. The sea came over the quay and into the foot of the street. On the second night it began to drive up the shingle towards the boats, and the whole town went down in the dark to haul them higher, and the humans came out of the tent with ropes and blocks and a capstan-bar off the slip, and nobody asked them to. Eilidh was on a line with her father and Seonag's grandsons and Samuel Hale and Nathan Cobb, heaving the coaster that the humans had built for Iain mac Chaluim up over the crest of the shingle, a foot at a time. The rain came at them level. Nobody could hear anything, and so nobody spoke anything but the one word, on the pull, which in the end they were all shouting in the town's tongue, humans and all. When the boat was over the crest Samuel threw a hitch round the post at the top of the shingle to hold her, and it was the net-maker's knot of the south-west, and he threw it one-handed.

Her father saw it. He was holding the lantern.

The storm blew itself out on the third morning. Nothing in the town had fallen down but the end of the salt-house chimney, and the humans' tent, which had lost half its roof, and which the humans put back up in a day and a half with Ruairidh's help, on the shingle where it had stood, the council having said nothing about taking it down.

The town had watched the carpenter in the chair for half a moon by then. He had sat under the same slates and at the same table, and settled what came before him by the same rule the town had always kept, and written it into his own book in his round slow hand, and nothing whatever had happened to the town that it could see, except that it had been paid for a rope.

One evening at the end of Faolach Ruairidh came down onto the shingle where his daughter was at her frames. He stood beside her for a while looking at the tent, where there was a lamp in the glass window, and the cooper's shadow going to and fro.

"Tell the cooper," he said, "that if he wants his bowl filled he can come up for it himself, like a christened man."

He meant it as a joke. He had learned the word from the humans that winter, and had no notion what it meant, except that they used it of a man who behaved as he should. Eilidh laughed so much that she had to sit down on the shingle, and she did not tell him.

That was the end of the first winter of the council of six. The two books stood on the shelf in the net-loft side by side, the one dated by the moon and the other by the day, with the letter from Inis thais between the pages of the one and nothing between the pages of the other. The lamp at the quay-head burned for the boats. The tent kept its crooked place on the shingle, with its back to the west wind and a new patch on its roof, and the gulls came back to it.

# Chapter Five: Of the Five Headlands

*AE 6 – 7*

## I. Of the Nine on the Western Shore

Of the walk round the headlands there are three witnesses, and none of them is whole. There is James Fenn's chart, which survives; there is the roll of the custodians of Cathair dhearg, which gives the walk four lines; and there is what Torcall Clachair told, when he was old, to the households of the southern cape, who kept it as coast people keep the names of drowned men. Where the three disagree, the copyists have trusted the chart for distances and the mason for everything else.

In the winter of that year Torcall was at Baile fhiadhaich on the west coast, setting a new face of stone on the harbour wall. He was a man of some forty-six winters, broad in the back and short in the leg, with a mason's hands, split at the knuckles and grey with dust in every crease. That autumn he had raised the frame for the new bells in the tower at Cathair dhearg, and the custodian of Baile fhiadhaich had sent for him after, because her sea-wall was falling into the harbour a stone at a time. He lodged with a rope-maker, and liked the town, whose people had a name on the coast for good cordage and bad manners, and deserved both.

On 30 am Faoilleach, AE 6, the fog came in off the western sea in the afternoon and did not lift. Torcall worked on at the wall until he could not see the end of his own line, then went up to the rope-walk to sit by the fire. In the night the fishermen heard a gun fired twice out on the water, and stood on the quay in the fog and argued over what it meant.

In the morning they found out. A human supply-brig, bound down the coast for Cuan shean with stores for the post at Ros dhomhain, had struck the reefs off the point south of the town, where the sea breaks white on a still day and no boat of Baile fhiadhaich goes without a man in the bow. By first light her masts lay along the water. The fishermen took off eleven men from the rigging and the rocks. The rest came ashore over the next three days, one or two at a tide, on the shingle under the dunes.

Torcall helped to carry them up. He had never touched one of the strangers before. They were heavier than they looked, and their clothes held the sea, and their faces had the pale of people who had lived under a greyer sky. There were nine of them. One was the ship's master, a man with a grey beard cut close and a brass ring in one ear, and in the breast of his coat, sewn into oiled cloth, was a chart.

The master's mate had come off the rocks with a broken arm and a face like chalk, and he knew a few words of Dia-thìris, as most of the strangers now did. He spread the chart on the rope-maker's table, and Torcall looked at it with him.

It was a drawing of the island's western coast in ink, with the headlands and harbours marked and soundings written small along the edges. It was a good drawing, and it was wrong. The point where the brig had struck was set down a mile and more further out to sea than it lay, and the reefs below it were not there at all.

"He drew it," the mate said, and put his finger on the dead man's name in the corner. "From his head. From other voyages." He had no word for what he wanted to say next, and in the end he tapped his own forehead and then the chart and shook his head.

"On your coast," he said, "there is no light. Only the fires. The fires are small."

Torcall said that the fires were for the boats of the coast, whose men knew the reefs.

"Yes," said the mate. "Yes. That is what I am saying."

The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich gave the dead ground above the tide-line, on a shelf of turf among the dunes where the sea-holly grew, and the strangers who had come off the rocks dug the graves with borrowed spades. One of them read from a black book in their tongue while the rest stood with their hats in their hands. The townsfolk stood a little way off, not knowing what was proper, until an old woman went down to the tide and came back with her cupped hands full of sea-water and wet the turf over each grave in turn, as the coast did for its own drowned. The strangers let her. Torcall cut nine flat stones from the spoil of his wall and set one at the head of each grave. Not knowing their letters, he cut on each a line for the sea, and the mate scratched the names under it with the point of a knife.

## II. Of the Asking

Torcall finished his wall in an Gearran, and on his road home he came down to Ros dhomhain to buy iron.

The post stood on the lake-shore below the capital, a long house of the strangers' building with a counter across one end, and that morning it was full of men who had nothing to buy. The masters of two ships at anchor off the quay were there, and the trader Thomas Pike behind his counter with his tally-book shut. The dead master's chart lay open between them, and they were arguing over it in their own tongue, fast and loud.

Pike knew the mason, who had bought bar-iron from him twice, and called him over and asked him, in careful Dia-thìris, whether he built towers.

Torcall said that he had built a bell-tower, and a sea-wall, and a great many byres.

Then Pike turned the chart round on the counter and spoke for the whole company. What he said stands in his letter-book of that month and in the custodians' roll, and the two do not quite agree. In the letter-book the seamen "request of the natives that standing lights be raised on the principal headlands of the coast, for the safety of shipping." In the roll the strangers "ask the council whether the old sea-fires may be built higher, and kept all night, and kept in all weathers." It comes to the same thing. The strangers had seen the old driftwood fires burning low on the headlands, and had thought, reasonably enough, that a people who kept fires already could keep them better.

Torcall took the question up the hill to Cathair dhearg. On 28 an Gearran, AE 6, it came before Comhairle a' Chùraim, and Tormod mac Ailein, who sat at its head, heard it read and passed it to the masons. Seven men in the capital were counted master builders, and they sat that evening at a table in the lower hall with the humans' question in front of them on a sheet of the humans' paper.

They were not long about it. A tower on a headland was a season's work for a crew of twelve, the strangers offered iron for it, and they had lost nine men on the rocks. The oldest of the seven, a man from Dùn thais who had built most of the granaries in the south, said that a light which kept men off the rocks was a good light whoever the men were, and the rest agreed with him.

Only Torcall asked about the coal. Every child on the island who had learned the old rulings at a custodian's knee knew that no coal might feed a sea-fire. Coimheadaichean na Lasrach had ruled it long ago, and their reason was short. *Lasaidh an teine-rabhaidh do choigrich:* the beacon-fire burns for strangers. A fire in a hearth warms the house; a fire on a headland is for whoever is out on the water and cannot be seen, and the coal of the vein was not to be burned for anyone the burner could not see. So the old fires had been fed on driftwood and seal fat and dried wrack for as long as anyone could count, and were small, and burned low.

"They have not asked for coal," said the man from Dùn thais.

"They will want the fire bigger," said Torcall.

"Then they can bring their own oil for it."

That was the end of it. The masons wrote on the back of the humans' sheet that the headlands might be built on if the custodians of each place gave leave, and that a Dia-thìreach builder should choose the ground; and they chose Torcall to choose it, since he had asked the only question and had walked the west coast twice for the sea-walls. Pike wrote under their answer that the natives had agreed "without difficulty and without asking what the lights would cost." It is the first time in his letter-book that he calls them the natives.

## III. Of the Southern Cape

The strangers sent their own man to walk with him, and Torcall met him on the quay at Ros dhomhain in am Màrt, with the wind coming cold off the lake.

James Fenn was twenty-six that spring, long in the leg, with fair hair the island's wind would not let lie and a face burnt red across the nose. He had come out as a navigator's mate with Harrow's four ships and had stayed when they sailed home. Across his back on a strap he carried a leather case, and in it, packed in wool, a brass instrument with a glass eye and a swinging arm, a compass in a wooden box, a roll of paper and a bundle of pens; on his other shoulder he carried a staff banded black and white, taller than himself. Of Dia-thìris he had some two hundred words, most of them the words of ships and weather, and he spoke them fast and with great confidence and little grammar. Torcall had perhaps forty words of the strangers' tongue, most of them the names of tools.

They went south and east by the carters' road, four days down out of the hill country, and on the evening of the fourth day they came over the last rise and saw the sea.

Tobar dhearg was a village of fishers and salt-boilers round a well whose water ran red over the stones, and it stood a few miles back from the cape, out of the wind. The cape ran out beyond it in a long spine of grey rock. On its end stood the oldest sea-light on Dia-thìr: a round tower no taller than a byre, of rough stones laid without mortar, its flat top black from more fires than anyone could reckon, with pegs set into the wall to climb it by. The households of the village kept it in turn. That night it was the turn of a man called Fionnlagh and his two sons, and Torcall and Fenn went out along the spine in the dusk and climbed up to them.

The fire was a heap of driftwood on the flat stones, no bigger than a cart-load, with a pot of seal fat beside it that the younger son ladled over the wood whenever the flame sank. Its yellow smoky light lit the three men's faces and did not reach the sea at all.

"How far?" Fenn said to Fionnlagh. "How far do boats see it?"

Fionnlagh said that the boats of Tobar dhearg saw it from the fishing ground, which was as far as they went.

"And the big ships? From far out?"

Fionnlagh said that there were no big ships, and then remembered that there were, and was a little put out. The fire, he said, was for the boats of Tobar dhearg.

In the morning Fenn set up the brass instrument on its three legs on the end of the cape and sighted along it to the headlands east and west, and sent Torcall out along the rocks with the banded staff to hold it upright where he pointed, and wrote numbers in columns. Toward evening he unrolled a clean sheet on the top of the old tower, weighted the corners with four stones, and began his chart of the southern coast: the cape, the village behind it, the well, the rocks off the point. Then he wrote a name on the end of the cape in the strangers' letters.

Torcall asked him what it said.

It was the name of a headland on the coast where Fenn was born, the one his father's boat had rounded to come home. It had been the last thing he saw of an Tìr Thall when he sailed, and he had thought it right to give it to the first light he found here.

Torcall looked at the name for a while. Then he said, "*Tha ainm air.*" It has a name.

"This one?"

"Every one of them."

Fenn did not argue. The name was for the chart, he said, and the chart was for men who came from the sea and would never hear the Dia-thìris name of the cape, and needed to call it something. That was fair, and Torcall said so. But that evening he gathered stones from the beach in a sack, and on the highest point of the cape, a few yards inland from the old tower, where the rock was sound and a new tower could stand, he built a cairn as high as his chest, laid dry, each stone on two below it, with a flat stone for a cap. The roll of Cathair dhearg enters it on 29 am Màrt, AE 6: *the mason Torcall has marked the ground at the southern fire.* It was the first of the five.

## IV. Of the Eastern Cape and the North-East Steps

From Tobar dhearg they walked east along the southern coast and then north with the sea on their right hand, and in an Giblean they came to the eastern cape.

Baile ìseal was a handful of low houses on the far edge of the island, with their backs to the moor, and its people kept a fire on the cape for their own boats. But the tellings of that coast said that it had always been lit to bring the boats home in a storm, and the old men of Baile ìseal were proud of the difference. On the southern cape, they said, the fire was a mark to steer by. Here it was a call. A woman whose husband was out in a blow would climb up and feed it herself, and he would see it and know she was there. Fenn wrote that in the margin of his chart.

The east coast was also the raiders' water, broken by low bare islets where men lived by taking what they could from the strands. On the second night Torcall and Fenn sat up with the watch, and near midnight the watchman pointed out a small red spark on the nearest islet that came and went as someone passed in front of it.

"They see us too," he said.

Fenn asked whether a greater light on the cape would help or hinder that. The watchman thought about it for a long time. Then he said that a greater light would bring more men home, and more of the other kind too. Torcall built his second cairn above the old fire the next morning, and the watchman helped him lift the capstone.

North of the eastern cape the land ran up steep out of the sea, and they walked the cliff-tops for the best part of a week with the wind in their faces. At Àth dhearg, above the passage in toward Seann Tarr, the fire had no tower at all. It was built on a shelf of rock near the top of the cape, and from the shore below a stair had been cut up to it in the living rock, turning back and forth across the face, a hundred and more steps, narrower than any stair Torcall had seen, and little worn.

Torcall went up them slowly with his hand on the rock. At the top he sat down on the fire-shelf and looked back down the stair for a long while. When Fenn asked what he was looking at, he said he was counting the cuts of the chisel, and that the man who had cut them had been left-handed, and patient, and had been dead a long time.

The custodian of Àth dhearg would not give leave for a cairn. The fire, she said, belonged to the households of the coast, who had cut the stair; she could not give away a place that was not hers, and if the strangers wanted a tower they must ask the households, one hearth at a time. So Torcall and Fenn went round the hearths, and it took eleven days. Most said yes. Two said no, and one of those came round when Torcall told him the tower would have a stair inside it, so that nobody need climb the old one in a gale again. The third cairn went up at the end of the shelf, where the rock was broad enough to bear a tower, and the custodian came up the stair to watch it built, and brought bread.

## V. Of the Northern Point and the North-West Headland

The north coast they walked in an Cèitean and an t-Ògmhios, going west, with the hills of the interior blue on their left. They slept in byres and once on the open heather, where each named the stars in his own tongue, and neither remembered the other's names in the morning.

It was on that stage that Fenn first spoke of the line. His chart of the coast was a chain of bearings from one headland to the next, all the way round, and it would close; but it had no measure across. Nobody knew how wide the island was. The ships' masters knew the west coast well enough now, and guessed at the east, and all guessed differently. What Fenn wanted was one straight line of sights across the whole island, from the open sea off the north-west to the water off the eastern cape, every station within sight of the next and every distance between them measured. Then the chart would have a spine.

Torcall asked how he meant to see across the middle of the island, where the hills were.

"From the tops of them," said Fenn. "With a mark on each top. A pile of stones, a pole, anything I can see from the next." He looked at Torcall sidelong. "You build good piles of stones."

At Muileann bheag, on the northern point, the old fire stood on a knob of turf above the shore, and the ground round it was red. Fenn wanted to know how deep the footing of a tower would have to go, and he borrowed a spade and dug a pit beside the fire-place with Torcall and a boy of the village. They went down through black ash and red earth, and black ash and red earth again, in bands like the rings of a felled tree, and at three yards they had still not come to rock. Torcall put his hand into the side of the pit and brought it out red to the wrist, and wiped it on the grass, and set his fourth cairn a little way inland where the rock was sound.

They came to the north-western headland at Baile chrom at midsummer.

This was the oldest fire of the five, and it had never been lit to bring anyone home. The tellings of Baile chrom said that it had been lit in the first days of the island to warn boats off the water beyond the headland, where Uilebheist na Mara had been seen, and every child in the town knew why the ash under it lay a man's height deep. The boats of Baile chrom kept south of the fire. Out beyond, some miles off the north-west cape, lay the water where the boats of Achadh àrsaidh had met the strangers' ships in the first winter they came, and beyond that the open sea and the north.

The households of Baile chrom heard Torcall out, and then an old man of the town put the matter plainly. The fire on the headland said *keep away*. The strangers wanted a fire that said *come in*. It could not say both, and the town would rather it went on saying what it had always said.

Fenn answered him in his bad Dia-thìris. The ships would come in whatever the fire said, he told the old man, because they were coming from an Tìr Thall and this was the first land they saw; the only question was whether they came in on the rocks or clear of them. The old man looked at him for a long while and said that this was the first true thing he had heard a stranger say, and that he did not like it any better for being true.

The town gave leave in the end, on condition that the old fire be kept alight beside whatever tower was built, and fed with driftwood as it always had been. Fenn agreed at once. Torcall built the fifth cairn above the fire, and when it was done he stood beside it looking north-west, where the line of the open water showed clean and hard in the evening light, as the fishers said it had only begun to show in their fathers' time.

## VI. Of Fenn's Line

The line began at sea, and the sea end was Torcall's doing.

Fenn wanted to know how far out a ship coming down from the north first saw the island, for there his line must begin. He could reckon it on paper from the height of the headland and the height of a mast, but he had seen what a chart from memory had done on the reefs south of Baile fhiadhaich, and he wanted to see it done. So at Lùnastal he went down the coast to Achadh àrsaidh and found a crew who would take him west in their boat, out past Coinneachadh nan Long, as far into the open sea as they dared go; and Torcall stayed on the headland at Baile chrom to keep a fire.

He built it on a platform of flat stones beside the old fire-place, so as not to disturb the ash, of driftwood that the households brought up in creels, and he fed it with seal fat as the old fire was fed. He burned no coal. On the first night the wind was wrong and the boat did not go out. On the second there was haze. The third came clear and still, with a small moon, and the fire stood up on the headland in a column of yellow light with the sparks going up out of it. Torcall sat beside it all night and fed it, and the households of the town watched him from below, and none of them came up.

Out on the sea Fenn sat in the stern with his compass and a lantern shaded under a cloth and his eyes on the headland, and when the fire sank to a spark on the rim of the water and went out he called to them to stop. He took the time by his watch and the bearing by his compass and the run of the boat by a line paid out astern, and reckoned it through the rest of the night. It came to something near thirty of his miles. The fishers, who had never been so far out, rowed home, and Fenn was sick over the side twice on the way.

This is the one piece of the line told from both sides. Fenn's letter to Pike says that "the native fire on the north-west headland was raised by Clachair to a great height for the purpose, and was visible until thirty miles." Torcall told the households of the southern cape, many years after, that he had sat all night beside a fire lit for a stranger, to measure how far off strangers could see the island, and that he had fed it with his own hands and burned no coal on it, and that he still did not know whether he had done right.

From the headland the line went east and a little south, over the whole breadth of the island, and they ran it through the autumn. Fenn chose each station from the one before, sighting to the highest ground in the right direction, and Torcall went ahead to the chosen top and built a cairn on it, tall and narrow, with a white stone on the cap that Fenn could find through the glass. Then Fenn came up and sighted forward to the next top and back to the last, and two boys hired from the nearest village carried a chain of iron links between the stations to measure them. When the cloud sat on the hills they made no stations at all, and sat in a byre, and Fenn copied his columns fair and Torcall mended his boots.

The cairns went across the middle of Dia-thìr in a string, over the moors south of Cnoc bheag and the rough hills where the carters' roads went round, through country with no village for a day in any direction, where they slept against the cairns they had built.

In an t-Samhain they came up into the Doire uaine hills, and the next station on the line was the highest ground on the island.

Binnean a' Chlachair stood up over the bare moor above Muileann gheal, a great shoulder of grey rock with the cloud on it half the year, and the line ran over its summit as near as made no difference. Fenn saw it from two stations off and was glad, for from its top he could sight a long way east and cut a week off the work. He wanted a fire on it: a great fire, at night, that could be seen from station after station all the way to the eastern cape.

Torcall said that there would be no fire on Binnean a' Chlachair.

The herders of Muileann gheal said the same when they fed the two of them oatcakes and broth that night. Every child of those hills knew the telling of Clann a' Chlachair, that a man of that kindred had carried coal up to the summit in the old days and let it fall, and that one coal had caught fire in the air as it fell. Since then no one had lit a fire there. The herders who went over the top left a stone on it as they passed, one stone each, and that was all they did.

"*Cha las sinn teine an seo*," said the oldest of them. We light no fire here. He said it to Fenn directly, slowly, as to a child.

Fenn asked Torcall whether it was the same ruling as the coal on the beacons. Torcall said that it was a ruling of the hills, and the herders kept it.

They went up on a clear morning in the last week of an t-Samhain, with frost on the heather in the hollows and the whole eastern half of the island laid out below them in brown and grey, and the sea shining at the edge of it far off. On the summit there was a cairn already, broad and low and shapeless, built of the stones the herders had left there one at a time for longer than anyone could count. Torcall did not build on it. He took out of his coat a stone he had carried up from the burn at Muileann gheal, and laid it on the herders' cairn as the herders did, and stood back.

Fenn took his sights from the summit by daylight, to a square of white linen stretched on a pole on the next station east, with a boy of Muileann gheal beside it to hold it into the sun. It cost him four days more than a fire would have. He wrote in his columns that "the natives will not suffer a fire on the high point, for a reason connected with their religion," and went on with the work.

Winter shut down on them in an Dùbhlachd, and they wintered at Muileann gheal with the herders, and went on again in am Màrt when the cloud lifted off the moors. The last stations ran down out of the hills over the long slopes of the east to the cape at Baile ìseal, where Torcall's second cairn stood above the old fire and the households of the coast came out to see the chain carried the last of the way.

On 26 an Giblean, AE 7, Fenn sat down in the watchman's house at Baile ìseal with all his columns in front of him and added the line up from end to end, twice, and then a third time. He made it a hundred and fifty-five miles, from the point in the open sea off the north-west where a ship coming down from the north would first raise the fire on the headland, to the water off the eastern cape; and some thirty of those miles were sea at the western end. It was the first measure that had ever been made of Dia-thìr from side to side.

He told Torcall the number, and Torcall asked what it meant in days.

Fenn thought about it and said, on a good road, walking hard, a little more than five.

Torcall said that it had taken them from Lùnastal to an Giblean.

"We were stopping," said Fenn.

"We were building," said Torcall.

## VII. Of the Two Books at Baile dhìreach

They walked west from the eastern cape together, since Fenn was bound for Baile dhìreach and Torcall's road home to Cathair dhearg lay the same way for most of the journey.

Fenn had a wedding to go to. The human cooper Samuel Hale, who had come out with him in Harrow's ships and had settled at Baile dhìreach among the boatbuilders, was to marry a net-maker of that town, Eilidh nic Ruairidh, and had written in the autumn to ask Fenn to stand for him. The letter had found them at Muileann gheal in the snow.

Baile dhìreach was a small harbour on the south-west coast, built along one long street that ran straight down to the quay, and it was the only town on Dia-thìr where the two peoples lived under one council. They came in over the last hill on an evening late in an Cèitean, with the sun going down into the western sea at the end of the street, and the street full of people carrying benches.

That night the council of six told the two walkers about the ruling. Before the spring, Iain mac Chaluim, the fisherman who sat for the Dia-thìrich on the council, had written to the custodians at Cathair dhearg to ask whether such a marriage could be entered in the custodians' roll as any other was, and whether its children would stand in the roll as the children of a Dia-thìreach mother. A rider had carried the letter to the capital and come back with nothing. The council there had heard it read, he said, and gone on to the next matter.

"Then we shall write it down ourselves," said Iain mac Chaluim, "and they can rule on it when they please."

The council of Baile dhìreach kept two books, one in each tongue, as its compact was written in each, and on 26 an Cèitean, AE 7, it entered the marriage in both.

The wedding was held on the quay, the only open place in the town wide enough for everyone, and everyone came. The tide was full and the fishing boats rode at their moorings with green boughs tied to their mastheads. An old woman of Òrd Mhanannain, whose people had founded the town, poured sea-water on the stones at the couple's feet, and one of the human carpenters read a few lines from the strangers' black book while the townsfolk of both peoples stood through it. The two of them said their promises twice, once in each tongue, Eilidh haltingly in the strangers' tongue and Samuel worse in Dia-thìris, and nobody laughed at either. Then William Rook sat down at a table on the quay with the humans' book open in front of him, and Iain mac Chaluim beside him with the other, and each wrote the marriage into his own book in his own letters.

Each book needed a witness of each people. Fenn signed for the bridegroom in the humans' book. For the Dia-thìreach book the council had meant to ask a custodian, and no custodian had come; so Iain mac Chaluim looked round the quay for a Dia-thìreach of some standing who was not of Baile dhìreach, and found Torcall on a bollard at the edge of the crowd with a cup of ale, and called him to the table.

Torcall could write his name and not much more. He wrote it slowly under the names of the bride and bridegroom, and Iain mac Chaluim sanded it and blew on it and closed the book. Beside him William Rook closed the other.

There was dancing on the quay until the tide turned, and fish and bread and the strangers' ale. Late in the night, when the fires had burned down, Fenn brought out his chart and spread it on the council's table under the lamp, beside the two books where the clerks had left them. The whole coast of the island was on it, all the way round, and across the middle ran the line, straight as a stretched cord from the open sea to the eastern cape, every station marked with a small triangle, and at each of the five headlands a small circle, and at each circle the name Fenn had written in the strangers' letters.

He had learned enough of the Dia-thìreach letters that winter at Muileann gheal to spell a word he heard, and he asked Torcall to tell him the names. So Torcall told him. The southern cape, Tobar dhearg. The eastern cape, Baile ìseal. The steps in the north-east, Àth dhearg. The northern point, Muileann bheag. The north-western headland, Baile chrom. Fenn wrote each under his own, carefully, in the island's letters, and at the mountain in the middle of the line, where he had written nothing, he wrote Binnean a' Chlachair and drew no triangle.

The chart survives, with two names at every headland, one above the other in the same hand. The two books of Baile dhìreach that were closed on the quay that night hold the one marriage in two tongues. Of the cairns that Torcall built, the five above the old fires and the long string of narrow ones he laid across the island for Fenn's line, most have been pulled down by herders for their walls or have fallen in the winters and gone back into the hills. The stone he laid on Binnean a' Chlachair is on the summit still, among all the others, and there is no telling now which one it was.

# Chapter Six: Of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg

*AE 7 – 9*

## I. Of the Letter from Baile dhìreach

In the summer of AE 7 a letter came up the road from Baile dhìreach to the council hall at Cathair dhearg, and lay on the table of Ceann a' Chùraim for the better part of a season.

Tormod mac Ailein was fifty-two years old that summer, and heavier than he had been when the ships came, and he had begun to feel the damp of the lake in his knees. He kept the table under the east window of the hall, where the light came in over the smoke of the smiths' lane, and he kept it clear. A custodian could lay a matter there in the morning and have his answer, or know that he would get none, by the time the lamps were lit. The clerks of the roll said that Tormod's table was the only flat place in Cathair dhearg that was never wet.

The letter from Baile dhìreach did not go from it. The council of six in that small port on the south-west coast, three of the island's people and three of the strangers, had entered a marriage in both its books: the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh to the human cooper Samuel Hale. Now they asked the custodians at Cathair dhearg for a ruling on what they had done. The letter was in two hands and two tongues. Iain mac Chaluim had written the Dia-thìris half, in a fisherman's square letters, and at the foot of it the carpenter William Rook had put his own name in the strangers' writing, with a flourish under it like a wave.

Tormod read the Dia-thìris half twice. The other half he could not read at all, and he looked at it a while all the same, as a man looks at a field in a strange country, trying to tell barley from grass.

"They want to know whether it is a marriage," said Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, who had come in with the letter under her arm and stayed to watch him read it.

"They have married them. It is in both their books."

"Then they want to know whether it is a marriage to us."

Tormod set the letter down. "And what are we?"

She gave no answer, and he had looked for none. Gormshuil was five years younger than he, and in the five years since the season of words she had learned the strangers' letters from Samuel Wren, one at a time, with the patience of a woman threading beads. She could read Rook's line. She read it to him: his name, and the words *for the council*, and the date by the humans' reckoning, which meant nothing to either of them.

Tormod laid the letter in the chest under the window, with the other things that were waiting. The council did not take it up that summer, nor in the autumn. When at last a custodian of the south-west asked in the hall what answer had been sent to Baile dhìreach, Tormod said that the town had made its own compact with its own hands, and a town that could do that could keep what it had made; and the clerk wrote that no ruling was given.

He had other things on his table. He had the iron.

## II. Of Tormod's Reasons

There were three of them, and he could have counted them off on his fingers, and more than once he did.

The first was the iron. In the lane below the bridge the smiths of Cathair dhearg had learned the strangers' bar-iron in a single winter, and Gilleasbuig Gobha, the best of them, could draw a blade now that would shave the hair off a man's arm. Tormod had a hoe of it himself, for the garden behind his house, and a spade, and a pair of shears; and the old bronze hoes of the capital's fields had been melted down and cast into bells, which he heard every evening. No one in the fields wanted the bronze back.

The second was the surgeon. Jonas Tull had set the leg of a Cuan shean fisherman whom the whole town had given up for lame, and the custodian of Cuan shean had entered it in her roll as the first debt owed to a stranger. In the winter before the letter came, a back tooth had rotted in Tormod's own jaw and kept him from sleep for a month, and the capital's physician had given him willow-bark and told him to wait. Tull, passing through to the post, had looked in his mouth by the east window, asked for a stool and a cup of spirit, and drawn the tooth in the time it takes to say so. Tormod kept it in a box.

The third was the ships.

Edmund Harrow had sailed home with hides and cloth in his holds and come back with four ships in place of three. He could come back with forty, and had never needed to say so. A big man gone grey at the temples, who laughed easily, Harrow had held out an empty cask on the strand at Cuan shean and been given water, and every custodian on the island liked him for it. But Tormod had asked him once, at the post, through Thomas Pike, how many ships there were in an Tìr Thall. Harrow had thought about it honestly, then laughed and said that he could not count them, and that most of them were not his, and that the men who owned them did not always ask for water.

That was the third reason. Tormod never wrote it down.

In the autumn of that year Harrow came up the lake road to Cathair dhearg with Pike beside him to put his words into the island's tongue, and sat at the table under the east window, and asked that the terms on which his people stayed be written.

"You have your leave," said Tormod. "It is in the roll."

"It's in your roll," Harrow said. Pike gave it over word for word, with an apologetic look, as a man hands on a pot too hot to hold. "In my country nothing is so until it's written by both sides and signed by both. A man is coming who will ask for it. Better it's written now, between friends, than later between strangers."

"We are strangers," Tormod said.

Harrow laughed at that, and when Pike had given it him he laughed again. "So we are. Well. Between strangers who've eaten each other's bread, then."

He told them that the man who was coming would bear a title that Pike could not put into Dia-thìris and did not try to, and which the island came afterwards to render An t-Àrd-mhaor, the high steward; that he would speak for the government of an Tìr Thall and for no trading house; that Harrow himself had asked for him, since a ship's master was no one to be making laws; and that he would come with the spring sailing. Then he stood, and shook Tormod's hand in his fashion, and went down the stairs to the street whistling.

Tormod sat on at the table after they had gone, while the new bells rang for the evening, and thought of Oighrig nic Leòid's letter from her sickbed six years before, which the clerk had not read out: that a leave given in the roll cannot be ungiven by the next roll, and that the strangers would know it better than the council, since they would be holding it. He had thought her an old woman afraid of the sea. He read the letter again that night by the lamp, and put it back.

## III. Of the Man Who Asked for a Horse

Josiah Pell landed at Cuan shean in the early spring of AE 8, off the first ship of the year to come down from the north.

The custodian of Cuan shean was still Oighrig nic Leòid, who had given Harrow water. She walked with a stick now, and kept her custody from a chair by the harbour window. She sent a rider up the valley road to the capital the same day with a letter, and the letter is in the council's roll. It says that the ship came in on the morning tide; that the man got down into the boat in a black coat, with a leather case under his arm that he would let no one else carry; that he came up the shingle dry-shod, on a plank the sailors laid for him; and that he did not ask for water. He asked for a horse. She lent him her own, the gentlest in the town, and he thanked her by name, having learned it on the ship. He was a man of about fifty, she wrote, clean-shaven, grey, with good manners and a cold, and he looked at everything once and seemed to remember it.

He rode the twenty-six miles to Cathair dhearg in a day, with two of his own people and a Cuan shean boy to show the road, and came up the hill into the capital at dusk with the rain beginning. Instead of the post, he asked for the council hall, and there for Ceann a' Chùraim; and Tormod, who had been told he was coming and had not believed he would come the same night, went down to meet him in the hall with his house-shoes still on his feet.

There was no one there that night to carry words between them. Pell took off his wet hat, bowed a short neat bow from the neck, and said a sentence in his own tongue, and then two words in Dia-thìris that he must have learned on the ship, careful and wrong in every sound: *Beannachd leibh*. It is the island's word of leave-taking. Tormod bowed back and did not correct him. Pell was given a room in the guest-house by the temple, and in the morning Wren came up from the post to put his words into the island's tongue, and the talking began.

It went on for most of a moon.

Wren sat between them at the long table in the council hall, or on fine days at the post at Ros dhomhain, where Pell laid his papers out on a board across two casks. He was thinner than he had been in the season of words and coughed in the mornings, and sometimes he stopped and said to Tormod in Dia-thìris, "There is no word of yours for this. I will say it as near as I can," and then said it. Pell's secretary, a young man with a clean hand, wrote down each day what was agreed and read it back at evening.

Tormod asked at the start that the terms be written twice, once in each tongue, as the compact of Baile dhìreach had been.

Pell heard this through Wren and said that he honoured the custom, and that at Baile dhìreach it had been well done. Only an agreement between his government and the island must go before the lawyers of an Tìr Thall, who could read only their own tongue, and a writing in two tongues was two writings, and the day would come when they did not agree. One text should govern. A copy in Dia-thìris would be made for the council's use, as a courtesy, when there was leisure to make it well.

"When will there be leisure?" Tormod asked.

Pell said: after. Wren gave it over as *an dèidh làimh*, which is the island's way of saying it, and means *after the hand*, and the council clerk wrote it down.

Six of the council sat through the talking, from the capital and the lake towns and the west; the roll gives their names, and sets down that no one of them spoke against the terms. What there was to speak against, they could hear only through Wren, a sentence at a time, and a sentence at a time the terms were fair. The strangers might dwell where they had leave and trade where they found buyers. They would keep their own law among their own people and answer to the council for harm done to the island's. The harbour dues would be shared as they were shared already. A man of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach would keep order among the humans and speak for them to the council. There was a line about goods, and the working of goods, which Wren gave twice over and frowned at.

Gormshuil was not at the table.
