She had gone east in the month of Bearnach with the season's copies for the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol, as she went every year, near sixty miles of hill road with a chest on a pony. When Tormod saw how the talking went he sent a rider after her. She started back the day he found her, and the rain was on the hills, and the fords were up.

On 27 an Giblean, AE 8, the terms on which the humans stayed were set down in writing for the first time, fair, on six sheets, in the humans' tongue only. The secretary wrote them. Pell signed nothing yet, and said that the signing should be done in the council hall, before the council, as was proper; and Tormod, who had been given a great many reasons that morning and had followed all of them, found that he agreed.

## IV. Of the Line Read Twice

Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg was signed on 7 an Cèitean, AE 8, in the moon of Bealltach, a week after the bright fires.

The fires of Bealltainn had smoked more than they blazed that year, and it rained all the morning of the signing. The rain came off Loch chrom in grey sheets and walked up the hill over the roofs, and the windows of the hall ran with it, so that the lake and the harbour and the far shore went to smears of grey behind the glass. The custodians sat in their cloaks by the two fires, and the cloaks steamed.

Josiah Pell sat on the far side of the long table in his black coat, newly come over the sea as An t-Àrd-mhaor of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, the first of them; and on the near side sat Tormod mac Ailein, in the chair of Ceann a' Chùraim, with his hands folded in front of him. Between them lay the six sheets, squared together and covered edge to edge in the strangers' close black writing.

Tormod could not read a word of it. The letters stood on the sheets like a fence of thorn, and he looked at them, and then away.

Someone read it to him. The roll keeps the name of every custodian in the hall that day, and Pell's name, and the names of the two humans who stood behind him, and the name of the clerk; it keeps the name of the boy who fed the fires. It does not keep the name of the reader. The copyists of the cellar have looked for it in every roll that came down to them, and have not found it. Tormod sat with his hands folded and his eyes on the rain and listened to the voice go down the sheets, sentence by sentence, the strangers' tongue and then the island's, and the custodians along the table listened with him.

Gormshuil had not come. Her rider had sent word from the hills the night before that the ford at the foot of the long glen was up to a horse's belly, and that she would cross it in the morning.

About the middle of the fourth sheet Tormod lifted one hand from the table.

"*Leugh a-rithist e*," he said. Read that again.

The voice went back to the beginning of the sentence and read it again. It was the line about goods: that the humans might trade in such goods as the island afforded, and in the working of them, under licence of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, and that the council would not hinder such trade. It read the same the second time. Tormod listened to it with his head a little on one side, the way he listened to a custodian of the hill country who was taking the long way round to a point, and then he nodded and put his hand down, and the voice went on.

He thought, as the voice went on, of wool from Cathair naomh and dyes for Baile Mòr mhòr, of the salt of Seann Warr, of hides and cloth. Those were the goods the island afforded; he had seen them go across Pike's counter for six years. The working of them was the spinning and the dyeing and the curing, and the strangers wanted a licence for everything. It did not come into his head that a trader might want to work anything else on Dia-thìr. The vein was the vein, and no one had ever carried it to a counter.

When the reading was done Pell turned the last sheet round on the table so that it faced Tormod, and took a pen from the secretary, and dipped it, and held it out across the table.

Tormod took it. It was a goose quill, cut fine, and it was lighter than he had thought it would be.

He looked for a long while at the place where his name should go, a space at the foot of the sheet above a ruled line. He looked at it as a man looks at a ford before he wades it: at the colour of the water, and the set of it over the stones, and the far bank, and whether the far bank is as near as it looks. The custodians along the table watched him. Pell did not move. The rain ran down the windows. Then Tormod bent and wrote his name in the island's letters, square and heavy, and gave the pen back.

Pell signed after him for Riaghaltas nan Coigreach. His name was short and went quickly, with a line under it.

The strangers had dated the sheets at their head by their own day, month and year, and the secretary read the date aloud. The custodians' clerk had the roll open at the end of the table, and when the signing was done he entered it under its name, Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg: the names of those present, the terms as near as he could catch them, and the signing. At the head of the entry he wrote the year of the count of An Diosal, and the moon of Bealltach. Then he came to the day. The humans' day was a number out of their own month, which ran by another measure than the moon, and no one in the hall could tell him how to turn the one into the other. He sat with his pen over the page a while. Then he left the day empty and went on to the next line.

It was the first page of its kind in the council's roll, and no one remarked on it. The clerk ruled off the entry and sanded it, and Pell's secretary rolled the six sheets into a leather case with a cap to it and gave the case to Pell, who put it under his arm and kept it there.

Gormshuil came in two days later, with the mud of the long glen up to her knees, and the pony lame. She went straight to the hall without stopping at her house, and found the chair of Ceann a' Chùraim empty and the clerk at his table, and she asked him for the roll, and read the entry standing. Then she went to find Tormod, and what was said between them neither of them ever told. That afternoon she asked Pell, through Wren, for a copy of the terms in the strangers' tongue, since the copy in hers was to wait for leisure; and Pell, who was courteous in all things, had his secretary make one and sent it to her house within the week, with his compliments.

She began to read it with her finger, a word at a time, the way Wren had taught her. The strangers' law had words that were in none of Wren's lists, and she wrote each one on a slip and took the slips to Wren, who was often ill that year. She did not bring it before the council, and no one asked her to. It was signed.

## V. Of the House on the Rise

That summer Pell asked the council for ground.

He wanted the rise above Ros dhomhain, the bare shoulder of hill behind the harbour where the town's goats grazed, to build on it a house of dressed stone for Riaghaltas nan Coigreach. The goat-keepers were paid in iron pots, and were glad of the bargain. The council gave the ground, with no vote needed, since it was a matter of goats.

Pell had no masons of his own, and asked for the best of the masons' lane at Cathair dhearg, who had rebuilt the council hall's east gable when Tormod was young. They were paid in bar-iron by the day, and by the humans' day, which began at midnight where the island's began at dusk, and they grumbled at it and took the iron. They floated the stone over from the old quarries across the lake on rafts, and dressed it on the rise with the wind cutting at their hands.

Tormod rode down to see it in the autumn. The house was going up square and plain, of the grey stone of the lake shore, two floors high and five windows wide, with a slate roof on it from the hills behind Cathair dhearg; and it faced the harbour. From its windows Pell would see every mast in Ros dhomhain and every boat that came up Abhainn gheal into the lake. From its door he would not see the capital. Tormod stood on the rise in the wind with the master mason and asked him why the house was turned so.

"He drew it that way," said the master mason. "On a paper he brought with him." He spat on his hands and picked up his mallet. "A good paper. You can see every stone on it before it's cut. We could build him the other way round, if the council asked it."

The council did not ask it.

On 10 an Cèitean, AE 9, Pell went up the hill from the post and slept for the first time in the stone house on the rise, and called it by the name it had in his tongue, which the island came to call Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, the house of the high steward. A flag went up on a pole before its door. From that day the humans on Dia-thìr answered to that house.

Edmund Harrow was needed ashore no longer, and he went back to the sea.

He came up the lake road to Cathair dhearg to say so, with Pike beside him. Tormod gave them bread and cheese in the room behind the hall, and Harrow ate like a man who would be at sea again tomorrow. He said that Pell would govern now and that it was right he should; that a ship's master had no more business in a council hall than a council in a ship; that he had been ashore on this island eight years, longer than he had been ashore anywhere since he was twelve, and that it was time.

"And the post?" Tormod asked.

Harrow wiped his mouth. He and Pike, he said, were to have a licence from Riaghaltas nan Coigreach to trade: a trading house, the two of them and some men of an Tìr Thall who had put money into it. Pike would keep the books ashore, and Harrow would keep the ships at sea, and between them they would carry what the island had to sell to the people who wished to buy it. He said it cheerfully. Pike, putting it into Dia-thìris, said it more slowly.

"It's a charter," Harrow said. "Pell seals it. You'll have a copy. You'll find it's all in order."

He shook Tormod's hand at the door, and went down the stairs whistling, as he always did. He sailed on the next tide but one from Ros dhomhain, north-about, the way the ships went. Tormod did not see him again.

## VI. Of the Charter Read in Private

Harrow and Pike founded their trading house on 18 an Cèitean, AE 9, under licence of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach and Pell's seal. It had a long name in the strangers' tongue, and the island never learned it. From the first the island called it A' Chompanaidh, since that was the word Pike used for it at his counter, and nobody asked what it was a company of.

A copy of its charter came to the council, as Harrow had said it would. It came in the strangers' tongue, on four sheets, with a red seal at the foot of the last, and the clerk entered its coming in the roll and laid it in the chest under the east window, beside the letter from Baile dhìreach. There it lay a month.

Gormshuil took it out. She had been a year at the terms by then, and read the strangers' tongue far better, though still with her finger. She took the charter home one evening at the end of the moon of Ògach and read it twice through by her lamp, and wrote something on a slip. Then she put on her cloak and walked across the town in the long summer dusk to Tormod's house, below the temple, and knocked.

He was at his supper. He had a fire lit, though it was midsummer, because of his knees; and he sent the girl who kept his house to bed and poured Gormshuil a cup of ale and sat across the hearth from her, and she read him the charter.

She read it slowly, the strangers' sentence first and then her own, and where she had no word of the island's for a word of theirs she said so. It was long. It named Harrow and Pike and the men of an Tìr Thall, and the licence, and the seal; it spoke of ships and of goods and of the post at Ros dhomhain; it spoke of tools and stores. Tormod listened with his cup in his hand. It was all in order, as Harrow had said.

Then she came to the clause, and stopped.

"There is a word here," she said. "I know it. I have known it since the season of words."

It was the word Wren had written in the window-light on the morning she tipped the basket of broken coal out on the table and named its colours: the one word, the word for the black fuel of the strangers' own hearths, with which he had tapped the whole heap to show that it stood for all of it. In the charter it had grown. It stood in a list, and the list was a long one. She read it to him in the strangers' tongue first, and then she put it into Dia-thìris as close as the island's tongue would go, word by word.

*All fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield.*

Tormod did not say anything.

"The charter gives them the first refusal of it," Gormshuil said. "All of it. Whatever the island yields that burns, and whatever is dug. Before any other trader of their people. It is sealed by Pell under the licence." She laid a second paper on her knee: her own copy of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, worn soft at the corners by a year of her finger. "And the licence hangs from here."

She found the line on the fourth sheet and read it to him. That the humans might trade in such goods as the island afforded, and in the working of them, under licence of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, and that the council would not hinder such trade.

He had heard it twice. He had asked for it twice.

"I thought it meant wool," Tormod said.

"Yes."

"I thought of the salt at Seann Warr. The hides. The dyes." He set his cup down on the hearthstone as though it might break. "There's Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig. No household burns more than its handful. It has been so since An Aois Naomh."

"That measures hearths," said Gormshuil, "and has nothing to say about a ship's hold. The men who made it never saw a ship go out that was not coming back." She folded the charter along its creases. "They did not ask for our word for the coal, Tormod. They never asked. Now they have written theirs down, and put a seal on it, and you have signed the paper it hangs from."

The fire had burned down. Neither of them made it up. Outside the town had gone to bed; a dog barked down by the bridge, and stopped, and the bells of the capital rang for the middle of the night, the bronze of the old hoes speaking over the dark roofs.

After a while Tormod asked her whether it could be undone.

She did not know. In the strangers' law, as far as she had been able to learn it from Wren, a thing signed by both sides stood until both sides unsigned it; and that Pell had no reason to unsign anything; and that no ship had yet come asking for coal, and none might. The charter was a list of what the strangers might want, she said, and a list was not a pit.

"Then there is time," Tormod said.

"There may be."

"Keep it between us," he said, "until I have thought."

She looked at him a long time across the dead fire, and then she said that she would; and she did. She gave him the slip she had written on, which had the clause on it in both tongues, and walked home through the dark. Tormod sat up with the slip in his hand until the window greyed. He did not bring the charter before the council that year, nor the next. There was no ship in the harbour asking for coal. There was only the list.

## VII. Of the Door at Cathair dhomhain

The first building of A' Chompanaidh was a warehouse, and it went up that summer and autumn at Cathair dhomhain, along the lake shore from the capital, where the fishing town runs down to the water between its two stony points.

Pike chose the ground. He said, when anyone asked, that it was to keep its tools and stores out of the reach of the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain, who had had two of his axes and a coil of good rope in a single winter. The ground was a strip of shingle and rough grass above the high-water line, with a spring behind it, and it belonged to a family of Cathair dhomhain that had drawn its nets there since An Aois Naomh. They sold it to Pike for a keg of nails, two lamps and a sheet of window-glass. The custodian of the lake shore entered the sale in his roll. It was the first ground on Dia-thìr that the strangers held by sale and not by the council's leave.

The masons who had built the house on the rise built the warehouse too, of the same grey stone, long and low with no window on the landward side and two high narrow windows on the lake, like a byre; and Pike roofed it with slate.

Tormod walked out to see it on 28 an Dàmhair, AE 9.

It was the stags' moon, Damhrach, and the first cold day of the autumn. He went alone and on foot, since it was only five miles by the lake road. The road ran along the shore with the lake on his left hand, grey and still, and the geese coming down on it out of the north in long wavering lines, calling. At Cathair dhomhain the warehouse stood finished on its strip of shingle, all but its door. The doorway stood open, a square of dark smelling of new lime. There were men of the strangers inside, stacking tools: picks and bars and shovels, and heavy hammers with long hafts, and coils of rope and chain, all new, with the grease still on them. Tormod stood in the doorway and looked at the picks a long while. They were not the tools of a fisherman or a dyer or a man who cures hides.

Pike came out to him, with his tally-book under his arm and his pen behind his ear, and greeted him in the island's tongue, which he spoke well by then. He showed him the warehouse end to end, and the tally of every tool in his book, balanced to the last line.

"For the post?" Tormod asked, and put his hand on a pick.

"For whatever's wanted," said Pike. "We keep them against the day."

The door came down the shore road that afternoon on a cart from Cathair dhearg. It was a heavy door of oak planks, a hand's breadth thick, pegged and studded with iron, and it took six men to lift it down. Its hinges had been forged in the smiths' lane below the bridge. Tormod knew them when he saw them: long iron straps drawn out and folded round a pin, with the ends split and curled back like fern, which was the mark Gilleasbuig Gobha put on everything he made. The strangers had paid for them in bar-iron. Pike had asked for Gilleasbuig by name.

They hung the door as the light was going. The six men lifted it and walked it to the doorway, and held it upright with their shoulders against it while a seventh stood on a cask and guided the straps down over the pins; and it dropped onto them with a clank that went out over the lake. Pike swung it. It turned without a sound, and closed, and he took a long iron key from his coat and locked it; then he unlocked it again, to see that it worked, and locked it again, and put the key away.

"There," he said, in the island's tongue, pleased as a boy. "That's ours."

Tormod walked home along the lake road in the dusk. The geese had settled on the water for the night and were talking among themselves out in the dark, and away along the shore the lamps of Ros dhomhain were coming out one by one, and above them, on the rise, the windows of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, five across, all lit. Behind him at Cathair dhomhain there was no light at all. The warehouse had no window on the landward side. There was only the door, and the key in Pike's coat, and whatever was kept behind them against the day.

The custodian of the lake shore wrote in his roll that night that a door had been hung on the strangers' building by the water, and that it was a good door, of oak, with a smith of the capital's hinges on it. The copyists of the cellar found that line when the rolls came down to them, and kept it, and asked the reader to remember that door.

# Chapter Seven: Of the Fever and the Sacks of Coal

*AE 9 – 11*

## I. Of the Carriers at Cuan shean

Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill was nineteen that autumn, a hewer's son of Muileann chrom, and he had never seen the sea.

His father sent him west with the carriers late in an Dàmhair, in the ninth year of the strangers. It was the custom of the hill households that the coal for the far hearths went down from the store at Taigh na Fèithe before the dark of the year, on the backs of ponies and young men, so much for each hearth and no more, as the law of the handful had it; and a lad who had carried it once to the coast was held to have seen the island. Raghnall had asked for three years to go. When his turn came he went with a pony called Donnag, eleven carriers, and an old custodian's clerk who could not walk fast and rode the whole way on a cart of meal, complaining.

They were five days on the road. Past the capital the country flattened and the wind got up, and it came off the west smelling of wet sand and rot, a smell he did not know, and Donnag put her ears back at it. On the fifth evening they came over the last rise and he saw the water. It lay grey to the edge of sight, heaving slowly, and a long way out on it the light ran in a white bar where the sun was going down. He stood with the pony's rope in his hand until the clerk shouted at him.

Cuan shean was bigger than any town of the hills and smelled of fish and tar. Its houses stood with their backs to the weather along a bent harbour, and in the harbour, among the Dia-thìreach boats, lay two of the strangers' ships, so high out of the water that the carriers stopped in the street to look at them. The humans had been coming to that harbour nine years by then, and the town had the habit of them.

The custodian of Cuan shean was Oighrig nic Leòid, who had given the first of the strangers water on that shingle and had been abed the winter the council gave them leave. She was old now and walked with a stick, and she came down to the custodians' store herself to see the coal counted in. She had each carrier open his baskets on the floor, and she went along the rows with a lamp, stooping, and turned the coal over with the end of the stick. Raghnall stood by his baskets with his heart knocking. She stopped at them and held the lamp low.

"Whose cutting?"

"My father's, lady. Dòmhnall's, of the old cutting above the mill."

"It is good coal," she said. "See the green in it." And she moved the lamp so that the green came up out of the black like weed under water, and Raghnall, who had broken that coal himself in the hill, felt his face go hot.

On the third day the carriers were to start home. That morning a ship came in from the north, a big hull low in the water and so crowded at the rails that from the quay she seemed to have a hedge along her sides. She had come the long way about, past the north cape and down the western coast, and she had been six weeks at sea. The humans on the quay went out to her in boats. Those who came ashore were thin and grey in the face, and some of them had to be lifted over the side. There were women among them, which Raghnall had not seen before, and children, and a man with a fiddle in a bag, who stood on the stones and wept.

Oighrig's people gave them water, as Cuan shean always did. The ship's master asked for more than water, and got it, and the town took some of the sick into the sail-lofts, where the humans said their prayers.

Within four days the first Dia-thìreach was sick. It was a woman of the net-sheds, who had carried water to the lofts. She burned, and shook, and talked all night in a voice that was not hers, and on the second day a rash came out on her chest like the marks of wet sand, and on the fourth day she died. By then there were eleven more. The custodians' roll gives the day the fever came ashore as 5 an t-Samhain, AE 9, and names it Fiabhras nan Coigreach, and that is the name it kept.

The carriers did not go home. The clerk would not have them walk the roads with the fever in the town, lest they carry it into the hills, and Oighrig said the same. So Raghnall stayed in Cuan shean through an t-Samhain and saw the whole of it.

He carried water, because the custodians asked for strong backs and he had one. He carried the dead out of the net-sheds on hurdles, two to a hurdle, with cloths over their mouths that did no good. In a week he knew the smell of the fever houses and the sound a house makes when no one inside it is well enough to answer the door. The humans died of it too, but fewer of them, and slower, and some of those who took it at sea got up again. The Dia-thìrich who took it seldom got up. The old men of the harbour sat on the upturned boats and said that the strangers had brought it in their clothes, in their blood, in their bread; and a younger man said that it made no odds where they had brought it, since here it was.

On the ninth day Oighrig nic Leòid called the custodians of the town to the store and shut Cuan shean to ships. No hull was to come in and none to go out until the fever was gone, and the boats of the town were to fish within the harbour mouth or not at all. She had them bring her chair down to the quay so that the masters of the two human ships could hear it from her. One of them laughed. The other went white and asked how his cargo was to reach the capital, and she said by the road, like anyone's.

Eight days after that a rider came in from Ros dhomhain with a letter. It was from Josiah Pell, An t-Àrd-mhaor, and it was written in the humans' tongue, on three sheets, and sealed. There was no one in Cuan shean who could read it but the humans, and so Oighrig sent for the trader who kept the humans' store by the quay and had him read it to her in the store-room, standing, with the carriers and the town's custodians round the walls.

Raghnall understood none of the words. He understood the voice. It went on a long time, level and hard, and now and then the trader stopped to put a sentence into Dia-thìris for her: that the harbour of Cuan shean was open to the ships of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach under Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg; that the custodians had no power to close it; that Pell protested in writing, and would protest again, and would hold the town answerable for the goods spoiled in the holds.

Oighrig heard it out. Then she asked the trader whether the letter said anything about the dead.

He looked through the sheets. "No, lady."

"Then write him that there are forty-one of them in this town," she said, "and that the ships may wait."

The roll of Cuan shean enters the protest, and beside it the number, which was forty-one that day and went on rising.

## II. Of the Dunes and the Road Home

They buried the fever dead of Cuan shean beyond the dunes, in the sand, where the town had never buried before. The custodians would not have the fever lie in the old ground by the harbour, among the town's grandmothers; and so the hurdles went out along the shore path past the last net-shed and up over the marram and down again on the far side, out of sight of the houses, where the wind comes straight off the open sea. Raghnall carried on that path more times than he let himself count.

It rained most days. The sand took the rain and did not hold it, and the graves were easy to dig and hard to keep, for the sides slid in. The human dead went into the same ground, a little apart, in a row of their own, because their priest asked it. He read over them from his book in the rain, and the Dia-thìreach carriers stood back with their hands under their arms and waited for him to finish so that they could fill in.

Once, on the path, the man at the other end of Raghnall's hurdle stopped and said, "Look at them," and Raghnall looked back at the town and saw the two tall ships riding in the harbour with their sails furled, and a boat going out to them with fresh water, and a man in the stern of it singing.

"They are well," the carrier said. "Most of them are well."

By the dark of the year the burying slackened, and a little before Là Fhèill Brìde it stopped. The custodians opened the harbour at the season's end. The roll of the west gives the whole count down the coast as ninety-one Dia-thìrich dead and eleven humans, and the numbers stand in the copy at Muileann chaol exactly as the custodians wrote them.

Raghnall walked home with the carriers when the roads were opened. They did not talk much. At the capital the clerk left them to report to the council, and they went on east without him, up the long road into the hills, and the country rose round them and the wind lost its salt. On the fifth evening he saw the mill at Muileann chrom with its wheel turning in the bend of the river, and the smoke going up flat from the roofs, and he sat down on a stone at the roadside for a while before he went down.

His father met him at the door and looked at him a long time and said, "You are thinner."

"I carried," Raghnall said.

His father said nothing to that. Dòmhnall was a hewer of the old cutting, as his father had been, a short man with shoulders like a yoke and black in the seams of his hands that no washing took out. He had cut the measured coal of the hill for thirty years, so many baskets in the season and not one over, and he had never been further west than the capital. Raghnall told him about the ships, and the sea, and the sand, and Oighrig's lamp, and the letter; and his father listened, and at the end he asked only whether Oighrig had liked the coal.

"She said to look at the green in it."

"So she should," said Dòmhnall.

## III. Of the Word from the West

News came up the road that year in the carters' mouths, and none of it good.

On 9 an Gearran, AE 10, the fever reached Baile àrsaidh, a short way up the coast from Cuan shean, where the druids of Manannan kept their school. It killed the custodian of the town and both her sons, and a number of households besides, and the school shut its doors and kept them shut until the summer. The thing the custodians of the west wrote down, and the thing the carters told in the hills, was this: that no human lived in Baile àrsaidh at all. No strangers' ship had put in there. The fever had walked up the coast by itself, on Dia-thìreach feet, from house to house.

The custodians of the hills met at Taigh na Fèithe above Muileann dhearg in the spring to speak of it. Raghnall's father went, as a hewer of the old cutting had the right to do, and came back late and sat by the fire with his boots on.

"They talked of shutting the roads," he said.

"Will they?"

"No." He pulled at a boot. "The road is the meal and the salt. It is the lamp-oil from Ros dhomhain, which half the hill has got the use of now. They said a hill that shuts its road starves slower than it sickens, but it starves." He got the boot off and looked at it. "Old Seonag Liath, who keeps our cutting, said we had eaten salt with the strangers nine years and it was a little late to be afraid of their bread. They wrote that down."

So the hills did not shut their roads, and the roll of Taigh na Fèithe gives the reason in Seonag Liath's words. The fever did not come to Muileann chrom that year. Whether that was luck, or the hills' distance from the sea, or the grace of the hill, nobody in the district could agree, and they argued it at the mill all summer.

In the south-west, at Cnoc àrsaidh, where Imrich nam Pantar passes and Òrd na Cloiche keeps its oldest shrines, the townsfolk did what the hills had talked of. When the fever came down the coast towards them, on 14 an t-Samhain, AE 10, they dragged their carts across the road on either side of the town, wheel to wheel, and set men with staves behind them, and turned back every traveller for a season: carters, drovers, custodians, and the humans' traders with their packs. The fever went round them and did not come in. The carters told next, with relish, that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had fined Cnoc àrsaidh for hindering trade, and that the town had paid it in wool, sacks of it, and the humans had not known what to do with so much wool.

Dòmhnall laughed at that, which he seldom did. Raghnall remembered the dunes, and did not.

## IV. Of the Two Prospectors

Near the end of an t-Samhain in the tenth year, when the hills were brown and the rain came across them in sheets, two humans came up the road to Muileann chrom with a letter.

They came on foot, with a pony carrying their packs, and they stopped at the mill because it was the largest house in sight. One was a broad man of five-and-thirty, bald, with a red face and a red beard and a voice that could be heard across the river; his name was Abel Stone. The other was younger and taller and stooped, with spectacles that he took off every few minutes to wipe, and a book in a waxed cover that he never let go of; his name was Hugh Mercer. The letter was from A' Chompanaidh, the trading house that Harrow and Pike had founded under licence of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, and it asked in both tongues, badly in one of them, that the bearers be given lodging and a guide into the hills, for which a fair price would be paid.

The miller read the Dia-thìris half aloud to the room and gave it back.

Nobody would go. The men of the hill were courteous to the strangers and gave them the miller's back room and a fire and a supper of mutton, and the miller's wife lent Mercer a dry shirt. But when Stone spread his hands and said "Coal?" and pointed up at the hills, and made a hammering motion with his fist, the men at the fire looked at one another and looked away. The hill was the custodians'. What a man broke out of it he broke by their leave, in its season, in the measure. No one in Muileann chrom had ever led a stranger up it with a hammer, and no one wanted to be the first.

Raghnall was at the fire that night. He had been thinking since the spring, when he thought at all, about the ships riding well in the harbour at Cuan shean and the man singing in the stern of the boat. What he thought of it he could not have said; but he was tired of the mill and the cutting and the same eleven faces, and he had seen the sea.

Stone had taken a coin out of his purse and laid it on the table, a disc of silver with a man's head on one side, stamped, and letters round the edge. The firelight ran on it. He tapped it and said a word in his own tongue and looked round.

"I will go," said Raghnall.

His father was not there. He heard of it the next morning from the miller, and he came to the mill yard where Raghnall was loading the pony and stood and watched without a word. When the loading was done he said, "You will not go into the cutting."

"No."

"Nor into any gallery the custodians keep."

"No. Only the hill."

"The hill is the custodians'," said Dòmhnall. Then he turned round and went home, and Raghnall watched his back until the corner of the byre took it.

They were eleven days on the hill. Stone and Mercer knew what they were looking for and had only a little of the tongue to ask for it, and Raghnall had none of theirs, and between them they made a talk of hands and a few words that got better as the days went on. Stone wanted water: streams, gullies, the places where rain had cut down into the hillside and bared the rock. Raghnall took them up the burns north of the mill, into the high ground towards Doire mhòr and east along the flank of the hills above the river, where the heather gave way in the stream-cuts to banks of shale and clay, and where every child of the hill knew that the black showed through.

It showed. In the second gully Stone went down on his knees in the wet and scraped at the bank with his hammer and a shout went out of him that sent a hare bolting. There was the seam, a hand's breadth of it and then an arm's length, running into the hill under the turf like a black river under a bank. Stone broke off a piece and turned it in his fingers and rubbed it with his thumb, and smelled it, and put his tongue to it, and gave it to Mercer, who wrote in his book.

Raghnall stood above them on the bank with the rain running off his hood. He looked at the broken piece in Mercer's hand. It was fresh coal of the upper seam, the sort that comes near the surface, and in the grey light it showed its brown at the edges, deep brown going into red where it had split, and under that the green, and along one face a sheen like the inside of a mussel shell. Any child of the hill could have named them. He had the words in his mouth.

"Gual donn-ruadh," he said, and pointed at the edge where the red ran into the brown. "An sin. Agus an sin, gual airgid."

Mercer looked up at him, pleasantly, and wiped his spectacles, and looked at the piece of coal, and looked at Raghnall again, waiting. Raghnall touched the sheen with his finger. Mercer nodded, the way a man nods at a child who has shown him a pebble, and said something to Stone, and Stone laughed, not unkindly, and said a word that Raghnall had heard in Cuan shean. He heard it a great many times on that hill. It was the only word either of them had for what they were breaking, and it stood for all of it alike.

They broke a great deal. They broke it at every gully where the seam showed, and they put it in sacks, coarse sacks of the humans' weaving with letters on them, a sack for each gully, and Mercer wrote the place in his book and a number, and Raghnall learned after a while that the number was the paces from the last. On the fifth day Stone took to walking the seam. He went along the hillside with his head down, from one stream-cut to the next, counting under his breath, and where it showed he broke it and went on, and where it did not show he dug until it did. Mercer came behind with the book. Raghnall came behind Mercer with the pony, and the sacks.

On the eighth day, far out along the hills to the north, where the high ground looks down on the valley of Abhainn uaine, Stone stopped on a knoll in the evening and looked back the way they had come, and then forward, and scratched his beard. He said a long thing to Mercer. Mercer wrote it down. Then Stone turned to Raghnall and said, slowly, in Dia-thìris that he had been practising, with his hand held out flat along the line of the hills:

"Black. Further than a man can walk in one day."

He seemed very pleased with it. He said it again in his own tongue, and Mercer wrote that too. Those are the words the letter-books of A' Chompanaidh keep, "further than can be walked in a day," and they are the only words of that walk the humans kept.

That night they camped under a peat-bank, and Stone and Mercer drank from a flask and talked late in their own tongue, fast and happy, and Raghnall lay in his cloak and listened to the rain and could not sleep. He was thinking of the old cutting above the mill, of the baskets his father filled in the season, eleven and not twelve; of the custodian with her lamp going along the rows; of the old words that are said at the rock face before a man puts his pick in, which every hewer's son learns before he learns to swing. He had not said them once on the hill. Nobody had asked him to.

They came down on 13 an Dùbhlachd, AE 10, with the pony so loaded that Raghnall carried a sack on his own back the last miles, and Stone and Mercer each carried one, and all three of them were black to the elbow. At the mill Stone paid him the coin. Raghnall took it and held it and looked at the man's head on it, and put it in his shirt.

The men of Muileann chrom stood at their doors to watch the sacks go by. Nobody said anything. The next morning the prospectors went down the road towards the capital and Ros dhomhain, with the pony and a hired cart, and the sacks in the cart.

## V. Of the Half Carried West

The custodians of the vein wrote to A' Chompanaidh before the year was out.

They wrote in Dia-thìris, for they had nothing else to write in, and the letter went down to Ros dhomhain with a carter who had orders to give it into the hand of Thomas Pike and nobody else's. It asked that the coal broken on the hill above Muileann chrom without leave be brought back, all of it, to be laid in the rock again with the proper words, as the custodians had always done with coal taken out of season. There was no threat in it. The custodians wrote as they had written to their own people for a thousand years, as if there could be no question of the answer.

The answer was a long time coming. Raghnall heard of the letter at the mill, and of the carter's going and coming, and of a second letter in the spring, and a third. Men looked at him in the mill yard and said nothing. His father spoke to him about the work of the day and about the weather, and not about the hill. Raghnall kept the coin in a crack of the byre wall and took it out sometimes and looked at it.

At the summer's end in the eleventh year a cart came up the road from the capital with a human driver and six sacks in it, coarse sacks with letters on them, and stopped at the mill. The driver gave the miller a paper. The miller could not read it and sent for Raghnall, as the one man in Muileann chrom known to have talked with the strangers, and Raghnall could not read it either. He counted the sacks. Stone had filled thirteen.

"Where are the others?" he said to the driver, in the few words of the humans' tongue he had got on the hill, and made the number with his fingers.

The driver shrugged and pointed down the road the way he had come, west, towards Ros dhomhain and the lake and the ships, and said a word Raghnall knew, and turned his cart round.

The custodians came to the old cutting three days later, on 17 an t-Sultain, AE 11. There were four of them from Taigh na Fèithe and Seonag Liath, and they had sent word through the hill, so that most of the households came up behind them, the hewers first. Raghnall's father was among the hewers. Raghnall was not asked to come and went anyway, and stood at the back, and when the custodians looked round for strong backs to carry the sacks up the last steep path to the rock face, it was Seonag Liath who looked at him and lifted her chin, and he went forward and took up the first sack.

He carried all six. Nobody helped him, and he did not ask. At the face, where the old cutting goes into the hill under an overhang of grey rock, black-mouthed and dry and smelling of the inside of the earth, the custodians had the sacks opened and the coal laid out on a cloth in the lamp-light, piece by piece; and they sorted it, as a custodian sorts, by colour and by the gully it had come from, as near as they could tell. Then the hewers took it up in their hands and carried it into the cutting and laid it back into the rock, into clefts and old workings, packing it with clay; and the custodians said the words over each handful, the old words that are said when a thing taken out of season is given back, the same words, over and over, until the words and the dark and the lamp and the slow hands made one thing.

Raghnall stood outside with the empty sacks. He could hear his father's voice in the cutting saying the words with the rest, low, and the tap of clay being pressed in.

When it was done the custodians' clerk sat down on a stone at the cutting mouth with the roll on his knees and asked how much had been taken from the hill and how much given back.

"Thirteen sacks," said Raghnall. "Six."

"And the rest?"

Raghnall thought of the driver and his pointing hand. "West," he said.

The clerk wrote it. The roll of Taigh na Fèithe enters the other half of the coal as "carried west," and it is still so entered in the copy that lies in Seilear Muileann chaol, the first coal of the vein in all the records that went out of the hill and was not accounted for. Seonag Liath, who read over the clerk's shoulder, put her finger on the line and looked at Raghnall a long while, and said nothing, and went down the hill.

## VI. Of the Contract and the First Ton

Two days after the laying-back, on 19 an t-Sultain, AE 11, A' Chompanaidh brought its first contracts into the hills.

Abel Stone brought them. He came up the road to Muileann chrom on a good horse this time, with a clerk behind him and two carts of goods: iron. There were picks with steel points, shovels, wedges, hammers, bar-iron in bundles tied with cord, and on the second cart casks of lamp-oil, more oil than the whole district burned in a year. He had the carts drawn up in the mill yard and the covers taken off, and he stood beside them with his thumbs in his belt while the hill came to look.

The contract was read in the mill in the humans' tongue by the clerk and in Dia-thìris by a young man of Ros dhomhain whom A' Chompanaidh paid to put its words into the island's. Raghnall stood at the wall. It was short, as such things went. A crew of the hill was to cut coal from the seam at a place A' Chompanaidh would name, on the hillside below the old cutting and well away from it; and for every ton the crew brought to the pit-mouth, weighed on the strangers' beam, the crew would be paid in iron tools and lamp-oil, at so much the ton, the rate written in figures on the paper. The ton was a thing of the humans' reckoning. The young man of Ros dhomhain tried three ways to say it in Dia-thìris and settled for "a great load, weighed".

Some of the older men walked out before the reading was done. Some stayed. The hill had lamp-oil to think of, and iron, and the good years of trading behind it, in which nobody had yet been cheated at the humans' counter. A bargain was a bargain. And A' Chompanaidh was careful that year: the place it named was on no custodian's lot, and the paper said nothing about the old cutting at all.

When the reading was done Stone looked round the room and found Raghnall at the wall, and grinned at him, and pointed.

"This one," he said, in his practised Dia-thìris. "He walked the hill. He knows the black. Let him lead the crew."

So Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill was made the leader of the first crew of the hill. It was thirty men, the number the contract asked for: young men mostly, sons of hewers and sons of shepherds and two from the mill, and three older hewers of the old cutting who had sons to feed and said so. His father was not among them. Dòmhnall heard the reading from outside the mill door and went home before it was over, and when Raghnall came in that night with the paper folded in his shirt beside the coin, his father was sitting at the fire with his hands on his knees and did not look up.

"They will pay us in iron," said Raghnall. "Picks with steel points. You have seen them. And oil, enough to light every house on the hill through the winter."

"I have seen them," said his father.

"The place is on no lot. It is below the old cutting. They have not asked for the cutting."

"No," said Dòmhnall. "Not this year." And then, after a while, to the fire: "Who will say the words at the face?"

Raghnall found that he had no answer, and his father did not ask again.

They opened the working on 16 an Dàmhair, AE 11. It was on the south face of the hill, a mile below the old cutting, in a gully where Stone had broken the seam the winter before; and the crew cut back the turf and the shale above it with the new shovels from the carts and went in along the black with the new picks. The steel points went through the coal like a spade through turf. Men who had swung the old picks of the hill all their lives stopped and looked at the new ones in their hands and laughed out loud. By midday there was a heap at the pit-mouth taller than a man.

Stone had the beam set up that afternoon at the pit-mouth: a great iron bar hung from a tripod of timbers, with a hook at one end and a weight that slid along the other, and a board of marks. He showed Raghnall how it worked. The coal went into a sling of chain and hung from the hook, and the weight was run along the bar until the bar hung level, and the clerk read the mark and wrote the figure in a book. The crew stood round in the drizzle and watched. It was the first weighing of coal most of them had ever seen, and they did not know yet what they were watching.

At dusk the clerk added his figures and said something to Stone, and Stone turned round to the crew and held up one finger, and shouted.

"One ton!"

The crew cheered, because he was so pleased, and because they had cut it. Raghnall cheered with them. He stood at the pit-mouth with the black to his elbows and the new pick in his hand, in the rain, and watched the clerk write the figure down in the book of A' Chompanaidh, one ton, the first ton weighed in the hills of Muileann chrom, and he was proud of it. His crew was the best on the hill, the first and the best, and he had led them, and it was all written down.

He walked home in the dark. Up the hill above him the old cutting was black against the sky. There was no lamp in it. The season of the handful was over, and his father's eleven baskets had gone to the store a month since, measured, and the custodians would not light the cutting again until the spring.

## VII. Of What the Hill Had Never Been Weighed By

*Here the copyists who set down the age from its four witnesses leave Raghnall at his pit-mouth, and look back.*

In all the years of the vein before the strangers came, from the first keeping to the last, the coal of the hill had been measured and it had been counted; but it had never once been weighed. It was measured by the handful, a hewer's two hands cupped together, which is the measure of the law, and by the basket, which is so many handfuls, and by the season, which is so many baskets. It was counted by the hearth. The custodians knew how many hearths the island had, and how many handfuls each might burn, and they cut that much and no more, and what was cut out of season was given back. The roll of every cutting is kept that way. It speaks of hands and hearths and seasons, and of colours, which it names each time, and of the words said at the face; and in all its leaves there is no ton, and no beam, and no figure written by a clerk who was not a custodian.

After AE 11 a second book was kept beside it, at the pit-mouth of A' Chompanaidh below Muileann chrom. It opened with a single figure in the humans' letters, under a date in the humans' reckoning, and against the figure the name of a crew-leader written as the humans heard it. The custodians' book went on counting handfuls in their season; the other counted tons.

So ended Bliadhnachan na Malairt Cothromaich, that began with a cask of water on the shingle at Cuan shean. Nobody on the island marked the day. The crew at Muileann chrom were paid on the first market-day after in picks and lamp-oil, at the rate on the paper, to the last ounce of oil; and the book of A' Chompanaidh balanced to the line.

# Part Two: Of the Hill Sold by the Ton

# Chapter Eight: Of the Door at Doire mhòr


*AE 12 – 16*

## I. Of the Shortest Roll

Of all the rolls of the hill villages that came down to Seilear Muileann chaol, the roll of Doire mhòr for these years is the shortest, and the copyists have handled it more than any other. It is nine leaves stitched with linen thread, in a square black hand that presses so hard on the pen that the letters stand up from the back of the page like the marks of a nail. The hand is Beathag Dhubh's. She was custodian of Doire mhòr through the years of the first contracts, and she wrote the roll as she said everything, with as few words as would carry the thing and none to spare.

Beside it stands the second witness. In the letter-books of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, among the reports sent down from the hills to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in the fourteenth year of the strangers, there is a sheet in the humans' tongue from an agent of A' Chompanaidh, who climbed to Doire mhòr with a contract under his coat and came down again without it. It is the only place where her answer to him is set down. The telling that follows is made from the nine leaves and the one sheet, and from what the carters of the hill remembered.

Doire mhòr stood on the shoulder of the hills north of Muileann chrom, a morning's walk above the mill and the bend of the river. Its name was the great oak grove, and in those years the grove still stood: old oaks on the slope behind the houses, broad and low and crooked from the wind, with a stream coming down between them out of the heather and running past the doors to the fields. There were seven households, stone-built and turf-roofed, with their byres at their backs. They grew oats and barley in small walled fields along the stream, and in the season of the handful their young men went down to carry at the old cutting above Muileann chrom. The custodian's house stood highest of the seven. Its door faced down the hill, and from the step on a clear day you could see the smoke of the mill, and past it the green line of the Abhainn uaine going away between the hills towards the sea.

Beathag was some thirty-two years old in the year the quay was built below her. She had black hair, which gave her the byname, and black brows that met, and a way of standing with her arms folded while other people talked that made the talkers talk faster. She had been custodian since her mother's death, and she kept the roll and the count of the village's hearths, and went to the council at Cathair dhearg when it called the custodians of the hills. Children she had none, and said when asked that she had seven households, which was enough.

## II. Of Nails by Weight

In the summer of the twelfth year she walked down to Ceann fhada to buy salmon, and found A' Chompanaidh building on the shore.

Ceann fhada was a hamlet of river-fishers and pilots on a long spit where the Abhainn uaine ran slow and deep below the hills, a short hour's walk under Doire mhòr. The foreshore of the spit, where they drew up their boats and dried their nets and split their fish, was held by the hamlet in common, as a thing no one household could buy or be sold. Beathag came out of the trees on a hot morning and saw the spit covered with men.

There were masons from over the lake at the capital, and human overseers in shirt-sleeves, and carts of cut stone drawn up on the turf where the nets had hung. A wall was going out into the river on a bed of rubble, square-ended, straight as a rule. At its root, where the fish-shed had stood, a clerk sat at a table under a sailcloth awning with a book open before him and a steelyard hung from a tripod at his elbow, and before the table the men of Ceann fhada were standing in a line.

She stood at the back of the line and watched it for most of the morning. Each man came to the table in his turn, and a human with a measuring-chain paced out on the turf the strip of foreshore where that man's boat had always lain, and called the figure to the clerk. The clerk wrote it. Then a boy tipped nails out of a keg into the scoop of the steelyard, and the clerk ran the pea along the arm until it hung level, and the nails were poured into the man's cap or his shirt or his two hands, and he stepped aside. So many pounds of nails for so many paces of shore; and the next man came up.

An old pilot near the front had his nails poured into his hat and stood looking at them.

"What does a man do with these," he said, "who has no house to build?"

Nobody answered him. The old man carried his hat down to the water's edge and sat on a stone with it on his knees. Beathag went and sat beside him.

"They are good nails," he said after a time. "I bit one." He turned one over in his fingers. "My father's boat lay on that shore. And his father's. Now there is a wall on it, and I am paid for it by the pound." He looked at her sidelong. "You are Beathag of the oaks. Tell me, custodian, whose shore was it, that they could buy it off me?"

"It was the hamlet's," said Beathag.

"Then why did they pay me?"

"Because you were standing in the line," she said, "and the hamlet was not."

That evening the men of Ceann fhada took their nails to the fish-shed that had been moved up the bank, and weighed them again, each man's share, on their own old beam that they weighed salmon on, to see whether the strangers had cheated them. The strangers had not. Every man had his weight to the ounce. The copyists found it in the roll of Ceann fhada, in a pilot's hand: that the weight was true, and that the men were ashamed of having doubted it, and ashamed besides, though of what the roll does not say.

The quay was finished on 23 an t-Iuchar, AE 12. Beathag was not there. But in the autumn she went down to the edge of the oaks on her own hill and watched the first carts of coal from the new pit at Muileann chrom come jolting along the river track and down onto the spit, and tip their loads into the first flat barge moored against the new wall. The barge went away downstream with two pilots of Ceann fhada at the sweeps, since nobody else knew the river.

The coal in the carts was all colours. She could see it from where she stood, even at that distance, the way anyone of the island could see it: the black that is green at the edge, and the black that holds a blue in it like the back of a mussel, and the rust and the plum and the grey that go purple in rain. The two carters walking at the horses' heads were humans, and they looked at the road.

## III. Of Three Words in a Grammar

Samuel Wren finished his grammar of the island's tongue at Ros dhomhain in AE 12, in the last weeks of summer, and sent a fair copy to the council at Cathair dhearg with his compliments. He had been at it ten years, since the season of words at the capital. The council gave it to Gormshuil nic Fhearchair to read, because she had learned the humans' letters for that purpose, and she took it home and read it through, and at Samhain, when the custodians of the hills came down to the council for the winter sitting, she brought it into the hall under her arm.

Beathag had not met her before. She found a woman past fifty with a long grey face and ink on her thumb, who sat by the fire in the side room with the book on her knee and a candle at her shoulder, reading out whatever anyone asked for, and putting it into Dia-thìris as she went.

"It is a good book," Gormshuil said. "He has the verbs right. He has most of the words for the weather. He has all the words for the sea, because he came over it and was frightened of it." She turned a leaf. "He has one word for the coal, which is his own, and he has put it where ours should be. And he has this." She put her finger on a line. "This is what he calls us. You and me and every custodian of every cutting on the island."

"Read it," said Beathag.

Gormshuil read it out in the humans' tongue, slowly, three words, and then put it into Dia-thìris. It came out as *the keepers of the coal*.

"That is near enough," said a custodian from the east, and one or two others nodded.

"It is near," said Gormshuil. "Ask what a keeper is, in his tongue." She shut the book on her finger. "I asked him. I sat in his room at the mission-house with this on the table and asked him, what is a keeper, and he told me, a man who keeps a thing. So I asked him what kinds of keepers there are over the sea. A keeper of sheep. A keeper of a gate. A keeper of a shop, which is a man who has goods on his shelves until somebody pays him for them. An innkeeper. A storekeeper. He was pleased to be asked. He gave me eleven." She looked round at them. "In his tongue a keeper of the coal is a man who has the coal."

Nobody spoke. The fire settled.

"Then when they read this over the sea," said Beathag, "they will think the coal is ours to sell."

"Or they will think we are standing in the way of it," said Gormshuil, "which is what a storekeeper does, until he is paid."

Beathag went home to the hills in the snow before the sitting was over, and the copyists find the thing in her roll that winter in two lines. The first says that the strangers' book of words calls the custodians keepers. The second says: *We do not keep it. We keep it back.*

The grammar went out over the sea on the next ship, and copies of it were made at the mission-house for the strangers' own use on the island. In the summer of the thirteenth year, on 4 an t-Iuchar, AE 13, a hawk-priest came down to Ros dhomhain from Cnoc bheag, a thin man in a brown cloak with a feather in his hair, and asked at the door of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise for a copy for the priests of his shrine, so that they might read what the strangers wrote of them. The mission-house gave him one, and was pleased to. He carried it home a day's walk on his back in a satchel of oiled hide.

That copy came down to the cellar among the hawk-priests' papers, and it has more notes in its margins than any other copy the copyists have seen. Where Wren writes of the gods the hawk-priests have written corrections, and where he writes of the hawk they have written a good deal. And beside the three words on the custodians, in a small hand of the old kind with a hawk's head drawn after it for a signature, somebody has written in Dia-thìris: *He writes as a man counts sacks.*

## IV. Of the Bell before the Fleet

The council called the custodians of the hills again at the dark of the thirteenth year, for the contracts were beginning to come up from Muileann chrom into the villages round about, and the council wished to know what the hills made of them. Beathag walked down to Cathair dhearg in the frost, two days on the road with a pony and a bag of oatcake, and sat through four days of talk in the hall. The council heard that iron was good and lamp-oil was good and the young men liked the look of the picks, and made no ruling; and on the last evening of the sitting word came up from the lake shore that the strangers' chapel at Ros dhomhain was finished, and that they would hang their bell in it and ring it in the morning for the first time.

Some of the custodians went down to see it, Beathag among them. Ros dhomhain was two hours' walk below the capital along the shore of the lake, and they went in the dark before dawn, because the strangers' service was to be at first light, and stood with the fishers on the cold stones of the quay on 30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 13.

The chapel was of timber, on the quay itself, with its back to the water: a long plain hall of new planks, tarred black, with windows of the strangers' glass down each side and a little open tower at the landward end. In the tower, hung on an oak beam, was the bell. It hung against the grey of the sky like an upturned cauldron. It was the first bell of iron that had ever hung on the island.

The fleet of Ros dhomhain was going out. The lake-fishers were loading their boats along the quay in the way they had always loaded them, with lanterns shuttered and no word spoken. The rule of that quay was an old one. What is said on the stones before the boats are out is heard on the water, and the water keeps it; so the men went down to their boats without a word and cast off without a word, and a boy who laughed aloud on the quay in the dark was sent home. Beathag stood among the silent men and was careful not to cough.

Then the strangers rang their bell.

It was a great noise. It went out over the black lake and came back off the far shore, and rolled back again, and went on ringing, twenty strokes, thirty; and every man on the quay stopped where he was, with a net or an oar or a basket of line in his hands, and stood with his head down as though he had been struck. One boat had cast off already. Its men lay on their oars in the dark water and did not row. Then an old man on the quay put down the net he was holding and walked home, and then another, and one by one the crews unloaded their boats again, not hurrying, still without a word, and went up the quay and away into the town. Only three boats went out on the lake that morning out of more than twenty. The bell rang on over the empty quay until the service began.

The custodians went up to the chapel door when the strangers came out of it. The minister was a young man with a cold, and Samuel Wren was with him, thin and grey and coughing into a cloth. Wren put the custodians' words into the strangers' tongue.

The custodian of Ros dhomhain did the speaking. He told them the rule of the quay, and that on that quay a bell over the water before the boats were out was the bell for the drowned, and that the men had gone home because they would not go out on a lake that had been told to expect them. He asked that the bell should not be rung again before the fleet was out.

The young minister listened to Wren with his head on one side, and looked at the empty quay, and was troubled; and it is to his credit, and Wren's, that he agreed at once. After that morning the bell of the chapel was rung at Ros dhomhain only when the last boat was clear of the harbour mouth, and the chapel held its first service late.

Beathag walked back up to the capital with the others. The sun was up by then, and the three boats that had gone out were small on the lake behind them.

"He was a decent young man," said one of the custodians. "He did what we asked."

"He did," said Beathag. "And the morning is gone all the same."

## V. Of the Paper at the Hearth

The contract came up to Doire mhòr at the end of the winter of the fourteenth year. A boy of Muileann chrom carried it up in oilcloth inside his shirt, and gave it to Beathag at her door. It was written in the humans' tongue, two pages of it, close, with a space at the foot for marks. Beathag could not read a word of it. The next morning she walked down to the mill at Muileann chrom with the paper and found the young man of Ros dhomhain who put A' Chompanaidh's words into the island's tongue, and made him read it to her twice in the mill-house, sitting on a sack.

It was the same paper the hill had heard read at the mill in the autumn of the eleventh year, save in the one thing that mattered to her. The place it named for the working was the south slope of Doire mhòr's own hill, under the oaks, where the stream came down.

"They have found the black there," the young man said. "The prospectors found it in the stream-bank four winters back. There is more of it under your fields, they say, than under all the rest of the hill together."

"I know where the black is," said Beathag. "My grandmother knew."

She took the paper home and put it on the shelf by the door, and did not put a mark on it, and did not send it back. On 29 am Màrt, AE 14, the day A' Chompanaidh had set for the marks, the boy came up the hill again for the answer, and she gave him none and sent him away with an oatcake. That was the first refusal of the age. Other villages of the hills had put their marks to the contracts, and one or two had haggled first; but none had let the day go by with the space at the foot of the paper empty. The clerks at the pit-mouth entered it in their book as a delay.

That same evening she called the seven households to her hearth.

They came in out of the rain and sat round the fire on stools and on the floor, with the children at the back on the heaped fleeces. She had the paper read to them in her own words, since there was nobody on the hill who could read it in the strangers' own. Then she let them talk.

They talked a long while. Some of the young men wanted the iron: a spade that did not bend, an axe that held its edge through a winter's wood. One of them said that the pit at Muileann chrom paid better than oats. One of the women said that the strangers had been fair at every counter on the island for ten years, which was true. An old shepherd asked where they would put their sheep when the hillside was a heap of shale, and nobody knew. Another asked what A' Chompanaidh would do if they said no, and nobody knew that either.

Last of all the oldest woman of the hill spoke from her stool by the door. She was near ninety and had carried baskets at the old cutting since before any of them were born, and she did not say much. She said:

"Chan ann leinn an cnoc."

*The hill is not ours.*

Then she said that the custodian should answer for the hill, since that was what a custodian was for, and she went home through the rain, and after a while the others followed her. The roll for the night has a single line: that the households were called, and that they gave the answer to the custodian to give.

## VI. Of the Door

The agent of A' Chompanaidh climbed to Doire mhòr himself on 27 an Giblean, AE 14.

It rained. It had rained on that hill for eleven days, and the agent came up through it from the mill on foot, because no horse would take the last of the path. He was a man of forty or so, well-fed, in a good dark coat that was mud to the knee by the oaks, with the contract buttoned inside it and a hand held flat over the place as he walked. The young man of Ros dhomhain came behind him with a satchel and a face that said he would rather be somewhere else.

By the time they reached the stream the doors were full of faces, and nobody came out.

Beathag was at the top of the village, at her own door, with the door open behind her and the fire lit inside. She had been told they were coming. Ruairidh of Doire mhòr stood behind her in the doorway, and said nothing.

The agent stopped at the foot of her step and took off his hat, and the rain ran off his hair. He was civil. The copyists allow him that; everything in his report is civil. He had a good deal of the island's tongue for a stranger, got at the counters and the pit-mouths, and what he did not have the young man of Ros dhomhain gave for him. He told her who he was, and whom he spoke for. He told her of the contract and the rate and the iron: picks and spades and bar-iron, lamp-oil by the cask, more than the hill had ever had. The young men at Muileann chrom, he said, had new boots. There would be a road up the hill, so that no one of Doire mhòr would ever have to carry a load on their back again. He told her the seam under her fields was the best A' Chompanaidh had found, and that it was a sin to leave it where it did nobody any good. He said it all in order, and then he said some of it again.

It is the custom of the island, and was in those years a custom older than any law, that a stranger who comes to a door in rain is asked in to the fire. Oighrig nic Leòid, who had no liking for the strangers, gave their captain water on the shingle at Cuan shean because he had come with an empty cask; the humans had lived on that custom for thirteen years. Beathag Dhubh let the agent stand on her step in the rain until he had said all he had come to say, and she did not ask him in.

When he had done she answered him. She spoke a few words, and then she shut the door.

What she said at the door, in her own tongue, the roll of Doire mhòr does not set down. It lives only in the agent's report, which he wrote that night at the pit-office by the mill, by the light of A' Chompanaidh's lamp-oil, in the strangers' tongue, and sent down to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir with the week's figures. The copyists give his words as they stand in the letter-books:

> The woman who is custodian there heard me through at her door, in the rain, and did not ask me in. Her answer I set down as near as I have it: that the hill was not hers to sell, nor mine to buy. Then she shut the door. I judge that nothing is to be had of that place by persuasion at present, and recommend that the working be opened elsewhere.

He went back down the hill with the contract still dry inside his coat. The young man of Ros dhomhain went with him. At the stream, the carters used to say, he stopped and turned round and looked back up at the shut door for a long time, and then went on.

## VII. Of the Road round the Fields

Doire mhòr was not punished. The hill talked of it all that summer: that the custodian of the oaks had shut her door on A' Chompanaidh, and nothing had come of it, and the boy of Muileann chrom did not come up again with any papers. Beathag, when she was asked why, said she did not know.

In the fifteenth year, on 28 an Gearran, AE 15, A' Chompanaidh opened its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich, below Doire mhòr on the south, where a wild hill rose over the road to the river landing and nobody lived but a few households of hunters; and it began a cart-road to carry the coal of both its pits down to the quay at Ceann fhada.

The road came up from the south by the shortest way, and the shortest way lay over Doire mhòr's fields.

The surveyors came in am Màrt with a chain and a staff and a bundle of white-painted pegs, two humans and a boy, and walked straight up the hill from Cnoc fhiadhaich with the staff before them. They crossed the stream at the lower ford and went on across the barley ground, and every forty paces the boy knocked a peg into the earth. By evening there was a line of white pegs up the middle of the village's three best fields, from the stream to the edge of the oaks, and on over the shoulder of the hill towards the river.

Beathag walked the line of pegs the next morning with her arms folded. She did not pull them up. She sent to the custodian of Muileann chrom to say that the pegs were on the fields of Doire mhòr, which were not in any contract, and she waited.

Five days later the surveyors came back. They pulled up their white pegs one by one and put them back in the bundle, and they went down to the lower ford and started again; and this time the line went east along the foot of the fields, outside the field walls, round the whole of the village ground in a long bend, and joined the first line again on the far side of the oaks where the hill fell away towards the river. It was a mile longer that way. The carters complained of it from the first day to the last.

They built it that spring and summer with a crew of hill men paid in iron, bridging the stream with timber at the lower ford, and finished it at the end of the summer. The first carts came up it from Cnoc fhiadhaich in the autumn, heavy with coal, the horses leaning into the collar on the bend below the fields, and went on round the oaks and down to Ceann fhada and the barges.

Beathag let the carters water their horses at the stream where the road crossed it. They asked her leave the first time, in bad Dia-thìris, and she gave it, and they did not ask again, and she did not mind. In wet weather they ate their bread under the oaks before the last pull down to the river. The children of Doire mhòr went down to the road to watch the carts pass, and learned the strangers' words for horse and wheel and whip before they learned their letters.

In the autumn Beathag went down alone to the bend of the road below her fields and walked the length of it from one end to the other. The road was well made. It ran in a wide smooth curve round the foot of the field walls, never more than a stone's throw from them, and at every point along it she could see her own barley stubble over the wall, and beyond it the roofs of Na Seachd Taighean, and above them the oaks. Nowhere did it go away from the village; the whole way round, it kept as close as it could go.

She stood at the far end, where the bend joined the straight road again, and looked back along it. It seemed to her a road made by people who had marked a thing and meant to come back for it. They had not gone another way. They had gone the same way, and left a space in the middle of it the shape of Doire mhòr, and made the space as small as they could.

## VIII. Of the Light at Tobar dhearg

*That same spring, far off on the southern cape, the first of the new beacons was lit; and since the keepers of the lights are the third witness of this age, the copyists give its beginning here, as the keepers tell it.*

Torcall Clachair and James Fenn had walked the five headlands of the old driftwood fires, and the first of the towers went up at Tobar dhearg, the village of the red well on the southern cape, over the stump of the old fire-tower the village had kept since An Aois Naomh. A' Chompanaidh paid for it, since its ships would use it most. Torcall built it. He was past fifty and stiff in the knees: a round tower of grey stone with a stair inside it going up in the thickness of the wall, and a room at the top with windows on the sea. Fenn set the lens: a great glass of the strangers' making, ground over the sea and carried up from Ros dhomhain on a cart packed in straw, which nobody in the village was allowed to touch.

It was lit on 9 an Cèitean, AE 15. The village stood on the headland in the dusk and watched the light come up in the room at the top of the tower and go out over the water in a long beam, and the old people said it was a poor small thing beside the driftwood fires of their youth; and then a fisherman came back from the open sea after dark and said he had seen it three leagues out, and nobody said anything more against it.

The keeper was Anna nic Dhòmhnaill of Tobar dhearg, a fisherman's widow of twenty-five or so, whose husband had been lost off the cape two winters before. The village chose her. It held the light as a trust, the way it had held the old fire, and it chose the keeper from among its own families as it always had; and it chose Anna because she lived nearest the headland and had sat up nights for a boat that did not come home, and knew how long a night was. The council confirmed her in the spring of the next year. After that the keepership stayed in the families of the village.

She climbed the tower twice a night, once at dusk to light the lamp and once in the black middle of the night to trim it, and she went up and down that stair every night that she lived. She could not write. So she kept her count on the wall of the stair, at the turn below the lamp-room: one stroke cut into the stone with the point of a knife for every night the light was lit, and a stroke across every thirty, like a gate across a field. The copyists have not seen that wall. The keepers who came after her say that the strokes low down are cut deep and straight and the highest are shallow and crooked, and that there is not one night missing.

It was the keepers of Tobar dhearg who first said that a keeper has nothing to gain from a ship that is not there. They meant that the count is true. Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg was paid for by A' Chompanaidh so that its coal ships should come round the southern cape by night; but the tally on the stair counts nights, and not ships.

## IX. Of the Brig and the Bend

The word of the southern light came up to the hills with the carters in the summer, and they were pleased with it, since it meant that the barges could go out of the river mouth and round the cape without waiting for daylight. Beathag heard them say so at the stream, and understood what the light was for, and said nothing.

In the sixteenth year, on 10 an Giblean, AE 16, a brig of A' Chompanaidh coming down from the north with a cargo of iron tools for the pits was boarded off the north-west coast, in the empty waters beyond the capes, and stripped of everything in her hold. Her crew were put in their own boat and came ashore at Cuan shean, cold and whole. The raiders were never known. Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir wrote to the council that the custodians of the coast should have prevented it. The custodians of the coast wrote back that those waters had always kept their own law, and that the island had never asked the sea for leave.

The answer of the coast came up to the hills in the spring, copied by the council for every district and read out at the mill at Muileann chrom by the custodian of the district, and the hill men laughed at it for a week. Beathag heard it read. She did not laugh; but the copyists find that she went home and wrote it into the roll of Doire mhòr word for word, which is more room than she gave to anything else that year.

Then she went down to the bend.

It was a clear spring evening, the first dry one after a wet month, and the carts had stopped for the day, and the road lay empty round the foot of her fields in its long smooth curve, with the ruts of the winter filled with light.
