The barley was up green behind the walls. The stream ran loud at the ford. Up the hill the smoke of Na Seachd Taighean went straight up into the still air, and the oaks stood black above it. Down the valley the smoke of two pits went up now instead of one.

She stood at the bend a long time. She had shut her door on A' Chompanaidh and A' Chompanaidh had gone round her; and in two years it had not come back. The hill thought that a custodian's word at a door still counted against paper, as it had counted against everything else since An Aois Naomh. Beathag stood on the new road and looked along the bend of it, and knew better.

She went up to her house in the dusk and took down the roll, and under the sixteenth year, after the brig and the answer of the coast, wrote the road into it: the road round the fields, made in the fifteenth year, a mile the longer for Doire mhòr, well built. Then she wrote two words more, pressing hard enough on the pen that they stand up from the back of the leaf, and they are the last words she wrote that year.

*For now.*

# Chapter Nine: Of the Mark and Its Hundred Pence

*AE 17 – 20*

## I. Of Carragh Cnoc bheag

Samuel Wren went up to Cnoc bheag at the end of the dark of the year, in the seventeenth winter since the ships came, with a pony, a boy from the clergy-house to lead it, and a satchel of white paper wrapped in oilcloth against the rain. He was near fifty then. The damp of the island had never agreed with him. He coughed on the lake road out of Ros dhomhain and on the long rise north through the sheep-country, and at night in the houses where they lodged he sat up against the wall to cough, so as not to wake the household, and woke it anyway.

He had been asked. Some years before, the hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag had written to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise for a copy of his grammar, to read what the humans wrote of them, and had been sent one. Now they wrote that there was a stone near their town with writing on it older than any hand on the island, and that a man who wished to know the island's tongue from its roots should see the oldest thing in it.

The priest who met him on the road was a lean man with a hawk's feather pinned in his cloak and a voice much bigger than his chest; Wren's day-book calls him only the priest of the feather. He talked the whole of the last miles in the clipped Dia-thìris of the north, and Wren caught one word in three and nodded at the rest.

At the priest's house that night, after they had eaten, the priest brought out Wren's own grammar.

Wren knew the binding, but not what had become of the pages. Every margin was written in, in two hands and three inks, in the stag-letters of the island, running up the edges and between the lines; there were small crosses beside some words and a drawn hawk beside others; and on the leaf where Wren had put the name of the vein's custodians into his own tongue as *keepers of the coal*, someone had written the island's word in the margin three times over and scored a line beneath it.

"You have it wrong there," the priest said, with great good humour. "A keeper keeps a thing in a box. The custodians have the care of it. As a man has the care of a sick child, or a ewe at lambing." He tapped the page. "We wrote it in so that the next one who reads your book will know."

Wren asked whether he might copy the notes.

"Copy all of them," said the priest. "That is what they are for."

He sat up by the priest's fire until the candle was a stub, copying, and coughing.

The stone stood some four miles off, south and west of the town, on a green shoulder of ground above a burn. The town had fenced it long ago with a ring of oak stakes against the cattle, and each generation renewed the stakes as they rotted, so that the fence was always new and the stone always old. It was a little taller than a man, grey, narrowing to the top, and it leaned as if it had been listening to something in the west for a long time. The rain came across the shoulder from the sea, fine and cold, and Wren stood inside the stakes with his paper pinned to a board under his cloak and looked up.

On the upper face ran a single line of marks. They were cut deep and cleanly, with the edges still sharp after all the weather, and they were like no letters Wren knew in any tongue of his own world or any tongue he had learned on the island. Lower down, cut with a narrower tool, shallower and less sure, were four words he could read.

"*Bha teine sa chloich*," he said aloud.

"There was fire in the stone," said the priest. "That is the easy part."

The custodian of Cnoc bheag had come out with them, an old woman on a stick who had said nothing all the way from the town. Now she laid her hand on the top of a stake and told him what the custodians of that town had told every asker since the stag-letters were made. The stone was older than the Dia-thìrich. The scholars of the old schools had carried their own letters to it when those letters were new, and found that they matched nothing. Somebody of the island had cut the four words below, later, knowing no more than they did. None living could read the rest.

"Then who can?" Wren asked her.

"Nobody here," said the custodian. "Perhaps nobody anywhere. You may try."

He tried. He copied the line mark by mark, three times over, with his back to the wind and the boy holding the ink-horn in both hands to keep the rain out of it; he measured each mark with a rule and wrote the measures under it; and he copied the four words also, and the lean of the stone, and the stakes. It took him the whole of that day, which was 5 an Gearran, AE 17. When he came away his fingers would not close on the pony's rein.

He sent the best of the three copies over the sea on the first ship of the spring, north-about, to the scholars of an Tìr Thall who kept such things, asking what the line was and who had cut it. Through that summer and the next he asked the master of every ship that came in whether there was a packet for him. No answer came. The custodian of Cnoc bheag, when she was told, is said to have laughed.

## II. Of the Ship on the Coin

While Wren was in the north the coin came in.

On 13 an Gearran, AE 17, Wren's clerk, making up the quarter's accounts, found that the stores of A' Chompanaidh at Ros dhomhain would take his notes of hand no longer, but only coin: the humans' own, shipped from over the sea in small iron-bound kegs and brought in beside the old barter of the island, as the proclamation of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach put it, for ease. Nobody on the island had asked for it. The post went on taking wool and fish that year as before. The iron began to cost coin, and the fish went on costing fish.

That summer Riaghaltas nan Coigreach set up a striking-house on the quay at Ros dhomhain below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, a long stone shed with a press brought over in pieces and bolted to a floor of new oak, and silver and copper came over the sea for it in bars. On 10 an Lùnastal, AE 17, the first coins of the island's own striking came out of the press into a wooden tray: the mark and its hundred pence.

Wren was there, because Josiah Pell had asked the clergy to send somebody to bless the press, and they had sent the man who spoke the island's tongue best, in case any of the island came to watch. A dozen fishers stood in the shed door with their caps in their hands, and a knot of children who had been told to go home and had not. Wren said a short prayer over the press in his own tongue and then said it again in theirs. The press came down. The workman lifted the first mark out of the die with a pair of tongs and dropped it in the tray, and it rang.

Pell turned it to the light from the door and showed it round. On one face was a ship under full sail, very finely cut, with every rope drawn. On the other were letters in the humans' tongue that gave the coin's worth and the year of the humans' own reckoning. There was nothing of Dia-thìr on either face. No hill, no hawk, no word.

Wren said so, afterward, in Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, over a glass of the strangers' wine. He said that it might be well to have some mark of the island on the island's coin, since it was to pass from hand to hand among the island's people, and they would look at it.

Pell said the dies had been cut over the sea. He said it pleasantly, and poured Wren more wine, and asked him about the stone at Cnoc bheag.

Wren kept one of the first marks. At the end of that month he walked up the hill to Cathair dhearg with it in his coat, to the long room on the east side of the council hall where Gormshuil still kept her papers, and where he had sat across a table from her fifteen years before and pointed at cups and bread; and he put it on the same table, in the same window-light, ship-side up.

Gormshuil picked it up. She was grey by then, and wore spectacles of the strangers' glass, which she did not like and could not do without. She held the coin close to them a long while, both faces, and weighed it in her palm.

"Which ship is it?" she asked.

Wren said it was no ship; it was a ship. A figure for all ships.

"No," said Gormshuil. "It is the ship that came." She put the coin down between them. "Where is the island on it?"

He had no answer to give her, and gave none.

Muireall was at the far end of the table, copying. She was a woman near thirty by then. She took the mark from her aunt without asking and laid a sheet of thin paper over it and rubbed it with a soft lead until the ship came up grey on the white, every rope of it, and then did the letters. Under the rubbing she wrote the island's year and moon, and the humans' day in the humans' figures. Under that she wrote: *the island is on neither face.*

The rubbing went east that autumn with the season's copies, in the chest for the loft at Muileann chaol. Gormshuil gave the coin itself back to Wren. She said she had no use for it yet.

## III. Of the Two Books

From the first day of the next year the market of Cathair mhòr, the greatest market below the hills east of the capital, would not take the mark at all.

The custodians of that town met in their hall on 1 am Faoilleach, AE 18 and gave their ruling in a sentence: what was sold in Cathair mhòr would be sold as it always had been, thing for thing, by the old measures, and a man who wanted iron could bring wool. The tool-sellers of A' Chompanaidh were told it at the bridge-foot and took it back to Ros dhomhain, and Pell wrote to Tormod mac Ailein, and Tormod put the letter in the chest under the east window of the council hall.

At the capital there was no ruling. There it happened stall by stall.

Wren saw it that first winter after the striking, on a market-day at the end of am Faoilleach, when he went down to buy stockings. The market lay below the hill along the lake road, and the lake wind set the awnings cracking. At the bridge end stood the tool-sellers of A' Chompanaidh with their carts, and their prices were chalked on boards in the humans' figures, in marks only. At the other end the cloth-women and the fish-wives sat as they had always sat, and a fleece was worth so many ells and a creel of herring so many loaves, and a stranger with a purse of new pence had to find an islander to change them, at a loss, before he could buy anything.

Between the two ends, under the arch of the old gate, sat the custodians' market-clerk with two books open in front of him.

He was a sharp-nosed man called Tadhg. In the left-hand book he entered the market's dues by the old reckoning, so many fleeces and so many creels; in the right-hand book, ruled in the humans' manner, he entered the tool-sellers' dues in marks and pence. They would not pay in fleeces. The cloth-women would not pay in pence. At the end of each month he must make the two books into one figure for the council, and there was no figure that would do it.

He showed Wren the foot of the left-hand page. Under the last tally he had written, in the stag-letters: *This book cannot be added to the other.* Then he turned to the foot of the right-hand page and showed him the same sentence, written again, laboriously, in the humans' letters and the humans' tongue, with one word misspelled.

"So that both sides will know," said Tadhg.

Wren bought his stockings at the far end for a fleece's worth of goods he had brought in a bag for the purpose, having learned. On the bridge one of the tool-sellers called out to ask whether it was true that the strangers' priest had gone to Cnoc bheag to read a stone, and Wren said that it was true he had gone, and not true that he had read it.

## IV. Of the Winter at Dùn thais

That summer a letter came from Dùn thais, in a beautiful hand in the stag-letters, so courteous that it took Wren and his clerk a week to be sure what it asked. The masters of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, the school of the deer, had read the grammar also, and heard of the stone. They would receive the man who made the grammar for the dark of the year, when the school sat, if he would come and dispute with them; and they would give him a bed near the fire, since they had heard he coughed.

He went east with the carriers at the end of an t-Samhain, with a trunk of books on the cart, over the capital road through Cathair mhòr and on into the hills, where the road narrowed and the carriers walked at the horses' heads and sang to keep the pace. They were five days on the sixty miles, in the rain. He came down into Dùn thais on the last afternoon with the light going: grey houses at the head of a long valley, smoke lying flat over the roofs, and a dark wood on the hill behind.

The disputation began on 3 an Dùbhlachd, AE 18, in the hall of the school: a long, low room with a hearth at each end and rushes on an earth floor, where some twenty masters sat on benches down both walls in undyed wool and the students sat on the floor between. The eldest of them was a woman so old that she had to be helped to her bench, and so sharp that the others looked at her before they answered anything.

Wren put his question on the first evening, standing, in his best Dia-thìris, with the fire loud behind him.

He asked why the vein should be holy.

He meant it honestly. In seventeen years on the island he had seen the custodians go up to the cuttings in their season with their baskets and their words, and seen the handful set down at the shrine and burned there, measured, and the rest left in the hill. He had seen a people who were cold every winter keep a fuel under their feet and not burn it. He had written it into the grammar and never understood it. In his own country, he said, God had given men the earth to use, and the black stone in it with the rest, and a man who froze beside a coal-seam for want of leave would be thought a fool.

The old woman heard him through. Then she asked him, in her turn, why his fuel should be burned.

He began to answer, and found he did not know how to begin. In his own country nobody had ever asked it. The fuel was there; it burned; the house was warm. She asked him what the fuel had been before it was fuel, and he told her what the philosophers of his country said, that it was the wood of old forests pressed under the earth for ages. She nodded, as if she had expected it, and asked him whether he burned his grandmother's house because it was made of wood.

So it went all that winter. Each side put its question and the other put its question back. They sat in the long hall through the short days with the rain on the roof, and argued in two tongues, with a young master to interpret when Wren's Dia-thìris failed him, which was often when they came to the old words for the vein. The school's way was to hold a question up to the light like a piece of coal and look for the colours in it. Wren's way was to answer, and write the answer down. By the turn of the year the students had taken sides, and argued on the floor after the masters had gone to bed.

Neither telling of that winter names a winner. The register of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh sets down the two questions, and under them a line the students took up among themselves: that it is a poor question that can be answered in one winter. Wren's letters call the masters the most learned company he had met on the island or off it, and the old woman a person he would not willingly face again across a table.

On a night near the year's end, when the talk was done, the masters told stories at the hearth, and the old woman told one of a voyage west. A holy man of the island's first days, she said, put out from the western shore in a boat of hides with a few companions to look for the isle where the blessed live; and they came to many islands, one of sheep and one of birds that sang the hours, and landed on a great fish's back and lit a fire on it, until it moved; and at last they came to the isle of the blessed, and were shown it, and sent home to tell of it.

Wren sat without moving while she told it, and afterwards asked her to tell it again, and wrote it down as she spoke.

In the last days of the year Wren wrote home to the house of his order over the sea, and sent it by the packet of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, so that the letter lies in the letter-books of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach still. It tells of the school and the questions, and then tells the story as the old woman had told it, and says that it was very like the telling in an Eaglais of the voyage of Naomh Breandan, a saint of his own country's coasts, who sailed west in a boat of hides to look for the land of promise and found the fish and the birds and the isle; told from the other shore, as though the people at the end of that voyage had watched the boat come in. Wren did not know what to make of it, he wrote, and should be glad of any light his superiors could give him.

That letter, too, had no answer the island ever heard of.

He went home at the end of the dark season, west over the hills, coughing, with a second trunk of copied pages and a gift from the school, a small deer carved of black bog-oak.

## V. Of the Bridge and the Carriage

Cathair mhòr held out its whole year. All that year the tool-sellers came to the bridge-foot on market-days and went away with wool. When the year turned they came no further; they stopped their carts on the far bank of the river and would not cross the bridge, and a man of Cathair mhòr who wanted a spade or a pot had to walk out over the bridge to them with coin in his hand. By the second month of the new year the custodians of Cathair mhòr had given way, and entered it in their roll without comment, and the market took the mark like everyone else.

Gormshuil read that entry to the council. She was the only custodian of the council who could read both the island's letters and the humans' without help, and the chest under the east window, where the strangers' papers went, had come to be hers in all but name.

That spring the masons of A' Chompanaidh came up to rebuild Drochaid Cathair dhearg.

The bridge had carried the capital's road over the Abhainn dhomhain on the same piers time out of mind, and the carts of the hill country crossed it every market-day with their wheels a hand's breadth from the parapets. A' Chompanaidh wanted it wide enough for coal-carts to pass two abreast, and wanted it in dressed stone. The work began on 28 an Gearran, AE 19. The masons took down the old parapets course by course and stacked the stones on the bank.

Gormshuil went down on the second morning with a single stone in mind. On the downstream parapet near the middle of the bridge was a block with a name cut in the old letters, much worn: the name of Queen Sìleas, who had widened the bridge in her day for two carts to pass. The children of the capital were taught to find it with their fingers on the way to market. Gormshuil had found it so herself.

She found it already down, lying on its face in the mud of the bank. The master mason was a big, red-faced man from over the sea with a voice like a gravel-cart, and he came up the bank wiping his hands, and heard her in his own tongue, which surprised him, and asked her what she wanted with one old stone out of three hundred.

She told him whose name was on it.

He had the block turned over, and could not read it, and she read it for him. He said the new parapet would be squared true and this block would never sit square with the others. Gormshuil said it had sat square with the others for some hundreds of years. In the end he had it dressed on its back and sides and left the face as it was, and set it again in the downstream parapet near the middle of the new bridge, a little proud of the new stones and a little darker. The children found it again by midsummer.

The bridge was finished by the autumn. On 30 an t-Sultain, AE 19, Pell drove over it.

The wheelwrights of A' Chompanaidh had built him a carriage over the summer: a closed black box on springs, with a glass window in each door and a pair of greys shipped over the sea to draw it. It was the first carriage on the island. He drove in it from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir along the lake road and over the new bridge and up the hill to the council, with a coachman on the box and a boy up behind, and the whole of the lake road came to its doors to see it go by.

Tormod mac Ailein was walking to the council that morning with Gormshuil beside him. He walked slowly by then, with a stick in each hand because of his knees, and they were halfway over the bridge when they heard the wheels behind them and stood in to the downstream parapet, by Sìleas's stone, to let it by. The carriage drew up level with them and stopped, and Pell let down the glass.

He greeted them both courteously, in Dia-thìris, and offered Tormod a seat as far as the hall.

Tormod thanked him. Then he said, in the island's tongue, so that the coachman and the boy and the people on the bridge could hear it: "*Coisichidh sinne.*" We will walk.

Pell bowed, and put up the glass, and drove on. Tormod and Gormshuil walked up the hill after him, with Tormod's two sticks knocking on the new stones, and reached the hall long after the carriage had been put up in the yard. The roll of that day notes that An t-Àrd-mhaor came to the hall in a carriage, and that the custodians came on foot, as they had always come. The custodians said it aloud often after, to anyone who would listen.

## VI. Of Puingean a' Chalaidh

Puingean a' Chalaidh, the articles of the harbour, came before the council at the end of that year.

They came as Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg had come, in the humans' tongue alone, eight sheets with Pell's seal at the foot, to be signed with the council on 16 an t-Samhain, AE 19. This time the council had the sheets a month beforehand. On the first evening Gormshuil took them out of the chest and carried them home, and read them twice by her lamp, with her finger and her spectacles, and made a slip of every clause.

They were articles for the harbour of Ros dhomhain. They fixed where a ship might lie in the lake and what she must pay for lying there, and the dues on goods landed and taken off. A harbour-master of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach was to be set over the quay, with the keeping of the anchorages. At every turn the dues fell in favour of A' Chompanaidh, whose hulls lay at the best berths for a third of what any other boat paid; and every boat that anchored off Ros dhomhain paid something, the boats of the island's own lake towns among them, which had anchored there free since there had been boats.

Gormshuil went to Tormod's house with her slips. He heard them by the fire, as he had heard the charter ten years before, with a cup in his hand and his feet on a stool. When she had done he was silent a long time.

"We need the quay," he said at last. "We need what comes to it."

"So we do," said Gormshuil. "We have had the quay since before there were strangers. What we are asked to sign is that it is theirs."

"Does it say so?"

"The harbour-master is to be theirs. That comes to the same."

He asked her what she would do. She said that she would read the articles aloud in the hall, in both tongues, before anyone signed, so that every custodian would know what was on the sheets; and that she would not sign them herself. He let her be. He was tired.

On the day the hall was full. The rain came in off the lake as it had on the day of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, and Pell sat at the far side of the long table in his black coat with Wren at his elbow to carry words. When it came to the reading, Gormshuil stood up.

She read the articles through, every clause, first in the humans' tongue as it was written and then in Dia-thìris as close as she could bring it. It took most of the morning. Where she had no island word for a word of theirs she said so, and turned to Wren and asked whether she had the sense right; and Wren, who had not been asked for this, said each time that she had, and each time Pell looked at him. When she came to the clause on the anchorages, a custodian at the lower end of the table, Ailean Ruadh of Baile ghlas, whose town's boats had lain free off Ros dhomhain every season of his life, stood up and asked to hear it again. She read it again.

Then she sat down.

Tormod signed first. He wrote his name slowly, looking a long while at the place before he put the pen to it, and the custodians signed after him one by one down the table, with Pell watching each name go on.

When the sheet came to Gormshuil she did not take up the pen. She passed the sheet on to the next place. When it came to Ailean Ruadh he did the same.

Pell asked, through Wren, whether the custodian of the capital was unwell.

Gormshuil answered him herself, in his own tongue. She said that she was well. She said that she had read the articles, which none at that table but she had done, and that she would not put her name under what she had read. Ailean Ruadh said, in the island's tongue, that he would not put his name under anything that charged Baile ghlas to lie where Baile ghlas had always lain. Pell heard them out. He thanked them. Then he signed, for Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, below the names of those who had signed, and the articles stood.

The council's roll enters the signing, and the names under it, and says that two custodians refused: Gormshuil nic Fhearchair of Cathair dhearg, and Ailean Ruadh of Baile ghlas. It was the first time since the strangers came that any custodian had refused to sign a thing the strangers put before the council. Muireall, who copied that leaf for the loft, drew a line round the two names.

Walking home in the dark, Tormod said to Gormshuil that it had done no good.

"No," she said. "It is written, though."

## VII. Of Grazing, and Chimneys

Puingean a' Chalaidh took effect with the new year, and the harbour-master took up the keeping of the quay, and by the autumn after, on 5 an Dàmhair, AE 20, he was charging anchorage.

The fishermen of Baile ghlas paid it once. Then they talked it over on the shingle and sent word up the lake that they would not pay it again. They took their catch to their own small harbour under the town, a stone jetty and a slip with room for a dozen boats, and sold it there off the boats to anyone who would walk the seven miles out from the capital, and to anyone at all but A' Chompanaidh. Gormshuil walked out one bright morning at the end of an Dàmhair and found the jetty crowded with the capital's fish-wives and their creels, and the herring going from hand to hand for pence and for loaves both, and Ailean Ruadh at the top of the slip with his arms folded, very pleased. The letter-books complain that the salting-house of A' Chompanaidh had herring that season only from its own boats.

A month later the council granted Riaghaltas nan Coigreach grazing.

There were human families on the island by then who had come over the sea to work for A' Chompanaidh and would not go down the pits; they had sheep and cattle of their own breeds and no land. The council gave them, on 3 an t-Samhain, AE 20, summer grazing on the empty uplands of the north-west about Muileann àrsaidh, where the fields had gone back to rush in the last age. The grant was for grazing. Gormshuil had the word read back three times, in both tongues, before anyone signed, and noted on her slip that the humans' word meant the eating of grass by beasts and nothing else. She signed that one.

Before the winter a short letter came down to the chest under the east window from the custodian of Muileann àrsaidh. The families on the grazing had built houses, the custodian wrote. They had built them of stone: good stone, quarried from the hill and squared, with chimneys and slate from somewhere, and walls a man could not kick down. The shielings of the island were built of turf and wattle, to stand a summer and be let fall. These would stand a hundred years. Did the council mean it so?

## VIII. Of Tormod's Burying

Tormod had been ailing since the harvest, in the chest and then in the heart. When Gormshuil brought the letter from Muileann àrsaidh he was in his bed, propped on bolsters, with the fire made up and the girl who kept his house on a stool by the door. He asked her to read it to him.

She read it. When she came to the chimneys he began to laugh, and the laugh turned to coughing, and the girl brought him water.

"Grazing," he said, when he could.

"Grazing," said Gormshuil. "I had it read three times."

"I know you did." He lay back on the bolsters. "You had it right. It meant grazing when we signed it. It is only afterward that their words grow." He was silent a while. "Write to them that the council meant summer grazing, and shielings. Write it in both tongues. They will not pull the houses down."

"No."

"Write it all the same."

She wrote it that night, in both tongues, and sent it north in the morning. Tormod died on 15 an Dùbhlachd, AE 20, in the dark of the year, in the house below the temple, with the fire lit and the girl at the door and Gormshuil asleep in the chair by the bed. He was sixty-five years old. He had sat at the head of Comhairle a' Chùraim, in the crown's place, for longer than most of the council had been grown, and he had given the strangers leave to stay, and signed Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg and the harbour articles, and there were those in the capital who had not forgiven him for it, and came to his wake anyway.

They waked him three nights in his own house, by the old custom, and on the second night the council chose Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh after him, a broad, slow-spoken man from twenty miles up the east road, who had never set eyes on a human before An t-Aiseag and had dealt with little else since, and the choice was made in an evening. The roll gives it as unanimous. It was.

They buried Tormod on the fourth day, in the ground behind the council hall, on a cold wet morning with the cloud down on the hill. Six custodians carried the bier out of his door and down through the town, with the council walking after, Coinneach Glas at their head and Gormshuil among them in her grey cloak, and the bells of Cathair dhearg rang for him all the way, the old bronze of the hoes. At the grave they went round sunwise, each with a stone from the lake shore, and laid the stones on the turf one by one, and said the words.

Josiah Pell came. He left his carriage at the bridge-foot and walked up the hill in the rain behind the custodians, bareheaded, and stood at the edge of the ground through the whole of the burying, and went away at the end without speaking. At the back of all the crowd, by the gate, stood Samuel Wren in his black coat. He had walked up from Ros dhomhain in the rain, as he always walked, and he did not come nearer. Through the words and the stones he stood by the gate with a handkerchief to his mouth, and coughed, and tried not to, and coughed again; and when it was done and the crowd went down the hill he was still there, and Gormshuil, passing, stopped, and they went down together.

# Chapter Ten: Of the Going Out of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig

*AE 21 – 24*

## I. Of the Ship That Did Not Come Home

In the roll of Comhairle a' Chùraim for the twenty-first year of this age there is a page the copyists of the cellar turned back to more than once. At its head the clerk has written its year of An Diosal and the moon, and under them two lines in his quick hand. The first says that the humans at Ros dhomhain were in mourning for their captain. The second says that the fee of the counters was held over to the next sitting. Nothing on the page joins the two lines, and the clerk did not think they were joined. Of the second line the copyists could find no later entry anywhere. The next sitting did not take it up, nor the one after, and no council ever struck it out. So Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig went out of the island on a line held over; and the one custodian who stood up to speak for it was a woman of the eastern hills who had come to the capital that summer on other business, and who happened to be at Ros dhomhain on the day the humans stopped waiting for their ship.

Fionnghal nic Artair was thirty-six years old that year, custodian of Dùn dhearg, and she had sat in the council eleven winters. She was a tall woman, long in the jaw, with the grey come early into her hair, and she rode her own horse to the capital and would not be driven. Her town stood three days' ride east of Cathair dhearg, on a hill with a double bank round it and a stone wall inside the bank, where the old hall of the crown had stood before Beathag Mhòr carried it west to the bridge-foot in the long centuries. Dùn dhearg had kept its granaries and its graves and its pride, and an old habit of sending its accounts to the capital in no hand but its own. Fionnghal wrote her own letters, and wrote them long.

She had come west in an t-Iuchar because the council had called in its custodians to hear Coinneach Glas, who had been chosen Ceann a' Chùraim at the turn of the year, after Tormod mac Ailein was buried. He was a broad, slow-spoken man of Ceann àrsaidh, twenty miles up the east road, and he had spent the twenty years since An t-Aiseag dealing with the humans at one table or another, so that he spoke their tongue better than any man in the hall and read it slowly, with his finger under the line. He wanted the council to know the state of the dues. That took four days. On the fifth the sitting rose, and Gormshuil nic Fhearchair asked Fionnghal to walk down with her to Ros dhomhain, where she had business with Samuel Wren at Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise. Fionnghal went, for she had never seen the humans' town close to.

Ros dhomhain lay a short walk below the capital on the lake shore, and in twenty years it had grown a second town beside the first, of sawn timber and dressed stone, with Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir above it on the rise and the chapel down on the quay with its iron bell. That day the bell was being rung slowly, one stroke to every few steps of a walking man, and a flag that Fionnghal had seen at the mastheads of the humans' ships hung halfway down its pole over the warehouse of A' Chompanaidh. The humans stood about the quay in their dark coats and did no work. Gormshuil asked a carter what had happened. He told her that Harrow's ship was a month past her day, and that A' Chompanaidh's men had given her up that morning.

"He went north-about in an Cèitean," said Gormshuil. "I saw him go. He said he would be back before the hay."

Wren came out of the chapel to meet them. He was grey now and thinner than ever, and he coughed into a cloth before he could speak. He took them in out of the wind off the lake and sat them on a bench at the back while the humans' prayers were said, and Fionnghal watched Thomas Pike stand at the front with his hat in both hands and read names from a paper: Harrow's, and after it the names of the men who had sailed with him. She could not follow the words. She could hear that the first name was read in another voice from the rest.

Afterwards Wren told them, in his careful Dia-thìris, what the letter-book at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir would say of Harrow, for he had been asked to help write it. It would say that Edmund Harrow was the man who found Dia-thìr.

Fionnghal turned that over on the long climb back to the capital. At the top of the hill she stopped.

"Lachlann Odhar of Achadh àrsaidh found him," she said. "Off the north-west cape, in the cod season. And led him down the coast to water."

"That is in our roll," said Gormshuil. "It is not in theirs."

"Then theirs is wrong."

"Theirs is theirs," said Gormshuil. She had been twenty years at the humans' letters, and two winters before she had refused to set her name to Puingean a' Chalaidh and had watched Puingean a' Chalaidh take force on the quay without it. She said nothing more on the road.

Within the month A' Chompanaidh was Pike's alone, and the humans' clerks wrote to the council to say so, in their own tongue, on good paper with a seal. Coinneach Glas read the letter to the sitting and it was entered in the roll. Nobody in the hall had ever spoken with Pike about anything that mattered except Gormshuil, who had watched him weigh wool at a counter in a net-loft when the humans on the island could be counted on two hands. She said he was a fair man by his own measures. Then the custodians rode home, and Fionnghal went east to her hill, and did not think about the ship again that year.

## II. Of the Empty Board at Dùn dhearg

The counters of Dùn dhearg kept their board in the old granary under the north wall, where grain had been stored for the crown in the long centuries and where nothing had been kept since but the board and the measure. The board was a plank of black oak the length of a man, hung on two pegs, with a row of holes bored for every household of the town and its farms. The measure was a cup of turned alder made in the shape of two hands held together, worn pale at the rim. Twice in the year, at Samhain and at Bealltainn, the households came up with their sacks for the coal of the shrine-cutting and had it measured out, one double handful to each hearth for the season, and the counter put a peg in the hole. So it had been done since An Aois Naomh, when the custom of the handful was made law. A household that burned twice its measure lost its coal for the season after. The roll of Dùn dhearg held three such sentences in six hundred years, and the town could still name all three families.

The counter was Pàdraig Cam, who had kept the board forty years, as his father had before him. He was paid out of the dues of the vein. A share of every cutting in the hills had gone to the council's chest at Cathair dhearg since An Aois Naomh, and out of it the council paid each town that kept a board, so that the counting should be no one's favour. When the contracts came in, the cuttings went to A' Chompanaidh by the ton, and A' Chompanaidh paid the council for them in marks. The marks came fewer than the old shares by the council's reckoning, and more by A' Chompanaidh's; and the council, which had its part of the new bridge to pay for and a hall roof that let in the rain, found at its autumn sitting that it could not meet every fee. The counters' fee was held over. That was the line the copyists turned back to.

Pàdraig Cam heard it at Samhain from Fionnghal's own mouth. She rode home with the news and went up to the granary to tell him, and found him at the board with his bag of pegs on his knee.

"I'll count this season for nothing," he said. "I have counted for less."

He counted it. Half the households of Dùn dhearg came up the hill with their sacks that Samhain, and those that came were the old. The young households had bought their coal that summer at the market of Cathair mhòr, a day's walk to the west, off A' Chompanaidh's carts, by the sack and for marks, as much as they could pay for. A sack off the carts never came up to the granary to be measured. Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig had been made when every coal on the island came out of the shrine-cuttings through the counters' hands, and it had nothing to say about a cart. Fionnghal walked through the town at dusk and saw it through the open doors: black coal on hearths where there had been peat, a heap of it in the corner of a kitchen, a child set to break the lumps with a hammer. The smell of it hung in the lanes. It was a warm smell, and the town liked it.

Her own steward, Tòmas Bàn, had bought four sacks for her house in an Lùnastal while she was away at the capital, because the young men who cut the peat for the town had gone down to the pits at Muileann chrom for the ton-wage and there was no one left to cut her bank. She found the sacks in the byre when she came home. She said nothing about them. That winter was a hard one, and she burned them.

On 2 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21, the council sent round to the towns a letter saying that its chest held nothing for the counters until the spring. The copyists have set that day against the end of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, for want of any other, and the keepers at the hill hearths tell the end of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig as they would tell of a fire that went out for want of feeding. No council repealed it. It went on standing in Leabhar a' Chùraim with the three sentences of Dùn dhearg written under it, and after that winter hardly anyone kept it.

At Doire mhin, in the valley below the hills two days' ride west of Dùn dhearg on the capital road, the custodians went on keeping the count through that winter as though the letter had not come. Theirs was the older half of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, the count of the hill: how much coal the cuttings of their valley might give in a year and never more. On 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 21, the last night of the year, they entered the count in their roll, and wrote under it that no one had asked for it.

## III. Of the Letter and the Road West

Fionnghal began to write in an Gearran, the week Pàdraig Cam died.

He died in his bed in the ordinary way, of his years and a winter cough, and his son did not take the board, having gone to the pits at Muileann chrom two summers before and married there. The board hung in the granary with the pegs of the last Samhain in their holes, and nobody took them out, since nobody would be putting new ones in. Fionnghal went up to look at it after the burying. Then she went home and sent Tòmas Bàn to Cathair mhòr for paper.

She wrote all that spring. She wrote at the kitchen table with the bought coal burning in the grate behind her, because it was what there was, and it is told at Dùn dhearg that she would get up from the table and stand with her back to the fire and look at the wall, and then sit down and go on. Five drafts were written and four of them burned in that grate. The one that survives is dated 11 an t-Ògmhios, AE 22, in her own hand, by An Diosal's year and moon, and it runs to eleven pages.

It is the only defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig that has come down. The copyists give the heart of it as she wrote it:

*Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was made for the people more than for the coal, for a people becomes whatever its burning makes it. A house that burns the handful keeps a peat bank and a man who knows how to cut it, and a hedge, and a child who knows which willow burns green and which dry, and it goes up the hill twice in the year and says its name to the counter. A house that burns by the sack keeps a purse. I have seen my town go warm this winter, and I have seen my counter die with his pegs in the board. The council need fine no household. Let it pay the counters, and write in the roll that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig stands. Our grandmothers' grandmothers made the handful when there was no one watching them. If we let it go now, it will be said that we let it go because strangers were watching, and paying.*

She sewed the pages into a cover of calfskin, wrapped it in oilcloth against the weather, and rode west in the middle of an t-Ògmhios with the packet inside her coat and Tòmas Bàn beside her on a hill pony. The road went down off the eastern hills through birch and bracken into the long valley, and the fields on either side were green with oats that would be late. At every ford she met coal-carts coming the other way, empty, going back up to the pits for another load. The carters walked at the horses' heads and did not look up.

On the second evening she came into Doire mhin. It was a village of a few long houses round a green, with its shrine-cutting a mile up the valley side, and its custodian was Anndra mac Eòin, a small bald man with a carpenter's hands, who had kept the count of the valley since his youth. He knew her name from the council. When she told him what she carried, he went to his chest without a word and brought out his roll and opened it on the table under the lamp, at the last page of the year.

The count was there in its columns, cutting by cutting, and under it the line: that no one had asked for it.

"You are the first to ask to see it," said Anndra mac Eòin. He said it in Dia-thìris, in the plain speech of the valley, and then again as though to himself: "Cha do dh'iarr duine e."

"I am asking," said Fionnghal.

She read him her letter that night by his lamp, all eleven pages, while his wife banked the fire with peat from their own bank, for Doire mhin had not bought coal. When she was done he asked her to read the page about the board again, and she read it. In the morning he walked beside her horse to the end of the village and stood there until she was over the rise.

## IV. Of the Filing

The council sat that summer in the old hall at Cathair dhearg under its leaking roof, with buckets set along the south wall to catch the drips when it rained, which it did on the day Fionnghal read. Twenty-odd custodians sat at the long table and on the benches behind it. Coinneach Glas sat at the head with his hands flat on the board in front of him, and the clerk at his elbow with the roll.

She read standing. It took most of an hour. The hall was close with wet wool and the rain loud on the slates, and some of the old men on the benches slept, and one snored, and was nudged, and slept again. Gormshuil nic Fhearchair sat near the door with her eyes shut, and Fionnghal knew that she was awake by the way she lifted her head at the sentence about the strangers watching. Coinneach Glas did not move once. When Fionnghal came to the end she folded the pages and stood waiting, and for a while no one in the hall said anything at all.

Then Coinneach Glas thanked her. He said that the council had heard the custodian of Dùn dhearg with respect, that her letter would be kept with the rolls, and that the matter of the counters' fee would come before the council when the state of the dues allowed. He said it kindly and he said it well, and the clerk wrote it down. The line in the roll reads that a letter of the custodian of Dùn dhearg upon Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was read and filed.

The next matter was a paper from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, brought up by a young clerk of the humans who stood in the doorway dripping. Josiah Pell asked the council's leave to widen the road from the capital to Muileann chrom so that two coal-carts might pass on it. Coinneach Glas read the paper aloud in the humans' tongue and then in the island's. There was some talk about whose fields the road would take. The leave was granted before the candles were lit.

Fionnghal found Gormshuil afterwards on the old bridge, which was A' Chompanaidh's bridge now, of dressed stone, wide enough for the carts to pass two abreast. The rain had stopped. The river ran high and brown under them, and down the valley the lamps were coming out along the quays of Ros dhomhain.

"They filed it," said Fionnghal.

"They wrote my refusal in the roll too," said Gormshuil. "It is there, a line under the Articles. The Articles are on the quay." She was sixty-two that summer, and she had begun to lean on the parapet when she stood. "You did the right thing. You put it in the roll. Someone copies the roll."

"Who reads the copy?"

"Nobody yet." Gormshuil looked at her sideways. "Give me a fair copy for Muireall. She sends such things to the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol, where they are kept dry. The loft is a small place, and still a better one than the press in the hall."

Fionnghal sat up that night in her lodging and made the copy with her own hand, and gave it to Gormshuil's niece at the door in the morning. Then she rode home. At Doire mhin she did not stop, for she had nothing to tell Anndra mac Eòin that he would want to hear.

## V. Of An Seabhag Acrach

On the north coast of the island, where the hills come down in heather to a bay of grey sand, stands Seann Skell of the hawk, the other town of that name, where the fowler households have kept birds on the fist and fed them before their own children since An Aois Naomh. Once, long before, the priests of An Seabhag Biadhte had been driven there from Cnoc bheag, and from its shrine they had asked the king's council for a quarter more of the handful for the cold hearths of the north coast, and been refused. The town had not forgotten it. By this age the shrine of Seann Skell kept the teaching of Òrd an t-Seabhaig as Cnoc bheag kept it, that the hawk of the rite is Mòd, Seabhag Acaill, as old as Fionntan and remembering all things with him; and that the vein is An Seabhag Acrach, to be fed the measured handful and no more.

Its priest in those years was Murchadh Seabhag, a fowler's son of forty-two, spare and weathered, with a hooked nose that his people said had given him his byname before the order did. On 6 an t-Sultain, AE 22, a bright day at the end of the harvest, he preached on the steps of the shrine with a grey hawk hooded on his fist, to the fowler households and to the carters who had come up the coast with A' Chompanaidh's coal for the town's new hearths.

The copies of that sermon differ in small things, as copies made by ear will. They agree in this: that Mòd starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them. The hawk remembers every meal it is given, said Murchadh, and every meal it is kept from, and it keeps the reckoning longer than any clerk. Feed it the handful and it hunts for you all your life. Feed it past its fill and it sits on the perch and grows fat and will not fly. And a people that eats the hill faster than the hill can grow is a hawk overfed, and it will not hunt, and in the end the hill will not feed it. Then he said the old line of the order over the hooded bird, which every copy keeps in the island's tongue:

*Ma bhiadhas tu an seabhag thar a leòir, cha sheilg e.*

If you feed the hawk past its fill, it will not hunt.

A scribe of the shrine wrote the sermon down that night from the priest's own mouth, and the fowlers who took birds south to sell at the autumn markets carried copies with them in their bird-bags. From the markets the copies went on by carters and pedlars into the camps at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, where there were few who could read and many who could listen, and a man who could read was given his supper for reading it in the huts after the shift. It was the first writing of the Dia-thìrich to go among the crews in that way.

A copy came to Dùn dhearg at Samhain in a carter's pack, folded small and worn soft at the creases. Fionnghal read it at her kitchen table, twice, by the coal fire. She had written eleven pages, and here a man who kept hawks had said the thing in a line. She put the copy in her chest beside the draft of her own letter, and did not burn it.

## VI. Of the Peat Hearths and the Pumps

In the spring of the next year word came east over the hills from Achadh naomh, a village of the uplands north of the workings, some fifteen miles inland from the hawk's town. Its households kept Na Seann Spioradan, the old spirits of the hearth and the dead, and on 16 am Màrt, AE 23, their elders had given out that no hearth of Achadh naomh would be lit with coal bought of A' Chompanaidh. They burned peat, as their grandparents had. They had heard of the letter from Dùn dhearg, for a copy had come to them folded inside a copy of Murchadh's sermon, and they sent to ask whether the custodian who wrote it would come and read it at their hearth.

Fionnghal went in an Giblean, a two days' ride north and west through the bare hills, with the peat banks black and wet on either side of the track and nobody cutting them. Achadh naomh stood in a fold of the moor above a burn, a score of low houses roofed in heather rope, and every roof smoked blue. The smell of it came down the hill to meet her a mile off. She had not smelled a whole village of peat smoke in two years, and she had not known that she missed it.

The eldest of the elders was a woman named Sìleas nic Uilleim, bent nearly double, who received her at a hearth in the middle of the floor with the peats built up round it in a ring, and a flat stone at the head of the hearth where no one sat. Sìleas told her what the stone was for. Every night at the smooring of the fire the woman of the house told the dead at the stone what had been burned that day and where it came from: this peat from this bank, cut by this man in this summer. It was a short telling. It had been the same telling for the whole life of the village.

"We tell them what we burn," said Sìleas. "I would not know how to tell them the other."

Fionnghal read her letter at that hearth to the whole village packed into the one house, with children on the rafters and the door open for the ones who could not get in. They heard it through without a sound. When she was done Sìleas asked her, in front of them all, what burned on the hearth of the custodian of Dùn dhearg.

Fionnghal told her.

Sìleas did not say anything to that. In the morning, when Fionnghal went to her horse, there was a creel of dry peats tied on behind the saddle, and nobody would say who had put it there.

In an Lùnastal Coinneach Glas sent three custodians to Muileann chrom to ask A' Chompanaidh, in the council's name, that the tally of the hill be kept: that its agents learn what the hill might give in a year, as the custodians of the valley had always reckoned it, and cut no more. Fionnghal was one of the three, because Dùn dhearg was nearest. They came down into the valley on a hot still morning and saw the smoke before they saw the town.

The camp of the crews had doubled since she was last there. Rows of timber huts ran up the slope from the pit-head, with the washing strung between them and the ground trodden black, and at the head of the rows A' Chompanaidh's agents were going from hut to hut with a basket. Women stood in the doorways with their arms folded. Fionnghal asked a girl at a water-butt what the men were looking for, and the girl said: the hawk-priest's paper. The agents had been told to take every copy they found. They took eleven that morning, by the girl's count, from under mattresses and behind the hearth-stones, and carried them off in the basket to the agent's office. One woman, as they came to her door, put her copy in the fire in front of them and stood on the hearth until it had burned, and they wrote down her name.

The crew-leader who took the custodians down to the pump-house was a man of Muileann chrom named Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, broad and soot-grained, who had led the first thirty into the pit twelve years before. He did not say much. He showed them the thing as they asked, the way a man shows the road.

The pump stood in a house of stone at the mouth of the deep gallery, a great beam rocking on its pin over a shaft, and the water came up out of the hill in a black gush at every stroke and ran away down a trough to the burn. Beside it were the furnaces that drove it. Carts came up the track from the heaps in a line, and at each furnace-mouth a man knocked out the tail-board and the coal went in by the cartload, straight off the cart, without anyone looking at it. Fionnghal stood in the heat and watched six carts go in while Raghnall told the others how deep the gallery ran. Anndra mac Eòin's count, a whole year of his valley's cutting, would not have kept those fires a month.

A' Chompanaidh's chief agent heard them out in his office with the basket of papers on the floor beside his desk. He was civil. He said that he would send the council an account of the yield. Nine days later a packet came to the council at Cathair dhearg in the humans' tongue: a copy of A' Chompanaidh's accounts for the half-year, in columns of tons and marks, carefully ruled. Coinneach Glas read the totals aloud. The clerk put the accounts in the press in the corner of the hall, on the shelf where Fionnghal's letter lay.

## VII. Of the Oaks of Cathair fhada

The council's winter sitting of the twenty-fourth year was the last that Josiah Pell attended. He came to it in his closed carriage over A' Chompanaidh's bridge, as he had come for five years, and sat at the table in the chair the council kept for him, a grey heavy man by then, and heard the council's business through, and said at the end in his slow Dia-thìris that he was going home. On 15 an Gearran, AE 24, he sailed from Ros dhomhain, north-about, and did not come back. He had sat at the council's table for sixteen years, and Fionnghal, who had disliked him for most of them, found that she was sorry to see the carriage go down the hill for the last time.

Henry Maddox came to the council a week after in the same carriage. He was twenty-eight, fair and quick and pleasant, and he had learned a greeting in Dia-thìris on the ship, which he said to each custodian in turn round the table, with a small bow, getting it nearly right. He told the council that his orders were to double the yield of the pits. It came out as good news, a thing for the island to be glad of, and he looked round the table for the gladness. He did not speak of the letter in his pocket from A' Chompanaidh, which promised him a share of that doubling. The council never saw it. The copyists found it in the letter-books.

On 12 am Màrt, AE 24, Maddox bought the oak woods about Cathair fhada for pit-props. The custodians of Cathair fhada sold them for marks, being in debt to A' Chompanaidh's store for seed after a wet harvest, and the woodreeve of the town came up to the council to ask that the sale be undone. He was Eòghann mac Phàdraig, a lean man with bark-stained hands, and he stood where Fionnghal had stood and said his piece in a quarter of the time. The council heard him. Coinneach Glas said that the custodians of Cathair fhada had had the right to sell. The clerk entered it.

Fionnghal rode south with Eòghann the next morning. It was a day's ride down the valley into the country south of the capital, and they came into Cathair fhada at dusk, a town of grey stone on a long ridge with the oaks round it on three sides, bare and black in the last of the light, older than any house in it. Eòghann showed her the rule of the wood as they walked out into it at first light. Every spring at the feast of Brìde the town cast lots for one oak, and that one was felled for the town's need, a roof-tree or a keel or a mill-shaft, and six acorns were planted in the ring of its roots. So they had cut since An Aois Naomh. There were oaks in that wood that had been acorns in the time of the queens.

The lot had been cast that year before the sale. The oak it had fallen on stood at the wood's edge above the town, a broad old tree with a split crown, marked with a band of red ochre round the trunk at the height of a man's chest.

"The fellers come on the morning after next," said Eòghann. "We will cut ours first."

They cut it the next day, Eòghann and his two sons and four men of the town, with axes, the old way, taking the whole day over it. Half the town came out to watch, and the custodians who had sold the wood came too, and stood at the back. The oak went over in the late afternoon with a noise like a door slammed in a great house, and lay down along the slope with its crown in the bracken. Then Eòghann went down on his knees in the ring of its roots and planted six acorns out of his pocket, and his sons filled in the earth over them with their hands.

The fellers came on the morning after, as he had said, forty men in a line along the wood's edge with long saws from over the sea that two men worked between them, and A' Chompanaidh's carts waiting on the road below. Fionnghal did not stay to see them start. She heard the first saw as she rode out of the town, a harsh rasp, over and over, that followed her down the ridge.

She rode home east across the country, three days on the road with the creel of peats from Achadh naomh still tied behind her saddle, for she had not burned them. The coal-carts passed her at every ford. She came up the hill into Dùn dhearg on the third evening in a thin rain, and went into her own kitchen, where Tòmas Bàn had the grate heaped with coal against her coming, red and roaring, the whole room hot with it.

She had him rake it out. He looked at her, and did it, and carried the coals out in the scuttle to the midden and came back. Then she knelt at the cold grate and built the fire again herself out of the Achadh naomh peats, in a ring as she had seen it built at Sìleas nic Uilleim's hearth, and lit it. It was slow to take. The smoke went blue up the chimney and the smell of it filled the kitchen, and after a while it drew and burned low and red, and gave out less heat than the coal had. In the morning she sent Tòmas Bàn to find a man in the town who still knew how to cut peat, and to pay him whatever he asked.

Up in the old granary under the north wall the board of the counters hung on its two pegs in the dark, with the pegs of the last Samhain still in their holes.

# Chapter Eleven: Of the Eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich

*AE 25 – 29*

## I. Of the Heading under the Wild Hill

There is a leaf in the roll of Taigh na Fèithe, copied in Seilear Muileann chaol from a page gone brown at the edges, that holds nothing but eleven names. It has no heading. Each name stands on its own line with the name of a father or a mother after it and the name of a hearth after that, and at the foot, in a smaller hand, the day and the moon and three words for the place: under the wild hill. The letter-books of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach keep the same day in the humans' reckoning, and against it a single line from the agent of A' Chompanaidh at the workings: that a length of gallery had come down in unsound ground, and that the yield of the quarter would be short by so many tons. Between those two pages lies the tale of Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill in the years when the hill first began to take back what was taken from it, and the copyists, who had both before them, set down what the one knew and the other did not.

Raghnall was five-and-thirty in the spring of the twenty-fifth year. He had led a crew at the pit-mouth below Muileann chrom since the first ton was weighed, fourteen years before, and when A' Chompanaidh was sent away from Doire mhòr and opened its new working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, a short walk east along the hill, it was his crews it sent there first. He had three crews under him by then, near ninety souls, and a house at the top of the mill street with a byre and a good door, and a wife, Ciorstaidh, who had been a miller's daughter and could reckon faster than the clerk. They had one son, Dòmhnall, called after Raghnall's father, who was five that spring and followed his father to the pit-mouth whenever he was let.

The working at Cnoc fhiadhaich went into the hill on the level from a gully on its southern side, where the seam showed in the bank. The first gallery was the carters' road: a broad drift, high enough for a pony, with rails of oak laid down its floor and props of oak along its sides, square-cut and set in pairs with a cap across. That oak had come up from Cathair fhada the summer before, cartload after cartload, when Henry Maddox bought the woods about that town for the pits. Raghnall's crews had set every pair.

From the head of the drift the new gallery was driven north into the hill after the seam, and there the props stopped.

Maddox had come over the sea in the spring before with a letter that bade him double the yield, and he had read it aloud at the pit-mouth, in his own tongue and then through the young man of Ros dhomhain who put A' Chompanaidh's words into the island's. He was not thirty, with a clean jaw and a quick walk. What he wanted of Cnoc fhiadhaich was the heading: the gallery driven forward fast along the seam, so that the rooms could be opened off it on either hand and the coal come out of the hill from a dozen faces at once. The props, the agent said after him, would follow when the yield allowed. The oak was costly. It had come a long way.

So the heading went north, a yard and a yard and another yard, on the pay of the ton, with bare rock over it.

## II. Of the Colour in the Roof

Raghnall asked for timber the first time at the end of an Gearran. The heading was forty yards beyond the last pair of props, and the roof over it was a grey shale that split in leaves, and in the lamp-light, along the partings where it had begun to open, it had taken on a colour the old hewers had a word for. It was a sick yellow-green, like a bruise going off, or the underside of a toad; and every hewer's son of the hill had been taught to see it and to stop.

He took the agent in to look. The agent held his lamp up to the roof and looked for a long time, conscientiously, and then looked at Raghnall.

"Grey," he said. Then he said in his own tongue that the roof was dry and rang when he knocked it, and was the same rock as in the drift behind. That was true. The rock was the same. The colour was not, and the agent could not see it, any more than Stone and Mercer had seen the green in the sacks, fifteen years before, on the hill above the mill.

Raghnall asked a second time in am Màrt, and a third in the first week of an Giblean, when a leaf of shale the size of a door had come down in the night and been found across the rails in the morning. Ailean mac Dhùghaill, who led the second crew and had been his friend since they were boys on the mill-lade, came with him that time and stood beside him while he asked. The agent wrote the request in his book. He wrote that the crew-leaders wished for timber at the heading, and under it that the timber would be sent up when the next oak came from Cathair fhada, and he read both lines back to them through the young man of Ros dhomhain so that they should know it had been written.

"When is the next oak?" said Ailean.

The young man asked. The agent said the summer.

They went back to work. There was nothing else to do. The rate was on the paper, and the ton was on the beam, and the crews had had three hungry winters since Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig lapsed and the custodians' measure stopped paying; nobody on the hill that spring had a store of meal that would carry a family through a season with no pay. Raghnall told his crews to keep an ear to the roof and to come out if it spoke. Ailean told his the same. They set wedges of their own under the worst of it, split from old hurdles and fence-posts, which the agent did not forbid.

On 26 an Giblean, AE 25, the roof spoke, and nobody came out in time.

It was the middle of the forenoon. Raghnall was at the pit-mouth with the clerk, arguing over a tub that the clerk said was short and he said was full, when the air came out of the drift. It came in one push, like a breath from a man struck in the belly, and it carried a cloud of dust that rolled out over the tipping-floor and went up the gully in the sun, and after it, a long way behind, the sound. The men at the pit-mouth that morning said it was like a door shut in a far room of a great house.

He was in the drift before the dust had settled, with a lamp he did not remember lighting. The props stood, every pair, all the way to the head of the drift. Beyond the last pair there was no gallery. There was a wall of broken shale from floor to roof, and the roof had gone up into a black hollow over it that the lamp would not reach, and from somewhere in the hollow small stones were still coming down, one and then another, with a sound like rain beginning.

## III. Of the Eleven

They dug for three days. Every crew on the hill came, and men from the old cutting, and farmers from the villages who had never been underground in their lives and stood in a line passing baskets back into the drift, and the women at the pit-mouth taking the baskets and tipping them and passing them back. Raghnall would let no one go beyond the last pair of props without a timber over his head. They cut the timber out of the oak rails of the drift, board by board, prising up the carters' road to prop the fall, and the agent saw it and said nothing. On the first night they heard knocking. On the second they did not.

They brought them out one by one, as they were found. Calum mac Eòghainn came first, and his son Anndra, who was fifteen and had been hurrying tubs for his father since the winter, lay a yard behind him with an arm across his back. Then Pàdraig mac Coinnich; Murchadh Liath; Iain Crùbach, who had a bad foot and could hew sitting better than most men standing; Alasdair mac Fhionnlaigh; Lachlann Beag; Fionnlagh mac Sheumais; Mòr nic Artair, who dragged the tubs for the second crew and sang while she did it; Eòghann Donn. Ailean mac Dhùghaill was the last. They found him at the very head of the gallery, where the seam went on into the hill, with his pick under him and one of the wedges he had split from a hurdle still in his hand.

Raghnall carried him out himself. At the pit-mouth there was a crowd, silent, the whole hill; and among them, at the front, a short old man with shoulders like a yoke, who had not come down to the working in fourteen years.

Raghnall's father walked past him to where the eleven were laid out on the tipping-floor under their coats. He stood at their feet and looked at them each in turn. Then he turned to the mouth of the drift, black in the bank, with the dust still hanging in the light at its edge, and he began to say the words that are said at the face before a man puts his pick into the hill. He said them slowly, the whole of them, and the old hewers among the crowd took them up. Nobody had said them at that pit-mouth since the day it was opened. Most of the young men of the crews did not know them to the end, and stood with their mouths moving, a word behind.

When it was done old Dòmhnall looked at his son once, and went home up the hill.

The eleven were buried at Muileann chrom, in the ground above the mill where the hill's dead had always lain, on the fourth day after the fall. The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe came down to them. Seonag Liath was two winters dead, and the cutting was kept now by Marsaili nic Sheumais, a tall grey woman with ink on her fingers; and she stood at the head of the row of graves with the roll open on a board held by a boy, and read the names out, and wrote them in as she read them, each with the father and the mother and the hearth. She asked Raghnall the name of Mòr nic Artair's mother, which she did not know, and he did not know it either, and a woman in the crowd called it out, and Marsaili wrote it.

Then she asked him the name of the place, and he said, "Under the wild hill," and she wrote that.

That leaf is the one the copyists found. The agent's full report was slower. It went down to Ros dhomhain in his hand when the heading had been cleared, and was entered at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on 14 an Dàmhair, AE 25. It named no one. The agent gave the length of the fall in yards and the tons lost from the quarter, and it said that the gallery had been driven in unsound ground, and that the natives had been warned of the roof; and where it spoke of the dead at all, it called them *hands*.

Raghnall heard it read, later, by a carter who had got it from a clerk. He was quiet a long while after. Then he said that the ground had been sound enough when the oak was over it, and the carter, who had not been there, agreed that it likely had.

## IV. Of the Breakers at the Pit-Mouth

The heading was cleared by the midsummer, and timbered as it was cleared, pair by pair, with oak that came up from Cathair fhada in an t-Ògmhios after all; and the yield of the year was short, as the agent had written it would be, and nobody was paid for the days of the digging. That winter the cough came.

It began among the breakers. At every pit-mouth of the hill the coal came out of the drift in the tubs, and was tipped on the floor in the open, and there the children broke it. They sat in rows on low benches under a roof of hurdles, with a hammer each and a heap in front of them, and broke the big coal into the sizes the humans' furnaces wanted, and picked out the stone and the shale, and were paid by the basket. It was a thing that had come in with the ton. In the old cutting the custodians had never let a child near the face until he was old enough to say the words; but the old cutting worked a season in the year, and the pit-mouth worked every day there was light, and there was always more coal on the floor than hands to break it. The families were glad of the pence.

Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill went to the benches in the autumn after the fall, the month he turned six. He asked to go, because the other boys of the mill street went, and Ciorstaidh said he was too small, and Raghnall said no harm could find him on the floor in the daylight with his father fifty yards off. So Dòmhnall went, with a hammer that the smith cut down for him, and came home black every night, and was paid his first pence at the end of the week and gave them to his mother and would not eat his supper for pride.

The dust at the benches was thick on a still day. It hung under the hurdle roof in the low sun like smoke, and the children breathed it all the daylight long, and coughed, and spat black, as the breakers always had. Nobody thought much of that. Then in the new year, on 11 an Gearran, AE 26, a boy of nine at the Cnoc fhiadhaich benches coughed at his heap until he could not stand, and was carried home, and was dead within the week; and by the end of the month there were twenty coughing at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and most of them were breakers.

It was a dry cough. It had no wet in it and no fever, which the women said was the worst kind, because there was nothing to bring up and nothing to break. The fits came without warning, and the child would bend double with it and fight for breath with a noise like a saw in wet wood, and then it would pass, and the child would lie grey and tired and ask for water. Some had it a month and grew well. Some had it a month and did not. The hill called it An Casad Tioram, and had no other name for it, since there was nothing it was like.

Dòmhnall took it in am Màrt.

Raghnall sat with him through nine nights. He had the boy on his knee by the fire, wrapped in a blanket, upright, because lying down the cough was worse; and Ciorstaidh boiled water with pine-needles in it and held the steam to the boy's face, which an old woman of the mill street said would help and which did not. He would go an hour, two hours, sleeping, with his head on his father's chest and a small rattle in him like a stone in a jug, and then he would wake coughing and fight, and Raghnall would hold him and feel the whole of the small body go hard with it.

On the fifth night the surgeon of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise came up from Ros dhomhain, sent by A' Chompanaidh when the agent had counted the empty benches. He was a tired, kindly man who went round the houses of the mill street with a lamp and listened to each child's chest with an ear-trumpet of wood, and told each house through the young man of Ros dhomhain that it was a winter complaint and would pass with the spring. He left a brown bottle in every house that tasted of honey and something bitter. Dòmhnall spat it out.

On the tenth morning Dòmhnall slept through the dawn and woke without coughing, and asked for bread. Raghnall gave it to him, and went out to the byre, and stood with his forehead against the cow's warm flank for a long time before he came in again.

The spring came, as the surgeon had said, and the cough did not pass with it. It went on through an Cèitean, and through the summer, when the dust was dry and blew about the benches all day and the children came home with it in their eyes and hair. The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe asked the agent to shut the benches until the cough was done. He wrote the asking in his book. The benches stayed open, because the furnaces at the pit-mouth burned day and night now to drive the pumps, and wanted broken coal. By the end of an Lùnastal, when the first rains laid the dust and the coughing thinned, thirty-eight were dead at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and most of them were boys who broke coal at the pit-mouth, and some were their mothers and fathers, who had nursed them.

Dòmhnall lived. He was thin that year and small the next, and had a catch in his breath when he ran; but he lived, and in the autumn he went back to the benches with his cut-down hammer, and Raghnall let him.

## V. Of the Cart to Cill thais

When the cough was done there were children on the hill with nobody to keep them. Some had lost a father under Cnoc fhiadhaich and a mother to the cough after; some had lost both to the cough; and there were Anndra mac Chaluim's two small sisters, whose father and brother were both in the row above the mill, and whose mother had gone back to her own people at Muileann dhearg and not come for them. The neighbours took them in for the winter, as the hill always had. But the hill that winter was short of meal and shorter of marks, and the neighbours had breakers of their own coughing still, and by the spring of the twenty-seventh year there were fourteen children sleeping in other folk's byres whom nobody could feed through another season.

The word of it went west along the road with the carters. It came, in the way of such things, to the custodians of Cill thais, a large village on damp ground two long days west towards the capital, whose wardens kept the sacred wood; and in an Ògmhios the custodians of Cill thais sent a letter to Taigh na Fèithe to say that they would take the children in and keep a house for them at their own cost, for as long as the children needed a house. The roll of Cill thais sets it down on 6 an t-Iuchar, AE 27. The custodians of the hill, on the same page of their own roll, asked A' Chompanaidh to give something toward it. A' Chompanaidh sent a crate.

Raghnall drove the cart. Nobody asked him to. He had the loan of the miller's two ponies and the long cart with the hooped cover, and he put straw in it, and blankets, and the crate, and a sack of oatcake that Ciorstaidh baked, and on a grey morning in an t-Iuchar he stood at the top of the mill street while the fourteen were lifted in. The smallest was three. The eldest was Anndra's sister Seasaidh, who was eleven and held the three-year-old on her knee and would not let anyone else take her. Dòmhnall stood at the byre door and watched them go. He had broken coal on the benches beside four of them.

They were two days on the road. The first night they lay at a farm below the watershed, where the farmer's wife brought milk and would take no penny for it. The second day they went down the long road west through the hill country, past the old carters' house at the half-way stage, roofless now, with nettles in its yard and its sign-post leaning. The children looked at everything.
