Cill thais was a long street of low houses on a rise above wet meadows, with the dark edge of the sacred wood behind it, and the custodians had a house ready at the end of the street: a long house of stone with a new thatch, and beds of heather and blankets along both walls, and two women of the village to keep it, and a fire lit on the hearth, though it was high summer, because the children would be tired. Taigh nan Dìlleachdan, the village called it, the house of the orphans, and it had no other name. The warden who met the cart was an old man with a staff of black wood, and he lifted each child down himself, and asked each its name and its mother's name, and a girl beside him wrote them.

Then two of the village men took down the crate, and the warden had it opened in the street.

It was full of books. They were small books, bound in grey board, all alike, perhaps a hundred of them, and they were in the humans' letters, and in the humans' tongue; they were the primers from which Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise at Ros dhomhain was teaching the children of the humans' clerks to read. There was a picture of a lamb on the first page of each.

The warden took one out and turned the pages over slowly, the whole book, and looked at the lamb a while. Then he closed it and laid it back in the crate with the others and had the crate carried into the house and set on a shelf.

"They may learn to read them," he said. "Somebody may."

Raghnall drove home with the empty cart. On the long hill up from the half-way stage he stopped the ponies and sat on the tail of the cart for an hour with his head in his hands, and a carter coming down with a load of props from the south asked him if he was ill, and he said no.

## VI. Of the Light on the Eastern Cape

*Here the copyists leave the hills for a while, as the roll of Taigh na Fèithe does, and go east with the carters to the sea.*

In that same summer the second beacon of the island was lit, on the eastern cape at Baile ìseal, where the long slopes of the east run down out of the hills and the land ends in a shelf of black rock over the open water. There had been a fire on that cape since before An Aois Ailein, a driftwood fire in a ring of stones, kept by the households of the coast to bring the boats home in a storm. Twenty years before, Torcall Clachair had walked out to it with James Fenn and built the second of his five cairns above it; and the cairn had stood there, with the white stone on its cap, while the tower at Tobar dhearg went up in the south-west and was lit, and while the town waited for a tower of its own.

A' Chompanaidh came in the end, because its ships had begun to come round the south coast from Ceann leathan and go up the eastern shore, and two of them had touched on the rocks below the cape in the dark. It paid the masons and sent a lamp. It sent no mason of its own. The tower was built by the masons of the eastern coast under Torcall's direction, as the tower at Tobar dhearg had been, of the grey stone of the cape, and its lime was burned in a kiln on the shore with coal carted over the hills from Muileann chrom, a few loads of which, by the tally, had been cut by Raghnall's crews under Cnoc fhiadhaich in the spring of the fall.

Torcall was old by then, near seventy, and his knees had gone. He could not climb the headland. So they carried a chair out for him, a high-backed chair from the custodian's house, and set it at the foot of the headland on the flat turf above the shingle, where he could see the whole height of the tower against the sky; and he sat in it through the whole of a summer and an autumn and most of another summer, with a rug over his knees and a boy beside him to run messages up the path, and a long stick he pointed with. He could see a stone a finger out of true from the foot of the cliff, and he would send the boy up to say so.

The tower was lit on 4 an Lùnastal, AE 27. The whole town was on the cape to see it, and the households of the coast for a day's walk round, and the old fire in its ring of stones was lit beside the tower as it always had been, with driftwood. When the lamp caught at the top of the tower and the light went out over the water, the fishermen in the boats below the cape set up a shout; and Torcall, in his chair at the foot of the headland, was seen to take off his cap.

The keepers came from the fishing families. That was the first thing the custodians of Baile ìseal asked for, and they got it: the lamp would be trimmed and the stair climbed by the households who had kept the driftwood fire, and by no one else, and the families drew lots for the watches each Samhain as they had always drawn them for the fire. The second thing they asked for came the next spring, and they got that too, on 9 an Cèitean, AE 28. On the nights the boats went out to the deep grounds beyond the cape the lamp was to be lowered, lest the fish take fright at the great new light on the water and leave the grounds. The rule was kept. When it lapsed no one wrote down.

In the spring after the lighting, when the rule was granted and the keepers were at their watches, Torcall Clachair was put on a cart to go home west. A mile out of Baile ìseal, where the road tops the first rise of the moor and a traveller going east sees the tower for the first time over the heather, he had the carter stop. He had himself lifted down, and sat by the road on a stone, and had the boy bring him stones from the ditch, one by one, and laid them himself with his own hands on the turf beside him in a small cairn, no higher than his knee, each stone on two below it and a flat one for a cap. It took him the morning. Then he was lifted back onto the cart, and went home, and built no more. The cairn is there by the road, the carters say, and they put a stone on it when they pass.

## VII. Of the Offer and the Huts at the Ford

In the hills the yield of A' Chompanaidh was short three years together. Maddox's letter had bidden him double it, and it had not doubled. It had gone down.

The reason was not hard to find. The crews of the hill were hill men. They had fields, most of them, or their fathers had, small fields of oats and barley in the valley bottoms and on the lower slopes, and a few beasts on the hill; and when the harvest came in an Lùnastal they went home to cut it, as their grandfathers had gone home from the old cutting when its season was done. They had always done so. The contract said nothing against it. The first summer after the fall, a third of the crews went home to the harvest and stayed there through the autumn; the summer after the cough, it was half. Men who had carried their friends out of the heading, or buried a child from the benches, found they could do without the pence. The agent wrote it in his book.

In the spring of the twenty-ninth year he sent for Raghnall.

He received him in the new office A' Chompanaidh had built at the pit-mouth, a room of dressed stone with a glass window and a stove in it that burned the hill's coal. The agent had been at the hill five years and had some Dia-thìris now, and he did not send for the young man of Ros dhomhain. He gave Raghnall a chair, which Raghnall had not had in that room before, and a cup of something hot and brown that the humans drank, and then he made his offer.

Raghnall's crews were the best on the hill, the agent said; everyone knew it; and Raghnall was the man the hill listened to, as the agent had seen at the fall. A' Chompanaidh would pay him, over and above the rate of the ton, a leader's share on every ton his three crews brought up, paid to him and not to the crews, if he would keep them at the face through the harvest and the winter together. The share was written on a paper, and the agent turned it round on the table so that Raghnall could see the figure, and Raghnall looked at it for a long time.

Then the agent said the other thing, in the same voice. A' Chompanaidh had been buying the foreshores of the coast for its quays, he said, at Ceann fhada and elsewhere, and a good many fishing families of the coast had nails and no foreshore now, and would come up to the pits for pay if there was a roof for them. There was talk at Ros dhomhain of building one. If the hill men would not keep the face through the year, men from the coast would; and there would be no need then of a leader's share.

Raghnall said he would think on it. The agent said, of course.

He thought on it a month, and told nobody what he thought. The letter-books keep the paper, with his mark at the foot of it and a date in an Cèitean. He told Ciorstaidh the figure, and she reckoned it out on the table with beans, in marks and in meal, the way the mill had taught her, and it came to more than a hewer of the old cutting had seen in ten seasons. He did not tell his father. Old Dòmhnall heard it at the mill a week after, and came to the door of the house at the top of the mill street, and did not come in; he stood on the step and looked at his son, and at his grandson behind him, who was nine now and black from the benches, and then went back up the hill. They spoke after that of the weather, and of the boy.

So Raghnall kept his crews at the face through the harvest of the twenty-ninth year. He did it by going to each man's door, and sitting at each man's fire, and saying what the agent had said about the coast; and most of them heard him out and stayed, because he was Raghnall, who had led the first thirty and carried Ailean out of the heading, and because a man who goes home to his oats and finds his place at the face given to a stranger has neither oats enough nor a face. The yield of the year came up. The leader's share was paid on the first market-day after, to the penny.

And the coast men came anyway.

That same season the traders' boats of the new quay at Ceann òg, on the Abhainn ìseal, had begun to run their long lane round the capes to the capital's water, down the river past Cnoc bheag to the north coast and west along it, and round the western capes and south, the lane the boatmen called Seòlaid Ceann òg; and in the autumn A' Chompanaidh used the lane the other way about. It gathered the men of the foreshores at the capital's quays and shipped them in the traders' boats round the western capes and east along the north coast and up the Abhainn ìseal to the quay at Ceann òg, and they walked the last long day over the hills with their bundles. They were fishers and net-menders and the sons of salters, and they had never been under the ground. They came in companies of twenty, with a clerk of A' Chompanaidh in front and their wives and children behind.

For them A' Chompanaidh built the camp at Àth ìseal, a few miles north-west of Cnoc fhiadhaich, at the low ford below the new workings where the ferrymen of the hill had always put the carts across in the wet season. It was built in a month, of sawn plank on sills of stone, in rows: long huts with a door at each end and a stove in the middle, and a store at the head of the rows, and a well. There was no field and no byre and no burial ground, and no shrine. The roll of Taigh na Fèithe enters it on 6 an Dàmhair, AE 29, with a note in Marsaili nic Sheumais's hand that it had no custodian and had asked for none; and it was the first settlement on the island that had been made for nothing but the pit.

Raghnall walked over to see it on the evening the first crews moved in. It was raining. He stood on the rise above the ford with his hood up, where the ferrymen's path comes down, and looked at the three long huts with the smoke of their stoves going up flat into the rain, and the rows marked out in pegs beyond them for more. A man came out of the end of the nearest hut with a bucket and went to the well. He was a broad man with the rolling walk of a boat, and he stopped at the well and looked up at the hill to the east, where the workings were, and the heather going up black into the cloud; and he stood a long while at the well with his bucket, looking at it, as a man looks at a sea he does not know.

Raghnall did not go down to him. After a time he turned and walked home along the hill in the dark, past the mouth of the working at Cnoc fhiadhaich, where the drift stood dark under its oak, and down into Muileann chrom, where Ciorstaidh had kept his supper warm on the hearth over a fire of the hill's coal.

# Chapter Twelve: Of the Green River Run Black

*AE 30 – 35*

## I. Of the Stream at Doire mhòr

Seònaid Bhàn was twenty-five years old in the summer the stream stopped, and she had driven her father's cart on the hill road since she was fourteen. Her father was a carter of Cuan chrom, the little river town where the carriers' road from the capital comes down to a bend of the Abhainn fhionn and crosses it by the ford below the quay. At that quay, since An Aois Naomh, there had stood a carters' house with a hearth at either end, one for carriers going up to the hills and one for carriers coming down; and in the winter of Fiabhras nan Coigreach its roof had fallen in, and nobody had put it back. The carters cursed it as they passed, as men curse a friend who has died on them.

She was called Bhàn for her hair, which was the colour of oat-straw. She was tall and long in the arm, and the carters of the road let her sit at their fires as one of themselves, and said of her that she drove like a man and bargained like a custodian, and that the second was worse.

On 23 an t-Iuchar, AE 30, she took a load of lamp-oil up to the washing-floors at Cnoc fhiadhaich for A' Chompanaidh, twelve casks at so much the cask, paid in marks at the pit-head. It was a two-day haul from Cuan chrom, over the ford of Àth chiar and up into the hills. The washing-floors were new that spring. They lay in the valley bottom below the pit where the eleven had died five years before, long troughs of plank on trestles, down which a race of water ran over the broken coal to carry off the dirt; and the dirt went on down the valley in a grey stream to find its own way to the river.

She saw at once that the race was running higher than it had in the spring. She saw too where the water came from. Above the troughs, where the valley narrowed under the shoulder of the hill, there was a new bank of turf and clay faced with planks, and behind it a long brown pond with the drowned heather standing up in it. The stream that fed the pond came down off the high ground from the north, from the side of the hill where Doire mhòr stood among its oaks. It had watered Doire mhòr since there was a Doire mhòr. Now it went into the pond, and out of the pond by a wooden sluice into the race, and down the troughs over the coal.

Below the bank, in the old bed, there was a green trickle between dry stones, and a woman was kneeling there with a wooden pail, scooping.

Seònaid unloaded her casks and was paid. Then she walked up the old stream-bed towards the village. All the way up the stones were dry and the cress in the pools had gone brown, and at the top, where the path came out of the oaks into the village fields, she met a line of people coming down the slope with yokes on their shoulders and a pail at each end of the yoke. They were going down to the spring at the foot of the brae, below the oaks, which had been the cattle's spring and was now the whole village's. It was the better part of a mile each way, and a steep mile.

There were men in the line, and women, and children carrying jugs. The roll of Doire mhòr, which Beathag Dhubh kept in her own hand, names the households that carried that summer, and one of those who carried is Tormod, the son of Ruairidh who had stood behind Beathag at her door when she sent the agent of A' Chompanaidh down the hill. The roll gives him his name and his yoke and nothing more.

Seònaid slept that night in the byre of the custodian's house, and in the morning she went down to the washing-floors again with Beathag Dhubh.

## II. Of the Order That Was Not Written

Beathag Dhubh was forty-nine years old that summer, a small dark woman with a jaw like a quern-stone, and she walked down the hill with her hands clasped behind her back. She had asked Seònaid to come because Seònaid knew which of the strangers kept the book.

The man who kept the book at Cnoc fhiadhaich was Amos Tanner, an agent of A' Chompanaidh, a heavy young man with red wrists who sat in a timber office by the washing-floors with a ledger open in front of him and a stove going in the corner in the middle of summer. He spoke some Dia-thìris, badly and fast, and he stood up when Beathag came in, which was more than most of them did.

"The stream," said Beathag. "The stream of Doire mhòr. Show me the order."

Seònaid said it again for him in the carters' speech with the strangers, half of one tongue and half of the other, and he looked relieved, as a man looks who has been asked a question with an easy answer.

There was no order, he said. Nobody had ordered anything. The washing needed water and the stream was there. The bank had been thrown up in the spring by the washing gang, to hold a head of water for the dry months, and that was all.

"Then let it go," said Beathag.

Tanner said that he could not do that. The washing needed water.

"Who said you might take it?"

Nobody had said so, Tanner answered patiently. It had not needed saying. It was a stream on the hill, and the hill was worked by A' Chompanaidh under its contracts, and the water went with the working. If the custodian of Doire mhòr had a complaint, she might write it, and he would send it on to Ros dhomhain.

"To whom at Ros dhomhain?"

He did not know to whom. To the office.

Beathag looked round the timber room: at the ledger, at the stove, at the chart of the valley pinned to the planks, with the pond drawn as a neat blue shape and the stream above it as a line that came from nowhere. She put out one finger and touched the place on the chart where Doire mhòr would have been, if anyone had drawn it. Then she turned and went out without another word, and Seònaid went after her.

"He has no paper," Beathag said on the path. "So there is nothing to undo."

She wrote to the council all the same. The letter went down the road in Seònaid's cart, and Seònaid put it into the hand of a custodians' clerk at Cathair dhearg, and the council entered it; and the stream was not let go that season, nor the next.

## III. Of the Wet Harvest

The summer broke at the end of an t-Iuchar and it rained for a month.

In another year the hill villages would have taken their oats in between the showers, every hand in the field at the first dry hour. That year there were not the hands. The pits had been drawing the young men off the farms for twenty years, and faster in the six since the new Àrd-mhaor came over the sea with orders to double the yield: a son here for the ton-money, a brother there, a husband who came home at the week's end with coal in the lines of his face and slept the rest-day through. The old men and the women and the children cut what they could. The rest stood in the fields and sprouted in the ear, and in AE 30, by the end of Lùnastal, the hill villages of Muileann chrom had lost the better half of their harvest.

Seònaid carried meal that autumn. She carried it for A' Chompanaidh, from the quay at Ros dhomhain where it came off the ships in sacks stencilled in the humans' letters, up the carriers' road to the store at Àth ìseal, where the camp of timber huts stood at the ford below the new workings. She was paid for the haul in marks. At the store the meal was sold, over a counter, by a clerk with a steelyard, and it was sold for marks.

The hill villages had few marks. They had oats in a good year, and wool, and cheese. The clerk at Àth ìseal would not take cheese; he had no book for cheese. So the women came down to the store with the coins their men had brought home, and when those were spent they sent the men back to the pits for more.

Seònaid stood at the store door one wet evening in an Dàmhair, waiting for her own pay, and watched a woman from the high farms above Doire mhòr count coins onto the clerk's counter. There were not enough. The clerk pushed the sack back towards the wall. The woman stood and looked at it, and then she took off the brooch at her shoulder, which was bronze with a knot on it of the old kind, and laid it on the counter. The clerk looked at it and pushed it back to her with one finger.

Seònaid put two marks down beside the brooch, and the clerk took them, and the woman took the sack and went out without looking at either of them. Seònaid drove home the next day two marks short, and her father said nothing about it, which in her father was a kind of speech.

## IV. Of the Meal-Carts from the South

The south had had its own wet autumn, and it waited on its next harvest before it gave from it. In the autumn of the next year, when that harvest was in, the villages of Doire fhiadhaich, far down in the oak country of the south, loaded carts with meal and sent them north to the hill villages. They did it as Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte bade in a hungry year, as it had bidden since An Aois Naomh, and nobody asked them to and nobody paid them.

There were nine carts, with oxen, and they came up by Dùn chrom and struck the carriers' road below Cuan chrom in the second week of an Dàmhair, in the rain. They came down to the ford at dusk and stood looking at the roofless house at the quay with the rain running out of its doorways, and Seònaid's father went down with a lantern and brought them up to his own byre and hearth, and Seònaid made the porridge. They talked late, in the slow broad speech of the south.

The eldest of the drivers was a man named Gille-Brìde, an oak-keeper's son, who had brought his own grandson with him to show him the road. He asked how the hill villages were keeping, and what the meal was selling for at the stores, and Seònaid told him. He sat a while with his cup between his hands.

"For coin," he said at last.

"For their coin," said her father. "The marks."

"And where do the hill folk get their marks?"

"From the pits."

Gille-Brìde nodded slowly, like a man working a sum he did not like the end of. Then he said, "Well. They will not need to buy this."

The carts went on in the morning, over the ford at Àth chiar and up into the hills, and Seònaid went with them the first day to show them the road. She turned back at the Muileann chrom fork. It was not until the next week that she heard, at the store, what had become of them.

At the ford below Àth ìseal the agents of A' Chompanaidh had met the carts on the road. They wanted meal for the store and the camp, and they offered the southern drivers marks for it, more than it would fetch at any market in the south. The drivers said the meal was not for sale. The agents doubled the price. Two of the drivers, young men with debts at home, sold their loads there on the road and went home by another way. The other seven went on up into the hills and gave their meal away, sack by sack, at the doors of the villages, as the law bade.

Gille-Brìde's was one of the seven. He came back down the road a week later with his empty cart and stopped at Cuan chrom to thank her father for the byre, and Seònaid asked him about the two who had sold.

"They were paid," he said. "The agents paid them fair. More than fair." He rubbed his face. "That is the thing about it I cannot get round."

He went away south. Seònaid did not see him again. But that was the night she began to count in her head, as she lay awake, what a cart could carry, and what it could be paid in, and who could pay.

## V. Of the Chest for the Loft

In the same season a woman in a grey cloak came up the road from the capital driving a hired pony-cart with a chest roped into the back of it, and she stopped at Cuan chrom and asked for a bed.

She was Muireall nic Fhearchair, a copyist, a lean woman of forty-two with ink under her nails. Her aunt Gormshuil nic Fhearchair had died at Cathair dhearg in the last days of an t-Sultain, in her seventy-first year. Gormshuil had kept the council's list of the island's words since the ships first came, and she had been the custodian who would not sign Puingean a' Chalaidh, and she had taught herself the humans' letters at an age when most women are teaching their grandchildren. Now she was dead, and her papers were in the chest, and Muireall was carrying them east to the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais at Muileann chaol, where the old copies were kept, because Gormshuil had asked her to and because she did not trust them to stay safe anywhere nearer Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir.

Seònaid carried the chest in from the cart herself. It was heavier than it looked.

"What is in it?" she asked.

"Words," said Muireall. "Forty years of them. Hers and the strangers'."

She would not open it that night. But the next morning the rain held on, and the road was a river, and she could not go on; and in the afternoon, sitting at the hearth with nothing to do, she unroped the chest and lifted the lid and took out, from the top, a single leaf in a wrapping of oiled cloth. It was her own copy of the first leaf she had written, she said, in the third spring of the strangers, when Gormshuil and the cleric Wren had sat across a table at Cathair dhearg with a basket of coal between them. It was Clàr nan Dà Fhichead Dath, the colours of the coal, each with its name, forty names in two columns, in the old strokes and in the humans' letters side by side.

Seònaid could not read either. Muireall read the names to her, down one row and up the other: the purples and the greens and the fire-colours, the white of gual sneachda, the brown-red that is almost black. Seònaid knew most of them, as every carter of the hills did, for a carter who could not tell good coal from dross by its colour did not stay a carter long. She had never heard them said in a row before.

At the bottom of the leaf there was a note in a smaller hand. Muireall read that too. It said that the strangers had one word for all the coal of the vein, and that no word of the island answered it, and that they had not asked for the island's words.

"One word," said Seònaid.

"One."

"For all of that?"

Muireall wrapped the leaf again and laid it back in the chest.

"They cannot see it," she said. "My aunt was a long time understanding that. She thought at first they would not see it. It took her years to believe that they could not." She shut the lid. "The one word is the word for what it burns like. It is a good word for that."

The rain stopped in the night. In the morning Seònaid roped the chest back into the pony-cart and saw it over the ford, and Muireall went on east alone towards Muileann chaol, three days away, a grey figure beside a grey pony, until the road turned behind the shoulder of the hill.

That winter, as the copyists count it, the mountain began to be dug by the ton. A' Chompanaidh had weighed its coal by the ton since the first contract. From AE 31 it cut by the ton as well: the crews were set a weight for the week, and the galleries driven to meet the weight, and the hill was worked for ends that no custom of the Dia-thìrich would have chosen. At Dùn chrom the rope-walks that had spun cable for the fishing boats turned all their hemp to winding-rope for the pit-heads, and A' Chompanaidh paid well, and the town grew by half. Seònaid hauled the rope up to the hills in coils as thick as a man's thigh.

## VI. Of the Going Down from Doire mhòr

In the spring of AE 32 word came up the road that A' Chompanaidh had been chartered afresh in an Tìr Thall, with new money and a new name. The name was long, and the carters tried it out at their fires and gave it up, and went on calling it A' Chompanaidh. What they did take note of was that its agents at Ros dhomhain now outnumbered the clerks of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach four to one, and that a carter with a quarrel over a haul had stopped going to the office of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach at all. He went to the office of A' Chompanaidh, since that was where the quarrel would be settled.

The second summer of the carrying came, and the stream at Doire mhòr was not let go. The pond behind the bank had grown. The washing gang had raised the bank another two feet in the winter, and the drowned heather was gone under, and the brown water lay nearly to the oaks.

Seònaid went up to the village in an t-Ògmhios with a load of salt, and found it half empty.

The households had begun to go that spring, one family and then another, with no meeting called: a man away to the pits since the winter, his wife left carrying water for a field he would not come home to cut, and at last the wife packing the kist and the pots onto a borrowed pony and going down to him. Most went to the huts at Àth ìseal, where there was work breaking coal for the children and water that someone else carried. Others went on to Muileann chrom, or down the road to the capital. Seònaid passed them on the road, sitting on their bundles in the backs of carts.

The roll of Doire mhòr sets the first households' leaving under that year, and gives their names. Tormod, who had carried water up to Doire mhòr for two summers, went down to Àth ìseal with the rest.

Beathag Dhubh did not go. She stood at the door of the custodian's house as Seònaid unloaded the salt, with her arms folded, and watched the empty cottages across the green.

"You could go down to the council," Seònaid said. "Again."

"I have written to the council three times," said Beathag. "They have entered it three times." She took a pinch of the salt from the open sack and tasted it, and nodded. "They cannot give back a thing that nobody took."

In an t-Sultain of that year A' Chompanaidh began to load barges at Cidhe Beag. Cidhe Beag was the little quay on the Abhainn uaine, below Baile thais, where the river comes out of the hills wide enough to float a boat; it had been a canoe landing since before a' Scaradh, a shelf of flat rock at the water's edge with a ferryman's hut above it, and a shrine on the rock, a grey stone the height of a child with a hollow worn in its top where the boatmen had left their offerings going out. A' Chompanaidh widened the shelf with cut stone into a quay, and built a chute down to it from the cart-road for the coal.

Seònaid brought the first loads down to it herself, and she was there when the masons came to the shrine. The foreman, a Dia-thìreach of Ros dhomhain who did not like the work, sent for the ferryman before he touched the stone. The ferryman was old and weary in the face. He looked at the stone, and at the chute, and asked where they meant to put it.

The foreman said: wherever the ferryman liked, so long as it was off the quay.

So the ferryman chose a place on the bank above, under a rowan, where the stone could still see the water; and four masons carried it up on a hurdle, with the ferryman walking in front, and set it down where he showed them, and the ferryman put a little meal in its hollow from his own pocket. Then the masons went back to their work, and the first barge was loaded before dark.

## VII. Of the Green River

The Abhainn uaine is called the green river for the colour of the water under its alders, which in the old songs is the colour of a trout's back. That winter it turned black.

The washing-floors at Cnoc fhiadhaich and Muileann chrom, and the new ones built that year, all sent their dirt down into the streams, and the streams carried it into the Abhainn uaine. At first there was a dark edge along the banks after rain. Then the pools below the landing silted, and the gravel of the fords went under a grey mud that stank when it was stirred. By the turn of AE 33 the whole river from Cidhe Beag to the sea ran thick and dark, and the barges went down it to Seann Toll and the river mouth on water the colour of a slate roof.

The strangers called it black. To a Dia-thìreach eye it was never only black. When the sun came through onto it at a bend there was colour in it, the colours of the coal ground to dust and gone to sludge, purple and bottle-green and a dull fire-colour, drifting in long streaks the way oil drifts on a puddle. Seònaid stood on the bridge at Cidhe Beag one bright morning with the ferryman and watched the streaks go under, and neither of them said anything about it. There was nothing to say that the other could not see.

At the river's mouth, at Ceann leathan, the fishermen had netted salmon on the spring run every year that anyone could remember. The town took its share at the mouth and let the rest go by to spawn in the gravel of the hills. In the spring of that year the run was thin. In the summer it was thinner. The last salmon netted at the mouth of the Abhainn uaine was taken that year, a hen fish of no great size, and the man who landed it is remembered by name at Ceann leathan, and he did not want to be; for he gutted it and found it empty of eggs. In the next spring no fish came in at all. The gravel where they had spawned was under the grey mud, and the fish of the sea do not go up a river that has nothing for them at the top.

The fishers of Ceann leathan went on calling it the Abhainn uaine. They said it with their mouths turned down, and the bargemen laughed at them, and the fishers did not laugh back.

Other coal went north from Cidhe Beag by the river road to Baile Mòr dhomhain, the old walled market town on its deep river, and the town grew fat on it. Its people doubled in number, most of the newcomers bargemen from the coast who slept in the lofts over its stables; and the old families complained of them at every market and let them rooms at every chance. Seònaid hauled there twice that year. It had too many inns, she said, and none of them any good.

That was the year she married. Her husband was Pàdraig mac Artair, a carter of Doire chaol, the carters' village just east of the capital, a broad slow man who sang when he drove and was the only carter on the road who could outbargain her; and she said afterwards that she married him to have the benefit of it, which may have been true. They lived in her father's house at Cuan chrom. Their son Murchadh was born there the next winter, in the room above the byre, while the roofless carters' house stood by the quay with the frost in it.

## VIII. Of the House at the Half-way

In the first month of AE 34 a surveyor of A' Chompanaidh went out to a valley in the hills north-west of Muileann chrom with a chain and a book of squared paper, and laid out a town. He drew it before a stone of it was set, streets set square to one another and a row of little houses all alike on either side, with a store and a pay office at the end. The camp was called Baile dhomhain, the first town of the Dia-thìrich drawn on paper before it was built. Within two seasons it was full, a hundred souls and more. Seònaid hauled timber for its roofs. She said to Pàdraig that it was a town for people who would not be staying, and he asked her where else they would go, and she did not answer.

That spring the traffic on the road was heavier than it had ever been, and every night there were carters at Cuan chrom with nowhere to sleep. Some slept in their carts, and some in her father's byre until there was no more room in it, and the rest built fires under the broken walls of the old carters' house and drank and quarrelled there; and in an Giblean one of them knocked another into the ford.

Seònaid went and stood in the roofless house the next morning. The two hearths were still there, at either end, under a litter of fallen thatch and nettles. The walls stood to the height of a man. The lintel over the western door was a single stone with a groove cut in it, worn smooth by the hands of the carriers of An Aois Naomh who had touched it going in, and of every carrier since.

She went home and told her father and Pàdraig that she meant to put the roof back.

Her father thought it a great deal of money. Pàdraig thought it a good idea, and went round the carters of Doire chaol, and came back with twenty of them who would give a week's work each for a year's lodging at half the price. Seònaid went to the custodians of Cuan chrom, who held the quay, and they gave her the house for a rent of one cheese a year, since nobody else had wanted it for twenty years and more. The timber for the roof came up from the oak country of Doire fhiadhaich, on carts she sent south for it. The slates came from the quarry at Àth chiar. The strangers' iron was in the nails and the hinges, and nowhere else.

She opened the doors on the first day of Lùnastal, 1 an Lùnastal, AE 34, on the feast, with a fire lit at both hearths and a bowl of new ale for any carter who came in; and she kept the old name, An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, because nobody on the road had ever called it anything else.

On the first night a carter from the hills came in with his crew, and asked the price of a bed and a supper, and when she told him, he put down a round cheese and a fleece on the table.

"I have no marks," he said. "Not till the week's end."

A carter of the capital, at the other end of the table, laughed and said that she would want marks. Every house on the road wanted marks now. A' Chompanaidh paid in marks and the stores sold in marks, and a cheese was a cheese.

Seònaid picked up the cheese and turned it over and smelt it. Then she weighed it in her two hands.

"That is a bed and a supper," she said. "And the fleece is two."

The carter from the capital stopped laughing. "And if I pay in marks?"

"Then it is a bed and a supper for marks. The same bed. The same supper." She put the cheese on the shelf behind her. "I will take the one or the other. I will take them at the same rate. And I will not ask which a man has before I tell him the price."

That was the rule of the house, and she had it cut on a board and hung over the hearth at the eastern end, in the old strokes, since that was what most of the hill carters could read: *Bonn no bathar, an aon bhobhla.* Coin or goods, the same bowl. She kept it all the years she kept the house, the only keeper on the road who took both; and the carters of the hills, who had cheese and wool and no marks, came to her, and the carters of the capital came to her also, since the ale was good.

In an t-Sultain the road-gangs of A' Chompanaidh finished metalling the carriers' road from the capital by Doire chaol and Cuan chrom and the ford of Àth chiar, up to the workings in the hills, broad enough for two coal-carts to pass. They laid it in crushed stone and rolled it with an iron roller that twelve men pulled. At every mile there stood an old post with the crown's sign cut in it, the posts that had marked the road since An Aois Scaraidh, and the road-gangs left them standing, since it was less trouble to go round. The carters, whose road it had been since An Aois Naomh, began to call it Rathad na Mèinne, as if it had been made the day before. Seònaid called it that too, after a while.

## IX. Of the Carters at Her Table

The carters of Doire chaol met first in her house in the winter, round the eastern hearth, because they were on the road and it was the only house on the road where they could all afford to sit down.

There were some thirty of them in the end, with Pàdraig among them, and they had one grievance, which was the rate. A' Chompanaidh paid by the ton for coal hauled from the hills to the capital, and set the rate at its office in Ros dhomhain, and had lowered it twice in two years; and a carter who would not haul at the new rate found carters from the coast who would. Each man had gone to the office in his turn. None had gone together.

They sat in Seònaid's house through the dark of the year and argued it. Some of them were for refusing the hauls outright. Some of them were for going to the custodians. Pàdraig, who was slow, and who had listened to his wife count carts in her sleep for three years, said that they should go to the office all together, all thirty, on the same day, and ask for the old rate, and that no man should take a haul at the new one until they had it. And they swore to that at her table, on the ale, with their hands on the board with the rule on it; and in an Giblean of AE 35 the carters' guild of Doire chaol went down to Ros dhomhain, thirty carts in a line, and stood in the yard of A' Chompanaidh.

It was the first Dia-thìreach guild of the age. A' Chompanaidh might have broken it with the carters from the coast; but those men did not know the road or the fords, and they lost wheels and loads in the ditches; and the clerks at Ros dhomhain did the sum, and found that it came cheaper to bargain with thirty men who knew the road than to break them. So A' Chompanaidh let the guild stand. It sent an agent up to meet the carters. And since the carters would not come to Ros dhomhain again, the agent came to them, to the house at the half-way stage of the road, where they met.

The agent was Amos Tanner, older and heavier now, who had been given the carriage of the coal as his charge. He came up Rathad na Mèinne on a grey horse on a hot evening at the start of an t-Iuchar, and tied the horse at the door, and ducked his head under the grooved lintel, and stood a while at the eastern end of the room reading the board over the hearth, or looking at it, since he could not read it.

"What does it say?" he asked her.

She told him.

He thought about it. "And the ale, if I pay you in marks?"

"The same," said Seònaid, and gave him a bowl.

The carters were at the long table under the window. Tanner sat down at its head, with his book in front of him, and Pàdraig sat down at its foot. The first thing Tanner told them was that the landing at Seann Toll on the Abhainn uaine had been taken for a coal stage three days before: that A' Chompanaidh had built a loading-stage of timber there below the workings, and moved the town's fishing boats to the next reach down, and that from now on a good part of the coal of the hills would go down the black river by barge to Ceann leathan, and on by ship, and never come near the capital at all. There would be less hauling on the road.

The carters had seen the barges at Cidhe Beag, and heard it without surprise. Pàdraig asked how much less.

Tanner told him. Then he named the rate for what was left.

Pàdraig named the old rate back to him. Tanner shook his head and named a figure halfway between. Pàdraig looked down the table at the others and then at his wife, who was standing at the hearth with the jug, and she did not move, and he named the old rate again.

Seònaid filled the bowls. The windows were open for the heat, and the long light lay across the table between the agent's ledger and the carters' hands. Across the room at the other hearth a hill carter was paying for his supper with a basket of eggs, and she went and took them from him, and counted them, and gave him his change in a quarter of a cheese.

At the long table they were still bargaining when the light went. She lit the lamps.

# Chapter Thirteen: Of Raghnall Maor

*AE 36 – 41*

## I. Of the Barges Going Down

In the winter of the thirty-sixth year the coal of the hills began to go to sea by the river.

A' Chompanaidh's stage at Seann Toll stood finished below the workings, three miles down the valley from Muileann chrom, a loading-stage of timber with a crane on it, where the town's boats had been drawn up for as long as the town had stood. The barges loaded there. They went down the Abhainn uaine on the current, and at Ceann leathan, where the river comes out through the flats into the southern sea, A' Chompanaidh's ships lay at the mouth and took the coal aboard in baskets. From there the ships went out by Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, west along the south coast to the wild strait and the open sea, and round, the long way, north-about, for home.

The fishers of the south coast had worked that lane for five hundred years. On 31 am Faoilleach, AE 36, the custodians' roll of Ceann leathan enters that a coal ship coming out on the ebb ran down a fishing boat of the town off the river bar, and that the two men in her were taken out of the water alive by their neighbours, and the boat was not. The harbour-men said afterwards that she was too big to stop, and that likely nobody aboard her had seen the boat at all. Within a season the boats of Ceann leathan had learned to keep inshore of the ships' track and to lie to at the bar when a hull came down.

Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill walked down to Seann Toll the week the first barges loaded, to see it for himself. He stood on the new stage in the rain among A' Chompanaidh's men, and watched his own crews' coal go into the hold of a barge and the barge go off round the bend of the river with the current under her. The water of the Abhainn uaine had been green when he was a boy. It ran the colour of slate now.

He was forty-five that winter, and had led crews on the hill since the first ton was weighed. He had three crews under him and a leader's share on every ton they cut, a son grown tall, a wife who could reckon faster than the clerk, iron picks for every man he worked with, and lamp-oil to spare. As he walked home up the valley, a hewer he had known all his life stood aside for him on the stones of the ford, which had never happened before.

## II. Of the Staff

The agent sent for him in an Cèitean.

The agent of A' Chompanaidh at the pits of Muileann chrom in those years was Enoch Pratt, a narrow, bald, careful man who had come up from Ros dhomhain the year before the fall under the wild hill and had not been down again since. He kept the office of dressed stone at the pit-mouth, with a stove in the corner that burned the hill's coal day and night, and he used his Dia-thìris sparingly, as a man spends coin in a strange market.

This time Pratt came round the desk and shook Raghnall's hand, as the humans did with each other. Then he took up a thing that had been leaning against the stove, and held it out across his two palms.

It was a staff of ash, a little taller than a man's shoulder, straight and pale and new, with a cap of brass at the head and a ferrule of iron at the foot. On the brass were cut the letters of A' Chompanaidh, and under them a small ship with three masts.

"For you," said Pratt in Dia-thìris. For the rest he sent for the young man of Ros dhomhain who had put A' Chompanaidh's words into the island's at the first contract, and who was not young now.

A' Chompanaidh, the interpreter said, had watched the crews of Muileann chrom since the first ton. Raghnall's crews cut more than any on the hill, and other men listened to him, and its agents could not stand at every face. It wished to set one man of the island over all the crews of the hill of Muileann chrom: to see the work done, to keep the tally of the tubs, to put men on and put them off, and to answer for all of it to the agent. For this he would have a wage paid in marks, weekly, whatever the tubs came to; a house, to be built at A' Chompanaidh's charge; and this staff, so that any man on the hill might know him.

Raghnall looked at the staff for a long time. He did not take it.

"Over the crews," he said at last. "Over the hewers of the hill. Over my own people."

The interpreter put it into the humans' tongue. Pratt answered without any pause.

"Over the work," the interpreter said. "The agent says, over the work. The men are your people still."

Raghnall knew what the old men would say, and what his father would say, standing on the step and not coming in. He knew too what the hill had been these last years: the eleven under the fall, the boys coughing at the benches, the agent's men with their watches shouting at crews who had not the words to shout back. He thought that if there must be a man set over the crews it had better be a man who could say the words at the face and knew where the ground was bad. Then there was the wage in marks, every week, in rain or drought; and there was his son. Afterwards, when men asked him why, he gave each of these reasons at one time or another, and every one of them was true.

On 19 an Cèitean, AE 36, he put out his hands and took the staff, and the clerk wrote it down. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill was forty-six years old.

It was lighter than it looked. He walked home with it down the mill street in the evening, holding it a little away from his body, as a man carries a thing he has been lent. The men on the bench outside the smithy stopped talking as he came by, and looked at the staff, and then at the ground. At his own door his son Dòmhnall was sitting on the step mending the strap of a coal-basket, and he looked up, and his hands stopped.

"What is it?" the boy said.

"It is A' Chompanaidh's," said Raghnall, and went in, and stood the staff in the corner by the hearth where the peat-spade stood, and it was taller than the spade.

Ciorstaidh asked him what the wage was, and he told her, and she did not reach for the beans to reckon it. She said it was a fair wage, and set the supper on the board.

Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill was sixteen that spring. He had broken coal at the benches from the autumn he turned six, the year of An Casad Tioram, and lived, and at twelve had gone below into his father's crews. He was a long, rawboned lad with his grandfather's shoulders and his mother's quick eyes and a way of watching before he spoke. All through supper his eyes went to the staff in the corner with the firelight on its brass, and he did not ask about it again.

## III. Of the Slate Roof

The house went up that summer on a shelf of the hillside above the mill, where the ground had been common grazing, with A' Chompanaidh's masons from Ros dhomhain to build it and A' Chompanaidh's carts to bring the stone. It had two rooms below and a loft above, glass in the windows, and a roof of slate, the first in Muileann chrom, where the hill roofed with heather and rushes. When the roof was done it stood out above the mill from as far off as the ford, and threw back the light like the water of a loch.

On 17 an t-Ògmhios, AE 36, the roll of Taigh na Fèithe enters, in the hand of Marsaili nic Sheumais, that Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom has taken A' Chompanaidh's staff and a house with a roof of slate, and is set over the crews of the hill. It is the last entry in that roll to give him his father's name alone.

It was the miller's wife who said the other name first, or so the hill told it. She was a sharp woman, and she had known Raghnall since he was a boy stealing her apples. The week the family moved into the new house she stood at the mill door and watched him go by up the road with the staff, and said to the women at the well, loud enough to carry, "There goes Raghnall Maor to his castle."

The women laughed. The name went down the hill before nightfall. By the end of the summer it was the only name the crews used.

The Dia-thìrich had called the strangers' governor at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir An t-Àrd-mhaor since the first of them came, the high steward. A maor was the lesser thing: a bailiff, a man who held another man's keys and gathered another man's rents. The name said whose keys Raghnall held.

He heard it before the summer was out. He was going along the heaps at the pit-mouth with the tally-board, counting tubs, and one of the boys at the benches said it behind him, not meaning him to hear. Raghnall turned round. The boy went white. Raghnall looked at him, and then went on counting, and did not turn round again; and that night he sat long at the fire in the slate-roofed house and listened to the rain on the roof. It made a harder, thinner sound than rain on thatch, and he found he did not like it.

## IV. Of the Number in the Roll

A' Chompanaidh did not stop at one.

Within the year there were overseers at Achadh dhomhain, where the new galleries were being opened into the hill, at Àth ìseal among the timber huts, at Cnoc fhiadhaich over the old fall, and at the pits along the valley towards Seann Toll; and at each of them a man of the island with an ash staff and a brass cap, answerable to the agent.

Marsaili nic Sheumais had entered Raghnall in the roll by name. She entered the second overseer by name, and the third, and the fourth. Then she laid down her pen, and closed the roll, and walked over the hill to Taigh na Fèithe to put it to the custodians of the vein.

What the custodians said to her is not in the roll. What the roll holds is the entry of 21 an Lùnastal, AE 37, in Marsaili's hand, which reads: "Over the crews of the hill, set by the strangers, overseers: seven." There are no names. The next year the number is nine, and the year after that it is twelve, and the roll goes on so, a number under the date, through all the years after. Asked why, she said that the roll was for the vein and for those who kept it.

Raghnall could not read, but he knew what was in the roll, as everyone on the hill knew, and one evening at Taigh na Fèithe, where he had gone with the tally for the custodians as crew-leaders had always done, he asked Marsaili to read him the line.

She read it. "Overseers: seven."

"And my name?"

She turned back the leaves to the summer before and found it and read it out: Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, the staff, the slate roof. Then she turned the leaves forward again and closed the book.

"That is the last of it," she said. "There will be no other."

Raghnall stood a while in the doorway of Taigh na Fèithe with his staff. Then he said good night, and Marsaili said good night, and he walked home in the dark over the hill and did not light his lamp.

Raghnall was good at the work, and that was the worst of it. Knowing where the roof was rotten, and which roof had the sick colour in it that no human could see, he could tell the agent so, and sometimes the agent listened. That year there was no fall on the hill of Muileann chrom, and the tonnage went up, and Pratt wrote to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in praise of the first overseer of the island.

What he minded was the singing. The crews had always sung below, the old slow songs of the vein that go with the swing of a pick, and he had sung with them for twenty-five years. Now he would come along a gallery with his lamp and his staff and hear the singing ahead of him in the dark, and it would stop before he reached it, and the men would be working without a word, and would look up and say "Raghnall," civilly, and wait for him to go by. When he had gone by, after a while, the singing began again behind him.

His son was in one of those crews. Dòmhnall said nothing about it at home, and Raghnall did not ask.

## V. Of Seumas Dubh

Seumas Dubh had come into Raghnall's crews as a lad of fifteen, in the fourth year of the pit.

He had been born in the winter before the ships came down from the north, a black-haired hewer's son of the valley below Muileann chrom, strong and quick and given to laughing. When A' Chompanaidh opened its new pits at Cnoc mhòr, a morning's walk south of the hill over the moor, and asked Raghnall for a man to set over them, Raghnall gave Seumas's name; and Seumas took the staff and went south in the spring of the thirty-seventh year with a cart of tools and his wife and his two children, to a crew of the new men of Cnoc mhòr who had never worked a seam before.

The pits at Cnoc mhòr were driven down a slope, and the coal came up out of them in tubs on a haulage, a rope of hemp from the rope-walks of Dùn chrom running over a drum at the top that a horse turned. A' Chompanaidh wanted the tubs hurried. Maddox's orders were still to double the yield. Seumas hurried them. He ran the tubs up three at a time on the one rope, which the crews said it would not bear, and set the boys to run the empties down the slope so that the horse need not stop.

On 14 an Lùnastal, AE 38, the rope parted with three full tubs on it. They came back down the slope and through the gallery-mouth, and a boy was coming up the rails with an empty and could not get out of the way. His name was Coinneach Beag and he was eleven. The custodians' roll of Cnoc mhòr has his name and his age, and the name of his mother; A' Chompanaidh's report of the day gives "a boy" and the cost of the rope.

What happened then happened below, in the dark, and the men who were there did not tell it the same way twice. Seumas came down the slope with his staff when he heard the tubs go, and went into the gallery-mouth, where the crew had the boy out from under the iron and were kneeling round him. Somebody said something. Seumas said something back. It is told that he said the boy should have jumped, and it is told that he said nothing of the kind and only asked whether the tubs were broken; and either way a hewer stood up with a pick-helve in his hand. When the agent's man came down the slope with a lantern there were two dead in the gallery-mouth, the boy and the overseer, and the crew standing about them, and nobody running. Seumas Dubh was thirty-eight years old.

Before that month was out A' Chompanaidh hanged two men at Ros dhomhain for the killing of him.

Maddox ordered the overseers down to see it. Every man of the island who held A' Chompanaidh's staff was to be at Ros dhomhain on the day and stand in front. Pratt told it to Raghnall in his office without looking at him, and then the interpreter told it again in Dia-thìris.

Raghnall went, thirty-five miles by the road in A' Chompanaidh's cart with the four other overseers of the hill, and none of them said much. They lay a night at the carters' house. Seònaid Bhàn served them and took their marks and said nothing, but the carters at the other end of the room drank up and went out.

They hanged them on the open ground between the lake shore and the rise where Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir stands, on a frame of new timber put up the day before, with the guards of A' Chompanaidh round it in a square. It was a still, bright day at the end of summer, and the lake behind the gallows lay flat as a board. A great crowd had come, humans and Dia-thìrich both, and they made almost no sound. The overseers were put in a row inside the square, in front of the crowd, with their staffs, where the crowd could see them. There were fourteen of them, from all the workings of the island. Raghnall stood at the end of the row nearest the gallows.

The two men were brought out of the guardhouse under the rise with their hands tied. One was a big man with a cut over his eye, and the other was young. The roll of Cnoc mhòr gives their names, Eòin Ruadh and Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, hewers of that town, and the day, and that they were carried home and buried in the town's ground on their neighbours' shoulders; the letter-book of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir gives "two of the crew." A clerk read the sentence in the humans' tongue from a paper, and nobody put it into Dia-thìris. A chaplain of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise said a prayer, which nobody put into Dia-thìris either.

As they were brought past the row of overseers the young one, Fionnlagh, turned his head and looked along them. He looked at every face, one after another, as though he were counting them, and when he came to the end of the row he looked at the staff with its brass cap in Raghnall's hand, and then at Raghnall. He did not say anything. Then they took him up.

Raghnall watched it. He had been ordered to, and he found afterwards that he could not have looked away if he had tried. He had carried the fever dead of Cuan shean and dug out the eleven, and had thought there was no way of dying left that he had not seen. This was slow. The crowd made one long sound when the young man's feet left the cart, and then was silent, and in the silence Raghnall could hear the water of the lake lapping at the shore stones behind the gallows, and a gull.

The roll of the custodians of Ros dhomhain enters that day as the first on which a man of the island was put to death by the strangers' law on the island's ground. It enters too, in a line of its own, that the overseers of A' Chompanaidh stood in front.

On the road home they lay again at Seònaid's house, and one of the overseers of the hill, a man of Àth ìseal, left his staff leaning against her wall when he went up to bed. In the morning it was gone. He told the agent he had lost it, and A' Chompanaidh gave him another.

Raghnall kept his. He carried it into the house above the mill and stood it in the corner by the hearth, and sat down at the fire with his hands on his knees, as his father had sat on the night of the first ton, and did not speak all evening. Ciorstaidh put his supper by him and took it away again cold. Dòmhnall, who was eighteen now, sat across the fire and watched him. At last the young man got up and made up the fire and went to bed. On the stair to the loft he stopped and said, without turning:

"The men at the face are saying that you gave Seumas Dubh his staff."

"I did," said Raghnall.

Dòmhnall waited, but there was no more, and he went up.

## VI. Of the Priest at the Gate

A few weeks after the hanging Maddox barred the priests of the hawk from the camps.

The order came down from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on 12 an t-Sultain, AE 38, and the overseers read it at every pit-mouth on the hill. It said that the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig were not to come within the bounds of any working or any camp of A' Chompanaidh, for their preaching slowed the work and put the crews in fear. It said nothing of the chaplains. The chaplains of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise kept their chapels of plank in every camp as before.

The hawk had many friends in the camps. Men who worked below found the old teaching of Mòd, An Seabhag Acrach, easier to believe than most things: that the land feeds whoever eats in measure, and the hawk starves whoever eats faster than the land can feed him. The hawk-priests came up from the west in ones and twos, with a hawk's feather bound in the hair behind the ear, and preached at the pit-mouths at the change of shift.

Several of the overseers were hawk-faithful themselves. The roll of Taigh na Fèithe says so, under the number, which is the only thing it ever says about them.

Raghnall was at the gate of the camp at Àth ìseal the week the order came, with Iomhar Bàn, the overseer of the huts there, a heavy grey man of the coast who had worn the hawk's feather behind his ear at every feast since he was a boy, and had taken it out when he took the staff. A priest came along the road from the west in the evening. He was old, with a bag on his back, and the crews coming off the shift began to gather at the gate.

Iomhar went out into the road to meet him. Raghnall stayed at the gate, and heard it.

"You cannot come in, father," said Iomhar. "It is A' Chompanaidh's order."

"I have not come for A' Chompanaidh," said the priest.

"The crews are A' Chompanaidh's while they are inside the fence. I will lose the staff, father. I have children."

The priest looked at him a while. Then he put down his bag in the road and sat on it. "Then the crews may come out," he said.

They came out. They came out through the gate past Raghnall and Iomhar, forty and fifty of them, black from the shift, and sat down in the road round the old man in the dusk, and he preached to them there, outside the fence, where the order did not run. When the sermon was done and the men were going back in, he went out into the road himself, and knelt in the mud, and the priest put his hand on his head.

Raghnall did not kneel. He had never been much given to the hawk. He stood at the gate and watched, and when Iomhar came back past him with mud to his knees neither of them said anything about it, then or after. Pratt heard of the sermon in the road and wrote to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that the order had been obeyed, as it had.

## VII. Of the Spotted Pox

In the autumn of the thirty-ninth year a ship of A' Chompanaidh came up the Abhainn gheal into the lake and tied up at the quays of Ros dhomhain with sickness aboard, and on 11 an Dàmhair, AE 39, the custodians of Ros dhomhain entered the first of their dead of A' Bhreac Bhallach.

It did not stay on the quays. It went up Rathad na Mèinne as the coal came down, stage by stage, and in the last days of an Dàmhair it came into the camps.

Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill turned twenty that autumn. He was a hewer at the face in the gallery below Cnoc fhiadhaich, and his crew was the first on the hill to lose a man, a carter's son of Àth ìseal who had fetched a cask up from the ford. The fever came first, then the spots, which filled and broke. Some lived and were marked for life. More died, the children most, in the huts at Àth ìseal where the families lay six and seven to a room, and at Achadh dhomhain, which was the worst on the hill.

A' Chompanaidh did not stop the pits. The ships lay at Ceann leathan waiting for their loads. It was the overseers who went round the huts each morning with the agent's list to see which men were fit for the face, and stood in the doorways, and saw what was inside, and went on to the next. Dòmhnall went down to the face every day that winter with the men who were left, and in the evenings he carried with the others. They buried the pox dead in new ground below Achadh dhomhain, stony ground, dug by lamplight.

Twice that winter Dòmhnall saw his father at the burying ground with the staff in his hand, standing at the edge, where the agent's clerk stood with A' Chompanaidh's book. He did not go to him. Once, coming up from the pits with a hurdle, he found his father at the door of a hut at Àth ìseal where a whole family was down, a hewer and his wife and four children, with no one to fetch water; and Raghnall had put the staff down against the wall and was carrying the water in himself, two buckets at a time from the ford, with the brass of the staff shining by the door where anyone going by could see it. Dòmhnall stopped. His father looked up and saw him, and said, "Take the other buckets," and Dòmhnall took them.

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise kept a count. The chaplain at Àth ìseal, a young man lately come over the sea, went among the huts with a vinegar cloth over his mouth and wrote down every dead man, woman and child he could find, in a fair hand; and his list went down to Ros dhomhain with the lists of the other chaplains, and the chaplains' count of the whole sickness was twenty-seven.

The custodians kept a count also. Marsaili nic Sheumais went round the hill in the spring with her book, from hearth to hearth and camp to camp, and wrote down the dead as the households gave them to her, the ones the chaplains had not found and the ones who had gone home to die among their own people. Then the custodians of the hill asked the chaplains for a copy of their list, and the chaplain gave it to them readily, for he was proud of it; and they wrote their own names in the margin of it, down the whole length of both sides, in the old letters, with the total at the foot. They sent it back to Ros dhomhain, where it was filed.

The pox went on south from the harbour through the winter and into the next year. On 9 an t-Samhain, AE 40, it reached Baile chiar, a day's walk down the country from Ros dhomhain, and the villages about it. The carters brought the news up the road in the spring of the fortieth year, and with it the news of what the custodians of Baile chiar had done: they had set the town's masons to cut the names of every one of their dead into the stone lintel over the door of the council house, the whole length of it, so that no one might go in to the council without passing under them.

At Muileann chrom the pox burned out with the spring. In an Cèitean the pits were full again, with new men from the coast in the dead men's places.

## VIII. Of the Last Door at Doire mhòr

In the dead of the next winter news came up the road that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had moved its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain, on 31 am Faoilleach, AE 41, and that the harbour dues the little town had shared with the strangers since the fifth year would go now to the strangers alone. The mixed council there, left with half an income, cut itself from six to four. Seònaid Bhàn said at her table that it was the first time the strangers had taken back a thing they had shared.

In the spring of the forty-first year Beathag Dhubh died at Doire mhòr.

She was sixty-one years old. She had been custodian of Doire mhòr on the day A' Chompanaidh's agent climbed up with the first contract under his coat, and she had heard him out at her door and sent him down the hill again, and the road had gone round her fields. Then the stream had been dammed, and one household after another had gone down. By the fortieth year there were only a few hearths left lit on Doire mhòr, and the bed of the stream below her door was dry stones with nettles growing in it. She would not go down. The households that had gone sent meal up to her, and peat, and she took it.

The word came down to Muileann chrom on a wet morning of an Giblean. By noon the hill was walking up to Doire mhòr, many of them households who had lived on Doire mhòr and gone down; and the crews came up from the galleries with the black on them and did not stop to wash. Pratt did not stop them. He looked out of his window at the road and said something to his clerk, and the clerk did not write it down.

Dòmhnall went up with his crew. At the bend where A' Chompanaidh's cart-road curved wide round Beathag's fields, the people left it and went straight up over the old walls, the way the path had gone before the road was made, through grass unmown and wet to the thigh.

She was laid out in her own house on the board, in her dark gown, with coal of Doire mhòr's own cutting at her head and her feet, as the custodians of the hill have always been laid out. The house was too small for the people who came. They went in by the door and out by the back in a slow line, the whole of the afternoon, and each one as they went by her laid a hand on the board, or on the coal. Outside they stood in the wet among the empty houses, some hundreds of them, and waited.

Dòmhnall was in the line with his crew when he saw his father.

Raghnall had come up by himself, late. He did not have the staff. He had left it, Dòmhnall learned afterwards, leaning in the corner of the slate-roofed house, and had walked the eight miles in his old coat and his hewer's boots; and he stood now at the back of the crowd by the wall of the last empty cottage, bare-headed in the rain, where the people could see him and could choose not to. Nobody spoke to him. Nobody moved away from him either. He did not go into the line, and he did not come forward when they carried her out to the burying-ground under the oaks; but he stood where he was, at the back, until the last of the earth was in, and then he was gone down the hill before anyone else had turned for home.

The roll of Doire mhòr that Beathag Dhubh kept in her own hand ends a few leaves after the year the stream stopped, with the names of the households that went down. The last leaf of it is in another hand, and gives her name, her age and the day, and that the hill came up. Marsaili nic Sheumais entered the same in the roll of Taigh na Fèithe, and a line more: "The last door of Doire mhòr that did not open."

## IX. Of the Bound Book

Henry Maddox left Dia-thìr that summer, in the seventeenth year of his office, a rich man.

The hill saw his going only in the carts. For a week the carts went down Rathad na Mèinne loaded with his goods, and a clock taller than a man lashed upright in a cart of its own; and at the quays of Ros dhomhain it all went into the ship that had brought his successor. The carters who hauled it said that he had come out with one chest.

Arthur Lisle came to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in his place. He was forty-one years old, a lawyer, thin and clean-shaven, with a bad knee and a dry voice, and he came up the Abhainn gheal to the lake in the grey weather with two clerks and a chest of books and no letter in his pocket from anyone.

On 28 an t-Iuchar, AE 41, his first order went out from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in his own small hand. Every compact, charter, contract and agreement made between the strangers and the island since the leave was given was to be found, wherever it lay, and copied fair, and bound in one book.

A rider of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach came up the hill to Pratt's office in the week after with a satchel and a letter, and carried down to Ros dhomhain the contract of the first thirty and the paper of the leader's share with Raghnall's mark at the foot. He asked too for the agreement by which the staff had been given; and Pratt found that there was none, and the rider wrote that down.

Raghnall Maor carried his staff through all of it, at the heaps and the gallery-mouths and the huts, in the forty-first year of the strangers and the fifty-first of his own age, and the crews stopped singing when he came by. He had learned to walk a little faster through the galleries than he used to, so that they might begin again the sooner. Dòmhnall was twenty-one that summer, a hewer at the face in his father's district, and he took his turn with the others at the singing.

Down at Ros dhomhain, on the evening the rider came in, Lisle had the papers of the hill laid on the table in his room at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir with the rest, under the window that looks down across the gallows-ground to the lake. The clerks had carried up the old letter-books of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir from the cellar that week, Pell's and Maddox's, more than thirty years of them, and stacked them against the wall. The first of them had Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg copied into it, in Pell's hand, on its opening leaf.

Lisle sent the clerks away. Then he sat down, and lit the lamp, and drew the first letter-book towards him across the table, and opened it at the first leaf, and began to read.

# Part Three: Of Silver, Steam and A' Phlàigh Uaine

# Chapter Fourteen: Of the Ledgers at the Adit


*AE 42 – 45*

> *Chan eil an t-airgead naomh.*
> Silver is not holy.

## I. Of the Bound Book

Of all the hands in the letter-books of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, the copyists of the cellar learned Arthur Lisle's first. It is small and level and leans a little backward, like a man reading with his chair tipped from the table, and it never blots. He came to the island in the summer of the forty-first year of the strangers, a lawyer of forty-one, thin, clean-shaven, with a bad knee that he favoured on stairs, and he brought with him two clerks, a chest of books, and no letter from A' Chompanaidh promising him a share of anything. Henry Maddox had gone home rich by the same ship.

His first order as An t-Àrd-mhaor was that every agreement made between the island and the strangers since the day of the leave should be found, copied fair and bound in one book. The two clerks were at it all that winter in the long room over the stair of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, with the rain on the glass. They copied Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg and Puingean a' Chalaidh; the contracts of the pits one by one, with the crew-leaders' names spelled as the humans had heard them; the grants of foreshore at Ceann fhada, paid in nails by weight; the leases of the concession grazing; the orders about the hawk-priests; and at the back, in a separate gathering, Cairt na Companaidh. The charter had been made over the sea between A' Chompanaidh and its own masters, before any Dia-thìreach had seen it, and it bound nobody on the island; Lisle had it bound in all the same, because he wanted it where he could lay it beside the rest.

When the book came back from the binder at Ros dhomhain, in calf with brass at the corners, he read it through with a pen in his hand. The letter-books keep his notes on it, forty pages of them. Where the humans took something that no page gave them, he wrote *on what ground?* in the margin. Where the Dia-thìrich paid something that no page asked of them, he wrote *why do they pay?* He was a hard man and meant the island no particular kindness; but he could not bear an account that did not balance, and the first account he found out of balance was the northern coast.

The coal ships of A' Chompanaidh went home north-about, past the north cape, and along that coast lay fishing towns that had never been asked for a penny of harbour-due. Their boats went out to the coal ships as they passed and sold them fish and water and fresh greens, and took marks for it, and nobody had told them they owed any share of the marks to anyone. Lisle looked for the page that made them owe it and found none. So he made one. On 2 am Màrt, AE 42, a customs house was opened at Ros gheal on the northern coast, in a hired loft by the fish-steps, with a table, a book, a brass scale and an officer from the harbour office at Ros dhomhain to keep them.

Ros gheal was a hawk town, and had been since the pupils of Gormshuil founded the second house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig there in An Aois Scaraidh. Its priests had kept the measured burning for all the country up the river to Cnoc bheag while Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was still kept, and the fishing families there held that what the sea gave, the sea gave to the hand that went out for it. The officer had been in his loft eleven days when the hawk-faithful came down from the hawk-house at dusk, some thirty of them, fishermen and their wives and a priest with his hood up. They carried out the table with the book still open on it and set it down in the street. They carried out the scale and the officer after it. Then they walked him, not unkindly, to the last house on the road south and left him there with his book under his arm.

He came back in a month with a letter from Lisle and two clerks to bear him company, and he kept the loft through the summer. At the herring in the autumn the town put him in a boat with his table, his scale and his clerks and rowed him two miles down the coast and set him ashore on a beach with no road. The roll of Ros gheal says only that the officer "went away by water." The letter-book says a good deal more. Lisle wrote under the report, in his level hand, that the town had broken no page, since no page yet bound the town, and that he would write one.

The news went east along the carriers' roads, as news did, and came up the valley to Muileann chiar at the back end of the year, told at the smelting-floors by a carter with his hands held out to the heat. Ùna nic Choinnich heard it standing in the door of the guild hall with a ledger under her arm. The carter told it for a laugh, the fishwives and the table in the street, and the men at the floors laughed. Ùna did not.

"He reads," she said. "That one reads what he signs. Mark him."

## II. Of the Silver Town

Muileann chiar lay in the far east of the hills, on a shelf of the valley under the moor, a day's walk above the southern sea and an hour's walk from the old walls of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal. It was a small town, a few score households in stone under turf and slate, with the adit in the hillside above the last houses and the smelting-floors below them by the stream, and in those years it was the only place on the island where the smoke that went up from the work was not the smoke of coal. The guild burned charcoal from the eastern woods and peat from the moor, as the first silver-workers had done. There was a sweet, sharp smell over the whole valley that the carters said they could taste in their bread for a day after.

The silver had been found in An Aois Naomh, near the great vein but apart from it, and the first question anyone had asked of it was whether it belonged to the mountain. Muireach Liath answered it then. Silver shows no colour when it breaks, he said; it breaks grey and bright and the same all through, like water; and so it is not the mountain's.
