From those words Muileann chiar had been let dig as deep as it liked. From those words, too, every quarrel over the silver had begun. When Ruairidh Liath demanded one ring in five, Sliochd Fhearchair shut the workings for three seasons sooner than pay, and the road-guards went unpaid; that was Falachd an Airgid, in which nobody died, and which Coimheadaiche na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal settled by giving each side half of what it asked. The weights of Muileann chiar had been the lawful weights of every road on the island since that settlement. Twice in An Aois Scaraidh Clann Choinnich had asked the queen's council for leave to burn coal beyond the measured handful for the smelt, since the coal burns hotter than charcoal; and twice the council had refused, the second time by one voice. The last asking still lay in Taigh na Fèithe, unanswered, when the strangers came.

Ùna was of Clann Choinnich by her father and of the refiners' families by her mother, and she had been head of Comann an Airgid for eleven years. She was fifty-seven in the winter this telling begins: a short square woman with a burn-scar up the inside of one forearm, grey hair plaited and pinned flat so that it would not catch, and a voice that did not rise. As a girl of twenty she had carried the guild's rings down to the humans' counter at Ros dhomhain in the years of fair exchange, and she had learned their tongue across Pike's counter, word by word, the way the carters learned it; and later, in a winter when the snow shut the valley, a clerk of A' Chompanaidh who was lodging in the town had paid for his board by teaching her the humans' letters. She read them slowly. She read everything slowly, and forgot none of it.

The guild kept two ledgers, and they were the pride of the town.

The older was hardly a book at all. It was a stack of thin boards of ash, each notched along one edge in the stag-letters that the teachers of the grove had made out of the cutters' tally-marks at Muileann chiar long ago, bound between two planks with thongs through holes at the corners. In it was set down every member of the guild since the first, the name and the house and the year of taking-on, and every gallery driven into the seam, and who had driven it, and how far. The newer ledger was a book of the island's own paper in the island's own letters, begun in An Aois Scaraidh and kept since in a dozen hands. In it were the weighings: every bar and every ring that went out of Muileann chiar, to whom, and for what, down to the last ring traded for salt fish. Between them the two ledgers held the whole life of the seam from An Aois Naomh to that winter, and in all their boards and leaves there was not one word of the humans' tongue.

On 3 am Faoilleach, AE 43, a rider came up the valley in sleet with a letter in a leather case. It was from the agent of A' Chompanaidh at Muileann chrom, and it was written in the humans' tongue with a Dia-thìris version under it in a clerk's cramped hand. The agent gave notice that A' Chompanaidh, holding under its charter the first refusal of "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield," would send its surveyors to the silver seam at Muileann chiar with the spring, to measure the workings and value the yield, so that the silver might be brought under the same terms as the coal.

Ùna read it at her own table by the fire, first the Dia-thìris and then the humans' version, and then the humans' version again, with her finger under the words. The rider stood dripping by the door. When she had done she folded the letter along its creases and gave him a bowl of broth, and asked him whether he had come by the Muileann chrom road or the moor road, and how the fords were running. Then she sent her grandson round the houses to call the guild.

They came to the hall in the dark, forty-one of them, in their work-clothes with the ash still on them, and sat on the benches along the walls under the hanging scales. Ùna read the letter to them in both tongues. Nobody spoke for a while.

"The charter is theirs," said Seumas mac Fhearchair at last. He was the oldest refiner in the valley, seventy-three that winter, and his house had worked the seam longer than any. "They wrote it for themselves. What has it to do with us?"

"Nothing," said Ùna. "So they will say it has everything, until someone shows them where it stops."

"And who will show them?"

"The council," said a young man by the door, and a few of the others laughed, not kindly. The council at Cathair dhearg had been shown a good many things in forty years and had filed most of them.

Ùna let them laugh. "I will go and ask it," she said, "and I will see what it has in its chest."

## III. Of the Council's Copies

She rode west in the second week of am Faoilleach with her grandson Fionnlagh, who was sixteen and had never been further than Dùn ìseal, and a pack-pony with oats and a sack of silver rings for the road. It was fifty miles and more to the capital. They went by the moor road to Muileann chrom, where the smoke of A' Chompanaidh's furnaces lay along the valley so thick that the boy put his sleeve over his mouth, and then down Rathad na Mèinne, cart-ruts frozen hard as iron, among the long lines of coal-carts going west. It took them three days. At the inns the carters talked of the Ros gheal fishwives, and the tale grew every night.

Coinneach Glas received her in the room behind the council hall, where the custodians' rolls were kept in presses along the walls. He was Ceann a' Chùraim, and had been since the death of Tormod mac Ailein twenty-three years before; he had come to the seat at forty-five and was sixty-eight that winter. He had never set eyes on a human before An t-Aiseag, the council's clerks said, and had dealt with little else since. His hair and beard had gone the grey that gave him his byname long before he was old, and now his skin was going the same way. He had a cough that he did not trouble to hide, and a brazier by his chair, and a rug over his knees. He heard her through without a word, and then sat for a long time looking at the brazier.

"I asked them to keep the tally," he said. "In the twenty-third year. I asked them to burn no more coal in a year than the hill could give. They sent me a copy of their accounts." He coughed. "It was a very fine copy."

"I have not come for the council to write to them," said Ùna.

"No. I did not think so." He looked at her properly then. "What have you come for?"

"Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg," she said. "And whatever else was signed. The council's own copies."

The clerk who kept the presses made a small noise, and Coinneach Glas lifted one hand without looking round.

"They are in the humans' tongue," he said. "Only in that."

"I can read the humans' tongue."

He had the clerk bring them: Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg on six leaves of heavy paper, sewn with green thread, with Tormod mac Ailein's mark at the foot and Josiah Pell's name beside it in a great looping hand; and Puingean a' Chalaidh, which two custodians had refused to sign; and a bundle of the pit contracts tied with tape. No promise was asked of her that she would bring them back. Coinneach Glas only said, as she was wrapping them in oilcloth for the road, that nobody in that room had read them through in a long while.

"Look for the silver," he said. "If it is there, better you find it than they do."

She read them at the inns going home, by rushlight, at the end of the long tables, with the carters singing at the other end and Fionnlagh asleep with his head on his arms. She read them the way she read a ledger, a line at a time, and when a word was strange to her she wrote it on a scrap of paper and asked the next human she met what it meant, which on that road was never long. The leaves of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg spoke of the humans' leave to stay and to build, of the post and the harbour, of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach and the council and how each should send to the other. It spoke of the dues, and of such goods as the island afforded and the working of them. Puingean a' Chalaidh spoke of anchorages and moorings and nothing else. The contracts, which hung from that one line of goods, spoke of the coal, and of how the coal should be cut and weighed and paid for, at a length that surprised her, and of tons.

On the third night, at the inn below Muileann chrom, she laid the leaves down on the table and put her hand flat on them.

"What is it?" said Fionnlagh, who had woken.

"There is no silver in it," said Ùna. "No metal in it at all but the iron they paid with. Coal on every page, and not a word about anything else under the ground."

"Then they cannot have it."

"Then they have no paper that gives it to them," said his grandmother. "Which is a smaller thing. Go to sleep."

## IV. Of the Ledgers at the Adit

The surveyors came up the valley on 31 am Màrt, AE 43, the last day of am Màrt, in a thin cold sunshine after a week of rain. There were five of them, the chief surveyor on a grey horse and the rest on foot, with two carts of chains, pegs, staves and a tripod in a canvas bag, and a Dia-thìreach of Muileann chrom walking at the horse's head to speak for them. The town saw them from a mile off. Nobody went down to meet them.

Ùna had made her plan in the hall two nights before, and it was short. Every member of the guild would be at the adit at the hour the carts came up, man and woman and apprentice, in the leather aprons of the smelting-floors, and every one of them would hold their tongue. Seumas mac Fhearchair and old Mòr nic Fhearchair, the two eldest, would hold the ledgers. Ùna would speak, and nobody else.

"And if they will not go?" somebody asked.

"Then we will all be standing at the adit," said Ùna, "and they will have to measure round us."

When the carts came up past the last houses the whole membership of Comann an Airgid was already there, filling the yard in front of the adit and the slope above it, forty-one people in leather aprons standing in the sun. Seumas and Mòr stood at the front, one on each side of Ùna, and each held a ledger open across the forearms, the way a priest holds a book at a rite: Seumas the notched boards of the old ledger, strapped open at the first board, and Mòr the paper book of the weighings, open at the page where the old brown hands of An Aois Scaraidh gave way to the hands of the present. Behind them the black mouth of the adit breathed out its cold. Down by the stream the smelting-floors were banked but not dead, and a thread of smoke went straight up from them into the still air.

The chief surveyor was a big, red-faced man in a good coat, with a clerk's case on a strap across his chest. He got down from his horse and looked at the yard full of silent people, and then at the woman in the middle of it, and he did not seem to know which to speak to. The man from Muileann chrom said something to him low. He took a paper from his case and began to read out his authority.

It was a long paper and he read all of it, in the humans' tongue, in a loud flat voice as if reading to a crowd that could not hear: the charter, the first refusal, the fuels, ores and minerals, the seal of An t-Àrd-mhaor, the agent's instructions, the rights of entry and of measurement. The man from Muileann chrom tried to put it into Dia-thìris and fell further behind at every line. The yard stood and listened. Nobody moved. A dog barked somewhere down in the town and was hushed.

Ùna let him finish. Then, when he had folded his paper, she turned toward him the first ledger, the notched boards in Seumas's arms, and after it the second, the paper book in Mòr's; and she said to him, in his own tongue and quite pleasantly, "These are the books of the seam since it was found. Find me your name in either of them."

He looked at her. Then, because he could think of nothing else to do, and perhaps because he was an honest man in his way, he looked at the books.

He could not read the boards at all, and she did not help him. He looked a long time at the paper book, turning the leaves back and back with one thick finger while Mòr held it steady, through the weighings of the last season and the season before, through the rings for salt and the bars for bronze and the weights sent to the inns of the roads, back into hands so old that the ink had gone brown. The yard waited. The wind came down off the hill with the smell of the smelting-floors in it, charcoal and hot stone and the sharp sweet smell of the silver, and moved the hair on forty-one heads and the pages of the book.

After a while the surveyor closed his own book, the one in his case that he had been ready to write the seam into. He said something short to the man from Muileann chrom, and turned his horse, and the carts creaked round in the yard; and the men of A' Chompanaidh went back down the valley the way they had come, with their chains and pegs and their tripod still in its bag.

Nobody in the yard spoke until they were out of sight below the last houses. Then Mòr nic Fhearchair shut the paper book with a clap, and somebody at the back began to laugh, and then all of them were laughing, forty-one people in leather aprons laughing in the sun at the mouth of the adit, and old Seumas sat down on the edge of the ore-trough and wiped his eyes with his sleeve.

Ùna did not laugh. She took the ledgers from them and carried them back to the hall herself, one under each arm.

"They will come again," she said that night at her own fire, to Fionnlagh, who could not sit still. "Or somebody will come in their place with a better paper. We have won nothing yet. All we have shown them is that the paper they carried was too short."

## V. Of What the Lawyer Found

The chief surveyor's report reached Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir a fortnight later, and it is in the letter-books, in a hand that is none too steady. He wrote that he had been met at the working by the whole population of the place in a body, silent and in an attitude he could not call threatening and would not call anything else; that he had been shown two books of accounts, one in no writing he knew, and had found no trace in either of any grant, lease or payment to his masters or to any of his countrymen; that he had not thought it prudent to proceed; and that he awaited instruction.

Under it, in the small level hand, Lisle wrote one line: *Nor would I have found it. Bring me the bound book.*

He read it through again that summer, from the first leaf to the last, with the charter laid open beside it. The letter-books keep that reading too, in a long letter he wrote in an Lùnastal to the master of A' Chompanaidh at Ros dhomhain, and the copyists have kept a copy of the letter in the cellar because it is the plainest account any human wrote in all the age of what the humans on the island held and by what right. The charter, Lisle wrote, was a promise that A' Chompanaidh's own masters had made to it: that whatever the island should yield to their own people, A' Chompanaidh should be offered first. It gave A' Chompanaidh nothing on the island. It could not give what the island had not first given, and the only writings by which the island had given anything were Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg and the contracts that hung from its line of goods. He had read them. They were careful about coal, and the contracts spoke of coal at great length and on every page; of silver they said nothing whatever, or about any other metal or ore, or about any ground but the ground of the coal. "They gave us the hill," he wrote, "and we have been reading it as the whole island. The silver of Muileann chiar was never ours to refuse or to be offered, and a surveyor sent to measure it has no more right on that hillside than a stranger has in my garden."

The master of A' Chompanaidh wrote back angrily and at length. Lisle's answer was two lines long and is also kept. He did not mean to lose another customs officer, it said, and he did not mean to lose a war over a seam that no page had ever given him.

In the autumn he wrote to Comann an Airgid. The letter came up the valley by the same road the surveyors had taken, in the humans' tongue only. It proposed that An t-Àrd-mhaor and the guild set down together, in a compact, that the silver seam of Muileann chiar and its workings belonged to the town and its guild, and that A' Chompanaidh had no claim on them under its charter or any other paper; and it proposed that the compact be signed at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on a day to be named.

Ùna wrote back herself, in the humans' letters, slowly, on a sheet of the guild's paper. The copyists found her letter in the letter-books, bound in between a complaint about harbour thieves and an order for lamp-oil. It says that the guild would sign such a compact gladly; that the seam was at Muileann chiar and not at Ros dhomhain, and the compact had best be signed where the seam was; and that the guild asked for it to be written in both tongues, the humans' and the island's, line against line, so that neither side should have to trust the other's reading of it.

Lisle's clerk put a question mark in the margin beside that last sentence. Lisle struck it through. He wrote under the letter, *It costs me a clerk's week and it will save me a war of glosses. Do it*, and sent word to Muileann chiar that he would come himself on Là Fhèill Brìde.

He came in a closed carriage, over roads so bad that he and his clerk walked the last three miles up the valley beside the horses with their boots full of snow-water. The town turned out to watch him come, as it had turned out for the surveyors, but this time Ùna went down the street to meet him. He was a smaller man than she had thought, and older in the face, and he limped. He bowed to her in the humans' way. She did not know what to do with that, so she bowed back.

The compact was signed in the guild hall on 1 an Gearran, AE 44, Là Fhèill Brìde, the first day of an Gearran, at the long table under the hanging scales, with the brazier lit and the whole guild on the benches along the walls. It was short. There were two copies, each of two leaves, each written in two columns, the humans' tongue on the left and the island's on the right, and a young man of Ros dhomhain whom Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir paid to put its words into Dia-thìris had made the island's column and Ùna had gone through it with him line by line the night before and made him change four words. It said that the silver seam at Muileann chiar and all its workings, galleries and floors were the town's, held for it by Comann an Airgid as they had been held since An Aois Naomh; that A' Chompanaidh had no claim upon them under its charter or any other writing; that the guild might sell or send its silver where it chose; and that neither An t-Àrd-mhaor nor any officer of his should enter the workings without the guild's leave.

Lisle signed both copies at the foot of the humans' column. Ùna signed both at the foot of the island's, in the island's letters, and then, because the humans set store by it, in theirs as well. Old Seumas mac Fhearchair signed as witness with a mark, and Lisle's clerk with a flourish.

Before he left Lisle asked to see the seam. Ùna took him up to the adit herself, with a lamp. He stood a long time in the mouth of the gallery, holding the lamp up to the face where the last cutting had broken it, grey and bright and the same all through, and then he said a thing that Fionnlagh, who had come behind them with a second lamp, remembered and told to his own children.

"On the coast they tell me there are colours in the coal," Lisle said. "I have never seen them. I have stood at the pit-mouth at Muileann chrom with a custodian at each elbow pointing, and I saw coal." He turned the lamp so the light ran along the seam. "This I can see."

"We see it the same as you," said Ùna. "That is why it is not holy."

He looked at her as if he would ask what she meant, and did not ask; and they went back down to the hall.

That evening, when the carriage had gone down the valley in the dusk with its lamps lit, Ùna had the compact read aloud to the guild from the Dia-thìris column, all of it, by Mòr nic Fhearchair, who had the best voice. Then it was read again, because the apprentices at the back had not heard. It was the first writing of the whole age of the strangers in which the island's side kept the better terms. Nobody in the hall said so. They did not know it yet. They knew only that the surveyors had gone down the valley and a paper had come up it, and that the paper said the seam was theirs, in their own tongue, in a hand they could read.

## VI. Of the Guild Chest

The guild chest of Muileann chiar was a box of black oak bound with silver bands, older than anyone could say, that stood at the end of the hall under the scales. It held the ledgers and the weights and the guild's seal, and it had three locks, and the three keys were kept in three houses. Ùna had the compact laid in it the night it was signed, on top of the paper book of the weighings, and the three keys turned.

In the spring word came east that Coinneach Glas was dead at Cathair dhearg. He had died in his chair by the brazier in the room behind the council hall, with the rolls in their presses round him, at sixty-nine, having held the seat twenty-four years. The clerk who wrote to Muileann chiar with the news added that Ceann a' Chùraim had heard of the compact before the end, and had had it read to him twice from the copy Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir sent the council, and had said that it was a better paper than any he had signed. The council's leaves were still at Muileann chiar. Ùna sent them back to the council by Fionnlagh, wrapped in the same oilcloth, with a bar of silver for the clerk who kept the presses, for his trouble.

The council chose Alasdair Liath after him, a custodian of forty-nine, who had sat on the council since before Puingean a' Chalaidh and had voted to sign them. The roll gives his choosing in a single line. It gives his age, and the number of voices, and nothing else. Ùna, when she heard, said that she had met him once and he had a good memory, and did not say whether that was praise.

In an t-Ògmhios the guild tried its compact for the first time. A' Chompanaidh had asked, through the agent at Muileann chrom, that the guild's silver should go to the sea by its own quays at Ros dhomhain, where it might be weighed at the customs house and entered in the books. Ùna read the compact again, the island's column and then the humans', and found that the guild might send its silver where it chose. So on 26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 44, the first carts of bar silver went south instead, eighteen miles down the valley road to Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast, where the oyster-beds lie in the shallows and the coasting boats had loaded Muileann chiar silver since An Aois Naomh. The guild paid the custodians of Seann Bhral for the use of their quay in the old way, in silver by the Muileann chiar weight, so much on every bar. The agent at Muileann chrom wrote to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir to complain. Lisle's clerk wrote back that it could find no ground in the compact to object, and the agent's letter and the answer both are in the letter-books, one under the other, with nothing written between them.

It was a good summer in the silver town. The floors worked from dawn to dark, and the paper book of the weighings, which had lasted the guild a lifetime, was full by the autumn and a new one begun.

In the winter came news from the other end of the island that the guild marked in its ledger, though it had nothing to do with silver. The carters of Baile gheal, in the south-west, had taken up the carrying of the brine-salt of Seann Warr round the lake to the capital, with their own carts and their own ponies, on the old roads. A' Chompanaidh had never troubled to claim the salt trade, and nobody had told the carters of Baile gheal that they might not have it; so they had it. They were paid in salt and in marks both, and their young men stayed home from the pits. A carter from the west told it at the smelting-floors in the month of am Faoilleach, in the forty-fifth year of the strangers, a week after the thing was done. He told it as a small thing, which it was. Ùna had it written into the new ledger all the same.

"Write it down," she told the weighing-clerk. "Salt at Baile gheal. Their own carts. Put the year."

"It is not silver," said the clerk.

"It is a thing they did not take," said Ùna. "There are not so many of those that we can afford to forget one."

At the end of that month, on the day the guild reckoned its year and read out the weighings, the three keyholders came to the hall with their keys, and the chest was opened, and Ùna took the compact out and had it read aloud again to the whole guild, both columns, the island's and then the humans'. She was fifty-nine that winter. She stood by the chest while it was read with her hands folded in front of her apron, and when Mòr nic Fhearchair had finished she took the two leaves and looked at them a while, at the two columns and the three names, Lisle's small level one and her own twice over and the old man's mark. Then she laid them in the chest on top of the new paper book, beside the notched boards of the old ledger, and the three keys turned, one after another, in the three locks.

# Chapter Fifteen: Of the Keeper's Daybook

*AE 45 – 48*

## I. Of the Fire-Shelf and the Tower

Of the four witnesses in the chests at Muileann chaol, the copyists say the daybooks of the beacon-keepers are the dullest to read and the easiest to trust. A custodian writing to the council wanted something of it. So did a clerk of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach writing home. A keeper on a headland wanted oil for the lamp and a dry wick, and what he wrote down was the wind, the weather, the hour he lit the flame and the hour he put it out, and every sail that went by his light. A keeper has nothing to gain from a ship that is not there. So the copyists have leaned on the daybooks wherever the other witnesses quarrel, and the first daybook of them all was begun at Àth dhearg, on the north-eastern cape, by a mason named Tormod mac Pheadair.

The fire on that cape was older than any roll. The households of the coast had kept it on a shelf of rock near the top of the headland since before An Aois Naomh, and had cut a stair up to it from the shore, turning back and forth across the face of the cliff, a hundred and more steps, each narrower than a man's boot. Forty years before, the mason Torcall Clachair had sat on that shelf with the human navigator James Fenn, counting the chisel-cuts, and had raised a cairn at its end where the rock was broad enough to bear a tower. The custodian of that day had made them go round every hearth of Àth dhearg to ask leave, and it had taken eleven days.

The cairn stood a long while with nothing beside it. The beacons at Tobar dhearg and Baile ìseal were lit, both of Torcall's building; then Torcall died, and A' Chompanaidh, which paid for the towers, let the third wait while it paid for props and pumps and winding-rope in the hills. When at last it sent word up the coast that it would pay for a tower on the north-eastern cape, it sent no mason with the word. Its masons were building at the pits.

So the custodian of Àth dhearg called the hearths together again, in the long room over the net-store where the town held its councils, and put it to them. The strangers would pay half the cost in marks, their coin with the ship on one face, and would send the lens and the oil; the town would find the stone and the hands. The other half of the pay, she said, was a promise: that the tower would bring home the boats of Àth dhearg as the old fire had done, and better. Some in the room laughed. A promise, said one old fisher, was a poor thing to put in a pot. But the households of that coast had lost boats on the reef below the cape in every generation, and nobody in the room had to be told whose, and the town said yes.

Tormod mac Pheadair was among the first to put his name down. He was twenty-nine that winter, a mason's son, broad and slow-moving, with a burn-scar across the back of one hand from a lime-kiln and a way of looking at a wall for a long while before he touched it. Byres and sea-walls he had built all along that coast, and he had worked on the new quay at Seann Bhral, where he first saw the humans' figures chalked on a stone to be cut. The custodian's clerk had taught him his letters as a boy, and he wrote a square, careful hand, like a man laying courses.

They built through a year and more. The stone came from the landward side of the headland on sledges. They raised the tower over the end of the fire-shelf, and Torcall's cairn they took down stone by stone and set into the footing, facing out to sea, because that was what Torcall would have done. Inside the tower they turned a stair in the thickness of the wall, so that no keeper need climb the old stair in a gale again, as the town had been promised forty years before. The old stair they left as it was.

In Teasach of the forty-fifth year the lamp-room was roofed, and the lens came up the coast road in a crate packed with straw, with a human of A' Chompanaidh riding beside it who would let nobody else touch it. He set it on its iron frame, polished it for most of a day, and then asked who would keep the light. The keeper would be paid a little, in marks, and must keep a book: his masters wished to know how many ships went by the cape, and whose, and when, and which of their own captains kept to their sailing-days. Most of the household elders could not write. Among the masons of the tower there was one who wrote a fair hand and knew the humans' figures besides.

So Tormod mac Pheadair was made keeper of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg. He said afterwards that he had only gone up the stair to fetch his hammer.

## II. Of the First Line

The lamp was lit at dusk on 10 an t-Iuchar, AE 45. The whole town came out along the cliff-top to see it, and most said it was brighter than the old fire. The man of A' Chompanaidh noted the hour by his watch. In the morning he rode south, and Tormod was alone in the tower with the lamp, the oil-casks, a bundle of wicks and a book of the humans' paper, bound in grey board, left on the table.

He sat a long while before he wrote in it. The paper was better than anything the custodian's clerk had, and he did not like to spoil it. In the end he wrote as he would have cut a line in stone, slowly, pressing hard. The copyists found the book among the first chests from the north-east, its grey boards warped by the damp and its first leaf gone brown at the edges, and the first line reads:

> *Air a lasadh aig ciaradh. Gaoth an iar, beag. Cha robh long ann.*
>
> Lit at dusk. Wind west, light. There was no ship.

Under it, in the same hand, stands the night of the moon: the tenth night of Teasach. The humans' day stands above the line, in a different ink.

The man of A' Chompanaidh came back at the end of Lùghnas with a cart of oil and read the book through at the lamp-room table, and was not pleased, for he could not tell from the nights of the moon on what day any ship had passed. He sat Tormod down beside him and wrote out a list of the humans' months and days to the end of their year, each against its night of the moon as well as he could reckon it, which was not well. From then on Tormod wrote two dates at the head of each entry, the humans' day above in their figures and the night of the moon beneath in words, and went back and wrote the humans' days over the entries already made. Some of them he got wrong, and the copyists have set them right from the letter-books.

The entries of that first autumn are short and much alike. The lamp was lit and put out. The wind went round. Fog came in off the sea on the nineteenth night of Pailteach, and he wrote that the lamp was lit and did no good. The fishing boats of the coast went in and out, and he left them out of the book, for the man of A' Chompanaidh had said *ships*. Then, on the fourth night of Damhrach:

> *A ship of the strangers, three masts, going south. Deep in the water. She showed a lamp at the stern.*

She went by within two miles of the cape with every sail set, and Tormod watched her out of sight from the gallery. He did not know her name, or her cargo, or her port. He wrote down what he had seen.

By the end of the humans' year he had written down nineteen of them. By the end of the next, forty-four.

## III. Of the Boats Brought Home

That winter the masons went on working, though the lamp was lit. The outer face was half-pointed when the weather closed in and the keeper's house at the tower's foot was unroofed, and Tormod slept in the lamp-room on a pallet by the oil-casks and wrote by the light of the lamp, the best light he had ever written by. Few ships came round the north coast in the dark months, and the daybook shows them late on their sailing-days, and early never.

On the second night of Bealltach, in the forty-sixth year, a gale came up out of the north-east in the afternoon, when four boats of Àth dhearg were out on the long lines beyond the reef. Tormod saw it coming from the gallery: a dark edge on the sea far out, and the gulls coming in ahead of it. He lit the lamp an hour before dusk and stood in the wind and rain watching the grey water below the cape, where the reef showed white when the swell drew back.

The first boat came in at dusk. The second came an hour after, low in the water and baling. Then nothing came for a long time, and the women of the four households stood on the cliff-top with lanterns, as the women of that coast had always stood in a blow, under the shelf where the old fire had been fed by hand. There was no fire on the shelf now. The tower's light went out over their heads to sea.

The third boat came in near midnight, from the wrong side of the reef, having run north past it in the dark and come round. Her steersman said afterwards that he had not known where he was until he raised the light, and then he had known exactly, because it could be nowhere else. The fourth came in at first light, a man short. He had gone over the side in the afternoon, before the gale reached them, where no light could have helped him.

Tormod wrote it all down, which was more than the man of A' Chompanaidh had asked: the four boats by name, the hour of each, and the lost man and his name. It is the only entry in the first daybook that names anyone of Àth dhearg. The copyists think he wrote it so that the promise could be seen to have been kept.

On 28 an Cèitean, AE 46, the work was done. The keeper's house was roofed and the outer face pointed, and the man of A' Chompanaidh came up the coast road with a clerk and a strong-box and paid the masons in marks from a table set out on the grass at the tower's foot. There were eleven of them, and Tormod came down the stair and stood in the line and took his pay with the rest. The custodian's clerk wrote the payment into the town's roll, and wrote beside it that the masons of the tower had been the town's own men, and that the other half of their pay had been made on the second night of Bealltach, in four boats and three of them home.

## IV. Of the Glow in the South

In the autumn of that year a ship of A' Chompanaidh went south past the cape:

> *A ship of the strangers, two masts. Coal. Going south close in, with the wind behind her.*

He knew her for a collier by the way she sat low and square in the water, and because as she passed below the cape the wind brought him the smell of her cargo, the smell of broken coal that nobody on the island mistook. At that distance he could not see the colour in it. He could smell it.

Two nights after, at the change of the watch, he went out onto the gallery and saw a redness low in the south, under the cloud, where there should have been nothing but the dark coast running away towards Ceann leathan and the islets beyond. It was too steady for lightning and too far off for a fire on any hill he knew. He watched it grow, and towards morning sink.

> *A light in the south under the cloud, red, from the middle watch until near dawn. I do not know what it was.*

Four days later a carter came up the coast road with salt and the news. Raiders in low black boats had come out from the islets off the eastern shore in the night and taken the collier, and stripped her of what they wanted, and set her afire, and she had burned to the waterline with her coal in her. Her crew had been put in their own boat and set rowing for the land, and came ashore alive at a fishing village near Ceann leathan, and the village fed them. The copyists set the burning at 20 an Dàmhair, AE 46, which is the day the letter-books give.

The raiders of the eastern islets had taken Dia-thìreach boats in every generation since An Aois Naomh, and nobody on that coast was surprised that they had taken a stranger's at last. Within the month its agents were saying at Seann Bhral and Ros dhomhain, and writing to Arthur Lisle, An t-Àrd-mhaor, that Comann an Airgid had paid the raiders, out of spite for the surveyors turned back from the adit at Muileann chiar.

The guild said nothing. The copyists have looked for a word from it in every chest that came to the cellar, and have found none.

In the dark days of Dubhlas a clerk of A' Chompanaidh rode up the coast road to Àth dhearg alone and asked to see the daybook. He had some Dia-thìris and could read the humans' dates, and he found the collier and the red light, and went over them with his finger. Then he asked Tormod whether he had seen any boats go south along the coast in the days before the burning. Low boats, black-painted, with many oars.

Tormod said that he had written down every ship he saw.

The clerk said that such boats were hardly ships, and Tormod might have seen them and thought them not worth the writing. There was room at the foot of the page.

Tormod looked at the page for a while. Then he said that he had seen no such boats, that if he had seen them he would have written them down, and that he would not write down a boat he had not seen, for his own people or the clerk's.

The clerk did not argue. He thanked the keeper for the use of the lamp-room fire and rode south in the morning. The daybook says nothing of his coming. His report lies in the letter-books of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir among the papers on the burning of the collier, and says that the keeper at Àth dhearg was "civil, but of no assistance," and that his book "throws no light on the matter"; and somebody at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir has underlined the words about the light.

## V. Of the Gunboat and the Cove

The next summer A' Chompanaidh sent a ship of war.

Tormod saw her come round the north coast on a clear morning in Teasach of the forty-seventh year. She was smaller than the colliers and lower and a great deal faster, two-masted, painted black with a white band along her side, and there were more men on her deck than any trader carried. Through the glass A' Chompanaidh had given him for reading sails he made out the gun in her bows under a canvas cover, and wrote her down with more care than he had given any ship before:

> *A ship of the strangers, two masts, black with a white band. A gun in the bows under canvas. Many men. Going south along the coast.*

On 25 an t-Iuchar, AE 47, the gunboat found a cove near Ceann leathan with boats drawn up on the shingle and the smoke of a fire among the rocks above. Her master wrote in his report that he had tracked the raiders there. He put a boat's crew ashore with torches under cover of his gun, and there was nobody on the shingle to stop them. They burned every boat drawn up there, eighteen of them. The gunboat stood off through the day, waiting for the raiders to come down out of the rocks, and nobody came.

Most of the boats were the fishermen's. The households of Ceann leathan drew up their small boats in that cove in the summer, when the lining was good off that shore, and slept in the bothies above the rocks, and it was their fire the master had seen. When the torches came up the shingle they had run into the rocks with their children, having heard what a gun could do, and from the rocks they watched their boats burn. The raiders were not found. Nobody on the coast believed they had been there.

Tormod wrote the gunboat going back north on the third day after, running before a southerly wind:

> *The gun-ship, going north. The gun uncovered.*

The news came up the coast road behind her, with a Ceann leathan man who walked nearly forty miles north with two of his sons to ask Àth dhearg for the loan of a boat. The town had boats to spare that year, since the masons had been paid in marks and two households had bought new boats with the money. The households talked it over into the night in the long room over the net-store, and gave the loan of two, to be returned when the Ceann leathan men had built their own. The man and his sons sailed them south in the first days of Lùghnas, and passed under the cape on the way, and Tormod saw them go. He left them out of the book, as he left out all the boats of the coast.

## VI. Of the Wall on the Shingle

That same Lùghnas, on the other side of the island, the council of Baile dhìreach broke apart.

It had sat for forty-two years, and every year it had sat on less. When the customs house went to Ros dhomhain six years before and took the harbour dues with it, the council had cut its members from six to four. William Rook and Iain mac Chaluim gave up their seats then, being old men, and sat on the salt-house step on fine evenings with their pipes and watched the others go up the ladder to the net-loft without them. The two books stood on the shelf there side by side, and most months there was little to put in either.

Iain Hale was thirty-eight that summer, the son of the marriage entered in both books on the quay, of the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh and the human cooper Samuel Hale. He had been born in the tent on the shingle and grown up in the yard, and he was a boatwright. The carpenter Nathan Cobb had taught him the humans' way of setting up a keel, and his grandfather Ruairidh the salter had taught him the town's knots before he could walk. He spoke both tongues as a child speaks them, without choosing. He had his father's long arms and his mother's broad hands, and people of both peoples in the town were a little shy of him, as they were of the tide-line, which is neither sea nor land.

In the spring of that year the yard-master, Daniel Lusk, the sawyer's son who had come ashore as a boy with the first seven, came back from Ros dhomhain with a promise from A' Chompanaidh of oak and pine by the shipload, more than the yard had ever had, if the yard would build for it. He had nowhere to stack it. The yard stood on the shingle north of the quay by the town's leave, and above the wrack the shingle was held for the whole town and built on by nobody; so both books said, each in its own words.

Lusk wanted to build a wall.

He put it to the council in the net-loft on an evening in Lùghnas, with the rain on the slates. A wall of dry stone, he said, no higher than a man's chest, from the foot of the slip up the shingle to the old post at the top. It would keep the timber in and the town's children out. It would not be a house, and the compact said nothing against walls.

Eòghann mac Iain, Iain mac Chaluim's son, who sat for the town, said that the compact did not need to. A wall was a building, and the first thing that anybody would ever have built on that shingle, and a wall had two sides.

The other town member was Mairead nic Aoidh, Seonag's granddaughter, who kept the salt-house as her grandmother had. She said that before there could be a wall somebody had to say where the line was, and the town had never said that the yard went this far and no further. The yard was on the shingle by leave, as the curers of Inis thais had been in her grandmother's grandmother's day. A wall would make it a piece of ground.

"It has been a piece of ground for forty years," said Lusk.

The fourth member was Nathan Cobb, seventy and deaf in one ear, who had sat on the council since the night the compact was written. He took the humans' book from the shelf, opened it at the compact, and read out the clause about the shingle in the humans' tongue: *The shingle north of the quay is the property of the town.* If it was the town's property, he said, not unkindly, then a wall would show where the town's property ended and the yard's began, and that was the whole use of a wall.

Mairead asked for the other book. Iain Hale was sitting at the foot of the table, having been asked to carry the talk from one tongue to the other when either side stuck, and it was he who took down the Dia-thìris book and found the page and read it out: *The shingle north of the quay is kept for the town.*

Everyone at the table looked at him then, from both sides, and waited for him to say which of the two books was right. He had read them both, the only man at the table who could.

He closed the book, put it back on the shelf, and said nothing.

They argued for four nights. While they argued Lusk had the footing of the wall laid, a line of big stones from the slip half-way up the shingle, and on the third night somebody of the town took the stones up and carried them below the wrack-line and left them in a heap. Nobody on the council would say who. On the fourth night, 23 an Lùnastal, AE 47, Lusk stood up and said that he would not sit with people who pulled down a man's work in the dark, and Eòghann mac Iain said that he would not sit with people who built on the town's ground by daylight, and Lusk went down the ladder. Cobb sat on a while, looking at the table. Then he got up and followed.

The council of Baile dhìreach never met again. On the last written page of the Dia-thìris book a line in Eòghann mac Iain's hand says that the council rose without its business done. The humans' book has nothing on its last page but the date, in Cobb's shaking hand.

## VII. Of the Yard That Went East

The human families began to go before the harvest was in. There were not many of them now, and most were the families of the yard. Two went up the coast to Ros bheag, the citadel harbour of the west, where there was a human chandler and a chapel. The rest went to Ros dhomhain, where A' Chompanaidh had its yards and counting-houses and work for any man of their people who could hold an adze.

Of the households that were of both peoples it is not told which went and which stayed, save one. The Hales stayed, and said nothing about it. They went neither to the quay to say they were staying nor to the salt-house to say they had taken the town's side. They kept to their house at the head of the street by the well, where they had lived since the tent grew too small for them; Samuel Hale mended the town's barrels as he had for forty years, and Eilidh mended nets on the frames outside the door, being too stiff in the knees now for the shingle. The humans who were going came to their door to say goodbye, and the Hales gave them bread and a jug of ale. When the town spoke of the wall in their hearing, they spoke of other things.

In the first days of Samhnas Lusk came to find Iain in the yard, where the men were breaking up the stacks and caulking the yard's own boats for a voyage. The yard was going east, he said, to Inis chrom, a day's sail along the coast: a walled harbour of sailors on its bent island in the mouth of the river, with ground to spare, where A' Chompanaidh had promised the timber and the town would take them in and say nothing about walls. A' Chompanaidh wanted boats, and would want more every year. Lusk needed a foreman who could set up a keel of the humans' pattern and talk to the island's timber-men in their own tongue, and he offered Iain the place, for more marks than the yard had ever paid.

Iain asked for a night to think. He went down that evening to the shingle and sat on the heap of footing-stones below the wrack-line and looked at the yard: the long shed open to the sea, the slip of split logs bedded in the stones, and the tent. It stood where Rook's men had set it up in the first summer, a little crooked, with its back to the west wind and a lamp in its window of real glass. Rook had written in the compact, in his round slow hand, that the tent would be taken down when the council told him. Now there was no council to tell anybody anything.

His father found him there after dark. Samuel Hale was sixty-nine and walked with a stick, and he came down the shingle slowly and stood beside his son and looked at the tent, as his father-in-law had looked at it forty years before, when the town was still deciding whether it was a house.

"Your mother says you'll go," he said. He said it in Dia-thìris, as he always did in the town. His Dia-thìris had grown little better since the day of the wedding, and in forty years the town had come to hear it as the way the cooper talked.

"And you?"

"I said you'd stay." Samuel poked at a stone with the end of his stick. "We didn't wager on it. She wouldn't."

After a while Iain asked his father whether he had ever thought of going back over the sea. Nobody in the family had ever asked him.

Samuel laughed. He had a sister over there somewhere, he said, if she was living, who would not know him, and a town that would not know him either. When the men of the yard talked of home they meant a place; when he thought of home he thought of a bowl of whatever was in the pot, on the salt-house step. And he was not the one being asked.

In the morning Iain went to Lusk and told him no.

The yard sailed for Inis chrom on 18 an t-Samhain, AE 47, three boats deep with tools and timber and families, on a cold bright morning with a north wind. Half the town came down to the quay to see them off, which was more than anyone had expected. The last boat out was steered by Nathan Cobb, deaf and upright at the tiller, and he did not look back.

When they had gone round the point Iain climbed the ladder into the net-loft. The humans' book lay on the long mending-table where Cobb had left it on the last night of the council, open at the page with the date and nothing under it. Iain closed it and set it back on the shelf beside the Dia-thìris book, the two side by side as they had always stood, and the copyists found them there in that order.

That winter he took over the slip with the town's leave and under the town's rule, and built the town's boats on it, a keel at a time. The tent stayed where it was on the shingle. Nobody told anybody to take it down.

## VIII. Of the Dry Year and the Seed

At Àth dhearg the daybook went on as before. The forty-seventh year gives fifty-one ships of the humans going by the cape; the forty-eighth gives fewer colliers and more ships bound for Seann Bhral and the eastern harbours with goods from over the sea. Tormod had a wife by then, Ciorstaidh nic Phàdraig of Baile ruadh, a red-haired woman who laughed at his handwriting and could not read it. They lived in the keeper's house at the tower's foot, and in the evenings she climbed the inside stair with his supper and stood on the gallery with him and named the boats of the coast as they came in.

In the spring of the forty-eighth year the rain began to fail.

The daybook does not say so at first. It says, night after night, *wind west, dry*; *wind south-west, dry*; *no rain*; and the copyists noticed the word before they noticed the season. A keeper writes down the weather because the weather is what brings ships ashore. By Ògach he was adding what he saw from the gallery: the fields inland going yellow before midsummer, and a heath fire on the hills to the south that burned three days. In Teasach he wrote that the burn below the town had stopped running, which it had never done in anyone's memory, and that the women were carrying water from the spring on the landward side of the headland.

The farming country south and east of the cape, the old fields of Achadh shean and the red-earth country beyond, lived by its grain. The rain failed over all of it through the summer. It rained a little in Pailteach, and the daybook marks the night with a word it had not used for four months, and then the rain stopped again. On 21 an t-Sultain, AE 48, the custodians of Achadh shean wrote to the council at Cathair dhearg that the harvest of their country had failed for want of rain, and that the granaries of the custom of An Aois Naomh would carry them through the winter. The council's roll enters the letter. No answer is entered.

Baile ruadh had sown its winter corn early, in the last days of Lùghnas, trusting to the rains of Pailteach as the farmers of the red-earth country always did. The rains came for three nights and stopped. The seed swelled and sprouted and withered in the dry ground, across the whole of the town's fields. By Damhrach there was nothing to be done but sow again, and no seed left to sow; the granary had gone to feed the town through the summer.

Ciorstaidh's brother Pàdraig sat on the council of Baile ruadh, and he sent a boy up the coast road to the tower. Tormod left the lamp in the charge of the old clerk's grandson, who had learned to trim the wick, and walked south-east over the brown hills to Baile ruadh, a long day. At the council's table in the custodian's house sat a clerk of A' Chompanaidh from its store at Seann Dunn, a thin young human with a ledger and an ink-pot, and beside him a Dia-thìreach of Seann Dunn to put his words into the island's tongue.

The store at Seann Dunn had seed. A' Chompanaidh had brought it over the sea in grain ships, some of which Tormod had written down going south past his cape, and it would lend enough to sow the fields again before the frosts, at a price to be paid back in grain over five harvests. The terms were written out in the humans' tongue and the figures in the humans' figures. Nobody at the table could read them. The custodian of Baile ruadh, who was old and had a cough, turned to Pàdraig and asked whether it was true that his sister's man could read the strangers' numbers.

So Tormod read them. He stood at the custodian's elbow and put his finger on each figure in turn and said it aloud in Dia-thìris: the measure of seed lent, the measure of grain to be paid back at each harvest, and the number of harvests. He read them twice, as he would have read a line on a stone twice before he cut it. The figures were what the man of Seann Dunn had said. The price was high, and there was nothing in the paper that the council had not been told, and he said so.

The council talked a little, not long, since there was nothing else to talk about. Then the custodian made his mark on the humans' paper, and the clerk sanded it and blew on it, and on 20 an Dàmhair, AE 48, the town of Baile ruadh borrowed its seed corn from A' Chompanaidh. The custodians' roll of Baile ruadh enters the debt under the night of the moon, with the measure and the five harvests. It is the first debt in grain to the strangers that stands in any roll of the island. Beside it the clerk of the roll has written, in a smaller hand, the name of the man who read the figures.

The seed-carts came up from Seann Dunn three days later, and the town sowed its fields again in the dust and waited for rain.

Tormod walked home the next morning. He came up the coast road in the late afternoon and saw the tower on the headland ahead, grey against a grey sky, and Ciorstaidh on the gallery. The boy had lit the lamp early, since there was cloud coming in from the west, and Tormod climbed the inside stair in the last of the light and read over what the boy had written while he was away, which was *lit* and *no ship* and *lit* again.

Before midnight the rain came, and a ship went by below the cape, going south. He knew as well as anyone on that coast what the deep ships going south carried that autumn, and to whose store. He wrote down what he saw, with the humans' day above and the night of the moon beneath, and it is the last line on that leaf:

> *Wind west. Rain before midnight, a small rain. A ship of the strangers going south, deep in the water.*

# Chapter Sixteen: Of the Question at Dùn thais

*AE 49 – 56*

## I. Of the Basket on the Master's Table

Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais, Taigh na Deasbaid, stood at the top of the town where the street gave out into oak and hazel, a long hall of grey stone with a turf roof and one door. Over the door the old question of the schools was cut in the lintel, *Carson an làmh seo?*, why this hand, and the letters had been cut so long ago that moss grew in them and the students scraped it out with their thumbnails on the first day of every year. Inside there were benches down both walls, a hearth at the far end, and a table before the hearth where the master sat. On the table lay the register. It was the third of its name. The first two, filled, stood in a press behind the master's chair, and between them they held every question that had been set in that hall since Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn first set one, with the year, and the name of the master who set it, and whatever the master had chosen to say.

In the summer of AE 49 the master was Aonghas mac Coinnich. He was forty-nine that year, a long lean man with a shepherd's stoop and a grey beard he cut himself with a knife, and he had sat at that table for eleven years. He was born in the last summer before Ceò Mhanannain lifted, and his mother used to say that he had lain in his cradle through the winter the ships came, listening to the whole island ask where they were from. At eighteen he had been a student on the benches of that hall, and had heard the cleric of the humans argue there through the winter of Wren's disputation, and he could still do Wren's cough, which he did sometimes, when the students were slow.

It was the custom of the house that the master set one question at midsummer and the house argued it the year round. Most masters took a question out of the press, one of the old ones turned a little to catch the light of the year. On the eve of midsummer Aonghas came up the street with a basket on his arm, and the students on the benches saw that it held coal.

It was the coal of A' Chompanaidh. He had bought it at the weigh-house by the river, in marks, and he said so. It was broken small, the sort the carts shed on the road, and he tipped it out on the table beside the register and went through it with his long fingers until he found a lump the size of a fist that had split clean in the cart. He held the broken face up to the window.

"Màiri nic Ailpein," he said. "Tell me what you see."

She was the youngest on the benches, a smith's daughter of the town. Up she came, and looked, and told him, as any child of the island would have told him, beginning at the edge: the grey that the old lumps have where the air has been at them, then the brown like wet bracken, then the deep green that lies under the black at the fresh break and seems to go down into the lump further than the lump goes, then the red that grows when you breathe on it. She breathed on it, and the red grew. In all she gave the names of eleven colours, which was good for a girl of fifteen, and sat down.

"Fearchar," said Aonghas, and Fearchar Beag gave him fourteen. Seumas mac Artair, who kept the register and was vain of his eyes, gave him nineteen and was stopped.

"Now," said Aonghas. He put the lump down on the table. "There is a man at the weigh-house by the river who weighed this coal for me this morning. He is one of theirs, a decent man, and careful with his beam. I held up this same lump and asked him what colour it was, and he looked at me as though I had asked him the colour of water, and he said the word they have. He said *black*. The cleric said it in this hall thirty years ago. The keeper of A' Chompanaidh's books at Ros dhomhain says it, and An t-Àrd-mhaor in his house above the river, and the girl who sells ribbons off their ships. Every one of them looks at this and sees one thing." He turned the lump over. "Why?"

Nobody answered him. He had not expected an answer. He sat down at the table, pulled the register to him, and wrote the question in his own hand, in the tongue of the hall, and turned the book round so that Seumas might see it:

> *Carson a chì sinne an dath, is iadsan dall air?*
>
> Why do we see the colour, and they blind to it?

That is how it stands in the register, under the date 19 an t-Ògmhios, AE 49. Below it, in Seumas's hand, which is smaller and neater than the master's, is the note that has been copied into more books than the question: that when the house asked the master what the answer was, he told them it was the wrong question, and would not give them the right one.

## II. Of the Summer of Arguing

They argued it all that summer, as the custom was, on the benches in the wet weather and under the oaks behind the hall when it was fine.

Seumas mac Artair held that the humans' eyes were made differently, as a dog's are, or an owl's, and that there was nothing more to be found out than that. Fearchar Beag held that it was the burning. He had it from the old tellings of Wren's winter: when the cleric had asked the masters why the vein should be holy, they had asked him back why his fuel should be burned. A people who had burned coal by the cartload for as long as they could remember, said Fearchar, would have stopped looking at it long ago, as a man stops seeing the colour of the peat he cuts. Màiri nic Ailpein, who was fifteen and afraid of nobody, said that she had once seen a human child at Inis bheag pick up a lump from the road and turn it in the sun for a long time; and the house argued for a week about whether the child had seen anything, or had been looking at the shine, and nobody could say, since nobody had asked the child.

Aonghas let them. He sat at the table with his hands folded on the register and said almost nothing, except to stop a student who was shouting, or to send one out for more peat. When they pressed him, and they pressed him every week, he said only that the question was a poor one, and they were welcome to it.

A student from the west who had come for the summer said aloud one evening what several of them were thinking, that the master had set them a question he did not believe in so that they would find the one he did.

"Then find it," said Aonghas, and went home to his supper.

In the autumn three of them set out for Baile Mòr uaine, a long day's walk to the west over the high moor, where there was a hall of disputation of its own, older in its benches than Dùn thais and prouder. They carried the question in their heads and a copy of it in Seumas's hand, sealed. The masters of Baile Mòr uaine took it up at the dark of the year. On 15 an Dùbhlachd, AE 49, it was put to their hall for the first time, and the argument ran through that winter and the next, and the record of it, which the students sent back to Dùn thais leaf by leaf with the carriers, runs to four hundred leaves. It is the longest argument in the press. It ends, as the question did, without an answer. The last leaf is a list of the names of those who spoke, and at the foot of it the master of Baile Mòr uaine has written that the hall adjourned because the peat was done.

Aonghas read every leaf as it came. The students saw him at it late in the hall with a rushlight, turning the leaves slowly and sometimes going back. He never said which argument he thought the best. When the last leaf came, he had the whole bundle tied up with the others, and went out, and walked a long while in the oakwood in the rain.

## III. Of the Town with No Custodian

Those were the years when the humans began to build towns of their own.

The concession country in the north-west had been theirs to graze for thirty years, and the families there had built in stone for a generation. In the spring of the year after Aonghas set his question, they founded a market town at Cathair gheal, with a stone hall for their magistrate and a chapel with a bell, and Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, sent them up a charter under its seal. The copyists have that charter, Cairt Chathair gheal, in a fair copy from the letter-books of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir. It gives the date of the founding as 28 an Cèitean, AE 50, and the bounds of the market, and the tolls, and the rights of the magistrate over weights and measures and the ringing of the bell; and nowhere in it, in all its three sheets, is any custodian of the island named, or asked, or thanked, or told.

That same summer farmers out of the concession cleared land beside the old village of Cnoc ghorm, up in the high country of the north-west, and put up a mill on its stream. The people of Cnoc ghorm had lived under their pillar and its saying since the first ford-gatherings, and they had seen strangers come before. They sold the newcomers grain through the first winter, at a fair price, and carried it to them on their own ponies. When the mill-wheel turned in the spring, they stopped. Nobody at Cnoc ghorm said why, and the humans did not ask; but Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's letters speak afterwards of "a coolness at the old village," and of a boy of the farms who went up there to buy eggs and was sold none.

On the coast a few fishing families from the concession settled at Ceann mhòr under the north-western headland, on 14 am Màrt, AE 51. They were the first humans on the island to fish its waters for their own living and not for A' Chompanaidh's table, and the Dia-thìrich fishers of that coast, who had watched A' Chompanaidh's boats for fifty years, watched these more closely. The newcomers' boats went out when theirs did. They learned the marks of the reefs from them, and the set of the tides round the headland; and they took, in the second summer, to planting a leaf on the sheltered slopes behind the harbour, a coarse broad plant that they hung in their sheds to dry and sold to A' Chompanaidh's ships. By AE 52 there were whole terraces of it behind Ceann mhòr. Of all the plants the humans brought, that leaf alone took to the ground of the island.

The news of the charter came to the council at Cathair dhearg in the humans' tongue, since Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir sent everything in its own tongue by then, and the council sat a whole afternoon over three sheets that most of its members could not read.

## IV. Of Eachann Mòr's Seat

One of those who could not read them was Eachann Mòr of Ceann àrsaidh.

He had sat for Ceann àrsaidh on the council for nine years. Ceann àrsaidh was an old market town on the roads some twenty miles east of the capital, with a stone crossing over its river and a great many opinions of itself. It had given the council Coinneach Glas, and it expected to be listened to. Eachann was fifty that year, a big slow man with a voice that filled the council hall without his raising it, and he knew every boundary-stone and every well-right in his country, and the names of the grandfathers of the people who used them. He had the old reckoning by heart, and the rolls of his town back to An Aois Scaraidh. Of the humans' tongue he had perhaps ten words, and he was ashamed of none of them. 

He stood up in the council when the charter had been read, first in the humans' tongue by a clerk who had it and then in Dia-thìris by the same clerk, stumbling. He said that a town had been founded on the island under a writing that did not know the island had custodians, and that the council ought to send the writing back. The council agreed with him. It wrote to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir. Some weeks later an answer came in the humans' tongue, and the clerk who read it aloud stumbled again, and nobody on the benches could say afterwards with any confidence what it had meant, except that the charter stood.

Eachann went home and told Ceann àrsaidh what he had said in the hall. He told it well. But A' Chompanaidh had a weigh-house on the river at Ceann àrsaidh by then, and a road-agent, and a clerk who came through twice a month to settle the carting; and in the autumn, when the households met at the crossing to choose who should sit for them, a man spoke up who had never said anything at a choosing before. He was Dùghall Òg of the carting families, who had worked five years at the weigh-house and spoke the humans' tongue as fast as his own. The town needed a custodian, he said, who could read what was sent to him. There was no heat in it. Eachann Mòr, he said, was the best man in the country, and could not read a bill of lading.

They chose Dùghall. The roll of Ceann àrsaidh gives Cunntas nan Làmh, and it was not close.

Eachann walked home from the crossing with his wife Mairead nic Ìomhair beside him, and his son and daughter behind. He did not speak on the way. At the door of the house he stopped, and stood a while looking at the lintel, and then he turned round and looked at his son. Calum was twelve that autumn, a thin dark boy with his mother's eyes, who could already do the old reckoning faster than his father and had a way of listening at doors.

"You will have their tongue," Eachann said to him. "Better than Dùghall has it, and better than their clerks. And from their own schools."

Mairead said nothing then. She said a great deal afterwards, in the house, through the whole of that winter; and the copyists, who had the family's letters from a granddaughter's chest, found her side of the argument only in what Eachann wrote back to her from the road. He was never a man to put a thing on paper twice.

## V. Of the Ship That Went North-about

There was a school in the humans' tongue on the island that spring, and he would not send Calum to it.

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise of the humans' faith, opened its school at Ros dhomhain on 9 an Cèitean, AE 51, in a new room built on the side of the chapel. It took thirty children in its first year and taught them their letters and their catechism and their sums, all in the humans' tongue. Most of the thirty were the children of overseers, who were paid in marks and wanted their sons to be paid in more of them. Among them, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise wrote home with great joy, were its first converts of the island's own people.

Eachann Mòr would not have his son at a bench among overseers' sons. That was his pride, and Mairead knew it for his pride, and told him so. But he had spoken in the autumn to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's cleric at Ros dhomhain, and the cleric had spoken of schools over the sea, true schools, with libraries and masters, where a clever boy might learn the humans' law and come home able to read any charter Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir could send. The cleric wrote a letter for the boy to carry. Eachann paid for the passage in marks, and he gave Calum besides a purse of marks sewn into the lining of his coat, which was nearly all the silver the house had.

They went down to Ros dhomhain in the spring, the four of them in a cart, a long day on the road through the farms and the coal-dust. The ship lay at the quay below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, a ship of A' Chompanaidh going home with coal and hides, low in the water. Her master was a short man in a blue coat who looked at the boy, and at the letter, and at the purse when it was shown to him, and then wrote a line in his book. The quay was full of carts and barrows and the shouting of the men at the weighing-beam. There was nowhere to sit. The family stood by the bollards in the rain.

Calum went aboard on 10 an Giblean, AE 51. He went up the plank without looking back, since his father had told him to, and then at the rail he did look back, and lifted his hand. Ciorstaidh, who was nine, waved both her arms until her mother caught them.

The pilot of Caol leathan took the ship down the Abhainn gheal on the evening tide, and at the river's mouth she stood out to sea and turned north, as every ship of the humans turned, to go up the west coast past the headlands and out past the north cape into the grey water beyond, and so round by the north to the humans' land. That is the only road. The strangers' first ships had come down by it, and Cabhlach an Scaraidh had gone out by it long before. Mairead said afterwards that she hated to think of him going the long way, round the whole island, when the land he was going to lay somewhere off to the east where the sun came up. Eachann said that the ship knew its road. He stood on the quay until the masts had gone down the river out of sight behind the reeds, and then he went up to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise and thanked the cleric, and gave him a cheese.

## VI. Of the Letters That Did Not Come

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's cleric had said a letter would come by the autumn ships. None came.

Eachann went down to Ros dhomhain when the autumn ships were in, and stood at A' Chompanaidh's counter and asked, through a pupil of Scoil na Teachdaireachd whom he paid a penny, whether any letter had come for the house of Eachann Mòr of Ceann àrsaidh. The clerk looked through a box and said none had. The ship that had carried Calum was not among the ships in, and the clerk did not know when she would be.

In the winter Eachann wrote a letter himself. He wrote it in Dia-thìris, since he could write nothing else, and took it to Ros dhomhain, and paid the pupil to put it into the humans' tongue under his own lines; and he gave it to the master of the first ship going north in the spring, with a mark for the trouble. It went, and there was no answer to it. He wrote another the next winter. The copyists found copies of four such letters among the family's papers, each longer than the last, all of them telling the boy about the harvest and his sister and the price of oats and the dog, and none of them asking him outright to write back. Mairead's hand is on the fourth, below her husband's, one line: *Scrìobh gu do mhàthair.* Write to your mother.

In the year after Calum sailed, the custodians of Inis bhàn in the north opened a school of their own, twenty-odd miles up the road from Ceann àrsaidh, on 7 an t-Ògmhios, AE 52. They said openly that it was an answer to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's. They taught the old reckoning of years and moons and the reading of the rolls, and the names of the hills, every hill that could be seen from the school's door and a great many that could not, with the tale that went with each name. Eachann sent Ciorstaidh there. She was ten. She came home at midsummer able to name forty hills and argue with her father about the boundaries of his own parish, and the next year Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise complained in writing to the custodians of Inis bhàn that the children who came to its school from theirs arrived already knowing how to argue. The custodians of Inis bhàn had that letter read aloud at their gathering and then kept it, as a testimonial.

In the third year Eachann went down to A' Chompanaidh's counter again and asked for the ship by name. This time the clerk found her in his book. She had come in to the island twice since the spring Calum sailed, he said, and gone out again, and her master had since been given another run. Against the day Calum sailed, the book had one line, which the clerk read out and the pupil turned into Dia-thìris for the old man: a passenger, a native boy, his fare paid in full.

Eachann asked what had become of the passenger. The clerk said that was not a thing his book would know.

## VII. Of the Coal Road in the East

While Eachann Mòr waited at Ceann àrsaidh, A' Chompanaidh came east.

It had opened workings in the eastern hills, and it wanted a road to the sea for their coal that did not go the long way round by the capital. Up the valley from Inis bheag there was an old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn, Drochaid Ros fhionn, which Ailean Clachair had first built and whose piers the masons of An Aois Naomh had mended. The river had silted below it in the last generations, and the salt trade had gone off to the coast, and the carts had stopped crossing; the office of the bridge-keeper had been done away with, and the grass had grown up between the stones. In the spring A' Chompanaidh's masons came and rebuilt it for heavy carts. They left Ailean Clachair's sign in the keystone where it was, since it bore nothing up; and on 1 an Giblean, AE 53, the first coal-carts went over.

Aonghas walked over to see them, since Ros fhionn was no great distance from Dùn thais, and he took the students with him. They sat on the bank below the bridge all one afternoon and watched the carts go over, forty in the afternoon, each with its load heaped and roped and a boy on top to hold the rope. The drivers were most of them of the island, hill-men from the camps, and when the students shouted to them from the bank to throw down a lump, some of them did, laughing. Two of the drivers were humans. The students watched them closely. The humans looked at the coal they drove as a man looks at a load of stones, and at the students on the bank as though they had lost their wits.

"There," said Seumas mac Artair to the master. "The eyes."

"Perhaps," said Aonghas, and threw the lump he was holding back up to the next cart, and the driver caught it.

The coal went down over the bridge to the river quays of Inis bheag and there onto barges for Caol chrom at the river's mouth, where the ships took it. A' Chompanaidh deepened the river at the quays with a gang of men and a great iron scoop worked by a horse, and to make room for the coal-stage it moved the town's fish market, which had stood on that quay since before there was a town, up the hill to a yard behind the tannery. By the winter of AE 53 the quays at Inis bheag could load no more, and the barges began to go on down the Abhainn bheag to Baile mhin, a short way below, whose people took the overflow and were paid by the barge. On 13 am Faoilleach, AE 54, the first barge was loaded there, and within two years Baile mhin had its first houses of stone, built out of A' Chompanaidh's money by the men who loaded A' Chompanaidh's coal.

Caol gharbh on the coast had hoped for the traffic. It had taken the salt trade when the river silted, a lifetime before, and its people had watched the bridge go up and made ready. But A' Chompanaidh's road ran down to the river quays and passed Caol gharbh by a mile, and all Caol gharbh ever had of the eastern coal was the dust, which came over on the east wind and lay on the washing. Its custodians wrote to the council at Cathair dhearg, on 11 an Gearran, AE 54, that they had not known a town could be harmed by a road it was not on. The council filed the letter. Aonghas had a copy of it from a student of that country, and he pinned it to the door of the hall, beside the lintel, where it stayed until the rain took it.

## VIII. Of the Things the Clerks Could Not File

There were things in those years the clerks of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir never knew where to put.

In the spring of AE 55 the crew of a brig of A' Chompanaidh came into Ceann mhòr with their mainsail split and their master white to the lips, and said that off the north-western headlands, on a clear morning, a beast had come up beside them that was longer than their ship. It had lain on the water, they said, and looked at them, and gone down. The report went to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, as all reports did, and the clerk there read it, and filed it on 12 am Màrt, AE 55, among the complaints about pirates, having no other box it would fit. The fishers of that coast heard of it and were not surprised.
