Uilebheist na Mara had been seen off those capes since An Aois Àrsaidh, and had fouled their nets within living memory; they said they had wondered how long the humans would sail there before they saw it too.

In the autumn of the same year a brig bound for the northern landing with tools was caught by a gale in sea-mist off Eilean fhada and driven onto the skerries there. Her crew waited for the ebb and waded ashore through the weed, and walked along the coast in the wet to the harbour at Caol bheag, where the fishers took them in and dried them by their fires. On 13 an t-Sultain, AE 55, her master made his report. Thereafter A' Chompanaidh's charts marked the northern passage as foul from midwinter to the end of spring, which were the months of the gales and the mist, and its masters were bidden not to sail in them without need; and so, from that year, few ships came to the island or went from it for a third of every year. At Ceann àrsaidh Mairead nic Ìomhair heard of the new rule from a carter and asked what it meant. When it was explained to her, she said that she would stop going to the door in those months, then, and mostly did.

That winter the human fishers of the concession taught the boats of Àth fhionn to go out after the whales with the hand-lance, and not wait for them to strand. The men of Àth fhionn had taken whales as the sea gave them since the first harbour there, and had thanked Manannan for each one. They went out now in the humans' way, six to a boat, and killed them in the open water, and rendered the oil in pots on the shore and sold it to A' Chompanaidh for its lamps. After 9 an Dùbhlachd, AE 55, the whale-boats went out from the north coast every summer.

And in the summer of AE 56 two of A' Chompanaidh's surveyors came up to Doire uaine in the hills above Muileann chiar with chains and pegs and a boy to carry the instruments. The hills there are cut with the old writing that nobody can read, lines of it yards long, some of it scored across by the same kind of tool that cut it; and the people of the villages under them hold that the writing speaks of a thing that walks without breath, the Marbh-bheò, which falls on anyone who lights a fire in its sight. No fire has been lit where those hills can see it since An Aois Àrsaidh. The villagers told the surveyors so, through the boy. They told them not to go up. The surveyors thanked them and went up on 21 an Lùnastal, AE 56, with a tinder-box in their pack, and camped on the high ground, and were not seen again.

A' Chompanaidh sent a search party of eight men. They went up into the hills one morning and came back down that same evening. They had found the surveyors' last camp and their chains laid out along a ridge, they said, and a fire-ring of stones with no ash in it; and past that they would not go, not for the agent's pay nor for his threats, and not one of them would say why. The agent wrote to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that the men were idle.

The villagers of Doire uaine did then what their grandparents had done after any death on the high ground. They took salt and coal to the foot of the hills and left them on a flat stone there, for the sìth. A' Chompanaidh's agent for that country heard of it, and sent men on 19 an t-Sultain, AE 56 to gather up the coal, since he would have no coal left lying about the country to be picked up by anyone who liked, and he had it carted back to the stockpile and weighed. After that the villagers left salt alone on the stone. A' Chompanaidh's men came up the next season and looked at the salt and let it lie.

## IX. Of the Question Put Back

Eachann Mòr came to Dùn thais at the end of the harvest of that year, when the rowans were red.

It was forty miles and more from Ceann àrsaidh, two long days on a borrowed horse, and he was fifty-six and had grown heavy, and he came into the town stiff and grey with the dust of the coal-road. He asked in the street for the master of Taigh na Deasbaid. They sent him up the hill to the hall. Aonghas was at the table with the register open, and the students were out under the oaks, and there was nobody else in the hall at all.

Eachann had not met him before. He had heard of the question, as everyone on the island had heard of it by then, from the carriers and the carters and the hearths; and he had heard, from a carter, of the salt on the stone at Doire uaine, and of the men who would not go past a cold fire-ring. He sat down on the end of the nearest bench, since nobody asked him to sit and he could not stand any longer, and told the master who he was. Then he told him about the ship.

He told it straight through, as a custodian tells a matter to the council: the choosing at the crossing, and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's letter, and the purse sewn into the coat, and the quay in the rain, and the four letters, and the clerk's one line. He did not hurry it. Aonghas did not stop him. When it was done he sat with his big hands on his knees, and the rooks went over the roof, and after a while he came to what he had ridden two days to ask.

"He could see it," he said. "He could name more in a lump than I could, by the time he was eight. His mother used to set him to it for a game, by the fire." He looked at the basket, which was still on the table, with A' Chompanaidh's coal in it. "Five years he has been among them. Eating what they eat. Burning what they burn, by the cartload. Hearing their word for it and no other." He stopped. "When he comes home, will he see it?"

Aonghas looked at him for a long time.

Then he took the split lump out of the basket, the same one, and turned its broken face to the window, and held it out across the table; and Eachann took it, not knowing what else to do, and looked, and the colours came up out of it for him as they always had, the grey at the edge and the brown and the green under the black and the red when his breath touched it.

"You see it," said Aonghas.

"I have always seen it."

"And you want me to tell you whether your son does, in a country none of us has seen, among a people I cannot see into." He took the lump back and laid it in the basket. "Seven years ago I set this house a question. Why do we see the colour, and they are blind to it? The house has argued it ever since, and so has Baile Mòr uaine, four hundred leaves of it. You have ridden two days to ask me the same question turned round. I told my students it was the wrong question. I will not answer it for you any more than I would for them."

"Then what is the right one?"

"I do not know," said Aonghas. "If I knew it I would have written it down."

Eachann Mòr sat a while longer. Then he got up off the bench, heavily, and thanked the master for his time, as a custodian thanks a man who has told the council nothing, and went out into the yellow evening and down the hill to find his horse.

Seumas mac Artair, coming in from the oaks, met him at the door and asked the master afterwards who the big man had been. Aonghas told him, and told him why he had come. Seumas asked whether he should put it in the register.

"Put in that a man came from Ceann àrsaidh to ask the question," said the master, "and that the master did not answer it."

Seumas wrote it down. It is the last entry in Aonghas mac Coinnich's hand of that year, or rather in Seumas's under his dictation, dated at the end of the harvest of AE 56. Below it the rest of the leaf is empty. The basket stood on the table in the hall through the winter, with A' Chompanaidh's coal in it, and the students took lumps from it to argue over and put them back, and none of them was ever burned.

# Chapter Seventeen: Of the Tithe and the Flux

*AE 57 – 62*

## I. Of the Schedule Read Twice

The paper came down from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in am Gearran of that year, folded in three and sealed with Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's wax, and the custodian who broke the seal at Cathair dhearg could not read a word of it.

Nobody at the council table could. It was the humans' writing, close and slanted, three sheets of it, and under Lisle's hand at the foot a line in Dia-thìris so cramped it might have been an afterthought: *the schedule follows below.* The council sent for Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's pupil, a girl of fifteen called Barabal nic Dhùghaill who had learned her letters at Ros dhomhain and her sums from a clerk who liked to be flattered, and she stood at the table's end with the three sheets shaking a little in her hands and read Lisle's schedule into Dia-thìris while the custodians listened.

What it came to was this. Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's part of the mined coal, which had stood at one sack in five since Maddox's day, was to rise to one sack in three. Barabal read the figure twice, thinking she had misheard herself, and the second time it was the same.

"One in three," said the custodian of Cnoc bheag, an old man who had sat at that table longer than anyone living. "Read the reason."

There was no reason given. Barabal turned the sheets over to be sure, and turned them back, and said there was none.

"Ask her to read the figure a third time," said a younger custodian at the foot of the table, a woman new enough to her seat that she still thought a wrong sum might be undone by the asking.

Barabal read it a third time. It came to the same.

The hall at Cathair dhearg where the council sat was the same low stone room it had sat in since before the strangers came, with a hearth at one end that smoked in a westerly and a table scarred by three generations of knife-cuts where clerks had trimmed their pens against the wood rather than find a board. Barabal stood at the foot of it in Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise grey with the three sheets in her two hands, and she has said since, to the one custodian who ever thought to ask her, that she was more afraid of the room than of the news, since she had never before been looked at by so many people at once who wanted something from her that she could not give them, which was a smaller figure.

The old custodian of Cnoc bheag asked her to read Lisle's line at the foot once more, the cramped one that named the schedule. She read it. He asked whether there was anything above the fold, any mark of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's council or seal beyond Lisle's own hand. There was Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's wax and nothing else. He sat a while with his hands flat on the table, and then said that the roll should have her rendering copied into it entire, with her name at the foot, so that no one might ever say the island had not been told what was done to it, only that it had not been able to stop it. Barabal, who had expected to be thanked or dismissed and had not thought to be asked to sign anything, wrote her name under the copy in a hand rounder than her fifteen years, and it stands there yet.

AE 57 is remembered on the coal roads as the year of the schedule, and Lisle's is the hand under it, though whether the figure was his own asking or an order sent to him from over the sea that he only signed, no one at Cathair dhearg could say. His letter-book, which survives, gives no reason either. It gives an account of the cost of the new customs house at Ros gheal, and a note that Comann an Airgid's compact must on no account be touched, and then, three lines down, the new fraction, as if it followed from the customs house and the silver both.

The custodians wrote a copy of Barabal's rendering into the roll of every coal town on the island, word for word, with the date and her name at the foot of each, so that whoever asked how the tithe had doubled without a war to explain it would find one paper that said so in the island's own tongue, made by one of its own, and not only Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's sealed sheets that few could read.

## II. Of the Weighing at Dùn fhiadhaich

At Dùn fhiadhaich, which stood among the barley fields under Cnoc naomh and had never dug so much as a bucket of coal, the tithe-gatherer arrived in the spring with a wagon, a set of scale-beams, and a paper that named the town among those that must pay.

The town's grain, he said, fed the men who worked the pits at Muileann chrom and Achadh dhomhain, and so the town shared in the pits' gain and would share in their tithe. He set his scales up in the market square between the well and the mill, and the farmers brought their sacks and stood in a line that ran the length of the square and back, and watched one sack in three of the year's barley go into the wagon while the rest went home with them.

A farmer near the head of the line, a man called Griogair Fada who held the largest acreage under Cnoc naomh and so had the most sacks to lose, asked the gatherer straight out whether it was the pits' fraction that had gone up or the farms' fraction that was new. The gatherer, who was a young man himself and plainly uneasy with the question, said only that his paper named Dùn fhiadhaich and gave a weight for grain against it, and that he had not written the paper and could not answer for what was in the mind of the man who had.

"Then who can," said Griogair, "since he is not here to be asked."

The gatherer had no answer to that either, and weighed the sacks as his paper said, and by evening the wagon stood a third heavier than the town's own store, and the line of farmers going home carried two sacks in three back through the same square where their grandfathers had once carried salt to trade for iron before any human had set foot on the island at all.

The custodians of Dùn fhiadhaich wrote the thing into their roll under a name of their own, since no name for it had come down from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir: *deachamh an deachaimh*, the tithe on the tithe, for it seemed to them a strange doubling, to be taxed for feeding men who were themselves taxed. The name held. It is the name the town still gives that spring, when old men there are asked about it, though the grandchildren of the men who stood in that line no longer quite remember what the first tithe had been for, only that it is called by a name that means twice paid, and that this is reason enough not to like it.

## III. Of the Sick-House in the Chapel

Anne Colby came ashore at Ros dhomhain on 16 an Gearran, AE 57, twenty-two years old, with a chest of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's linen and a case of instruments she had been shown how to use twice on the crossing and never once before. She had asked to be sent to the island because her brother had gone out with Harrow's ships years before and never written home, and she had a notion, which she kept to herself, that she might find some word of him among the quays. She found no word of him on the island, and in her third summer she found the flux instead.

It broke first in the crowded lodgings above the harbour, where the men who worked the counting-house and the steelyard slept eight and ten to a room A' Chompanaidh let them for what it cost A' Chompanaidh nothing to build. By the second week of an t-Iuchar the sick lay two to a bed in those rooms, and by the third the well behind the counting-house had been fouled, though no one owned to knowing how; and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chapel, the long timber hall on the quay with its iron bell, stood shut between its services, the width of the quay from the lodgings.

Colby had the door opened and the benches carried out into the yard and did not ask leave of anyone to do it. She laid down what straw she could buy and what linen Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise would give her, and she and two women of the harbour quarter, a widow called Mòr nic Amhlaidh and her daughter, began to carry the sick up from the lodgings on a hand-barrow, six and eight a day, until the long timber room held as many as could lie down in it and the yard held the rest under a sailcloth awning that Colby had begged off a shipmaster for the promise of prayers for his crossing.

Mòr nic Amhlaidh had lost a husband to the sea and two children to A' Bhreac Bhallach years before Colby ever landed, and she is said to have told the young nurse, on the first night the two of them washed the chapel floor together by lamplight, that she had buried enough of her own to know the trick of it: that the dying wanted their names said to them more than they wanted the fever broken, since the fever generally broke or did not on its own account regardless of what hands did to it, while a name said plainly by someone who meant it could be given to a man right up to the last hour, cost nothing, and was sometimes the only thing left to give. Colby, who had come out with instruments and had been taught nothing at all about names, took the advice as if it had been part of her training from the start, and it may be from that one night's washing of a floor that the whole of what she did afterward followed.

The days ran much alike. She rose before light, walked the yard and the room together and marked who had worsened in the night, then spent the forenoon at the lodgings themselves, since A' Chompanaidh's own physician would not go into them and someone had to judge which of the newly fallen could still walk to the chapel on their own legs and which must wait for the barrow. At midday she ate standing, generally bread and whatever fish Mòr's daughter had got cheap at the quay, and in the afternoon she boiled linen in a copper Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had once used for washing altar cloths and now used for nothing else. The custodians' roll, which took to noting her comings and goings as it noted little else about Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, records that she was seen to sleep, in the worst of that season, no more than four hours together, and generally on a bench in the yard rather than in the room Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had given her in the town, since the room was a mile off and the sick were not.

She was told by A' Chompanaidh's own surgeon, who came once and did not come again, that she would do better to let the sick lie where they were and keep the well-off away from them. He stood in the chapel doorway with a cloth held to his own face and would not come further in than the threshold, and told her, in the tone of a man passing on a kindness, that a chapel crowded with the dying was no place for a young woman to make her name. She answered him that the well-off were already dying, since the flux never troubled to ask a man's wages before it took him, and asked him to leave, which by his own account, written years after in a letter to his son, he was glad to do.

He did send, before he left the harbour for good that season, a case of the salts he judged best against the flux, with a note that she was welcome to try them though he held out no great hope of them, and Colby used every grain in the case and kept the empty box afterward on the chapel's one shelf, since it was, whatever the man's manners, the only help A' Chompanaidh's own physician ever sent her.

What she did instead, and what the roll of the custodians credits her for, was to learn the sick by name. Not A' Chompanaidh's names for them, which were their number on the pay-roll and the gang they worked in, but the names the custodians already kept, each man and woman with a house and a mother and a place of birth set down against them in the town's own roll. She sat at the door of the chapel each evening with that roll open on her knee and a clerk's boy to read her the entries, and she wrote against each name who lived and who did not, in her own hand, in the humans' tongue, a column the custodians could not read, and turned the roll round on the table each evening so they could see for themselves that it was there.

Fourteen died in her chapel before the flux burned out in the autumn, and the custodians' roll, which counted the quarter's dead with care, credits her with keeping them under fifteen. The town remembers her less for the number than for the list she kept, of the men who died in her chapel, every name spelled right, and that when the families came to ask, she did not need the roll open on her knee to tell them.

## IV. Of the Barges to Seann Vell

The coal barges that ran the river east from Ros dhomhain to the port of Seann Vell had no part in the flux at first, or none that anyone marked until a bargeman fell sick at his pole on 7 an t-Ògmhios, AE 60 and was put ashore at the Seann Vell landing rather than carried on, since the barge-master judged, wrongly as it turned out, that a man on dry land had a better chance than a man on the water.

Within the fortnight the sickness was in three of the landing's houses, and within the month it was in a dozen. The custodians of Seann Vell, a river town that had never before had cause to shut anything, shut the only quay the town had for the coal traffic that fed it, and let no barge tie up there for the length of a season.

A' Chompanaidh fined them for it. The letter that came down from the pay office cited the loss of a season's landing fees and made no mention of the flux at all, as though the town had shut its own quay for no better reason than mischief. The custodian who received it, a woman called Mairead nic Amhlaidh who was no kin to the widow at Ros dhomhain though she shared her name, as the island's names will run twice and thrice over between towns that never knew each other, read the fine to the town council standing on the landing steps, within sight of the graves the town had dug that season on the rise above it, and said only that A' Chompanaidh's letter had been well timed, if nothing else, to arrive on the day the last of the dead were being sung over.

The custodians of Seann Vell paid the fine out of the same purse that had buried their dead, since there was no other purse to pay it from, and wrote in their roll, in the flat hand the roll keeps for things it does not trust plain words to say, that A' Chompanaidh had weighed a season's coin against a season's dead and found the coin heavier.

Colby heard of it at Ros dhomhain from a bargeman who had carried the news downriver along with a cargo of empty sacks, and she walked the eighteen miles to Seann Vell on a day when the chapel could spare her, along the towpath where the barges no longer ran, with the river low and brown beside her and the landing, when she reached it, as quiet as she had ever seen a coal port. She stayed a week helping to lay out the last of that town's dead before she went back to her own, and it was at Seann Vell, sitting with Mairead nic Amhlaidh over the town's own roll one evening, that she first thought to ask whether any other town kept such a list, and was told that most did, after their own fashion, and that no one had ever thought to keep one list of the sickness across every town it touched, only each town's account of its own.

## V. Of the Seal Passed On

Arthur Lisle died at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on 3 am Màrt, AE 61, of a fever that settled in his chest and then, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's own physician wrote, in his heart, so that he was a fortnight dying by inches with his clerks bringing him papers to the last, since he would not be told he could not sign them. He was one and sixty years old, a lawyer by training who had come to the office at forty-one and never in his twenty years at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir raised his voice at a council table, which the custodians who dealt with him counted, on the whole, in his favour, though they did not forgive him the schedule.

Walter Crane, who had been A' Chompanaidh's chief agent at the pits since before Lisle's time, took Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's seal within the month. He was six and forty, a heavier man than Lisle, quicker to anger and quicker to forget it, who had spent his years among the coal camps rather than at a desk and knew the roads between Achadh dhomhain and Muileann chrom better than he knew Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's own corridors. He came to the seal in his own riding coat, still splashed to the knee from the pit roads, and it is told, though not in any hand that signed its name to the telling, that he sat at Lisle's own desk on his first morning and pushed the dead man's inkstand a foot to the left before he would so much as open the first paper on it, for Lisle, he said, had kept it in a fool's place for a right-handed man.

Crane was the first man to hold A' Chompanaidh's office and Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's one after the other, and the custodians noted the thing without saying what they thought of it, though what they thought is not hard to guess: that the two offices, which had been kept carefully apart since Harrow's day so that neither office might answer only to its own master, now answered to one man's convenience. Crane himself, when a custodian of Cathair dhearg put the question to him plainly at his first council, said only that he saw no sense in the island having two masters where one would do the work of both more cheaply, and that the council might take that for whatever comfort it was worth. It was taken for none.

Crane's first order from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, given within the week, was that the pits should not slacken for the change of one Àrd-mhaor to another. His second, given the same week, moved A' Chompanaidh's pay office for the southern workings from the pit-heads themselves to the town of Ceann mhin.

## VI. Of the Day's Walk to Ceann mhin

The reason given, when a reason was given at all, was that a single pay office serving the whole southern district would keep truer books than a paymaster riding from pit to pit with the coin in his saddlebags, as had been done till then, and lose fewer sacks of silver to bad roads and worse arithmetic. It may even have been true. What it meant for the crews was a day's walk to Ceann mhin and a day's walk back, twice in every month, to stand in a line at a window and be paid what they were owed, and no pay at all for the two days spent walking to collect it.

Uisdean Ruadh, who hewed at Muileann chrom and had a wife and three children to feed on what he carried home, walked it the first time in company with forty other men of his gang, setting out before light on a morning of frost with their breath standing in clouds ahead of them on the road. His wife had packed him bread and a twist of dried fish the night before and asked him, only half in jest, whether he meant to be paid or only to walk, since the two seemed to have become separate undertakings, and he had no answer for her beyond that a man went where the coin was kept and not where it was easiest to fetch.

They reached Ceann mhin at midday, stood in the pay line till near dusk behind the crews of two other pits who had the same idea of an early start, and walked the road home again in the dark, so that the two days it cost them to be paid were, by his own reckoning kept afterward on a stick he notched at his door, worth rather less than the pay itself. The line at the window moved slowly because the clerk within counted every coin twice, being new to the office and afraid of a wrong tally more than he was troubled by the length of the queue outside, and the men waiting had time enough to talk among themselves of little else but the road, so that by the third pay-day the walk, and not the wage at the end of it, had become the thing the gangs of Muileann chrom spoke of first when they met men of other pits.

The custodians of Ceann mhin, whose town gained a fortnight's trade in bread and small beer from every pay-day and complained of it to no one, kept no roll of the walk at all. It is Uisdean Ruadh's notched stick, kept by his family three generations after him and shown still to those who ask, that is the only record of what the day cost the men who walked it.

## VII. Of Raghnall's Burying

Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, whom the crews and the custodians both had come to call Raghnall Maor, died at Muileann chrom in am Màrt of AE 62, seventy-two years old, in the slate-roofed house A' Chompanaidh had built him above the pit he had first walked into as a guide to A' Chompanaidh's men who did not know one seam of coal from another.

He had been ill through the winter with a wasting the surgeon called an old man's cough and treated as one, and Colby, sent for from Ros dhomhain in his last week by a message from his son that she never learned the whole of, sat with him two nights before the end, more for the son's sake than for any doctoring she could do, since there was none left to do.

The house surprised her, though she had heard it spoken of often enough on the coal roads: a slate roof over dressed stone, the only one of its kind for miles, with a hearth big enough to be a custodian's and a window of real glass looking down on the pit-head, so that a man lying in the bed A' Chompanaidh had given him could watch, if he chose, the crews going down and coming up without ever leaving it. Raghnall did not choose to. He had the bed turned, in the last weeks, so that it faced the door and not the window, and when Colby asked him once, more to have something to say than because she expected an answer, why he had it so, he told her that he had looked at that pit-head every day for fifty years and saw no cause to spend his last ones at it as well.

He said little to her that she thought worth setting down, being a man who had never been given to speaking of himself even in his own house, but on the second night he asked her, apropos of nothing that had passed between them, whether she wrote her dead down by name, as the town said she did. When she told him yes, he said that was a good thing to keep doing, and spoke no more before morning. In the small hours before he died he spoke once more, to the room rather than to her, a few words in Dia-thìris that his son, sitting on the other side of the bed, kept from Colby then and always, though the son is said to have written them down somewhere in his own hand, in a paper that has not survived.

Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill, his son, was two and forty that year and had broken his first coal at six in the year of An Casad Tioram and lived, which the custodians had not expected him to. He had grown into a quieter man than his father, by every account, and had worked twenty years at his father's side without any sign that he wanted the staff for himself, and it is said of him, by the one custodian who thought to ask him afterward, that he had hoped, as much as any man in the town, that the office would go elsewhere.

A' Chompanaidh gave him his father's staff within the week of the burying, the office and the slate roof and the crews together, as though the three were one inheritance and not three separate things a son might have been asked whether he wanted. A clerk came up from the pay office at Ceann mhin with the paper already drawn, needing only Dòmhnall's mark at the foot of it, and stood in the slate-roofed house's own doorway while Dòmhnall read it through twice before he signed, less because he doubted the terms than because he seems to have wanted, for those few minutes, to be a man still deciding rather than a man already decided for.

The custodians of Muileann chrom, who had buried eleven men under Raghnall's first gallery and watched him take A' Chompanaidh's pay to keep his crews at the face rather than lose it, had hoped, without quite saying so to one another, that the office might die with him and the crews go back to choosing their own foreman as they had before the pits opened. It did not die with him. It went from father to son as if it had always been meant to, and the custodians' hope, which had never been written down anywhere and so cannot properly be said to have died either, went with it.

Raghnall was buried on the hill above Muileann chrom beside the eleven, in ground the town had kept for its own dead since before A' Chompanaidh came, on a morning of thin rain that put out the torches twice before the custodian gave up lighting them and let the burying go on in the grey light alone. The whole pit turned out, both shifts together, which had not happened for any death at Muileann chrom in living memory, since a pit that stops both shifts at once stops its coal as well, and A' Chompanaidh had never before let that be reckoned worth the cost of one man's grave, whoever the man.

Colby stood at the edge of the grave among the crews with her list from the chapel still in the bag she carried everywhere, though there was no name to add to it that day but his. She had walked down from Ros dhomhain the day before on hearing the word, arriving too late to sit with him again but in good time for the burying, and she stood a little apart from the townsfolk, as she generally did at such gatherings, being neither of the crews nor of the custodians nor, any longer, entirely of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise either, but something the coal roads had made of her that had no ready name.

Dòmhnall stood at the graveside in his father's place and said nothing that any account sets down, though one among the crew is remembered to have said afterward that he had watched Dòmhnall's hand close twice on nothing, as a man's hand will close on a staff it has not yet been given and already knows the shape of. When it was over he walked back down the hill to the slate-roofed house alone, and the crews went back to the pit within the hour, since the pit did not stop for a burying any longer than A' Chompanaidh judged it must, any more than it had stopped for the schedule, the flux, or the day's walk to be paid.

Colby wrote Raghnall's name into her roll that evening in the same hand she had used for every name before it, with the date and the place, and under it, because she had begun by then to think it worth doing for everyone she buried and not only for the flux dead, a line of who he had been: *hewer, then Steward, father of Dòmhnall*. It was the only line in the whole roll that named an office. Why she wrote it there she never said to anyone the roll names, though a person who had watched five years of schedules and tithes and pay offices come down from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir without a single name attached to any of them might have guessed at her reason well enough.

# Chapter Eighteen: Of Lowe's Spade

*AE 63 – 68*

> *Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc.*
>
> Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill.

## I. Of the Coloured Flame at Muileann bheag

Four beacons burned on the coasts of Dia-thìr by the sixty-third year of the strangers, and three of them still burned oil, the old way, a wick fed from a cistern and trimmed each watch by a keeper who climbed the stair in the dark and came down again at dawn with his fingers black. The fourth was at Muileann bheag on the north shore, and it burned coal.

Edwin Lowe came up from Ros dhomhain to see it that winter, riding a mule of A' Chompanaidh with a satchel of paper across his knees, sent by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise to look into a complaint the beacon's own keepers had laid before the custodians and the custodians had, in their way, laid before nobody. He was thirty-eight years old that year, a cleric without a parish, thin in the shoulder and going grey early, and he had been eleven years on the island without once finding the thing he had come to find, which was proof, of one kind or another, that the god An Eaglais preached had been here before him, or that no god had, and either answer would have done, so long as it was an answer.

He had come out from an Tìr Thall a young man with a licence to preach and a private letter of introduction to a bishop who had since died without reading it, and had drifted, in the way of men whose first errand fails them quietly, into Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's smaller work: the copying of custodians' rolls that some clerk in Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir wanted translated, the measuring of ruins nobody else had time for, the answering of complaints too strange for A' Chompanaidh's own agents to be troubled with. Eleven years of it had made him into a kind of scholar the island had no name for and did not quite trust, a man who asked the custodians questions a cleric of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had no business asking and wrote down their answers in a hand too careful to be idle curiosity. The road to Muileann bheag, three days of mule-track and one of open coast, was nothing to him by then; he had ridden worse for less.

The keeper at Muileann bheag was a broad, weathered man named Ailig mac Griogair, who had tended the light since it burned oil and had asked, three winters running, to be let go back to the old lamp. He took Lowe up the stair himself.

"There," he said, at the top, and pointed down through the lantern glass at the black water below the point, where the beam swung slow across the swell. "You'll not see it. None of your people see it. But it's there."

Lowe looked, and saw firelight on water, the ordinary orange wash of a flame thrown wide by a curved glass, breaking and mending on the chop. He said as much.

"It's a green under the orange," said Ailig. "A green like nothing that was ever in a flame before, and it lies on the water a long way out, further than the beam itself should carry, and it comes and it goes with no wind to account for it. The herring won't come in under it. Ask any boat on this coast."

"And before the beacon burned coal?"

"The oil flame never did it. No flame ever did it before this one." Ailig's own son had gone twice to the custodians of the town about it, and had been heard and sent away with nothing added to the roll, for the custodians could find no law the flame broke; a man might burn what he liked in his own lamp, and the beacon was A' Chompanaidh's now in all but the keeping of it. "They say it drives the herring off. I say it lays a colour on the sea that was never laid there before, and that a colour laid on the sea is a thing worth minding, whatever it does to the fish."

Lowe wrote the complaint down as he had been asked, word for word, and climbed down the stair, and stood a long while on the point in the cold with his collar up, looking at the black water and the orange wash on it, trying to see the green the keeper saw, and the more he stared the more certain he became that there was nothing there to see, only firelight doing what firelight had always done to water, breaking and mending, breaking and mending.

He came back to the point twice more before he left the district, once at dusk and once before the dawn watch, and stood the same span of the same cold each time, and saw the same nothing. On the second visit Ailig's own son, a boy of perhaps twelve who had never known the beacon burn anything but coal, came down and stood beside him without being asked and looked where he looked.

"Well?" said Lowe.

"You're looking too hard," the boy said. "It's not a thing you look for. It's a thing you see, the way you see it's raining before you feel the first drop."

Lowe asked him what colour it was, precisely, and the boy considered a long while, the way a child considers a question put to him seriously for the first time, and said only that it was a green that made him think of nothing else he had ever seen, which was, Lowe wrote afterward, the most honest answer given him in eleven years on the island, and the least useful.

He wrote in his own book, that night, in the humans' letters, a single line that he did not send to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise with the rest: *I begin to think there are two islands here, laid one over the other, and I have been sent to survey only mine.*

Within the season the herring came back in under the light as they had always come, in their numbers, as if the sea had settled some dispute of its own and moved on; and the letter the fishermen of Muileann bheag had first sent was withdrawn in a second letter, which A' Chompanaidh kept beside the first, and neither was ever answered. The keepers did not change the lamp. They never did, in all the years it burned.

## II. Of the Dig at Làrach an Teampaill

Lowe's true errand that season lay further south and east, at a low ruin among gorse and standing water that the island called Làrach an Teampaill, the temple that had stood, empty and unclaimed by any faith the Dia-thìrich kept, since before the oldest roll of any custodian house began. Three ages of scholars had measured it and gone away no wiser. Lowe meant to be the fourth, and to dig where the others had only measured.

He got A' Chompanaidh's labourers for the digging, six men off the coal contracts at Doire ghlas who wanted the winter wage and had never held a spade for anything but coal, and a custodian of Doire ghlas, Griogal Odhar, came out with them most mornings to watch, never to work, and sat on the fallen lintel with his hands on his knees the way a man sits at a wake.

The ruin itself was low, little more to the eye than a rise of gorse and grey stone in a hollow of poor grazing land, with a single lintel still standing over what had once been a door and the rest of the walls sunk to their footings under a century of turf. Sheep grazed the mound in every season but this one, and the shepherds of Àth mhòr, whose flocks it was, had turned them off it without being asked, and would not say why beyond that it had always been the custom, on the days the ground was opened, to keep beasts from a grave until the grave was shut again.

They opened the ground inside the western wall first, where the old measurings had marked an altar, and found in the first week worked stone below the turf, cut square and laid without mortar, in courses too even for any wall the labourers' own grandfathers had raised. Lowe measured each course as it came clear, and noted that the stone was not of the district, a hard pale grey unlike the darker rock of the hills round about, and must have been carried some distance, by what means over what road he could not say, for no road the island now kept ran anywhere near the place.

In the second week they found bone, burnt through, packed in a shallow pit beside the altar stone with ash and a scatter of small worked flints that answered to no tool any smith of the island had ever made or named. The bone crumbled at a touch, and Lowe had the labourers stop digging round it and clear the earth away with their hands instead, a spoonful at a time, so that what came up came up whole; and it was slow, cold work, the men on their knees in the wet through the shortening days, breathing on their fingers between handfuls, and none of them complained of the wage, though more than one of them complained, quietly, to Griogal Odhar, of the work itself.

The labourers stopped there. Lowe pressed them to go deeper, and the eldest of the six, a broad quiet man called Tormod Ruadh, drove his spade upright in the loose earth at the pit's edge and would not lift it again.

"It's bone under an altar that was old before the vein was cut," he said. "I'll dig coal all my life and glad of the wage. I won't dig a man out of his own grave for a stranger's paper."

Lowe did not press him further. He wrote out what the pit held, the stone, the ash, the flints, the burnt bone he judged too old and too cold in the ground to be any recent thing, and sent word to Griogal Odhar to bring the custodians of the district to see it before he covered it again.

Four of them came, two days later, from Doire ghlas and Doire fhiadhaich and Àth mhòr, walking the last mile together though their three towns lay a half-day apart from one another, and stood at the pit's edge a long while without speaking, the way the labourers had stood, and then Griogal Odhar crouched and turned one flint over in his palm and set it down exactly where it had lain.

"It is not ours," he said. "The stone is not ours, and the bone is not ours, and whoever laid it there is not ours, and I do not think the god it was laid for is any god that is prayed to on this island now, if it is prayed to anywhere at all." He stood. "Cover it again. Say the word over it that we say over any grave whose kin cannot be found, and no more than that."

Lowe asked what word that was, and was told, and it was said, briefly, in Dia-thìris, by all four custodians together over the reopened pit, and none of them offered to teach it to him, nor did he ask twice.

Before they left he asked Griogal Odhar one thing more: whether any order of the island's own faiths, the hawk-order that kept the vein's old rites, or the order that held the capital's shrines, or any other, claimed the ruin or the bone under it as its own.

"None," said Griogal. "I have heard it said that Mòd himself does not claim what was old before the vein was found, for a god that eats the hill can only eat what grew in the hill's own time, and this was here before the hill was a hill worth eating. Whether that is true, no one has told me. No order has ever asked to be given this ground, and none has ever been refused it, for none has asked."

He wrote afterward, in the letter-book he kept for Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise and did send: *They agree with my own reading of the stone entirely, and add nothing to it. I had thought a people so old in their own land would have some tale for a ruin older still. They have none. I begin to wonder whether that is the more remarkable fact of the two.*

## III. Of the Pillar and the Column

There were two other marks in the district that Lowe had been asked to copy before he left it: a pillar of grey stone near Cnoc chiar, weathered past most reading, and a column near Cnoc ghorm that stood a little taller and a little plainer, with lines cut round its shoulder that might have been words or might have been only the marks of the tool that dressed it.

He went to Cnoc chiar first, in the spring, and spent nine days with paper and charcoal rubbing the face of Colbh Cnoc chiar a hand's width at a time, working from the ground up in the wet wind off the hill, while an old woman of the town below came up most afternoons to sit on the stone's shadow-side and watch him without a word of greeting either way. She brought her own work with her, a basket of wool she carded as she watched, and by the fourth day Lowe had stopped expecting her to speak and had begun, instead, to find some comfort in the small sound of the carders, back and forth, under the wind. The pillar stood alone on a shoulder of open hill with no wall or ditch about it that any digging had ever found, and the grass grew close about its foot as it grew nowhere else on that slope, cropped fine by sheep that came to no other patch so willingly.

On the ninth day, folding his last sheet, he asked her, in the little Dia-thìris he had, whether the pillar had a name.

"It is a stone," she said. "It had a name once. We have not kept it."

"Was it a wicked thing, that the name was lost?"

She thought about that longer than she had thought about anything else he had asked her in nine days. "No," she said at last. "Names are lost the way anything is lost that nobody carries any more. Nobody has carried this one in a long time. It does not mean the stone minds."

He set her answer beside Samuel Wren's old copy of Carragh Cnoc bheag, made some forty years before and sent over the sea to scholars who had never troubled to answer it, and judged, laying the two side by side on an inn table at Cnoc chiar, that the hands were not the same hand, and that neither pillar's writing answered to the other's, letter for letter, though something in the shapes of both put him in mind of the same idea, the way two strangers' faces can share an expression without sharing a feature. He copied Wren's copy twice more into his own book, from memory and then checked against the paper, for he did not trust A' Chompanaidh's post with the original and would not risk the only rubbing he had of Carragh Cnoc bheag on a road he had never travelled.

At Cnoc ghorm, in the autumn, he copied Calbh Cnoc ghorm in four days, quicker work, for less of it had worn away; and he wrote in the last page of his notebook, in a smaller hand than the rest, as if he grudged the paper it took: *Like the pillar, but not near enough to help. I do not think these three markers, the obelisk, the pillar, the column, were raised by three peoples, or by one people at three times only. I think they were raised by one people who no longer needed, by the third marker, to say all that the first marker said, because by then everyone who read it already knew. That is the mark of an old and settled thing, not a new one. And no one now living can read a word of it.*

He left Dia-thìr the following year, on a ship of A' Chompanaidh out of Ros dhomhain, with his notebooks in a sealed case under his berth and nothing else of the island in his baggage that he had not paid for. He did not write again to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise that had sent him, nor, so far as the custodians' rolls record, did any answer ever come back over the sea to the stone he had copied, or the bone he had uncovered and covered again. What he had come to prove, in eleven years and more, he never once claimed to have proved; and the last line of his own book, set down the night before he sailed, said only that he had looked a long while at a colour he could not see, and had come, by looking, to believe in it a little, which was as much faith as the island's own god had ever asked of the strangers, and more than most of them gave.

## IV. Of Voss's Glass-House

*Here the copyists of Seilear Muileann chaol leave Lowe at the rail of his ship, and turn to a man who did not sail.*

Peter Voss had come to the island as a glazier under A' Chompanaidh's contract, to set Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's windows and the panes of the counting-house at Ros dhomhain, and when his contract ran out in the sixty-sixth year he did not take passage home with the rest of his gang. He gave no reason to the clerk who struck his name from the muster roll, only that he had found white sand on the shore below Baile Mòr dhìreach the like of which he had not found in three counties of an Tìr Thall, and a hill of good charcoal-wood behind it, and he meant to see what the two of them, put together in a furnace, would make.

He built the furnace himself over a summer, with two Dia-thìrich labourers he taught as he went, a stone drum lined with clay and fired for a week before he trusted it with sand, and for that whole week he slept beside it on a heap of sacking, waking every few hours to feed the fire and read its colour through a slit in the clay, a trick of the trade he had learned as a boy in his father's own glass-house over the sea and had thought, coming to the island, he would never use again. His two labourers thought him half mad for the sleeping, and said so, and stayed to watch all the same.

What came out of the furnace the first three times was a black cinder, no glass at all, and the town's children carried it off for luck and the custodians' clerk recorded, dryly, as "Voss's first stones, being none." Voss broke each failed batch himself with a hammer before it cooled fully, turning the pieces in his hand and muttering over them in his own tongue, and each time changed some small thing, the heat of the fire, the grain of the sand, the ash he mixed into it, and tried again. The fourth firing, on a wet morning in an Iuchar, gave him a pane the size of two hands, pale green, thick as a wall, and clear enough to see a gull through.

He held it up to the light in the furnace door, and one of his two apprentices, a girl of the town called Cairistìona nic Griogair who had carried sand for him all that summer and asked, more than once, to be shown the fire, laughed out loud at the sight of it, the first laugh anyone had heard in that yard since the furnace was raised.

"There," said Voss. "There's your first glass made on this island, and not a scrap of it came from over the sea."

Within the year he had orders from three towns for window-panes, more than he and his two apprentices could cut, and within a generation, as the copyists who set this down already know though Voss himself did not live to see it, his craft had gone out from his own two hands to glass-houses at Cathair dhearg and Seann Skell and half the towns of the capital shore, every one of them tracing its fire, in the telling if not always in the truth of it, back to a glazier left behind at Baile Mòr dhìreach because a ship's berth was not worth losing a beach of good white sand.

## V. Of the Answer of Comann an Airgid

*And here they turn from a furnace to a hall.*

Martha Gale came to Muileann chiar in the spring of the sixty-seventh year, on 29 am Màrt, AE 67, an agent of A' Chompanaidh of thirty-seven with a paper case under her arm and an offer inside it that her own letter-book called generous, and generous, by A' Chompanaidh's reckoning, it was: a partnership in the silver of the guild's own vein, half the yield to A' Chompanaidh and half kept by the guild, with A' Chompanaidh's beam to weigh it and A' Chompanaidh's road to carry it, in place of the old road down to the quay at Seann Bhral that the guild had used since before any strangers came.

The guild's head by then was Ùna nic Choinnich, who had stood with the ledgers at the adit some twenty-four years before, and who was some eighty winters old that spring, bent now at the shoulder but sound in the eye, with a voice that still carried the length of the hall without rising. She had come to the hall that morning on a stick and on her grand-niece's arm, as she had come to every guild meeting for a decade, and had sat through the winter's ordinary business, the ore counts and the smiths' dues, with her eyes half shut, so that more than one in the hall thought her asleep before Gale's letter was ever read; and then, at the reading, she opened her eyes fully and did not shut them again until the hands had been counted.

She had the offer read aloud once by Gale's own clerk, in the humans' tongue, and once more by a guild boy who put it into Dia-thìris, sentence by sentence, so that no hand in the hall could say afterward it had not understood what it voted on. Ùna made him read the paragraph on A' Chompanaidh's beam a third time, slowly, and asked him twice to explain, in his own words and not the paper's, what the weight on that beam would be measured against, and was not satisfied with either answer, and said so.

"You are offering us half of what we already have," Ùna said, when both readings were done, "in exchange for a road we do not need and a weight we do not trust. Is there anything in this paper that is not that?"

Gale said there was A' Chompanaidh's protection, in years when the silver ran thin, and A' Chompanaidh's markets, which reached further than any cart the guild had ever sent round the lake.

"We have had thin years before A' Chompanaidh came to this island," said Ùna, "and we are here yet, and so is the guild, and so, I think, will both of us be when your paper is dust." She turned to the hall. "Hands, then, as the guild has always answered."

The hands went up, and the count was taken by two clerks of the guild's own, one for and one against, as the custom held, and the offer was refused by every hand in the hall save one, an old silversmith too deaf that year to have followed the second reading, who put his hand up, as his neighbour told the clerks afterward, only because his neighbour's hand had gone up first. Gale took the count without argument, folded her paper case, and thanked the hall for its time in a Dia-thìris of her own, careful and correct, learned, the guild's clerk noted, entirely for that one visit and never used by her again on the island.

## VI. Of the Camp at Achadh dhomhain and the Cloth of Dùn chiar

*And here, last, to a hillside, before the copyists close this book.*

The deep galleries that A' Chompanaidh's surveys had marked below the hill at Achadh dhomhain were opened for cutting at the turn of the sixty-eighth year, on 1 am Faoilleach, AE 68, and within a few seasons the farming village that had stood there since An Aois Naomh, its granaries feeding the mining camps already a generation old on either side of it, found itself the most crowded place in the district, larger than any market town, though it had no market, no charter, and no custodian sent to it who did not also serve three villages besides.

A' Chompanaidh built nothing there that first season but a pay-hut and a store. The crews built the rest, out of what the ground gave them, which was spoil: the broken rock and shale thrown up from the new galleries, stacked and packed and roofed over as the season allowed, so that a man's house at Achadh dhomhain was, in a sense the custodians' rolls were careful to note, cut from the same hill he worked, only nearer the surface of it. The old farms stood apart from the new stacks of spoil at first, a field's width between the two, as if the village itself were unsure whether to call the camp a part of the town or a separate thing entirely grown up beside it; within two winters the field between them was houses too, and the question was no longer asked.

A hewer of the western workings, Cormag mac Ailein, raised the first of these houses for his own household that first winter, four low walls of stacked spoil chinked with clay, and asked the district's weavers for canvas to close the roof until timber could be got, for there was none to spare that year, every beam on the coast going to shore up the new galleries before the winter wet.

The weavers who answered him were of Dùn chiar, the hill fort south-east of the capital, whose looms had woven for the capital's own custodians since An Aois Naomh and had never, in all that time, taken a contract of A' Chompanaidh, holding, as their eldest weaver Ealasaid Bhuidhe put it to the town council that had to vote on it, that a loom that wove for the vein-country's temples should not also weave sacking for a coal camp. The council voted for the contract all the same, twenty-six against nine, the nine led by Ealasaid herself, who signed the roll of dissent and then, the record is careful to add, sat down at her own loom the next morning and wove canvas with the rest, for the town's custodian had ruled it, and a vote lost is a vote kept, in Dùn chiar as everywhere else on the island.

The first bolts of Dùn chiar canvas went up to Achadh dhomhain at the end of that first month, on 30 am Faoilleach, AE 68, and Cormag mac Ailein's roof was the first of the camp to be closed against the winter, four walls of spoil and a roof of borrowed cloth, tarred at the seams against the rain by his own hand, with his wife and their two children under it before am Faoilleach of the sixty-eighth year was out.

He stood back from it in the last light, to look at what he had made. He knew that the roof would hold, and that it was his, and that the winter, this year, would not come in on his children while they slept. Of the coloured flame at Muileann bheag, and the bone under the altar at Làrach an Teampaill, and the glass held up to the light at Baile Mòr dhìreach, and the hands raised and counted in the guild hall at Muileann chiar, he had heard nothing at all, and would hear nothing for some years yet; and so ends, at one man's roof and not at any of the others, the account the copyists have kept of what was seen, and not seen, in the six years after the fourth beacon was lit.

# Chapter Nineteen: Of the Smoke in the Gallery

*AE 68 – 72*

## I. Of the First Winter of Achadh dhomhain

The camp had no name before it had houses, and it had houses before it had a name that anyone but A' Chompanaidh used. Beitris Bhàn came to it in its first winter with a wool blanket, a horn cup and the small knife her mother had laid out three husbands and eleven neighbours with, walking the short road up from Àth ìseal because word had gone round the huts there that a new camp at Achadh dhomhain needed a woman who knew how to close a dead man's eyes and not flinch at a wound the coal had made.

She found the camp built of itself. A' Chompanaidh had sunk its shaft into the hillside for the deep galleries, and the spoil that came up out of it, broken rock and coal-dross too poor to sell, went into walls; so that the houses of Achadh dhomhain were grey and black together, low, roofed with turf cut from the same hill, and every one of them stood a little crooked, for spoil does not lie true the way a quarried stone does. The crews called them houses of spoil without meaning anything by it, the way a man calls his own boots his boots. Beitris took the end room of one such house, next the well, and hung her mother's knife on a nail, and within the week she had work.

That first winter the camp buried nine. Two were old hewers brought down from Àth ìseal for their skill and dead of the damp before the first snow; one was a child of five crushed under a cart of spoil that a tired horse let run back on its heel; the rest went of the cough that every camp has, deeper some years than others, and that winter deep. Beitris washed them in the well water, which came up black in a bucket until it had stood a night, and laid them out on the plank table in her room with a coal set on the breast for the going-down, as the custom is in every pit town from Doire mhòr to the last camp on the eastern road, and the custodian of Àth ìseal, whose roll then still reached as far as the new camp, rode up once a season to write the names and the days.

The name Donnchadh mac Thormoid meant nothing to her yet. He was one hewer among three hundred, and his crew worked the far end of the deepest gallery, where A' Chompanaidh had run its air-shaft down from the hillside above, and men who work an air-shaft's draught keep to themselves, for the wind down there is cold enough to work in a coat where other crews strip to the waist. She had heard, as everyone in the camp had heard, that his grandfather had once stood behind Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr on the day she sent A' Chompanaidh's man back down the hill unanswered, and that his father Tormod had carried water up to Doire mhòr for two summers after A' Chompanaidh took the stream, and then gone down with the rest to the huts at Àth ìseal. It was said, too, that Donnchadh himself had broken coal at a pit-mouth before he could read his letters, and gone below at twelve, a beginning that raised no eyebrow in that camp, where most of the men had made the same one or a harder. She knew him, that first winter, only as a name on the custodian's roll when his crew lost a boy to the damp, and as a back going down the ladder in the grey of the morning with the rest.

The nine of that first winter were laid in a field A' Chompanaidh had not yet found a use for, above the last of the spoil-heaps, in ground too broken with old workings to carry a cart-road. Beitris cut the turf for each grave herself, since the camp had as yet no man spared from the pit for the work, and found under it, more than once, the black seam showing through where an older digging had come near the surface and been left. She set nine cairns that winter with her own hands, small ones, for the camp could spare no more stone than that, and when the custodian of Àth ìseal rode up in the spring to write the names, he stood over each cairn a while, as though counting them meant something more than the writing did.

## II. Of the Coach and the Steelyard

A' Chompanaidh put its road in before it put in anything else that eased a life. In the spring a coach began to run twice in the week between the quay at Ros dhomhain and the camps about Muileann chrom, changing its horses at the old waypoint houses that had stood empty since the post first came up the coast, and the clerks and the overseers rode in it, dry, with their ledgers on their knees, while the crews who dug what filled the ledgers walked the same road on their own feet, in whatever weather the road had that day. Beitris saw it pass twice a week for years after and never once saw a hewer's boot inside it.

The next year A' Chompanaidh raised a great steelyard on the quay at Ros dhomhain, a beam and a basket and a chain of iron links taller than two men, and from the day it was hung the island's yield was no longer spoken of in the old way, in baskets filled and carts drawn and seasons of a crew's labour, as the custodians' rolls had always kept it, but in tons and hundredweights read off a scale by a clerk of A' Chompanaidh who had never gone below in his life. The custodians' old count went on a while in the margins of the rolls, out of habit, and then it did not. Ùna nic Choinnich, who kept Comann an Airgid's own scales at Muileann chiar and had refused twice already to let A' Chompanaidh's weights anywhere near her own, said when she heard of it that a hill weighed by the ton and a hill worked by a crew's own reckoning of what a day was worth were two different hills, and that the island had let the wrong one be written down. Beitris heard the saying secondhand, as everyone in the camps heard everything Ùna said, a season late and twice removed, and thought little of it at the time.

That was also the year A' Chompanaidh opened its second coal stage, at Ros dhìreach on the southern coast, to carry off the yield of the workings south of the hills without the long haul round to Ros dhomhain. Its first cargo went down in a squall not a mile off the harbour mouth, boat and coal and two of the crew who had gone out with her to trim the load, and the fishermen whose grounds had been given over to make room for the new stage would not put out past the wreck for a season after, saying the sea there had taken against the place. And in that same year, or the year after, for the camp's memory of dates ran together the way a hewer's years run together below ground, a ship came into Ros dhomhain driven by no sail at all, with a wheel turning in a housing at either side and smoke coming off her instead of spray, and the harbour's own fishermen rowed out in a ring to look at a hull that went against the wind. It was said in the camp, by men who had seen her, that within a few years A' Chompanaidh would send nothing else, and that the sailing ships that had first come down from the north with Harrow would soon come no more.

Beitris marked these things the way the camp marked them, as weather is marked: noticed, talked over at a door on a wet evening, and then folded away under the next thing.

The road brought the camp its wonders, and Beitris listened to all of it at the well, the way the whole camp listened to everything, and weighed it against the small, unremarkable fact that a hewer at the far end of the deep gallery had stopped coughing on the night his daughter was born, which nobody outside a handful of women had yet troubled to notice at all.

## III. Of What the Wife Told the Women

It came to Beitris the way most things came to her: at a laying-out, in the small hours, when the work of the hands leaves the tongue free and grief makes people say what they would otherwise keep.

In the fourth winter of the camp, the old woman who had first taken Beitris in, and taught her the way of setting a coal on a still breast, died in her sleep with no mark of the pit on her at all, which the camp took as a mercy and marked so. The women who came to sit the night with the body were Achadh dhomhain's own: wives and daughters of hewers, two widows, and Donnchadh mac Thormoid's wife, who had never before sat such a night in Beitris's room, and who sat now with her hands in her lap and said little until the small hours had worn the room down to its plainest talk.

It was Beitris who asked, in the end, only because the woman's silence had a shape to it that Beitris's trade had taught her to know. She asked how her husband had come to lose his cough, for the camp had seen him coughing black through a winter and thinning through a spring, and had begun, as camps do, to reckon how soon they would be laying him on this same table; and then the cough had stopped, all at once, like a door shut.

The wife told it then, low, with the other women leaning in to hear, and she told it as her husband had told her, which is the only way she would tell it, for she said more than once that the words were his and she would change none of them.

He had been alone at the face, she said, in the first winter of the camp, at the far end of the deepest gallery A' Chompanaidh had opened, with his lamp hung on a nail behind him and the shaft's draught running past him steady and cold, so that his flame lay over on its side all day and the dust of his cutting drifted away toward the dark in a thin grey thread. He had stopped to spit, and turned, and seen the thread of dust part around something that was not dust.

It stood the height of a tall man, she said, and it was made of smoke, grey smoke such as a peat fire gives in a shut room, and the draught went past it on either side without so much as bending it, though it bent the flame of his lamp and carried off every grain of dust he had cut. He had heard of the smoke in the grove all his life, at his grandmother's knee, with Marbh-bheò and the white stag and the rest of the fireside tales a child puts away when he goes below; and he had put this one away too, until it stood in front of him in the dark, and he found there was nowhere to run to but past it, and he did not want to run in any case, though he could not afterward say why not.

It spoke to him. "You are Tormod's son," it said, and its voice was low and very clear, and the draught that carried off everything else in that gallery did not carry off a word of it.

"I am," he said.

"And Somhairle's, and Ailean's." It seemed, he told her, to be looking about the gallery, at the props and the black walls and the cut face, the way a guest looks about a house where things have plainly gone badly for the people in it. "They are taking the hill."

"They are," he said.

"I will not fight for the kin. I never have; that is not my charge. But I was set to keep the kin, and a kin with its hill dug out from under it is not kept." It came nearer him then, close enough that he caught its smell, which was a hearth in the morning, when the fire has been banked all night and only just stirred. "I made a promise once, in the grove, to the one you come from. Breathe."

He breathed, because it had told him to, and the smoke went into him along with the dust of his own cutting, and it was warm, he said, warm all the way down, like a coal carried home under a cloak on a cold walk.

"What is it?" he asked, when he could speak again.

"A gift," it told him. "It is not for you. You will carry it, and the carrying will not be easy. It will wake in your daughter." The draught had begun to move through it by then, and it was thinning as it spoke. "It is in the dust of the deep places now, for every one of the kin who goes down; and where it wakes, it wakes. Tell no one of it but the one who will bear the child."

Then the draught went clean through the place where it had stood, and his lamp flame righted itself, and there was nothing in the gallery but the dust, settling.

He had coughed from that day, his wife said, black, and grown thin, and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's surgeon at the camp had listened at his chest and written him down with the miners' lung, the same dust-rot the humans brought with them from the pits of their own country, which the crews called Grodadh nan Scamhan among themselves, and had given him, the surgeon said, a year. And then, on 7 am Màrt, AE 69, his daughter was born to them in their own house of spoil, and that same night, his wife said, his cough stopped, and it never came back, not once, in all the years since. He had told her what he had met in the gallery the night the cough left him, and she had never told a living soul of it until this night, in this room, over another woman's body, with the coal already set on the dead breast between them.

Nobody in the room asked her the child's name. Everybody in the room already knew it. It was Aisling.

## IV. Of the Child the Rolls Gave Three Things

Beitris saw the child herself, in the way everyone in a small camp sees every child, at doors and at the well and asleep in a shawl on her mother's back while the mother queued for meal. There was nothing to see, at first, but a child. The custodian who rode up that spring wrote her down as the roll requires, a birth, a name, a father's name, and rode on to the next camp, and that was the whole of what the record ever meant to say of her.

It was the camp that said more, and it began, as most things in Achadh dhomhain began, with the women who laid out the dead. Beitris was one of them by then in her own right, and she heard it said first over a washing, in the flat voice women use for a thing they are only half in earnest about and half not: that the child was of the old king's blood. They meant Ailean Mòr, whom the gods crowned in the grove in the first years of everything, who was king four thousand years and more before he fell at Àth na Fala, and whose children, the tale ran, lived thousands of years after him. Not one woman in that room believed a word of the thousands of years; Ailean Mòr was a tale for the dark end of the year, set among the tellings by scribes long dead, and there was not a soul in the camp who had ever heard the whole of his line said out in order. But the child did not thicken through the shoulders as the other children of her year thickened, and did not lose her milk teeth when they lost theirs, and the women noticed it the way women who wash the dead notice everything about a body, early and exactly, and the whisper grew with her rather than dying the way most camp gossip dies.

They called her *nighean an rìgh*, half in jest and, as the seasons went by without her growing the way a child should, half not; and it began to be said of anyone in the camps who kept their youth past its season that they had *Aisling-aois* upon them, though there was as yet only the one Aisling for the saying to be named after. A people whose hill was going out of the island in ships by the ton took its comfort where it found one, and Achadh dhomhain found it in an old tale nobody believed and a girl of the spoil-houses who would not grow old. Nobody could prove a word of it, then or for years after, and nobody in that camp tried; a whisper that could be proved would have stopped being theirs.

Beitris herself was as much a watcher of the child as any of them, by the ordinary chance of a laying-out room standing close by the well where every mother in that row of houses of spoil came morning and evening. She saw Aisling grow as far as a small child grows. What she did not see, season after season, was the child changing the way a child changes: no new tooth lost and grown again, no stretching of the wrist past the cuff of last year's smock, no voice dropping into the huskier register a growing throat takes on. It was a stillness so gradual that no single week of it could be pointed to, and that, Beitris came to think, was why it took the women of the wash-house to notice it before anyone else did, for they were the ones who handled the camp's dying by the hand and the wrist and the throat, and knew exactly what a year should do to a body and what it should not.

Of what had passed in the gallery, and of what the smoke had told Donnchadh to keep, the women who had sat that night with Beitris said nothing outside the room where it was said. It was Beitris, in the end, who set the rule, though no one voted on it and no meeting was ever called: she told the others plainly that a thing a spirit had charged a man to keep close was not theirs to spend on the rest of the camp's talk, whatever they made of the child in their own kitchens, and the others agreed, and held to it. What was happening to the child had no name in any tongue spoken on the island, then or for years to come; it was the camp's own secret before it was anyone's mystery, kept the way the camp kept everything it valued, close, and among its own.

## V. Of Ùna nic Choinnich and the Shrines

In the child's second year word came down from Muileann chiar that Ùna nic Choinnich, who had led Comann an Airgid for near forty years and had twice turned A' Chompanaidh away from its seam, once at the adit and once by a show of hands, was dead at last in her own bed, eighty-five years old, having outlived An t-Àrd-mhaor who signed her compact. The camp had never seen her, most of it, and knew her only by the sayings that came down the road ahead of the coach; but Beitris, laying out a hewer's wife that same week, found the women of Achadh dhomhain talking of Ùna's dying with more feeling than they had shown for Àrd-mhaoir who had actually ridden through their own camp, and thought that a guild which had said no twice, and been believed, was worth more to people who had never once been asked than any office that only ever gave orders.

The camp kept its own shrines through those years as it had always kept them, A' Chompanaidh suffering the custom because it cost little enough to suffer. At Cill dhìreach, on the edge of the workings, the custodians held a small shrine where the crews of every new gallery brought the first piece cut from it and set it down before they carried the rest to the steelyard, and A' Chompanaidh let the practice stand, for a stone of coal a gallery was cheaper than a quarrel. At Cill ghlas, in the hills among the deepening pits, the custodians of Brìde's flame kept the older rite, at the mouth of the oldest cutting in those hills, tending the stone and the flame there while A' Chompanaidh's new shafts went down all around them; and of every shrine in that district it was the last the crews still climbed to on the old feast days, at Samhain and Imbolc, at Bealltainn and at Lùnastal.

Beitris went up to it for the first time in the same season Ùna's death came down the road, more from the habit of a woman who had spent a hard winter laying out neighbours than from any settled faith, for her own people had kept no particular custom of the shrine before the camp gave her one. She found the path already scored by other feet, hewers' boots mostly, going up before a shift or coming down after one, leaving nothing behind them but a nod to the custodian and sometimes a coin, sometimes nothing at all. It struck her, standing there the first time with the flame small and steady against a hard wind, that A' Chompanaidh, which begrudged a stone a gallery to the shrine at Cill dhìreach, had never once tried to close this one, whether because the cost was smaller still or because even an Àrd-mhaor who could not see the colour in the coal knew better than to be the man who put out Brìde's flame in a camp already burying its dead by the dozen.

## VI. Of the Climb to Cill ghlas

In the fifth Lùnastal of the camp, with the child three years old, Beitris climbed the hill path to Cill ghlas alone, before first light, as she had taken to doing since the night of the telling, though she could not have said to another soul why that night had put the habit in her.

The path went up past the newest of the spoil-heaps, black even in starlight, and past the mouth of the gallery where Donnchadh mac Thormoid still worked his shift, cough long gone, saying no more of what had happened to him there than his wife had said of it in Beitris's room, and by all report never once saying more. At the top the custodian was already at the flame, feeding it the last of the night's peat before the sun took over the work, and the old cutting behind her stood open and black and ordinary, a hole in a hill like any other hole a people had ever dug in search of what it needed.

Beitris set down the coal she had carried up, one piece, no bigger than the ones the crews left at Cill dhìreach, and said nothing to the custodian, who said nothing to her, for it was not a shrine that asked for words.
