Below her the camp was waking, doors opening onto the grey light, smoke starting from a hundred low chimneys built of the hill's own dross, and somewhere down among them a child not yet four years old.

What the camp had been given, that Lùnastal morning, Beitris could not have said, nor what the giving would yet cost it; a layer-out of the dead learns early that not every debt comes due while the one who owes it is still watching. She knew only that a promise made once in a grove, to someone whose name none of them now living had ever heard said whole, was being kept in the one way a promise so old can be kept: quietly, underground, in the dust, where nobody stood by who could put a word to it. A while longer she stayed at the flame with the custodian, neither of them speaking, and then turned back down the path to see who else the winter had left her to lay out, and did not speak of the child again to anyone outside that first room for a long time after.

Remember it.

# Chapter Twenty: Of A' Phlàigh Uaine

*AE 73 – 76*

## I. Of the Green Acre

Beitris Bhàn had laid out the dead of Achadh dhomhain for six years before the sickness came, and she thought she knew every way a body could leave the world underground. She had washed the crushed and the drowned and the cold, the old who went quietly in a house of spoil and the young who did not go quietly at all. She had not washed anyone the colour of a candle held behind glass, and when Fearchar Iasgair's wife sent for her on a wet morning in an t-Ògmhios of the seventy-third year, and she came into the hut and pulled back the blanket, she stood a long moment with the cloth in her hand before she could make herself begin.

He was green. Not the green of a drowned man, which she knew, nor the green-white of a man dead of poison, which she had seen twice; a green under the skin, as though a lamp with a coloured shade had been set behind his face and left burning. His lips were dark. When she washed his chest the water in the basin turned grey with the dust that had come up out of him in his last hours, more dust than she had ever wrung from a living man's coughing, as if the hill itself had been washing out of him from the inside.

"He was well at Bealltainn," the wife said, from the door, not coming in. "Well enough to dance at it."

"How long was he taken?"

"Nine days. Ten." The wife's hands were working at her apron, twisting it. "He went the colour first. The overman said it was only the bad air of the new gallery and he'd come right in a week above ground. Then the cough came, and then he couldn't stand."

Beitris finished him and covered him and went out into the rain and stood a while under the eave, because that was her way; she gave herself the length of one held breath for each body before she went to the next thing. Before the month was out she had given herself that breath thirty-nine times more. The camp buried its dead that summer in a field beyond the spoil-heaps that had never been used for anything, too stony for a garden and too far from the huts for convenient burying, and by the end of an t-Iuchar the field had a name the whole camp used without anyone deciding it should: an Acair Uaine, An Acair Uaine. Beitris helped dig the first of it herself, on a day when the grave-diggers proper were laid up sick themselves, and she never after that let herself forget the particular heft of a spade going into ground that had not been turned before.

She did not know then what the sickness was, or that it had a name yet to be given it, or that within the year every custodian's roll from the coast to the hills would be keeping a tally of it under one heading. Only this she knew: that Fearchar Iasgair had been a strong man at Bealltainn and green in the ground by midsummer, and that this was the fourth summer running in which the camp at Achadh dhomhain had buried more of its own than it had the year the deep galleries opened. Beitris laid out the camp's dead and did not think, that summer, of the hewer whose cough had stopped on the night his daughter was born. The one thing had nothing to do with the other, so far as anyone could see.

## II. Of the Blank Line

It went along the coal roads the way water goes along a furrow, taking the low ground first.

From Achadh dhomhain it followed the carts to Muileann chrom, and from Muileann chrom by the same roads that carried the coal itself, to Àth ìseal and to Cnoc fhiadhaich, and from those three camps it spread wider than any of the custodians who kept the count had thought a sickness of the lungs could spread, out along the lines the ore and the timber travelled, as though it rode the carts and not the men. It fell on Ros dhìreach, on Ceann òg, on Inis ìseal, on Baile dhomhain, on Achadh fhada, on Cnoc bheag, on Muileann uaine, on Cuan àrsaidh, on Inis bhàn. It fell on Baile chrom in the hills, not the Baile chrom of the north-west, whose beacon burned coal above a different sea entirely; and the clerks of that year took a particular care, twice underlined in one hand, to keep the two apart, for they had heard already of copyists elsewhere confusing towns of one name, and did not mean to be the ones remembered for it.

The custodians' roll for that year lists twenty-six settlements with cases set down against them, in the order the word of them reached Cathair dhearg, and after the twenty-sixth name the clerk who kept the roll left a line blank. Nobody now living can say why he left it, whether by habit, meaning to fill it when the next report came in, or because he could not make himself write the page full and close it. The line stayed blank through that autumn and into the winter, and was still blank when a different hand took up the roll the following spring, by which time a twenty-seventh settlement might as well have been entered, and was not. It is there still, in the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais, a line of nothing between one town's dead and the empty bottom of the page, and every custodian who has read it since has understood it without being told what it was left for.

At Àth ghlas the custodians did a thing no other camp thought to do until it was too late for the thought to help them. When the first three died within a week of one another, the custodian of that place, a stern woman named Sìne Ruadh who had buried her own father to the fever thirty years before and never forgot the smell of a sick-hut, ordered every hut in which a death had happened burned to the ground, roof, walls, bedding and all, before the next dark. A' Chompanaidh's agent at Àth ghlas protested the loss of its property in writing, three times, and was answered each time with the same line copied out fresh: the hut is A' Chompanaidh's; the ground under it is the custodians'; and the custodians will keep what stands on their own ground safe from what killed the man in it. Sìne Ruadh burned nine huts before the summer was out. Of every camp on the coal roads, the sickness left Àth ghlas soonest, and though the roll does not say it plainly, every custodian who has since compared the counts has drawn the same line between the burned huts and the empty ones.

At Cnoc naomh there was no burning, and no early stopping. The dead there were laid first in the burial-ground of the town's old shrine, in the ordered rows the shrine had kept since it was built, and when that ground filled, in a field outside it that had never held a grave before. The field at Cnoc naomh was never ploughed again after. Fifty years on, a woman who farms the land beside it can point to where the fence turns to go round it, and will tell you, if you ask, that nothing was ever sown there because nothing would grow; and if you ask her how she knows that, since nobody has tried it in living memory, she will say only that nobody in living memory has needed to.

## III. Of Doctor Bright's Table

Nathaniel Bright had been Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's physician at Muileann chrom nine years by the time the sickness reached the settlements around him, long enough to have buried three of his own household to fevers that were not this one, and long enough to have grown, in the Dia-thìrich way of speaking of a stranger they had come to trust a little, "the doctor who listens." He was a careful man, thin, with ink permanently under two fingernails of his right hand and a habit of repeating a patient's own words back before he wrote them down, so that the patient could hear whether he had understood.

His study began in the second summer of the sickness, in the small room behind Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's dispensary at Muileann chrom that the surgeon before him had used for storing bandages. He asked the custodians' leave to open the chests of the dead before burial, and was given it, on the condition that a custodian stand by the whole time and that nothing of the body be kept afterward. This he agreed to without argument, understanding, as few of his own people troubled to, that the custodians asked it as a plain point of law and no more. What he found, he weighed. A table grew in a black-bound book, ruled in columns: the name, where known; the years worked below; how much the lungs themselves weighed; and how much, so far as his scales could reckon it, of what was not lung in them. Beside each entry he wrote, in a small cramped hand, whatever the family or the crew could tell him of how the man had died, how long it had taken, and whether the green colour had come before the cough or after.

Anne Colby came to his room once, in the second winter, carrying a list of her own: the sick-house's tally, kept by name and settlement, that she had begun keeping without being asked to by anyone in Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, because nobody else was keeping it in any form the living could be traced by afterward. She set her list beside his book on the table and they went down both together by lamplight, matching names.

"There is no pattern I can find in who takes it and who does not," Bright said. "A hewer at the face fifteen years may live. A boy of six months below may die of it in a fortnight. I had thought it might follow the deepest galleries, and it does not; Cnoc fhiadhaich's shallow workings have as many dead as Achadh dhomhain's deep ones, by the head."

"What do you think it, then?"

"The dust. I can find no other thing they share." He turned the book round so she could see the column of his weighings. "Every lung I have opened is dark with it, more than a man could take in from ordinary air in a lifetime of ordinary work. I mean to weigh a hundred before I say so in writing, so that no one can say I guessed from ten."

He did not weigh a hundred. He fell ill himself in the third season of the work, in the spring of the seventy-fifth year, with the same colour and the same cough he had spent two years describing in other men's chests, and his own hand grew too unsteady for the small cramped writing before the summer was half over. The last page of his book breaks off in the middle of a row: a name, the years worked, the weight of the lung, and then nothing where the weight of the dust should have been, the pen having been set down, it seems from the mark it left, and never taken up again over that line. He died at Muileann chrom the following spring, and was buried by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise with the honours Riaghaltas nan Coigreach gave its own, in ground apart from An Acair Uaine and the field at Cnoc naomh, though the colour that took him from it was the same colour, and Anne Colby, who came to the burying, thought so and said nothing, because there was no one there it would have helped to say it to.

## IV. Of the Seal and the Letter-Book

Walter Crane had been Àrd-mhaor twelve years when the sickness reached the camps, and in all that time he had walked them himself, twice a season, in a coat that grew steadily shabbier because he would not send it to be brushed while other men's coats went unbrushed for want of a wife to do it. He walked the sick-rows at Achadh dhomhain in the worst of the second summer, when the stink of the huts kept even the huts' own children playing at a distance, and he did not walk faster past the bad ones than the ordinary ones, which the custodians noticed, and which Beitris Bhàn, who saw him there twice, noticed too, and remembered afterward in his favour, the only human besides Anne Colby she ever remembered so.

The sickness caught him in the autumn of the seventy-fourth year, most likely from the very rows he had walked so faithfully, though no one could say which visit. Before the winter was out he was dead, at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir above Ros dhomhain, in a bed his own physician had ordered him to twice and he had twice got out of to answer letters. Martha Gale, A' Chompanaidh's agent, held his seal for the months there was no one else to hold it, and ran the pay office and the ore contracts and the sick-house grants exactly as Crane had left them running, changing nothing, because she said afterward that a dead man's arrangements were owed at least that much respect until a live one came to say otherwise.

The live one came over the sea in the spring of the seventy-sixth year: George Tolley, sent out with orders, set down plainly in the papers he carried and read aloud once, without apparent discomfort, to the clerks of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on his first morning, that the yield of the pits must not fall on account of the sickness, whatever else was done about it. He set a quarantine at Caol mhin on the northern coast within his first month, holding every ship from an Tìr Thall offshore until her crew had been looked over by a physician sent out in a boat for the purpose, a measure so plainly sensible, and so plainly aimed at keeping the sickness from crossing the sea rather than at the men already dying of it on the island, that the custodians approved it without reservation and said so in writing, the only order of his whole rule they ever did approve.

He did not visit the camps. Not Achadh dhomhain, not Muileann chrom, not Àth ghlas nor Cnoc naomh nor any of the twenty-six named in the blank-lined roll; not once in the two years of his rule that the sickness ran its worst. He kept his own letter-book at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, in a fair clerk's hand that was not his own, dictated of an evening, and in it, when at last he set down his opinion of the cause of A' Phlàigh Uaine for A' Chompanaidh's directors over the sea, he gave three causes and gave them in this order: the coal dust of the workings; the custom, as he understood it from his clerks, of the Dia-thìrich sleeping close by their own hearths in ill-ventilated huts; and the custodians' shrines, which he believed, on no evidence he troubled to name, might be a means by which the sickness passed from the sick to the well through the gathering of crowds at them. Anne Colby was shown a copy of the letter some years later, by a clerk who thought she would want to see it, and read it through twice before she said anything, and what she said was not fit to be entered in any roll.

## V. Of the Feathers Over the Door

The hawk-priests had been barred from the camps since Maddox's day, an order Tolley found already standing and saw no reason to lift, and the crews had long since learned to do without them in body while keeping them in every other way they could. In the years of A' Phlàigh Uaine, the overseers' own reports, kept with more care than almost anything else Riaghaltas nan Coigreach wrote down in those years, since a matter of discipline was worth a clerk's ink where a matter of dying was not, begin to list, camp by camp, hut by hut, the finding of feathers nailed above doors.

A single feather, most often; sometimes two crossed. The overseers took them down as fast as they were found and entered the finding against the household's name, a mark that in some camps cost a week's pay and in others nothing at all, depending on which overseer happened to be walking that row. The crews put them back up as fast as they were taken down. Nobody was ever caught in the act of nailing one, in six years of the sickness and hundreds of feathers found; the custodians, when asked by an overseer once too many times who had done it, answered only that a hawk drops what it drops, and a door is a door, which satisfied no overseer and stopped no report and was, so far as anyone below the rank of Àrd-mhaor ever discovered, entirely true.

There was a saying that went with the feathers, said low in the huts at night and not to any human who might carry it up the hill, though by the second year of the sickness even some of the humans of the camps, the few who had married in and stayed, had it by heart in their own halting Dia-thìris, having heard it often enough at a neighbour's door to learn it the way a child learns a hymn without being taught the words of it on purpose.

*Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc.*

Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill.

Beitris Bhàn nailed a feather above her own door in the second winter, after she had laid out the fortieth of the season, and did not take it down when the overseer's boy found it and told his father, and paid the week's pay it cost her without complaint, and put another feather up within the month.

## VI. Of the Washing

It was in the third summer of the sickness that Anne Colby came to Beitris Bhàn's door for the first time. No one at Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had sent her and no custodian had asked her; she had heard, from a woman at the sick-house, that the layer-out at Achadh dhomhain had washed more of A' Phlàigh Uaine's dead with her own hands than any physician on the island had examined with instruments, and Colby had run out, that summer, of people who knew more about the sickness than she did.

Beitris let her in without a word and without surprise, as though she had been expecting a human at her door eventually and had simply not known which one. Colby had brought nothing with her but a clean apron rolled under her arm, which she put on in the doorway before she asked leave to help, and Beitris, who had never in six years let another pair of hands touch a body she was laying out, some old bone-deep unwillingness in her giving way all at once for reasons she could not afterward have named to herself, stood back from the table and let her.

They worked without much speaking, the way two women who have each done a hard thing alone for years learn to work together the first time without needing to be told how. Colby had the physician's way of it, methodical, naming what she saw as she saw it; Beitris had the older way, the custodian's rites said quietly under the working of the cloth, a word for each part of the body as it was washed, words that had been said over the dead of Achadh dhomhain since long before A' Chompanaidh came, said now for a woman whose name Colby had written on a list and Beitris had known since the woman was a girl.

"You say a word for every part of her," Colby said, once, not stopping her own hands.

"My grandmother's mother said it for her grandmother's mother. There is a word for each part because each part is owed its own leaving-taking, and none is owed more than the rest." Beitris turned the woman gently onto her side to reach her back. "Do the humans say nothing over their own dead?"

"We say a great deal. Over the ones we can afford a priest for." Colby's voice had gone flat in a way Beitris had heard before, in women who had buried more than they could carry the grief of properly and had learned instead to carry the work of it. "The camps' dead get none of it. I have buried forty with no more than my own two hands and a hole dug too shallow because there was no one spared from the pit to dig it deeper."

They finished the woman together and began the next, a boy of perhaps nine, and Beitris found, without deciding to, that she had begun saying the words aloud instead of under her breath, so that Colby, working opposite her, might have them too if she wanted them; and Colby, who understood no more than a handful of words of Dia-thìris and none of these particular ones, said nothing at all, but matched the pace of her own hands to the rhythm of them, so that the two of them moved together over the small body as though the words were being said by both, which in every way that mattered to either woman, they were.

They washed the camp's dead together through that summer and the next, whenever the sick-house sent Colby to Achadh dhomhain and the toll there was more than Beitris could face alone, which by the second of those summers was most weeks. Neither of them ever spoke of it to Riaghaltas nan Coigreach or to the custodians as anything but what it plainly was, two women doing a hard thing that needed two pairs of hands; but the camp came, in time, to speak of it as something else, and the phrase that grew up around it, *An Dithis a Nigh Còmhla*, was said in the camps for years after, though neither woman, so far as the record shows, ever heard it said to her own face.

## VII. Of the Letter-Book's Order

The sickness did not end. It slackened, the way a fire slackens when it has burned through the driest of what it was given and is left working more slowly on what is left, the deaths falling from forty a month at Achadh dhomhain to four, then to one in a season, then, in most of the twenty-six settlements, to none for a year at a stretch before another case would show and the whole camp would hold its breath until it was seen whether one case meant a new burning or only one grave. Nathaniel Bright's book, with its broken-off row, was filed at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and never taken up again by any physician who came after him; his question, what the dust did and how much of it a lung could hold before it stopped forgiving a man for breathing it, went unanswered on the island.

George Tolley's letter to A' Chompanaidh's directors, the one setting the sickness's causes down in the order he believed them to stand, was copied at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir into the bound letter-book that Lisle's successor had begun and every Àrd-mhaor after kept, each adding his own year's pages to what had gone before. It sits there still, among orders about the price of iron and the state of the harbour works, three causes given in three lines: the dust of the workings first, since that at least could not be laid at any door an Àrd-mhaor might one day wish to walk through; the habit of the hearth second, since a people's own customs were always the easiest blame to give and the hardest for them to answer; and the custodians' shrines last, named without one word of evidence beside them, because a shrine was a gathering, and a gathering could always be made to sound like a danger to a man who had never stood in one and watched what was actually done there.

Of the true cause, the dust that Bright had weighed and never finished weighing, carried up out of galleries driven faster and deeper than any before them into lungs that had never been asked to breathe so much of the hill at once, no Àrd-mhaor's letter-book ever said a plain word. The camps needed no letter-book to tell them. They had An Acair Uaine, and the field at Cnoc naomh that has never since been ploughed, and the feathers that went back up over every door as fast as the overseers took them down, and the saying that outlasted every one of the men who tried to stop its being said.

*Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc.*

They had, too, though few beyond Achadh dhomhain itself yet knew to connect the two things, a girl in a house of spoil who had been steeped in more of that same dust than any child before or since, and had not sickened of it at all, and did not age.

# Part Four: Of An Togail, the Hunger and the Drought

# Chapter Twenty-one: Of Stad-oibre Baile thais


*AE 77 – 79*

## I. Of the Spring after the Sickness

The dying at Baile thais had stopped by the time the first primroses came up along the moor-road, but the town did not look like a town that had stopped dying. Catrìona nic Eachainn walked out to the pit-mouth in the grey of that spring with her shawl over her mouth from old habit, though Anne Colby had told her months before that the habit did nothing and she might as well breathe free. She kept it anyway. A thing the body has learned to do against fear does not stop because the fear is told it was wrong.

Below Cill ghlas the ground still showed where the town's burial field had been cut wider twice in one winter. Grass had not yet taken the new turned earth; it lay the colour of a scar, paler than the field round it, and the shrine women left dishes of meal on the mounds because that was what you did when you did not know what else to do. Catrìona had buried her mother's sister there in am Faoilleach, and a niece a fortnight after, and had gone on leading her shift the whole time because A' Chompanaidh's book of hours did not stop for grief, and because thirty other households were waiting on her wage same as her own.

Anne Colby's sick-house still stood at Achadh dhomhain, an hour's walk north among the deep galleries, its canvas roof gone grey with two winters' smoke, and word came down that she meant to keep it open through the summer for the crews at Àth ìseal too, though the worst of the sickness there had passed. The camp people called it kindly, the only house of the strangers' building that they called kindly, and it was said without much thinking about it that this was because Colby herself had washed the dead with her own hands rather than sending a servant to do it, which was more than Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's own ministers had done.

At Cnoc gharbh, to the south along the ridge, the people who had worked the southern galleries did not wait for the sickness to be called past. They took their pots and their bedding and their children and walked back up to the old village on the hill their grandfathers had held before the pits, and left the camp huts standing empty with the doors swinging. A Chompanaidh's agent rode out to look at the empty huts and wrote in his book that the crews had deserted their posts, as though a plague were a kind of laziness. Nobody at Baile thais blamed Cnoc gharbh. Half of them had thought of doing the same and had stayed only because Baile thais, unlike Cnoc gharbh, had no old village on a hill to go back to. It had never been anything but the camp.

Catrìona was seven-and-thirty that spring, crew-leader of the seventh shift at the Baile thais gallery, a broad, dark, plain-spoken woman with a scar through one eyebrow from a fall of stone as a girl, and hands that the coal had got into so deep that even scrubbed they looked bruised. She had led the seventh shift for eleven years, since the crew-leader before her, an old man named Griogar, had coughed himself to a standstill and put the tally-stick in her hand himself and said she was the only one of them who would not be talked round by the agent's smile. Griogar was dead two winters now, of the ordinary lung-sickness that took hewers, not the green plague; he had at least been spared that.

The camp still kept, over most of its doors, a single hawk's feather nailed to the lintel, the overseers' reports calling it a matter for punishment and the overseers themselves too busy that spring to trouble over it. The hawk-priests had gone unwelcome in the camps for years now. A feather cost nothing, though, and a man could nail it up himself in the dark, and Catrìona had one over her own door, put there by her mother before her, and had never taken it down nor troubled to say a prayer under it either. It was less a faith to her than a habit, like the shawl over her mouth, and she thought, without much reflection, that a people who had been told for two generations that the strangers' book had all the say in what a hill might hold could be forgiven for keeping quietly to older things, whether or not they believed the old things any harder for the keeping.

There was no one at Cathair dhearg to write to about any of it, not that year. Ceann a' Chùraim's seat, Ceann a' Chùraim, had stood empty since Alasdair Liath died six years before, and Comhairle a' Chùraim had not agreed on who should fill it, being much taken up, so it was said, with the business of the tithe and the petitions of the towns, and finding, as councils will, that an empty chair causes less argument than a full one. Catrìona did not think about the empty seat often. But she thought of it that spring, walking past the burial field to the pit-mouth, because it meant that whatever she was about to ask, there would be no one great enough at the capital to be asked twice.

## II. Of the Agent's Answer

The agent at Baile thais that year was a man named Silas Crewe, thirty-seven himself, sent up from Ros dhomhain the autumn before to replace an agent who had died of the same sickness he had been sent to manage. He was neither the worst of A' Chompanaidh's men nor the best: he kept his ledgers straight, did not water the lamp-oil, and had once, to general surprise, paid a full week's wage to a crew that lost two days to a flooded sump through no fault of its own. He had also, in the same season, signed the order that kept the deepest gallery working through the height of A' Phlàigh Uaine, on the word of a surveyor from Ros dhomhain who had never gone down it himself.

Catrìona went to him on a wet morning with three other crew-leaders behind her, though it was understood between them without saying that she would do the talking. Crewe's office was a plank room built onto the counting-house, with a stove that smoked and a window that did not shut properly, and he stood behind his table rather than sitting, which she took, rightly, for a kind of politeness meant to look like the opposite.

"I'm asking you to close the third and the fourth gallery," she said. "Not the whole working. The third and fourth, where the dust hangs, till the surgeon says different."

"The surgeon has not said the dust does it," Crewe said. "He has said he does not know what does it."

"He has said it is worst where the dust is worst. He told me that himself, at my aunt's burying."

Crewe looked at the paper in front of him rather than at her, which she also took rightly, for he had the figures of the quarter's yield laid out on it and knew them without needing to look. "The yield in the third and fourth is a third of the whole working," he said. "If I close them I have to write to Ros dhomhain and say why, and the why I have to give them is a physician's guess. I can't close a gallery on a guess, Catrìona. The yield must not fall. Those are the words I was sent with, near enough."

"The yield," Catrìona said, "or the dead."

"I did not choose the words," Crewe said, and for a moment, briefly, something in his face agreed with her, and then put itself away again, as a man puts away a coin he has been shown he cannot spend. "I'll write up what you've told me. That's what I can do."

"Write it up," she said, and did not thank him for it, and went out into the rain with the other three crew-leaders behind her, none of whom had said a word, and none of whom needed to; they had heard the same answer given a dozen times in a dozen shapes since the sickness began, and they knew by now what shape came after a shape like that one.

## III. Of the Coal-Tub

She let three weeks pass before she stood on the tub. She was not, whatever the camp said of her afterward, a woman who acted from a single hot morning; she went first to the custodian of Baile thais, an old woman named Sìneag who kept what rolls there were for a town that had never properly had a custodian's house, only a room over the smithy, and asked her what the old law said about a hill and its rest, in case there was a word from An Aois Naomh she could set against A' Chompanaidh's paper. Sìneag found nothing that would serve; Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig spoke of the coal burned, not the coal cut, and there was no law anywhere, old or new, about how deep a gallery might be worked while men sickened in it, because no one before this age had needed to write one.

So on a grey morning near the middle of the summer, with the shift gathering at the pit-mouth in the usual half-light and the usual noise, wet boots and lamp-checks and somebody's dog getting under everybody's feet, Catrìona turned over one of the empty coal-tubs that stood by the weigh-house, climbed up on it, and told the whole shift, which by then was near enough the whole working, since word had gone round in the night, what she had asked Crewe for and what he had answered.

"He says the yield must not fall," she said, from the tub, her voice carrying flat and hard over the yard the way it carried down a gallery when a fall had to be called. "I say the yield can wait on the living. I'm not asking any man or woman here to leave their family without bread. I'm asking that nobody go below today, into the third or the fourth, until Crewe writes to Ros dhomhain and gets back a better answer than a guess. If that costs us the day's pay, it costs us the day's pay. I'll stand it same as you."

There was no great shout of agreement, no crowd surging forward with fists in the air, of the kind the camp songs like to make of such mornings. What there was instead was a long quiet, boots shifting in the mud, a woman coughing somewhere at the back who was not sick, only cold, and then, one by one, men and women turning their lamps down and setting them on the ground rather than carrying them to the gallery mouths. Raghnall Breac, a hewer's boy of seven who was too young that year to be paid a man's wage and was there only to carry water and pick slate from the tubs, stood at the front the whole time with his water-pail still in his hand, not understanding all of it, understanding enough of it to stay.

Catrìona stepped down off the tub, and rather than going to stand over the crowd or address them further, sat down on it, in the mud, in her working clothes, and folded her arms, and did not go below. She had planned no speech to make with her body; the speech made itself, and it was the one that held. A woman sitting on an upturned tub, arms folded, in the rain, saying nothing further, is a harder thing to argue with than a woman shouting, because there is nothing in it to answer.

Crewe came out within the hour, saw the yard full and still, and went back in again without a word to anyone. By noon two riders had gone from the counting-house, one south to Ros dhomhain and one, it was said later though nobody at Baile thais ever had it proved, north to Muileann chrom, where Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor kept the staff of the Stewards and had, by then, eight-and-fifty years and no love at all for a stoppage he had not ordered.

Sìneag came down from her room over the smithy at midday and stood a while at the edge of the yard. She joined no crowd, being too old by her own reckoning to sit in mud for anybody, yet she kept her place at the edge of it a long while too, and when a young overseer's clerk asked her, civilly enough, whether the custodian meant to order the crews back to work, she told him that a custodian's rolls recorded what was done and did not order what should be, and that he was welcome to write that down too if he thought it worth the ink. He left it unwritten, and stayed near her the rest of the afternoon regardless, as though an old woman who would say such a thing to a clerk of A' Chompanaidh was worth keeping an eye on, which in its own way told Catrìona, watching from the tub, that the day's stand had already gone further than the yard.

## IV. Of the Eleven Days

The first three days were the easiest, because the town still had its own bread and its own stored meal, and because there was something in the crowd of the yard, the fires kept up after dark, the songs Fearchar sang years later having their true root in mornings such as these, that felt for a while like a kind of holiday, wrongly earned yet taken all the same. By the fourth day the easiness had gone out of it. Catrìona took to walking the town each evening. A crew-leader who does not walk her own streets in a stoppage she called is asking to be thought a coward, and there, walking, she counted, without meaning to at first and then quite deliberately, the loaves standing in the windows.

There was one store in Baile thais that sold bread, and it belonged to A' Chompanaidh, same as the huts and the weigh-house and the smithy's lease. On the first evening there had been loaves stacked three deep behind the glass. On the fourth there were perhaps a dozen. On the sixth, six. She did not need Crewe to tell her what he already knew, which was that a camp that owns its only store can starve a stoppage without lifting a hand against it, and does not even have to be cruel to do it; it need only wait.

Ros gharbh's fishermen, fifteen miles off on the southern coast, heard of the stoppage by the seventh day, nobody afterward could say quite how fast such things travelled, and began carrying salt fish up into the hills by night on the moor tracks, past A' Chompanaidh's own watch at the crossroads, and left it at back doors without asking payment or thanks. It fell short of feeding eleven days of a mining town, but it kept every child at Baile thais from starving outright, and the custodians' roll, when it came to be written years later at Muileann chaol, called it the one trade of that whole decade that ran the right way, from the giving hand to the needing one and asking nothing back.

On the ninth day Crewe sent word that he would open the store's back room, where flour was kept for the counting-house's own table, to any family with children under five, if the crews would go below. Catrìona refused it in front of the yard. She wanted the children fed as much as any mother there; what she would not have was a store opened halfway, which stays owned however it is opened, breaking a strike along exactly the line A' Chompanaidh would choose to break it. "Feed them all or feed none," she told him, at his own door, "and if you feed none, I'll answer for that to God and not to you." He did not open the room.

On the tenth night it rained without stopping, and half the yard fires went out, and a woman named Beathag Ruadh, whose husband had died in the third gallery two winters before the stoppage and who had five children and no bread left at all, came to Catrìona in the dark. She asked her plainly, as a tired woman asks another, no accusation in it, whether it would not be better to send the crews back down and keep what strength they had for another day, another year, since the third and fourth galleries would go on being worked whether Baile thais stood in the yard or not. Catrìona had no good answer for her, and gave her the only one she had, which was that she did not know, and sat with her by what was left of the fire until Beathag's children were asleep against her. In the morning Beathag went to the yard with everyone else and did not go below.

## V. Of the Twelfth Morning

On the twelfth morning Catrìona went down to the store herself before first light, before anyone else was in the yard to see her go, because she did not want to be watched deciding. She stood at the shutters, which had not yet been opened for the day, and looked in through the gap where the wood had warped, at shelves she already knew were bare, having counted them bare the evening before, and stood there long enough that the cold came up through her boots.

There was nothing in the shop but the counter, the scale, and, on the top shelf, out of easy reach, a single sack of meal that Crewe, she supposed, had kept back for his own table, or for a bribe he had not yet had cause to pay. She looked at that sack a long while too. Then she walked back up through the town, past the shrine women already at the burial field with their dishes of meal that they, at least, had never stopped finding somewhere, and came to the yard, and climbed up on the same tub, which had stood in the same place, rained on, eleven days running, and told the shift to go below.

"We did not win the third and fourth," she said. "I won't tell you we did, because you'd know it for a lie inside the hour. What we won, if we won anything, is that they know now it can be done. Eleven days is not nothing. Go below. Feed your children. I'll go below with you." And she did, that morning, walking into the second gallery herself for the first time in eleven days, her lamp lit, her hands shaking a little in a way she did not let the shift see, and the work went on as though nothing had stopped it, which was the worst part of going back, that the hill did not care one way or the other how long a person had refused it.

The third and fourth galleries were not closed. They ran another four years before the seam in them thinned and A' Chompanaidh abandoned them for reasons of its own that had nothing to do with anyone's asking. No answer of any kind ever came from Ros dhomhain, nor, so far as anyone at Baile thais ever learned, from the empty chair at Cathair dhearg, which sat empty still.

## VI. Of the Granary

Within the month a wagon-train came up from Muileann chrom with timber and stone, and A' Chompanaidh began building a granary of its own beside the pit-mouth, a squat building with one door and a lock, and word went round the camps, all of them, not Baile thais alone, that from now on no household was to keep more grain in its own house than a week's ration, the rest to be held in A' Chompanaidh's granary and drawn against a crew-leader's tally. The order was read out at Baile thais by an overseer none of them had seen before, and it carried, at the foot of the paper, the mark of Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor, Steward at Muileann chrom, a man Catrìona had met twice in her life and liked neither time, though she allowed, thinking it over afterward, that he had likely signed a good many orders that summer he had not troubled to read closely, being a man more given to the staff's ceremony than its use.

Sìneag the custodian said, when she heard of it, that she had never in all her rolls read of a granary built to answer a stoppage rather than a harvest, and that this alone told her more of what the stoppage had done than anything Crewe had put in writing. Catrìona thought there was truth in that, though it was cold comfort to a household now walking to a locked building with a tally-stick to ask for its own week's bread.

The overseers enforced the granary rule with more spite than the order itself asked for, as overseers on the whole will, and searched huts for hidden meal, and twice that autumn fined a family a day's wage for a sack of flour found under a bed, though the sack, in both cases, had come up from Ros gharbh by night and never passed through A' Chompanaidh's own scales at all, a fact the overseers either did not know or chose not to ask about.

## VII. Of the Road East

Catrìona was not dismissed outright, which would at least have had the honesty of a plain blow. She was, instead, over the two years that followed, quietly refused. The seventh shift was given to another crew-leader before the winter was out, a young man loyal to Crewe and glad of the wage; Catrìona was offered work at the surface, sorting slate, at half a hewer's pay, and took it because there was nothing else, and kept it eleven months, until the overseer over the sorting-sheds, a different man from Crewe but reading from the same book, told her the sheds had more hands than they needed and hers, this quarter, were the ones not needed.

She walked to Cnoc fhiadhaich and asked for work and was turned away at the gate before she had said her name twice; the agent there knew her by sight, which told her plainly enough what had gone round in A' Chompanaidh's own letters, whatever face Crewe himself might have kept at Baile thais. She walked to Àth ìseal, and to the timber camp beyond it, and had the same door shut in the same quiet way each time, no shouting, no threats, only a man looking past her shoulder and saying there was nothing that quarter, come again another season.

She did not, in all that time, ask the guild of Muileann chiar for anything, having no claim on it and no trade in silver, and it did not occur to her until the second year of her refusing that a hill which owed A' Chompanaidh nothing might be the one hill left on the island that would look at her without first looking at Crewe's letters. Sìneag, when Catrìona came to the smithy room to say her goodbyes, gave her what little the custodian's own store could spare, a heel of cheese and a pair of stockings darned past their first darning, and said only that Baile thais would remember the tub longer than it remembered the granary. Catrìona did not fully believe it, standing there with the cheese in her hand and the road east still ahead of her.

In the autumn of the third year after the stoppage, with her savings gone and her sister's household unable to keep her much longer without going short themselves, Catrìona took what she had, a change of clothes, her mother's ring, and the tally-stick Griogar had given her eleven years before, which she had kept though it named a shift she no longer led, and walked east over the hills toward Muileann chiar, two days and the best part of a third, sleeping the first night in a shepherd's bothy and the second under a wall, with the country changing under her feet from the black spoil-heaps of the coal hills to the paler grey of the silver country, where An Seann Urram for the vein still held in a way it had stopped holding at Baile thais some years before.

Comann an Airgid, had never worked easily with A' Chompanaidh, holding as it did its own seam under the compact Ùna nic Choinnich had won from Lisle, which the humans had never managed to unwrite; and its head that year, a woman who had stood at the adit with the ledgers as a girl, heard Catrìona's whole account without interrupting it once, asked her three questions about the ore she had never in her life seen, and put the matter of taking her on to the guild's own hands rather than deciding it herself, which was the guild's way in most things that mattered. The hands voted to take her, by a wide margin, and Catrìona had little doubt it was less for love of her than for the pleasure of taking from A' Chompanaidh a hewer it had gone to some trouble to be rid of.

A' Chompanaidh wrote to the guild within the season, in the correct and distant hand of its counting-house at Ros dhomhain, asking that Catrìona nic Eachainn, lately of Baile thais, be sent back to answer for the stoppage of two years before. The guild's answer was drafted by its own clerk, read aloud once in the guild hall to general satisfaction, folded, sealed, and sent south by the ordinary post; and what it said, whether short or long, courteous or otherwise, no one at Muileann chiar troubled to keep a second copy of, thinking the matter closed the day it was sent. The letter that was filed against it at Ros dhomhain has not survived either. Of the words themselves, then, nothing more can be told than that they went, and that Catrìona nic Eachainn, refiner of Comann an Airgid from that autumn to the end of her days, never again set foot at Baile thais, nor, so far as the rolls know, ever wished to.

# Chapter Twenty-two: Of the Priced Silver and the Blessed Coin

*AE 80 – 87*

## I. Of the Silver Priced by Dia-thìreach Hands

At Muileann chiar in the autumn of the eightieth year Catrìona nic Eachainn weighed her first bar of guild silver alone, without Ùna nic Choinnich's hand at her elbow, because Ùna nic Choinnich had been ten years in the ground and there was no one else the guild trusted with the scale on a market morning.

She had come to the silver town a year before with nothing but the clothes she stood in and a name A' Chompanaidh had marked as one not to be hired again in any pit on the island, and the guild had taken her on as it took on anyone with steady hands and no fear of the acid vats, and had not asked what she had done at Baile thais. She learned the trade fast: how to read the ore by its weight in the hand before the fire ever touched it, how to keep the ledger that answered to no clerk of A' Chompanaidh, how the guild's own price for a bar of silver was set by the guild alone, at a hall table, by seven refiners' vote, and was the one price on the whole island that no human hand had ever moved.

It was a small thing to be proud of and she was proud of it anyway.

The town had grown around her without her much noticing the growing, the way a wall grows a foot at a time and is only a wall when you look up from your work and find you cannot see over it. Two years before there had been one street of stone houses and a smithy; now there were five streets, and a second town besides, a mile to the west, that the guild had raised for its carters and coal-breakers when the old town's lanes could no longer hold them, and which was called by the old town's own name, so that a stranger asking the way to Muileann chiar was as often as not sent to the wrong one. The custodians' rolls, when they had cause to write of either, called them the old town and the new, and did not always trouble to say which they meant.

Below the town, where the burn ran warm out of the hillside, Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had built a bath-house that autumn for its officers who came up sick from the coast fevers to take the water. The springs had been the island's own since before any custodian now living could say; the Dia-thìrich of the district had bathed there each Bealltainn and each Samhain time out of mind, for the joints and for the skin complaints of the deep galleries, and had never paid a penny to do it. Now they were let in on two days of the humans' week, and charged a penny at the door for the water that had been theirs to walk into unasked. Catrìona went once, in the second winter, to see it for herself, and paid her penny, and sat in water that scalded exactly as it always had, and came out and told the guild hall that the water had not changed at all, only the door.

Silversmiths began that year to settle along the carters' road at Muileann bhàn, half a day's walk west, working the guild's bar into brooches and clasps and buckles for the humans' own market, since a piece of worked silver crossed the sea for far more than a bar of it ever had. It was, Catrìona came to understand, turning the guild's ledgers over of an evening, the one craft of the island sold across the water under its own name and no other; every bolt of cloth, every keg of salt fish, every cask of the island's own barley beer went out under A' Chompanaidh's mark, but a Muileann bhàn brooch went out under its own maker's mark, because the humans who bought it liked to say where it had come from.

A' Chompanaidh asked, that same year and the next, whether the guild would sell its silver at A' Chompanaidh's price rather than its own, and was refused both times, and asked a third time with a paper naming a magistrate at Ros dhomhain who might be brought to rule on the question, and was refused a third time, more shortly. Catrìona was in the hall for the third refusal and watched the seven refiners vote it down without one dissenting hand, and thought, though she did not say it aloud, that this was the whole of what she had walked east over the hills to find: one table in the whole width of the island where the Dia-thìrich still set the price.

## II. Of the Seat Ten Years Empty

In the autumn of the eighty-first year Fearghas went up the hill to a council he had no vote in but had been asked to bless: the seating of a new Ceann a' Chùraim, the first in ten years.

Alasdair Liath had held the seat twenty-seven years and had been dead ten; since his burying the council had sat without a head of its own choosing, unable to agree on one, and had said among itself, in the hearing of no clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, that an empty seat answered no letters and signed no papers Riaghaltas nan Coigreach might afterward hold against the whole council, and that this was not the worst thing a seat could be. Fearghas had heard Ealasaid Liath say once that ten years without a head was an answer of its own kind, though not one anybody had meant to give.

The council chose, at last, Artair mac Iain, a custodian of the eastern shires six-and-fifty that winter, a quiet man who had kept his own town's rolls without a blot for thirty years and had never once, in all that time, been summoned to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir for anything. He took the seat in the same hall where Tormod mac Ailein had signed Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, under the same beams, and said, when he was asked for words, only that he would keep the rolls as they had always been kept, and sat down.

Fearghas said the order's blessing over him, both horses named, the dark and the light, and found the words came easier over a man than they had come over a coin, though he could not then have said why, only that a man could answer for himself and a coin could not.

## III. Of the Two Horses

Fearghas mac Mhuirich had kept the fire of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg for eleven years before Tolley's letter came, and in that time he had blessed ploughs, byres, bridges, the first-born of three custodian houses, and once, at a fisherman's asking, a boat that sank within the month with the blessing still wet on her bow. He did not think himself proud about any of it. A blessing was a word said in the right order over a thing that could not say it for itself, and Òrd Mhacha had said such words at Cathair dhearg since before Rìghrean na Cloiche were a memory anyone kept whole.

The letter was carried up from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir by a boy in a coat of A' Chompanaidh who did not know what he carried and did not wait for an answer. It asked, in the courteous hand Riaghaltas nan Coigreach used for everything it meant to have, that the priests of Òrd Mhacha bless the new coin of the realm before it was struck a second time, so that the humans' subjects on the island might take it without fear of ill luck.

The eldest of the order, a woman named Ealasaid Liath who had held the fire longer than Fearghas had been alive, read the letter twice and laughed once, without much humour in it. "They want the horses to run for them," she said. "Well. The horses have run for stranger riders."

She meant the rite of the two, Dubh Sainglenn the black and Liath Macha the grey, that stood at the heart of every blessing the order gave: the dark hour and the bright, the labour and the rest, the thing spent and the thing kept, each with its due and neither without the other. It was the oldest teaching the order had, older than any building at Cathair dhearg, and Fearghas had said the words of it over a hundred doorsteps and a thousand infants without once doubting that the two halves were equal, and that a blessing given to one alone was no blessing at all, only a wish dressed as one.

"The coin is one thing," he said. "It is spent, and it does not rest. What is the grey horse's part in it?"

Ealasaid Liath looked at him with the patience she kept for the youngest of the order, though he was forty-five that year and had buried his own teacher. "The grey horse's part," she said, "is that the coin passes from a full hand to an empty one, and comes back full again, in its season, as the tide does. That is the rest it takes. You are thinking of the box it sits in. Think of the road it walks."

He went with her to the temple on the morning appointed, 24 an Gearran, AE 85, with the whole order in their grey and black and Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerk standing at the door with a satchel of the new-struck marks, bright as fish-scale, a ship stamped on the one face and nothing of the island on the other. Tolley himself did not come; he sent word that the ordinance of an Àrd-mhaor's presence would overweight a religious matter, which those of the order who cared to be amused found a fine thing for a man to say who had ordered the blessing in the first place.

Ealasaid Liath said the words over the satchel, both halves of them, the dark and the light, in the old order, and the fire took the smoke of the burnt hazel the rite asked for, and it was done. Fearghas stood at his place in the second rank and said the words with the rest, because that is what a member of an order does, and because he could not, that morning, have told anyone in what particular the thing felt wrong. Only that when the clerk gathered up the satchel and thanked them and went, he found himself watching the door a long while after it had shut, the way a man watches a place where he has mislaid something without yet knowing what.

Three of the younger priests would not stand at their places that day and stood instead at the back of the hall with their arms folded. Nothing was said to them then. Ealasaid Liath was not a woman to make an example in front of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerk. But that night, over the last of the fire, she told Fearghas what she had not troubled to tell them: that a coin blessed with both horses' names was still, in the end, only a coin, and that the order's business was the rite done rightly, not the uses a stranger's hand put a rightly-blessed thing to afterward. "We do not answer for the road it walks," she said. "Only that it is a whole horse that walks it, and not half of one."

Fearghas turned that over for years before he understood he did not believe it. He said nothing of that yet. He kept the peace of his order that year, and kept it.

He kept it, too, at the cost of small things he only noticed afterward, looking back. That year he stopped walking the lower town on the mornings Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerks changed their coin at the money-tables by the bridge, where a queue of Dia-thìrich waited with barter goods to be weighed against the new mark and went away with fewer coins than the goods, by the old reckoning, ought to have bought. The bridge road was longer and quieter, he told himself, and left it there. He kept the fire, said the hours, blessed what was brought to him, and did not again stand at the temple door to watch a satchel of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir carried out into the town, though he heard, from those of the order less careful of where they walked, that the second and third strikings of the coin went out from that door much as the first had.

## IV. Of the Fleece and the Boats

The second cheapening of the coin fell in the year after the blessing, read out at every market cross by a crier of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir who did not trouble to soften it: the barter goods of the Dia-thìrich, wool and hide and dried fish and the rest, were marked down a second time against the mark, on a table Riaghaltas nan Coigreach alone had drawn, and no custodian's council was asked to sign it or shown it before it was cried.

Word of it reached Muileann chiar three days after Cathair dhearg, carried by a carter who had heard it cried at Baile Mòr fhionn on his way east and had thought the guild ought to know, since silver was not named in the table and the guild's own price stood as it had. He told it at the hall table over his supper, and told also what he had seen at Baile Mòr fhionn itself: the weavers standing about the market cross with their wool in baskets at their feet, working out on their fingers what a fleece was worth under the new table, and finding it was worth what half a fleece had been worth the week before.

The weavers of Baile Mòr fhionn would not sell at the table. That winter they carried no wool to the humans' market at all, and the wool sat in their warehouses through two winters until the moths had the better part of it.

At Caol fhiadhaich, a fishing town on the same coast that had never dealt in coal or silver at all, the harbour dues were called in marks that year for the first time, where they had always been called in fish or in kind, and the town could not raise the sum any way but by selling boats. It sold eleven of its two-and-twenty, at A' Chompanaidh's own asking price, which was low, since A' Chompanaidh was the only buyer on that coast with marks to spend; and the men who had sailed the eleven boats went into the pits the following season under A' Chompanaidh's contracts, because a man who has sold his boat must eat from somewhere.

Catrìona heard all this the way the guild hall heard everything, as news carried by carters and confirmed or corrected by the next carter after, and set it beside what she had seen with her own eyes at the bath-house door, and thought that she was coming to understand the shape of the thing A' Chompanaidh was building, one small cheapening at a time, the way a tide takes a shore in ten thousand waves, each so small a man standing on the sand would swear the water had not moved at all.

## V. Of the Second Asking

Riaghaltas nan Coigreach struck a new coin the year after, when the barter was marked down the second time, larger than the old and stamped, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter said, so that no forger on the island might easily copy it, though there had been no forger caught in all the years of the first. The letter asked, in the same courteous hand as before, that Òrd Mhacha bless it as the first had been blessed.

Ealasaid Liath had died in the winter between, of a lung complaint that took her slowly and without complaint, and Fearghas kept the fire in her place, the eldest now among a much younger order, most of whom had not stood in the hall the first time.

He read the letter at the fire that night and did not sleep, and in the morning called the order together and told them he would not say the words over this coin, and that any who wished to say them without him might, since he held no rule over another priest's mouth, only over his own.

None went.

It was not, he told them, a matter of the humans' coin being unworthy of a blessing; a plough was no worthier and he had blessed a hundred ploughs. It was that the order had been asked, the year before, to bless the road a thing walked and not the thing that walked it, and had told itself it answered only for the horse and not the rider; and he had watched the road a year now, through the second marking-down of the barter, and did not believe that any longer. The coin did not pass from a full hand to an empty one and back again in its season, as the grey horse's part required. It passed from an empty hand to a fuller one, always in the one direction, down the same road every year the same way, and no rite he knew how to say could make a one-way road into a wheel.

"Then bless the wheel," said the youngest of them, a woman named Sìne who had joined the order the winter before, "and let the road answer for itself."

"I do not know how to bless a wheel that only turns one way," Fearghas said. "If you know, teach me, and I will say the words gladly."

She did not know either. Nobody in the hall that morning knew, and the not-knowing sat among them a long while before anyone spoke again.

Word of the refusal reached Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir within the month, as such words always did, carried by whichever clerk had cause to visit the temple on other business and found the fire kept but the coin unblessed on the shelf where it had been left. Tolley did not send for Fearghas. He had larger matters on his desk than one priest's obstinacy over a rite the coin did not in any case require to pass current; the letter asking the blessing had been courtesy, not law, and the coin was spent in every market on the island with or without it. But Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-book that year notes, in a clerk's hand, that the order of Òrd Mhacha at the capital was "divided on a religious nicety," and does not trouble to say what the nicety was, which is as much as most Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's papers ever granted the order's reasons in all the years of the age.

## VI. Of the Name at the Wash-Stones

It is told from these same years, though no roll sets the day of it, that the name the washing-women of Achadh dhomhain had given the girl of the spoil-houses went out of that camp and down the coal roads, to Àth ìseal and Muileann chrom and the huts at Cnoc fhiadhaich, and was said at wash-stones where nobody had ever seen her.

By the count of the years she was near grown. By the look of her, the women said, she was not; and the women who washed the dead knew better than anyone what a year does to a body. They called her *nighean an rìgh*, meaning Ailean Mòr, whom the gods crowned in the grove and who fell at Àth na Fala; and most of those who said it did not believe a word of the thousands of years, or said they did not, which came to the same thing at supper. A king four thousand years old was, to a woman with a week's ration to stretch and a husband on the night crew, a tale for the dark end of the year. They went on saying the name all the same, because it was a good name, and because a people whose hill was going out in ships will take its comfort where it finds it.

Nobody wrote it in a roll. The custodians of the camps had learned, in these years, to keep out of their rolls whatever Riaghaltas nan Coigreach might read as a claim, and a king's daughter, even a jest of one, was such a claim.

## VII. Of the Fire under the Trees

Fearghas mac Mhuirich left the temple at Cathair dhearg in the spring after his refusal, with eleven of the order who had come to think as he did, and walked north to Cnoc bheag, where Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag had stood since before the order was founded and where a fence of oak stakes, renewed generation on generation, still kept the cattle from the old stone that no one living could read.

They were not driven out. Nobody at the capital's temple forbade them the door; the eldest of those who stayed, a mild man named Griogair who had said the second blessing without Fearghas's help and thought no worse of him for the refusing, walked with them as far as the north road and told them the fire at Cathair dhearg would keep both horses' names as it always had, and that this was no falling-out between them, only two roads to the one rite, and that he hoped they might one day agree which was the truer.

They did not agree, not then and not for years after. But the custodians of Cnoc bheag, whose own seat at the council's table had gone begging more than once in these hard years, and several custodians of other towns who had lost their seats outright to A' Chompanaidh's magistrates and Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's displeasure and had nowhere else the old forms were still kept whole, came to the dissenting priests' hall by ones and twos through that first summer, until the forest held near as many custodians without a town as priests without a temple, and the two kinds of the dispossessed began, without either quite meaning it, to keep each other's company.

On the last evening of that first spring, Fearghas lit a fire under the oaks with hazel cut from the grove, as the rite asked, and said the words of the two horses over it, both halves in the old order, the dark and the light, exactly as Ealasaid Liath had taught him and exactly as he had said them over the first coin two years before. He asked nothing of anyone to walk any particular road that night. He asked only that the fire be a whole fire, spent and kept both, as a rite ought to be; and the custodians who stood in the ring about it, most of whom owned no seat and no roll and no staff any longer, watched it burn down to embers under the old stone's shadow, and said nothing at all, which among that company had come, in these years, to be its own kind of prayer.

## VIII. Of the Staff Passed On

In the spring that Fearghas walked north, word reached Muileann chiar by the usual road of carters and market gossip that Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor, overseer of the coal country these five-and-twenty years, had died at Muileann chrom in his sixty-seventh year, of no illness the guild's informant could name, only of age and the staff's long weight.

Catrìona had cause to remember him without kindness: it was his hand that had signed the order forbidding the camps to keep more than a week's grain against her own Stad-oibre Baile thais, years before she ever came east, and the granary his order had built still stood at Muileann chrom, locked of a Friday evening the way it had always been locked. She felt, hearing of his death, less than she thought she ought to feel, and told the hall table only that a hard man was gone and a harder trade would go on without him.

The staff passed, as everyone in the coal country had long known it would, to his son Iain, seven-and-thirty that year, the first of the overseer's line schooled at Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise at Ros dhomhain, who was said to keep his household in Dia-thìris and his reports to A' Chompanaidh in the humans' own tongue, and to walk the galleries himself rather than send a clerk. What that would mean for the crews under him nobody at Muileann chiar could yet say, and the guild's answer, when the news was set before the hall table, was the same answer the guild gave most tidings out of the coal country now: that they would learn it soon enough, and that until they did there was silver to weigh.

# Chapter Twenty-three: Of An Togail and Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh

*AE 88 – 91*

> *Ghearr sinn ar n-ainmean sa chloich mus do scrìobh iad sinn às.*
>
> We cut our names in the stone before they wrote us out.
>
> — cut into the lintel of the lamp-room at Taigh-solais Baile chrom

## I. Of the Reading at Caol mhòr

The camps under the hawk-feather burned their fires that winter as they had burned them the winter before, and Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's clerks at Ros dhomhain wrote in their ledgers that the yield still climbed. It was George Tolley's thirteenth year as Àrd-mhaor, and by then he had learned what the island's soil would give up and what its people would, and had stopped troubling to ask which was which. On a hard morning at the turn of the year he set his seal to a single sheet and called it An Togail: from every farming village of the west and north, one soul in five of the able grown folk, taken for two years, to go down into the pits where A' Chompanaidh's coal was cut. The villages would be paid for it, in marks, at the rate the second reform of the coin had lately fixed; a rate that bought less bread each season it was reckoned in, though the ledger did not say so.

Word of a law travels a country faster than the law's own officers, and slower than the fear of it. It reached Cnoc thais as a rumour before it reached Caol mhòr as a list, and at Caol mhòr, in the far north-west where the strangers had first raised the land, it came as both together.

The officers rode in on a market morning, four of them and a wagon, with a guard of A' Chompanaidh's men the town had not asked for. They set up at the steelyard by the quay, where the fish were weighed, and one of them stood on the weighing-stone with a paper and read from it in the humans' tongue, flat and fast, a list of names that were not the names anyone in Caol mhòr answered to. The custodians of the town stood below him with their own clerks and wrote each name down again as it was said, guessing at the shapes of it, and only when the whole list was read and the officer had gone back to his wagon for a cup of something did they go from house to house with their own paper and match a guessed name to a face. Twice they guessed wrong and took the wrong son from the wrong door, and it was three days before the mistake was mended, by which time the right son had already been marched a day's walk east.

The custodian who kept that day's roll, an old woman with a bad hip who had held the post since before An Togail was thought of, wrote at the end of it a single line that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own reader, when the roll crossed his desk months later, let stand unremarked: that a people may be counted twice, once by those who take them and once by those who love them, and that the two counts never come out the same.

The wrong son was found on the third day, sitting under guard in a barn a day's walk east with eleven other taken men, none of whom had thought to say, until a rider from Caol mhòr caught them up, that the paper's name and his own were two different shapes that had only looked alike to a guessing clerk. He was sent home, and the right son was fetched in his place, and the officer who had made the error entered it in his own tally as a delay of one day, with no further word, so that the roll of Caol mhòr and the roll of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach disagree to this hour on how many men that town gave up, by exactly one.

It was the first tally taken under the new law, and Caol mhòr's grief was loud and short, as a first grief is. Grief travels a country too. By the time the officers' wagon had gone from three villages to thirty, the households of the hills had stopped weeping where the officers could hear it, and had begun instead the older, quieter work of hiding what could be hidden and choosing, among those who could not be hidden, who should go. Some sent their eldest, on the thought that the eldest was hardest to spare and so ought to bear the hardest thing; others sent their youngest, on the thought that a young back mended faster than an old one; and there was no counsel from any custodian's roll, and none from the Council at Cathair dhearg either, on which of the two thoughts was the kinder.

## II. Of the Two Tallies

An Togail's writ ran over the whole west and north, but it did not run evenly, no more than rain runs evenly over uneven ground. It fell heaviest about Baile chrom and the province the humans called their northern concession, the upland grazing of the north-west that the council had granted for the humans' flocks two generations before, and that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had since leased whole to its own farmers. The concession's fields were sown that spring as they had always been sown, by the same hands; only the hands that worked them now were fewer, for every Dia-thìreach household within the concession's bounds paid An Togail in full, while the human farmers who held the leases paid nothing at all. The officers' own list, when the custodian of Baile chrom's roll got sight of it, gave the reason in one line: that the concession's leaseholders were tenants of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach and its charter, and An Togail touched Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own subjects only by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own leave, and that leave had not been given.

At Baile ìseal the tally took forty-one, the largest of any single town that year, out of a town of some seventy hearths. Nineteen came home again when their two years were done. The custodian's roll names the other twenty-two, town by town among the camps they were carried to, and against four of the names writes nothing at all, neither camp nor date nor word, only the name and a line drawn under it, which the copyists have kept exactly as it stood, understanding it no better than the roll's own keeper had.

Muileann naomh tried what no other town on the list is known to have tried, and its trying is remembered for the manner of its failing. Its custodians met An Togail's officers before the reading and offered silver, a purse weighed out on the town scale in front of witnesses, that the tally might be cut by half. The senior officer, a heavy, patient man who had done this work in a dozen towns before Muileann naomh and would do it in a dozen more after, took up the purse himself and weighed it a second time on his own small scale, as though a custodian's weights might not be trusted, and only then said that the town's offer was noted and would be honoured in full. The custodians took this to mean the tally would be halved, and stood by while the whole list, uncut, was read to the end. When the eldest of them asked, before the townsfolk, what had become of the silver, the officer said that it had been honoured as an offering toward Sìol-lann na Companaidh, and that An Togail answered to no offering a town cared to make, and rode on. The complaint that Muileann naomh sent after them to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir at Ros dhomhain was received, logged, and filed, and no answer to it has ever been found, though the custodians kept a fair copy against the day one might come.

The tale of it went ahead of the officers into every town they had not yet reached, and did Riaghaltas nan Coigreach more harm, in the way such tales do, than the silver was worth to lose; for after Muileann naomh no other town on the list is recorded to have offered a bribe, custodians having learned in one hearing what Caol mhòr had learned in one reading, that there was no bargain to be struck with a list, only a length of road between the reading of it and the leaving.

Dùghall Clachair heard all of this the way a man hears weather from over the next hill, as talk carried by carters and by the officers themselves, who liked well enough to tell what they had done in one town when they rode into the next. He was three-and-thirty that spring, a mason of Cnoc thais, master of a crew of six who had cut and set stone together since he was a boy carrying their water. He heard the talk and thought, as every man in every village thought that spring, that his own door would not be spared for long, and went on cutting stone, because there was nothing else a mason could do about a law.

## III. Of the Shut Halls and the Trees of Flidais

In the same season, and by the same Àrd-mhaor's hand though under a different seal, the hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Dùn thais was shut. Its offence, as the order that closed it gave it, was a lecture the masters had let stand unanswered: whether the humans' plain blindness to the colours of the coal, the blindness Gormshuil nic Fhearchair had first met across a table two generations before, was a kind of sickness in its own right, and if so, whose. Tolley's clerk who drew up the order did not trouble to say which answer had offended him. He shut the hall on the strength of the question alone.

The masters of Dùn thais did not disperse. They went on teaching in their own houses, in rooms that grew smaller each year as more households thought it wiser not to send their sons, until at Doire chiar, on the eve of Bealltainn, they held the last open disputation the schools held in the old way, in the open air on the village threshing-floor, before whoever cared to stand and listen. Folk came from three parishes to hear it, more than the floor could well hold, and stood in a ring beyond the stones with children on their shoulders. Its matter was whether a question might rightly be forbidden at all, and it was argued the whole of one long evening by two masters who had taught together thirty years and did not agree at the end of it any better than they had at the start, which the old men in the crowd took as proof that the matter had been well chosen. Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's clerk who was sent to note it down sat apart on a cart-shaft with his own lamp, and wrote in his own report, without seeming to feel the weight of writing it, that it might.

After that the masters who would still teach took their pupils under the trees, to the sacred forest of Flidais near Muileann chiar, where the white stag was said to walk and where Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had no hall to shut, having never troubled to learn that a grove could serve the office of one. There was no threshing-floor there and no cart-shaft for a clerk to sit on; the pupils sat on roots and stones in a rough half-ring, and the master who spoke walked as he spoke, so that on a wet day the lesson moved from tree to tree with the shelter.
