It is told that the first lesson given under those trees was the very question that had closed the hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, taken up again from where the order had left it standing, and that the master who put it that day answered it herself before any pupil could, saying that a question forbidden by one hand could always be asked again under a roof that hand had not thought to look for.

Dùghall's own younger brother had gone to Dùn thais as a boy to learn his letters from the masters there, in years before the hall was shut, and it was from him, home for a season between one crew's work and the next, that Dùghall first heard the tale of the threshing-floor at Doire chiar. His brother told it standing in the doorway with the light behind him, the way a man tells something he has decided not to be afraid of, and Dùghall, who set stone for a living and had never in his life stood up in a hall to ask a forbidden question, thought his brother the braver of the two of them, and said so, and his brother laughed and said a mason's hands asked questions too, only slower.

## IV. Of the Masons of Cnoc thais

The officers came to Cnoc thais in the high summer of the ninetieth year, with the same wagon and the same list, and Dùghall's name was on it, and the names of his whole crew besides: Ailean, the two brothers Cailean and Seumas, old Pàdraig who had taught Dùghall to read a stone's grain, and the two youngest, Anna and her cousin Murchadh, who had been apprenticed to the crew not two years before and had not yet cut a stone worth the name of a mason's work. Dùghall stood in his own doorway and heard his name read from a paper by a man who could not have said it back to him if his life had hung on it, and understood for the first time what the custodian of Caol mhòr's old roll had meant, that a people may be counted twice.

He thought, as the officer moved on down the list, that they were bound for the pits like every other village's chosen, and had already begun in his head the reckoning a mason makes of any road, how many days, what weather, what he would need to carry. It was two days into the march east, on a stretch of the coast road above Baile ìseal, that the guard captain rode down the line and called for any among them who knew stone-work, and Dùghall and his whole crew put up their hands together, for there was no sense in six masons pretending otherwise to one another's faces. They were turned out of the line then and there and marched north instead of east, along the headland road toward Baile chrom, and it was three days more before any officer troubled to tell them why: that the fifth and last of the coast beacons was to be raised on the headland above the town, the ring of towers that had stood four strong since builders older than any roll now kept, and that masons were wanted for it more than diggers were wanted underground.

It did not feel, to Dùghall, like a mercy, and he came in time to think it was not meant as one. The fields of Cnoc thais that his crew would have worked between commissions, the small plots that kept a mason's household fed in a lean season, stood untilled that whole year for want of the very hands An Togail had taken to build a light that would serve no plough and no byre of theirs. He set that thought aside most days, because a man cannot cut good stone while nursing a grievance, and took it up again most nights, because a man cannot help what comes to him lying still in the dark.

"You should be glad of it," the guard captain told him, on the second evening of the march, meaning glad to be spared the pits, and waited as though a man ought to thank him for the saying. Dùghall said nothing, because there was no way to tell a guard-captain that a mason parted from his stone-yard felt the parting no less than a hewer parted from his own hill, only that the shape of the loss was different, a field going to weed instead of a family going hungry for want of a wage; and a captain with a wagon to keep moving had no patience for a difference of shape. He touched his cap instead, which cost him nothing, and the captain rode on satisfied, and Dùghall walked the rest of that evening beside old Pàdraig, who had heard the whole exchange and said only that a man who explains himself to a guard has already lost the argument he meant to win.

They were housed, the six of them, in a hut of turf and driftwood on the headland above Baile chrom, alongside crews taken the same way from four other villages, so that within a month the camp held above sixty masons and their apprentices, none of whom had chosen one another's company and all of whom now shared one fire, one well, and one quarry. The work went by the light there was, longer in summer than any of them had worked before, shorter in winter than any of them had hoped, and the officers who oversaw it kept a tally of stone cut that mattered to them more than any tally of men fed. Anna, who was seventeen that first winter and had never before slept a night away from her mother's hearth, wept the first three nights in the hut where she thought no one heard her, and was heard by all of them, and on the fourth night old Pàdraig without a word got up from his own straw and mended the gap in the turf wall nearest her sleeping-place, through which the wind had been finding her all along, and after that she did not weep where they could hear it again, though Dùghall never once believed she had stopped.

The tower rose through that autumn and the winter after, coarse grey stone from a quarry the officers had opened on the headland, so that the masons need not even be spared the labour of hauling it far. Dùghall set the courses and taught Anna and Murchadh to read the lie of a block before they touched a chisel to it, the way old Pàdraig had taught him; and Pàdraig, whose hands had grown too slow for the finer cutting, sat most days on an upturned barrow and told the younger ones what he could no longer show them, and the crew came in time to work as well by his voice as by his eyes. Cailean broke a finger that winter and would not leave off working for it, and Seumas, his brother, quarrelled with him about it every evening and dressed the finger every morning, and the two of them were never once heard to agree, on that or on anything else, in all the time Dùghall knew them.

The worst of that winter was a gale out of the north-west that took two days to blow itself out and stripped the scaffold from the tower's third course as easily as a man strips bark from a green branch. When it had passed, Dùghall climbed what stood of the walls alone, before he would let any of the others up after him, to judge whether the stone had shifted; and standing in the wind that still gusted hard enough to lean a man sideways, with the sea below him white to the horizon and no ship anywhere on it, he understood for the first time in his own body why a light was wanted on that headland at all, and forgave the tower, a little, for the fields it had cost him. He did not forgive An Togail. A tower, he thought, climbing down again with his hands raw from the cold stone, owed nothing to the law that had raised it, any more than a child owed anything to the manner of its getting.

By the second summer the walls stood to their full height and the crew began the finer work at the top: the stair turning always to the right, hand over hand up the cold stone, and the lamp-room, no bigger than a byre, lit on every side by narrow windows against the weather. It was slower work than the coursing below, and Murchadh, who had grown in a year from a frightened boy to a mason who could be trusted with a door-jamb, cut the last of the window-sills himself, under Dùghall's eye and without a single stroke wasted, and Dùghall told him so in front of the others, which was the only wage of that kind either of them ever got for An Togail's taking.

They built the tower to a height a man could not see the top of from its own foot without stepping well back, round and tapering. It was Dùghall who cut the lintel of that room, the stone that would stand over whoever kept the light for as long as the tower stood, and it was Dùghall, on the last evening before the tower was done, who took a chisel he had no order to take and cut into the underside of that lintel, where only a man climbing the last step and looking up would ever see it, the names of his crew: Ailean, Cailean, Seumas, Pàdraig, Anna, Murchadh, and his own beneath them, each letter as clean as any he had ever cut for a custodian's hall or a dead man's stone. It is the only writing on any of the five towers of the ring, and no order asked for it and no order struck it out.

## V. Of the Ring Made Whole

The ring of coast beacons was finished in the summer of the ninety-first year of the strangers: Taigh-solais Baile chrom last of the five, standing to Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg as a hand's fifth finger stands to the rest, so that a ship might now run the whole coast of Dia-thìr by night and never lose a light from sight before the next one rose to take its place. A' Chompanaidh's clerks at Ros dhomhain called it the completion of the coast trade and entered the date in three ledgers. The keepers' own daybooks, kept in a plainer hand, called it the end of the dark crossing, and the two names meant the one thing.

What it meant for Cuan ruadh, on the eastern shore, was the end of a trade the town had kept since before any beacon stood at all: the old coasting boats that had carried goods by day from harbour to harbour, hugging a shore too dangerous to run by night, put up their sails for the last time within a few years of the ring's completion, for A' Chompanaidh's steamers no longer needed to put in anywhere along that coast, and ran the whole circuit of the island without touching Cuan ruadh's quay from one season's end to the next. A master of one of those boats, a woman named for the same red headland as the town, sold her hull for firewood the winter the last cargo failed to come, and is remembered to have said, to whichever custodian's clerk thought the sale worth entering, that a light built to keep ships from wrecking on a coast had wrecked her trade instead, and no less surely for doing it slowly. The town's custodian entered the last coasting sailing in her own roll with no comment beyond the date, which the copyists have judged, from the small unevenness of the ink, was written with a hand that trembled.

An Togail held Dùghall's crew at Baile chrom until the tower was lit, and they would have stayed for it in any case; a mason likes to see a thing finished that he has raised with his own hands. The keeper appointed to it was a young man of the headland villages named Uisdean mac Lachlainn, thirty years old that autumn, chosen for the post, Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's letter said, on the recommendation of the very masons who had built the light he was to keep; which recommendation, though the letter does not say so, Dùghall had himself written out and signed, along with Ailean and old Pàdraig, in a hand none of the three would have called fine.

On an evening of an t-Sultain, with the last of the year's warmth still in the air and the sea below the headland gone the colour of hammered lead, Uisdean climbed the turning stair to the lamp-room for the first time as its keeper, with Dùghall and what remained of his crew behind him, for they had asked to be there and no one had thought to refuse them. Ailean carried the coal up in a leather sack himself, saying that a light built by six masons' hands ought to be lit with coal carried by at least one of the same six, and Anna, who had grown a head taller in the year since she first slept in the turf hut, went up last of all and touched the newel of the stair as she passed it, the way she had seen old Pàdraig touch a finished stone before he would call it done.

At the top of the stair Uisdean stopped under the lintel, as every keeper after him would stop there without knowing why the stone at that particular step seemed to want a man's eye lifted to it, and asked Dùghall, since he stood nearest, whether the mason who had cut it thought it plumb. Dùghall said that he did, and did not say that he was the mason, and Uisdean, who had signed his own name to the tower's finishing without ever learning that the recommendation for his post had come from these six hands, struck the light.

It caught on the second strike, a coal flame steady behind glass, and threw its first beam out over water that had never in the island's whole memory carried a light so far. Below on the darkening sea, and for a distance beyond guessing, the beam found nothing to answer it that night; but the keepers' daybooks would show, within a very few years, A' Chompanaidh's sailings past that headland doubled, and doubled again, ships running by the new light at hours no master would once have risked the coast at all.

Dùghall stood at the foot of the lamp-room, under the lintel he had cut, and looked up at the names no order had asked for and no order had struck out, and thought that a tower raised by taken hands might yet be made to answer, in its small way, to the hands that raised it, though the light, once lit, answered only to the ships it was built to serve, and asked no man's leave to shine for them and not for him.

# Chapter Twenty-four: Of Gorta Baile chrom

*AE 94 – 97*

## I. Of the Empty Road

Uisdean mac Lachlainn kept the first daybook of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, and its first pages are given over to nothing but weather and wicks: so many hours burning, so much oil drawn, the wind from such a quarter. He had asked for the keeping himself, the year the ring was finished, on the notion that a keeper who wrote nothing down could never answer for what he had seen. He did not, that first winter, know what he would be asked to answer for.

In am Màrt of the ninety-fourth year he began to write other things.

The tower stood on the headland above Baile chrom, a climb of a hundred and nine steps he had counted more than once in the dark, and its gallery looked two ways: out over the water where the light he tended went round all night for ships that were not his, and inland over the fields that fed the town. That spring he stood his morning watch at the rail and saw a farmer he knew, a man called Alasdair Ruadh, walk the length of his own ploughland with a hand-harrow and no one behind him. The year before there had been six at that work, sons and cousins and a hired man from the shore. Uisdean wrote in the daybook: *Alasdair Ruadh ploughs alone. No hands for the seed but his.* It was not a thing a keeper of lights was asked to note. He noted it anyway.

The hands had gone to the pits under An Togail, which had come down from Ros dhomhain six years before and was read out at the market cross in the humans' tongue and then again, badly, in Dia-thìris by a clerk who stumbled over the numbers: one in five of every village's grown men and women, for two years, to work under A' Chompanaidh, paid in marks at the new rate. It had fallen on the coast and the hill villages round Baile chrom harder than anywhere else, for the concession farms to the north, worked by the strangers' own people, sent no one. Uisdean had watched the first draft go down the coast road with its bundles on its backs, twenty-three from a town of a few hundred, and had thought, climbing the tower that night, that it was a hard thing but a passing one, the kind of hardship a people bears and is done with.

He had not thought, that first year, to ask who would plough.


By the spring of the ninety-third year the fields round Baile chrom stood half sown, and the ones that were sown were thin, for there were not enough hands to weed them either, and by midsummer the grain that stood was short in the ear and beaten flat in two storms that in another year would have cost a farmer a week's worry and no more. The harvest came in light. Uisdean watched the carts go up to the granary and counted them against the carts of the year before, which he had also, without meaning to, kept a tally of, and the count came out at less than half.

The winter after was hard. The one after that was worse, for it came on a country that had eaten its own reserve to get through the first.

He wrote, on a night in am Faoilleach of the ninety-fifth year, with the wind driving spray to the top of the tower and the lamp burning steady behind its glass: *Nothing crosses the road below tonight. Not a cart, not a dog. The town is shut against the weather, or shut against something else.* He read the line back before he blew out the small lamp at the desk, and thought it was not a keeper's business to write such things, and left it standing.

## II. Of the Bounds of the Hunger

The custodians who kept the count called it, before the year was out, Gorta Baile chrom, and gave it bounds: thirty-four settlements from the coast to the hill road east of the concession, worst at the centre and thinning at the edges, as a fire thins at the edge of what it burns.

At Doire ghlas, north along the coast, the hunger took the old first and then the very young, as hunger does when there is grain enough for one meal in three and a household must choose who eats it. The custodian of Doire ghlas, a woman whose name the roll gives and this telling need not repeat, walked from door to door in the last weeks of that winter and wrote down who still stood and who did not, and in the spring she sent the town's young people south to the camps for the ration A' Chompanaidh gave its crews, which was more certain than anything the fields could promise that year.

A woman of the town called Mòr nic Aonghais, whose son was fourteen and had never worked a day underground, walked with him as far as the hill road and no further, because the custom of the coast held that a mother did not follow her child past the boundary stone. She had baked him what bread the house could spare that morning and wrapped it in a cloth that had been her own mother's, and told him to mind the overseers and to write, though there was no one at Doire ghlas any longer who could read a letter to her but the custodian, and the custodian had her own dead to see to. Mòr stood at the boundary stone a long time after her son had gone out of sight round the bend of the road, and then she walked home to a house with one mouth fewer in it and no more grain in the store than it had had that morning. By the year's end Doire ghlas held half its former number, though half of those who were gone had only gone south and would come back, in their own time, to fields that would need them more than ever.

At Inis mhin on the north coast the second winter of the hunger found the town with seed corn in its store and nothing else, and the choice a coastal town makes in that pass is older than any custodian's roll: they ate the seed, and trusted to the fish and to what charity came, and did not plant that spring at all. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's kitchen at the harbour, which had stood empty three parts of the year since it was built, fed some scores a day the whole of that season, fish broth and biscuit brought round by sea from Cathair gheal, and the harbour-master's wife, who kept the tally at the kitchen door, told Uisdean once, years after, that she had never in her life counted so high a number so many days running and never wanted to again.

At Seann Bhrenn, east of the hunger's worst ground but inside its bounds all the same, the custodians did a thing that had not been done in living memory: they opened the grain-pits of An Aois Naomh, sunk in the chalk hill above the town so long ago that no one now living had seen them opened, kept against a need no one now living had thought would come. The lids were levered up with bars, and the whole town stood round the mouths of the pits in the rain while the custodians went down on ropes with lamps, and came up again with nothing but the dust of grain long generations gone, and a smell that the older people said was the smell of the deep earth, and no comfort in it at all. An old man of the town, who had come to watch with the rest, said afterward that he had always been told the pits held enough to see Seann Bhrenn through any winter the sky could send, and that it had never once crossed his mind, in seventy years of hearing it told, to ask through how many winters that telling had already worn thin.

Uisdean heard these things as a keeper of lights hears most things, from the boats that put in below his tower and the carters who climbed to see the lamp lit and to ask, always, whether the weather would hold. He wrote what he was told into the daybook beside the weather and the oil, because he had begun, without deciding to, to think that a record which held only the light and not what the light shone over was no record worth the keeping.

## III. Of the Ship at Ros dhomhain

Word came to the island, in the second winter of the hunger, that a ship of grain was crossing from an Tìr Thall, sent by An Eaglais's own people who had heard, from the letters of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, what was happening on the coal coast. It reached Ros dhomhain at the dark of the year and lay at anchor in the roads a full month with its holds unopened, for Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir held that unloading and carriage were A' Chompanaidh's charge, being the party whose ordinance, An Togail, had emptied the fields, and A' Chompanaidh held that famine relief was Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's office and none of its own, being no party to the failure of a harvest it had not sown or reaped.

Anne Colby was in Ros dhomhain that spring, come back to the island after some years over the sea, and she went down to the harbour more than once to look at the ship riding at her cable with the gulls working the water round her and her crew idle at the rail. She had nursed the flux on those same quays years before and thought she had seen the worst that argument over a ledger could do to people who had none of the say in it, and found she had not. The ship's master, a quiet man who had made the crossing twice before with cargo Riaghaltas nan Coigreach wanted badly enough to have it off his decks within a day, told her once, leaning on the rail with nothing better to do, that he had never in thirty years at sea been kept waiting so long for a cargo nobody seemed to want unloaded at all.

She wrote to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir herself, once, a short letter asking only who should be told to unload the ship, and had no answer for eleven days, and when the answer came it named no one and settled nothing, and only said that the matter was under consideration between the two offices, and that Àrd-mhaor Tolley had noted her concern. She kept the letter folded small in the same case she carried her lancets in, as though it were a kind of instrument too, and showed it to no one else at all.

On the last day of that month she went down to the harbour again and found the grain still standing in the holds and the town's own children, thin already though the true want had barely begun, playing at soldiers on the quay below the idle ship. It was then, she said afterward, that she stopped writing letters and began instead to walk from office to office in person, since a woman standing in a doorway, she found, could not be answered with a note passed to a clerk.

The ship was unloaded at last, in the first days of the new year, when a clerk at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and a clerk of A' Chompanaidh between them, and neither by any order from above, simply set men to the holds one morning without waiting for either office to finish arguing, and the grain went out by cart in the following weeks to the kitchens Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had by then opened at Cathair gheal and at Baile chrom. Anne Colby went north to Baile chrom herself to run the one there, since she knew the coast and the coast, by then, knew her a little.

## IV. Of the Kitchen Below the Tower

The kitchen at Baile chrom stood in what had been a net-shed by the harbour, its floor still smelling of tar under the smell of the pot, and Anne Colby kept it through the rest of that winter and into the summer with whatever the relief ship's grain and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's own store could supply, stretched with fish when the boats could get out and with nothing at all on the days they could not.

Uisdean came down from the tower most evenings that he was not on watch. The light did not need him at the kitchen door; he came because he found he could not climb his own stair afterward without having seen, once in the day, what the town below him looked like close to. He carried water for her sometimes, and split wood, and once carried a child too weak to walk the length of the quay on his own back, a boy of six or seven whose name he never learned and whose face he did not forget.

The kitchen kept no fixed hour, for the boats' luck and the cart's arrival from Cathair gheal governed it more than any bell could, and there were mornings the queue at the net-shed door stretched past the fish-curers' sheds and mornings it was three old women and no more, the young and the middling having gone, by then, south with the rest. Anne Colby ladled with her own hand at the start and end of every serving, and left the middle of it to whoever she could find to trust with the pot, saying that a person who has served the first bowl and the last knows the whole of a day's want, and everything between is only arithmetic. Uisdean thought, watching her, that she had the custodians' own habit of keeping a roll, though hers was written in faces rather than in ink, and that she seemed to hold every one of them in her memory at once, the way he held the wind and the oil.

Anne Colby knew the crews of the coast by the custodians' names before she knew them by their faces, having learned long before, in another town in another sickness, that a name written correctly in a ledger was sometimes the only thing a dying stranger was given that was truly theirs. She kept a private book of her own at the kitchen, apart from Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's, with every name she fed written once, and crossed through, gently, in the corner of the page, whenever one of them did not come again.

Uisdean asked her once, standing at the kitchen door with the light already lit behind them on the headland, whether she thought A' Chompanaidh knew what An Togail had done to the ploughing.

"They know," she said. "They have the figures. I have seen the figures."

"Then why does nothing change?"

She looked past him, up at the tower, where the beam was already sweeping its slow circle over the black water. "Because the figures they keep," she said, "are the figures for the ships, and the ships are not short of anything."

He had no answer to that, and did not try to find one.

## V. Of the Light He Did Not Put Out

There came a night in that second winter, the coldest of the two, when Uisdean climbed the hundred and nine steps with the wind trying to take the door out of his hand at every landing, and stood a long while at the lamp with his hand on the valve that fed it, and thought, not for the first time and not lightly, of turning it down and letting it go dark.

It was not a thing done from spite, or not only from spite. He had watched, that whole two years, coal go out past his light by the shipload, to hearths and forges over the sea that had never gone hungry a day in their history, while the fields that grew the food for the men who cut that coal lay half worked for want of the hands the coal trade had taken from them. It seemed to him, some nights, a plain enough account: that his light served the taking, and nothing of what it served came back. If the lamp went dark an hour, a night, a week, some ship somewhere would run onto the reef his own grandfather's generation had asked the beacon built against, and A' Chompanaidh's trade would falter, and perhaps, in some way he could not trace from the top of a tower in the dark, the fields would be given back their hands the sooner for it.

He stood with his hand on the valve a long time. The wind came in under the door and made the lamp gutter, then steady, the way it had steadied every night since the ring was finished, keeping its rhythm the way the tide keeps its own regardless of who is drowning or who is fed.

He thought of the nine drowned on the western reef, buried long before his time, whom the beacon had first been asked for. He thought of Alasdair Ruadh walking his empty field with the hand-harrow. Torcall Clachair had built the first of the ring and never lived to see it whole, walking the headlands once with a human navigator, in the years before either of them had reason to think the light they were planning would ever serve anyone's harm. A light built for the drowned did not choose afterward whose ships it saved, any more than a well chose whose bucket drew from it, and a keeper who let it go dark to punish one use of it would be punishing every other use along with it, the fishing boats and the coasting trade and whatever, on some night he could not foresee, might come up that coast needing it for a reason he would never be told. A ship wrecked on the rocks below would drown men who had no more say in An Togail than Alasdair Ruadh had, deckhands and boys signed on for their bread; the coal in her hold would go down with her unburned and change nothing at all in the fields above Baile chrom. The light he kept was near the wrong, he decided at last, standing there with the wind working at the door. It was not the cause of it, the way a man standing near a fire is not the fire.

He took his hand off the valve, and wrote in the daybook, in a hand steadier than his thoughts had been: *Wind north-west, fresh. Lamp trimmed at the second hour. Burning well.* Then, under it, because he had begun to think a record that held only the light was no record at all: *Thought tonight of letting it go dark, and did not. I do not know that I was right. I know only that I could not answer, after, for the ones it would have drowned.*

## VI. Of the Order That Came Too Late

An Togail was set aside in the famine districts early in the ninety-seventh year, three years after the harvest that had shown what it cost, and the order was read at the market cross of Baile chrom on a morning in an Gearran with the same clerk who had read it out first standing in the same place to read that it was ended.

There was no crowd of the size that had gathered for its beginning. Those who came stood in a thin late-winter sun, and heard that the villages of the famine country need send no more of their hands to the pits, and some of them nodded, and some of them looked at the empty houses along the street, shut up since their people had gone south and not all of them come back, and said nothing at all.

Uisdean stood at the back of the small crowd that morning, having come down from the tower to hear it read, and thought that a law lifted three years after the harvest it had ruined was a strange kind of mercy, offered to fields that had already, by their own hard way, worked out how to feed themselves without the hands An Togail had never meant to give back. He wrote the day into the daybook when he climbed the stair that evening, between the wind and the oil, in the same plain hand he kept for everything: *An Togail read ended at Baile chrom this day. Two harvests too late for those it took the hardest. The custodians say it was never repealed, only set by, and that no one here expects to hear it named again. The coast has learned by now what such a word is worth.*

Cnoc mhòr, in the north, past the worst edge of the famine's bounds, had not waited for any order to reach it either way. Its people had watched two winters take what the fields could not replace, and in the summer of the ninety-seventh year, though An Togail was by then set aside, the whole of the village walked south together, the old carried and the young walking, to take A' Chompanaidh's ration and A' Chompanaidh's work rather than starve waiting for a harvest that might fail a third time. A carter who passed through some weeks after told the kitchen at Baile chrom that he had walked the length of the street at Cnoc mhòr and found every door shut but none of them barred, in the way of a people who mean to come back, and a cat sitting on a doorstep that had watched him the whole way through without moving, as though it alone had been left to keep the place. The grass came up in the street the first summer, and by every account that reached the tower at Baile chrom, no household came back to it.

Uisdean climbed to the gallery on an evening at the end of that summer, as he had climbed it near every evening for six years, and lit the lamp, and stood at the rail while the beam went out over water that had drowned no one that season, over a coast where the fields, thin as they were, stood green again. Below him, past the last houses, the road that had carried away Cnoc mhòr's people and Doire ghlas's and so many others lay empty in the last light, the way it had lain empty the whole two years of the hunger, and would, he thought, lie empty a good while yet before it carried anyone home.

# Chapter Twenty-five: Of the Petition on the Bench

*AE 98 – 99*

## I. Of the Word from Ros dhomhain

Peigi Ghlas was forty-eight years old and had kept the shrine of Cill ghlas for eleven of them when the word came down from Ros dhomhain that Àrd-mhaor Tolley was going home.

It came the way most word came to Cill ghlas: by a carter who had it from a carter, three days old and worn smooth by the telling, so that by the time it reached her at the shrine door she could not have said which parts were the letter and which were what men had made of the letter on the road. Tolley was old, the carter said, and rich, and going home with honours, whatever honours were, to the country across Ceò Mhanannain that none of them had seen and none of them missed. A new man was coming to sit in his chair at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and this one, the carter went on, straightening up over his empty cart with the pleased look of a man delivering good news, had let it be known that he meant to ask the custodians' council what it thought before he set anything down.

Peigi heard it out, and thanked him, and gave him water for his horse, and went back into the shrine and trimmed the lamp, because it wanted trimming, and because her hands wanted occupying while the rest of her turned the news over.

She had been eleven years at Cill ghlas by then, since her mother died of the wasting cough, and in all that time she had watched three things come down from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir wearing the shape of good news, and none of the three had kept it past the first winter. She kept this from the carter, and told the flame instead, that night, the only thing at Cill ghlas old enough to have heard it all before her and unlikely to repeat it.

Cill ghlas was a small place even by the reckoning of that country, a scatter of stone houses and byres along a burn under the shoulder of the hill, with a shrine no bigger than a good barn set into the slope above the last house, at the mouth of the oldest cutting in those hills, where a flame that the roll called Brìde's had been kept since before anyone now living could say by whom. It stood an hour's climb above Baile thais, where A' Chompanaidh's galleries went deepest and the walls had lately gone up round the pithead, and it had given men to those galleries the way every village of that country gave men, in ones and twos, and had them come back, when they came back, grey in the face before their time. Peigi had buried four of her own kin out of the pits in eleven years, and had blessed the coal a household kept back from the vein for the shrine, and had gone up the road herself in her season to lay the custodian's handful at the door and burn it, small, the way it had always been burned. She was custodian in a line that was never written down; nobody had appointed her; the flame had simply been hers to keep since her mother's death, as it had been her mother's before her, and the village had never thought to ask whether there was another way of coming to it.

She had also, since the famine years, kept something else: a slate by the shrine door on which she scratched, in the stag-letters her mother had taught her from an old primer bound in sheepskin, every household of Cill ghlas that had lost someone to An Togail, the fever, or the two winters when the granary at Muileann chrom had been full and the village had not. The slate was short. Its weight had nothing to do with its length.

The letter that named the new order of things came a month later, in the last week of an Dàmhair, carried by a rider sent specially, a young man of Ceann àrsaidh with a good horse and a look of a man pleased with his errand. He asked for the custodian by name, which told Peigi before she had broken the seal that whatever was inside had been thought about by more than one person.

It was from Aonghas Ruadh, custodian of Ceann àrsaidh, and it said, in the plain hand of a man more used to counting than writing, that Robert Haskins, the new Àrd-mhaor, had sent word round every district that Comhairle a' Chùraim would be asked its mind on the tithe before anything was fixed, as a mark, the letter he had sent said, of the new order's good will; and that within the month, before any custodian outside Ros dhomhain had so much as replied to the asking, the tithe had gone up on the boards at every store of A' Chompanaidh from Baile thais to the coast, fixed, at the new rate, with the seal of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach at the foot of the notice and no mark anywhere on it of any custodian's mind.

Nowhere did Aonghas Ruadh write that this had surprised him. He wrote instead that it should not, in his judgement, be let pass unanswered a second time the way the granary order had been let pass, and An Togail after it; and that he had it in mind, if enough of the custodians of the east and the hills gathered with him at Ceann àrsaidh, to draw up one paper in one hand that could not be filed apart, settlement by settlement, the way single letters always were. He named a day in am Faoilleach, and asked Peigi to come. Cill ghlas was small, he wrote plainly enough, but its roll of who had been lost was better kept than most, and that was worth more to him than size.

Peigi read the letter twice by the lamp, and then went out and stood a while at the shrine door in the last light, looking down the burn toward the road that went, eventually, everywhere.

## II. Of the Store at Seann Dunn

She was not the first to arrive at Ceann àrsaidh when the day came, nor the last. She had walked it in two days, sleeping the one night at a cousin's house at Muileann dhearg and coming down into the walled town on the second afternoon with her feet sore and her good cloak, the one she kept for burials and for this, rolled tight against the rain in a bag on her back.

Ceann àrsaidh stood behind its old wall on a rise above the eastern road, a town of some size for that country, with a market square inside the gate where the custodians of the nineteen settlements that answered Aonghas Ruadh's letter had begun, by the second day, to make a kind of camp: fires in the lee of the wall, horses picketed along the inside of it, and everywhere the low talk of people comparing what had been done to them, as if putting it side by side might show the shape of it better than any one of them could alone.

It was there, on the second night, over a fire shared with three others, that Peigi heard properly of Seann Dunn.

The custodian who told it was a spare, quiet man named Coinneach Òg, from a fishing town on the far eastern coast that Peigi had never seen and would likely never see again, three days' ride past Ceann àrsaidh by his own account and further than that on foot. He did not tell it as a grievance. He told it the way a man tells a thing he has watched happen slowly enough to have stopped believing it could be stopped.

Haskins, in his first year, had opened a customs house at Seann Dunn, on the coast below Coinneach Òg's own town, and a store of A' Chompanaidh beside it, the first store the district had had. It came in, Coinneach Òg said, as help. The east had no smith to speak of and no source of iron nearer than a week's cart-journey, and the store sold seed against a bad year and tools against a broken one, on A' Chompanaidh's note, to be paid back in fish or wool or coin when the year turned. Most years the debts had been paid. But there had been a bad year, and then, close behind it, the hunger years and the two winters of An Togail's taking, and by now, Coinneach Òg said, turning a stick in the fire without looking up from it, the store's ledgers held the debts of near half the district, entered against named households, generation to come reckoned in against the last.

"They will tell you it is owed fairly," he said. "It is owed. I will not say it was not lent." He looked round the fire at the others. "But there is no year now in which the debt grows less. Only years in which it grows more slowly."

Nobody at the fire had an answer to that, and nobody tried to give one. Peigi thought of her own slate at the shrine door, the names scratched into it, and thought that Coinneach Òg's district must have a slate a great deal longer, and said so; and he said that it did, and that it was not his to keep, since the old shrine of Seann Dunn had gone to ruin long ago and the store stood where its keepers' house had been.

It was past midnight before the fire burned down and the talk with it, and Peigi lay that night under her cloak with the wall's stones cold at her back and did not sleep well, turning over the shapes of it: the granary, the store at Seann Dunn, An Togail that had taken hands from every field in the west and left the harvest to rot standing two winters running at Baile chrom, and now the tithe fixed before the asking about it had so much as reached half the men it was fixed on. She had thought, walking down from Cill ghlas, that she was coming to speak for eleven households and a dead mother's flame. She began, that night at the fire, to understand what Aonghas Ruadh had meant by one hand.

## III. Of the Nineteen at Ceann àrsaidh

They drew it up over three days in the hall behind the market square, a low stone building the town used for its own councils, with a fire at one end and windows too small to let in much of the grey light of that am Faoilleach, so that most of the work was done by lamp, at noon as much as at night.

There were, in the end, custodians of nineteen settlements, from Ceann àrsaidh itself out to the coast where Coinneach Òg's town lay and up into the hills as far as Àth fhionn in the south-east; and it was, so far as any of them could say, and several of the older ones tried to say it, the first time custodians of that many places had sat down together in one room to speak with one voice at all, rather than each writing alone to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and each being answered alone, or not answered, which had been the way of it since the first years of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg.

It did not go smoothly. Peigi had thought, walking down, that the grievance would come plain once enough people were in a room with it; she found instead that nineteen people who agreed entirely on what had been done to them could argue for the better part of a day over how to say so. One custodian, an old man from a hill village north of Ceann àrsaidh, wanted every death named, every year, every settlement, on the ground that a list could not be argued with the way a sentence could. Aonghas Ruadh, who had called them and who took, without anyone quite deciding it, the chair of the drafting, said that a list a hundred pages long would be filed unread where a single page might, just possibly, be read; and that they should say the true thing once, plainly, and let the naming wait for another day if it came to naming. The old man was not satisfied, and said so, twice, and in the end put his name to the shorter paper anyway, because there was nothing else on offer to put it to.

The paper that came out of the three days was not long. It set down, in a page and a half of the stag-letters copied fair by Aonghas Ruadh's own clerk, that the tithe had been fixed without the asking that had been promised; that An Togail, though set aside in the districts the harvest had failed in, had never been repealed and could be laid on again at any Àrd-mhaor's word; that the granary built of the Dia-thìrich's own coal money had in two winters been the only store between the west and starving, and had been A' Chompanaidh's the whole time; and that the custodians who signed it asked, in the humans' own phrase that Aonghas Ruadh's clerk had found for it in an old letter of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's own, for their council to be consulted before, and not after.

They read it through together on the last evening, each of the nineteen in turn, aloud, in the hall by the lamp, so that no one could say afterward he had not heard every word of what he put his name to. When it came Peigi's turn she read her part with her thumb pressed white against the edge of the sheet, and heard her own voice come out steadier than she had thought it would.

Then they signed it.

It was Ruairidh mac Thormoid, custodian of Àth fhionn, who signed last, and slowest, and it was he, of all the nineteen, that Peigi remembered longest after. A small, bent man, with a hand that shook a little at rest and did not shake at all once the pen was moving, he had walked to Ceann àrsaidh from the south-east, a good many days' road, on his own two feet, refusing every offer of a cart the whole way, as the man who had carried him the last few miles told it round the fire with some wonder. By his own count, and by the count of Àth fhionn's own roll, he was the oldest custodian at the gathering by a great many years: he remembered, or said he remembered, and none there doubted him, a world before the mark was struck at Ros dhomhain, before the strangers' coin had ever passed hand to hand on the island at all, when a fleece was still worth a fleece and nothing needed to be changed into anything else to be worth it.

He read his own line last of all, in a voice gone thin but not unsteady, and then he signed his name in the stag-letters, small and careful, at the foot of the page below all the rest, and beside it, where none of the others had thought to write anything but their names, he added a line of his own, which Aonghas Ruadh's clerk copied into the fair copy exactly as he gave it: *born before the coin*. He offered no more than that. Nobody at the table asked him to.

"They will not read the rest of it," the old man from the hill village said, low, to Peigi, as the paper was being sanded and rolled. "Perhaps they will read that."

## IV. Of the Bench in the Passage

It fell to Peigi to carry it.

She was not sure, afterward, quite how it had fallen to her rather than to Aonghas Ruadh, who had called them all together and might rightly have claimed the carrying as his own; she thought, turning it over on the road, that it was the roll at Cill ghlas that had done it, the slate of names by the shrine door that Aonghas Ruadh had heard was well kept, and that having asked her to come for that reason he had gone on, without either of them quite saying it aloud, to think her the right one to finish it. She did not refuse. She had walked further for less.

She went down to Ros dhomhain in the first days of am Màrt, alone but for a lad of Ceann àrsaidh sent along to carry the second copy and bring word back, two days on the eastern road with the petition rolled inside oilcloth against the rain, next to her skin under the good cloak where a purse would have gone had she had one worth guarding.

Ros dhomhain, when she came down into it off the last hill, was larger than any town she had stood in since her one visit to the capital as a girl: the harbour full of masts, A' Chompanaidh's sheds along the quay, and above it all, on its rise, the long grey house of stone, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, with a flag she did not know the meaning of hanging still in the wet air over its gate.

She found the door easily enough; it was finding what lay past the door that took the better part of two days.

The first day she was turned back at the gate by a man in a coat with buttons who told her, not unkindly, that the office that received such papers did not sit on the day she had come, and that she should come again in the morning. She came again in the morning and was let through the gate and left to wait in a yard, and then in a passage, and then, when the light in the passage windows had gone from grey to greyer, told that the office had closed for the day and that she should come again the morning after.

She came again.

The passage she was shown into the third time was of stone, narrow, lit by lamps set in the wall at long intervals because no window opened onto it at all, and it smelled, she noticed at once and never afterward forgot, of lamp-soot: not the clean burnt smell of a shrine flame, which she knew as well as she knew her own hands, but a heavier, closer smell, oil and smoke folded close in a space with no wind to carry it out. There was a bench along one wall, of the same grey stone as the passage, worn pale in the middle where a great many people had sat waiting before her, and she sat on it, with the lad from Ceann àrsaidh standing at her shoulder because there was room on the bench for one, and waited.

She waited the better part of that morning. People passed along the passage on errands of their own, humans mostly, in the black coats of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerks, and one or two Dia-thìrich among them, dressed in the same coats, who did not look at her as they went by, or looked and looked away, she could not afterward have said which. Doors opened and closed along the passage. Somewhere beyond one of them a bell rang at intervals, for reasons she never learned.

At last a door opened nearer to hand than the rest, and a young man put his head out and asked, in Dia-thìris good enough to be understood and poor enough that she knew at once it was not his first tongue, whether the custodian with the paper for An t-Àrd-mhaor's office would come in.

He was younger than she had expected, no more than five-and-twenty by the look of him, with ink on two fingers of his right hand and a high desk behind him stacked with paper in a way that told her, before he said a word, that hers would not be the only paper on it by the day's end. He asked her name and the name of the settlement, and wrote both down, carefully, in the humans' letters, checking the spelling of Cill ghlas with her twice. He asked whether she had come far. She said that she had, and that eighteen others besides her had put their names to what she carried, from as many settlements, meeting as one body for the first time that the roll of any of their towns recorded.

He said that this was noted, and thanked her for the trouble of the journey, in a tone she thought was meant kindly and might even have been kind.

Then he took the petition from her hands, unrolled it just far enough to see that it was indeed a petition and not some other paper mistakenly brought, rolled it again, and laid it on the pile at the corner of the high desk, a pile she saw, in the moment his hand left it, was neither the top of the stack nor the bottom of it but somewhere unremarkable in the middle, among papers she could not read the headings of and had no way of knowing were older or newer or of more or less weight than her own.

Then he bent his head again to the sheet he had been writing on when she was shown in, and went on with it.

Peigi stood where she was a moment longer than there was any reason to stand. She did not know, afterward, what she had been waiting for; not an answer, she told herself on the road home, for she had known before she came down off the last hill above Ros dhomhain that no answer would be given her that day, or that week, whatever came after. Perhaps she had been waiting only to see the young man look up again. He did not.

She thanked him, because it seemed the thing to do, and he returned some answer she did not fully catch, and she turned and went back out along the passage, past the bench worn pale in the middle, and out through the yard, and out through the gate, into the grey light of Ros dhomhain, with the lad from Ceann àrsaidh following a step behind her and neither of them saying anything at all until they were past the bridge.

They went home.

## V. Of Brìde's Lamp

The answer, when it came, did not come.

Through the rest of that year and into the next word passed among the nineteen settlements, as it always passed, slowly and by carter and by letter three days worn on the road, and none of it was an answer from Ros dhomhain. The tithe stood at the rate it had been fixed at before the asking. An Togail stayed unrepealed on its shelf, ready, the custodians said to one another, for the first bad harvest that gave Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir an excuse to take it down again. At Seann Dunn, Coinneach Òg wrote once, briefly, to say that the store's ledgers had grown by one more name that winter, his own cousin's, and that he supposed it made no difference now whether that was written into a petition or not. Aonghas Ruadh wrote to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir twice more, in his own name, asking only whether the paper of am Faoilleach had been received and read. To the first letter there was no reply at all. To the second, in the autumn, a clerk's hand, not the same clerk's, Peigi was fairly sure from the letters, wrote back that the matter remained under consideration.

Peigi kept the slate at the shrine door as she had always kept it, and in the course of that year and the next she added three more names to it, none of them, this time, of the famine or An Togail, but of the ordinary business of a country with a hill in it and men going down into the hill: a fall of stone at Baile thais that took two crews out of Cill ghlas's own households, and an old man of the village who had gone down every day of his working life and finally did not come up one evening in an t-Sultain, of nothing that any physician, human or otherwise, could put a name to but the descent, done too many years too many times.

On a still evening near the end of an Dùbhlachd, with the first hard frost of that winter white on the burn-stones outside, Peigi went up to the shrine at Cill ghlas as she went every evening of her life, to see that the flame that was called Brìde's had not gone low.

It had not; it had burned steadily through the whole of that year of petitions and answers not given, as it had burned through An Togail and A' Phlàigh Uaine and the years before either, needing from her only what it had always needed: oil enough, and a wick trimmed square, and someone to come up the hill in the cold and see to it. She knelt at the small stone trough before the flame and drew the old shears from the ledge where they always lay, and took the wick between finger and thumb, and trimmed it, careful, the way her mother had taught her, until the flame stood up clean and even and threw its light square across the little room and out through the open door into the frost beyond.

She did not know, kneeling there, whether the petition that had gone into the pile in the passage at Ros dhomhain would ever be taken up off it, read, answered, or refused; whether Aonghas Ruadh's third letter would fare better than his first two; whether Ruairidh mac Thormoid, who remembered a world before the coin, would live to see any Àrd-mhaor's answer at all, or whether his line at the foot of the fair copy, *born before the coin*, would be the last word of his that anyone at Ros dhomhain ever troubled to read. She only knew the wick was trimmed, and the flame stood clean, and that in the morning she would go down to the village and see who needed seeing to, and that this, at least, no clerk's pile could take from her hands.

She banked the fire, low, for the night, and went down the hill in the dark, and the frost held all across Cill ghlas until morning.

# Chapter Twenty-six: Of Fearchar Bàrd's Songs

*AE 101 – 105*

> *Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic*
> *gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh.*
>
> The ship is eating the hill
> to carry the hill away.

## I. Of the Book That Would Not Stay Shut

Fearchar had broken coal at Muileann dhearg since he was tall enough to reach the picking-belt, and by the winter the book came to him he had done it so long that his hands knew the weight of a lump before his eyes had found it, the good clean weight of coal against the duller drag of shale, and could throw the one into the cart and the other onto the spoil without his mind once leaving whatever verse it was turning over that day. His father had done the same work before him at the same belt, and had died of the cough the old women called by no name in those years, and Fearchar had gone on breaking coal and turning verses because there was no third thing to do.

The book came to Muileann dhearg folded inside a meal-sack, passed hand to hand from Baile thais by a carter who would not say whose it was. It had no cover and no title anyone had given it; the custodians' copyists, when a page of it at last reached the loft at Muileann chaol, called it Leabhar Baile thais for want of a better word, and the name held. Inside it, in perhaps thirty different hands, some sure and some barely able to shape their letters, were the things nobody had found anywhere else to put: a wage not paid, a death not answered for, the week the granary at Muileann chrom weighed short, the stream at Doire mhòr that had been dammed for the coal-washing without any order anyone could find.

Fearchar sat up two nights reading it by a tallow light borrowed from the pit stores, and found that he could not add a line to it. It was not want of a grievance. He had buried a father and watched a famine and knew the granary's short week as well as any man at that belt. But he found, turning the pages, that a wage not paid written down in a column looked like nothing at all, a bare fact among bare facts, and that what he wanted to do with it could not be done in a column.

"Then don't write it," said old Griogair mac Aonghais, who broke coal at the same belt and had known Fearchar's father. "Sing it. You've been singing since you could talk. Nobody's stopped you yet."

"Nobody's listened either."

"They will if you make it worth the listening." Griogair spat into the spoil-heap and went back to his sorting. "A column's for men who've given up hoping to be heard. You haven't given up yet, or you'd not be sitting up two nights over another man's book."

It was not the first time Fearchar had been told he sang too much for a man who broke coal for his bread. His mother had said the same, gentler, when he was a boy too small yet for the belt and was set instead to carry water along the row of pickers, singing whatever came into his head to keep his own feet moving; she had died before the famine, of nothing more than the years, and it was one of the few mercies Fearchar counted from those seasons, that she had not lived to see the granary's short week or the wall that came after it. His father had lasted longer and gone harder, coughing through his last two winters in a bed by the same hearth Fearchar still slept beside, and had said, near the end of it, that a man ought to leave something behind him besides coal, since the coal itself went into A' Chompanaidh's cart and was never seen again by the hand that broke it. Fearchar had not understood him rightly at the time. He understood him better with the book from Baile thais open on his knees, two nights running, and no column in it that would hold what he meant to leave.

Fearchar carried the book back to the carter in the spring, since it belonged at Baile thais. He carried something else away from it that no one could take back off him: the knowledge that the wrong done to Doire mhòr's stream and the wrong done to his own father's lungs were pages of the same book, whether anyone ever bound them together or not. He began, that spring, to put verses to the granary's short week, working them out under his breath at the belt the way another man might work out a debt.

## II. Of the Song That Was Forbidden and So Written Down

By 27 am Faoilleach, AE 101, it was known across the coal country that the grievances of thirty years had at last found a book to sit in; and a year after, on 17 am Faoilleach, AE 102, Fearchar sang his first finished song at the pit-mouth of Muileann dhearg, on an evening when the crews were waiting out a delay in the winding-gear with nothing else to do with their hands.

It was a short thing, four verses on An Togail and what it had cost the villages round Baile chrom, no name in it that could be hauled before a magistrate, only a field left to itself and a mother counting heads that did not come home. He had not meant it for more than the pit-mouth. But a song sung once at a pit-mouth is sung again at the next one, and within the month it had travelled from Muileann dhearg to Baile thais without Fearchar carrying it there himself.

The overseer at Baile thais heard it from a crew coming up off shift, singing it under their breath the way men sing something they have not decided yet whether they are allowed to know. He had them stopped and the words taken down from one of them, a boy who could not write and had to say it over three times before the overseer's clerk had it right, and the boy was docked half a week's pay for it and told the song was not to be sung again on A' Chompanaidh's ground.

It was sung again within the week, twice as far as before.

Fearchar heard of the docking before he heard of anything else, and went to Baile thais himself to find the boy and pay him back the half-week out of his own wage, which was not much, coal-breakers being paid less than hewers. The boy would not take it.

"Keep it," he said. "I'd rather have sung it than not, and I'll sing it again the first chance I get, so you may as well save your coin for the next one they dock."

It was the overseer's clerk, in the end, who did the greatest service to the song without meaning to. Ordered to write down every word of it so that it could be shown to be forbidden, he made, in the neat hand A' Chompanaidh had taught him, the only complete copy of Fearchar's first song that survives from that year, since Fearchar himself had never troubled to set it on paper and the crews who sang it kept it only in their heads. It sits now among A' Chompanaidh's own confiscation orders, filed under the offence it names, in a hand that never meant to keep it.

## III. Of the Roadside House in the East

The song went east before Fearchar did, carried by carters who worked the road between Muileann dhearg and the coast and had no more idea than A' Chompanaidh's clerk what they were carrying. By the second year it had reached An Taigh-òsta Grianach, the great road-house on the eastern road where the carriers from the north met the southern coast path, and the keeper there, a broad, slow-spoken woman who had buried two husbands and outlasted both, took to it because her custom liked a tune with their ale and asked no questions about where a tune had come from.

Fearchar went there himself only once in those years, in the third summer, riding on a grain-cart with a load of the guild's barley that had nothing to do with him beyond the ride. He came into the taproom at dusk, unknown to anyone there, and sat at the end of a bench with a cup he could barely afford, and heard six carters of A' Chompanaidh at the next table sing his own song of the granary's short week through from the first verse to the last, missing only a line in the third stanza that they filled with nonsense words since none of them could remember it rightly.

He did not tell them whose it was, only sat with his cup and listened. Hearing it sung wrong by men who did not know what they sang hurt worse than hearing it forbidden, and stirred him more too, in some way he could at the time put no name to; the carters sang it the way they might sing any road-song, for the tune's sake and the company's, with no more notion that it named a grievance than a bird has that its call is a warning to other birds. When they had done, one of them called across for another verse of something, and Fearchar, still unknown to them, obliged with a verse of a song about a horse, and left before the barley cart went on without him needing to be asked who he was.

He walked home the last twelve miles rather than wait for another cart, and worked out on the road, verse by verse, a longer song than any he had made before, though it would be two years yet before the event came that would give it its ending.

The keeper of An Taigh-òsta Grianach he came to know a little better on later passes through, since a man who rode the guild's messages east twice a year could not help becoming a familiar face at the one house on that road worth stopping at. She never asked him outright whether the songs her custom sang were his own making, though he came to suspect, from the particular way she filled his cup without being asked a second summer running, that she had worked it out for herself and judged it none of her business to say so aloud in a room full of A' Chompanaidh's carters. It was as much acknowledgment as he ever wanted from her, and more than he got from most quarters in those years.

## IV. Of the Quay That Ate the Hill

A' Chompanaidh's new quay went up at Ros dhomhain across those same years, a deep-water quay built out into the harbour where the old wooden jetty had stood, built for ships that no longer needed a tide to float them, ships with iron in their hulls and a stack instead of a mast, that burned coal to carry coal.

Fearchar saw the first of them load. He had gone down to Ros dhomhain on guild business, carrying a message for the silver refiners that had nothing to do with coal at all, and stood on the new stone of the quay among a crowd that had come to see the first of the iron fire-ships, greater than any paddle-boat the harbour had yet seen. It came alongside under its own power, with no oars and no visible sail, and a noise came out of it like a kettle the size of a house, and black smoke stood up from its stack straight into a still evening as though the sky itself had gone the colour of the coal at last.

They loaded her through the night by lamplight, gang after gang carrying baskets up a plank that bent under the weight and did not break, and Fearchar stood at the quay rail until past midnight watching the coal go into her holds and the smoke go up from her stack, and understood, in the plain way a thing is understood when it is seen rather than told, that the ship was burning the same coal it carried to make the carrying possible, so that in some measure it ate its own cargo as it went, and would eat more of the hill to carry the hill away than any cart or barge had ever managed before it.

He made the song that night, sitting on a coil of the new quay's rope with the fire-ship's kettle-noise going on behind him, and it came faster and cleaner than any song he had made before, as though it had been waiting in him since the taproom at An Taigh-òsta Grianach for the right ship to arrive and finish it.

> *Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic*
> *gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh.*

He sang it first to the gang he had loaded beside that night, men too tired by then to do more than nod, and it was that song, more than any other he made, that the carters carried furthest, since it named nothing that could be forbidden and everything that everyone who had ever loaded a cart already knew in their arms.

## V. Of the Wall at Baile thais

Fearchar came home from Ros dhomhain to find that Baile thais had grown a wall while he had been away at the quay: a stone wall round the pithead where there had never before been so much as a fence, with a single gate in it and a watchman set at the gate with a book to write in, so that every crew going down and every crew coming up was counted through a single door.

No one at Baile thais could say when the order for it had come, only that the stone had gone up through the summer, drawn by cart from a quarry A' Chompanaidh had opened for the purpose, and that the watchman's post was the first thing built on Dia-thìr, so far as the oldest hewers there could remember, meant to keep a working's own crews from its own working rather than to keep anything else out.

The watchman himself was no stranger; he had been a hewer at Baile thais until a fall two years before had left one leg shorter than the other and unfit for the face, and A' Chompanaidh had given him the gate as a kindness of sorts, since it paid better than the poor-rolls and asked less of his legs than a shift underground. He greeted every crew through the gate by name, tallied them in his book without malice, and was, Fearchar thought, watching him work the evening he came home, as much a man walled in by that wall as any of the men he counted through it, since he could no more leave the gate for the belt than they could pass the gate without him marking it.

Fearchar walked the length of the new wall the evening he came home, from the gate to the place where it met the old spoil-heap and stopped, since the spoil itself served as well as stone for the last stretch of it. He did not make a song of the wall that year. He found, standing at the gate and watching the watchman tally a shift through it by lamplight, that some things came to him whole and some needed to sit a long while before they would give up a verse worth keeping, and the wall was of the second kind; it sat in him through that winter and the next, unfinished, while other things came first.

## VI. Of Catrìona's Burying

Word came to Baile thais at the dark of the hundred and fourth year that Catrìona nic Eachainn had died at Muileann chiar, an old woman by then, a refiner of Comann an Airgid to the last day she could stand at a bench. There were men and women still at Baile thais who remembered her from the eleven days she had held the pit-mouth against its own agent, though most of the crew she had led then were dead of one thing or another themselves, and the ones who remembered were the old ones now, as she had been.

A dozen of them asked leave to walk east to her burying, and were given it, and A' Chompanaidh docked every one of them a day's pay for the day they were gone, entered against their names as plainly as a wage or a debt. Fearchar was not among the dozen who had known her, being too young to have stood below the pithead in her time, but he walked with them anyway, since a burying at Muileann chiar was twenty miles east and no company was wasted on a road that long.

They buried her under the guild's own stone, among the refiners who had gone before her, and one of the dozen, a woman old enough to have carried water to the strikers in her own girlhood, stood at the grave's edge and said only that Catrìona had told the crews what she had told the agent and then sat down on a coal-tub and not moved, and that this was worth remembering longer than most things men wrote down about her, since it had cost her every pit on Dia-thìr and she had never once, in all the years after, said she wished she had done otherwise.

Fearchar made her lament on the walk home, twenty miles being long enough for a lament to find its shape if a man has the grief and the road both. It named the coal-tub and the empty shelves she had counted, and the guild's bench she had stood at afterward until her hands gave out, and it ended, as her own life had, without complaint, which he judged afterward to be the hardest thing he had yet made a song do, since a lament that does not complain has to find its weight somewhere else, and he had put the weight, in the end, on the single line that she had never once said she wished she had done otherwise. The dozen who had known her wept at it on the road, which he took, rightly, for the only judgment on a lament that was ever worth having.

## VII. Of the Fire on the Quay, and the Empty Seat

The fire-ships' quay at Ros dhomhain burned three days in the spring after, taking two streets of the harbour quarter down with the coal sheds, and by the time Fearchar heard of it at Baile thais the news had already grown three different causes in the telling: a dropped lamp, a spark from a stack left burning at anchor, a fire set on purpose by hands the tellers left unnamed, though plainly they had someone in mind. A' Chompanaidh's own inquiry, when its findings reached the coal towns weeks later, found no cause at all, which satisfied no one who had watched two streets burn and asked why.

It was at An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on his way east with the guild's business again that same year, that Fearchar heard the fire-ship's carters singing his own song of the ship that ate the hill, louder and rougher than the granary song had ever been sung, and understood only slowly, listening from the same end of the same bench he had sat on three years before, that they were singing it now because their own quay had burned and the words fit a grief they had not made the song to carry. They did not know his name. They did not know the song was his. He sat with his cup, as he had the first time, and did not tell them, and found that a song forbidden on A' Chompanaidh's ground could travel further inside A' Chompanaidh's own mouths than it had ever travelled by any road he had walked himself. It was simply the way a true thing moved once it was let loose, going where it liked and being sung by whoever needed it, without asking leave of the man who had made it.

He was still on that same road home when the second news reached him, carried faster than either fire or song by a rider changing horses at every post-house between the capital and the coast: that Artair mac Iain, Ceann a' Chùraim these twenty and four years, was dead at Cathair dhearg, eighty years old, and that Comhairle a' Chùraim, called to choose the next as it had chosen every one before him since the crown fell vacant at the close of the age before this one, had sat three days and risen without a name.

It sat so still through the rest of that year. No custodian would put forward another's name for fear of putting forward his own, and no custodian would put forward his own for fear of what a name given now, with the coal roads walled and the quays burning and the grievance book still passing hand to hand from Baile thais to wherever a copy could be made, might be asked to answer for later. The seat at the head of the council table stood empty through the Faoilleach that followed, and the one after, with the chair of the old Ceann a' Chùraim left where it had always stood, since no one thought to move it and no one yet had the right to sit in it. It was said, though no one at Baile thais could say who had first said it, that Robert Haskins at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir had written home across the sea that an empty seat suited him better than a full one, since a council with no head to answer for it was a council that answered to no one at all.

Fearchar made no song of the empty seat that year, nor for some years after. He had a lament in him for Catrìona and a song in him for the quay and the wall at Baile thais still sitting unfinished from the winter before, and some things, he had learned by then, needed to sit a long while before they would give up a verse worth keeping. The empty seat was of that kind.

He went back to the belt at Muileann dhearg, and broke coal, and let it sit. In the evenings, when the winding-gear was quiet and the crews sat out the last light before the huts, he sang what he had, the granary song and the ship song and Catrìona's lament, and let the empty seat go unsung, since a chair with no one in it made a poor subject for a verse next to a man who had sat down on a coal-tub and not moved, or a ship that ate its own cargo as it carried it away. Some griefs, he thought, needed a shape to them before a song could hold them, a coal-tub or a quay or a woman's name on a stone, and a council that had simply stopped, quietly, without anyone striking a blow or signing a paper, had as yet no shape he knew how to give it. He judged, breaking coal at the belt his father had worked before him, that the shape would come in its own time, as the ship song had waited three years at An Taigh-òsta Grianach for the right ship to arrive and finish it, and that until it came the plainest thing left to do was what his father had told him from the hearth-bed at the end: to leave something behind him besides coal, one song at a time, and let the empty seat sit empty a while longer, since it seemed, by every account that reached Baile thais that year, in no hurry to be filled.

# Chapter Twenty-seven: Of Tiormachd Achadh shean

*AE 106 – 110*

## I. Of the First Dry Summer

Iseabail nic Leòid had kept the roll of Àth mhòr eleven years before the first summer the wells would not fill, and she remembered afterward that she had not known, standing at the mouth of her own well with the bucket coming up a third full of grey water and grit, that she was standing at the beginning of anything at all. A dry summer was not a strange thing on Dia-thìr. She had seen three in her time as custodian, and each had broken in its own season with rain enough to fill the cisterns before the cattle suffered for it. She let down the bucket a second time, watched the rope go slack sooner than it should, and told herself the same thing the town had told itself since Bealltainn: that the rain was late this year, not gone.

It did not come. By an t-Iuchar the burn below Àth mhòr ran in a channel a man could step across without wetting his boot, and by Lùnastal it did not run at all, only stood in pools the colour of weak tea between stones gone white with dust. Iseabail sent word east to Achadh shean, whose custodian she had known since they were girls together at the loft, and the word that came back was worse than her own: the wells there had failed a full month before Àth mhòr's, and the burn that fed the town's mill had not turned the wheel since Meadhan an t-Samhraidh.

The roll that year, when it was written up at the year's turning, named ten districts as drought country: worst at Achadh shean, at Àth uaine, at Achadh àrsaidh and at Muileann chiar, the drought reaching down as far as Cuan ruadh on the coast and west as far as Baile chaol before it thinned into ordinary dry ground. Iseabail's own Àth mhòr sat near the middle of it, close enough to Achadh shean that the two towns' custodians began that first autumn to send a rider between them twice a week, more for the company of shared bad news than for anything either could do to help the other.

Riaghaltas nan Coigreach kept no count of its own. Iseabail heard this first from a carter who had asked at the pay office at Ceann mhin whether A' Chompanaidh meant to do anything for the districts that could not feed their beasts, and had been told, in the words he repeated to her at her own door with the particular flatness of a man passing on an insult he has decided not to be angry about until later, that the yield was not affected and the office kept no register of rainfall.
