She wrote the carter's words into her own roll exactly as he had given them to her, because she had already begun, without quite deciding to, the habit of writing down every answer she was given, in the words it was given in.

## II. Of the Cattle Column

The second dry season broke nothing that the first had not already cracked. By the summer of the hundred and seventh year the wells at Achadh shean had been dry two years running, and the district's grazing, which had never been rich, was burned to standing straw by the middle of an t-Iuchar. Àth mhòr's own grass held a little longer, being nearer the coast and catching what fog came off the sea at night, but Iseabail could see from her own byre door that it would not hold past Lùnastal, and she called the district's herders together on a morning in the last week of an t-Iuchar and told them what she had already decided before she called them: that the beasts would be driven west, to whatever water could be found, before the grass gave out entirely and the driving became a burying.

They set out three days later, a column that the roll she wrote that autumn said was a day long, though Iseabail, walking at its head with a stick and a dog and her own two milk-cows among the hundreds of another's driving, thought afterward that a day long was too plain a way to say it, and that no word she had would say it better. Cattle low differently when they are thirsty than when they are merely being driven; she had not known that before that summer, and she knew it after in a way she never afterward lost, so that thirty years later the sound of oxen complaining at a gate could turn her stomach cold before she had thought why.

They walked four days to the first standing water worth the name, a tarn on the moor above Doire fhionn that had never in living memory gone dry, and the beasts smelled it a mile off and quickened without being driven, and Iseabail let them go, because there was no holding four hundred thirsty cattle back from water once they had scented it, and no reason on earth to try. Fewer than half of what had set out reached the tarn on its own legs. The rest had gone down on the road, in the dust, in the ochre grass at the road's edge, too weak to rise again, and had been left where they fell, because a beast that cannot walk cannot be carried, not four hundred of them, not by drovers who were themselves three days on short water. No roll required it of her, yet Iseabail counted the dead as they passed them, unable to walk by a fallen beast without marking it, the way she had begun to mark every answer Riaghaltas nan Coigreach gave her. She had ninety-one marks in her book by the time the column reached the tarn, and she added seven more before the drovers turned the survivors for home. She never, in all the years after, told anyone which number stayed with her longest; it was the count of calves among the ninety-one of the road, which was eleven, and which she had somehow known, walking, she would carry the rest of her life.

Doire fhionn, whose tarn had saved what was left of Achadh shean's herd, was by then sending its own women half a day's walk to a spring beyond its bounds for water fit to drink, the tarn having been fouled within a week by every district's cattle using it at once. Iseabail spoke to one of them at the tarn's edge, a woman carrying two full skins on a yoke who had walked out from the town before first light and would walk back after dark, and asked her how long the town meant to go on so. "Until it rains," the woman said, and shrugged the yoke straighter on her shoulders, and walked on, and Iseabail understood that this was the whole of the answer anyone in the drought country had, for any question that began with how long.

## III. Of Baile chaol's Choice

Baile chaol, at the far western edge of the drought country, had no moor within four days' driving that still held water enough for a herd the size of its own, and its custodian, a broad quiet woman named Ealasaid Ruadh whom Iseabail had known only by letter until that autumn, sent word round every district asking whether any had grazing to spare rather than water to reach. None did. Iseabail rode to Baile chaol herself in the last days of an Dàmhair, on the strength of nothing more than the wish not to leave the letter unanswered by a stranger's hand, and found the town's council already met and its mind already made, the kind of decision a town comes to only once it has stopped hoping there is a better one waiting a day further off.

They killed the herd over three days at the edge of the dry burn, the meat salted and smoked in every shed the town had standing, the hides scraped and stacked, and nothing wasted that a hungry district could use, and Ealasaid Ruadh stood at the killing the whole three days without once turning her back on it, which Iseabail thought, watching her, took more out of a person than the driving had taken out of her own drovers on the road to Doire fhionn. "A beast I can raise again in three good years," Ealasaid said to her that first evening, over meat neither of them had much appetite for. "A well that's gone dry three years running I can't promise anyone will fill again in ten." She did not say it as a complaint. She said it the way a woman says a sum she has already done the arithmetic of and does not need to do again, and Iseabail wrote the words into her roll that night exactly as she had heard them, the way she had begun writing down every hard thing anyone in the drought country said to her, because she had come by then to believe that the words themselves, kept whole, were worth more than anything she might have added to them.

Baile chaol ate through that winter on its own slaughtered herd and lost fewer of its people to hunger than any other district of the ten, a fact the roll records plainly and without praise, because Ealasaid Ruadh, when Iseabail rode back through in the spring to tell her so, said only that she would rather not have needed to know how to make the choice, and changed the subject to the state of the road.

## IV. Of the Spring That Did Not Fail

There was one water in the drought country that held through all three dry years, and every district that could reach it sent to it before the second summer was out: Allt an Àigh, the holy spring in the east, of which the old telling said it had never failed since An Aois Naomh, and did not fail now. Iseabail went there herself in the summer of the hundred and eighth year, a custodian with dying beasts and a district running on borrowed water, and found the ground around the spring already trodden into mud a hundred yards out by feet that had come the same way she had.

The pilgrims of Na Seann Spioradan had begun arriving at Bealltainn that year in numbers nobody at the spring had seen before, walking in from every drought district and some that were not drought country at all, carrying water home in whatever they had brought to carry it in, and the spring's own keepers, an old brother and sister who had tended it without payment for as long as anyone could say, found themselves that season feeding pilgrims from their own stores as well as watering them; and word of the crowding went along the road to Inis uaine, the nearest town of any size, which opened its own granary to the walkers rather than see them go hungry on the road home, a kindness the roll notes without explaining, because none was needed.

It was in that same summer that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach set a watchman at the spring, a young man from Ceann mhin with a ledger and a rate written out for him by some clerk who had never seen the place: so much a skin, so much a beast, payable before the water was drawn. Iseabail was there the second week he stood his post, and watched an old woman of Achadh àrsaidh, who had walked three days with an empty cask on a barrow to fill it at the one water she trusted, set the cask down at the spring's edge and refuse, in words Iseabail did not think the young man understood in either sense, to pay a stranger for water that had run free since before his people came down from the north. The watchman did not press her. He stood his post through that season and was called back before the next one began, and the roll of Allt an Àigh, which Iseabail copied that autumn from the keepers' own tally, records no reason given for his recall, only the plain fact of it, and under the fact, in the old brother's hand, the single word restored.

## V. Of the Drought-Fever

The third dry season brought a fever that the two before it had not, and it came first, as fevers of bad water do, to the towns whose wells had been dug deepest into old ground. At Baile Mòr ruadh, whose wells had gone down years before into what had once been the town's own middens, seventeen died of it before the summer's end, more than the town had lost to any sickness in Iseabail's memory of it, and the fever went on from there to Cnoc shean, where it took fewer but took them just as surely, mostly the very young and the very old, whose bodies had least water in them to spare for fighting it.

Iseabail rode to Baile Mòr ruadh in the worst of it, at the asking of its custodian, a younger woman new enough to the office that she had never yet buried anyone by the fever's own particular manner: quick at first, a griping of the belly and a thirst no water eased, then a stillness that the women who sat with the dying learned to dread more than the griping, because it meant the body had stopped fighting what it drank. Iseabail sat two nights in a row with a household that lost a grandmother and a boy of nine within a day of each other, and held the boy's hand at the last of it because his mother could not, being with the grandmother in the next room, and she wrote nothing in her roll that night at all, being for once too tired and too sick at heart to trust her own hand with it, and made up the entry the following evening instead, dry and plain, as if a day's distance could put back into the words the steadiness they had lost at the boy's bedside.

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's physician at Baile Mòr ruadh, a spare young man named Coll who had been sent out only that spring and had not yet learned to hold his tongue in front of a custodian, said to Iseabail on the second night, turning a dipper of well-water in his hands as though it might answer him, that he had tested the water himself and found it foul enough to sicken a strong man on a single cup, foul with whatever had lain in the ground the well was sunk through before ever the well was dug. "The old midden," Iseabail said. "It has been the town's midden longer than either of us. Everyone knew it." "Then everyone knew, and dug there anyway," Coll said, "because the drought gave them no ground to choose from that was not one old thing or another." He did not say it unkindly. He said it the way a man says a thing he has only just understood and finds he cannot now unknow, and it was his report, sent to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's house at Cathair dhearg that autumn, that named the fever's cause rightly before any other account written that year did: the deep wells the drought had driven the towns to dig, down into ground that had never been meant to give up water and gave up, along with what little it had, whatever had been buried near it in years the towns themselves had half forgotten. The drought itself had only starved.

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise bored new wells at Achadh shean and at Àth chrom that same season, deeper again but dug clean, away from any old ground, and those wells held, and the fever did not follow them. Iseabail entered both facts into her roll on facing pages, as the custodians of the whole drought country had begun by then to do without any of them having agreed to it aloud: Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's wells on one page, A' Chompanaidh's quota on the other, the quota unchanged through three dry years and a fever that had killed more of Baile Mòr ruadh in one summer than the pits themselves had that year, and beside neither page did Iseabail write a word, because there was no word she could find that the facing pages did not say better by themselves.

## VI. Of Achadh chaol Going Down

Achadh chaol, whose own grazing had failed with everyone else's by the second year, sent its young men to the pits that summer in numbers its custodian had never before had to record. Iseabail heard the first of it from her own nephew, her sister's boy, who came to her door one evening in the autumn of the hundred and eighth year to tell her, before he told his own mother, that he had signed with A' Chompanaidh's agent at Ceann mhin for a hewer's contract at Cnoc fhiadhaich, and would go down after Samhain.

"Your father kept sheep," she said, not as a reproach, because she found she had none ready to give him, only the plain fact laid beside his own plain fact the way she had lately taken to laying plain facts beside one another and letting them speak for themselves. "So did his father."

"His sheep are dead, Aunt. Mine would be too, inside the year, if I kept any worth the name." He was not angry saying it, only tired in a way she thought no boy of nineteen ought yet to be. "A hewer's wage comes whether it rains or not. That's the whole of my reasoning, and I don't think it's a bad one."

She could not tell him it was. She wrote his going into her roll along with the others who followed him from Achadh chaol that winter and the winter after, families who had kept beasts and small fields for generations going down into the galleries because a hewer's wage, paid whether the year was wet or dry, had become the only certain thing left to a household in the drought country, and she noted the count without comment beside it, because by then she had stopped believing that comment changed anything a plain fact did not already say.

## VII. Of the Petition, Begun Alone

Every custodian of the drought country petitioned Haskins that third year, each in her own hand and her own time, none of them, so far as Iseabail ever learned, having agreed beforehand to do it together, though when she came to compare the copies afterward, in the loft at Muileann chaol where such things were kept, she found that nine of the ten districts had written some version of the same three sentences, as though the drought itself had dictated the wording and left each custodian only the work of the hand. She wrote her own in the autumn of the hundred and ninth year, a single page asking that A' Chompanaidh's quota for the drought districts be set aside until two seasons of ordinary rain had been counted, and rode it herself to Ros dhomhain, three days on a horse thinner than she liked to ride, through country that still remembered how to be green and had lost, in three years, the smell of it after rain.

Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir kept her waiting the better part of a day in a passage she did not think had been swept since the petition before hers had waited in it, and when at last a clerk took her page from her hand he did not read it while she stood there, only set it on a pile with others she recognised by their folds as having come from Achadh shean and from Muileann chiar, and told her, in words so evenly worn by repetition that she wondered how many times that week alone he had said them, that the matter was under consideration. She asked him what matter, precisely, and by whom, and he looked at her the way a man looks at a question he has never once been asked to answer and does not intend to begin answering that afternoon, and said only that he would see her petition placed with the others.

She rode home and wrote the words into her roll, under consideration, and looked at them a long while by lamplight, and understood, as she had half understood since the cattle column and fully understood now, that the words meant nothing at all, and would go on meaning nothing at all for as long as anyone above Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's stair found it convenient that they should.

It was in that understanding, and not in any single grief sharper than the others, that Iseabail began, on a wet evening in the winter of the hundred and ninth year that felt, after three dry years, almost too strange to trust, to write down everything the drought had cost, district by district, in a hand small enough to fit a great deal onto a single sheet: the wells failed and when; the cattle driven and how many did not arrive; the fever's dead by name where she had the names and by number where she did not; Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's wells that held against A' Chompanaidh's quota that had not moved; the watchman recalled from Allt an Àigh and the word restored under his going; the carter's flat answer about a register that was not kept. She wrote a page and found she was not finished, and wrote another, and did not stop at ten, because by then she had stopped writing for Haskins at all and had begun writing, though she could not have said so plainly even to herself that winter, for whoever might someday want to know what three dry years had actually cost a district that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own ledgers had never troubled to measure.

Her own household thought she had taken up the writing as a kind of grief, and let her be at it evenings when there was little else to do by lamplight in a dry year, and she did not correct them, because she had not yet found words that would explain to anyone, even to herself with any confidence, what exactly she believed the forty pages were for. Nor was she a woman of letters in the way the copyists at Muileann chaol were; she had learned to write well enough to keep a custodian's roll and no more, and the work of setting down three years in full, rather than in the short entries a roll allowed, went slowly, a page some evenings, half a page on others, crossed through and begun again when a fact came back to her sharper than she had first set it down. The cattle column she wrote twice, the second time longer than the first, because on rereading the first she had found she had left out the calves, and could not let the second draft go forward without them.

Forty pages deep in it, and still writing, she stood at her own well one spring morning in the hundred and tenth year when a rider came from Achadh shean with word that Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's new rig, boring a third well on the moor above the town, had struck water at last, clean and cold and running, deeper than any well the town had dug before the drought and deeper, the rider said, than anyone had believed water could lie under that particular stretch of moor. Iseabail rode out to see it for herself, and stood at the rig's edge with half the town around her, children who had never in their remembered lives seen water come up out of the ground on its own account crowding close enough that the drillers had to wave them back from the pipe, and watched the water come up bright over the driller's hands, and thought, watching it, of the tarn on the moor above Doire fhionn and the ninety-eight marks in her drover's book, and of the old woman who would not pay a stranger for water that had run free since before his people came, and of her sister's boy three years gone now into the galleries at Cnoc fhiadhaich, whose contract would not be undone by a well striking water far from where he stood.

She wrote that night, at the bottom of her fortieth page, in a hand no steadier than it had been on the first: this also happened, so that whoever reads this after me will know the drought did end, in its own place, in its own season, and not because anyone above Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's stair troubled to make it so.

# Part Five: Of the Word and the Line

# Chapter Twenty-eight: Of Lagh na h-Aon Loidhne


*AE 111 – 113*

## I. Of the Forty Pages and the Four Words

Iseabail nic Leòid's forty pages reached Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir at Ros dhomhain in the spring of the hundred and tenth year, and lay on a clerk's table through the summer, and were answered at last, in the winter that opened the hundred and eleventh, in four words written across the foot of the last page in Robert Haskins's own hand: *the quota stands unrevised*. The copyists who later held both leaves together in the chest at Muileann chaol remarked on nothing so much as the room the two witnesses took up side by side, the one nearly as thick as a ledger of A' Chompanaidh, the other four words and a signature, and left it at that, because there was nothing in the pairing that wanted explaining twice.

It was in that same winter, at Baile dhìreach on the western coast, that Thomas Hale first put his name to paper against Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, in a matter that had nothing to do with drought or grain and everything to do with a strip of hill ground no wider than a cart-track, and it is by his roll, and by the Ros dhomhain court's own record, kept afterward among Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books, that the copyists have told what came of it.

Baile dhìreach was a small town even by the coast's own measure, one straight street running down to a quay, and it had been, since before Thomas could remember, a town of two peoples under one roof more often than any other on that shore. His grandmother, Eilidh nic Ruairidh, a net-maker's daughter of the place, had married Samuel Hale, a human cooper off one of the early ships, in the seventh year after the strangers came, in the first of the marriages the custodians of that coast ever entered in two tongues in the one roll; and though Samuel Hale had died an old man's death long before Thomas was born, and Eilidh not many years after him, the house they had kept together still stood at the head of the street by the well, and Thomas's father, Iain Hale, had grown up in it a boatwright, mending the town's craft and building new ones, Dia-thìrich and human custom both come easily to his hands if not always to his tongue.

Iain Hale had died when Thomas was eighteen, of a fever that took three others of the town the same season, and had left his son the boatyard, the house, and a habit, which Thomas had never fully understood until he was a man grown himself, of speaking of his mother's people's ground as though it were a thing held in trust and not yet properly claimed. Eilidh nic Ruairidh's own mother's family had worked, since before any of them could say how long, a narrow cutting in the hill above the town, a seam no wider than a good man's shoulders that gave up perhaps two cartloads of coal in a good year, more often used for the town's own hearths than sold, and held by no writing at all, only by the custom that a family which has cut a seam for its grandmothers' grandmothers and asked no other family's leave to do it owns the seam as surely as it owns its own byre. Iain Hale had cut there himself, as a boy, at his mother's side, and had gone on cutting there as a man, quietly, on the days the boatyard gave him free, and had never once, so far as Thomas ever learned, thought to ask anyone's permission for it, because the question had never in his lifetime come up.

Thomas remembered his father at that cutting better than he remembered him almost anywhere else: a broad, unhurried man kneeling at the low mouth of the seam with a hand-pick worn smooth at the haft, humming some boatyard tune under his breath that had no words Thomas ever learned, and stopping, every so often, to hold a broken lump up to the light the way a man might hold up a fish to judge whether it was worth the taking. Iain Hale had never once, in Thomas's hearing, called the coal his own outright; he called it his mother's, or the town's, or simply the hill's, as though ownership of it were a question he saw no profit in asking, being a question the hill had never troubled to raise in all the years it had let the family cut there. It was only after his father's death, going through the small chest of papers the boatyard's accounts were kept in, that Thomas found the copy of his grandmother's marriage entry his father had had made in his own hand, years before, from the custodian's roll, folded small and kept at the very bottom beneath the boat contracts, as though it were a thing Iain Hale had meant, one day, to make some use of, and had died before the day came.

It came up in the hundred and eleventh year because A' Chompanaidh's surveyors, working the southern seams along a line of workable coal that ran, as such lines will, without regard for any family's custom, marked the same hill for a new gallery, and sent an agent down to Baile dhìreach with a paper naming every holding on the slope that A' Chompanaidh judged owed to it, the narrow cutting among them.

## II. Of the Paper on the Table

The agent, a young man named Pryce who had been three years in A' Chompanaidh's survey office and had learned, in that time, to read a Dia-thìrich roll well enough to find the names he wanted in it, sat at Thomas Hale's own table on a wet morning in the second month of the year and laid the paper flat between them with the particular patience of a man who has done this in a dozen other houses and expects no trouble in this one.

"Your family has worked this ground," Pryce said, "under no charter A' Chompanaidh recognises. I am not saying you have done wrong. I am saying A' Chompanaidh's claim runs beneath the district's whole, and yours does not run beneath anything at all, in A' Chompanaidh's law, unless you can show it does."

"It has been my mother's people's ground since before A' Chompanaidh had a name," Thomas said. "That is the whole of my showing."

"It may be true and still be no showing, in the court A' Chompanaidh will bring this to if you refuse the offer." Pryce named a sum, small enough that Thomas understood, hearing it, that A' Chompanaidh had already reckoned the seam worth little on its own and wanted it chiefly to close a gap in its own map. "I would take it, if I were in your place. A court costs more than it returns, oftener than not, to a man arguing custom against a charter."

Thomas did not take it that morning, nor the following week, when Pryce came again with the same paper and a slightly larger sum written beneath the old one. He had, by his own account, no clear plan in his head beyond a stubbornness he could not at the time have named any more precisely than his father's habit of speaking of the seam as a thing held in trust; it was his wife, sitting at the table's far end through both of Pryce's visits and saying nothing until he had gone, who put the plan into words for him.

"Your grandmother's marriage is in the roll," she said. "Two tongues, one page, the custodian's own hand. If A' Chompanaidh's law knows anything of lines and charters, it will have to know what a marriage entered in the register of its own Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir is, or say plainly that it does not, and I do not think it wants to say that plainly, not with every other marriage of the coast standing behind yours asking the same question."

It was, Thomas said afterward, more courage than he had felt himself in the matter, and he went that week to the custodian of Baile dhìreach, an old woman named Mairead nic Aoidh who had held the office since before he was born, and had her make him a copy of the roll's page from the second year, the marriage of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale in the two tongues, sealed with the custodian's own mark as it had stood unaltered for a hundred and four years. With that copy in his coat, and no other paper to his name, he walked the two days to Ros dhomhain in the third month of the year to file his claim at A' Chompanaidh's court.

## III. Of the Walk to Ros dhomhain

The road to Ros dhomhain ran along the coast for the first day and inland for the second, through country Thomas had known since boyhood, boatyards and net-sheds giving way by degrees to the carting roads and the smoke of the hills, and he said afterward that he had spent most of the walk turning over, without ever quite settling, the question of what exactly he thought a court at Ros dhomhain owed a claim it had never in a hundred years been asked to answer. He had no lawyer, no letters of A' Chompanaidh's tongue beyond what his grandfather's house had given him, and no friend at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir to tell him what manner of hearing his paper would get once he had filed it.

Ros dhomhain he had seen only twice before that spring, both times as a boy come with his father to buy timber the boatyard could not get nearer home, and he found it, walking it now alone and on his own business, a harder town to read than he remembered: the quay stacked three deep with coal for the steamers that had begun, that year, to call there more often than the old sail ever had; Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's long grey front with its rows of shuttered windows giving nothing away of what went on behind them; and everywhere along the streets nearest the court, clerks and agents and A' Chompanaidh's men moving at a pace no coast town Thomas knew ever kept, as though every one of them had somewhere more pressing to be than the place they were walking to. He lodged the one night before his business was done at a boarding-house kept by a Dia-thìreach widow off the harbour road, one of a dozen such houses along that street that kept custodians and petitioners and claimants of every district, and she told him over a thin supper, without his asking, that she had housed men come to argue every kind of claim A' Chompanaidh's court would hear, and that in eleven years keeping the house she could not, that evening, call to mind a single one of them who had come away from Ros dhomhain with more than he had walked in with.

What the counter got him, the next morning, was a clerk's fee, four marks, paid in A' Chompanaidh's own coin over a table no wider than a door, and a date given him a full season off, the tenth month of that same year, for a hearing before the magistrate. He asked the clerk, before he left the counter, whether it was usual for a claim of this kind to take so long in the coming, and the clerk, a tired man who had clearly answered the question before, told him it was usual for every claim to take exactly as long as the court's own list allowed, and that a claim from a district with no agent of A' Chompanaidh resident in it went, as a rule, to the back of that list.

Thomas walked the two days home again with the fee's receipt in his coat where the marriage roll had been, and told his wife, and the custodian, and Pryce, when the agent came a third time with the paper and a sum unchanged from the second offer, that the matter would be heard in the tenth month, and that he did not mean to sell before it was.

The season between filing and hearing was, by every account Thomas ever gave of it afterward, the longest he had lived through since his father's death. The boatyard's work went on as it always had, and his wife kept the house, and their daughter Eilidh, thirteen that summer, understood the waiting better than her father wished her to; but Thomas himself found the hill above the town harder to walk past than he had ever found it before, the narrow mouth of the cutting sitting in the hillside exactly as it had sat in his father's day and his grandmother's, asking, he said, no question of anyone, and yet somehow, that year, seeming to ask everything of him.

## IV. Of Dunstan's Ruling

Oliver Dunstan, magistrate at Ros dhomhain, had sat on A' Chompanaidh's bench at that town for six years by the time Thomas Hale's claim came before him, and was known along the coast, so far as a Dia-thìreach could be said to know a human magistrate at all, chiefly for a manner that gave nothing away until the ruling was read, courteous to every party in a room and unmoved, so the custodians who had watched him rule on other matters said, by anything either party thought to say to him.

Thomas stood before him in the second week of the tenth month, in a room that held perhaps thirty people, most of them A' Chompanaidh's clerks with business of their own on the list that day, and had, when his own turn came, only the marriage roll's copy and his own plain telling of a seam worked without dispute by four generations of one family. Pryce spoke for A' Chompanaidh, briefly and without heat, laying out the survey's line and the charter it ran from, and did not, Thomas noted afterward, so much as mention the marriage roll at all, as though it were a paper that had not been filed.

Dunstan asked few questions. He asked Thomas once whether his grandmother's family had ever held any writing, charter or grant, naming them owners of the cutting, and Thomas said no, only the custom of the ground and the roll of the marriage, and Dunstan wrote something in the book before him and asked nothing further of it that day.

The ruling came a fortnight later, posted at A' Chompanaidh's counter along with a dozen others of that same list, and read, in the plain terms the copyists later set beside the master record of the case: that customary rights of the kind claimed descended, in Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's law, only through a line Riaghaltas nan Coigreach recognised as continuous in its own registers of holding, and that no marriage entered in a custodian's roll, however old, however honoured in the custom of a district, created such a line where none had existed before it; that Thomas Hale's claim, resting as it did on custom and on a marriage rather than on any grant of A' Chompanaidh, therefore failed; and that the cutting, together with the whole of the hill the survey had marked, stood confirmed to A' Chompanaidh under its existing charter.

Thomas read the ruling standing at the counter, with Pryce, by chance, two places down the same board reading a different notice, and said afterward that what struck him hardest that morning was not the ruling's substance, which he had half expected from the length of the wait alone, but its plainness: that a line the custodians of his own coast had kept in two tongues for a hundred and four years could be set aside in four sentences by a man who had never once, in the whole hearing, asked to see it read aloud.

## V. Of the Eleven Cuttings

The ruling named only Thomas Hale's cutting, and might, had it stood alone, have passed from the district's memory within a generation as one family's hard luck and no more. It did not stand alone. Within three years of Dunstan's ruling A' Chompanaidh's agents had brought eleven further claims of the same kind before the Ros dhomhain bench, each resting A' Chompanaidh's title on some marriage, generations back or recent, between a holder in a customary line and a human, and each decided, without exception, on the same ground Dunstan had first set out: that no such marriage created a line Riaghaltas nan Coigreach recognised, whatever the custom of the district or the age of the roll that recorded it.

The oldest of the eleven was the working at Cnoc dhubh, held by one household since An Aois Naomh, lost because a great-grandmother of that line had married a human sailor two generations back and the marriage, like Eilidh nic Ruairidh's, stood written in a custodian's roll and nowhere else. The custodian of Cnoc dhubh, an old woman who had known the family three generations deep, wrote in her own roll, when the ruling reached her, only that A' Chompanaidh had found a use, at last, for every marriage her district had ever entered in good faith, and set down no further word beside it.

A second of the eleven, decided in the hundred and thirteenth year, took the working at Seann Bhral on much the same ground: a cooper's daughter married, three generations back, to a human pilot off one of An t-Aiseag's own ships, the marriage entered in the same good faith as Eilidh nic Ruairidh's, and the cutting it had once secured passed, on Dunstan's own reasoning applied a second time by a magistrate junior to him, to A' Chompanaidh without further hearing at all, the ruling in that case running to no more than a page and citing the Hale case by name as settled law. Thomas read that ruling when a carter brought word of it to Baile dhìreach, and said to his wife, folding the notice away, that he had not thought, filing his own paper two years before, that he was writing the very sentence a second magistrate had now used against a family he had never met and a hill he had never seen.

It was Mairead nic Aoidh, custodian of Baile dhìreach, who first stopped entering such marriages in her own roll, in the spring of the hundred and twelfth year, on her own plain reckoning: a marriage written into the roll had become, under Riaghailt Dunstan, a paper a family's enemies could use against it, and had stopped, in her judgement, being a paper that protected anything at all. She told Thomas so herself, standing at her own door, and he said afterward that he had never in his life heard a woman say so hard a thing in so level a voice. Other custodians of the coast, hearing of Baile dhìreach's decision within the year, did the same, quietly, without any word passed between the districts to agree it, so that within a decade the two-tongue marriages that had once stood as the coast's own proof of a hundred years' living together had all but stopped being written down at all. The marriages themselves went on; only the writing of them had failed, because no custodian any longer trusted Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's court with it.

Thomas understood, by the second year, that his own suit, brought in good faith to save one narrow seam his family had cut for four generations, had become the very door through which A' Chompanaidh had walked to take eleven others, and he never afterward spoke of the case without some version of the same plain reckoning: that he had gone to Ros dhomhain to ask a court to honour his grandmother's marriage, and had come home having taught it, instead, exactly how to use that marriage against every family on the coast that had made one like it.

## VI. Of Faire nan Lòchran and Griogair mac Ailein

It was in the third year after the ruling, in the winter of the hundred and thirteenth, that word reached Baile dhìreach of a fellowship newly begun among the pit crews of Baile thais and Cnoc chaol, calling itself no more than a burial club, the kind of quiet society that put a little of every member's wage aside against the cost of a decent burying, of which there were a dozen along that coast already and nothing remarkable in one more. Thomas Hale, who had by then some name among the coast's custodians as a man who understood, better than most, exactly how far Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's law would and would not reach, was asked by a letter from Baile thais, carried by a carter who said little about who had sent it, whether he would come and speak for a man of the club who had died in A' Chompanaidh's lock-up at Cnoc chaol, and whose burying the club meant to see done properly, in A' Chompanaidh's own eye as well as the district's.

The man was Griogair mac Ailein, a breaker of some sixty years who had worked the sorting-floor at Cnoc chaol since before the pits there had needed a night shift, and who had been taken up by A' Chompanaidh's watchmen in the autumn of that year for a matter the letter described only as a dispute over short weight at the pay office, and had died in the lock-up before any hearing was set for him, of a fever A' Chompanaidh's own surgeon recorded as already advanced when he was taken. He had no family living to claim him, and the club, gathering what it could from its members' wages, had bought the ground and the box and asked only that someone stand at the graveside who could read, aloud, in A' Chompanaidh's own tongue, the surgeon's note releasing the body, so that no clerk afterward could say the burying had been done without A' Chompanaidh's own leave.

The man who carried the letter to Baile dhìreach, a crew-leader of Baile thais named Dòmhnall Ruadh, said little of Griogair mac Ailein beyond the plain facts of the dispute, a matter of a short-weighted cartload the pay clerk had charged against him and Griogair had refused, in words the clerk did not care to repeat afterward, to sign for; but he said a good deal, walking the last mile up to Cnoc chaol at Thomas's side, of why the club wanted the surgeon's note read openly and not merely filed. "A man who dies owing A' Chompanaidh money," Dòmhnall said, "is a man A' Chompanaidh is glad enough to forget, and forgetting is a cheap way to be rid of a debt. We mean the pay office to know he was buried honestly, and that somebody stood at the grave who could read what was owed him back." Thomas asked what, precisely, was owed a dead man, and Dòmhnall said only that a name entered correctly, and a note read aloud, and a stone that would carry his name after the club that raised it had itself been forgotten, were the whole of what Faire nan Lòchran could promise anyone yet, and that they had learned, the hard way, not to promise more.

Thomas walked the four days to Cnoc chaol in the last week of am Faoilleach, in weather no better than the winter that had carried his own suit to its ruling, and stood at a grave dug on the bare hill above the pit-head with some thirty men and women of the club around him, most of them pit crews he had never met, drawn from a fellowship he understood, standing there, to be a good deal more than a burial club, though nobody that day said so aloud and he did not ask. He read the surgeon's note in the flat, careful humans' tongue his grandfather had taught him as a boy, folded it, and gave it to the man beside him, who he learned afterward was one of those who had first proposed the club and had chosen, for reasons of his own that Thomas never asked after either, to call it Faire nan Lòchran among its own members and nothing so plain as a burial club at all, though the name it gave A' Chompanaidh's clerks stayed the same.

No one else in that company that day could have read the paper Thomas held, and he understood, standing at the grave's edge with the thin cold wind coming off the pit-head and the box already lowered, what his own hard winter at Ros dhomhain had left him. The seam was A' Chompanaidh's now, and the eleven cuttings had gone the same road behind it. What remained was a plain skill, bought at the cost of a ruling that had taught him exactly how little Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's law honoured any custom, and it was worth more, standing at a stranger's grave, to the men and women around him than any cutting on any hill had ever been.

# Chapter Twenty-nine: Of the Night Shift

*AE 114 – 120*

## I. Of the Man Who Spoke It Badly

Robert Haskins left Ros dhomhain on a wet morning in an t-Ògmhios of the hundred and fourteenth year, over a quarrel with A' Chompanaidh about the price of a steamship berth, a matter so small that the custodians who watched him go could not afterward agree what it had been. He had held Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir sixteen years and never once, in sixteen years, said a full sentence in Dia-thìris without a clerk at his elbow to mend it. He went down to the quay in a coat too heavy for the season, sixty-nine years old and glad, by every report, to be leaving, and the ship that took him stood off Ros dhomhain until the tide served and was gone by evening.

His successor came up from the same quay eleven days later, and half the town turned out to look at him, because Edward Vane was a thing Ros dhomhain had not seen before: an Àrd-mhaor who had been born there. Not born in an Tìr Thall and sent over grown, as every Àrd-mhaor before him had been, but born at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, four-and-forty years before, to a mother who had crossed the water once and never again and a father who had crossed it only the once and stayed. He had a Dia-thìreach nurse as a child, the custodians said, and had run barefoot on the strand at Ros dhomhain with the fisher-children before anyone thought to stop him, and something of that had stayed in his mouth, because when he stepped down onto the quay and the custodian of the port made him the customary greeting, he answered it. Badly. The tenses came out wrong, and he put the stress on the last syllable of every word the way the humans do, and afterward opinion was divided for a season on whether he had wished the custodian a fair wind or a long life, since the two are one letter apart in the mouth of a man who has not troubled to learn the difference. But he had answered, in Dia-thìris, unprompted, with no clerk beside him, and no Àrd-mhaor had done that in living memory.

He went up to Cathair dhearg himself that autumn, which Haskins had done twice in sixteen years and both times under summons. Comhairle a' Chùraim sat for him in the crown's place, Ceann a' Chùraim's seat empty still, as it had been empty nine years, and Vane stood before the council in the humans' good coat with his hat in his two hands and spoke to them in their own tongue for the length of three sentences before his nerve or his grammar failed him and he finished in the humans' speech through Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's interpreter. What he said, in the part that was his own, was that he had come home. The council's clerk wrote the sentence down exactly as he gave it, wrong tense and all, because it was the first time in the roll's memory that an Àrd-mhaor had used the word at all, home, of the island, and whatever else Vane proved to be, the clerk thought that worth the ink.

He kept a room at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that Haskins had never used, a small chamber off the counting-house with a shelf of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's Dia-thìris grammars in it, worn at the spine from a boyhood's handling, and in the evenings of his first winter he was known to sit with a clerk and a lesson-book like a schoolboy twice the age of any schoolboy, going over the cases of a language he had spoken badly since the cradle and never once been made to speak well. The clerks who taught him said afterward that he learned slowly and minded being corrected less than any human they had taught before or since, which they took, in their different ways, either as a mark in his favour or as proof that a man born on the island, however he had been raised, could never quite be brought to feel the shame of it that a man sent out fresh from an Tìr Thall felt on his first mangled sentence.

He was not loved for it. A custodian of the eastern hills, an old woman past her eightieth year who had buried three husbands and outlived two Àrd-mhaoir already, said within Vane's own hearing, in Dia-thìris too quick for him to follow, that a wolf raised among the sheep is still a wolf, and worse for knowing the sheep's own bleat. The saying went round the coal towns before winter and outlasted the man it was said of. But he had answered the greeting, and he went on, in the years that followed, answering more of them, and the custodians who kept the rolls could not decide, then or later, whether that made him easier to deal with or only easier to resent, since a wrong done in your own tongue by a man who has troubled to learn it cuts different from a wrong done at a clerk's remove, though it is not, in the end, a different wrong.

## II. Of the Iron Road and the Order That Followed It

Vane's first year of building was the tram-road, an iron track laid on wooden sleepers from the southern workings down to the coal port at Ros dhìreach, drawn by mule teams A' Chompanaidh shipped in from an Tìr Thall in crates that stank the length of the quay. It cost A' Chompanaidh less in a season to move coal by the tram than it had cost by cart in ten, and it cost the carters of the old coal road their whole trade inside two years; the villages that had lived on the carting, small places with no name the maps had ever troubled to learn, emptied a household at a time down toward the pits, where there was work still, of a kind. The tram-road opened without ceremony on a morning of an t-Iuchar in his second year, a string of mule-carts running loaded for the first time down the grade that generations of carters had walked with their own backs bent to it, and the custodian who wrote the day into the roll noted only the weight carried and the hour, thirty tons by the third bell, and nothing of the road it had put out of work, for a custodian's roll counts what moves, not what stops moving.

It was Vane, too, who signed the order that came down from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in an Lùnastal of the year after and was read out at every pit-mouth from Cnoc chaol to Muileann chiar by an overseer standing on an upturned crate: that the digging was thenceforward to run without ceasing, day following night following day, and no season of it given over to rest at all. The order named no reason. A' Chompanaidh's own letter-book, which the custodians never saw, gave the true reason plainly enough, that the tram-road had made it cheap to move more coal than the day shifts alone could cut, and idle rails cost A' Chompanaidh money the way idle hands never had.

The custodian of Cnoc chaol, a narrow camp of new galleries in the hills above Muileann dhomhain, wrote the order into her roll in the hand she used for weather and for deaths, and then wrote under it a single line and left the rest of the page blank: *the hill is given no silence at all.* She was a young woman, new to the roll that year, and an older custodian who read it afterward said she had never seen a page left so bare on purpose, as though the custodian judged that anything more she might add would only crowd out the one true thing the page had to say.

## III. Of the Two Shifts and the Week It Lasted

The night shift at Cnoc chaol worked by coal-lamp, small clay bodies with a wick and a horn window that threw a light the crews said was worse than none at all, for it showed a man just enough of the gallery to trust it and not enough to see what the trust cost him. Two shifts split the day and the dark between them, twelve hours each, with an hour at each changeover when both crews were below together and the air in the deep galleries, thin already, had to serve twice the lungs it had ever been asked to serve before.

The crews bore it through a winter, and in the summer after they refused it. There was no vote taken that the custodian's roll records, no meeting called under any name; the day shift simply did not go down when the bell rang for the night change, and stood instead in the yard above the pit-mouth in the last of the daylight, a hundred men and women with nothing in their hands, saying nothing to the overseer who came out to ask them what they thought they were about. He asked it twice. The second time somebody at the back of the crowd, a hewer nobody afterward would name to the overseer's face, said that the hill had never yet been dug in the dark by anyone who meant to keep digging it, and the crowd took up no chant and made no threat and simply did not move, which an overseer used to threats did not know how to answer.

A' Chompanaidh answered it in a week with crews brought up from the coast towns under new contracts, humans mostly, dockers and out-of-work carters glad of a wage the coast no longer offered steadily, and Dia-thìrich from camps far enough off that the word of the stand at Cnoc chaol had not yet reached them plainly. They came up the tram-road in the same mule-carts that carried the coal down it, and were set to the night shift within two days of arriving, and the crews of Cnoc chaol who had stood in the yard went back to the day shift they still had, because a stand that costs a household its whole wage inside a fortnight is not a stand a household can afford to keep making, whatever it costs the hill.

Muileann dhomhain, the milling town two hours' walk below Cnoc chaol on the road to the coast, would not house them. Every door in the town, the custodian's roll says, plainly and more than once, for the custodian who kept it seems to have taken some pride in the counting: every door was shut to the new crews, the inns would not bed them, the millers would not sell them meal at the counter, and the well at the crossroads, the only water on that stretch of road that did not belong to some household's own yard, was found blocked with stones on the second morning by no hand the custodian troubled to guess at. A' Chompanaidh's overseers housed the new crews in barns of A' Chompanaidh's own outside the town, and several of the newcomers, humans and Dia-thìrich alike, went home to the coast before the season was out, unable to say afterward, when asked, exactly what had driven them, only that a town that will not sell a man his bread is a hard town to work beside for wages that were never generous to begin with.

Faire nan Lòchran, the fellowship of pit crews that had begun four years before under cover of a burial club, at Baile thais and at Cnoc chaol both, kept the households of the men and women who had stood in the yard through that first week and the season after, out of a purse built a penny at a time from crews who could ill spare the penny. By the second winter the purse was empty. The society's own reckoning, kept in a hand nobody has since put a name to, closes the account for that year with a line that gives the sum remaining, nothing, and under it, in the same hand, a second line that says only that the hill was not given back its silence, which was not, whatever else it was, an accounting entry, and the custodian who copied the reckoning years later left it standing all the same.

## IV. Of the Sermon at Ros dhomhain

Matthew Dunne had held Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chapel at Ros dhomhain three years when Àithne na h-Oidhche came down, a narrow young man of one-and-thirty with a Dia-thìris better than any minister Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had sent before him and a temper, his own bishop said of him once, better suited to a soldier than a priest. He had walked the coal towns in his first year the way Walter Crane had once walked the sick-rows of A' Phlàigh Uaine, on his own feet and without an overseer beside him, and had come to know the camps better than any human at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, Vane not excepted.

He preached against the order on the humans' rest-day in an t-Ògmhios of the hundred and eighteenth year, when it was two years old and the stand at Cnoc chaol a year gone; and when word of it reached Cnoc chaol and Muileann dhomhain inside a fortnight, it did not go quiet. Standing that morning in the chapel pulpit at Ros dhomhain before a congregation half of it A' Chompanaidh's clerks and half of it dockers, he said, in the humans' own tongue so that no clerk could later claim to have misheard him through an interpreter, that the Dia-thìrich were right in the thing they had not been given leave to say for themselves: that the ground A' Chompanaidh dug was owed a season of quiet the same as any ground the humans' own scripture called holy, and that a people who would not let their own fields lie fallow a year in seven had no right to ask a hill to give more. The whole chapel knew what he meant without his naming it.

He had written the sermon three times before he stood up to give it, his housekeeper said afterward, and burned two drafts in the grate, and on the morning of the sermon he walked the strand below the chapel for an hour before the bell, alone, in a wind off the water that took his hat twice, and came in with salt on his coat and his text unchanged from the second burning. He was afraid, he told the housekeeper once, years after and from the other side of the water, not of A' Chompanaidh's answer, which he had judged rightly from the first, but of standing in a pulpit built by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's own money and telling the men who paid for it that they had misread their own scripture; a fear, he said, that a soldier does not carry into a battle he has already decided to lose.

A' Chompanaidh's agent at Ros dhomhain wrote to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's own house in an Tìr Thall within the month, and the letter, which a clerk copied before it went and which found its way years later into the same roll that keeps the custodians' counts, called the sermon an interference in matters the cloth had no competence in and asked, plainly, that the minister be recalled before his words did A' Chompanaidh more harm than his ministry did it good. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, which depended on A' Chompanaidh's ships for every letter and every year's stores that crossed the water, recalled him inside the season. He preached a last sermon at Ros dhomhain at the end of that same year, three-and-thirty years old, to a chapel fuller than it had ever been in his three years, and said nothing in it of the night shift at all, only the ordinary words for a minister's leaving, and went down to the same quay Haskins had gone down from four years before, in the same wet weather, though nobody who watched him go thought the two departures were alike in anything but the rain.

Faire nan Lòchran had a copy of the sermon inside the week, taken down, it was always said afterward though never proved, by a clerk of A' Chompanaidh who had sat in the chapel and did not care to give his own name to the copying. It went from Baile thais to Cnoc chaol to Muileann chiar in the space of a season, read aloud in the camps of an evening by whoever among the crews could read well enough to be trusted with it, and the line the crews kept longest of the whole sermon was the one about the fallow year, which passed into the coal towns' own speech soon after as a saying that owed nothing, by the time it had been said a hundred times over, to the minister who first gave it words.

## V. Of Donnchadh's Cough

A wasting sickness of the lungs came into the night crews of Cnoc chaol and Baile thais the same winter the sermon was preached, and stayed three years. It was not A' Phlàigh Uaine; it killed slowly, over a season or two, a cough that would not clear and a weight the sick could not keep on and a colour to the skin that was grey rather than green, and it took the humans of the crews first and hardest, the dockers and carters brought up from the coast, whose own country's pits had killed their fathers the same way before they ever crossed the water to find a hill that would kill them too.

The Dia-thìrich hewers coughed as hard through that winter, working the same galleries in the same lamp-lit dark, and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's own physician, a careful man named Colquhoun who had come out after Anne Colby's years and kept her habit of writing plainly, set the same word against their names in his book that he set against the humans'. But the custodians' roll, which knew every hewer of Cnoc chaol by name and had known most of their mothers, kept its own separate count, and the count said a different thing: that of the Dia-thìrich who coughed that winter, few died of it, though the cough lasted as hard and as long as any human's.

The old women of the camps knew the telling of the hewer of Achadh dhomhain whose cough had stopped on the night his daughter was born. They called any such cough among the Dia-thìrich crews Casad Dhonnchaidh, and would say no more. A' Chompanaidh, for its part, paid the widows of the dead a pension for a year and then stopped, the pension being, the agent's letter says without apology, a matter of A' Chompanaidh's grace and not of any debt owed.

## VI. Of Iain Maor's Letter

Iain Maor had kept the staff of the overseers at Muileann chrom two-and-thirty years, since he was seven-and-thirty, and had buried a wife and raised a daughter in the slate-roofed house above the mill that came with the staff, and at nine-and-sixty, the winter Àithne na h-Oidhche fell hardest on his own galleries, he did a thing no overseer of Muileann chrom had done in the office's whole history: he wrote to A' Chompanaidh that its own order was costing it more than it gained.

He wrote it in the humans' tongue, in the schooled hand Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had given him as a boy, and he did not soften it. The night shift, he wrote, was killing his crews faster than the coal they cut in the dark was paying A' Chompanaidh back, counting the cost of every dead man's training against a new one, the wage lost to every widow's household falling onto the parish and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise both, and the slower cutting of tired crews working by coal-lamp against crews that had once worked the same seams by daylight and rested. He signed it with his own name and the office's, and sent it down with the ordinary post, and heard nothing for two months.

His daughter Mòrag, four-and-twenty that winter and already keeping her father's own daybook for him in a hand steadier than his had ever been, was the one who found the answer when it came: a notice from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, unlike any reply to a letter she had ever copied for him, that Iain Maor, overseer at Muileann chrom, was relieved of the staff for conduct unbecoming his office. She read it to him at the kitchen table by lamplight, and he heard it out without a word and then asked her, when she had finished, to read it again, and she did, and he said only that he had known the answer would come dressed as something other than itself, and went to bed.

He had known the letter would cost him something even as he sealed it, he told Mòrag that same evening; a man who has kept a staff of A' Chompanaidh two-and-thirty years learns to read the shape of an answer before it comes, the way a hewer learns the sound a roof will make before it falls. She asked him why he had written it all the same, and he said only that a true thing costs the same to say whether it is answered honestly or not, and that a man who waits to speak until the cost is nothing has generally waited until the thing is no longer worth the saying.

The dismissal did not stand a month. There was no other overseer at Muileann chrom A' Chompanaidh trusted with the galleries, and the crews, who had heard within a day what had been done to him, worked the next fortnight at a pace so far below what the night shift demanded that A' Chompanaidh's own agent wrote up the road that the pits could not be run without him. The second notice came unsigned by anyone above a clerk's rank, restoring him to the staff with no mention made of the first notice at all, as though the office had simply forgotten, for a season, that it had ever taken the staff from him. Iain Maor kept both notices together in the same drawer, the dismissal and the restoration, ready to hand to anyone at his table who asked how A' Chompanaidh answered a true thing said to it plainly; and his letter, folded in with the dismissal that had answered it, survives in A' Chompanaidh's own files for that reason alone, filed by a clerk who thought the two papers belonged together and never troubled to think why.

## VII. Of the Iron Chariot

The potteries of Baile ghorm took A' Chompanaidh's contract for lamp-bodies in the spring the tram-road opened, thousands of clay bodies fired in a season, each with its horn window and its wick-hole turned on the same wheel that had turned bowls and pipkins for the coast trade a generation before. The potters' own book, kept as carefully as any custodian's roll though nobody at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir thought to call it one, notes that theirs were the first lamps made on the island for work commanded in the dark, and sets the number fired against the number of days, a column of figures that grows through that spring and does not shrink again.

Vane lived long enough to see the tram-road's true purpose finished. In am Màrt of the hundred and twentieth year A' Chompanaidh's iron road opened from the pits at Muileann chrom, down past the hill below Cathair dhearg, to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain, a proper railway of iron rail and a coal-burning engine, and the mule-drawn tram to Ros dhìreach was left, from that day, to the mules and to whatever coal the southern workings still had cause to send that way. Iain Maor stood at the pit-mouth at Muileann chrom on the morning the first loaded train went down, his daughter beside him, seventy years old and the staff back in his hand a season after it had briefly left it, and watched the engine take the grade that the tram-mules had taken at a walk, at a pace no mule had ever kept, trailing a smoke the colour of the hill itself.

The crews at the pit-mouth had no word yet for the thing. By the day's end they had made one, calling it carbad-iarainn, the iron chariot, and calling the road it ran on Slighe a' Ghuail, and both names outlasted every name A' Chompanaidh's own letter-book ever gave either. Mòrag, watching the smoke go down the valley toward Ros dhomhain and the sea beyond it, asked her father what he thought the engine would mean for the crews, now that the coal could travel faster than any crew that cut it ever would again, and Iain Maor, who had buried more of those crews in two-and-thirty years than he had ever troubled to count, said only that a thing which can carry more, faster, is a thing that will be asked to carry more, faster, and that the hill had not yet been asked the last of what it had to give. He did not live to see how far that answer would run. His daughter did, and kept it, in the years after, the way she kept most of what he told her at the pit-mouth that spring: filed away, unspoken, until the day it was needed.

# Chapter Thirty: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol

*AE 121 – 126*

## I. Of the Second Birth

In an Gearran of the hundred and twenty-first year a second child was born who did not take after the way of children, and word of it went up the east road in a season, from mouth to mouth, the way such word goes among a people who cannot write it down themselves and must trust it to carriers. His name was Fionnan. The custodians who kept the eastern rolls set down the birth and no more beside it, for there was no more that could yet be told; but every one of them who had heard, fifty years before, what the camps said of a girl called Aisling understood, on the reading of that single line, that the thing was no longer a wonder of one house. A wonder that happens once is a wonder. A wonder that happens twice is a question, and a question, once it is asked, does not go quietly back to sleep.

At Muileann chaol, where this telling is set down, the news reached the cellar in the ordinary way that all news reached it: folded small inside a roll of births and burials that a rider brought in on a wet evening, indistinguishable to look at from the fifty rolls before it and the fifty after. Nobody in the cellar that year thought to mark the page. It was only later, when the word had a name and the name had a use, that the copyists went back through the year's rolls to find the line again, and were a long while finding it, because it had been written the same size as every other line on the page.

## II. Of the Town and the Loft

Muileann chaol stands on the eastern slope where the mill road crosses the burn twice within a bowshot, a narrow town that had made the island's first paper from rags in an older age, and had gone on making it in a small way ever since, more from habit than from any great custom for the stuff. It was known east of the capital chiefly for one thing that had nothing to do with paper at all: the loft over the old mill, where a mill-owner's widow named Beathag nic Thòmais had once stacked the copies she bought up from houses that no longer read them, and left the loft and all that was in it to the town on the single condition that nothing kept there should ever be burned. The town had kept that condition longer than any of the families now living in it could trace their own descent, and since the strangers came the custodian houses of the east had grown into the habit of sending to the loft anything they wished to be certain of, since Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's writ did not reach into an old woman's roof-space over a paper mill, whatever else it reached.

Cailean mac Eachainn had grown up under that roof without ever once climbing the ladder to it. His father cut turf on the hill above the town; his mother wove the coarse grey cloth that Muileann chaol sold at the coast markets before the barter went out of the old towns' hands. He was a plain hand at his letters, no better and no worse than any boy who had sat through the winter months at the custodian's fire learning them, and he had thought, as far as he had thought about it at all, that he would cut turf as his father did, and grow old on the same hill, and be buried, in the end, under it.

What changed that was not the loft, which had stood over the town all his life and asked nothing of him, but the cellar, which had not.

## III. Of the Three Households

In am Màrt of the hundred and twenty-fourth year, at the end of a winter that had closed the coast road with drift, three families of Muileann chaol, the mac Ailpeins, the nic Rìghs, and the household of an old widow named Seònag Bhàn, took in more work than they had ever taken before, and it came from the east.

The custodians of the eastern hills, from Cnoc thais down to the shore below Dùn thais, had begun that winter to send copies of their rolls to Muileann chaol for the keeping, over and above whatever they had always sent to the loft. It was not, at the start, spoken of as anything more than good housekeeping: a custodian's roll, kept in one thin book in one damp custodian's house, could be lost to fire or flood or the plain wearing of the years in a way that three copies, kept in three different houses in a town Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir had no cause to visit, could not. But a roll copied is a roll read, twice over, once by the hand that first wrote it and once by the hand that copies it fair; and Na Trì Teaghlaichean reading, winter on winter, the whole record of the eastern hills, every birth and burial, every marriage with its seven names, every fine and fever and every shift lost to A' Chompanaidh's pits, came in time to know that record better than any single custodian who kept only his own corner of it ever could.

They worked in the cellar under Seònag Bhàn's house, because it was the driest of the three and had a chimney that drew well even in the worst weather, and because Seònag herself, being past the age for close copying, kept the peat going and the ink from freezing and fed whoever was at the table, which by the second winter was five or six people at a time. It became, without anyone deciding it should, the place the work was done, and the loft above the mill the place the finished copies went when they were done with; and the town, which had one word for the whole arrangement long before Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir ever heard of it, called it simply an Seilear, the cellar.

Cailean was four-and-twenty when the copying began, a turf-cutter's son with a plain hand at his letters and no other prospects, when Seònag Bhàn's own eyes began to fail her past the point of close work, and Na Trì Teaghlaichean, needing a hand that could be trusted with rolls no stranger's eye was meant to see, sent for him.

He remembered afterward that he had gone to the cellar the first evening expecting to be asked whether he could write a fair hand, and had been asked instead whether he could hold his tongue. That he could do. They gave him a corner of the table, a good pen, and the roll of a village he had never heard of, and told him to copy it exactly as it stood, mistakes and all, for a copy that corrected its original was worth less than the paper it was written on.

He was slow, that first winter, and made the ink run twice, and Seònag Bhàn scolded him for it in a voice gone thin with age but no gentler for that. By the second winter he was as fast as any hand at the table, and had learned, the way every copyist learns without being told, that a roll of births and burials read a hundred times over stops being a list and becomes something closer to the shape of the place it comes from: which families were dying out, which taking in strangers, which custodian's hand was failing along with his eyes, which village had gone three years without a marriage worth the name.

## IV. Of the Count of the People

Two years before the copying began, word went round the east that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had ordered a count made of every soul on the island, the first such count in the memory of anyone then living, and that its officers were riding out from Ros dhomhain with books and questions to every district in turn.

The count that came back, when the copies of it reached the cellar the following year among Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's other business that the custodians thought worth keeping a record of, was a strange document to read fair. For the humans of the coast towns and the concession farms it gave a number to the household, close as a tally of sheep: so many souls under this roof, so many under that. For the Dia-thìrich of the same district it gave a number rounded to the nearest hundred, and further inland, where the hill villages ran together in Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own maps into districts with names its officers had half invented, rounded to the nearest thousand.

"They count us the way a man counts trees," said Fearchar mac Ailpein, whose household had taken in the count among the rest of that winter's copying, laying the sheet down on the cellar table. "Near enough for the timber. Not near enough for the names."

Cailean, copying beside him, thought of the roll he had just set down, the roll of a village of forty-one souls that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own count gave as a round hundred, and said nothing, because there was nothing in it worth saying that the sheet had not already said for itself.

The same officers, riding the west and the outer islands that same season, had set the whole of the far coasts, Eilean bhàn, and the wind-scoured shore below the great moss that no chain of theirs could cross, and the harbour town of Seann Vell on Eilean ruadh where their revenue boats lay, into a single district ruled from Seann Vell itself, for want, the custodians' letters said, of anywhere closer that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach cared to build an office. The cellar's copies of that letter noted, in a hand Cailean came to know as Fearchar's, that the surveyors had walked the edge of the moss, found no way across it, and left the rest of the district's map blank; and that the custodians of those coasts, being no readier to be counted by a stranger's chain than the moss itself, had let them.

## V. Of the Death of the Last Teacher

In an Lùnastal of the hundred and twenty-third year, word came down from Dùn thais that Seònaid nic Dhùghaill was dead, in her seventy-eighth year, and that the school she had kept was closed with her.

She had been, for longer than anyone at the cellar's table could remember hearing otherwise, the last master of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh to teach openly in that age: the last to sit under the trees at Dùn thais with pupils in a ring around her and speak the philosophy of the schools aloud, in the hearing of whoever wished to stop and listen, as the schools had always taught before Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise between them made open teaching a thing best done quietly or not at all. She had gone on doing it for years after the last hall was shut and the last public disputation forbidden, on the grounds, she was reported to have said, that a philosophy that could not survive an Àrd-mhaor's displeasure had never been worth the keeping in the first place.

Cailean had never heard her teach. He had only heard of her the way a young man in a cellar hears of most things, at second hand, through a roll that another man's pen had already made history of before it reached his table: her death entered in the Dùn thais custodian's hand, plain as any other death that year, and beneath it, in the same hand, a line that said the register of her school ended with her name and would not be continued, there being none left of her house or her pupils willing to keep it in the open.

"They'll take it up again," said Fearchar, "when the strangers are gone."

"When will that be," said Cailean, not really asking, and copied the line as it stood, for a copy that corrected its original was worth less than the paper it was written on, and the register's silence was as much a part of the record as anything ever written in it.

## VI. Of the Copies Gone Astray

It was in the spring of the hundred and twenty-fifth year that the cellar first learned there was a second Muileann chaol.

It stood some hours to the north along the same eastern hills, a smaller place by every account, its whole population not so many as one good village of the coast; but it shared the name letter for letter, and more than one rider coming down from the northern custodian houses with a chest of rolls for the cellar had, over the years, asked the road to the wrong town and been told it plainly enough by carters who saw no reason to ask why a stranger with a locked chest wanted either.

Fearchar found the first of the misdirected copies by chance, going through a bundle newly arrived and finding among it a receipt, in a northern custodian's hand, for a delivery the cellar had never made and a roll the cellar had never received. He took it round the table without a word and let each of the others read it in turn. Seònag Bhàn, past copying but not past thinking, said only that a mistake three years old was a mistake worth mending before it became four years old, and looked at Cailean.

He went north on foot in am Cèitean, with a letter of Na Trì Teaghlaichean' own seal and nothing else, for there was nothing to carry until he found what there was to carry. It took him the better part of a day to reach the smaller Muileann chaol, along a road that climbed twice as high as it needed to and came down again for no better reason than the shape of the hill, and he arrived footsore and in no mood to be careful of anyone's feelings, custodian or carter.

He need not have worried. The custodian who met him at the northern town's door, an old man with a squint and a temper that had gone soft with disuse, showed him into a room no larger than Seònag Bhàn's own cellar and produced, from a chest under a bench, every roll the cellar at the true Muileann chaol had been missing for the better part of three years, sorted by year and tied with a cord, dry, unburned, and kept, the old man said with something close to pride, every bit as well as they'd have been kept anywhere else, mistake or no mistake.

"You could have sent word," said Cailean, not unkindly, for the old man plainly meant it as a kindness done rather than a wrong admitted.

"To who?" said the custodian. "Nobody told us we had what wasn't ours. We only knew we had rolls, and a roll's a roll. You keep it dry and you keep it whole and you wait for someone to come and say it's theirs." He tied the last cord himself, with hands that shook a little at the work, and handed the bundle over. "Well. Someone's come."

Cailean carried the whole of it back south on his own shoulders in two days, sleeping the one night at a hill farm that took him in for a story of the road, and reached Seilear Muileann chaol with his feet raw and the chest of copies unopened, exactly as he had received it, for a copyist who broke a seal that was not his to break was no copyist Na Trì Teaghlaichean wanted at their table.
