Fearchar broke it for him, that same evening, and the two of them and Seònag Bhàn went through three years of the north's own record by lamplight, matching what had been missing against what the cellar had pieced together from other hands in the meantime, and found, to their considerable relief, that nothing of any weight had been lost after all. It had only been kept in the wrong cellar for a while.

"It is a strange thing," said Fearchar, when the last roll was matched and put away, "to think how much of what we call lost is only misplaced, and how much of what we call found was never really gone."

Cailean, whose feet hurt too much that night for philosophy, said that he would rather it were all in one cellar to begin with, and went to bed.

## VII. Of the Change, and What the Years Would Not Do

Through all of this the copyists at the cellar table went on doing what copyists had always done with the thing that had no name.

It had been in the rolls, here and there, since before any of Na Trì Teaghlaichean were born to the work: a birth entered like any other birth, and beside it, in one hand or another, a mark, or a word set apart, that meant a custodian had noticed something in the child that he did not have a word to set down properly. Cailean had copied such lines himself, that first winter and every winter since, and had learned, as every hand at the table learned, that the custodians who wrote them wrote around the thing rather than at it, the way a man walks around standing water in the dark rather than say plainly that he cannot see the bottom of it. *The child does not grow as she should.* *He is much as he was at his naming, though four winters are past.* *She is called by the camp nighean an rìgh, though on what ground the roll does not say.* Cailean had heard the camps' own word for it too, from carters who had it from other carters, the kind of word boys use for a thing they are half afraid of and wholly certain will never touch them: Aisling-aois, they called the state of her, the age of Aisling, though nobody at the cellar's table had ever set that down in any hand that mattered.

It was, by the year of Fionnan's birth, thirty years and more since the first child had shown it and been written round in that fashion, and now there were two, and the custodians who had gone on writing round the thing for thirty years began, in ones and twos, to say in their letters to the cellar that a thing seen twice wanted a name a physician could enter in a column, whatever a teller might call it by the fire.

Cailean read a dozen such letters that winter and the next, in a dozen hands, each circling the same want from a different side, and none of them settling it. He asked Fearchar once, late at a table with the peat gone low, whether Na Trì Teaghlaichean ought to put a word of their own forward, since they had read more of the record than any custodian living. Fearchar said no, and said it hard enough that Cailean did not ask again. "We copy what is decided," he said. "We do not decide it. A cellar that starts deciding what the rolls should say stops being a cellar anyone can trust."

## VIII. Of the Call to Cill ghlas

The letter that settled it came to the cellar in am Faoilleach of the hundred and twenty-sixth year, from the custodian of Cill ghlas, a woman named Peigi Ghlas whose hand Cailean knew well from years of her own eastern roll, small and upright and given to underlining the word that mattered most in any sentence she wrote.

She had called, the letter said, every custodian within two days' walk of Cill ghlas to meet at the shrine there on the night of the coming full moon, at the mouth of the oldest cutting on the hill, where Brìde's lamp had burned since before any of them had a roll to keep; and she asked, further, that the cellar send a hand who could write a fair copy on the spot, since the custodians who would be there were, in her own words, more used to arguing than to agreeing, and a decision arrived at in the dark by candlelight and not written down clean before the company dispersed was a decision that would be argued over again within the year.

Seònag Bhàn looked at the letter a long while and then looked at Cailean, who was the youngest hand at the table and had the steadiest by then, and said that it was his to carry, if he was willing.

He was willing, though he did not say, walking west the following week with a folding writing-board strapped to his back and a stock of good paper wrapped against the weather, quite how much he minded the cold of a hill shrine in am Faoilleach, or how far Cill ghlas lay from anywhere a fire could be had along the way. He slept the one night at a custodian's house on the road and reached the shrine the next evening with the light already failing and the wind coming hard off the moor.

They came up the path in ones and twos through the last of the dusk, custodians he knew by their hands and had never before seen by their faces, cloaks steaming where the walk had warmed them and the cold struck through again the moment they stopped: an old man from Cnoc thais who had to be helped the last stretch of the climb; two sisters from villages on either side of the same burn who had walked separately and arrived within a minute of each other and seemed put out by it; Peigi Ghlas herself, last of all, small and upright as her hand, with a lantern that she set by the lamp at the cutting's mouth so that the two flames stood together, one old beyond telling and one carried up the hill in her own fist.

The oldest cutting still stood open in the hillside behind the shrine, black-mouthed, the timber at its lip gone soft and silvered with age, and all around it in the dark, under the wind, Cailean could hear the pumps of A' Chompanaidh's newer galleries lower down the slope, working on through the night the way they worked every night now, for the hill, since the order went out, was given no season of rest at all.

He set his board on his knee at the edge of the group, near enough to hear, far enough not to be in anyone's way, and dipped his pen, and waited.

## IX. Of the Naming

They sat on the benches of the shrine with their cloaks steaming and argued, as Peigi Ghlas had promised they would, for the better part of two hours before anything was decided at all.

Some wanted an old word, one out of the tellings, a word with weight already in it, so that whoever bore it would be seen for what the tellings said such children were. Peigi Ghlas herself spoke hardest against that. "An old word carries an old story with it, whether we mean it to or no," she said, "and the story it would carry is one we have not finished telling ourselves, let alone a child of five winters." Others wanted no word at all, arguing that a name is a door, and that a thing without a door could not be walked through by Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerks or Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's physicians or anyone else who might, given a word to hang a report on, hang more on it than the word was ever meant to carry. The man from Cnoc thais, who had said little on the climb up, said that a physician would write a word down whether the custodians gave him one or not, and that it was better the word came from a shrine than from a stranger's ledger.

It was full dark by the time the arguing narrowed. In the end it was one of the sisters from the burn villages, a woman Cailean never did learn the name of, who put forward the word that held: the plainest word there was, she said, fit for nothing grander than a physician's column, with no song in it and no story attached that any teller could make more of than the two words themselves already said. Fuil-ghuail. Coal-blood.

There was a silence after it long enough that Cailean, waiting with his pen above the paper, began to think it had failed, the way a proposal fails in a room grown tired of arguing, simply by not being taken up. Then Peigi Ghlas said that she, for one, could enter it in her own roll tomorrow without shame, and asked for a show of hands.

Cailean counted them by lamplight as they went up, dark shapes against the paler dark of the hillside, and there were more raised than not, though not every hand in the company went up, and nobody asked those that stayed down to account for themselves.

"Fuil-ghuail," said Peigi Ghlas, when the hands were down again, the way a custodian repeats a decided thing to fix it in the record. "Coal-blood, for the humans' books, if they must have it in their own tongue. Let it be entered so."

Nobody moved to argue it further. The pumps went on working somewhere below them in the dark, and the wind came round the mouth of the old cutting and made the two lamps gutter together and steady again, and one by one the custodians got up from the benches, stiff with the cold and the sitting, and began the walk back down to whatever fire waited for them at the bottom of the hill.

Cailean stayed a moment longer than the rest, because Peigi Ghlas had asked him to, and because the thing was not yet finished until it was written.

She dictated it to him there at the mouth of the cutting, by the two lamps, in the plain words a physician's register wanted and none other: that on that night, at that shrine, the custodians present had agreed a name for the change that had come twice now upon a child born of the pits, and that the name was fuil-ghuail, and that it was to be entered so in every roll that had cause to speak of it from that day forward, in the custodians' hand or, where Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerks required it, in the humans' tongue as coal-touched.

He wrote it in the fair, careful hand the cellar had taught him, the ink slow to dry in the cold, and read it back to her once before she would let him close the board. She listened with her eyes on the old lamp rather than on him, and when he had finished she said only that it would do, and that he had best get down off the hill before the paper froze in his hand and the pen with it.

He walked back to Muileann chaol over two days with the board strapped to his back exactly as he had carried it up, and gave the leaf, when he reached the cellar, to Fearchar to copy fair a second time for the loft, as every leaf of any weight was copied fair a second time before it was trusted to the years. Fearchar read it through once, in silence, and then read it again, and said nothing at all about the word itself, only that the hand was good and the ink had held despite the cold, which was, from Fearchar, as near to praise as a copyist's work ever got.

It was Cailean's own hand, in the end, that carried the word into the physician's column: a small, upright entry, no larger than any other line on the page, set down among the year's other births and burials and fines and fevers as though it were no more than any of them, though every copyist who came to that page afterward, in the cellar or the loft, would know exactly what it was, and would read it, whatever else the roll around it said, a little more slowly than the rest.

# Chapter Thirty-one: Of Sloinneadh Aisling

*AE 126 – 131*

## I. Of the Roll at Àth ìseal

Cailean mac Eachainn had been two years in Seilear Muileann chaol before he learned to stop reading the rolls he copied.

It was not a lesson anyone taught him. Seònag Bhàn, the eldest of Na Trì Teaghlaichean, told him only that a hand copies faster once it stops caring what it copies, and that a fast hand kept a place in the cellar longer than a slow one, whatever else was true of it. Cailean had taken her at her word the way a young man takes an old woman's word when he has not yet found a reason to doubt it, and by the second winter he could set down a page of births, burials, fines and shifts lost without his eye once catching on a name. The lamp smoked, and the roll in front of him went from one pile to the other, and that was the whole of the work, and he was glad of it in the way a man is glad of a thing that asks nothing further of him.

The roll of the camp at Àth ìseal reached him in the tenth month of the hundred and twenty-sixth year, bundled with three others from the eastern custodians whose rolls Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's own clerks could not be trusted to keep private, and whose copies therefore came down to Muileann chaol to be made again in a hand Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir never saw. Àth ìseal was a small camp, a hundred souls or so scraping at the thin seam above Achadh dhomhain, and its custodian had kept the new camp's people on the same pages as her own from its first winter, so that the roll ran heavier than its size would suggest: two settlements' worth of births and burials and shifts lost, pressed into one book by a hand that had grown worse with every winter it was asked to write in. Cailean did not know the custodian's name and had no cause to learn it. He set the roll on the stand, trimmed the lamp, and began.

He had copied perhaps sixty such lines that month, and read none of them, when his hand slowed over the marriages.

A camp's marriages are not written the way a town's are. Where a town custodian sets down only the two names and the year, a camp custodian writes them as the households at the ford first recited them, in An Aois Ailein, each side's line carried seven names back before the vow is called good: so-and-so, son of so-and-so, son of so-and-so, to the seventh father, and the same again for the bride, and only then the marrying. It is the oldest habit the custodians keep and, Cailean had always privately thought, the most useless one for a man paid to make a fair copy of a roll in the fewest hours he can manage; seven names back for every hewer and every hewer's wife in a hundred camps was a great deal of ink spent on the dead.

He had copied a hundred such lines that season and never once read past the first name in any of them. This one he read, and could not afterward have said why, except that the seventh name of it was a name nobody gives a child now, and something in his eye caught on it the way a boot catches on a root it has walked over a hundred times without ever quite tripping on.

*Donnchadh mac Thormoid, hewer,* the marriage began, and carried Donnchadh's line seven fathers back to a name that meant nothing to Cailean at all, and then gave the bride's line the same courtesy, and then the marrying. Cailean copied it as he copied everything, and went on, and would have thought no more of it, except that further down the same page, in the same custodian's failing hand, a birth was entered with a small mark beside it, a third mark, neither the mark for a birth that lived nor the mark for one that did not, one Cailean had seen perhaps four times in a year of copying, always against one name only, never explained in any book he had been given to copy from.

*Aisling.*

Every copyist in the cellar knew what the camps said of a child marked so. Cailean had said it himself once, as a boy at Muileann chaol, the way boys say a thing they have heard grown men say and do not trouble themselves to believe: *the girl who does not grow.* He had not thought of it in years. He thought of it now, sitting with the lamp guttering, and found that he did not want to go on to the next line until he had gone back and read the first one properly.

He read it three times. Donnchadh, hewer, son of Tormod, and Tormod's line running back seven names to one that struck him as being older than a hewer's grandfather's grandfather had any business being, in a hand that gave no sign of thinking it strange. He sat with it a long while by the lamp, long enough that Seònag Bhàn came down once to see why his pile had stopped growing and went away again without asking, because she had kept the cellar long enough to know the look of a man who has found a thing he does not yet understand is his to keep or to give away.

In the end Cailean finished the page, as the work required of him. Then he took a scrap of the cellar's poorer paper, the kind kept for false starts, and copied the seven names of Donnchadh's line onto it in his own hand, folded it once, and put it inside his coat where the ledger's ink could not mark it. He told himself, walking home along the millrace that night with the folded paper against his chest like a stolen thing, that he only meant to ask someone who would know whether such a line as Donnchadh's could truly run as old as it looked on the page, and that this was no more than any careful copyist owed to a roll he had failed to understand. A thin excuse, and he knew it, and walked on anyway. In the morning, instead of walking down to the cellar, he walked out along the hill road to Tobar dhìreach, where it was known, if a man asked at all, that the last of Clann na Ceiste who still said the old lines kept a house not far from the standing slab.

## II. Of Tobar dhìreach

It was raining by the time he reached the house, the fine grey rain that comes off the western sea in the tenth month and does not trouble to announce its coming with wind first, and he stood at the door a moment working out what he meant to say before he knocked, and found he had worked out nothing at all.

The woman who opened to him was old in the way the very old are old, past the age where a stranger can guess at the years by looking, with a face gone to folds around eyes that had not dimmed with it. She looked at him the way, he thought afterward, a woman looks at a fox that has come to her door in daylight: not afraid of it, and not glad of it either, only certain that its coming meant some wrong had been done somewhere, to bring it to her door at all.

"You'll want to come in out of that," she said, "since you've come this far in it," and stood aside.

Her name was Ealasaid, and she told it him herself when he had not thought to ask, the way the old sometimes give a thing freely that a younger person would have made him earn. The house was one room and a loft, with a fire built up higher than the day's cold quite called for, and no sign in it of the things Cailean had half expected to find in the house of the last of a house that said the old lines: no bones, no carved stones; nothing but a chair drawn close to the fire and a shelf of ordinary crockery and, over the mantel, a length of plain cord hung in loops that he did not understand and did not ask about.

He told her what he had, badly, starting twice and beginning again, until she stopped him with a raised hand and said only, "Read it me, then, and stop telling me what you think of it before I've heard it," which steadied him more than any kindness would have.

He drew out the folded scrap and read the seven names of Donnchadh's line aloud by the fire, slowly, the way a man reads a thing he is not sure he has copied without error. Ealasaid sat with her eyes shut through all of it, her hands still in her lap, and did not open them until he had said the seventh name, the old one, the one that had first caught his eye in the cellar.

"Where did you get that?"

He told her: the roll of Àth ìseal, a hewer's marriage, copied down the way the camp custodians write such things, nothing more.

"That is Somhairle's line," she said, and said it the way a woman says a fact so old it has stopped surprising even her. "The son who asked for nothing. We have kept that line since Somhairle himself, and in a thousand years nobody of it has come asking after it. They went down into the valleys and forgot us, all of them, generation on generation, until there was no one left above ground who remembered there was anything to come asking for." She was quiet a while, looking at the fire rather than at him. "Whose is the child?"

"Donnchadh's," Cailean said. "His daughter. Her name is Aisling."

He had not meant to say more than that. Something in the old woman's stillness pulled the rest out of him almost before he had decided to give it: the mark beside the birth, the whisper the camps carried about a girl who did not grow, the boy's grin with which he himself had once repeated it, not believing a word of it, the way boys repeat any strange thing that is said around them.

Ealasaid said nothing at all for so long that Cailean began to think she had not heard him, or had heard him and judged the matter beneath answering. Then, without turning her head, in a voice that had gone flat and careful, as a woman reads a thing off a wall rather than out of her own mind, she said: "When strangers hold this island, the fire will wake again in your line."

She looked at him then. "That is the end of the vigil, as we keep it. I have said it every winter of my life at the hearth on the night of the lightning, and I never once thought I would live to see what it meant." She rose, slowly, with the particular care of the very old getting up from a low chair, and Cailean understood without being told that what she meant to give him required her to be standing to give it. "The lines are said standing," she said, as if he had asked. "Sit where you are and write, if you've brought anything to write with. I'll not say it twice in a night."

He had a stub of pencil and the back of the same poor paper. She gave it him as it is given at a naming, from the child back to the fire. Clann a' Chlachair has kept the years of its dead beside their names since the mason, but it says them to no stranger except where they are strange; and so in the short form only the long lives are given their years. Cailean wrote it down as she said it, as fast as his hand would go:

> "Aisling, daughter of Donnchadh, who hewed in the deep galleries of Achadh dhomhain;
> son of Tormod, who carried water up to Doire mhòr two summers, and then went down to Àth ìseal;
> son of Ruairidh of Doire mhòr, who stood behind Beathag Dhubh when she sent A' Chompanaidh down the hill;
> and seventy generations whose names we keep;
> son of Fionnlagh, who stood on the quay at Seann Skell when the ships went out, and did not go;
> and a hundred and sixteen generations whose names we keep;
> son of Ceallach, the last of us whose years were long; and all the days of Ceallach were a hundred and forty years, and he died;
> son of Gille-Brìde, who carried a coal of A' Chiad Lasair home to the hills; and all the days of Gille-Brìde were two hundred and twenty-four years, and he died;
> and six generations whose names we keep, each longer-lived than the one after, and their days were three hundred and eight years, and four hundred and thirty-one, and five hundred and ninety-seven, and eight hundred and twenty-six, and one thousand one hundred and forty-eight, and one thousand five hundred and ninety-four;
> son of Beathan, who sat by the slab through the dark half of the year; and all the days of Beathan were two thousand two hundred and thirteen years, and he died;
> son of Somhairle, son of Ailean, who asked for no share of the kingdom and went before his father to the grave; and all the days of Somhairle were two thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven years, and he died;
> son of Ailean Mòr, the first king, whom the gods crowned in the grove, and who was king until he fell at Àth na Fala; and all the days of Ailean Mòr were four thousand six hundred and twenty-six years, and he died;
> son of Suibhne, and fourteen fathers whose names we keep;
> son of Seathan, who snapped his fingers, and the fire was in his hand; and ten fathers;
> son of Colla, in whose days they called us Luchd-ceasnachaidh a' Ghuail Dhìomhair; and fifteen fathers;
> son of Eòghann, who tasted the river; and twenty-one fathers;
> son of Cormac of the Misstrike, who bled in the grove; and thirty fathers;
> son of Brian, who buried the five like the dead; and twenty-eight fathers;
> son of Fearghas, who climbed to the top of the island; and thirty-one fathers;
> son of Aodh, who threw the seven into the sea; and eighteen fathers;
> son of Diarmad, who spoke with Coimhdeach na Fine in the grove; and thirty-four fathers;
> son of Conall, who kept the vein while it burned;
> son of Neachdan, who found the fire;
> son of an Dia-shluagh, who grew out of the island like grass;
> and the island was born of Caoran's fire."

When it was done she sat again, and for a while neither of them spoke, and the rain went on against the shutter as it had gone on the whole time, indifferent to what had just been said in the room it fell on.

"They'll say it's a tale," Cailean said at last, looking at what his own hand had written, not quite believing the numbers even as he read them back. "Four thousand years. Two thousand. Nobody will believe a word of it below."

"The years, they will call a tale," Ealasaid said. "Let them call it that. I never told you a man lived four thousand years, Cailean mac Eachainn. I told you whose son he was." She looked at him a moment longer, and something in her face eased, very slightly, as though a weight she had carried a long time without expecting to set it down had shifted onto someone else's shoulder at last. "Go home now, and write it where it will keep. That's all that was ever asked of either of us."

## III. Of the Return, and the Report that Named No One

He walked back to Muileann chaol in the last of the light with the paper inside his coat, wet through at the edges where the rain had got at it despite him, and sat up past the cellar's own hours copying the line fair onto a second sheet before the pencil could smear past reading. In the morning he did the only thing that seemed to him, then, both possible and right: he wrote the seven names, and Ealasaid's line after them as she had given it, small, in the margin of the Àth ìseal roll, beside the entry for Aisling's birth, in a hand no larger than the mark that had first caught his eye. He told no one at the cellar what he had done, and Seònag Bhàn, who saw the margin filled and might have asked, chose that year, as she had chosen other years before it, not to ask a young copyist what he did with an evening that was rightly his own.

So it was found, as far as a line of names can be said to find anything: that the girl of the spoil-heaps at Achadh dhomhain, whom the camps had whispered over since before she could walk, carried in her the blood of the first king of the island, more generations removed from him than any roll could count, and no less his for the distance. What it proved beyond that, the cellar did not ask, and Cailean, who had begun the matter, was careful afterward never to be the one who raised it again.

Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir heard of the word the custodians had agreed within the year, as Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir heard most things that were said twice within a day's ride of one of its clerks, though by what road neither the custodians nor Na Trì Teaghlaichean of the cellar ever learned. What reached it was not the line, which no clerk of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach would have believed if he had heard it, but the plainer fact: that certain children of the Dia-thìrich did not grow as other children grew, that the custodians had a word for it, and that they appeared to know a good deal more about which children these were than they had troubled to report.

The order came down at the end of the hundred and twenty-seventh year, over An t-Àrd-mhaor's own seal, and was read out to every custodian's gathering from Cathair dhearg to the coast: any child of the Dia-thìrich showing the change the custodians had lately named was to be reported at once to An t-Àrd-mhaor's office, with the child's name, place and parentage, that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach might keep its own account of a matter touching the Dia-thìrich body it had not previously thought to number.

The custodians obeyed the order in the only way most of them ever found themselves able to obey an order of that shape. They reported none. Not Aisling, not Fionnan, not any child born with fuil-ghuail in the years that followed, though every custodian's roll from Cathair dhearg to the coast went on quietly keeping its own note of them, in the plain hand the physicians had settled on, where no clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir thought to look for it. A custodian at Cill ghlas, asked once by an agent of A' Chompanaidh whether she knew of any such child in her own district, is recorded as having answered that she kept no roll of miracles, only of births and deaths, and that the office in front of her was welcome to search her books for either.

## IV. Of the Third Coin

The order on the children was not the only order that year, nor, as it happened, the one that changed more households than any single ruling in a generation.

Barter had been marked down against the mark twice already, and had gone on regardless in a hundred quiet corners Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerks never fully reached: cloth for fish at the steps of Inis mhòr, a day's labour for a day's milk between neighbouring crofts, the old exchanges that had outlived the marks and the mint and every change of coin that came before them, because a clerk cannot fine a transaction he never learns took place. In the spring of the hundred and twenty-ninth year Riaghaltas nan Coigreach struck barter down as lawful payment altogether, and in the autumn it closed the last door as well. The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and at Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish and every manner of goods besides had changed hands without a coin passing since before the humans first came over the sea, were shut by written order, their doors nailed, their keepers turned to other work. A clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, setting the closure into the year's account, wrote that A' Chompanaidh's ledgers were now, for the first time in the island's keeping, *complete*, and meant it as praise of his own office's thoroughness rather than as anything said against the households the closing cost.

The fishwives of Inis mhòr, who had sold their catch at the river steps by barter since before any of them could say when the custom began, took no coin at all for a full week after the order reached them, giving their fish away to whoever came down to the steps rather than sell it for marks they had not asked for and did not want. A' Chompanaidh's own clerks, coming down to the steps to see what the disturbance was, recorded the week as a glut in the season's catch and set it down so in the account, and never once asked a fishwife why so great a glut had chosen that particular week to appear.

It did not last, of course; a week is a week, and a family must eat past the end of it. Within the year the hill villages that had always paid their seed and their rents in kind now had no lawful way to pay in anything but marks, and the villages around Muileann chrom, having no marks of their own to spare, began borrowing them at interest from A' Chompanaidh's own stores, the only lender within a day's walk willing to lend at all. It was a small thing at first, a mark here, two marks there, against the next year's crop. Within a few years most of the villages about Muileann chrom owed A' Chompanaidh more marks than a year's crop could answer for, and every custodian who kept a roll of debts as well as of births knew it, and none of them knew what to write against it that would change the sum.

The old market at Muileann òg, where the hill folk and the coast folk had met to trade with each other directly since An Aois Naomh, without A' Chompanaidh or Riaghaltas nan Coigreach standing between them, closed after its last poor season in the hundred and thirty-first year. No order closed it; there was simply, one spring, nothing left worth carrying to it that could not be carried more profitably to a town with a mint. The ground it had stood on, a flat green shoulder above the ford that had given the old market its name, stood empty from that year on, and the grass that grew up over it grew thicker each season, since nothing walked it anymore to keep it down.

## V. Of the Staff at Muileann chrom

Peigi Ghlas died at Cill ghlas in the spring of the hundred and twenty-eighth year, the year before the barter houses' doors were nailed shut, an old woman by then, her petition long unanswered and the pile it had joined grown taller by every year that passed without an answer coming. She had trimmed Brìde's lamp herself the last week of her life, though her hands shook so that a younger custodian stood by to catch the oil if she spilled it, and she is remembered at Cill ghlas, where such things are remembered longest, as having said, near the end, that she had asked Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir for an answer once, and meant to leave the asking there for good. She was buried within the shrine's own ground, beside the cutting the custodians still keep open, and the roll of Cill ghlas records nothing further of her save the day.

Iain Maor, third of that name to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, followed her within three years, in the autumn of the hundred and thirty-first year, having held the staff since before most of the hill's present hewers were born and having spent no small part of it, in his last years, writing letters to Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, which dismissed him for the writing of them and then reversed the dismissal and took him back, because it could find no one else the coal camps would trust to keep order among them. He died at Muileann chrom, in the same house he had held the staff from, and was buried within the week, the custom of the camp allowing no longer delay for a man whose office could not sit empty.

His daughter Mòrag took the staff from his hand before he died, by his own wish and the custodians' agreement both, the first woman to hold it in the staff's whole history at Muileann chrom. She was thirty-six years old, born the year her father first took up the letters he would spend the rest of his life writing, and she had grown up, as she told a younger cousin once, "knowing the shape of that staff better than I know the shape of my own hand, from having watched it lie across his knees at every supper of my life." A' Chompanaidh wrote to confirm her within the month, in a letter that named her, without further comment, "a safe pair of hands," a phrase the custodians of Muileann chrom repeated to one another afterward with an expression none of A' Chompanaidh's clerks would have cared to see on their faces.

Mòrag took the staff home the evening of her father's burying, through a hill gone quiet with the particular quiet that follows a funeral, past the pithead where the night shift's lamps were already moving. Where her father had set it across his own knees by the fire, she hung it over her hearth, on two iron hooks he had never troubled to have fitted, where it caught the firelight along its worn grain every evening after. There, she told the same cousin years later, she could see it without having to hold it, which was, she had found, most of what a staff of office was actually good for.

She thought, hanging it there that first night, of a thing her father had told her once and again as she grew, a thing he said he had had from a copyist at Muileann chaol who had had it, in turn, from an old woman of Clann na Ceiste out at Tobar dhìreach, though neither he nor Mòrag had ever met the woman nor asked after her name: that somewhere on a roll no clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir had ever read, a girl who did not grow was written down as the daughter of a king four thousand years dead, in a line kept by people who had stopped expecting anyone would ever come asking for it. *I never told you a man lived four thousand years,* the old woman was supposed to have said. *I told you whose son he was.* Mòrag did not know, that first night with the staff cooling on its hooks and her father not yet a day in the ground, what use such a thing as a name kept four thousand years could ever be to a hill that could not keep its own coin, let alone its own children, out of a stranger's ledger. She only knew that she thought of it, standing there, longer than she thought she should have, and that she did not stop thinking of it, in the years that followed, whenever the staff caught the evening light in a particular way and she found herself, without quite meaning to, looking up at it from her chair.

# Chapter Thirty-two: Of the Grey Goose and the Dockers

*AE 132 – 135*

## I. Of the New Àrd-mhaor

Edward Vane died at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir above Ros dhomhain late in an Lùnastal of the hundred and thirty-second year, in the bed he had been born in sixty-two years before, the only Àrd-mhaor Dia-thìr ever gave a birth as well as a death. He had spoken the tongue of the island badly to the end, in the flat clipped way of a man reciting a lesson he had never quite trusted himself to feel, and the custodians who came to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in the old form to acknowledge the change of stewards found, as they always did with Vane, that they had liked him rather more than they had meant to and could not now say precisely why.

Charles Merriman came out from an Tìr Thall within the season, and with him came thirty men in a grey coat nobody on the island had worn before, each with a rifle slung and a look of having crossed a great deal of water to be told, on landing, that there was nothing yet for them to do. The custodians who received the ship at Ros dhomhain asked what the soldiers were for, and were told, courteously, that they were constables under An t-Àrd-mhaor's own commission, sworn to keep the harbour and the roads, and that this made all the difference in law, whatever it looked like standing on a quay with a rifle slung.

"It is the first standing force Riaghaltas nan Coigreach has kept here," said Mòrag nic Iain Maor, who had ridden down from Muileann chrom to see the new Àrd-mhaor land, more from a wish to look at his face than from any hope of learning anything from it. "A hundred and twenty years A' Chompanaidh kept order with an agent's signature and a locked storehouse. Now it keeps it with rifles."

"A hundred and twenty years A' Chompanaidh had no cause to do otherwise," Merriman said. He was a broad, sandy man who did not raise his voice, which the custodians came in time to find more unsettling than a man who did. "I hope, madam, to give it none now either."

He built his first post within the month, at Muileann shean on the northern coal road: a low stone house with a yard for horses and a flag that flew from a pole cut, the townsfolk noted without much surprise, from timber A' Chompanaidh had felled and never paid the custodian for. They called it the humans' second Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and did not mean it kindly, and the name outlasted every other name anyone tried to give the place. A second post went up that same autumn at Tobar ghorm, nearer the northern workings, where the custodian of the village was paid a rent for the ground it stood on and used the money, with a thoroughness that made A' Chompanaidh's agent write two letters of complaint to Ros dhomhain, to buy the village clear of every debt it owed A' Chompanaidh's own store.

Mòrag rode home from the landing with the picture of the thirty grey coats fixed in her mind the way a burn scar fixes, and told her crew-leaders only that the staff she held was the same staff her father had held, and that nothing about the water she had just seen them carry ashore changed what it was for.

At Tobar ghorm the constables who took up the new post found, in their first week, that the village gave them nothing to do at all: no theft reported, no quarrel brought for judging, no crowd gathered anywhere near the stone house with its yard and its flag. The custodian who had let the ground to them, an old man named Uilleam Glas who had buried two sons in the same gallery three years apart, told the sergeant set over the post, when the man asked him plainly why the village kept so quiet, that Tobar ghorm had learned long since to settle its own quarrels before any stranger with a badge could hear of them and offer to settle them differently. The sergeant wrote as much in his first month's report to Merriman, who read it twice and told his clerk that a quiet post was either a well-kept one or a lying one, and that he did not yet know Tobar ghorm well enough to say which.

## II. Of Hannah Webb

Hannah Webb had come to the hill country behind Baile chrom at nineteen, in the year Slighe a' Ghuail opened, following a brother two years younger who had heard there was steady field work to be had among the concession's tobacco slopes and steadier pay than either of them had known on the crossing. She was thirty-two now, broad through the shoulder from twelve years of stooping to the leaf, unmarried, with a face the sun had weathered past what her years alone would have done, and she kept, in the small room she rented from a tenant-farmer of A' Chompanaidh, a single object of any value: her mother's clasp-knife, brought over the sea and never once used for anything but cutting bread.

She had gone down to Ceann mhòr in the spring of that same year, on an errand for the farm that had nothing to do with what she came home carrying. The harbour under the north-western headland held perhaps forty houses of human fishing families, the first of their people to draw a living from the island's own sea rather than A' Chompanaidh's table, and among them an old woman named Ruth Pallant who mended nets on a bench outside her door and talked, without much needing to be asked, to whoever sat down beside her.

"You keep late hours, out on the field paths," Ruth said, when Hannah admitted, more from politeness than confession, that she often walked at night rather than sleep through the heat that hung on even after dark in the growing season.

"There's nothing to see by night but the dark."

"There's a deal to see by night, if you know to look for it." Ruth's needle did not stop. "My grandmother's people fished these waters before there was a Ceann mhòr to fish them from, and they kept a watch some nights, to hold the sea shut against whatever the dark lets loose on it if nobody watches. We learned it from the island folk, who've kept it longer than anyone can say, though Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise would have it we invented it out of our own fright at a strange coast. A grey goose flies over the watch, they say, and if you keep it faithfully and in silence, the goose carries the watching up, and nothing comes ashore that oughtn't."

"What do you say, keeping it?"

"Nothing at all. That's the whole of it. You keep still, and you keep quiet, and you let the goose do the saying." Ruth looked up from the net for the first time. "You've the look of a woman who doesn't sleep well. Try it, some clear night. It costs you nothing but the hours you weren't using anyhow."

Hannah kept the vigil for the first time in the last week of an t-Iuchar, alone, in the field behind the tenant-farmer's byre, sitting on an upturned crate with her knees drawn up and her mother's clasp-knife closed in her fist for no reason she could have given, watching the sky go from the last green of evening to a black so thick with stars she could not find, at first, the constellations Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's calendar named for her. She did not know, doing it, that she was keeping anything with a name; she knew only that the stillness asked for stopped, for the first time in twelve years, the endless small counting of her days that ran under everything else she did: the tally of what was owed and what was short and what her brother had said at breakfast that she ought to have answered better. Toward the middle of the night she saw, or thought she saw, low over the field, a long pale shape crossing east to west with its neck out straight before it, and she did not move, and it passed, and she went in afterward and slept the whole night through for the first time since she had come to the island.

She kept it again a week later, and then most weeks, telling no one, until a field hand named Colm Ashe, walking home late from a different farm, saw her sitting motionless in the dark by the byre two nights running and told the story at Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's rest-day meeting more from wonder than from malice. Within a month half the human labourers of the concession's edge had heard of it, and a handful had tried it themselves, and by the autumn there were nights when six or seven of them kept the field together, spaced apart and silent, each fixed on the same patch of sky.

## III. Of What Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise and the Priests Said of It

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise at Cathair gheal took the matter up formally the next summer, when its minister, a careful and not unkind man named Obadiah Renn who had buried more of his flock to fever than he had married, asked Hannah to sit with him in the chapel's cold vestry and tell him plainly what she did and why.

"We keep the sky," Hannah said. "That's the whole of it. Nobody taught me a word to say. There isn't one."

"You call it a prayer."

"I don't call it anything. Others have started to."

Renn turned his pen over twice before he wrote anything. "The scripture knows the dove, and it knows the raven Noah sent out and the one that did not come back. It does not, so far as I have ever read it, know a goose." He looked at her not unkindly. "You have done nothing wrong that I can name. But I cannot find you in the book, and a minister who cannot find his flock in the book grows uneasy, whatever the flock itself feels keeping the field. So I mean to write to Cathair gheal, plainly, that the practice is irregular, and unaccountable, and very likely picked up, however it came to you, from the island folk's own customs."

"It was an old woman of Ceann mhòr taught me the way of it. She's no more island folk than I am."

"Then she had it from someone who was, once, however many years back, and the water it has passed through since does not change the spring." He wrote his letter that week, and it went, as such letters did, up the chain to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's house at Cathair gheal and from there, in time, into a report that named the vigil irregular and its origin uncertain, and asked that no minister encourage it while it remained unaccountable to the scripture.

Baile chrom's own Dia-thìrich, when the thing came to their ears, for little stayed long unheard between the town and the fields about it, wanted no part of it either, though for reasons of their own. "We keep no watch with An Eaglais," said the custodian of Baile chrom's lower row, a stiff, careful woman who had buried enough of her own people in the hunger years to have no patience left for anyone else's borrowed grief. "If the field folk want a goose in their sky, let them keep it themselves and leave our name out of the keeping of it." The saying went round the town within the week, and the human labourers who had begun, hopefully, to call their watch a thing shared between the two peoples learned instead to call it, among themselves only, their own.

It was Manannan's priests at Ceann mhòr who, of everyone who heard of it that year, came closest to naming the thing rightly, and liked it least for having named it. An old priest of the harbour temple, hearing from Ruth Pallant herself what she had taught the field woman, walked the width of the concession to Baile chrom to see the vigil kept with his own eyes, stood at the field's edge through one whole silent night without once being asked or asking to join it, and told Hannah afterward, in the grey hour before dawn, that she had the form of the watching near enough right and its meaning hardly at all.

"The goose you keep you take for an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the bird of an Spiorad Naomh, your own, and your minister cannot find it in his book, and Baile chrom will have none of it. Your minister is half right. The watching under the goose is ours, out of our own harbours: the night prayer to keep the sea shut. Your fisher-wife's people learned it from mine, to keep the sea shut against what the sea lets in unwatched, and somewhere between her grandmother and you the sea got left out of it, and what's left is a good and a true thing, kept faithfully, that is nonetheless not the thing it started as. It has gone astray of us. I will not say it has gone wrong."

"Will you tell your own people to keep it with me, then?"

"I will not. It is not, any longer, entirely ours to keep, and I would not have my house's people standing silent in a field to a prayer that has wandered as far from its beginning as yours has. I have told Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's man at Cathair gheal, though, that it is not for him to stop it either, in words he did not much care to hear." He looked out at the field, empty now in the daylight, the crate Hannah sat on nothing more than an upturned crate. "Keep your watch, Hannah Webb. Whatever it is you are keeping, by now, is your own."

## IV. Of the Dockers of Ros dhomhain

Hannah's brother, whose name was Daniel, had left the tobacco fields for the quays at Ros dhomhain two years before, saying he had had enough of another man's leaf under his own nails and would rather break his back for wages he could see counted out to him at the week's end than for a crop A' Chompanaidh priced after the fact. He worked the coal berths, loading the steamships that had begun, since Slighe a' Ghuail opened, to carry more coal in a season than the sailing ships had carried in five, and he worked them beside Dia-thìrich dockers who had been loading the same berths since before he was born, men he had learned, over two years, to drink with and argue with and, on the one occasion a beam had come loose and nearly taken a Dia-thìreach docker's leg, to haul clear with his own hands fast enough that the man had thereafter called him, half in jest and half not, *a bhràthair*, brother, which was not a word given lightly on either side of that harbour.

The docker he had pulled clear was named Tòmas Ruadh, a broad quiet man twice Daniel's age who had worked the Ros dhomhain berths since the pit at Muileann chrom first sent coal down to them, and who took to bringing Daniel a share of whatever his wife had put up that week, a habit neither of them ever remarked on aloud. It was Tòmas who told him, on an evening in the spring of the hundred and thirty-fourth year, that A' Chompanaidh's agent had posted a new tariff on the loading-house door, a toll on every ton counted at the scale that had not been there the week before and that no docker of either people had been asked about.

"They'll say it pays for the new stone on the quay," Tòmas said. "It pays for the quay right enough. It does not pay us anything at all."

"Then don't load it."

"Easy said by a man who can be put on a ship home if it goes badly." Tòmas looked at him without heat, only the flat weighing look of a man deciding something. "But you're not wrong that it wants saying. We have never once, in all the years this harbour has stood, put down our hooks with the humans standing next to us instead of over us. It might be worth seeing what that looks like."

The berth charges went up that spring, a new toll on every ton loaded that A' Chompanaidh's agent said was owed the harbour works and the dockers said was owed nothing but A' Chompanaidh's own accounts, and the two peoples of the quay, who had never in the whole history of the port struck together over anything, put down their hooks on the same morning and did not pick them up again.

"You're mad to stand with them," a clerk of A' Chompanaidh told Daniel Webb on the second day, not unkindly, meaning it as a warning. "They'll strike you eleven days at Baile thais and forget you the day after. You're not one of them and never will be."

"I'm not striking for them," Daniel said. "I'm striking for the toll, same as they are. It happens we're both on the same side of it this year." He said the same, in rather fewer words, to Hannah when she walked down to see him on the fourth day of it, finding him thinner already and cheerful in a way she distrusted on sight, the way she had learned to distrust his cheerfulness their whole lives, since it generally meant he had decided on something before he had thought all the way round it.

The stoppage held nine days, the whole harbour idle, the coal piling on the quayside faster than any store could take it, before Merriman's constables came down from their new posts on the tenth morning and stood in a line the length of the quay, rifles slung and shown but never fired, enough of them that the dockers who had held nine days without a blow struck went back to their hooks within the hour rather than find out what the tenth day of standing against thirty grey coats might cost. A' Chompanaidh took the names of every human docker who had struck, and within the week a ship stood off Ros dhomhain to carry them over the sea. The passage was offered once, in a notice read to the men on the quay by A' Chompanaidh's agent himself, courteous and plainly worded and impossible to mistake for anything but what it was: it would not be offered twice, and no man there needed to be told what the ship's leaving without him might mean for the season's work he had left.

Hannah stood on the quay the morning the ship took on its passengers, in a crowd of families who had come to see off husbands and brothers and, in two cases, wives, and watched Daniel go up the gangway with a single sack over his shoulder and his back straight in the particular way she knew meant he would not turn to look at her again before the ship cleared the harbour mouth, because he had never in his life been able to say a proper goodbye and had settled, instead, on not making one. He did turn, once, at the rail, and lifted a hand, and she lifted hers, and that was the whole of it; the ship's whistle sounded, and it stood out past the headland with the morning tide, and she did not know, standing there, whether she would ever again in her life see the water this particular colour of grey without thinking of that sail going small against it.

The Dia-thìrich dockers of Ros dhomhain went back to their hooks that same week, having no ship offered them and nowhere else on the island to be sent. At Seann Vell, the neighbouring harbour, where no human had ever worked the berths, the dockers heard of the shipping and refused, on their own account and without a single human among them to strike beside, to load the coal that had been meant for the vessels the strike had held back. When the stoppage broke elsewhere they were not shipped over the sea, for there were none among them to ship; but neither were they hired again that season, nor easily the season after, and the harbour-master's rolls at Seann Vell show, for two years running, a quay standing half idle beside a coal-yard standing full, which no one at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir troubled to explain in writing, and everyone at Seann Vell understood without needing it explained.

## V. Of the Two Births

Hannah kept her watch through that winter and the next, in the field behind the byre, alone some nights and joined by two or three of the concession's own on others, the shape of it settled now into something Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise had stopped writing letters about and Baile chrom had stopped troubling to disown, since a thing left long enough alone in its own field becomes in the end too small a thing for anyone to keep minding. She wrote to Daniel twice that year, letters that took the better part of a season to cross and be answered, and learned, from the second answer, that he had found work on the docks of a great river port of an Tìr Thall, loading ships bound, as it happened, nowhere near Dia-thìr, a fact he set down without comment and she read with more feeling than she let herself write back.

That same spring, on 29 an Cèitean, AE 134, a third child of the coal-blood was born, Lorccan, the first of them born in a mining town and not in a camp; and the custodians, who had written the word *fuil-ghuail* in their columns for eight years by then against two names only, knew from it that the thing had outgrown any one place. Within a year, on 3 am Màrt, AE 135, a fourth was born, Cian. Never before had two of the coal-blood come so near together. The custodians who wrote the two births wrote them as the rolls required, the name and the day and the word in its column, and nothing more, and reported neither to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir.

Hannah heard nothing of either birth, keeping her own watch in her own field far from both, and knew nothing of any such children at all. The custodians' rolls kept the four names, and Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's register, which asked for them, kept none.

# Chapter Thirty-three: Of Scàineadh Cill ghlas

*AE 136 – 138*

## I. Of the Plan and the Mark Below It

The shrine at Cill ghlas had stood through the whole of the age. It was older than that: the custodians said the cutting had been worked before the strangers came, before the mark, before the first ton was weighed at Muileann chrom, and that Brìde's lamp had burned there since a time nobody now living could put a year to. It was there the word *fuil-ghuail* had been agreed, in the year the custodians gave the thing a name, and it was there the crews still climbed on the old feast days, as they had climbed since before any gallery had a name.

In the hundred and thirty-sixth year of the strangers A' Chompanaidh came to drive new workings under the hills about it.

The engineer's name was Robert Fairley, a spare, sandy man not yet forty, who had come out from the coalfields of an Tìr Thall with a case of instruments and a habit of measuring things twice. He set his levels on the moor above the shrine in the month of am Faoilleach, in a wind that took the surveyor's flags out of the ground three times before noon, and by an Cèitean he had his galleries marked on a sheet of linen paper pinned flat on a drawing-board in the site office at Baile thais: eight headings running north under the hill, numbered, with the old cutting shown as a hatched square at the top of the sheet, and the new workings stepping down below it toward the river.

The custodians of the shrine came to him twice. The first time it was Aonghas Mòr, keeper of the lamp that year, a heavy, slow-spoken man who had held the office eleven years and never once let the flame go out in all of them. He stood in the office doorway with the smell of the moor still on his coat and asked, through the clerk who did A' Chompanaidh's Dia-thìris, that no charge be set where the noise or the shake of it could be felt at the shrine. Fairley heard him out, asked the clerk to repeat the words a second time so he had them right, and wrote on the margin of his plan, in a small careful hand: *Custodians ask no charge in sight of old cutting.* He underlined it once.

The second time it was Aonghas Mòr and two others, in am Màrt, when the first blasting parties had begun to come up from the coast with their crates and their careful, unhurried carters. They asked the same thing again, in the same words, because that was the custodians' way with a thing once asked: to ask it again exactly, so that no one could say later that the asking had changed. Fairley looked at his own margin note, found it still there, and told them, through the clerk, that A' Chompanaidh had it marked and would keep to it.

He believed, when he said it, that he meant to.

The charges that summer were set according to the depth of good coal under each heading, and the depth of good coal ran deepest where the old cutting's own diggers had worked closest to the surface, in the years before anyone measured a working by the ton. The lowest headings, numbered six, seven and eight on Fairley's sheet, came up under the shrine itself, forty fathom down and rising, where the plan's careful ink line seemed from above to set them beside it. Fairley had marked the custodians' asking faithfully. He had not marked where the ground under his numbers actually lay, because on the sheet the shrine was a hatched square with no thickness to it, and the workings below were a set of numbers with no depth drawn in beside them, and the two things never touched on the paper at all.

The powder for the new headings came in that same summer, landed not at Ros dhomhain or Cathair dhearg, where the harbour-men had grown particular about barrels that hissed when they were dropped, but at the small stone quay of Caol ìseal on the north coast, away from the crowded southern ports. It came up from the hold in casks bound with iron hoops, stencilled in the humans' letters, and carted inland under an escort of four constables who rode a little apart from the carts, as men do who have been told what is in them and would rather not be asked. The custodian of Caol ìseal, an old woman named Oighrig Ruadh who had kept that small roll for thirty years, went down to the quay herself and asked the carter what the casks held.

"Lamp-oil," the carter said, not unkindly, and helped her count the barrels onto his manifest so the number would agree.

She wrote in her roll that night: *Forty casks landed, said to be oil. They did not smell of oil when I put my hand to a stave.* It is the only line in any custodian's roll that says plainly the lie was known for a lie before it was told, and it went unanswered, as such lines mostly did, into Seilear Muileann chaol with everything else.

## II. Of Baile thais in the Winter

Eilidh nic Raghnaill was thirty-one that winter and had led a crew at Baile thais for six years, ever since her mother died and the crew that had been her mother's would not be led by anyone from outside the family. She kept a room over Comann an Adhlacaidh's hall, two streets up from the pithead, with a window that looked down the row of grey roofs to the sea, and on the wall by the door, where another woman might have hung a carving of Coimhdeach na Fine or a sprig of dried heather from Brìde's shrine, she had a single sheet of paper pinned flat, copied out in her own hand from a longer one that had gone round the crews eight years before: the names of the eleven who had died under the fall at Cnoc fhiadhaich, long before her own remembering, and under them the names, added later, of everyone since whose death the crews had judged worth keeping.

Her father, Raghnall Breac, hewed at Baile thais still when she was a girl, one of the crews who had come out in the eleven days of the great strike before she was born, a boy then, and had never in all the years after let a Lùnastal pass without telling the story of the twelfth morning and the shelves. But the seam at Baile thais was old and narrow and paid by the ton at a rate that had not moved in a generation, and in the hundred and thirty-fourth year, with two grandchildren to feed and his knees gone stiff for the low work, Raghnall Breac had gone up the hill to Cill ghlas, where the new galleries paid better and a man his age could still find a heading tall enough to stand up straight in. He came down to Eilidh twice a year, at Bealltainn and at the turn of the year, and each time said the same four things: that the house was dry, that the food was fair, that the overseer left the old men alone, and that she was to mind her crew and not to worry for him.

She did not see him again after am Faoilleach of the hundred and thirty-sixth year.

It was in that winter, in the room over Comann an Adhlacaidh, that she was first asked to sit at the table where Faire nan Lòchran kept its business. Faire nan Lòchran had begun, twenty years and more before, as Comann an Adhlacaidh's own purse stretched a little further than the burying of the dead: a fund the crew-leaders kept among themselves for the widow of a man killed at the face, for the fine of a boy taken up by the constables, for the passage of a letter that A' Chompanaidh's post would not carry. By the time Eilidh was asked to the table it had become something else again, though no one at the table would have called it by any other name than what it had always been called. She was given the youngest seat and the least to say, and she went home from her first meeting with the club's minute-book under her coat, to copy its entries into a second book kept nowhere A' Chompanaidh's clerks would think to look, which was a woman's linen chest.

## III. Of the Ground that Spoke First

On 9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 137, an ordinary day of an ordinary week, the galleries under Cill ghlas were worked as they had been worked every day since the headings opened: the day crews down before light, the tubs running, the overseer's watch ticking in his waistcoat pocket at the pit-mouth as it had ticked every morning for two years.

The tellers of Cill ghlas, in the years after, all agreed on one thing before they agreed on anything else: that the ground spoke first. Those nearest the eighth heading said it was a grinding, long and low, like a quern turning under a great weight, felt through the soles of the feet before it was heard at all. Those on the surface, at the pit-mouth and in the cottages along the moor road, said the ground under their own feet answered it a breath later, a shudder that stopped the wheel on the headgear and set every dog in the district barking at once. Then, in the space of perhaps three breaths, the fault that ran unseen and unsurveyed beneath the whole of Fairley's careful sheet of numbered headings tore open along its length, and the hill above the eighth heading came down into the eighth heading, and the seventh into the seventh, and the ground above the old cutting, which had never been drawn with any thickness on any plan, went down after them into a working forty fathom below it that no one at the shrine had ever been told was there.

It killed dozens. The custodians' roll of Cill ghlas, written up at the year's end from what could be gathered of that morning, gives the number as thirty-one, and says under the number that four more bodies were never brought up at all, and were left to the hill. Raghnall Breac was among the thirty-one. He was found on the third day, with two other hewers of his heading, under a fall that had not reached the surface, in a gallery that by every account should have held for a week after the charges that opened it. The overseer who wrote his name into the roll spelled it wrong, and a later hand at Muileann chaol has corrected the spelling in the margin, and left the wrong spelling standing, as the copyists always did once a mistake had gone into the roll.

The shrine went down with the eighth heading, in the same three breaths as everything else: Brìde's lamp, the stone bench where the shrine-keepers sat their watch, the little cairn of coal from every gallery that had ever been opened at Cill ghlas, going back further than any roll now standing could say. Of the keeper on watch that morning, an old woman named Sìne nic Aonghais who had climbed to the shrine every day for nineteen years, nothing was ever found, not a bone nor a shred of her plaid.

The custodians' roll, in the hand that first set the day down, records the loss of the shrine in one line and the loss of the dead in the next line after it. A later copyist, working from the same leaves a season afterward, judged the order backward, holding that flesh must be set before stone, and wrote a second account with the two lines reversed, meaning to strike out the first. He did not strike it out. Both hands stand in the roll as it came down to Muileann chaol, one above the other on the same page, and Na Trì Teaghlaichean who copy there have never agreed which should be kept and which crossed through, so both are copied still, every time, the shrine before the people and the people before the shrine, side by side.

## IV. Of the Fenced Ground and the Stone on the Moor Road

A' Chompanaidh's surveyors were back on the hill within the week, this time to fence it. The district closed, by the order that came down from Ros dhomhain, ran from Cill ghlas to Àth chaol and took in every hamlet between, a stretch of hill country that had fed itself on oats and coal both for as long as anyone's grandmother could remember, and the order gave no leave for anyone to go on working any part of it, on any ground, for any wage. The fence was a poor thing, posts and three strands of wire strung by men who plainly did not expect it tested. No one tested it. The custodians read the order to their own households and then, one by one over that autumn and into the winter, the households of the closed district began to leave.

They went in twos and threes at first, and then, as the winter drew in and the last of the stored meal ran low, in whole villages together, walking the moor road south toward Muileann dhomhain with what a cart or a back could carry. The custodians of Muileann dhomhain met the eldest of them, not in the town hall, where a clerk of A' Chompanaidh sat most days on other business and might have seen who came and went, but at a standing stone on the moor road a mile short of the town, an old grey stone of a height with a tall man, that had stood there, by whose hand or for what first purpose nobody now living could say, since long before the strangers, before the mark, before any road had been metalled to run past it at all. There, at the stone, the custodians of Muileann dhomhain lent the dispossessed the poorest of their own common land, a stretch of thin ground at the edge of the fenced country that had never been worth enclosing for anything better than rough grazing. The meeting was given a name that winter, by whoever names such things: Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, and the stone has been called by no other name since.

On the ground lent them the people of the closed district raised, over the following spring and summer, a new village they called Achadh chaol, narrow field, for the shape of the ground it stood on. It was built without any surveyor of A' Chompanaidh's setting foot on it, without any clerk of A' Chompanaidh's hand in its laying out, house by house as the households that built it saw fit, on a common decided at the stone and a lease held from the custodians of Muileann dhomhain, in the old form, for the old dues, and from no one else. Of every settlement raised on the island in the years of the strangers, it was the only one built so, and the custodians who wrote of it afterward were at pains to say so, more than once, in words that were nearly the same words each time they said it.

Achadh chaol was raised through that summer in the ordinary way of a village built by people who had built villages before and had only ever lacked the ground to build one on: a well dug first, at the lowest point of the common where the water table lay shallowest, then the custodian's house, because a village without a custodian's roll to enter itself into was not yet a village at all in anyone's reckoning, and then the seven other households in the order their names had been drawn at the stone, so that no household could say afterward it had been given the worst plot out of spite or favour. Aonghas Mòr, who had kept the lamp at the lost shrine and had nothing left to keep it in, was given the custodian's house because the households that had followed him down off the closed hill trusted him more than any stranger among them, and told him so plainly enough that he could not well refuse. He opened the first roll of Achadh chaol on the day the well was finished, and its first line, in a hand still shaking a little from the digging, gives the well's depth in feet and says nothing at all of the shrine, or of Sìne nic Aonghais, or of the day the ground spoke.

Eilidh nic Raghnaill walked to Cill ghlas in the fortnight after Scàineadh Cill ghlas, though there was no house of her father's left standing to walk to, and no grave with his name over it that she could find among the rows the custodians had opened in haste along the moor. She found instead the fenced posts, and the wire strung between them, and beyond the wire a slope of broken ground with the headgear of the eighth heading lying on its side in it like a felled tree, and she stood at the fence for the better part of an hour before a constable, not unkindly, told her the ground was closed and she should move along. She wrote nothing of that hour in the second book kept in the linen chest. It was the one thing in those years Faire nan Lòchran's minutes never held.

## V. Of the Pumps Stopped to Save Fuel

The gallery that flooded at Muileann chrom that same season lay three miles up the valley from the barge-stage at Seann Toll, in the workings of Mòrag nic Iain's own district, under an agent new to the pit that year, a narrow, quick-spoken man named Edgar Holt who had come up from the coalfields with strict word from Ros dhomhain that the yield of every pit on the island was to hold, whatever the season asked of it.

The gallery's pumps ran on coal, as every pump on the hill ran on coal, and in the last week of an t-Ògmhios, with A' Chompanaidh's own stores at Seann Toll drawn low by the shipments south and a barge two days overdue, Holt gave the order that the pumps at the flooded heading should stand idle a night, to spare the fuel for the winding-gear until the barge came in. The overseer under him, a Dia-thìreach man named Fionnlagh who had cut coal at that face for twenty years, went to Holt's office himself the evening the order came down and said what a man of twenty years' standing at one face is entitled to say to any agent, however new: that the ground under that heading had never once, in his memory, gone a full night without the pumps running, not even in a dry summer, because the water came out of an old working above it that nobody living had ever mapped. Holt heard him out standing, and answered that the barge was expected within the day, that the winding-gear could not be spared its coal until it came, and that the crews would go down at the ordinary hour as they always did. The pumps were stopped at dusk.

By morning the gallery had filled to the roof for its whole length. Fionnlagh went down himself with the change of shift, to see for himself before he sent any other man in ahead of him, and so he was among the seven who did not come up again, though the roll that lists them gives his name no more weight than any of the others.

Mòrag nic Iain Maor was at the pit-mouth when they brought the seven up. She was forty-two that year, and had carried A' Chompanaidh's staff, the one her great-grandfather Raghnall Maor had taken from the agent's hand a hundred years before, brass-capped and iron-shod, for six years, since her father Iain Maor's death. She had stood at more pit-mouths than she could count by then, but she said afterward, to the one or two who asked her, that she had never in her life heard a silence like the one that morning, with the rain coming down steady on the boards and the seven laid out in a row on them and no sound anywhere but the feet of the women of the camp coming up the track, and no one yet weeping, because no one yet believed it enough to weep.

At noon Edgar Holt rode up from the office with four constables behind him, and stood over the row of the dead, and began, in the humans' tongue, to speak of the loss to the working.

The first stone came from somewhere behind Mòrag and took him on the shoulder before the interpreter had turned two of his words into Dia-thìris. After that the air was full of stones, and the constables were shouting one thing and the crews another, and Mòrag was shouting too, though she could not afterward say what, only that she had been trying to be heard over both. She saw a constable bring his rifle up to his shoulder before she understood what he meant to do with it. She saw the smoke of it before the sound of it reached her, which she said afterward was the strangest thing of the whole morning, stranger even than the stones: that the eye had time to see a thing the ear had not yet caught up to.

When it was over, four Dia-thìrich lay in the mud of the pit-yard beside the seven already laid out from the flood, and one constable lay with them, shot, the roll says, by his own fellow in the confusion of the crowd, though the inquiry that followed never settled whose hand had fired the ball that killed him.

## VI. Of the Inquiry and the Copy That Was Kept

The inquiry sat at Ros dhomhain in am Faoilleach of the next year, on 4 am Faoilleach, AE 138, in a long panelled room in Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that Mòrag had never before had cause to enter, before three commissioners sent out from the capital of an Tìr Thall for the purpose, none of whom had ever set foot at Muileann chrom nor meant to. She wore her good dark dress, the one kept for burials, and carried A' Chompanaidh's staff with her into the room, though nothing in the summons had asked her to bring it, because she judged, rightly as it turned out, that the sight of it in her hand would make it harder for the commissioners to pretend they were questioning some stranger off the hill and not the fourth Steward of Muileann chrom, whose family's name had stood on that staff since before any of the three commissioners had been born.

She was asked a great many questions about the stones, and fewer about the pumps, and she answered every one of them as it was put to her, in order, without hurrying to the part she had come to say. When at last a commissioner asked, almost as an afterthought, whether she knew anything of why the gallery had flooded at all, she told them: that the pumps had been stopped the evening before on the agent Edgar Holt's own order, to spare fuel for the winding-gear until a barge came in, and that the overseer Fionnlagh had told him plainly what the water would do, and that Holt had given the order regardless.

The clerk at the little table below the commissioners' bench wrote it down as she spoke it. She watched him write it, word for word, in a hand a good deal neater than her father's had ever been. Then the eldest of the three commissioners, without raising his voice or his eyes from the paper in front of him, said that the witness's account of an order she had not herself heard given was not evidence proper to the inquiry, and instructed the clerk to strike the passage from the record.

The clerk drew a single line through what he had written, not so heavy a line that the words beneath it could not still be read, and turned the page.

Eilidh nic Raghnaill was not in the room, and had no right to be, but the clerk who kept the second copy of the inquiry's minutes, the one made for A' Chompanaidh's own file and not for Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's, was a Dia-thìreach woman of Ros dhomhain whose brother sat at Faire nan Lòchran's table beside Eilidh's own seat, and within the month a fair copy of Mòrag's stricken testimony, struck-through line and all, had made its way north to the room over Comann an Adhlacaidh at Baile thais, folded small inside a length of sailcloth that had nothing else remarkable about it. Eilidh copied it a second time into the linen chest, struck-through line copied as struck-through, word for word, so that whoever read it after her would see exactly what had been said and exactly what Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir had chosen not to hear.

She was given a seat of her own at Faire nan Lòchran's table that same winter, no longer the youngest with the least to say. It was am Faoilleach still, the hundred and thirty-eighth year turning over the same as every year before it, the same cold rain on the same grey roofs down to the same sea, and if anything else had changed in Baile thais that winter beyond one more woman's place at one more table, the roll that came down to Muileann chaol does not say what it was.

## VII. Of What the Two Rolls Kept

A' Chompanaidh's letter-books show Robert Fairley posted the following year to workings on the eastern side of the island, and there his part in the telling ends.
