Of Sìne nic Aonghais, keeper of the lost lamp, this alone is told: the shrine-keepers who came after her at Achadh chaol lit a new lamp without her name on it, for want of any line to carry the name from. Elsewhere in that year's telling the copyists let every doubled hand and disputed order stand, for a reader to weigh one against the other. Here they let the page stand empty, and wrote nothing to fill it.

# Part Six: Of Cogadh nam Beann

# Chapter Thirty-four: Of the Warning and the Constables


*AE 138 – 141*

## I. Of the Grey Fever

Eilidh nic Raghnaill was three-and-thirty the winter the fever came in on the ships, and she had already buried her father.

Raghnall Breac had died the summer before under the hill at Cill ghlas, and there was no grave to go to, only the fence. She had gone back to Baile thais and to the crew she led at the pit-mouth, and to the room behind Comann an Adhlacaidh's hall where six or seven met at a time and called themselves nothing, because a thing with no name could not be struck off a roll of A' Chompanaidh. She had taken her father's place there without being asked to and without anyone saying she had.

On the second of Gearran a coal ship out of an Tìr Thall put in at Ros dhomhain with nine men too sick to stand, and by the time the harbour physician came aboard, four of the crew who had carried them up from the hold were coughing too. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's clerk who wrote the entry called it a fever of the chest, plain and grey, not the green sickness of the galleries and not the flux of the quays that the older custodians still remembered, but a thing of its own, and it went through the young and the strong before it troubled the old, which was against all the custodians' long experience of fevers and which no one below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir could explain. It ran inland along the coal roads the way every sickness on the island now ran, because every road on the island now led, sooner or later, to a pit.

At Baile thais it came up from the harbour in a carter's chest cough by the middle of Gearran, and Eilidh watched two of her own crew go down inside a fortnight, a hewer named Tormod Buidhe and his sister's boy who had not yet had his first wage. She sat with them by turns, because Comann an Adhlacaidh's rule was that no one died watched only by strangers, and she was better at sitting than most, having had the practice of it with her father. Tormod Buidhe lived. The boy did not.

"He asked me what month it was," Eilidh told the room behind the hall, the night after she buried him. "Near the end. He asked what month it was, and I told him, and he said it wrong back to me, and then he didn't say anything more."

Nobody answered her. It was not the kind of thing the room answered.

She had kept Comann an Adhlacaidh's rule of sitting long before it was hers to keep, because her father had taught her it before he taught her anything else about the crew she now led: that a man dying underground or above it had a right to a face he knew bent over him, and that the right did not stop being a right because the man dying was a stranger's hired hand rather than kin. Tormod Buidhe, when the fever had run its course in him and left him standing, thin and grey-skinned and slower on the ladders than he had been, thanked her for the sitting in the flat way men thanked her for things they had not expected a crew-leader to trouble herself with, and went back to the pit-head within the fortnight because A' Chompanaidh's wage did not wait on a man's convalescence. The boy she had no name to give beyond the one his mother had given him, because the club's rule was also that a name too new to the world was the family's to keep or share as it chose, and his mother, when Eilidh went to her afterward, chose to keep it, and Eilidh did not ask twice.

The fever did not confine itself to Baile thais, though Baile thais felt it worst of the hill camps that first season, being close-packed and close-breathing in a way the older, looser settlements were not. Along the coal roads it went the way every sickness on the island went now, following the carts rather than the weather, so that a camp a day's walk from the sea might catch it from a camp two days inland before either heard word of the other's dying. The custodians who kept the rolls that year learned to write the fever's progress the way a keeper wrote a tide, a thing that came and went and came again, worse in some towns than others for reasons no clerk below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir could set down with any confidence.

By the middle of an t-Iuchar the fever had reached Cathair mhòr, and there for the first time in the town's whole memory the market shut, stall by stall, until the custodians' roll for that week gave the dead by street and the longest list was the street of the carters, who breathed each other's coughing all day over the scales. Word of it came to Baile thais three days late, by a drover who had it from a drover, and Eilidh wrote it into the club's own book, which was not the custodians' roll and answered to no one, in the plain hand her father had taught her: *Cathair mhòr, market shut, the carters' street worst.* She had begun keeping that book the year he died, because she had watched him carry twenty years of names in his head and give none of them to anyone, and she did not mean to do the same.

The worst of it that year came at Dùn thais in the last days of an Dùbhlachd, where Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had for once sent a physician of its own rather than leaving the sickness to the custodians and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise between them. He took the fever from the patients he was treating and died of it inside the month, and two of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's nursing sisters with him, in the same week the old halls of the druid masters, empty since the teaching under the trees of Flidais had gone quieter than it used to be, were opened again as sick-rooms for want of anywhere else to put the dying. Eilidh had never met the physician and felt his death less than she felt the boy's, and was ashamed of that, and wrote it in the book anyway, because the book's rule, like Comann an Adhlacaidh's, was that a name went in whether or not the hand writing it had loved the person.

"They send us one doctor and the coal takes him too," said Griogal, an old hewer who had signed on with the club before Eilidh was born and outlived, by his own reckoning, three crew-leaders and two commissioners. "That's a fair trade, if you're counting."

"I'm not counting," Eilidh said. "I'm writing it down. There's a difference."

"Not much of one, from where I sit."

## II. Of An Dàrna Athchuinge

It was in that same fever winter, with the club's book already three pages longer than she had meant it to grow, that Eilidh began the thing that would carry her name into Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books whether she wished it there or not.

A' Chiad Athchuinge, the one drawn up at Ceann àrsaidh and carried by Peigi Ghlas to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir forty years before, which had ended, as Eilidh had heard it told a hundred times, with Peigi trimming a lamp at Cill ghlas and saying nothing more about it to anyone, had asked. Eilidh had grown up on the story of that asking and on the silence that came back for it, and she did not mean to ask twice in the same voice.

She drafted the new petition in Comann an Adhlacaidh's room by a single coal lamp, over three nights, with Griogal and two others reading each page back to her aloud so she could hear where it went soft. It was not long, and set out, in plain terms and without a grievance wasted on complaint, what the tithe had cost the settlements of the hills in the fever years and the drought years before them, what An Togail had cost before that and been ended too late to matter, and what the galleries themselves had cost in men, in tens counted plainly and not rounded the way A' Chompanaidh's own returns rounded them. Nothing in it was new. Its last line repeated the sentence A' Chiad Athchuinge had buried in the middle of a long paragraph where Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerks could read past it without noticing: that the hill would not go on being worked by people who were not asked whether it should be.

She did not write "would not be worked." She wrote "would not go on being worked," because Griogal made her say both aloud three times and told her the second one sounded like a woman who meant it and the first sounded like a woman asking permission to mean it, and she saw that he was right.

The petition went out from Baile thais on foot and by cart through the spring and summer of the next year, carried crew-leader to crew-leader and custodian to custodian by people who did not write down who had carried it to them, in case the list of carriers should ever be asked for by someone with the power to make it a list of the dismissed. By the twelfth of Lùnastal it had come to Cnoc dhìreach, where the custodian of that place, a broad quiet man named Coinneach Ruadh who had kept the post for eleven years and clerked for A' Chompanaidh's store besides, out of the same door most mornings, read it through twice at his own table before he signed it.

He was nine-and-forty that summer, old enough, he told his wife, to have signed worse things for less reason and to know the difference now that it mattered. He signed under his own name and his town's, the way the petition asked, rather than with the custodian's mark alone, because he judged, rightly as it turned out within the week, that a mark could be denied afterward and a name could not.

A' Chompanaidh's agent at Cnoc dhìreach had the letter of dismissal drawn up before the ink on Coinneach Ruadh's signature was properly dry, and delivered it to the store's door on the market-day, in front of the queue for the week's flour, so that everyone in the queue should understand plainly what a name under that petition was worth to a man who needed A' Chompanaidh's wage to feed a family. Coinneach Ruadh took the letter, read it standing in the queue where he had been handed it, folded it once, and put it inside his coat.

"Eleven years," he said to no one in particular, "and they didn't even wait for the week to turn."

He was one of eleven signatories who lost A' Chompanaidh's work that season for the names they had put to the petition, and of the eleven his was the one the custodians afterward remembered best, because he had been offered, twice, the chance to withdraw his name before the letter was drawn, and had twice declined it without argument, saying only that a name once given did not, in his understanding of the custodian's own law, belong to the giver to take back.

Word of it reached Eilidh at Baile thais within the week, carried, like the petition itself, by someone who did not give a name for the carrying. She had never met Coinneach Ruadh; it was some years yet before she did. Still she asked the messenger to describe him, and kept what she was told, a broad man, quiet, slow to raise his voice and slower still to lower his eyes; for she had begun, without quite deciding to, keeping a second kind of record alongside the club's book, a tally now of the living who had put a name to something and paid for it, so that if the day ever came when the petition's cost was totted up in full, the account would have more in it than hers alone. Griogal, when she told him, said only that eleven clerkships were a cheap price for Riaghaltas nan Coigreach to pay for silence and a dear one for eleven households to pay for a sentence, and that the two prices were never going to look the same from both sides of the ledger, whatever the petition said about being asked.

By the last days of an Dùbhlachd, when the petition had gathered the hands of custodians and crew-leaders across one-and-thirty settlements from the hill camps to the coast, it went up at last to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in a fair copy Eilidh made herself, in her own hand, because she would not have anyone say afterward that a woman's name had been put to words she had not written. Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's clerk who received it underlined the petition's last sentence in red ink before he passed it up the office, and it was that underlining, more than anything the petition itself said, that the custodians afterward agreed was the first sign Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had ever given of having read a Dia-thìrich word and understood what it meant.

"It's the first thing they've troubled to answer," Eilidh said, when word of the underlining reached Baile thais by the same slow relay of carts and drovers that had carried the petition out. "That has to be worth something."

"It's worth exactly what the answer turns out to be," said Griogal, "and not a hair more."

## III. Of the Answer

The answer, when it came, was constables.

In the last days of Gearran the following year word went round the coal roads that Merriman, who held An t-Àrd-mhaor's seat and had held it, by then, the better part of eight years, had ordered the constabulary tripled and posted companies at four of the largest camps at once: Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, each with its own fortified store built or refitted inside the month, and each paid for, the custodians' rolls noted with a particular flatness, out of the tithe the petition had complained of in the first place.

Eilidh watched the first company march into Baile thais on the twenty-fifth of that same Gearran, forty men in Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's grey with a wagon of timber and iron grille behind them for the new store's windows, and she understood before a single order was read aloud that the underlined sentence had not been answered so much as it had been priced.

"They read it," she said to Griogal, standing at the edge of the crowd that had gathered, silent, to watch the company make its camp on the ground below the pit-head that had until that morning been common ground for drying washing. "They read every word of it. And this is what they wrote back."

The store the constables built at Baile thais stood finished within the fortnight, walled and barred where A' Chompanaidh's old store had stood open on three sides, and from that week the settlement's own well, which had served the whole camp since before the concession was granted, lay inside the new wall and had to be asked for.

The officer who commanded the company, a young man named Prosser with a new coat and an old rifle, called the settlement together on his first rest-day to read the order that had sent him, and Eilidh stood at the back of the crowd with Griogal on one side of her and the old woman who kept the club's rolls on the other, and listened to a paper written in Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's flattest hand explain that the constables were come for the settlement's own protection, in these uncertain times, against disorder from any quarter. Nobody in the crowd laughed. The hill camps had long since learned the cost of laughing at a man with a rifle in front of his own company. Eilidh heard instead, all down the ranks of people around her, a particular silence, one she had learned to recognise from her own room behind the hall, where it meant a thing was being noted rather than accepted.

"For our protection," Griogal said afterward, low, "against disorder from any quarter. He didn't say whose disorder he meant. I don't suppose he needed to."

"He meant ours," Eilidh said.

"He meant ours," Griogal agreed, "and he's not wrong to. He just hasn't worked out yet how right he is."

A month later, in am Màrt, a barracks went up at Dùn chrom, on the capital side of the hills where the coal roads met the road to Ros dhomhain, built to hold two hundred men against a rising Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had apparently decided, on the strength of one petition and eleven dismissals, was now more likely than not to come. For most of that first year the barracks stood empty for want of constables to fill it, a fact the club's book recorded without comment, because Eilidh had learned by then that some facts were their own comment and needed no help from her pen.

"An empty barracks for two hundred men," Griogal said, the night she read the entry aloud, "built before there's anyone to put in it. That's a man building the wall before he's sure there's a war, and calling it an answer."

"Then we'd best not be the ones to prove him right too soon," Eilidh said, and put the book away.

## IV. Of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and the Sermon

The hawk-priests had their own answer, and it was not one Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir had asked for.

At Seann Skell that spring a priest of Mòd named Ìomhar Seabhag, who had kept the shrine there since before Eilidh could remember, began to preach that the hawk's long hunger, starved so many generations on the measured handful and the old teaching that a people who ate faster than the land could feed them would in the end be eaten by their own eating, had turned at last toward those who had done the eating: A' Chompanaidh, and Riaghaltas nan Coigreach behind it, and every hand that had signed a charter for a vein it had not asked leave to open. It was not a new teaching so much as an old one pointed, for the first time in most people's hearing, at a single target.

Word of the sermon travelled the way Murchadh Seabhag's had travelled two generations before, by fowlers carrying birds to the autumn markets and by carters who learned it by ear from men who had heard it whole, and within the season the hawk-shrines of the west had quietly become meeting-places for the club and for others like it across the settlements, without any order given that could be written down and used against them. The constables, garrisoned in their new stores and barracks, did not yet know it, and would not for some while, because a shrine was a shrine to them and nothing more, and no constable posted at a coal camp thought to ask why the hawk-priests of a dozen towns had lately grown so attentive to who came and went from their doors.

At Ros gheal, where the hawk-faithful fishing families had chased A' Chompanaidh's first customs officers off the harbour a hundred years before and had never entirely stopped being proud of it, they raised a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall itself that same season, in open sight of the customs house their grandparents had emptied. The constables ordered it down within the week, and a sergeant with four men pulled the stones of it into the water on a grey morning with half the town watching from doorways and saying nothing. It stood again inside three days, built in the dark by hands nobody in the town would name even to each other, and the constables pulled it down a second time, and a third, and by the third time they had stopped trying. No order had told them to stop; a sergeant who has torn down the same nine stones three mornings running begins, whatever his orders, to feel the particular foolishness of a man fighting a harbour rather than a person, and there is no rifle drilled that answers that. The fourth shrine stood at Ros gheal still, uncounted and unremarked, the ordinary furniture of a wall that had always had something on it.

At Inis bhàn, that same summer, the priests of the hawk sat down for the first time in living memory with a handful of the old teachers who still kept, quietly and mostly among themselves, the disputations of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean that Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had shut at Dùn thais years before. The two orders had disagreed for six generations over questions neither Eilidh nor anyone in her room behind the hall could have named with any confidence, the shape of the vein's own hunger, whether Mòd fed or merely watched, whether the school's old habit of answering one question with another was wisdom or evasion; and the meeting, by every account that reached Baile thais, settled none of it. The hawk-priest who had called the meeting was heard afterward to say that he had come away no surer of the druids' answers than he had gone in, and prouder of them for it than he had expected to be. It is written of that meeting only that it settled nothing between the two orders, and that both sides, having failed entirely to agree on the questions that had divided them for six generations, parted as friends, which struck Eilidh, when the news of it reached her, as very near the whole of what she had hoped the petition might do in the first place.

The fever, meanwhile, had not finished with the island. It returned that same summer and settled hardest in the north-west, about Baile chrom and the towns of the concession, where for the first time it took humans as readily as it took Dia-thìrich, sparing neither the concession farms nor the Dia-thìreach villages beside them. At Cathair gheal Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's hospital filled past anything it had beds for, and Hannah Webb, who had kept her night watch in the fields behind Baile chrom these eight years, went there to nurse, and found herself nursing in wards where Dia-thìrich and human sick lay side by side for the first time in the concession's history, because there was no longer room, or will, to keep them apart.

"They wouldn't share a well with us a year ago," she wrote, in a letter set down for her by a clerk of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise that went the rounds of the burial clubs as far as Baile thais, "and now they'll share a ward. I don't know if that's the fever teaching them something or just too tired to keep up the wall."

The letter went on, in the plain hand of the clerk who had written it out at Hannah's dictation, to describe a night when the ward had held eleven beds and twelve patients and a Dia-thìreach overman from the north-west galleries had given up his own cot without being asked to a human boy of the concession who could not have been more than nine, and had sat the rest of the night on the floor beside him with his coat rolled under the boy's head, and had said, when Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's sister thanked him for it in the morning, only that he had buried enough of his own that year not to want to watch a stranger's child go the same way for lack of a bed. Eilidh read that part of the letter three times before she read the rest of it, and thought of Tormod Buidhe's sister's boy, and did not write that part down, because some things she judged belonged to the person who had lived them and not to the club's book at all.

Eilidh put what remained of it in the book.

Further north the fever's returning was met each town in its own way. Muileann fhionn, a Dia-thìreach mill town of the concession country, shut its roads against it entirely that following spring and kept them shut a whole season, turning back the human carters of the concession at the town's edge with their loads still on the carts, a thing no custodian there had ordered and every custodian there afterward defended, and a thing the constables, still thin on the ground so far north, had neither the men nor, that season, the stomach to undo. A carter who tried the road twice and was turned back twice told it afterward as the only week of his working life he had been glad of a closed gate rather than aggrieved by one, because he had seen by then, on the roads behind him, what an open one let through.

At Tobar fhiadhaich, further north still, the fever took one household in three before it burned itself out, and the custodians of that small place, who had heard the old story of Sìne Ruadh's burnings at Àth ghlas from their own grandparents and had thought long about it, judged in the end that it had come on them too fast and too widely to be stopped by fire, and buried their dead instead without burning a single hut, a choice the roll records without praise or blame, in the same flat hand it used for everything else that year. One household in three was a count Eilidh made herself set down twice before she believed it, and she thought, writing it the second time, of the empty barracks at Dùn chrom built for a war that had not yet come, and of how much easier, in the end, it had proved for Riaghaltas nan Coigreach to build a wall for men who were not there than to send a single physician to a village that was dying by households rather than names.

It was the sermon from Seann Skell that Eilidh chose, in the end, to bring before the room behind Comann an Adhlacaidh's hall, on an evening in Giblean when the fever had gone quiet again for the first time in three years and the new constables' watch had, for once, let the road home from the pit-head pass without a search. A fowler passing through with birds for the spring market had left a written copy with the club's door-keeper, three pages in a copyist's hand, close enough to Ìomhar Seabhag's words, by the copy-keeper's account, to be trusted.

She read it by the same coal lamp she had drafted the petition by, a year and more before, and the room listened the way a room listens to a thing it has been waiting to hear said aloud by someone other than itself: Griogal with his hands still, the two youngest crew-leaders with their eyes on the lamp rather than on her, an old woman from Comann an Adhlacaidh's own rolls nodding at the parts she had already half known.

"The hawk remembers every meal it is given," she read, "and every meal it is kept from, and it keeps the reckoning longer than any clerk." She looked up once, at the line about the eating and the eaten, and saw on every face in the room the same thing she had felt reading it herself the first time: a thing nearer to hope than the petition, underlined in red ink and answered with constables, had brought them, and nearer still to the plain, hard patience of people who have waited a long time and mean to go on waiting a while longer.

She read it to the end and set the pages down and did not, for once, reach for the club's book to write anything in it. Some things, she had begun to learn that year, did not need her hand to be kept; they kept themselves, in the ears of everyone who had heard them said aloud in a room with the door barred and a lamp burning coal that had cost a man his life to cut.

# Chapter Thirty-five: Of the Houses on the Roads

*AE 141 – 146*

> *Cha tug mi dhut ach an rud a bha thu ag iarraidh nach fhaicinn.*
> I gave you only what you wanted not to see.

## I. Of the House at the Halfway Stage

Aonghas had kept An Taigh-seinnse Mòr for six years before he understood that the keeping of it had quietly become an answer to a question nobody had ever put to him straight. His great-grandmother Seònaid Bhàn had opened the house again in the first years of the digging, when Rathad na Mèinne was new mud and the carters still carried both coin and barter in the same pocket and would take either without a word said over it. The house had never once in three generations shut its door on a traveller who could pay. Aonghas kept that rule as he had been given it. He kept the accounts in the same ledger his grandfather had used, the covers gone soft as cloth, and he kept, without ever writing it anywhere, a second reckoning that had nothing to do with marks.

By the autumn of the hundred and forty-first year the second reckoning had grown larger than the first.

It began, as most things on Rathad na Mèinne began, with a man Aonghas had never met asking a favour he had not thought to refuse. A crew-leader from Baile thais came down with a cart of A' Chompanaidh of scrap iron and asked, over a cup he paid for honestly, whether the loft above the stable might hold six men a night or two, now and again, no questions wanted and none offered. Aonghas said the loft held what it held. He did not ask what the men carried, coming or going, and in time he stopped noticing that he had stopped asking. It was easier that way, and easier, he told himself, was not the same as blind.

He was not alone in it. Up the northern road, at An Leòmhann Buidhe, they took on six new ostlers in a single season, and every carter on the road remarked, laughing, that not one of the six knew one end of a horse from the other. At the singing house, An Taigh-òsta Grianach, whose songs had been Fearchar Bàrd's in the carters' grandfathers' day, they raised a wall round the yard and set a boy at the gate with a horn he had never once had cause to blow, though he kept it polished all the same. Down on the south-western road, at Am Buabhall Fortanach, Tormod Buabhall barred his gates at dusk and put a man on the roof with a glass, and once a week, on no fixed day, he sent a folded list up the road in the saddlebag of whichever rider was going that way, and never told anyone, not even the rider, into whose hand it was meant to come. Aonghas met him twice at the horse-fair at Muileann shean and never once asked him what was on the list. It was not a thing men on Rathad na Mèinne asked one another in those years. A house that asked too many questions of its guests soon found it had none.

Riaghaltas nan Coigreach called none of this by any name. There was no order posted, no notice nailed to a board of A' Chompanaidh, because there was nothing yet to forbid; six houses walling their own yards against thieves was no different in the letter of any law from An Taigh-seinnse Òir, the great house beyond Dùn dhearg, digging a well in its yard that same season and walling it round, against thieves, its keeper said. Aonghas turned it over some nights with his back to the fire and his ledger unopened on his knee, and came to call that the design of it, if design was the word for a thing that had grown up the way heather grows up a burnt hill, from no one plan and every man's smallest choice. A house could not be charged with sedition for keeping its gate shut after dark.

## II. Of the Landing Below the Fortunate House

Below Am Buabhall Fortanach, where the south-western road ran down toward the sea before it climbed again into the hills, there was a harbour too small to have a name in any chart of A' Chompanaidh, though the fishermen who worked it called it Doire shean, after the stand of old oaks on the point above it. It had never shipped anything grander than herring and the odd cargo of slate, and A' Chompanaidh's agents, who counted every barrel that moved by water on the west coast, had long since stopped troubling to count Doire shean's.

That was its use. What the great house on the road above could not carry by cart, for weight or for the eyes that watched the road, went down instead by the old fishing path to the little harbour, and came up again by the same path in the dark of the next tide. The fishermen of Doire shean, who had fished that water three generations under three different flags of custodian and A' Chompanaidh both, took to being paid, for certain nights' work that were never spoken of as work, in Comann an Airgid's bar, cut small, rather than in the coin Riaghaltas nan Coigreach minted at Ros dhomhain. Nobody asked where the silver came from and nobody, least of all the fishermen, was fool enough to spend it where a clerk of A' Chompanaidh might see it change hands. It went, most of it, into the ground under a hearthstone or into a widow's dowry chest, to be spent, if ever, by whoever came after, without asking what nights had earned it.

Aonghas went down to Doire shean himself twice that year, on pretence of buying herring for the house, and stood on the point in the wind with old Coinneach nan Ràmh, who had fished the water since before the first pit opened at Muileann chrom, and said nothing that either of them could not have said before a magistrate. It was Coinneach who told him, without being asked, that the loft at An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the northern road was never once, in two years, found empty by A' Chompanaidh's carters passing through, and never once held the same men two nights running. "They come like the tide," the old man said, "and go like it, and no man's ever caught the tide at its turning." Aonghas thought that a fine thing to say and a truer one than most things said on Rathad na Mèinne in those years, and he carried it home and kept it, the way he kept the ledger, without ever writing it down.

## III. Of the Post at the Far Shore and the Boys of the Ford

Word, in those years, moved slower than silver and faster than either A' Chompanaidh or Riaghaltas nan Coigreach ever managed to learn. It moved through An Sligeanach Fad' às, the post-house on the eastern road near the silver country, whose keeper took his rent, openly and by the season, from Comann an Airgid of Muileann chiar, and who never once in five years lost a letter that was worth the losing. Through him Faire nan Lòchran sent its word to the guild and the guild sent its silver back, and Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, whose own post rode the same road on the same days, never once thought to ask why a road-house should need two keepers' worth of trade to fill one keeper's ledger.

The letters themselves, once past the Sligeanach's door, went the last stage by boys. They came out of Àth fhiadhaich, sons and nephews of the ford's boatmen, twelve years old and thirteen, too small for a constable to trouble with and too quick on the causeway paths for a mounted man to follow. They carried nothing that looked like a letter: a fold of paper inside a boot, a line of words learned by heart and said over to a woman at a well who would say them over again to somebody else three villages on. Aonghas met one of them once, a boy called nothing worth remembering here, who came into the house's yard soaked to the knee from the ford and asked for bread as any boy might, and left an hour later having said not one word out of place, and having left, folded under the loose board by the stable door where Aonghas kept certain things, a scrap that named a date and nothing else. Aonghas burned it that night in the kitchen fire, the way he burned every such scrap, and watched it curl and thought, not for the first time, how small and how ordinary a shape a great and terrible thing can wear while it is still only beginning.

The money for it all, for the boys' bread, the Sligeanach's rent, the loft at the Reòta that fed men it never named, was kept, in those years, at Achadh mhòr, a village of no great size near the great house on the eastern road, in the roof-space of its own shrine, above the rafters where the sacred lamp burned and below the thatch where no constable's search had ever thought, or dared, to reach. The custodian there was an old woman who kept the ledger of it in a hand so cramped and so plain that a stranger, finding it, would have taken it for a list of candles bought and wicks trimmed. Aonghas never saw that ledger. He knew only that when the loft at his own house needed feeding, word came, and marks came with it, folded inside a psalter that travelled the road as innocently as any priest's book ever had.

## IV. Of the Fire Taken for Heath

The day of 27 am Màrt, AE 143, was a dry, hard, bright day with a wind out of the north-west that had been blowing three days running and had scoured the sky to a colour Aonghas remembered afterward as harder than any blue he had seen before or since. He was in the yard at midday, seeing to a cart of coal-tubs bound down for Ros dhomhain, when one of the carters straightened and pointed east, up toward the long shoulder of Cnoc an Rabhaidh, where a thread of smoke was going up thin and steady into the wind.

"Heath fire," the carter said, and shrugged, and went back to his harness, because in that wind, on that hill, in that month, it was the likeliest thing in the world, and every man in the yard had seen a dozen such fires start from nothing more than a spark off a flint and burn themselves out by nightfall. Aonghas watched it a moment longer than the carter did. He had heard, though from whom he could no longer afterward have said, that the hill above Doire mhòr, a poor place now, its households few since it refused A' Chompanaidh's first contract and lost its water after, was to carry, on a day and at an hour nobody named aloud, a fire that was not heath at all, lit by the children's children of a woman called Beathag Dhubh, whose name the camps still used the way other places used a saint's.

Aonghas did not move from the yard, having no order to give and no man of his own to send, and reasoning that if the fire on Cnoc an Rabhaidh was the thing he half suspected it to be, then moving would tell any watching eye more than standing still. So he stood, and watched the smoke, and within the hour every wheel and hammer and windlass within sight and sound of the yard had stopped.

Every working the coal country held stopped in the same hour, without a single order carried by any rider Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own scouts could find. At Muileann bheag, far off among the druid villages in the north-east, the pits stopped, and the custodian there wrote afterward, in words that reached even Aonghas's ears months later, that it was the first thing her town had done with the hills in a hundred years. At Àth dhomhain in the north a runner on foot brought the word rather than any beacon, and the pits stopped all the same; their crew-leaders were among those Riaghaltas nan Coigreach later took and never gave back. On the northern coast the loading at Ceann bheag stopped before the dockers there had even been told to stop it; the coal simply ceased to come down to them, and they laid down their hooks because there was nothing left to lift. Quarrymen at Cnoc gheal, who cut no coal and owed Faire nan Lòchran no debt that any ledger recorded, laid down their tools with the rest and gave, when asked, no reason at all.

At Muileann chrom itself, and with it Baile thais, Cnoc chaol, the silver town and the eastern pits at Ros fhionn, every wheel stood still in the same hour the smoke went up from Cnoc an Rabhaidh. Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own agents, writing it down afterward for A' Chompanaidh's ledgers, called it the first stoppage the resistance of the coal country had ever managed to hold together, and granted, in words Aonghas heard repeated on the road for years after with something close to pride, that scattered as the Dia-thìrich of the hills were, town from town and valley from valley, they could act as one people when they chose to.

The yard at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr held that day a dozen men who could do nothing but wait. Aonghas fed them all, coal-tubs man and idle carter alike, and took no coin from any of them, and a woman among the carters, a driver named Cairistìona who worked the eastern run and had never before sat down in his kitchen, asked him quietly why he gave away a day's custom for nothing. "Because a house that charges for waiting is a house nobody waits in," he told her, "and I would rather have them here where I can see them than scattered on the road where I can't." She laughed at that, the first laugh the kitchen had heard all day, and it did him more good than the coin he had given up.

## V. Of the Six Days

Aonghas kept his own house open through it, as he had always kept it open, and turned no traveller from the door, though there were fewer travellers in those six days than the house had seen in any six days of his keeping. Rathad na Mèinne itself stood nearly empty; the carts that would have carried coal down to Ros dhomhain had nothing to carry, and the drivers who would have driven them sat instead in his yard with cups they were slow to finish, listening for word from the hills the way men listen for weather.

At Ros dhomhain A' Chompanaidh's steamships lay six days at the quay with their holds as empty as the day they were built, and the agents there wrote, in letters that found their way back up the road by the same paths the silver and the psalters travelled, that they had never in their years on the coast seen the harbour so quiet, and that the quiet frightened them a good deal more than any crowd ever had. A harbour that shouts can be answered with constables. A harbour that says nothing at all cannot be argued with, because it has offered nothing to argue against.

Force ended it, and no agreement. As the year went out the constables shut A' Chompanaidh's stores in every district of the coal country at once, so that a man who had stopped work in solidarity found within a day that his household could not eat without going back to it. Forty crew-leaders were taken up in the same sweep, from the hills and the eastern pits and the quarries at Cnoc gheal alike. Thirty-two of them were let go inside the fortnight, Riaghaltas nan Coigreach having found, on reflection, no law under which to hold men for standing idle on their own ground. The remaining eight went aboard a ship of A' Chompanaidh at Ros dhomhain and were carried east, for trial, it was said, in an Tìr Thall, and no letter, no rumour, no word carried by boy or boat or silver-bought fisherman ever came back from any one of them. Aonghas asked, over the years that followed, more than once, of more than one man who might have known, and got nothing for an answer but a shake of the head, which in time he learned to give himself when others asked him the same question.

The constables burned the heather of Cnoc an Rabhaidh that same week, to deny the hill a second such beacon, and it grew back thin and late the following spring, the way burned heather does, and it was three years before anyone on that road spoke openly of the fire that had, everyone by then knew and no one by then troubled to deny, been no heath fire at all.

## VI. Of the Idle Harbours

The ships grew fewer after that, and older. No single season and no single order brought it about; it crept in the way frost creeps into a house through a door left an inch ajar, unnoticed until the cold is everywhere at once. The keepers' daybooks at Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh of the ring, whose only business had ever been to count the sails from over the sea, began to show, year on year, fewer ships making the crossing, and the ships that did come were older hulls, patched and repatched, as though the yards that built them had troubles of their own that A' Chompanaidh's letters never named outright, speaking only, when they spoke of it at all, of difficulties at home.

At Caol leathan the wool piled in the warehouses for want of ships to carry it to the humans' market, and the merchants there, who had for two generations sold nothing but by A' Chompanaidh's weight and at A' Chompanaidh's price, began quietly, against the plain letter of the law, to sell it inland again by barter, the way their grandmothers had sold it before the first ship ever came down from the north. At Caol bheag, on the northern coast, A' Chompanaidh's quay, built at no small cost for a trade in the eastern grain and the eastern cloth that had never, even in its best year, come to half of what had been promised for it, saw one ship in the whole of a season, and the agent stationed there, a solitary man in a solitary house at the edge of a coast that had never wanted him, wrote to Ros dhomhain that he had been forgotten, and got, so far as anyone on Rathad na Mèinne ever heard, no answer at all.

## VII. Of Leave No Longer Asked

The last of it, for Aonghas, came at Ros dhomhain rather than on the road, where he had gone in the autumn of the hundred and forty-sixth year, on the ordinary business of the house, to buy salt and nails and the small iron things a road-house could not make for its own use. He found himself in the market square, more by chance than by design, on the day Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's notice was read aloud from its own steps, as such notices always were, to whatever crowd the harbour cared to send.

It was known already, before the notice, that Charles Merriman had gone. He had held An t-Àrd-mhaor's seat fourteen years, since the year Iain Maor died and his daughter Mòrag took up the staff, and he left now in health too poor, it was given out, for the climate of the island, though there were those in the crowd that day who said it low, meant only for Dia-thìreach ears near them, that a man's health failed faster under a coal country that would not stay still than under any weather the island had ever sent him. In his fourteen years Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had begun, by such small and unspoken steps as the walling of a well and the manning of a roof, to give its commands without first troubling to ask the leave of anyone at all, and the pretence of leave asked and given, which had stood since the council's vote in the second year of the strangers, had worn thinner every year.

A stranger read the new notice, a soldier by his bearing and his coat both, unknown to every face in the square, and his name, given at the notice's head, was Lionel Strake. Aonghas listened, as the whole square listened, to the reading of his commission from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's own steps, a long document in the flat unhurried voice the humans kept for such things, naming his powers and his charge and the authority under which he held them. It named A' Chompanaidh. It named Riaghaltas nan Coigreach in an Tìr Thall. Nowhere in the whole length of it did it name Comhairle a' Chùraim, not once, not even in the old polite formula, *with the leave and counsel of*, that every Àrd-mhaor's commission before it, back to the first, had carried as a matter of course.

Aonghas stood in the square and understood, with no one beside him to say it aloud and no need for anyone to, that the pretence was over, let fall quietly with no vote and no battle to mark its falling, simply no longer thought worth the keeping up. He bought his salt and his nails and rode home up Rathad na Mèinne in the dark, past An Sligeanach Fad' às with its lamp lit and its post-bag hanging ready by the door, past the loft at the Reòta where a light showed and went out as he passed, and came at last to his own gate, where he stood a moment before going in, looking back down the road the way a man looks back at a house he has just left for the last time, though he had left nothing, and the house he looked at was only Rathad na Mèinne itself, running east into the dark toward whatever the soldier's commission, read without the council's name in it, was going to mean for all of them next.

He went in, and barred the gate, and did not, that night or for a long while after, write anything at all in the ledger with the soft covers his grandfather had kept.

# Chapter Thirty-six: Of the Breaking of the Staff

*AE 147 – 149*

## I. Of the Iron Bird

Mòrag nic Iain Maor was fifty-two that winter, and had held the overseer's staff of Muileann chrom for sixteen years, and had not slept a full night since the inquiry into the fight at the pithead, where she had told Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's table plainly that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order and had watched a clerk draw a line through the words as she said them. Faire nan Lòchran had a copy of her testimony all the same, kept in Comann an Adhlacaidh's box under the false bottom with the burying-money, and she knew it, and had never asked to see it, because a thing a woman does not hold cannot be taken from her hand.

She was at the weighing-shed door on the morning the bird came over, checking the tally against the agent's book as she had checked it every working day since her father died, when the crews at the pit-mouth below her stopped their barrows all at once and stood looking up. She looked up herself. It came from the south, low over the ridge, a long grey shape with wings that did not beat, trailing a sound like a swarm too large for any hive, and it went the length of the valley and back again before it climbed away toward Ros dhomhain and was gone.

Nobody at Muileann chrom had a word for it that morning. By evening every hearth in the district had one, borrowed from nowhere and understood at once: eun-iarainn, the iron bird, a thing that flew and was not alive. The old women said a bird that did not beat its wings had no soul in it and could carry none away, which was some comfort, though none of them could say what it had come to do, only that it had counted something from the air that the ground would not have given up so easily.

Mòrag wrote it into her own book that night, under the tally, in the private hand her father had taught her that no agent ever asked to read: *a grey bird went over the valley twice and did not sing.* She did not know yet that it had gone the length of every working district on the island that season, from Doire mhòr to the eastern silver country, and that Strake, new come to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, meant to have on paper what the ground would not give A' Chompanaidh's surveyors on foot.

Word of Strake reached the district before the bird did. Merriman had gone home sick the autumn before, an old man worn thin by fourteen years of a climate that had never once been unkind to him, and the man who came after him was a soldier, not a merchant, and did not trouble to send the custom letter asking the council's leave for anything. His commission was read out at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir to an empty bench where Comhairle a' Chùraim' seats had always stood, and no one from the council was there to hear it, because no one from the council had been asked. Coinneach Ruadh, who had lost his clerkship at Cnoc dhìreach for signing An Dàrna Athchuinge and had taken to riding the district roads with news nobody paid him for carrying, brought that word to Muileann chrom himself, sitting at Mòrag's table with his boots steaming by the fire.

"They've locked the hall," he said. "The whole council hall at Cathair dhearg, doors and all, and the keys gone down to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir in a soldier's pocket. The custodians are sitting in Macha's temple now, on the priests' own floor, because Macha's priests took them in when nobody else in the capital would risk Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's temper."

"The priests that blessed the coin," Mòrag said.

"The same," said Coinneach. "Half the order left the capital's temple years back for the forest at Cnoc bheag over that blessing, and it's the half that stayed and gave it who've opened the door to the council now. A blessing's a cheap thing to give, it turns out, and a dear thing to have given."

## II. Of Àithne a' Ghlacaidh

The edict came down in the autumn, printed in Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's own press and nailed to the counting-house door at every working on the island in the same week, so that no district could say afterward it had not been warned in time, though warning and consent are not the same thing and the edict asked for neither. It claimed for Riaghaltas nan Coigreach the right to take any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich that it judged needful for the widening of the workings, at a price Riaghaltas nan Coigreach itself would set, and it gave no appeal.

Doire mhòr was a morning's walk above Muileann chrom, close enough that Mòrag rode over herself when the first word came that the constables were there, though there was nothing in it that was hers to mend. It was the village whose custodian, Beathag Dhubh, had refused A' Chompanaidh's contract at her own door more than a hundred and thirty years before, and whose last few households were the first emptied now under the last edict A' Chompanaidh would ever write. She stood at the top of the lane while the constables carried out beds and looms and a loom-comb some grandmother's grandmother had carved, and stacked them at the roadside in the rain because the new shaft beneath the hill could not wait for dry weather any more than it could wait for leave. An old man sat on his own doorstone with his hands over his knees and would not move until two constables lifted him by the arms, not roughly, which was somehow worse than roughness would have been, because it meant they had been told to be gentle about a thing that could not be made gentle by the manner of the doing.

"Write it down," the old man said to nobody, to the rain, to Mòrag standing at the lane's head in her overseer's coat that marked her for a woman with some standing, though standing had never once turned back a cart. "Write down that they were gentle about it. Somebody ought to know they were gentle."

She had no book with her that day. She carried the sentence home in her head instead and set it down that night beside the grey bird that did not sing, in the private hand, because a thing written in two places is harder to unwrite than a thing written in one.

At Baile dhomhain, nearer still, the camp that had been laid out on A' Chompanaidh's own paper before a stone of it was cut, two whole streets came down within the month for a spoil-tip that the surveyors said the new galleries would need before winter. A' Chompanaidh offered huts at Àth ìseal and marks for the timber of the houses it took, which some families kept, weighing the marks against the winter coming, and most did not, going instead to kin in the hill villages where there was a floor to sleep on that no edict could nail a notice to. Mòrag heard the tally of it from the district's own custodian, a quiet woman named Sìneag who had never before had cause to ride to the steward's house and rode there now white about the mouth, asking whether the overseer's staff of Muileann chrom could do anything at all for a street that was not, strictly, Muileann chrom's to answer for.

"Nothing," Mòrag told her, which was true that week, though it would not stay true past the next summer, and she did not yet know how soon the edict's hand would close on her own district instead of her neighbour's, or that when it did she would have an answer ready that surprised her almost as much as it surprised A' Chompanaidh.

## III. Of the Order and the Staff

The order came to Muileann chrom itself in the height of the next summer, on A' Chompanaidh's own printed form with her own district's name filled into the blank by a clerk's hand, instructing the overseer to identify for clearance, within the month, such dwellings in the third and fourth rows of the camp as stood nearest the new gallery mouth, numbering not fewer than eleven households.

Mòrag read it twice at her table under the slate roof, the same table her father had sat at with the same order in a different year for a different widening, and had told A' Chompanaidh's man then that the staff would not do it, and had been overruled by a surveyor of A' Chompanaidh's letter that made his refusal no more than a delay. She thought of that, sitting with the paper flat under both her hands as if it might otherwise lift and fly out the window after the iron bird. She thought too of the old man on his doorstone at Doire mhòr, and the grey bird that did not sing, and Sìneag's white mouth asking for an answer the staff had not had to give.

No reply went back to Ros dhomhain. Instead she took the staff down from over the hearth, the brass-capped, iron-shod length of ash Raghnall had carried first and Dòmhnall after him and her own father Iain after Dòmhnall, its grip worn to the shape of three hands and now a fourth, and walked out of the steward's house and down through the town toward A' Chompanaidh's office with the staff in her fist like a woman going to a fight rather than a woman going to resign one.

The town came out behind her without being asked. A crew coming off the morning shift saw her pass the weighing-shed with the staff and left their barrows standing and followed; a woman hanging washing left the washing on the line; two boys who should have been minding a flock of half-wild goats on the slag heap left the goats to their own devices and ran ahead to be first at the office door, the way boys will run toward any commotion without troubling to learn first what it is about. By the time Mòrag reached A' Chompanaidh's door there were perhaps sixty people behind her in the street, not shouting, not yet, only walking at her pace the way a tide comes in, without hurry and without stopping.

The agent that year was a careful young man named Osgood who had never once, in three years at Muileann chrom, raised his voice to a Dia-thìreach worker, which the district had come, wrongly, to read as kindness rather than as the particular fear of a man a long way from home among people he did not understand and could not afford to provoke. He came to the office door at the noise and saw the staff in Mòrag's hand and understood at once, before she said a word, what she meant to do with it, because there was nothing else a woman carries a staff to a locked door to do.

"I won't clear the eleven households," Mòrag said. "Not the third row, not the fourth. Not this year, not on this order, not on any order that comes after it with the same seal on the bottom."

"The order isn't mine to withdraw," Osgood said. His hands, she noticed, were not quite steady on the doorframe, though his voice held. "You know that. I only carry what comes down from Ros dhomhain."

"Then carry this back," Mòrag said, and brought the staff down across her own bent knee.

It was old wood, dry through more than a hundred years of hearths, and the brass cap and the iron shoe did nothing to hold it, and it went with a crack that carried the length of the street and brought faces to every door along it that had not already come out on their own feet. She laid the two halves on the office step, not thrown, not flung, set down the way a woman sets down a thing she is finished carrying, and straightened, and found that her knee, where the wood had broken across it, had taken a welt she would feel for a week and never once regret.

"Send that to Ros dhomhain instead," she said, "and tell them the fourth of my line has done what the first three couldn't bring themselves to."

She walked home through the crowd that opened for her and closed again behind her, and did not look back at the office, and did not need to, because she had already heard, before she reached the top of the street, three other names called out from three other doors: Griogar Camshron of the north pit, who had held the eastern gallery's staff for six years and threw his own down in the yard within the week rather than be the one man left holding wood A' Chompanaidh had marked for treachery; the overseer of Cnoc chaol, whom Mòrag had never met but heard of before the month was out; and a third, at the silver country's edge, whose name did not reach Muileann chrom until the winter, whose staff, it was said, was found propped against the counting-house wall with no one there to break it, because he had simply walked away and left it standing.

A' Chompanaidh put humans in all four places before the season turned, men who had never held Raghnall's staff and never would, and the office at Muileann chrom kept its ledgers after that in a hand that did not know the names of the third and fourth rows it now governed. So ended, in one summer, the office that Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill had taken up more than a hundred years before believing it the only door left open to him; and the custodians who had once hoped the staff would simply lapse, unheld, when the first overseer wearied of it, got their wish at last from the fourth in his line, though not in the manner nor in the year that any of them, dead or living, had ever thought to hope for.

## IV. Of the Silver and the Forest

Mòrag was no longer overseer of anything when Comann an Airgid's rifles came ashore, and found, to her own surprise, that she had more time for the district's true business than the staff had ever left her, and less patience for waiting to be told what that business was.

The guild at Muileann chiar had held its seam under a compact a century old, granted back when A' Chompanaidh still troubled to grant things rather than simply take them, and had kept its own arms in name only, an old militia roll nobody had called out since the compact was signed. That summer the guild began to buy rifles from the raiders of the eastern waters, where no gunboat of A' Chompanaidh had patrolled in years for want of coal to spare it, and paid the raiders in bar silver by weight, and entered the whole transaction in its own ledger under the heading of refining tools, in a hand steady enough that any clerk who read it would have believed the guild meant to melt the rifles down rather than load them.

Coinneach Ruadh, still riding the district roads with his unpaid news, brought that word to Mòrag's door along with the rest, and something else besides: that the custodians who had fled to Macha's dissenting priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag meant to hold a council there before the summer was out, a single council for the whole mining country, custodians and crew-leaders and priests together, the first such gathering A' Chompanaidh had never once been able to prevent because it had never once been told of it.

"They want you there," Coinneach said. "A woman who broke a staff in the street has more to say to that council than most who'll be sitting in it."

She went by night, on a borrowed pony over the ridge road and then off it, along tracks she had known as a girl and had not walked since, twenty-eight miles by her own count and every one of them dark, because a moon on a night like that would have shown the way to more than the council's own people. The forest at Cnoc bheag stood older than any road A' Chompanaidh had ever cut, oak and thorn grown up thick enough that the fires inside it, when she came to them at last past midnight, showed as no more than a red haze through the trunks until she was almost among them.

There were perhaps two hundred people in the clearing when she arrived, more than she had thought the whole quiet business of custodians and dissenting priests could have gathered without a single A' Chompanaidh's clerk hearing of it: crew-leaders she knew by sight from three other districts, priests of Òrd Mhacha with the black-and-grey horsehair of their office still worn openly for the first time in years, and a woman younger than Mòrag had expected, standing near the largest fire with her back very straight, whom she recognised from An Dàrna Athchuinge's underlined sentence before anyone spoke her name aloud. Eilidh nic Raghnaill was crew-leader of Baile thais and one of Faire nan Lòchran, and had drafted the words Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir itself had thought worth underlining, and stood now listening to older voices argue the shape of a council that had, in truth, already chosen her before the argument began, because there was no one else in that clearing whose name every district already knew.

## V. Of the Silent Town

Strake learned of Comhairle na Coille within the month all the same, by what road the district never troubled to ask, and answered it the only way an Àrd-mhaor with no council left to argue with could answer anything: with an order to seize.

The order named Eilidh nic Raghnaill first and the members of Comhairle na Coille after her, and the constables who carried it went to Baile thais in the last days of am Faoilleach, five miles down the valley from Muileann chrom, expecting, by every account that reached Mòrag afterward, a house to search and a woman to take from it.

They found the house standing open and swept, the hearth cold three days by the ash in it, and the town around it silent in a way that a mining town at midday is never silent, no barrows on the road, no children sent for water, every door shut and no face at a single window, so that the constables' captain, new to the district and unused to its ways, is said to have asked aloud whether the whole place had died of the fever in a night, and been told by no one, because there was no one left in the street to tell him.

Eilidh nic Raghnaill had gone by night two days before, on word carried ahead of the order by hands faster than Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own post, taking nothing from the house that could not be carried on foot and leaving the hearth swept because a woman raised to keep a house does not stop keeping it merely because she is leaving it for the last time. Where she went that night the district did not learn for some while, and did not need to, since it was enough to know she had gone, and gone whole, and gone before Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's hand closed on the place where she had stood.

Mòrag heard the whole of it from Coinneach Ruadh on the twenty-eighth of an Gearran, riding into Muileann chrom at a pace she had not seen him keep in the two years she had known him, his pony blown and his own breath short, so that he had to say it twice before the words came out in an order she could follow.

"They've called it," he said. "Not the council, the district. Every district. Word's gone out from the forest since last night. The grievance is one thing now across the whole mining country, and there's no council left at Cathair dhearg to bring it before, only Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir has had its answer this morning already, from Muileann chrom and Baile thais both."

Mòrag stood in her own doorway, in the house she still kept though the staff no longer hung over its hearth, and looked down the valley toward the pithead where the barrows had stood idle since dawn without her needing to ask why, and toward the ridge beyond which Rathad na Mèinne ran, empty now of every cart that had ever carried A' Chompanaidh's coal down it, and understood, with a plainness that surprised her less than it perhaps should have, what answer Coinneach meant: the one that comes only after a petition, and a strike, and a staff broken on a doorstone, have each in turn been tried and struck out or overruled or simply, as her own testimony at the inquiry had been, drawn through with a clerk's pen and filed away as though the drawing-through made the thing unsaid.

She did not sleep that night, the twenty-eighth of an Gearran in the hundred and forty-ninth year of the strangers' coming, any more than she had slept the night after the inquiry, but for the first time in all the years since, the waking did not feel like grief. She sat at her father's table with her father's book before her and wrote, in the private hand, a single line under the tally she no longer had any staff to keep: *the bird that did not sing has brought the whole hill to its feet, and I broke the first wood of it myself, and do not wish that back.*

Outside, along the whole length of the coal country from Doire mhòr to the silver hills, the fires that had been lit in secret for two years were being carried openly to every beacon height the districts held, and the light of them, when Mòrag went out at last to stand in her own doorway and watch, showed her more of her own country at once than she had ever seen by daylight: ridge after ridge answering ridge, from the forest at Cnoc bheag to the coast, each fire lit from the one before it, until the whole dark shoulder of the island seemed to have taken up, in one night, the single word that no council hall, no locked door, and no iron bird flying twice the length of a silent valley had ever yet managed to carry the length of it. War had come to the hills, and the staff that had broken across Mòrag nic Iain Maor's own knee, she understood now, watching the fires answer one another into the distance, had been only the first small crack in a much larger piece of wood.

# Chapter Thirty-seven: Of the Rising in the Hills

*AE 149*

> *Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc.*
>
> They burned the book, but they did not burn the hill.

## I. Of the First Light at Muileann chrom

Mòrag nic Iain Maor had broken the overseer's staff across her knee on A' Chompanaidh's own step the summer before, and in the months since she had carried nothing in her hands heavier than a tally-stick. On the twenty-eighth of an Gearran she carried a pike cut from a fence-rail, and led thirty men and women up the spoil-road to the walled store at Muileann chrom before the sky over the eastern ridge had properly whitened.

She had counted the store's watch for a month by then without once being asked to, the way a woman counts the doors of her own house without meaning anything by it: eleven constables, a relief of four at the changing of the watch, a locked gate with a bar dropped from the inside and no bar dropped from the outside in all that month, because no one in Muileann chrom had ever given A' Chompanaidh cause to drop one. She had that from the boy who carried the store's slops out each evening and had never once been searched for it.

The gate went down under four men with a felled larch before the watch inside had properly woken. Mòrag came through it herself, because she would not send others where she would not walk, and found the eleven constables drawn up in the yard in their shirts, most of them not yet properly dressed, looking at the pikes and the felling-axes and the sheer number of the crowd behind her with the particular stillness of young men doing arithmetic they do not like the answer to.

Their sergeant was a Cathair mhòr man not five years older than the boy who had carried the slops. He held his rifle a moment as though he had forgotten what a rifle was for, and then set it down on the cobbles with a care that looked almost like an apology, and the other ten set theirs down after him without being told.

"You'll not be harmed," Mòrag said, "if you go where you're sent and go quietly." It was the only promise she made that morning that she was certain, standing there, she could keep.

They carried off the rifles before the sun cleared the ridge, and the grain of the store after them, sack by sack, down the spoil-road to the weigh-house that had not weighed a pound of A' Chompanaidh in a fortnight and would not weigh one again. An old hewer named Tòmas Odhar, who had worked the Muileann chrom galleries since before Mòrag was born, stood at the empty gate afterward with his hand flat against the stone the way a man rests his hand on a horse's neck, and said to no one in particular that he had carried coal out through that gate for six-and-thirty years and never once thought to see rifles carried out through it instead.

Word of Muileann chrom reached Ceann fhada by midday, carried by a runner from Faire nan Lòchran who had not slept the night before and did not sleep that one either. A' Chompanaidh's coal quay at Ceann fhada had loaded barges for the coast since before the first pit at Muileann chrom was sunk, and the crews who worked it had spent a generation watching coal go out and little enough come back for it. They took the quay before the light failed, and that evening they scuttled two loaded barges across its mouth with their own hands, working chest-deep in cold water to knock the plugs from hulls they themselves had caulked the summer before.

A boatman called Pàdraig Reamhar, who had built the larger of the two barges with his father twenty years gone and had loaded her a hundred times since, stood on the quay afterward and watched her settle by the stern into the mud of the harbour bed, and said only that she had been a good boat, and that a good boat sunk on purpose was a different grief from a good boat wrecked, though he could not, pressed, have said exactly how. No coal left the hills by water again that year, nor the year after.

## II. Of the Eleven Days

At Baile thais, where the walls round the pithead had gone up within the memory of most who now stood outside them, the constables did not lay down their rifles at first light nor at any light soon after. Seumas Ciar had led the seventh shift of the Baile thais gallery for three years, since the crew-leader before him had gone to Cnoc bheag for Comhairle na Coille and not come back to the pit, and it was Seumas the crews looked to when the word came down from Muileann chrom that the rising had begun.

He had expected a morning like Muileann chrom's: a gate down, a yard of frightened boys, a promise given and kept before the sun was properly up. Baile thais gave him eleven days instead.

The walls had been raised, everyone in the camp had said at the time and said again now, against exactly this: a moor country, no second gate, a well dug inside the circuit before the first stone of the wall was laid, so that whatever came against Baile thais would have to starve it rather than storm it. Seumas had a hundred men and women outside those walls and a dozen ways to fill their hands, but no way at all to fill the constables' water-barrels with anything but time.

By the seventh day the bread the camp could spare had gone to a half-loaf a household, and the seventh shift's own children, who had at first treated the siege as a holiday from the gallery and had run the whole ring of it shouting insults up at the wall, had grown quiet and stayed close to their mothers' fires instead, in the particular way children go quiet when they have understood a thing without being told it outright. Seumas walked the ring each evening with a lamp shuttered against the wall's own watch, counting his own people rather than the constables', because it was easier, some nights, to know how many of his were still standing than to guess how many of theirs still had the will to hold.

They were not longer, in the end, by more than a day. On the twelfth morning a white cloth went up over the gatehouse, tied, the watchers below said afterward, to the same pole that had flown A' Chompanaidh's own flag the week before. The well inside had gone to mud two days past; the last barrel had been shared out by the constables' own sergeant in cupfuls, and even a cupful, by the eleventh night, was more than the barrel had left to give.

Word had come down to Seumas from Comhairle na Coille two days before that, carried by a girl of fourteen who had walked from Cnoc bheag by night roads she would not afterward describe to anyone: whatever garrison yielded at Baile thais was to be sent to the coast, whole and unharmed, under whatever guard could be spared to see it done. Eilidh nic Raghnaill's own hand was on the message, the girl said, and no one asked her to say more than that, for the hand was known.

It did not sit easily with every man in that circle. A hewer named Coll Buidhe, whose brother had died of the coughing sickness in a hut of A' Chompanaidh the winter the walls went up, stood at Seumas's shoulder as the gate opened and said, low, that eleven days of thirst was mercy enough for men who had kept walls like that one standing over graves like his brother's. Seumas did not answer him at once. He watched the constables come out into the daylight blinking and unsteady, thirty-one of them by the tally, the youngest not much past the boy who had carried word from Cnoc bheag, and he thought of the promise given at Muileann chrom that morning a fortnight gone, and of what it would be worth, the next time a wall had to be talked down rather than starved down, if this one were not kept.

"They'll walk to the coast on their own legs," Seumas said, "and every one of them will walk there whole, because Eilidh says so, and because I say so after her." Coll Buidhe did not argue further. He fell in at the rear of the guard that walked the constables east that same afternoon, and saw them fed from the crews' own stores before the road, which no one had told him to do and no one afterward thought to remark on.

Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books, when Strake's clerks came at last to write up the loss of Baile thais, did not trouble to record that the garrison had been spared. It was not a mercy Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir had looked for, and it was not a mercy Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir returned.

## III. Of the Moor and the Forge

Before ever a shot was fired at Baile thais, the crew-leaders of Baile gharbh and the pits north of it had met by night on the moor above Cnoc naomh, where the shrine ground had filled two generations before with the dead of the green plague and the field beside it had never since been ploughed. Each man and woman who came to that meeting brought a stone of spoil carried up from their own pit's own heap, and the stones were set down together in the dark and left in a cairn that stood there after, uncarved, saying nothing to anyone who did not already know what it was for. They fixed the week of their rising in an hour, by the light of a single shielded lamp, and were gone from the moor before the shrine's own watcher came up at dawn to see to the flame, so that he found only the cairn, and no one to ask about it.

Within that week the pits of Baile gharbh rose together with the posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and took them the way Muileann chrom had been taken, at first light, with more men outside the gates than inside them. The constables of the three posts were sent south on foot under no guard at all, their own legs and their own fear judged guard enough, and every one of them reached Rathad na Mèinne inside two days, footsore and talking loudly, to anyone who would stand still long enough to hear it, of how the whole of the north had gone over in a single week.

It had not, quite, gone over in a week; it had been three years coming, though few outside the crew-leaders' own circle knew how long, and one of those who did know was the smith Uilleam Gobha of Muileann dhearg, who had spent most of those three years turning A' Chompanaidh's own blasting-powder, bought a keg at a time on a chit of A' Chompanaidh for work that was never quite finished, into something A' Chompanaidh had not sold him and would not have sold him if he had asked.

Uilleam was thirty-and-nine that year, a broad, quiet man who had shod more A' Chompanaidh's mules than he could count and had grown, over the counting, to dislike A' Chompanaidh rather more than he disliked the mules. He forged pike-heads by day out of rail-iron torn from the disused sidings of the galleries, plain honest work that any smith on the island might have been set to and no agent thought twice about; by night, in the same forge with the shutters drawn, he packed the powder into tin cut from the coal sheds' own scrap and crimped the seams by hand, a slow and unforgiving labour that had already cost one man three fingers before Uilleam came to it and was determined it would cost him none.

He tried the first of them on the open moor behind the forge on a night with no moon, alone but for his eldest son holding the lamp a good way off, as Uilleam had told him to. It went off with a flat, ugly crack that put the birds up out of the whole valley and threw a spray of rock and scorched turf a man's height into the air, and Uilleam Gobha stood looking at the small smoking hole it had left in the ground for a long moment before he said, to no one, that it would do. The rebels' council wrote afterward, in the roll it kept of that first season, that without Uilleam Gobha's forge the rising in the hills could not have been fought at all past its opening weeks, and whoever wrote the line had the right of it, though Uilleam himself would only say that a smith does what a smith is asked to do, and left the rest for others to judge.

Rathad na Mèinne that ran from the capital up into the hills had one house standing across its middle stage that mattered more than any fort: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, kept these three generations by the line of Seònaid Bhàn, and kept now by her great-grandson Aonghas, who had spent the autumn before filling its loft with more men than any innkeeper's licence allowed and telling A' Chompanaidh's inspectors, when they asked, that the extra hands were for the harvest. On the day the word came up from Muileann chrom, Aonghas shut the gates of his own house across the road with his own hands, and the men in the loft came down armed, and the road between the capital and the hills was cut at its half-way stage and stayed cut for the whole of that year and longer.
