No coal came down it, and no column went up it, without Aonghas's leave, which he did not give.

## IV. Of the Rising of the Capital

Word of the hills reached Cathair dhearg by the third day, carried faster than any rider by the simple fact that half the capital had kin working a gallery somewhere north of it and had been waiting, without quite admitting to themselves that they waited, for exactly this news. The custodians who had sat shut out of their own hall since the winter Strake came did not wait to be asked twice. They broke Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's locks on the council-hall doors with a coal-hammer borrowed from the smithy across the square, and sat down again in the chairs that had been theirs before any lock was hung on them, and the roll they kept from that day forward opens without a word of apology for the two years it does not cover.

The townsfolk of Cathair dhearg held the bridge that A' Chompanaidh had built for its own coal-carts against the constables sent up in haste from the harbour, and barricaded it with the very carts it had been built to carry, turned on their sides and lashed together with chain from the ironmonger's own stores. It was not a fortification any soldier would have approved, and it held all the same, for three days, until the constables who had been sent to clear it were called back to guard the harbour instead and never came again.

At Cathair dhomhain the townsfolk broke open the stone warehouse A' Chompanaidh had raised along the lake shore in the first years of Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, the first building the strangers had ever owned outright on Dia-thìr and the one the old tellings had asked their listeners to remember. They carried off its tools, its rope, its nails and its stored powder for the council's own companies, and left the warehouse itself standing empty and unlocked, its doors swinging, much as the huts of Cnoc gharbh had once been left standing in the years of the green plague, though this time a reckoning long owed, and at last collected, had emptied it.

At Muileann mhin, a river port a morning's walk east of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn, the townsfolk argued for three days over a decision that the towns north and south of them had each made in an afternoon. It was said afterward, by those who had stood in the market square through all three days of it, that the argument turned less on where their sympathies lay than on where their boats did business, for Muileann mhin's living came from carrying grain and timber to whichever bank paid for the carrying, and a boatman is slower than a hewer to burn a bridge he may need again. On the third evening the town sent its boats to the council at Cathair dhearg all the same, and through that winter and the hard one that followed them the Abhainn fhionn carried food down to the capital by night as steadily as it had ever carried A' Chompanaidh's coal down by day.

At Ros dhomhain, Lionel Strake drew what remained of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach back inside Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's walls and fortified A' Chompanaidh's own quarter of the harbour, setting what constables he still trusted at every gate and trusting the rest to stand where he could watch them. The town below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's hill, Dia-thìrich almost to the last household, neither rose against him nor lifted a hand to defend him, and it was this, more than any wall, that the letter-books afterward called the strangest siege of that first year: a garrison shut up against a silence rather than an army, in a city that went about its ordinary business at its ordinary pace on every street but the one that led up to the gate, and would not meet a constable's eye on that one.

## V. Of Blàr Àth chiar

It could not last, from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's side of it, without an answer, and the answer Strake sent was Major Peter Ashdown, with what constables and A' Chompanaidh's guards could be spared from the harbour, marching up Rathad na Mèinne to open it again and relieve whatever of the hills could still be relieved.

Ashdown found the road cut at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, as every rider before him had found it that season, and turned north about it along the older cart-track that ran down to the ford at Àth chiar, where Rathad na Mèinne crossed the river before climbing again into the hills proper. It was there, on the far bank, that the crews who had held Baile thais a fortnight before were waiting for him, dug in along the willow scrub with what rifles the walled store had given up and what Uilleam Gobha's forge had since sent up the road in a cart with a false floor of turnips.

The ford ran deep that season with a wet spring behind it, and Ashdown's column went into it waist-high and in poor order, the guns of the rear companies held up over men's heads and the horses of the baggage train balking at the current. The fire that met them from the far bank was neither heavy nor especially well aimed, most of those who held it being hewers and quarrymen who had never fired at a man before that week, but it did not need to be well aimed to do its work in a column standing chest-deep in moving water with nowhere to go but forward or back. Ashdown chose back. He lost forty men to the river and the fire together, and the whole of his baggage besides, abandoned on the near bank in the retreat and carried off by the same crews who had held the willows.

The rebels' own dead numbered nineteen, and it was Seumas Ciar, who had brought his Baile thais men down to the ford at Comhairle na Coille's summons and stood with them the whole of that wet afternoon, who carried the word back up to Cnoc bheag of who among them had not come home. The council's clerk, a woman named Fionnuala who had kept few enough happy rolls in her three years of keeping any roll at all, wrote the nineteen names down that same night by lamp-light, each with the pit or the crew it had come from, and read the whole list aloud the next morning to whoever stood near enough the hall to hear it, once, plainly, without a word added to it.

They were buried within the week on the moor above Cnoc naomh, near enough the cairn the crew-leaders had raised there in the dark before ever a shot was fired, so that the two piles of stone stood within sight of one another from that season on: the one raised in secret for a rising not yet begun, the other raised in the open for the first of what the rising had already cost. The council's roll gives the nineteen names in full, and does not say, because by the custom of that roll it was never asked to say, which was harder to keep: the stone laid down before the fighting, or the stone laid down after it.

# Chapter Thirty-eight: Of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe

*AE 150 Jan – Jun*

## I. Of the Word That Came to Cuan dhearg

Coinneach Beag was five-and-twenty that winter, and had been a boatman on the Abhainn uaine since he was old enough to hold an oar against the current, ferrying barrels and once, memorably, a bull calf that would not stand still, between the two landings at Cuan dhearg. He had never carried a letter further than the length of the town. He had never fired a rifle at anything but a scarecrow, on a dare, at fourteen. When the crew-leaders of the river towns asked for seven men who knew how to keep their feet on a hill road and their mouths shut on a matter that mattered, he put his own name forward before he had properly decided to, the way a man steps off a boat onto a landing before he has quite finished thinking about the jump.

The word came to Cuan dhearg all that spring in pieces, by carter and by boat and by the mouths of men who had walked further than they meant to, and each piece was turned over at the inn's fire until it had been handled by everyone in the room. Ashdown's column, beaten at the ford of Àth chiar and its forty dead left to the river, had fallen back through Dùn chrom and lain there a night; in the morning the town had shut its gates on the soldiers who slept in its barracks, and let the column go on to the coast without its own wounded, whom the townsfolk kept to nurse or to bury as it turned out. Coinneach heard that twice, once from a carter who swore he had it from a man who had seen the gates shut with his own eyes, and once from a boatman up from the coast who swore the same thing of a different town entirely, and he learned that spring, before he learned much else of the war, that a true thing and a thing a man wanted to believe could travel the same road at the same pace and arrive looking near enough alike.

Other word he trusted better, because it came with names attached and names could be checked. Comann an Airgid at Muileann chiar had declared for the council and put A' Chompanaidh's agents on the road east with their own papers under their own arms, untouched; the small post at Dùn ìseal had given up its rifles after one exchange of fire, and the whole eastern coast, from the silver hills to the sea, stood clear of any human arm that spring for the first time in Coinneach's life. At Dùn dhearg the custodians had sent grain south and read their declaration from the steps of the hall, quoting, an old man at the fire said with some pride, as though the words were his own kin's, the very sentence Fionnghal nic Artair had written against Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig a hundred and twenty-seven years before it mattered to anyone again. Riflemen had risen at Cnoc leathan to hold the eastern road. At Ros fhionn the crews had stopped the pumps in the same week and let the water have the lower galleries back, and the bridge on Rathad na Mèinne there, which Coinneach had crossed twice in his life on family business, stood silent, he was told, but for the birds.

Then in the early weeks of the year came the word that stopped the fire's talk dead for a night: a ship of A' Chompanaidh had come up the Abhainn uaine itself, not twenty miles below where they sat, and shelled the coal stage at Seann Toll to keep it from the rebels, and set the fishing town behind it burning. Three-and-twenty of the town's own people had died, and the ship had burned island coal to do it, the very coal the hills had raised and carried and weighed out for a hundred years, turned round in a boiler and fired back at the people who had raised it. Coinneach's uncle, who had fished those waters as a young man and knew every rock of the Seann Toll shore by name, said nothing for a long while after that word came, and then said only that he had not thought to live to hear of coal doing that, and went out into the yard and did not come back in until the fire had burned low.

It was into this spring, thick with word half-true and word too terrible to doubt, that the crew-leaders sent for the seven.

## II. Of the Waiting at An Cupa Dàna

They were told to come to An Cupa Dàna, the inn at Cuan dhearg, on a morning when the frost had not yet gone off the roofs, and to bring nothing that would mark them for what they were. Coinneach came in his oldest coat, with a whittled knife and a pair of boots resoled twice, and found six others waiting in the inn's back room already, men of the river towns he knew by sight if not always by name: a cooper's son from further down the water, two brothers who had worked a coal barge together since boyhood, a quiet man called Gillebrìde who had been a hawk-priest's server as a lad and knew the shrine roads better than anyone else in the room, and two more whose names Coinneach set himself that morning to learn and not forget: Ailig, who talked too much when he was afraid and said so himself, and Pàdraig Buidhe, who did not talk at all.

They were given letters, sealed, and told only that the letters went north to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig, to Ìomhar Seabhag at the shrine of Seann Skell and to whoever else along the road would hear the council's word and might be moved by it. They were given, each of them, a small thing cast in lead and shaped rough but unmistakably like a hawk stooping, and told these had been made from cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom that first morning of the war, melted down by a smith at Muileann dhearg who had more urgent work waiting and had done this first because someone had asked him to. Coinneach turned his over in his palm. It was heavier than its size argued for, and the edges where the mould had not quite closed were sharp enough to catch on cloth, and he thought, holding it, that he had never owned anything before that had once been meant to kill a man and was now meant only to be worn at the throat and shown to strangers as a token of trust.

They left at dark, when the last letter was in Gillebrìde's coat with the rest, each man's hawk at his throat on a cord of tarred twine, and the innkeeper's wife stood in the door a moment with a lamp and said nothing, because there was nothing to say to seven men going out into a war on a road that so far existed only as a hope: the hope that the letters would find hands willing to carry them further.

## III. Of the Road by Seann Toll

The first day's walking brought them down past the burned stage at Seann Toll, and Coinneach, who thought he had prepared himself for it on the strength of his uncle's silence, found he had not. The stage itself was a black frame over black water, and the houses behind it that had caught from the fire stood roofless, their thatch gone entire and their stone walls stained the colour of the smoke that had gone up through them. A woman was picking through what had been a hearth, sorting stone from ash with her bare hands, and did not look up as the seven passed, and none of them spoke to her, for there seemed nothing a stranger could say that would not be an insult to what she was doing.

They went on that day and the next through Baile thais, where the walled store the constables had held eleven days still bore, on its outer wall, the marks of whatever had been thrown or fired at it in that fortnight, and a boy of nine or ten showed them, unasked and with more pride than the matter perhaps warranted at his age, exactly where he had stood the day the constables came out with their water gone and their hands empty. Over the hills by Achadh dhomhain the road climbed out of the coal country proper into country Coinneach had never walked, heather going to purple-brown at its roots though it was not yet the season for its flower, and down the far side by the Abhainn ìseal to Cnoc bheag, where they slept a night in a byre by leave of a farmer who asked no questions and was given no answers, which both parties seemed to find the more honest arrangement.

At every hawk-house on the road, a low building of one room where the hawk-faithful of that district kept a fire and a bench and, more often than not, little else, one of the seven stood up among whoever sat there and read the council's letter aloud. It fell to Coinneach at a hawk-house he never learned the name of, a bare room with six benches and a fire down to embers, and he found his voice did not want to carry the way he had meant it to, and steadied it by thinking of the woman sorting stone at Seann Toll and telling himself the letter was, in its way, owed to her as much as to anyone in the room. He read it through once, the council's own words about the hill country and the war and what was asked of every district the letter reached, and when he had finished an old woman by the fire said only, "Well. So it has come to that," and no one answered her, because there was nothing to answer, the letter having said as much as needed saying.

Along Oirthir an t-Seabhaig the road ran easier, a track worn by shrine-goers rather than carts, and they came down to Inis mhin on the third day with their boots worn thin and their letters, Gillebrìde said, checking the packet each night by feel before he slept, all still dry and all still sealed.

## IV. Of Oirthir an t-Seabhaig and the Roads Off It

Inis mhin was a walled landing the humans had built and half abandoned when the trade that justified it thinned, and the seven lay twelve hours in a boat-shed there, sleeping in turns, while Gillebrìde went out to learn what could be learned of the roads ahead. He came back with word that undid, in a sentence, the ease of the last two days: Strake's constables rode the western roads out of Ros bheag every day now, in patrols of ten or a dozen, and a party of seven men on foot, however plain their coats, would be seen and stopped and searched before it had gone a mile past the town.

It was Pàdraig Buidhe, who had said perhaps forty words in three days, who found the carter willing to take them, a man of Inis mhin with a covered cart and a mule past its best years, who asked no more than a fair price and a promise that whatever was in the cart's bed under the sacking was not his business to know, a promise the seven kept to the letter by telling him nothing at all. They left the road that night and did not take it again, going by cart-tracks and field-edges known to the carter and to no map Coinneach had ever seen, and it struck him, jolting along in the dark with six other men and a mule that seemed to know the country better than any of them, that he had come further from home in three days than he had gone in the whole of the rest of his life, and that he had not, until that moment, had leisure to think about it.

## V. Of the Grass Above Tobar dhomhain

Above Tobar dhomhain the carter set them down before first light at the edge of a stretch of open grassland that ran along the ridge over the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession, and told them, with the flat certainty of a man who had lived his whole life within sight of that road, that from here they would see anything that passed on it for the better part of a day, and be seen by nothing, if they lay still and let the grass do its work.

They lay eleven hours. The grass was long enough to close over a man on his belly and cool enough, in the morning, to soak through a coat within the first hour, and by midday Coinneach's whole left side had gone from cold to numb to a kind of steady ache he stopped noticing only by giving his attention entirely to the road below. Ailig, three feet to his left, kept up a whisper of complaint for the first two hours and then, as the sun climbed and the road below began to show its traffic, fell as silent as Pàdraig Buidhe ever was, because there was, after all, something to watch.

They counted. A farm cart at dawn, going toward Ros bheag with what looked like wool. Two women on foot, going the other way, whom none of the seven could place as anything but what they seemed. And then, beginning perhaps an hour after the sun was properly up, the riders: constables in twos and threes and once a full dozen together, moving at an easy pace that told Coinneach, who had never sat a horse in his life but had watched enough carters manage tired animals to know the difference, that these were not men in any great hurry, nor men expecting trouble on this particular stretch of road that day.

By the time the light began to go, Gillebrìde's tally, kept on a strip of bark with a line for each rider and a cross for each group's leader, stood at forty-one. Coinneach checked it twice against his own count, made independently and kept in his head for lack of anything to mark it with, and came to the same number both times. What struck all seven of them, lying there in the last of the light before they dared move, was not the number itself, though forty-one riders was more than any of them had thought to see on one road in one day. It was the direction. Every rider, every cart, every single soul they had watched cross that stretch of road since first light, had been going south, back toward Ros bheag and the coast, and not one, not a single one in eleven hours of watching, had been riding north.

"They're none of them looking this way," Gillebrìde said, when they had at last crept back off the ridge into the shelter of a fold in the land where a man could stand upright and speak above a whisper. "Whatever Strake wants watched, it isn't this road. Not any more."

## VI. Of Inis thais and the Roads of an Fhianna

They came down to Inis thais on the evening of the sixth day out from Cuan dhearg, footsore and carrying, Gillebrìde reported once more, seven dry letters, and were brought before the priests of Òrd na Cloiche in the low stone temple above the harbour, where a fire of driftwood burned blue-white with the salt in the wood and the priests sat in a half-circle that made Coinneach, standing in the middle of it with the letters in his hand, feel more closely watched than he had felt lying in the grass above Tobar dhomhain with forty-one riders passing below him.

The priests heard the letter through without a word, and when it was done the eldest of them, a woman whose name none of the seven were told and none thought to ask, said that Òrd na Cloiche would send no men to the hill country's war, for that was not what Òrd na Cloiche was for. But she said also, turning her eyes from Gillebrìde, who had done the speaking until then, to Coinneach, who stood nearest the fire, that Inis thais would shut its harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships from that night, and that the hawk-faithful, wherever their roads led, would find an Fhianna's own ways open to them from here to the western city, a kindness she did not trouble to explain and Coinneach did not trouble to ask after, being by then too tired to do more than be grateful for it.

There Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe's road, as the letters had carried it, came to its end. What the seven had walked and ridden and lain eleven hours in the grass for was delivered, letter for letter, hawk-house for hawk-house, into hands that would carry its word further than any of the seven could have carried it alone; and at the western Seann Skell, some days after, when the company of the hawk-faithful was mustered under Ìomhar Seabhag's own eye, the seven of Cuan dhearg stood in its first rank and were told, by a priest who had heard already what they had done, that they were one thing now, with one name: Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe.

Word reached the muster at Seann Skell all that early summer the way it had reached the fire at Cuan dhearg, in pieces, and Coinneach, now a soldier of sorts though he still thought of himself most days as a boatman lent out for a season, learned to sort the true from the merely believed as he had learned it on the river road. The coal stacked on the quays of Inis mhòr, that A' Chompanaidh's ships had meant to burn in their boilers, went up instead at the townsfolk's own hand rather than fuel one more voyage like the one that had shelled Seann Toll, and the ships that would have taken it put in at Ros dhomhain and burned their own stores down to the last sack. Fishing boats out of both towns called Seann Chwen, sailing by night, boarded a coaster of A' Chompanaidh at anchor and burned her where she lay, and A' Chompanaidh drew what shipping it had left back into the two harbours it still held and kept it there. On the concession, Cathair gheal shut its gates and raised a militia that went nowhere and did nothing, its magistrate having written to both sides asking only to be left alone, a request the council granted and Strake did not trouble to answer; and at Muileann àrsaidh the town blocked its own road with carts and kept a watch on it against both armies at once, a watch no one on either side had yet tried to break.

The southern beacons went dark that spring, one after another: Tobar dhearg first, where the keeper, a woman named Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill of whom Coinneach knew nothing then but the name on a report read aloud at the muster, put out her own light with her own hand rather than let it go on guiding A' Chompanaidh's ships along a coast the council now held; and Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal followed her within the week. Two ships of A' Chompanaidh, feeling their way along that coast by night with no light to steer by, ran onto the reefs the beacons had been raised to warn them from, and were lost with what the letter-books, when they were read after, called regret and nothing more. From over the sea, in all that first half-year of the war, one ship came, bringing dispatches and a few crates of cartridges to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, which had asked for regiments, and sailed again inside the week, and Coinneach heard a priest at Seann Skell say, of that one ship and its light cargo, that an Tìr Thall had sent Strake exactly as much help as a man sends a drowning friend by shouting encouragement from the bank.

By midsummer, when the days over the western city ran long and pale into their evenings and the muster had settled into something less like seven strangers and a company of priests and more like an army, such as it was, the lines the war had drawn that winter had not moved. The council held the hills, the east, and the capital; Strake held Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, the harbour quarter below it, and the western ports; and neither, for all that had burned and all that had been counted on a strip of bark in a field above Tobar dhomhain, had found the strength that summer to break the other. Coinneach Beag, standing his watch on the road north of Ros bheag with a rifle he had been given and had not yet fired, thought sometimes of the forty-one riders, all bound south, and wondered, as Gillebrìde had wondered aloud on the ridge, what it was that Strake had judged worth watching instead of that road, and whether, wherever it was, the council's own eyes were on it yet. He did not know. No one at Seann Skell could tell him, that summer, and the watch went on.

# Chapter Thirty-nine: Of the Burning of the Ledgers

*AE 150*

> *Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc.*
> They burned the book, but they did not burn the hill.

## I. Of the Grain from Seann Warr

Dùghall Dubh had counted carts before, in the years he weighed coal for A' Chompanaidh at the Ros dhomhain scales, and he counted them now for the council out of the same habit, standing at the harbour quarter's upper gate with a tally-stick and a stub of chalk while the grain train from Seann Warr came in by the eastern road under a sky the colour of wet slate.

Nine carts, then eleven, then a gap the length of a held breath before the twelfth came round the bend with a wheel binding badly enough that the carter walked beside it, easing it over the ruts by hand. Dùghall let the tally rest a moment and watched the wheel. He had not eaten a full meal since the fourth day of the month and could not have said, if asked, whether it was the wheel or the hunger that made him watch it so closely.

Seann Warr lay two days east by the good road, a farming town in the flat country that had never seen a pit-head in its life and had sent grain to the hills every month since the winter the lines were drawn, by carts that went the long way round to keep clear of Strake's patrols out of Ros bheag. The council's roll in the yard behind Dùghall kept the count of every load: how many sacks, whose oxen, which nights the carters slept rough rather than risk a farm too near the coast road. It was a poor sort of harvest to be grateful for, twelve carts against a capital's hunger, but Dùghall had learned in a year of siege that a poor sort of harvest was still a harvest, and he thanked the carter by name and sent the last cart on to the sharing-yard with the rest.

The sharing-yard stood behind the custodians' hall, where Cathair dhearg's grain had been measured out by household since Strake shut himself up behind the harbour's gates the spring before: a scale, a clerk, a line that did not shorten by evening. The custodians themselves, Dùghall had heard it said more than once and had seen enough to believe, took no more from the scale than any weaver's widow in the line before them, and the saying had done more for the city's temper through that hard winter than any speech from the hall steps could have. Dùghall did not go often to hear speeches. He went to the sharing-yard the one day in five it fell to him, took his household's share, and went back to the harbour quarter, where the work that mattered to him was done with the hands and not the mouth.

That work, through the first year of the siege, had been watching. The harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain sat below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and above A' Chompanaidh's quays, close enough to the humans' lines to hear their bells and their drums and, on a still evening, the creak of their ships' timbers at anchor, and it had sat there a year now neither wholly for the council nor wholly against it, a narrow strip of stone houses and net-lofts caught between two powers that each wanted its gates and neither had troubled, yet, to take them. Dùghall's own house stood on the quarter's upper street, three doors from the counting-house where A' Chompanaidh had kept its tithe rolls since before he was born, and he had grown up close enough to that building's clerks to know most of them by their coughs before he knew them by their faces.

He had weighed coal at the counting-house scales for nine years before the war closed them, standing the same six hours of every working day on the far side of a steelyard from a clerk named Prentice, an easy-spoken man who kept a paper twist of peppermints in his waistcoat and offered one to every man whose load he entered against, Dùghall among them, without ever once asking whose account the entry would fall on come the year's reckoning. Dùghall had liked Prentice, in the plain way a man likes another he has stood beside for nine years without either learning much of the other's life outside the scales, and it was a strange thing, that summer, to find himself weighing in his own mind what he owed a man's peppermints against what the ledgers that man had kept owed the whole of the hills, and to find the second sum so much the larger of the two that the first could not be set against it at all.

He had not, until that summer, thought of the counting-house as a thing that could burn.

## II. Of the Roofs in Stocking Feet

The word to move came down from the council's captains in the first days of an t-Iuchar, carried as a question rather than an order, put to men who knew their own streets better than any captain could: could the harbour quarter reach the counting-house without a shot fired, and if it could, would it.

Dùghall put the question to six men he trusted before he answered it, all of them born within sight of the counting-house's slate roof, and all six said the same thing in different words: that they had watched A' Chompanaidh's clerks carry the tithe books past their doors for thirty years, entering against every settlement in the hills the debt the hills would spend the next thirty paying, and that a shot fired would only tell Strake's men where to look, while a fire lit quietly would tell them nothing until it was too tall to answer.

They went over on a night of low cloud with no moon in it, in their stocking feet, up the outside stair of the net-loft that backed onto the counting-house yard and along its roof-ridge on hands and knees, six men and Dùghall a seventh, each with a garret window he had marked in daylight and a rope coiled at his shoulder for the drop inside. Dùghall's own window stuck at the sash, swollen with the damp of a wet summer, and for the length of ten held breaths he worked it with the flat of his knife while below him, through the slates, he could hear the counting-house's night clerk moving about at his desk, entirely unaware that the roof over his ledgers had seven men crouched along it.

The sash gave without a sound worth the name. Dùghall went down the rope into a garret stacked with old tally-boards and out through a door that had not been locked in living memory, because no one in thirty years had thought there was a way in from above; and at the stair-head he found Fearchar Beag already waiting for him, having come in by the loading hatch on the ground floor with two others, the night clerk's lantern taken and turned down and the night clerk himself sitting on the counting-house steps in his shirt with his hands laced over his head, looking, Dùghall thought, more relieved than afraid, as though some part of him had been waiting a year for this night to come and was glad, now, to have it over.

The tithe books stood where they had always stood, in the long room above the loading floor, calf-bound and ranked on their shelves like a wall built of pressed hide, each one heavy enough that a man could not carry more than two at a stretch without his arms failing him before the yard. Dùghall had weighed coal by the ton for A' Chompanaidh once and thought he had lost the trick of being surprised by weight; the tithe books surprised him. It took the seven of them the better part of an hour to carry the whole wall down the stair and out into the yard, armful by armful, stacking them on the cobbles the way a mason stacks stone for a wall not yet begun, and by the time the last shelf stood bare Dùghall's shoulders ached in a way the coal scales had never made them ache, because the coal, at least, a man set down knowing it would be picked up again.

He struck the light himself, from a lantern-wick and a twist of oiled rag, and stood back while it caught along the bottom row and climbed. The sentry at the counting-house's front door, posted there every night of the siege against a raid from the water side, never turned round until the whole yard behind him stood lit like a hearth in a house with the roof off, and by then there was nothing left for him to do but blow the alarm bell and watch six men and their leader go back over the roofs the way they had come, unhurried, because a fire that size buys its makers more time than they need.

Dùghall stood a while at his own garret window afterward, watching the light of it redden the underside of the low cloud, and thought, without much satisfaction in the thought, that thirty years of a man's life could be made to weigh less than a garret full of old tally-boards, provided enough of it was burned at once.

## III. Of the Word from Ceann àrsaidh and Muileann chrom

The word of the other two fires reached the harbour quarter three days apart, each by a rider who had ridden hard enough to arrive gasping, and Dùghall heard both accounts standing in the same doorway where he had heard the first report of his own men's work, so that the three fires came to him afterward as one telling rather than three, the way a man remembers a single bad winter though it held a dozen separate storms.

The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh burned second, and the rider who brought word of it, a boy of Fearchar Beag's own age with Ceann àrsaidh mud still on his boots, told it with a care that made plain he had turned the telling over more than once on the road. The tithe-house held the portion owed by every settlement of the hills, entered against each in its own column since the first schedule was drawn, a record older by twenty years than the counting-house's tithe books and kept, by all report, more exactly. The Ceann àrsaidh companies had let the humans' clerks go unharmed before they carried the ledgers into the square, and it was there, the boy said, at the last, that Aonghas Ruadh's own successor in the custodian's chair had asked that one ledger be spared, to keep the record entire rather than soften the debt it named, so that in a settled year to come the hills might show by their own hand what had been asked of them and what had been paid. His own townsfolk had refused him. They had carried that one ledger to the pile with the rest, and a woman the boy would not name had said, loud enough for the custodian to hear it, that a debt kept on paper could always be raised again by whoever next held the paper, and that the only sure way to close an account was to leave no account to close.

The weigh-house at Muileann chrom burned third, and by the time that word came the harbour quarter had already had two days to grow used to the smell of old smoke on the wind off the eastern road, so that this third telling landed lighter than the first two, though the loss it named was, by every measure Dùghall knew how to take, the greatest of the three: the steelyard ledgers in which the coal of the hills had been set down by the ton since the earliest contract, the whole long reckoning by which A' Chompanaidh had known, to the ton and the shilling, what the hill had given it. The rider who brought that word, older than the first and less careful with his telling, said only that the rebels' own chronicler at Muileann chrom had written the fire burned green, from the damp in the old timbers or from something in the ink itself, nobody could say which, and that the camp folk who watched it were already making a verse of it before the ash had cooled.

Dùghall did not hear the verse whole until a week later, from a woman selling fish at the quarter's lower gate who sang it under her breath the way market women sing whatever is going about, without knowing or much caring where it came from: *they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill.* He bought no fish that morning and stood a while at the gate all the same, listening to her sing it twice through, and thought that whoever had made those eight words had done in eight what he had failed to do in a week of turning the Ceann àrsaidh woman's saying over in his own head.

## IV. Of Cnoc ghorm

Strake answered the fires the only way left to him, which was with the guns he still held inside his shrinking lines, and it cost him, by the harbour quarter's later count, the last strength he had to spend on the hills at all.

Word of Cnoc ghorm came to Dùghall as smoke on the wrong quarter of the sky rather than any rider's telling, a grey smear rising beyond the eastern ridge where no fire of the council's setting had any business standing, and for the better part of a morning the harbour quarter went about its work not knowing whether the smoke marked an advance of A' Chompanaidh or a defeat of A' Chompanaidh. It was Fearchar Beag, sent up to the net-loft roof with a glass borrowed from a fisherman, who brought the answer down at noon: A' Chompanaidh's guards and constables, sallied out from the capital's harbour under cover of the night to try the eastern road one last time and win back the way to the mining country, driven off at Cnoc ghorm in the hills beyond the city with losses the loft-roof glass could plainly see though it could not count them, riderless horses coming back down the road alone before the men who had ridden them.

It was the last such attempt Riaghaltas nan Coigreach made in the whole of that war, though no one in the harbour quarter knew it yet for a last thing; they knew only that the guns had gone quiet on the eastern road by evening and had not spoken again, and took what comfort a quiet road gave, which in a year of siege was considerable.

## V. Of the Lower Gates

Eight weeks after the counting-house burned, the harbour quarter did the thing Dùghall had watched it circle for the better part of a year without doing, and opened its lower gates to Buidhnean na Comhairle waiting beyond them.

It was not put to a vote, in the end, nor settled by any one man's word, though afterward more than one teller would claim the deciding of it. It was settled, as Dùghall came to understand it, by the plain arithmetic of a quarter that had fed Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's kitchens for thirty years and could no longer feed its own children while doing so, and by the counting-house yard standing burned the whole summer in full view of every window on the upper street, a black scar that made the old bargain look, each morning a family woke to see it, less like a bargain and more like a debt nobody now living had agreed to. Dùghall stood at the lower gate himself when the bar came off it, having asked to be there though the honour of the drawing had not fallen to him, and watched Buidhnean na Comhairle come up from the quays in good order, their captain a woman of Muileann dhearg he did not know by name, who thanked the gate-wardens plainly and asked, before anything else, where the wounded of the counting-house sentry's alarm bell had been carried, which struck Dùghall as a stranger's sort of first question and a better one than he had expected.

That same night, with the gates open and the companies bedded in the lower streets, men of the quarter went up to A' Chompanaidh's shed above the town where the flying machine had stood idle the whole length of the siege, grounded from the first month of the war for want of the spirit its engine burned, and burned the shed and the machine together. Dùghall did not go up with them; he had never much liked the look of the thing, an iron bird that had never once flown in his sight and had cost, by the tithe rolls he had weighed against in his working years, more than the whole harbour quarter's grain for a season, and he felt no want to stand over its burning the way he had wanted to stand over the tithe books'. He heard only, from his own street, the second glow of that night rising over the roofs to join the first, and thought that nothing had flown over Dia-thìr since Ceò Mhanannain first thinned that was not, in the end, a bird.

## VI. Of Cuan uaine and the Water Road

With the harbour quarter lost to him and the eastern road shut at Cnoc ghorm, Strake had one road left, and it ran by water: the Abhainn gheal down from Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir to the sea, and along it the river quays of Cuan uaine, a morning's row east of the capital, through which what little still reached him from the coast had been passed all that year.

Cuan uaine opened its own quays to the council's boats within the week, on terms Dùghall heard told two ways and believed neither wholly: that the town's boatmen had simply stopped turning the council's craft back, one morning, without a word said either way, the way a door left unbarred is not quite the same as a door thrown open, and is opened all the same. Whichever way it went, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir after that could be fed, if it could be fed at all, only by what a boat could carry past a watch that no longer troubled to look away.

## VII. Of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir Stripped

Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir fell to Buidhnean na Comhairle without a shot on the morning of the twenty-second of an t-Sultain, and Dùghall was among the first up from the harbour quarter to see it, walking the same streets he had weighed coal in half his working life, now empty of every uniform of A' Chompanaidh but for a handful of clerks too old or too frightened to have gone with Strake down the river the night before.

The house itself, when he came into it, told its own story before any clerk could tell it him: rooms stripped to the floorboards, presses standing open and bare, the great hall's long table left with nothing on it but the marks where other things had stood, dust-shadows in the shape of what a year of siege had taught its household to carry and what it had not. Strake had taken his officers, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's clergy and A' Chompanaidh's own agents down the water road in the night, by every account Dùghall gathered that morning, and had taken with them everything a careful man judges worth the carrying: plate, papers of account, the small close-held things a household gathers over thirty years and cannot bear to leave for an enemy's hands.

What he had not taken, because in his haste or his judgement he had not thought them worth the room in the boats, were the letter-books: shelf on shelf of them in a lower room off the hall, bound in the same calf as the tithe books that had burned three times over that summer, but filled with something the tithe books had never held, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's own correspondence back to an Tìr Thall since the first Àrd-mhaor's day, every dispatch sent and every answer, or silence, received.

He sent word to the council's clerks that evening, and by the next morning a table had been set up in the same stripped hall where A' Chompanaidh's long board had stood, with the first of the letter-books laid open on it under a good lamp, and men who had never in their lives been asked to read a stranger's hand bent over the close, foreign script with the same patience Dùghall had once given a scale that would not balance. He did not stay to read them himself, judging that he had done the part of that summer's work that was his to do, and went back down through the empty streets to the harbour quarter, where the counting-house yard still stood black three streets from his own door.

Dùghall passed it slowly on his way home, as he had passed it every day since the fire and would go on passing it, he supposed, until someone built something else there or the rains wore the black down to grey. A child of the quarter had chalked something on the standing wall in the days since, letters Dùghall could not fully make out in the falling light, and he did not go closer to read them; he had heard enough words made of that fire already, the Ceann àrsaidh woman's and the fish-seller's both, and judged that whatever a child had found to say of it belonged to the child and not to him. Prentice, he had heard from a clerk taken at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that morning, had gone down the river with Strake's household after all, peppermints and all, to whatever account was kept of him at Ros bheag or beyond it; and Dùghall found, standing in the last of the light with the black wall in front of him, that he could wish the man no particular harm and no particular good, only that the ledgers Prentice had kept so evenly for nine years were ash now on the same cobbles where he had once handed a boy his coin for the day's weighing, and that whatever came after the war would have to be reckoned by some other hand than that.

For the first time since the fourth day of the month he found, when he reached the sharing-yard, that there was bread enough to feed every household in the line before evening fell.

# Chapter Forty: Of the Truce and the Closing of An t-Aiseag

*AE 150 – 151*

> *Cha tàinig long.*
> No ship came.

## I. Of Ros Bheag and the Last Seat

By an Dàmhair there was no seat left to Riaghaltas nan Coigreach but Ros bheag.

Ros dhomhain was gone to Buidhnean na Comhairle, the harbour quarter first and then Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, stripped of its letter-books and its silver and left standing empty for the rats. Cuan uaine's quays had opened in the night without a shot fired. Lionel Strake, fifty years old that autumn and Àrd-mhaor of a government that now governed three streets and a wall, took what was left of it, his officers, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's clergy, a handful of clerks who had nowhere else to be A' Chompanaidh's men, down the Abhainn gheal by water and set it up behind the old walls of Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the earliest years, before Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had come into being to be housed there. He had been a soldier before he was ever an Àrd-mhaor, sent out young to a war he had never expected to end in a room with a view of a harbour and nothing left to command but the harbour's stores, and those who served under him in that last season said he gave his orders the way a man gives orders on a sinking ship, plainly, and without asking whether they would be obeyed a second time.

The human families of the west and the south came in behind him, a few thousand souls in all where there had once been tens of thousands, walking or riding or carried in A' Chompanaidh's carts with what they could load in a day, and Ros bheag, a town built to hold a few thousand of its own, took them in the way a burn takes a flood: badly, and not for long. The Dia-thìrich of the town, who had kept their own houses and their own market cross through three generations of A' Chompanaidh's officers coming and going at the quay below, watched the walls fill with strangers and found, most of them, that there was nowhere left in the town to be a stranger from, since the strangers now outnumbered them within their own gates.

Strake set constables along the coast road at Ros àrsaidh, to hold the way north and bring him word, and the townsfolk of Ros àrsaidh, who had watched three generations of A' Chompanaidh's officers come and go through their gates, brought the constables food and news both, the news always a day old by the time it reached them and older still by the time Strake heard it. At Cuan shean, where the first of the strangers' boats had ever touched the island, the custodians shut the harbour to every ship that flew A' Chompanaidh's colours, and set nothing further down about it. The roll that kept the record of that season wrote only that the harbour was shut, and let the silence stand for whatever else there was to say.

The roads cut and no ship from over the sea in months, Ros bheag ran short of food within weeks of the last family's coming in behind its walls. It was Eilidh Hale, Thomas Hale's daughter, who carried Strake's order down to A' Chompanaidh's store on the quay in the first days of an Dàmhair and read it out herself to the storekeeper, because the clerk whose task it should have been had taken fever and there was no one else free to send: that the stores were to be opened, from that day, to the human families and to the Dia-thìrich townsfolk of Ros bheag alike, at one measure, and no ledger kept of who took what.

## II. Of the Question at Baile Dhìreach

She left Ros bheag herself before the month turned, on an errand of her father's that no longer had anywhere to deliver its answer, and came south along the coast road to Baile dhìreach, where her mother's people had kept a house since before the walls at Ros dhomhain went up.

Baile dhìreach had sat, for as long as anyone living could say, under a council that was neither wholly the custodians' nor wholly Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's, three of each, chosen by the town and answerable to it before either side; and it had gone on sitting through the burning of the ledgers and the fall of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and the shutting of Cuan shean, because both the companies that might have broken it up had other towns to take first. Its children, the sons and daughters of the joint council's own families, were of both peoples in a way the rest of the war had stopped allowing anyone to be. Some had a human father and a Dia-thìreach mother, or the other way about; some had two parents of one people who had raised them, all the same, in both houses of worship and both sets of festival, because it was the custom of the town and no one before the war had thought to ask why. When the companies came at last, the council's men from the east and Strake's constables from the west arriving within the same week to claim the town for their own sides, each asked those children, one by one, which people they were.

Eilidh Hale was twenty-two years past being anyone's child and was asked all the same, because she had kept the joint council's books three winters running and everyone in Baile dhìreach knew her face. A young officer of the forest companies, no older than she had been when she first came to the town, put the question to her plainly, not unkindly, on the steps of the council hall with half the street watching: which was she.

She stood a while before she answered, long enough that the officer shifted his weight and looked past her at the crowd, as if the crowd might answer for her. She had her father's colouring and her mother's tongue and a ledger under her arm written half in each, and she had buried people on both sides of the question inside a year, and she found, standing on the steps with the whole of the street waiting, that she did not have an answer to give that would not be a lie to one half of what she was.

"I keep the books," she said at last, which was true, and no answer, and she went on keeping them.

Most of the joint council's children gave some version of the same reply, or none at all, and it is written of that season, plainly, without more said, that neither side made them choose. Eilidh Hale stayed at Baile dhìreach through what was left of the war, and stayed after, when staying had become the harder thing to do.

## III. Of the Last Ship

The last ship known to come from over the sea anchored off Ros bheag at an t-Samhain, in weather too rough for a longboat, so that she lay out a full day and a night before a boat could be got to her at all. Word of her went round the walls faster than any boat could carry a man, and by the time the harbour master's launch put out to her there were families standing three deep along the quay who had not been told to come and had come anyway, on the chance of it.

She brought no soldiers and no grain. What she brought, the harbour roll set down afterward, was one sealed letter for An t-Àrd-mhaor, carried up from the boat by a sailor who would not say who had written it or from how far it had come, and who took his passage money for the return in silver and would not be drawn into speaking of the crossing beyond that it had been long, and that he did not care to make it again. Her berths, once the letter was ashore, filled with every family in Ros bheag who could buy or beg a place in them, and she put out on the next tide, deep in the water and low on stores, and was not seen again from Dia-thìr.

What the letter said to Strake, no roll of the island ever recorded. He read it alone in the room the townsmen had given him for an office, by a window that showed him the harbour and the ship standing out from it, and he was seen afterward by his own clerks to burn the outer wrapping in the grate and to keep the letter inside his coat for the rest of that winter. No man who worked under him claimed to have read a word of it before or after, and those who watched him that evening said only that he stood a long while at the window once the ship was gone from it, looking at nothing the window still showed him.

## IV. Of the Truce of Àth Àrsaidh

Envoys of Comhairle na Coille and of what remained of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach met at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the country the humans had first settled and now alone still held, in the last week of an Dàmhair.

They met in the town's meeting-house, a plain building of stone and turf with a single long table down its middle, the council's men on the one side and Strake's officers on the other, and between them, because neither side would trust the other's clerk alone with the writing of it, two scribes, one of each people, setting down the same words in two hands at once. The first day went on the naming of who should sign for whom, since the council had no crown to speak in the name of and Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, by then, had scarcely a government; the second went on the line the two sides drew on the map between them, argued mile by mile along a coast neither delegation had walked in full; the third settled, in less than an hour once the argument was spent, what three days had failed to agree in a morning: that the humans still on Dia-thìr should withdraw into the north-west country under the council's safe-conduct, unharmed on the road and unhindered at its end, and that the council in its turn would leave the towns of that country standing, their walls unbroken and their people, human and Dia-thìrich both, in possession of what they held.

Baile Mòr ruadh, the greatest town of that country, was named the place the columns would be received, and its own Dia-thìrich folk, who had lived under the humans' governance longer than any other town on the island and knew no other, were given the choice, plainly put to them at a gathering in the market square, of staying under the truce or going south with the council's men. The roll that counted them afterward set the two numbers side by side, and they came out close, near enough that no one afterward could say the town had chosen with one voice.

## V. Of the Columns North

They went in an t-Samhain and the first weeks of an Dùbhlachd, the human families of Ros bheag, of Cuan shean, of Baile dhìreach and the towns of the south-west, walking the western roads under the guard of Comhairle na Coille's companies, in columns that took the better part of a day to pass any one point on the road.

Hannah Webb went with them, though the country they were walking into was the one she already lived in. She had come to the hill country behind Baile chrom at nineteen, following her brother to the concession's fields, and had kept her night vigil on the field paths there and nursed in the wards at Cathair gheal through the fever; and when the first columns came up the western roads she walked out to meet them at the concession's southern edge and walked back with them, with a bundle on her back and a woman older than her mother on her arm, one of the last of the families to leave Cuan shean, because the woman could not walk fast and would not be carried, and Hannah would not leave her to walk alone. "I have nursed harder cases than a slow road," she told the woman, more than once, when the woman apologised for the pace, and meant it kindly; and the woman let herself be walked at whatever speed Hannah judged safe, and stopped apologising by the second day.

At Àth chrom the custodians of the town stood at the ford and counted the column over, family by family, the last count the Dia-thìrich made of the humans on Dia-thìr in that age, and it is written that the counting took from first light until past noon, and that no one on either side of the ford spoke more than the counting needed.

At Àth leathan, the last stage before the north country proper, the columns camped a night in the fields below the town, cooking fires strung along the hedgerow further than any one watch could count them from the wall. It is written that several of the humans who camped there asked the custodians the name of the place, and wrote it down for themselves before they slept, in whatever hand and whatever tongue each of them had; one woman, brought to bed of a child that same night under a hedge with two of her own people and the town's midwife working over her by lantern, is said to have asked the name a second time in the morning, to be sure she had it right, and given it to the child as if it were a christening name and no other had yet been settled on. What the rest of them meant to do with the name, the custodians who gave it did not ask and were not told.

## VI. Of the Keeper's Watch

At Taigh-solais Baile chrom, on the north-western headland, Lachlann mac Uisdein kept the light his father had kept before him, and his father's daybook before that, the same worn cover, filling now with a second man's hand.

He was forty that winter, and had known no other work; his father Uisdean had lit the tower first in his own youth and kept it through the years of A' Phlàigh Uaine, and had died with the daybook's ink not yet dry on the last page he wrote, and Lachlann had taken up the pen the same evening because the light did not keep itself and the wind did not wait on grief. He wrote what his father had written before him: the wind, the state of the oil, the ships seen and their bearing, and, on the nights there were none, the same three words his father had written on nights there were none.

A boat came up from Baile chrom below one evening with word, third or fourth hand by the time it reached him, that the last Àrd-mhaor had gone down to Cuan shean to take ship, and that the ship would go north-about past the headland on the evening tide, as every ship bound over the eastern sea had gone since before Lachlann's grandfather kept any book at all. Lachlann had never seen an Àrd-mhaor, nor any human of rank higher than the surveyors who had once come up the coast road with their chains, and he found, turning the word over as he climbed the tower stair, that he had no picture in his mind of the man he was about to watch leave, only of the ship.

He watched for her from the gallery through the last of the light, and saw her come up past the point further out than the coasting boats ever ran, three-masted and low in the water, showing no lamp he could see until she was nearly past, when a single light appeared at her stern, small and steady, and held so a long while that he thought at first she had anchored. She had not. She was standing out, slow against the ebb, and the light went with her, smaller each glass, until the dark of the water and the dark of the sky came together and there was nothing left to tell one from the other, and Lachlann stood at the rail of the gallery a good while after that, in case his eyes had been wrong about the last of it, before he went in and lit the lamp himself, because it wanted lighting, and wrote in the daybook, in his father's hand more than his own: *a ship of the strangers, three masts, going north about, showing one light. Did not come back.*

It is that book, kept in the same hand and the same plain words night after night, more than any order of the council's, that the roll of that winter leans on for the day and the hour of the last human commissioner's leaving Dia-thìr.

## VII. Of the Keys at Cuan Shean

The harbour officers of Ceann mhòr, of Cathair gheal and of Inis àrsaidh, the three ports of the north that had kept Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's charts and tallies since the earliest post at Ros dhomhain, rode down together to Cuan shean in the same week, each with his town's chest of harbour keys strapped behind his saddle, to give them into Strake's own hand before his ship sailed.

It was no part of the truce that required it. The council's writ did not run to those ports, tucked as they were behind the northern capes where the truce had drawn its line, and the three men might as well have kept the keys, or buried them, or thrown them into the sea their towns looked out on. They chose instead to ride two days south with the weight of them, and stood on the quay at Cuan shean in the last of the daylight and set the three chests down at Strake's feet. They said, between them, no more than that the accounts were even and the harbours in good order; that who would want the keys after was not for them to say; and that they had brought them, all the same, to the one man whose office it plainly still was, for as long as he held it. Each of the three had kept his father's post before him, as Lachlann kept his; none of them, that evening on the quay, spoke of what he would do when he rode home to a harbour with no office left to answer to.

Strake took the chests aboard with him, and no roll of the island records anything further of them, on a sea no ship of Dia-thìr had ever followed.

## VIII. Of the Beacons Relit

Comhairle na Coille, once the truce was signed and the columns on the road, ordered Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh lit again from Baile chrom round the coast to Tobar dhearg, the same ring that had burned through the years of An Togail to count human ships coming in.

They burned now for nothing that came. The keepers' daybooks, Lachlann's among them, went on being kept as they had always been kept, oil bought, wick trimmed, wind recorded, and the line beneath the weather where a ship would once have been noted stood empty night after night through an Dùbhlachd, until the keepers stopped troubling to leave the line and simply wrote, some of them, the same three words that had first been Uisdean mac Lachlainn's alone and were now half the coast's. *Cha tàinig long.*

No ship came. It was not grief in the writing of it, by the time the winter was old, so much as habit; the sentence had outlived the asking it once answered.

## IX. Of the First Chest

The rolls of that age, what the custodians could gather of them before the year turned, the copies of the two petitions, the book kept at Baile thais through the eleven days, the letter-books left behind in stripped Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and whatever else had not gone west with Strake's own clerks, came to Muileann chaol by cart in the last days of an Dùbhlachd, four chests bound in oiled cloth against the weather, with a single custodian riding beside them the whole way and sleeping across the lids at night.

Cailean mac Eachainn was fifty-three that winter, copyist of Na Trì Teaghlaichean of Muileann chaol since before any of this had a name, and it was into his hands the chests were given, because there was no one else at the mill house whose writing every custodian on the island already trusted. He signed for them on the step, in the cold, with the carter still stamping to warm his feet, and had them carried down into the cellar he had cleared for them through the autumn on nothing more than the word that they would be coming.

He opened the first chest alone, by lamp, on the last evening of the year, and found it filled less neatly than he had hoped and more fully than he had feared: papers out of order, some scorched at the corner, some still smelling of the smoke of the rooms they had been carried out of, a petition in a hand he knew and a ledger in a hand he did not, and under them all, wrapped apart in its own cloth as if someone at the last had thought to spare it, the book kept at Baile thais through its eleven days, whole.

That one he set aside, unread, and sat a while instead with his hand flat on the closed lid of the chest, the lamp burning low beside him, thinking less of what had been kept than of what the other three chests, still bound, might turn out to lack.

Word came down from Cathair dhearg at am Faoilleach's turning, on the first day of the new year, that the war was ended and An t-Aiseag shut, whatever way had ever let the strangers reach the island closed behind the last of them. The humans still on Dia-thìr had gone north under the council's safe-conduct into the northern country; and Cian and Lorccan, neither of them yet twenty, would grow up in the wake of it.

Cailean set the news down in no roll of his own that night. He only lit a second lamp against the dark, and drew the second chest toward him across the cellar floor, and began, again, to see what had been kept, and what had not.

# The Annals of the Age

## The Years AE 1 – 10

- <a id="ev-IV-0001"></a>**5 am Faoilleach, AE 1** — *The Crossing*. Humans come ashore on Dia-thìr, bringing their Church with them, and are given leave to stay. They are the first strangers met since the Sundering.
- <a id="ev-IV-0001a"></a>**13 am Faoilleach, AE 1** — *The ships met off the north-west* (Coinneachadh nan Long). That winter the mist that had lain on the eastern sea since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it lifts from the northern water. Two fishing boats of Achadh àrsaidh, working the water off the north-west cape where the Sea-Watcher is seen, meet three ships coming down out of the thin grey from the north, and hail them; neither side understands the other. The fishers turn south and the ships follow them down the coast toward Cuan shean. The fishers call the place Coinneachadh nan Long, the meeting of the ships, and the boats of Achadh àrsaidh still slow there.
- <a id="ev-EV-1001"></a>**21 am Faoilleach, AE 1** — *The word brought home to Achadh àrsaidh* (Achadh àrsaidh). The second of the two Achadh àrsaidh boats that met the strangers' ships off the north-west cape turns home and brings the word to its households, while Lachlann Odhar's boat leads the strangers' ships south toward Cuan shean. Achadh àrsaidh is the first place on the island to hear of the strangers, and it hears of them from its own fishers.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0001a"><em>The ships met off the north-west</em>, 13 am Faoilleach, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1010"></a>**28 am Faoilleach, AE 1** — *Lachlann Odhar leads the ships down the coast* (Achadh àrsaidh). Lachlann Odhar steers south from the north-west cape the length of a winter day, past the empty headlands of the north-west, with the strangers' ships shortening sail to keep behind him. He runs his boat up the shingle at Cuan shean after dark and wakes the custodians.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0001a"><em>The ships met off the north-west</em>, 13 am Faoilleach, AE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-1001"><em>The word brought home to Achadh àrsaidh</em>, 21 am Faoilleach, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1011"></a>**29 am Faoilleach, AE 1** — *The ships stand off Cuan shean in the westerly weather* (Cuan shean). A run of westerly gales keeps Na Trì Longan standing off and on beyond the bar of Cuan shean for many days. The town watches them from the dunes, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid forbids any boat to put off to them or any fire to be lit on the strand.
- <a id="ev-IV-0002"></a>**5 an Gearran, AE 1** — *Three ships off Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). Three ships down from the north anchor off Cuan shean, the first hulls of their size seen from Dia-thìr since the fleet of the Sundering. Their master, a captain the rolls name Edmund Harrow, comes ashore unarmed with eleven men and asks by signs for water.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1010"><em>Lachlann Odhar leads the ships down the coast</em>, 28 am Faoilleach, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1011"><em>The ships stand off Cuan shean in the westerly weather</em>, 29 am Faoilleach, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1002"></a>**28 an Gearran, AE 1** — *The rider from Cuan shean reaches Cathair dhearg* (Cuan shean). A rope-maker's son of Cuan shean rides the valley road to the capital in a day with Oighrig nic Leòid's letter on the ships. The clerk of the council reads it standing. The council's answer, two days later, bids Cuan shean feed the strangers, keep them apart and decide nothing.
- <a id="ev-EV-1012"></a>**18 am Màrt, AE 1** — *Oighrig nic Leòid gives water on the shingle* (Cuan shean). Edmund Harrow wades ashore at Cuan shean with an empty cask, and the custodian Oighrig nic Leòid gives him and his eleven men water from the town well under the old law of the shore. She has seven casks filled and refuses anything more on her own word.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0002"><em>Three ships off Cuan shean</em>, 5 an Gearran, AE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-1002"><em>The rider from Cuan shean reaches Cathair dhearg</em>, 28 an Gearran, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1013"></a>**24 an Giblean, AE 1** — *Three of Harrow's men buried above the tide-line* (Cuan shean). Three of the strangers, sick from the long voyage, die on the strand below the dunes at Cuan shean. Their own people bury them above the tide-line with a reading from a book and kneeling on the sand, while the town's children watch from the dunes.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0001"><em>The Crossing</em>, 5 am Faoilleach, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1014"></a>**13 an Cèitean, AE 1** — *Harrow's men mend nets on the dunes* (Cuan shean). Recovered from their sickness, the strangers penned below the dunes at Cuan shean begin mending the fishers' nets spread on the strand, unasked. The fishers learn from them a flat knot that does not slip, and call it the strangers' knot.
- <a id="ev-EV-1015"></a>**31 an Cèitean, AE 1** — *Buttons traded for fish on the strand* (Cuan shean). The first trade between the island and the strangers begins on the strand at Cuan shean, yellow-metal coat buttons for fish. The custodians forbid it twice and it goes on behind the dunes; at last Oighrig nic Leòid lets it be, and the fishwives wear the buttons on cords.
- <a id="ev-IV-0003"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, AE 1** — *Forty days on the dunes* (Cuan shean). The custodians of Cuan shean will not decide alone, and send inland to the capital for counsel. For forty days the strangers are fed on the beach and kept below the dunes.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1002"><em>The rider from Cuan shean reaches Cathair dhearg</em>, 28 an Gearran, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1012"><em>Oighrig nic Leòid gives water on the shingle</em>, 18 am Màrt, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1013"><em>Three of Harrow's men buried above the tide-line</em>, 24 an Giblean, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1014"><em>Harrow's men mend nets on the dunes</em>, 13 an Cèitean, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1015"><em>Buttons traded for fish on the strand</em>, 31 an Cèitean, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1016"></a>**4 an t-Iuchar, AE 1** — *Manannan's priests keep the tide-prayer through the forty days* (Seann Skell). Through the forty days the strangers are fed below the dunes, the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut at every tide without missing one. The harbour scribe enters their number each week, nine, with the weather and the thinness of Ceò Mhanannain.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <em>The mist thins</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_IV/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_Sundering.pdf#ev-III-0239a">→ An Aois Scaraidh, LE 1,813</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0003"><em>Forty days on the dunes</em>, 16 an t-Ògmhios, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0004"></a>**10 an t-Iuchar, AE 1** — *The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich rides south* (Baile fhiadhaich). Word of the ships reaches Baile fhiadhaich, up the western coast, in two days. Its custodian rides south to see them, and writes to the council that the strangers' ropes are better than ours and their manners worse.
- <a id="ev-EV-1003"></a>**12 an t-Iuchar, AE 1** — *Oighrig nic Leòid's letter to the council from her sickbed* (Cuan shean). From her bed at Cuan shean Oighrig nic Leòid writes to the council that she gave the strangers water under the law of the shore and nothing more on her own word, and that a leave given in the roll cannot be ungiven. She asks that it be read before the vote. The clerk notes it received.
- <a id="ev-EV-1017"></a>**28 an t-Sultain, AE 1** — *The strangers sheltered in the net-lofts* (Cuan shean). With the autumn gales the custodians of Cuan shean let the strangers off the open strand into the net-lofts along the harbour. The ships lie in the harbour with their yards sent down and a few hands aboard. The roll enters the lofts as a shelter for the winter and no leave.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0003"><em>Forty days on the dunes</em>, 16 an t-Ògmhios, AE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-1003"><em>Oighrig nic Leòid's letter to the council from her sickbed</em>, 12 an t-Iuchar, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1018"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 1** — *Oighrig nic Leòid falls ill* (Cuan shean). At Samhain the custodian of Cuan shean takes a cough that goes into her chest, and by an Dùbhlachd she cannot leave her bed. Custodians riding up to the council at Cathair dhearg stop at her bedside on the way.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-1017"><em>The strangers sheltered in the net-lofts</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0005"></a>**11 am Faoilleach, AE 2** — *The Council of Custodians grants leave* (Cathair dhearg). The Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg, which has sat in the crown's place since the crown fell empty at the close of the Age of Sundering, confirms the strangers' leave to stay under the high custodian Tormod mac Ailein. The council roll gives the vote as with one voice; a later hand in the margin notes that three custodians were absent.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1002"><em>The rider from Cuan shean reaches Cathair dhearg</em>, 28 an Gearran, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1003"><em>Oighrig nic Leòid's letter to the council from her sickbed</em>, 12 an t-Iuchar, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1017"><em>The strangers sheltered in the net-lofts</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, AE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-1018"><em>Oighrig nic Leòid falls ill</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1019"></a>**14 am Faoilleach, AE 2** — *The leave read on the strand at Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). A custodian of Cuan shean reads the council's leave to the strangers from an upturned boat on the strand, with a stranger who has learned some words in the net-lofts putting it into his own tongue. The strangers cheer three times and begin to send their ships' yards back up.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0005"><em>The Council of Custodians grants leave</em>, 11 am Faoilleach, AE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0006"></a>**9 an Gearran, AE 2** — *The quarter of sea they came from* (Cuan shean). Old sailors at Cuan shean say that the strangers came in from the same quarter of sea the fleet of the Sundering sailed into. The council forbids the saying in its hall. It is written down all the same, and never answered.
- <a id="ev-EV-1020"></a>**11 an Gearran, AE 2** — *The struck line in the council roll* (Cathair dhearg). Bidden to strike from the council's roll the old sailors' saying about the quarter of the sea, the clerk at Cathair dhearg strikes it and writes beneath the striking what he was told to strike, so that the next clerk should know. The saying stands in the roll so, struck and unanswered.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0006"><em>The quarter of sea they came from</em>, 9 an Gearran, AE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1021"></a>**24 an Gearran, AE 2** — *Lachlann Odhar's words at the harbour wall* (Cuan shean). Going home at last to Achadh àrsaidh in an Gearran, Lachlann Odhar stands on the harbour wall at Cuan shean and says aloud that the ships came out of the quarter Cabhlach an Scaraidh sailed into. Nobody on the harbour answers him, and he puts out for the north.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0006"><em>The quarter of sea they came from</em>, 9 an Gearran, AE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0007"></a>**26 an Gearran, AE 2** — *The land beyond*. The strangers name their homeland in their own tongue, but no scribe of the Dia-thìrich writes the word down. From the first season the scribes call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and its people simply the humans.
- <a id="ev-EV-1004"></a>**2 am Màrt, AE 2** — *The humans pray in a sail-loft at Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). On the day the strangers keep for their god a sailmaker of Cuan shean lends them his loft against the rain. They kneel on the sailcloth, the captain with the rest, while a priest reads from a book; they light no fire and burn nothing. Two priests of Manannan watch from the stair and go down to the water to say their own prayer. It is the first entry of the humans at prayer under a roof.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0001"><em>The Crossing</em>, 5 am Faoilleach, AE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0005"><em>The Council of Custodians grants leave</em>, 11 am Faoilleach, AE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-1005"></a>**3 am Màrt, AE 2** — *Wren and the priests come up to Cathair dhearg* (Cuan shean). Two priests of the humans and a boy ride up from Cuan shean on ponies of the town, a long day's road, and come over the bridge at dusk soaked through. The council lodges them in a house below the temple and gives them a long room on the east side of the hall. The younger priest, Samuel Wren, coughs in the damp of the lake country.
- <a id="ev-EV-1022"></a>**11 am Màrt, AE 2** — *Crìosd and an Eaglais written in the council roll* (Cathair dhearg). In the same season as an Tìr Thall the clerk of Comhairle a' Chùraim enters the name of the strangers' one god as the island hears it, Crìosd, and calls their faith an Eaglais, after the word their priests use of the whole company of their believers. They are the first words of the humans' tongue that the island takes and keeps.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-IV-0007"><em>The land beyond</em>, 26 an Gearran, AE 2</a>.</span>
