Constables sent under Strake's order find Eilidh nic Raghnaill's house at Baile thais standing open, its hearth three days cold, and the whole town silent around it, its people gone from door and window before the constables' captain can ask why.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0323"><em>The order to seize</em>, 3 am Faoilleach, AE 149</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6502"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149** — *The turnip cart to the ford* (Àth chiar). A cart with a false floor of turnips carries Uilleam Gobha's grenades up Rathad na Mèinne, past the cut, to the crews waiting at the ford of Àth chiar, the first of his work to leave Muileann dhearg for open fighting.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0335"><em>The fight at the ford of Àth chiar</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6503"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149** — *The nineteen of Àth chiar buried* (Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh). The council's clerk Fionnuala writes down by lamp-light the names of the nineteen dead of Àth chiar and reads the list aloud the next morning; within the week they are buried on the moor above Cnoc naomh, within sight of the cairn raised there before the fighting began.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0335"><em>The fight at the ford of Àth chiar</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 149</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0336"></a>**3 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *Ashdown's retreat through Dùn chrom* (Dùn chrom). Ashdown's column falls back through Dùn chrom and lies a night at the barracks there. In the morning the town has shut its gates behind them, and the column goes on to the coast without its wounded, whom the townsfolk keep and nurse.
- <a id="ev-IV-0337"></a>**15 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *The silver town rises* (Muileann chiar). The silver guild of Muileann chiar declares for the council and opens its armoury, and the Company's agents in the town are escorted to the coast with their papers. The guild's ledger notes that here alone the rising took nothing, for the humans had never held anything there to take.
- <a id="ev-IV-0338"></a>**17 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *The surrender at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The small constable post at Dùn ìseal, cut off by the rising at the silver town, yields to the silver guild's riflemen after a single exchange of fire. The east of the island is clear of human arms.
- <a id="ev-IV-0339"></a>**27 am Faoilleach, AE 150** — *Dùn dhearg declares* (Dùn dhearg). The custodians of Dùn dhearg declare for the council and send it grain. Theirs is the town whose custodian wrote the only surviving defence of the Small-Burning Law, and their declaration quotes it.
- <a id="ev-IV-0340"></a>**1 an Gearran, AE 150** — *Cnoc leathan's riflemen* (Cnoc leathan). Riflemen raised at Cnoc leathan in the east join the silver guild's companies and hold the eastern road. The Company's carters on the road are let go home with their carts.
- <a id="ev-IV-0341"></a>**13 an Gearran, AE 150** — *The eastern pits at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The crews of the eastern workings about Ros fhionn stop the pumps and walk out, and the lower galleries flood. The Company's engineers there go down the Abhainn chaol and take ship at Seann Mhorn for Ros dhomhain. The bridge on the eastern coal road falls silent.
- <a id="ev-IV-0342"></a>**15 an Gearran, AE 150** — *Seann Toll shelled* (Seann Toll). A Company steamship comes up the Abhainn uaine and shells the coal stage at Seann Toll to deny it to the rebels, and sets the fishing town behind it burning. Twenty-three townsfolk die. For the first time the humans turn the island's own coal, burning in their boilers, against a town of the Dia-thìrich.
- <a id="ev-IV-0342a"></a>**19 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The Leaden Hawk company* (Cuan dhearg). At An Cupa Dàna, the inn at Cuan dhearg, seven hawk-faithful crewmen of the river towns wait nine hours for the council's letters to the Hawk coast, and leave with them at dark. Each wears a hawk cast in lead from the cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, and they are called Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company.
- <a id="ev-IV-0342b"></a>**21 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The Leaden Hawk walks to the Hawk coast* (Cnoc bheag). The company goes on foot and lightly laden: past the burned stage at Seann Toll, through Baile thais, over the hills by Achadh dhomhain and Cuan bheag, down the Abhainn ìseal by Ceann òg and Inis ìseal to Cnoc bheag, and along the Hawk coast by Inis bhàn, Ros gheal and Seann Skell to Inis mhin, some fifty-five miles in a little over two days. At every hawk-house on the way they read the council's letter aloud, and at Seann Skell they leave it with Ìomhar Seabhag.
- <a id="ev-IV-0342c"></a>**22 an Giblean, AE 150** — *Rumours at Inis mhin* (Inis mhin). At Inis mhin, the northern landing the humans had walled, the company lies twelve hours in a boat-shed and hears that Strake's constables ride the western roads out of Ros bheag every day. They hire a carriage of a carter of the town and leave the roads altogether.
- <a id="ev-IV-0342d"></a>**23 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The watch in the grasslands* (Tobar dhomhain). A day and a half by carriage across country, off every road, brings the company to the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain in the western hills. They lie eleven hours in the long grass above the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession and count the constables' riders who pass. Their own list gives forty-one riders, none of them going north.
- <a id="ev-IV-0342e"></a>**25 an Giblean, AE 150** — *The Leaden Hawk at Inis thais* (Inis thais). A day and a half more by carriage, still off the roads, brings the company down to Inis thais, six days after it left Cuan dhearg. The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the council's letter in the temple of the Stone. They will send no men, but they shut the harbour of Inis thais to the Company's ships and give the hawk-faithful the use of the Fianna's roads. There the Leaden Hawk's road ends, and its seven join the hawk company when it is mustered at the western Seann Skell.
- <a id="ev-IV-0343"></a>**29 an Giblean, AE 150** — *Coaling from Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). The Company's steamships take their fuel from the coal stacked on the quays of Inis mhòr, the river port just east of the capital, whose barges carry it down the Abhainn fhionn to the ships at Cathair dhomhain. The townsfolk set the stacks alight. The ships put in at Ros dhomhain instead, and burn their own stores.
- <a id="ev-IV-0344"></a>**10 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *The fishermen of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). Fishing boats of Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast, board a Company coaster at anchor and burn her. The Company draws its coastal shipping back to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.
- <a id="ev-IV-0345"></a>**11 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *The other Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, further west on the south coast, join the raids along the shore. The rolls tell the two towns apart by the names of their boats.
- <a id="ev-IV-0346"></a>**24 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *Cathair gheal behind its walls* (Cathair gheal). The human town of Cathair gheal in the northern concession shuts its gates and raises a militia, but sends none of it south to the Residency. Its magistrate writes to both sides asking to be left alone. The council grants it; Strake does not answer.
- <a id="ev-IV-0347"></a>**28 an Cèitean, AE 150** — *Muileann àrsaidh closes its road* (Muileann àrsaidh). Muileann àrsaidh, a town of the concession, blocks its road with carts and keeps a watch on it against both sides. No one attacks it. The watch is kept to the end of the war.
- <a id="ev-IV-0348"></a>**5 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The hawk-shrines open* (Seann Skell). From the shrine at Seann Skell Ìomhar Seabhag declares that the war is Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it. The hawk-shrines of the west become mustering houses, and a company of the hawk-faithful marches south to join the council.
- <a id="ev-IV-0349"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The hawk company at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The company of the hawk-faithful is mustered at Seann Skell, the western city, a short march north-east of the human port of Ros bheag. It holds the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war.
- <a id="ev-IV-0350"></a>**9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The southern beacon dark* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The keepers at Tobar dhearg put out the beacon, and the keepers at Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal do the same. Company ships feeling their way along the coast by night run on the reefs the beacons were built to light, and two are lost.
- <a id="ev-IV-0351"></a>**10 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *No relief from over the sea* (Muir Mhanannain). The Administration's letter-books ask again and again for troops and ships from an Tìr Thall. In the whole first year of the war one ship comes, with dispatches and a few crates of cartridges, and sails again within the week.
- <a id="ev-IV-0352"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150** — *The lines at midsummer* (Ros dhomhain). The lines stand at midsummer where the first winter of the war left them: the council holds the hills, the east and the capital; Strake holds the Residency, the harbour quarter below it, and the western ports. Neither side has the strength to attack the other.
- <a id="ev-IV-0353"></a>**4 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *Grain from Seann Warr* (Seann Warr). Seann Warr, the farming town in the south-east and not the salt port of that name in the west, has sent grain to the hills by the eastern roads since the winter. The council's roll lists the carts.
- <a id="ev-EV-6524"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *Dùghall counts the grain carts from Seann Warr* (Ros dhomhain). At the harbour quarter's upper gate Dùghall Dubh, once a weigher of coal for A' Chompanaidh, keeps the council's tally of the grain train down from Seann Warr, twelve carts against a capital's hunger, and sends the last load on to the sharing-yard behind the custodians' hall.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0353"><em>Grain from Seann Warr</em>, 4 an t-Iuchar, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0354"></a>**8 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *Hunger in the capital* (Cathair dhearg). Its harbour held by the Residency, Cathair dhearg has gone short since the winter. The custodians share out the grain by household, and the roll records that they took the same share as everyone else.
- <a id="ev-EV-6525"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *The sharing-yard of Cathair dhearg keeps an equal share* (Cathair dhearg). Through the siege the custodians of Cathair dhearg measure the city's grain out by household at a scale behind their hall, and take no more from it than any household waiting in the line before them, a fairness the city's own hunger remembers afterward better than any speech.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0354"><em>Hunger in the capital</em>, 8 an t-Iuchar, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6524"><em>Dùghall counts the grain carts from Seann Warr</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0355"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *The burning of the tithe-books*. In three raids the rebels destroy the tithe ledgers of the humans' Administration. Later chroniclers make much of it; it did little.
- <a id="ev-EV-6526"></a>**24 an t-Iuchar, AE 150** — *Dùghall puts the question to six men of the quarter* (Ros dhomhain). Asked by the council's captains whether the harbour quarter can reach A' Chompanaidh's counting-house without a shot fired, Dùghall Dubh puts the question first to six men born within sight of its roof, and all six answer that a fire lit quietly will hold Strake's men longer than a shot ever could.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0355"><em>The burning of the tithe-books</em>, 9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6525"><em>The sharing-yard of Cathair dhearg keeps an equal share</em>, 9 an t-Iuchar, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0356"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The counting-house at Ros dhomhain* (Ros dhomhain). The first raid was on the Company's counting-house at the Ros dhomhain quay, within the lines. Men of the harbour quarter under Dùghall Dubh came in over the roofs, carried the tithe books into the yard and burned them.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EV-6526"><em>Dùghall puts the question to six men of the quarter</em>, 24 an t-Iuchar, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6504"><em>The night clerk of the counting-house is taken without a blow</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6504"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The night clerk of the counting-house is taken without a blow* (Ros dhomhain). The counting-house's night clerk is found sitting on its steps in his shirt with his hands laced over his head before the raiders reach the ground floor, and Dùghall Dubh judges, from the look of him, that some part of the man had waited a year for the night to come.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0356"><em>The counting-house at Ros dhomhain</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6527"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *Seven men cross the roofs in stocking feet* (Ros dhomhain). On a night of low cloud Dùghall Dubh and six men of the harbour quarter cross the net-loft roof-ridge to A' Chompanaidh's counting-house on hands and knees, in their stocking feet, and go down by rope through garret windows marked beforehand in daylight.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0356"><em>The counting-house at Ros dhomhain</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6504"><em>The night clerk of the counting-house is taken without a blow</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6528"><em>Word of the spared ledger refused reaches the harbour quarter</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0357"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). The second raid burned the Administration's tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, where the share owed by every settlement in the hills had been entered since the first schedule. The clerks were let go. The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared for the record, and their own people refused them.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6528"><em>Word of the spared ledger refused reaches the harbour quarter</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6528"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *Word of the spared ledger refused reaches the harbour quarter* (Ros dhomhain). A rider from Ceann àrsaidh brings the harbour quarter word that the custodian there asked one tithe ledger be kept whole for the record, and that his own townsfolk, naming the danger of any debt kept on paper, carried it to the burning pile with the rest.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0357"><em>The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6527"><em>Seven men cross the roofs in stocking feet</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0358"></a>**7 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The weigh-house at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The third raid burned the Company's weigh-house at Muileann chrom with its steelyard ledgers, where the coal of the hills had been entered by the ton since the first contract. The rebels' own chronicler writes that the fire burned green.
- <a id="ev-EV-6529"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The camps set the burning of the ledgers to a verse* (Ros dhomhain). Before the ash of the Muileann chrom weigh-house has cooled, the camp folk are already singing eight words of it at market, and the verse travels the coast faster than any rider: they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0358"><em>The weigh-house at Muileann chrom</em>, 7 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6528"><em>Word of the spared ledger refused reaches the harbour quarter</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0359"></a>**25 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *The fight at Cnoc ghorm* (Cnoc ghorm). Company guards and constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road are driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital. It is the Administration's last attempt in the war to reach the mining district.
- <a id="ev-EV-6530"></a>**28 an Lùnastal, AE 150** — *Fearchar Beag sights Blàr Cnoc ghorm* (Ros dhomhain). Sent up to the net-loft roof with a borrowed glass, Fearchar Beag reads Strake's last sally on the eastern road by its riderless horses coming back down alone, and brings the harbour quarter word by noon that the guns have gone quiet.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0359"><em>The fight at Cnoc ghorm</em>, 25 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6529"><em>The camps set the burning of the ledgers to a verse</em>, 21 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0360"></a>**4 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *The harbour quarter changes sides* (Ros dhomhain). After the raid on the counting-house the Dia-thìrich of the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter open the lower gates to the council's companies, and Strake is left holding only the Residency and the Company's quays. The same night men of the quarter burn the Company's flying machine in its shed above the town. It had not flown since the war began, for want of the spirit its engine burned, and nothing has flown over Dia-thìr since that was not a bird.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6531"><em>The captain of Muileann dhearg asks first for the wounded</em>, 4 an t-Sultain, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6531"></a>**4 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *The captain of Muileann dhearg asks first for the wounded* (Ros dhomhain). When the harbour quarter's lower gates open, the council company's captain, a woman of Muileann dhearg unknown to Dùghall Dubh by name, thanks the gate-wardens and asks before anything else where the wounded of the counting-house alarm had been carried.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0360"><em>The harbour quarter changes sides</em>, 4 an t-Sultain, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6530"><em>Fearchar Beag sights Blàr Cnoc ghorm</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0361"></a>**5 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Cuan uaine opens its quays* (Cuan uaine). The river quays of Cuan uaine, east of the capital, open to the council's boats. With them and the harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain both lost, the Residency can be fed only by water, up the Abhainn gheal from the sea.
- <a id="ev-IV-0362"></a>**21 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Strake forsakes the Residency* (Ros dhomhain). Lionel Strake leaves the Residency by water, down the Abhainn gheal, with his officers, the Mission's clergy and the Company's agents, and takes the Administration to Ros bheag. The council's companies enter the Residency the next morning and find it stripped of all but its furniture.
- <a id="ev-EV-6505"></a>**22 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *The letter-books found whole at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir* (Ros dhomhain). Where Strake has taken plate and account-papers down the river by night, Dùghall Dubh finds a room of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books left standing untouched on an unlocked shelf, thirty years of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own correspondence with an Tìr Thall, and sends word of it to the council's clerks that evening.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0362"><em>Strake forsakes the Residency</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6506"></a>**22 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Prentice the counting-house clerk goes down the river* (Ros dhomhain). Dùghall Dubh learns from a clerk taken at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that Prentice, who weighed coal beside him nine years at the counting-house scales, went down the river with Strake's household the night Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir fell, leaving the ledgers he had kept behind as ash.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0362"><em>Strake forsakes the Residency</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6532"></a>**22 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Clerks of the council begin to read Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books* (Ros dhomhain). By the morning after Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir falls, a table stands in its stripped hall with the first of the letter-books open under a lamp, and men who have never before read a stranger's hand bend over the close foreign script with the patience of a scale that will not balance.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0362"><em>Strake forsakes the Residency</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-IV-0363"></a>**23 an t-Sultain, AE 150** — *Ros bheag the last seat* (Ros bheag). At Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the early years, Strake sets up what is left of the Administration. The human families of the west and south, a few thousand in all, gather behind its walls.
- <a id="ev-IV-0364"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *Outposts at Ros àrsaidh* (Ros àrsaidh). Strake posts constables at Ros àrsaidh, north of Ros bheag, to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh. The townsfolk bring them food and news, and the news is always a day old.
- <a id="ev-IV-0365"></a>**4 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *Hunger in Ros bheag* (Ros bheag). The roads cut and no ships coming from over the sea, Ros bheag runs short of food within months. By Strake's order the Company's stores are opened to the human families and the Dia-thìrich townsfolk alike, the one deed of his the Dia-thìrich rolls give him credit for.
- <a id="ev-IV-0366"></a>**20 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *Cuan shean refuses the humans* (Cuan shean). The custodians of Cuan shean, where the first humans came ashore, shut its harbour to Company ships. The council's roll sets it down and says no more.
- <a id="ev-IV-0367"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, AE 150** — *The families of Baile dhìreach* (Baile dhìreach). At Baile dhìreach each side asks the children of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, which they are. Most of them, it is written, would not answer, and neither side made them.
- <a id="ev-IV-0368"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The last ship from the east* (Muir Mhanannain). The last ship known to come from an Tìr Thall anchors at Ros bheag at Samhain. She brings no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and sails again on the next tide with as many passengers as she can hold.
- <a id="ev-IV-0369"></a>**2 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The truce of Àth àrsaidh* (Àth àrsaidh). Envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession, and agree a truce: the humans left on Dia-thìr shall withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, and the council shall leave the towns of the concession standing.
- <a id="ev-IV-0370"></a>**20 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns* (Baile Mòr ruadh). The truce names Baile Mòr ruadh, the greatest town of the north-west, as the place where the columns will be received. Its Dia-thìrich folk are given the choice of staying or going south. The roll gives the numbers of each, and they are close.
- <a id="ev-IV-0371"></a>**29 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The columns go north* (Cuan shean). The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west march north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies. Few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and none was helped.
- <a id="ev-IV-0372"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, AE 150** — *The columns at Àth chrom* (Àth chrom). The columns cross the ford at Àth chrom on their way north. The custodians of the town stand at the ford and count them over, and it is the last count the Dia-thìrich make of the humans on Dia-thìr in this age.
- <a id="ev-IV-0373"></a>**1 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Àth leathan* (Àth leathan). At Àth leathan, the last stage before the northern country, the columns camp for a night. The custodians of the town write that the humans asked the name of the place, and that several of them wrote it down.
- <a id="ev-IV-0374"></a>**5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The ship that sailed east* (Cuan shean). Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, sails from Cuan shean for an Tìr Thall with his officers in the last ship on the island able to make the crossing. The keeper at Taigh-solais Baile chrom sets down her passing in his daybook. Nothing on Dia-thìr tells of her coming anywhere.
- <a id="ev-IV-0375"></a>**19 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The beacons relit* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). The council orders the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, are still kept, with nothing in them.
- <a id="ev-IV-0376"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The rolls sent to Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). The custodians send what survives of the rolls of the age, their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais and the letter-books left in the Residency, to the cellars at Muileann chaol. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake is not known.
- <a id="ev-EV-6507"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Coinneach Beag puts his name forward* (Cuan dhearg). When the crew-leaders of the river towns ask for seven men who can keep their feet on a hill road and hold their tongues, Coinneach Beag, a boatman of Cuan dhearg raised on the river since boyhood and no stranger to A' Chompanaidh's rule over his own family, puts his name forward before he has properly decided to.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342a"><em>The Leaden Hawk company</em>, 19 an Giblean, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6508"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The letter read at a nameless hawk-house* (Seann Toll). On the road past Seann Toll, Coinneach Beag reads the council's letter aloud in a bare hawk-house of six benches, his voice unsteady at first; an old woman by the fire answers only that it has come to that, and no one else speaks.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342b"><em>The Leaden Hawk walks to the Hawk coast</em>, 21 an Giblean, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6509"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The boy of Baile thais shows the wall* (Baile thais). Passing through Baile thais, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe is shown by a boy of nine or ten the marks on the store's outer wall from the siege's eleven days, told with more pride than fear, the town's memory of its own fight already settling into telling.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0327"><em>The siege of the store at Baile thais</em>, 1 an t-Ògmhios, AE 149</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6533"><em>Word of Ashdown's retreat reaches Cuan dhearg</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6533"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Word of Ashdown's retreat reaches Cuan dhearg* (Cuan dhearg). Through the fire's talk at Cuan dhearg the news of Ashdown's beaten column travels garbled and half-doubted: that Dùn chrom shut its gates on the soldiers who had slept a night in its barracks, and let the column go on to the coast without its own wounded, whom the town kept to nurse.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0336"><em>Ashdown's retreat through Dùn chrom</em>, 3 am Faoilleach, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6509"><em>The boy of Baile thais shows the wall</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6534"><em>The seven wait nine hours at An Cupa Dàna</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6534"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The seven wait nine hours at An Cupa Dàna* (Cuan dhearg). Seven men of the river towns gather at the inn of An Cupa Dàna and wait nine hours for the council's last letter, and in the waiting learn one another's names and fears: Coinneach Beag, Gillebrìde the hawk-priest's server, the coal-barge brothers, Ailig, and Pàdraig Buidhe, who says nothing at all.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342a"><em>The Leaden Hawk company</em>, 19 an Giblean, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6533"><em>Word of Ashdown's retreat reaches Cuan dhearg</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6535"><em>The lead hawks given out</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6535"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The lead hawks given out* (Cuan dhearg). Each of the seven is given a small hawk cast in lead from cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, worn at the throat on a cord of tarred twine as a token of the council's trust to whoever along the road might read it rightly.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342a"><em>The Leaden Hawk company</em>, 19 an Giblean, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0325"><em>The stores taken at Muileann chrom</em>, 28 an Gearran, AE 149</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6534"><em>The seven wait nine hours at An Cupa Dàna</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6536"><em>The carter of Inis mhin</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6536"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The carter of Inis mhin* (Inis mhin). At Inis mhin, warned that Strake's constables now ride the western roads out of Ros bheag daily, the seven hire a carter with a covered cart and a mule, and leave the road for cart-tracks and field-edges known to no map, asking nothing of what he carries.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342c"><em>Rumours at Inis mhin</em>, 22 an Giblean, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6535"><em>The lead hawks given out</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6537"><em>Eleven hours in the grass above Tobar dhomhain</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6537"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Eleven hours in the grass above Tobar dhomhain* (Tobar dhomhain). Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lies eleven hours in the long grass above the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession, counting every rider that passes; Gillebrìde keeps the tally on a strip of bark, a line for each rider and a cross for each leader.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342d"><em>The watch in the grasslands</em>, 23 an Giblean, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6536"><em>The carter of Inis mhin</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6538"><em>Forty-one riders, all going south</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6538"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Forty-one riders, all going south* (Tobar dhomhain). The company's count ends at forty-one constables' riders in a single day, and not one riding north; Gillebrìde reads the sign as Strake's attention turned elsewhere, and Coinneach Beag cannot say whether the empty road is the safest on the island or the most dangerous.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342d"><em>The watch in the grasslands</em>, 23 an Giblean, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6537"><em>Eleven hours in the grass above Tobar dhomhain</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6539"><em>The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the letter</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6539"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the letter* (Inis thais). In the low temple above the harbour at Inis thais, the priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the council's letter through in silence and will send no men, but shut the harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships and open an Fhianna's own roads to the hawk-faithful.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0342e"><em>The Leaden Hawk at Inis thais</em>, 25 an Giblean, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6538"><em>Forty-one riders, all going south</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6540"><em>The seven become one company</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6540"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The seven become one company* (Seann Skell). At the muster of the hawk-faithful under Ìomhar Seabhag at the western Seann Skell, the seven of Cuan dhearg stand in the company's first rank and are told they are one thing now, with one name: Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0348"><em>The hawk-shrines open</em>, 5 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0349"><em>The hawk company at Seann Skell</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6539"><em>The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the letter</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6541"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill puts out her own light* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). At Tobar dhearg, Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill, keeper of the light since her mother's death, climbs the tower alone on a night of her own choosing and puts out the beacon on her own authority, before any order from the council reaches her; the order finds the tower already dark.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0350"><em>The southern beacon dark</em>, 9 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6542"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Word of the burned coal at Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). At the Seann Skell muster Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe hears that the townsfolk of Inis mhòr fired their own coal stacks rather than let a ship of A' Chompanaidh carry them off to burn against another Seann Toll, and that the ships put in at Ros dhomhain and burned their own stores instead.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0343"><em>Coaling from Inis mhòr</em>, 29 an Giblean, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6543"><em>Coinneach Beag stands his first watch</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6543"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Coinneach Beag stands his first watch* (Ros dhomhain). By midsummer Coinneach Beag stands watch on the road north of Ros bheag with a rifle he has not yet fired, still turning over the forty-one riders and what road Strake judged worth watching instead, while the war's lines hold unmoved from where the first winter left them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0352"><em>The lines at midsummer</em>, 26 an t-Ògmhios, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6542"><em>Word of the burned coal at Inis mhòr</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6510"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Eilidh Hale will not choose* (Baile dhìreach). Asked on the steps of the council hall at Baile dhìreach which people she is, Eilidh Hale, who has kept the joint council's books three winters running, answers only that she keeps the books, and no more. She is neither pressed further nor turned away, and stays in the town through the rest of the war.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0367"><em>The families of Baile dhìreach</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6511"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Hannah Webb walks north* (Cuan shean). Hannah Webb, who keeps her vigil behind Baile chrom and nursed at Cathair gheal through the fever, walks out to meet the columns at the concession's southern edge and walks back north with them, an old woman of the last families out of Cuan shean on her arm who will not be carried.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0371"><em>The columns go north</em>, 29 an t-Samhain, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6512"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The keys given up at Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). The harbour officers of Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh ride two days south with their towns' chests of harbour keys and set them at Strake's feet on the quay at Cuan shean before his ship sails, saying only that the accounts are even and that who wants the keys after is not theirs to decide. Strake takes the chests aboard with him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0374"><em>The ship that sailed east</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6544"><em>The sealed letter kept close</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6544"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The sealed letter kept close* (Ros bheag). The last ship from over the sea puts a single sealed letter ashore for An t-Àrd-mhaor at Ros bheag before filling her berths with passengers and standing out again. Strake reads it alone by a window over the harbour, burns its wrapping in the grate, and is seen to carry the letter itself inside his coat for the rest of the winter. No clerk of his ever claims to have read a word of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0368"><em>The last ship from the east</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6512"><em>The keys given up at Cuan shean</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6545"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Two scribes, one truce* (Àth àrsaidh). At the meeting-house of Àth àrsaidh, envoys of Comhairle na Coille and of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach set down the truce of the withdrawal in two hands at once, neither side trusting the other's clerk alone with the writing of it. Three days of argument over the line on the map are settled in less than an hour once the terms are agreed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0369"><em>The truce of Àth àrsaidh</em>, 2 an t-Samhain, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6546"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *A name given at Àth leathan* (Àth leathan). Camped a last night before the north country, several of the marching humans ask the custodians of Àth leathan the name of the place and write it down for themselves. A child born that same night under a hedge by lantern-light is given the name as though it were a christening name, none other yet being settled on her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0373"><em>Àth leathan</em>, 1 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6547"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *The keeper watches her out of sight* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). From the gallery of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Lachlann mac Uisdein watches Lionel Strake's ship stand out north-about past the headland at evening, showing one light at her stern until the dark of sea and sky close over it. He writes the passing into his father's daybook in his father's own words for a night with no ship left to come.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0374"><em>The ship that sailed east</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EV-6548"><em>Cha tàinig long</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EV-6548"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150** — *Cha tàinig long* (Taigh-solais Baile chrom). Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh burn again from Baile chrom to Tobar dhearg, relit by the council's order, but for nothing that comes. The keepers go on filling their daybooks through the winter, oil and wind and a line where a ship would once have stood, until most of them stop troubling to leave the line at all and simply write the three words that were once Uisdean mac Lachlainn's alone.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-IV-0375"><em>The beacons relit</em>, 19 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EV-6547"><em>The keeper watches her out of sight</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, AE 150</a>.</span>

## The Years AE 151 – 151

- <a id="ev-IV-0377"></a>**1 am Faoilleach, AE 151** — *The Severance*. The war ends, and the crossing itself is shut: whatever way let the humans reach Dia-thìr closes. The humans still on the island are led into the northern country that their children's children hold to this day. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in the wake of it.

# A Gazetteer of the Age

#### A

**Achadh àrsaidh** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 14 am Màrt, FE 603. The field village on the far western shore sent out the boats that first met Na Trì Longan, under the steersman Lachlann Odhar, who sent word home and went on south to Cuan shean. Its people told the story of that morning longer than any roll kept it, and they fished the same waters under Uilebheist na Mara through all the years the strangers held the coast. Gorta Baile chrom that began in the north-west in the ninety-fourth year, reached it in its second winter and emptied many of its houses, and in the drought years a decade after it was named among the ten districts of the drought country. The houses stand close to the sea-wall, and the steersman's boat was kept drawn up on the shingle under them for as long as anyone remembered whose it had been. Known for the boats that met the strangers.

**Achadh chaol** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 5 an Dùbhlachd, AE 137 by the dispossessed of the closed district. The narrow field was built by the people of the district A' Chompanaidh fenced and closed after Scàineadh Cill ghlas, on common ground lent them by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. They raised it through a spring and summer without a single A' Chompanaidh's surveyor setting foot on it: a well dug first, then the custodian's house, then the households in the order their names were drawn at the stone. Its shrine-keepers lit a new lamp without the old keeper's name on it. It stands on the edge of the fenced ground, and from its well the wire of the closed district can be seen along the slope. Known for a village built without a surveyor.

**Achadh chaol** (Achadh chaol). Founded 27 an Gearran, GE 2,475. The farm village of the north-east lost its grazing two years running in the drought, and sent its young to sign hewers' contracts at Cnoc fhiadhaich and elsewhere, the first villagers of the eastern farm country to go to the pits for wages. Families who had kept beasts and small fields for generations went down in a single season, and their custodian wrote it down as the end of the village, not a flitting. Known for the end of the village.

**Achadh dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 272. The large farming village in the deep fields above the workings became a camp when the new galleries were opened into its hill, and it was the worst place on the hill in A' Bhreac Bhallach. Beitris Bhàn laid out its dead at her own table, the washing-women first said there that the girl of the spoil-houses did not grow, and Anne Colby kept her sick-house of canvas there through A' Phlàigh Uaine, which began among its huts. Walter Crane walked its sick-rows. Its granaries fed the camps for a century. The feather Beitris Bhàn nailed over her own door was copied on doors across the camps as fast as the overseers pulled them down, and the roll of the camp keeps the first cases of A' Phlàigh Uaine under her name. Known for the camp where A' Phlàigh Uaine began.

**Achadh mhòr** (Achadh mhòr). Founded 2 an t-Samhain, GE 4,000. The granary of the east keeps the shared-meal custom of An Aois Naomh. In the years before the war Faire nan Lòchran's ledgers of the money it had from Comann an Airgid were kept in the roof-space of its shrine, above the rafters, and no clerk of A' Chompanaidh ever thought to look for them there. It is one of the largest settlements on the island though it is still called a field village, and its grain went to the capital in the siege year. Known for the ledgers in the shrine roof.

**Achadh naomh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios, GE 4,091. The village in the hills north of the workings kept Na Seann Spioradan, and its households would not light their hearths with coal bought of A' Chompanaidh; they burned peat as their grandparents had, and their elders taught that coal burned for wages was burned twice. Fionnghal nic Artair rode there in an Giblean of the twenty-third year and read her letter in defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig at the hearth of Sìleas nic Uilleim. Asked what burned on her own hearth, she answered bought coal, and was sent home with thanks. Known for the hearths that burned no bought coal.

**Achadh shean** (Achadh shean). Founded 21 an Giblean, GE 3,125. The old field gave its name to Tiormachd Achadh shean, which lay on the east from the hundred and sixth year to the hundred and tenth. Its wells failed a month before any other, its custodian wrote to Iseabail nic Leòid at Àth mhòr twice a week, and in the third year Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise sank deep wells there with a boring-rig from an Tìr Thall, and they held. The custodians set Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's wells and A' Chompanaidh's tallies on facing pages without comment. It stands at the heart of the farming country south and east of the cape, and in the first dry year its custodian wrote that the granaries of the old custom would carry them through the winter, which they did, once. Known for Tiormachd Achadh shean and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's wells.

**Àth àrsaidh** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 12 an t-Samhain, GE 3,458. The ancient ford in the north-west, on the edge of the country the humans first settled, is where the envoys of the council and of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach met in its meeting-house in the last week of an Dàmhair of the hundred and fiftieth year, with two scribes writing the same words in two hands, and agreed the truce: the humans to withdraw into the north-west under safe-conduct, and the towns of that country to be left standing. The meeting-house has a single long table down its middle, and both copies of the truce were signed at it on the third day. Known for the truce.

**Àth chiar** (Àth shean). Founded 21 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,362. The ford town east of the capital is where Rathad na Mèinne crossed the river before climbing into the hills. In the spring of the hundred and forty-ninth year Major Peter Ashdown turned his relief column north about An Taigh-seinnse Mòr to cross there, and met the crews of Baile thais dug in along the willow scrub of the far bank. His column went into the ford waist-high and in poor order, lost forty men to the river and the fire and all its baggage, and went back. The rebels lost nineteen, whose names the council's clerk read aloud once. The old field of battle at Muileann ghlas lies to its south-west. A' Chompanaidh's baggage abandoned on the near bank went up the hill road on the rebels' carts that night. Known for the fight at the ford.

**Àth chrom** (Muileann naomh). Founded 3 an t-Iuchar, LE 989. The drovers' town at the bent ford was one of the two where Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise sank deep wells in the drought years, and they held. In the last weeks of the age its custodians stood at the ford and counted the columns over, family by family, from first light until past noon; it was the last count the Dia-thìrich made of the humans on Dia-thìr in the age. Its people are drovers, and the ford is crossed by the drove road north. Known for the last count.

**Àth dhearg** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 364. The red ford-town on the north-eastern cape kept a fire on a shelf of the headland for its boats long before any roll, and when the humans asked for a tower there the custodian went round every hearth to ask leave, which took eleven days. The mason Tormod mac Pheadair built the tower and kept it, and began in it the first daybook of the five lights, so plain that A' Chompanaidh's clerk who read it called its keeper civil but of no assistance. On a night of gale in the forty-sixth year the light brought four boats of Àth dhearg home off the long lines. In the war its light went dark with the others of the south, and was lit again at the truce. A clerk of A' Chompanaidh rode up the coast road in the dark days of Dubhlas to ask to see the daybook about the burning of a collier, and went away with nothing. Known for the first keeper's daybook.

**Àth dhomhain** (Àth dhomhain). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, LE 1,611. The pits north of the hills at the town stopped with the rest on Là Stad nan Sloc, the word brought by a runner and not by the beacon. Their crew-leaders were among the eight shipped over the sea when the stoppage was broken, and never heard of again. Known for the runner's word.

**Àth fhiadhaich** (Àth fhiadhaich). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd, GE 4,325. The ford town of the south-eastern hills, at the meeting of the Abhainn gheal and the Abhainn bhàn, sent its boatmen's sons as runners for Faire nan Lòchran in the years before the war, boys of twelve and thirteen who carried the letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town along the causeway paths, too young for the constables to stop and too quick for a mounted man to follow. It has been a river landing since An Aois Naomh, and its boatmen's causeway paths across the flood-meadows are known to no map. Known for Faire nan Lòchran's runners.

**Àth fhionn** (Muileann shean). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 697. Human fishermen of the concession taught the boats of the north-coast town to hunt whales with the hand-lance in the fifty-fifth year rather than wait for them to strand. The oil was sold to A' Chompanaidh for its lamps, and from then on whale-boats went out from the north coast every summer. Known for the whale-boats.

**Àth fhionn** (Àth fhionn). Founded 26 an Giblean, FE 900. The fair ford at the crossing of the southern drove road sent its custodian Ruairidh mac Thormoid to Ceann àrsaidh in the ninety-eighth year, the eldest of the nineteen who signed the petition, born before the humans' coin was struck; he signed last and slowest. Human fishers of the concession had taught its boats to take whales with the hand-lance, and the oil went to A' Chompanaidh's lamps. It has been a resting place for herds and drovers since An Aois Naomh, and its people keep the ancestor rite of the old roads. Known for the eldest signature.

**Àth ghlas** (Àth ghlas). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, FE 373. The grey ford beside Cathair mhòr is remembered for Sìne Ruadh, custodian in A' Phlàigh Uaine, who ordered every hut where a death had been burned with its bedding. A' Chompanaidh protested the loss of its property, and the custodians noted that the sickness stopped sooner at Àth ghlas than anywhere else. The story was still told by grandparents in the fever years sixty years later. It lies a short way from the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, which is older than any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich, and the huts it burned were never rebuilt on the same ground. Known for the burning of the huts.

**Àth ìseal** (Muileann chrom). Founded 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 324. The low ford below the new workings became the first of A' Chompanaidh's camps: timber huts where the ferrymen had always put the carts across in the wet season, and a store of A' Chompanaidh where the clerk had no book for cheese. The families who came down from Doire mhòr and the hill villages went to its huts, and A' Bhreac Bhallach and the fever were worst among them. Its roll was the one in which the line of Aisling was first found. The ford floods every wet season and the ferrymen still put the carts across, and the camp grew into a town of rows beside the old crossing. Its chaplain in A' Bhreac Bhallach wrote every dead man, woman and child in a fair hand. Known for A' Chompanaidh's first camp.

**Àth leathan** (Seann Skell). Founded 8 am Màrt, LE 1,303. The drovers' village at the wide ford was the last stage before the northern country. The columns camped a night in its fields below the town with their fires strung along the hedgerow, and several of the humans asked the custodians the name of the place and wrote it down; a woman brought to bed under a hedge that night asked it twice and gave it to her child. It had been a gathering place for the drovers of the north since before the strangers came, and the fields where the columns camped were grazing again by the spring. Known for the name written down.

**Àth mhòr** (Àth mhòr). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios, GE 1,847. The town of the eastern drought country was kept through Tiormachd Achadh shean by its custodian Iseabail nic Leòid. In the hundred and seventh year she drove the herds of Àth mhòr and Achadh shean a day west to the tarn above Doire fhionn, and fewer than half the beasts reached water on their own legs; she kept a count of the fallen, ninety-eight marks. Of the ten drought custodians who petitioned Haskins, each unknown to the others, she rode her own petition to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and over the following winter wrote forty pages on the three dry years. Haskins answered in two lines, and a later clerk bound the two together. Known for the forty pages.

#### B

**Baile àrsaidh** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, FE 879. The coastal town a day's walk up from Cuan shean took Fiabhras nan Coigreach in the tenth year, which killed its custodian and both her sons, though no human dwelt in the town at all. The custodians of the west took note of it. Known for the fever without strangers.

**Baile chaol** (Baile chaol). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,339. The cattle town of the east had no grazing left within four days' driving in the second summer of Tiormachd Achadh shean, and its custodian Ealasaid Ruadh ordered the whole herd killed and salted rather than lose it on the road. The salt meat was sold to A' Chompanaidh for the camps at a price A' Chompanaidh named. The town lost fewer of its people to hunger that winter than any other in the drought country. Known for the herd salted.

**Baile chiar** (Baile chiar). Founded 1 an Gearran, FE 869. The southern town took A' Bhreac Bhallach when it spread south from the harbour in the fortieth year, and its custodians cut the names of the dead into the stone lintel of the council house, where they can still be read. Known for the lintel of names.

**Baile chrom** (Doire mhin). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, LE 270. The town in the hills, not the town of that name in the north-west, took A' Phlàigh Uaine in the seventy-fourth year. The scribes kept the two apart with care, for the tellings of the island's hungers confuse them. Known for the other Baile chrom.

**Baile chrom** (Baile chrom). Founded 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464. The bent town on the far north-western coast stands beside Taigh-solais Baile chrom, the last of the five lights built and the first as the ring is counted. Uisdean mac Lachlainn kept it from its lighting in the ninety-first year and his son Lachlann after him, and the daybook there first wrote the three words *Cha tàinig long*. Gorta Baile chrom, took its name from the town in the ninety-fourth year. Hannah Webb kept her night vigil in the fields behind it from the hundred and thirty-third year, and Am Fiabhras Glas settled hardest round it. Lachlann watched the last Àrd-mhaor's ship stand out past its headland. An Togail that built its tower was set aside in the famine districts in the hunger years, too late for the harvest, and never used again. Known for its light, and Gorta Baile chrom.

**Baile dhìreach** (Inis thais). Founded 14 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,392. The straight town on the west coast took in the first human families to settle beside the Dia-thìrich rather than apart from them. Samuel Hale tightened herring barrels on its quay, Torcall the mason witnessed in its Dia-thìreach book, and a marriage was made there in two tongues. The town was governed for a long season by a joint council of both peoples, six of each, and lost its harbour dues to A' Chompanaidh in the years of An Togail. Thomas Hale first set his name to paper against Riaghaltas nan Coigreach here. In the last autumn each side asked the children of the old council which people they were, and most would not answer; Eilidh Hale kept the books and stayed. Its quay is a single long street down to the water, and the humans' slip where the first boat was launched stood at its foot. The storm of the wolf-moon drowned men of both peoples off its harbour in one night, and both were lit for at the lamps of the drowned. Known for the joint council and its children.

**Baile dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, AE 34. The camp town of the deep workings was laid out on A' Chompanaidh's paper before a stone of it was cut, in straight rows, the first town of the Dia-thìrich drawn by a surveyor. Two of its streets came down in the year of Àithne a' Ghlacaidh for a spoil-tip, and the families took huts at Àth ìseal or went to kin in the hill villages. Most of its hewers came from the camps at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain, and the grid of its streets was the pattern for every camp A' Chompanaidh drew after it. Known for its streets drawn on paper.

**Baile fhiadhaich** (Baile fhiadhaich). Founded 17 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,709. The harbour town up the western coast heard of Na Trì Longan within two days of their coming, and its custodian rode south to see them. In the first years of the strangers Torcall the mason set a new stone face on its harbour wall, and when a human supply-brig broke on the reefs south of the town its custodian gave the drowned ground above the tide-line among the dunes. The town kept that ground apart for the strangers' dead for the rest of the age. The custodian who rode south in the first year to see the ships wrote the only account of them from the western coast, and it was her successor who asked Torcall to mend the wall. Known for the strangers' graves in the dunes.

**Baile gharbh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, GE 2,662. The crews of the northern pit town rose in the same week as the other northern pits in the hundred and forty-ninth year, took the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and sent the constables south on foot. Their crew-leaders had left a cairn of spoil-stones, one from each pit, on the moor above Cnoc naomh the night they fixed the week. Known for the northern rising.

**Baile gheal** (Baile gheal). Founded 27 an Giblean, GE 4,347. The carters of the south-western town took up the carrying of Seann Warr brine-salt round the lake to the capital in the forty-fifth year, a trade A' Chompanaidh did not trouble to claim; Comann an Airgid entered the salt in its ledger. The trade kept the town's folk out of the pits for the whole of the age. Known for the salt carts.

**Baile ghlas** (Baile ghlas). Founded 7 an Cèitean, GE 4,047. The fishing town whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain time out of mind was charged anchorage under Puingean a' Chalaidh in the twentieth year. Having paid it once, its fishermen took their catch to their own jetty and sold it there to the fish-wives who walked out from the capital and to anyone but A' Chompanaidh, whose salting-house had herring that season only from its own boats. Known for herring sold to anyone but A' Chompanaidh.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 22 an Gearran, FE 837. The open market town of the south-eastern farms has no walls. Its potteries took a contract in the years of the night shift for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year, and the potters' own book notes that they were the first lamps made on the island for work in the dark by command. Its people kept Na Seann Spioradan through the age. Its fairs bring the south-eastern farms' grain and wool, and its potters kept working the same clay for household crocks when the contract ended. Known for the night crews' lamps.

**Baile ìseal** (Àth bheag). Founded 14 an t-Samhain, LE 197. The fishing town on the eastern cape kept a driftwood fire to bring its boats home in a storm long before the strangers came, and Torcall Clachair laid his second cairn there in the sixth year with James Fenn beside him. When A' Chompanaidh raised Taigh-solais Baile ìseal in the twenty-seventh year, the lime for its mortar was burned on the shore with coal carted over the hills from Muileann chrom, and the keeping of the lamp went to the fishing households, who drew lots for the watches at Samhain as they had for the fire. The custodians won a rule that the lamp be lowered on the nights the boats went to the deep grounds, and the old fire was still lit beside the tower. Known for the fire beside the beacon.

**Baile ìseal** (Baile ìseal). Founded 16 an t-Sultain, LE 1,567. The Tuathaich town sent forty-one of its people to the pits under An Togail, the largest tally of any single town. Nineteen came back when their term was done; the custodians' roll names the other twenty-two and the camps they were carried to, four with no camp given at all. Known for the forty-one.

**Baile mhin** (Baile mhin). Founded 17 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,685. The quays below Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag took the eastern coal that Inis bheag could not load. Its townsfolk were paid by the barge, and with the gain the town built its first stone houses. Known for its first stone houses.

**Baile Mòr dhìreach** (Baile chaol). Founded 7 an Gearran, FE 2,051. The city of the white sand lay below the dunes of Cuan ruadh. Peter Voss, a glazier of A' Chompanaidh who would not take passage home when his contract ended, built a glass-house there in the sixty-sixth year and melted the sand with charcoal from the hills. His first three firings gave only a black slag that the children carried off for luck; the fourth gave a pale green pane, and his apprentice Cairistìona nic Griogair laughed at the sight of a gull through it. It was the first glass made on Dia-thìr, and the town's apprentices were blowing it without him within a generation. Its custodians were among those of the east whose petitions against the coal tally in the drought went unanswered. Known for the first glass of Dia-thìr.

**Baile Mòr dhomhain** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 24 an t-Samhain, FE 101. The city on the river road grew, as the coal came down to it from Cidhe Beag, into the busiest barge town of the north. Its people doubled in number in the thirties, most of the newcomers bargemen from the coast. Known for its barges.

**Baile Mòr fhionn** (Caol leathan). Founded 6 an t-Samhain, FE 584. In the wool city of the western coast a fleece had been the measure of every bargain until Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's table of the eighty-sixth year made it worth what a half-fleece had been before. The weavers stopped bringing wool to the humans' market and loaded it for their own crossing instead, and A' Chompanaidh, holding the only deep-water berths on that coast, let it lie until the moths had most of it. Known for the wool left to the moths.

**Baile Mòr mhòr** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616. The weaving city of the northern coast traded its cloth for the humans' dyes in the fourth year, a red and a blue brighter than any the island could make, and within a few years the old madder fields about the town went back to grass. Known for the humans' red and blue.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 3 an Gearran, FE 2,252. The red walled city of the north-west, the greatest town of that country, had lived under the humans' governance longer than any other on the island. The truce named it the place where the columns would be received, and its own Dia-thìrich folk were given the choice, at a gathering in the market square, of staying under the truce or going south. The roll set the two numbers side by side, and they were close. It was held by Dia-thìreach lords from An Aois Naomh, and the humans' magistrates sat in its hall for most of the age. Known for the choice put to its people.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Seann Tarr). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, GE 3,311. The walled city of red stone suffered worst from the fever of foul water that followed the drought into the towns, for its wells had been deepened into the old middens; seventeen died. Coll, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's young physician there, tested the water and was the first to name the cause rightly. Its citadel is the strongest place of its province, and after the drought its custodians had the old midden ground walled off and the wells sunk anew outside it. Known for Coll's report on the water.

**Baile Mòr uaine** (Cuan ghlas). Founded 22 am Màrt, FE 982. The city of the north-west kept a hall of disputation of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. In the forty-ninth year students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carried his question there, why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal, and the hall argued it until its record ran to four hundred leaves. The last leaf lists those who spoke and notes that the hall adjourned because the peat was done. Known for the four hundred leaves.

**Baile ruadh** (Baile ruadh). Founded 3 an Dàmhair, FE 971. The farming town of the east lost its seed corn in the ground in the forty-eighth year and borrowed seed from A' Chompanaidh's store at Seann Dunn, to be paid back in grain over five harvests. Tormod mac Pheadair, keeper of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg and kin of the town by marriage, walked there to read the terms to its council figure by figure. The custodians entered the debt under the night of the moon with its measure and its five harvests, the first debt in grain to the strangers in any roll of the island. Known for the first debt in grain.

**Baile thais** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,086. The pit town where the Abhainn uaine leaves the hills was the heart of the crews' own long resistance. The eleven days of its great strike in the seventy-seventh year won what the crews could win, and its roll kept Sìneag's search for an old law of rest. Its Comann an Adhlacaidh became Faire nan Lòchran, which kept a purse, a book and the copies of every petition; Eilidh nic Raghnaill led a crew there and kept the book. A' Chompanaidh walled its pithead, and in the first days of the war its constables held the walls eleven days until the well ran dry, and were marched to the coast unharmed on Eilidh's word. Sìol-lann na Companaidh built there against a stoppage was the first on the hill, and the overseer's clerk who copied the forbidden song kept his copy in its roll. Its boats have been launched at the landing since before any roll. Known for the eleven days, twice over.

#### C

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 15 am Màrt, FE 477. The small harbour on the northern coast took in the crew of a brig of A' Chompanaidh wrecked in sea mist off Eilean fhada in the fifty-fifth year; they waded ashore at low water and walked there. A' Chompanaidh built a quay at the town for the eastern trade, and by the hundred and forty-fifth year it saw one ship in a season. Its agent wrote to Ros dhomhain that he had been forgotten, and no answer came back to him that Rathad na Mèinne ever heard of. Known for the forgotten agent.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,547. The harbour town of the south-west paid its dues in fish until they were called in marks in the eighty-third year. They could be raised no way but by selling boats: eleven of its two-and-twenty went to A' Chompanaidh at its own asking price, and the men who sailed them went into the pits under the next year's contracts. Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, the lane the coal ships took west along the south coast, is named for its strait. Known for the eleven boats sold.

**Caol gharbh** (Caol gharbh). Founded 10 am Màrt, GE 4,128. The road for the eastern coal to Inis bheag passed the town by a mile in the fifty-fourth year, and it got only the dust of the traffic it had hoped for. Its custodians wrote that they had not known a town could be harmed by a road it was not on. Known for the road it was not on.

**Caol ìseal** (Caol ìseal). Founded 21 am Màrt, FE 1,450. The harbour on the low strait of the north coast has salt pans that supply the northern fisheries. The blasting-powder for the new deep galleries was landed there in the hundred and thirty-sixth year, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard; the custodians asked what was in the barrels and were told it was lamp-oil. It keeps the ancestor rite of the old coast, and its custodians wrote the lamp-oil into their roll with the weight the carters said the barrels had. Known for the barrels of lamp-oil.

**Caol leathan** (Caol leathan). Founded 12 am Faoilleach, GE 1,560. The town on the wide strait took its tolls from the strangers' shipping as it had from the western pilots, and for two generations its merchants sold wool by A' Chompanaidh's weight and at A' Chompanaidh's price. When the humans' ships thinned in the years before the war, the wool piled in its warehouses and the merchants quietly began to sell inland again, against the letter of the law. By the war its harbour stood idle. The tally-book of Pike's post named its merchants the hardest bargainers on the island, since they would take only iron by weight for their wool, and they sent the first wool-ship to the humans' post in Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg's second year. Known for wool, and its idle harbour.

**Caol mhin** (Caol mhin). Founded 17 am Màrt, FE 1,345. The harbour of the calm strait was chosen by Tolley in his first month as Àrd-mhaor for a quarantine station, holding every ship from an Tìr Thall offshore until a physician had looked her crew over. It was the first order of his rule the Dia-thìrich approved, and they said so. Its quays stand on Eilean chrom across the strait, and the physician's boat went out from them to every ship that came in under the quarantine. Known for the quarantine station.

**Caol mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462. The harbour of the great strait in the far north-west, near where the strangers first raised the land, took the first tally of An Togail, when the officers read the names of the chosen from a list in the humans' tongue and took the wrong son. The custodians wrote the names again in Dia-thìris, that they might know whom to look for. Its grief was loud and short, as a first grief is. Its yards took timber for A' Chompanaidh's hulls, and An Togail's officers used its quay as their first station in the north-west. Known for the wrong son.

**Cathair dhearg** (Cathair dhearg). Founded 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18. The capital held Comhairle a' Chùraim through all the years of the strangers, and the council's roll is the spine of the age's record. Here Gormshuil nic Fhearchair and the priest Samuel Wren made the first lists of words across a table, with a cup and a loaf; here Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg was read in one tongue and signed, and here the council sat without a Ceann a' Chùraim for ten years. When Lionel Strake came Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir locked the council hall and took its keys, and the custodians sat on the floor of Macha's temple for two years. In the spring of the hundred and forty-ninth year the townsfolk broke the locks with a coal-hammer, held A' Chompanaidh's bridge with overturned carts, and fed the city from a sharing-yard behind the hall through the siege that followed. Its bells were rehung in a new frame by Torcall the mason in the first years. Tormod mac Ailein, Ceann a' Chùraim when the ships came, was buried in the town, and Artair mac Iain was seated after the chair had stood empty ten years. Known for the council roll, and the sharing-yard of the siege year.

**Cathair dhomhain** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634. The deep city on the lake shore, five miles from the capital by the lake road, holds the first building the strangers ever owned outright on Dia-thìr: the stone warehouse Pike raised there in Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg's first summer to keep A' Chompanaidh's tools out of reach of the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. A' Chompanaidh's surgeon came to its sick only once in Fiabhras nan Coigreach, and it was here that Anne Colby first wrote the dead by name. In the rising the townsfolk broke the warehouse open and carried off its rope, nails and powder for Buidhnean na Comhairle, and left its doors swinging. The fishing town runs down to the shore beside the capital's deep water, and the old folk there said the warehouse door was the first door on the island ever hung with a lock the town could not open. Known for the strangers' first warehouse.

**Cathair fhada** (Cathair fhada). Founded 13 an Cèitean, GE 2,523. The long walled city of the south follows Macha, and its oak woods had been cut for A' Chompanaidh's pit-props since the first contracts. The age's rolls note the day the last oak of its own cutting came down, and the priests of Macha who would not stand for the blessing of the coin were many of them its people. Its priests of Macha were the first to refuse to stand for the blessing of the humans' coin in the capital's temple, and many of them followed the dissenters to the forest. Known for the oaks that went for pit-props.

**Cathair gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 5 am Màrt, GE 1,378. The walled city of white stone on the far western coast was a Dia-thìreach town until the human families of the northern concession made it their market in the fiftieth year. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise kept a chapel and, in the fever years, a hospital where Dia-thìrich and human sick lay side by side for the first time because there was no longer room to keep them apart; Hannah Webb nursed in its wards. In the war it shut its gates, raised a militia that went nowhere, and its magistrate asked both sides to be left alone. Its harbour officer rode south with his town's keys at the end. Obadiah Renn, the minister of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, sat with Hannah Webb in the chapel over her vigil, and wrote of it to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's house at Cathair dhearg. Known for the concession's market and the shared wards.

**Cathair mhòr** (Cathair mhòr). Founded 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847. The great city below the old ruin refused the mark when it was first made law, and went on paying in kind at its market for a season after the rest of the country had given in. Am Fiabhras Glas came to it in the high summer of the hundred and thirty-eighth year, and for the first time in the town's memory the market shut, stall by stall; the longest list of dead in the roll was the street of the carters. It keeps below its walls the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, and the market that refused the coin gave way at last only when A' Chompanaidh's tool-sellers would not cross its bridge for anything else. Known for the refusal of the mark.

**Cathair naomh** (Seann Toll). Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,162. The city above Seann Toll on the northern coast sent its first wool south to the humans' post by coasting boat in the third year, and its custodians took their payment in paper and ink and began the town's roll afresh with them. Thomas Pike added a quire of his own writing-paper uncounted, the one line of the post's first tally-book he did not balance, and marked it as a gift. Known for the roll begun on the strangers' paper.

**Ceann àrsaidh** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 17 an t-Sultain, GE 4,328. The walled river city on the old headland over the Abhainn fhionn sent Eachann Mòr to the council for nine years, and he lost his seat for what he said in the hall and wrote a letter over the sea. In the ninety-eighth year its custodian Aonghas Ruadh called the custodians of nineteen settlements to its hall behind the market square, and after three days of argument they set their grievance down in the petition that Peigi Ghlas carried to Ros dhomhain. In the war its companies burned the tithe-house and every ledger in it, though its custodian asked that one be spared. Its barges run down the Abhainn fhionn to Cathair dhomhain, and the custodians of the east met in its hall again in the war before the companies went out. Known for A' Chiad Athchuinge.

**Ceann bheag** (Ceann bheag). Founded 15 an t-Iuchar, FE 311. The coal stage of the northern-coast town stopped loading on Là Stad nan Sloc. Its dockers had not been told; they stopped because the coal stopped coming. Known for the stage that stopped.

**Ceann chaol** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 23 an Giblean, FE 145. A second deep-water quay was built at the village in the south-east in the hundred and third year for the eastern coal, by builders brought from the coast, and a village of forty houses became a town of four hundred. Known for the second deep quay.

**Ceann fhada** (Muileann chrom). Founded 27 an Cèitean, LE 1,359. The long spit on the Abhainn uaine, a short hour's walk under Doire mhòr, held its foreshore in common, and A' Chompanaidh's first surveyors found it covered with their own men. A' Chompanaidh built its coal quay there, and for a century barges loaded the hill's coal for the coast. On the first day of the rising the crews took the quay and sank two loaded barges across its mouth; the boatman Pàdraig Reamhar knocked the plugs from a hull he had built with his own father. No coal left the hills by water again in the age. Its pilots guided A' Chompanaidh's barges through the shoals below the spit for a century, and the rivalry with Inis ìseal downstream went on untouched by all of it. Known for the barges sunk across its quay.

**Ceann leathan** (Ceann leathan). Founded 27 am Màrt, FE 1,810. The fishing town on the southern shore sheltered the crew of A' Chompanaidh's collier when the raiders burned her in the forty-sixth year and set her men rowing for the land; its households fed them until a rider could carry word south. The next year a gunboat of A' Chompanaidh hunted the raiders to a cove near the town and burned every boat drawn up on the shingle, most of them its own fishermen's. The raiders were not found. Known for the burned cove.

**Ceann leathan** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, GE 2,061. The river-mouth city of the south coast was where A' Chompanaidh's ships loaded the coal that came down the Abhainn uaine from Seann Toll, and went out by Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich. Its fishermen netted the last salmon of the green river's mouth in the thirty-third year, a hen fish empty of eggs; the next spring none came in from the sea, their gravel under the grey slurry of the washing-floors. In the thirty-sixth year a coal ship on the ebb ran down one of its boats off the bar and did not stop, and after that the town's boats kept inshore. Known for the last salmon.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 18 an Lùnastal, FE 745. The city of the south got A' Chompanaidh's pay office for the southern workings in the sixty-first year, when Crane moved it there from the pit-heads. The crews of every southern pit walked a day there and a day back twice a month to be paid, with no pay for the walking; Uisdean Ruadh of Muileann chrom kept the cost of it on a notched stick. Known for the pay line.

**Ceann mhòr** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 6 an Cèitean, FE 163. The great harbour under the north-western headland took in the first human fishing families of the concession in the fifty-first year, the first humans to fish the island's waters for their own living. Tobacco grew on the concession farms behind it. Manannan's priests kept Oidhche Glaise on its quay, and Ruth Pallant, who taught Hannah Webb the night watch, lived near it. Gorta Baile chrom struck it hard. At the close of the age its harbour officer carried the town's chest of keys two days south to Cuan shean. Its harbour lies under the beacon of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, and in the hunger years it sent what boats it had south along the coast for grain. Known for the concession fishers.

**Ceann òg** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 19 an t-Sultain, AE 8. The quay town on the Abhainn ìseal gave its name to Seòlaid Ceann òg, the traders' lane that ran down the river past Cnoc bheag and Inis bhàn, west along the north coast and round the western capes to the capital. In the autumn of the twenty-ninth year A' Chompanaidh shipped the fishers and net-menders whose foreshores it had bought up that lane to Ceann òg and walked them over the hills to the pits. Known for Seòlaid Ceann òg.

**Cill dhìreach** (Cill dhìreach). Founded 12 am Màrt, FE 2,599.
