The temple village of Macha at the edge of the workings kept a small shrine where the pit crews left the first piece of coal from every new gallery. A' Chompanaidh suffered the custom, since it cost a stone a gallery, and the shrine was one of the two pit-mouth shrines where the crews kept the old words of the rock face in the strangers' years. It lies beside Ceann leathan, where the old contest is still held each year, and its druids tended the shrine through the whole of the age without a quarrel of A' Chompanaidh. Known for the first-coal shrine.

**Cill thais** (Cill thais). Founded 15 an t-Samhain, FE 1,933. The large village on damp ground beside the sacred wood of Macha took in the orphans of the Eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a long house of stone with new thatch that its custodians made ready at the end of the street, and raised them. The wood behind it gave shelter in the last years to the priests who had left the capital's temple, and Comhairle na Coille of the war sat among its fires. The long house the custodians made ready stood at the end of the street for the rest of the age, and the orphans raised there were counted in its roll as children of the town. Known for the orphans of the Eleven.

**Cnoc àrsaidh** (Cnoc àrsaidh). Founded 11 am Màrt, GE 2,405. The walled town of Òrd na Cloiche, where Imrich nam Pantar passes, did in the first fever years what the hills only talked of: it turned the fever back at its gates. Riaghaltas nan Coigreach fined it for hindering trade, and it paid the fine in wool, more sacks than the humans knew what to do with. Its priests kept the oldest shrines of Òrd na Cloiche open through all the age. Its wool fine was long told in the south-west as the one bargain the humans ever lost by weight. Known for the fine paid in wool.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, GE 3,908. The river port of the north-central country and heart of the hawk-faithful asked Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise for a copy of Wren's grammar in the thirteenth year, to read what the humans wrote of them; of all the copies that survive, theirs bears the most notes in the margins. In the war Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe slept a night in a byre near it on the road to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig. It lies on the Abhainn ìseal, and its hawk-priests kept that copy in the temple where anyone who could read the humans' letters might ask to see it. Known for the most-read copy of Wren's grammar.

**Cnoc chaol** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 22 an Cèitean, GE 2,404. The narrow hill was a mining camp worked by night crews in the last decades of the age. Griogair mac Ailein died in A' Chompanaidh's lock-up there, held for a short-weighted cartload he did not cut, and Thomas Hale came to read the surgeon's note over his grave. The day shift stood in the yard in silence for the night crews, Faire nan Lòchran's purse ran dry keeping the strikers fed, and the strike was broken by crews brought in through Muileann dhomhain. Grodadh nan Scamhan was worse there than on any other hill. In the hundred and forty-eighth year its overseer threw down his staff in the week Mòrag broke hers. Its crews were among the first to work by the clay lamps of Baile ghorm, and the pithead there was lit all night from the year the night shift began. Known for Stad-oibre Cnoc chaol.

**Cnoc dhìreach** (Cnoc dhìreach). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,845. The walled seat of the eastern mining district was walled by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach after the strikes. Its custodian Coinneach Ruadh signed An Dàrna Athchuinge in the hundred and thirty-ninth year and was turned out of his clerkship at A' Chompanaidh's store within the week, in front of the queue for the week's flour; he was one of eleven who signed and lost A' Chompanaidh's work for it, and he rode the district roads with news for the rest of the age. Its post as custodian Coinneach Ruadh kept eleven years before the petition, and he went on keeping it after he lost the clerkship. Known for the eleven who signed.

**Cnoc dhubh** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar, FE 93. The black hill of the charcoal burners kept an old customary cutting held by one family since An Aois Naomh. Under Riaghailt Dunstan the working was taken from them because a great-grandmother of the line had married a human sailor, and the rolls of the hill set down that this was the whole of the reason given. It is the largest of the cluster of charcoal hills, and its people burned charcoal for A' Chompanaidh's smithies after the cutting was taken. Known for the cutting taken.

**Cnoc fhiadhaich** (Muileann chrom). Founded 17 am Màrt, LE 488. The wild hill in the middle country gave its name to the Eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich, the crew of the first great fall, whose orphans went to Cill thais. Raghnall asked three times for timber at the heading before the roof came down. The road around Doire mhòr was cut through its ground, and A' Chompanaidh's huts followed. The wall of its old heading still stood above the camp at the close of the age, and the crews would not work the gallery beneath it. Known for the Eleven.

**Cnoc gharbh** (Ros gharbh). Founded 5 an Giblean, LE 1,014. After A' Phlàigh Uaine the people of the town, who had worked the southern galleries, left their camp huts and went back to the old village on the hill. The next year A' Chompanaidh built the huts again and brought in crews from the west. Known for the huts left empty.

**Cnoc gheal** (Cnoc gheal). Founded 5 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,928. The quarrymen of the north-eastern town, who cut stone for A' Chompanaidh's buildings, laid down their tools on Là Stad nan Sloc unasked. Why, no one said. Known for the quarrymen who stopped.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 15 an Dàmhair, GE 1,362. In the fiftieth year human farmers of the concession cleared land beside the Tuathaich village of the upland north-west and built a mill; through the first winter the villagers sold them grain at a fair price and carried it on their own ponies, and when the farmers' mill turned in the spring they sold no more and gave no reason. Known for the grain sold for one winter.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Ceann mhin). Founded 30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,292. In the hills beyond the capital, the guards of A' Chompanaidh and the constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road were driven back at the town in the last year of the age, in Blàr Cnoc ghorm. It was the last attempt Riaghaltas nan Coigreach made in the war to reach the mining district. Known for Blàr Cnoc ghorm.

**Cnoc leathan** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 11 am Màrt, FE 172. Riflemen raised at the eastern town joined the companies of Comann an Airgid in Cogadh nam Beann and held the eastern road. A' Chompanaidh's carters caught on it were let go home with their carts. Known for the riflemen of the eastern road.

**Cnoc mhòr** (Cnoc mhòr). Founded 8 am Màrt, FE 1,210. The hill town south of the coal country got its pits in the thirty-seventh year, with Seumas Dubh of Raghnall Maor's crews set over them as overseer. A year later the haulage rope parted under three full tubs and crushed Coinneach Beag, a boy of eleven, and the crew killed Seumas Dubh for the haste he had ordered. A' Chompanaidh hanged two hewers, Eòin Ruadh and Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging done by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach on Dia-thìr. The town's roll names the boy, his age and his mother, and the two hanged men, whom their neighbours carried home and buried in the town's own ground. Known for the first hanging.

**Cnoc naomh** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, GE 2,894. The holy hill south of the capital laid the dead of A' Phlàigh Uaine in its shrine's burial ground until it was full, and then in the field beside it, which was never ploughed again. In the months before the rising the crew-leaders of the north met by night on the moor above it and raised a cairn of spoil-stones from their own pits; the nineteen dead of the ford at Àth chiar were buried within sight of it. It has been a house of Macha since An Aois Scaraidh, and lies close by the old battlefield of Muileann ghlas. Known for the unploughed field and the two cairns.

**Cnoc shean** (Cnoc shean). Founded 18 am Màrt, FE 3. The drought-fever spread to the town from Baile Mòr ruadh in the hundred and ninth year and took mostly the very young. Its one well was found tainted and closed, and for a year the town drank from carts. Known for the year of the carts.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc thais). Founded 19 an t-Sultain, GE 4,328. The damp hill of the north-west heard of An Togail as a rumour before it came as a list. In the high summer of the ninetieth year An Togail's officers took its masons, Dùghall Clachair and his crew of six, to build the tower at Baile chrom, and their small fields stood untilled that year. Dùghall cut the names of his crew into the lintel of the lamp-room, the only writing on any of the five towers. It is the market of the country of the two Muileann àrsaidh, and An Togail's officers came to it again in each of the three years the towers were building. Known for the masons of the lintel.

**Cuan chrom** (Seann Vell). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, LE 1,231. The ford town on the northern road kept a carters' house at its quay that stood roofless for most of the age. Muireall nic Fhearchair, carrying her aunt's papers east to the loft at Muileann chaol in the thirtieth year, was held there by rain and read Clàr nan Dà Fhichead Dath aloud to the carters. That same autumn the town's carter, Seònaid Bhàn's father, lodged the drivers and oxen of the meal-carts of Doire fhiadhaich. Seònaid married Pàdraig mac Artair of Doire chaol there, took the old carters' house, and made her rule of marks and barter at its table. Known for Seònaid Bhàn's table.

**Cuan dhearg** (Muileann chrom). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, LE 1,789. The river town under the red cliffs on the Abhainn uaine lives on river fish and the short ferries between its two landings. In the first spring of the war the crew-leaders of the river towns met seven men in the back room of its inn, An Cupa Dàna, gave them sealed letters and hawks cast in lead from the cartridges of Muileann chrom, and sent them north to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig; they were Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, and the boatman Coinneach Beag was among them. The ring of small river towns on the Abhainn uaine above Cathair mhòr heard the news of the war first at its inn fire, where word was turned over until everyone in the room had handled it. Known for the inn where Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe set out.

**Cuan ruadh** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 1 an t-Sultain, GE 2,387. The harbour town of the eastern shore had carried goods by day along a coast too dangerous to run by night. When Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh was finished in the ninety-first year, A' Chompanaidh's steamers rounded the island without putting in, and the town's coasting boats were laid up within a few years. Voss's white sand came from its dunes. Known for the coasting trade that died.

**Cuan shean** (Cuan shean). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,755. The old harbour of the west was the first town of Dia-thìr to see the strangers, when Na Trì Longan lay off its cape in the first year and their people spent forty days on the dunes below it while the council decided what to do with them. Oighrig nic Leòid, its custodian, gave them water before any vote allowed it. The humans prayed in one of its sail-lofts in those first winters, and Fiabhras nan Coigreach went out from its quays into the country. For a hundred years coal came down to it from the hill and went out in the humans' hulls. In the last autumn of the age its custodians shut the harbour to every ship of A' Chompanaidh, and it was from its quay that Lionel Strake sailed, with three chests of harbour keys set at his feet. Its sail-lofts and rope-stores filled with the humans' trade for a generation, and its custodians kept their own roll of every ship that came in, beside the harbour master's. In the siege year it was the one western harbour that answered neither side's letters. Known for the first landing, and the last ship.

**Cuan uaine** (Doire fhada). Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,534. The river quays of the city east of the capital opened to the council's boats in the last year of the age. With them and the harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain both lost, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir could be fed only by water, up the Abhainn gheal from the sea. Known for the quays opened to the council.

#### D

**Doire chaol** (Doire chaol). Founded 3 an Giblean, AE 17. The carters of the village on the road just east of the capital banded together in the thirty-fifth year to bargain with A' Chompanaidh over the rates for hauling coal, the first Dia-thìreach guild of the age; A' Chompanaidh bought it, because that was cheaper than breaking it. Pàdraig mac Artair, who married Seònaid Bhàn of Cuan chrom, was a carter of the town, and its carters swore at Seònaid's table. Known for the first carters' guild.

**Doire chiar** (Doire chiar). Founded 8 an Giblean, GE 4,183. The village of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean north of the eastern workings held the schools' last open disputation on its threshing-floor on the eve of Bealltainn in the ninetieth year, before three parishes' folk, on whether a question may rightly be forbidden. The clerk of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach who attended noted that it may. Known for the last disputation.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Doire fhiadhaich). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, FE 1,981. The villages of the south sent meal north to the hill villages in the hungry thirty-first year, as the custom of An Aois Naomh bids. The agents of A' Chompanaidh at Àth ìseal bought two of the nine carts on the road; the seven that refused their marks went on into the hills and gave their meal away sack by sack at the village doors, as Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte bids, and their drivers came home by the carriers' road with their carts empty. Known for the seven carts.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire fhionn). Founded 20 am Màrt, FE 397. The village of the eastern drought country had its tarn fouled by the driven cattle of every drought district within a week of the drive, and its women walked each day to the spring at Àth ruadh and back for water, half a day's journey. The custodians recorded it for the three dry years, and then ceased. Known for the walk for water.

**Doire ghlas** (Doire ghlas). Founded 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470. The grey oak grove of Coimhdeach na Fine stood in the hunger's country. In the winter of the ninety-fifth year the hunger took its old and its very young first, its custodian walked door to door to write who still stood, and in the spring the village sent its young folk south to the camps for A' Chompanaidh's ration; by the year's end it was half empty. Some of its men had dug for Lowe on A' Chompanaidh's winter wage. Its grove was cut for the camps' timber in the famine years, and those who went south to the camps did not, most of them, come back. Known for its young sent to the camps.

**Doire mhin** (Doire mhin). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,260. The village of the south kept the old count of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, the measure of coal that might be burned in a year, one season longer than any other town on the island, and entered it in its roll with the note that no one asked for it. Known for the last count of the old law.

**Doire shean** (Doire shean). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 695. The fishing village below Am Buabhall Fortanach became in the war years the landing for goods the great road-house could not take by road. Its fishermen, old Coinneach nan Ràmh among them, took to being paid for certain nights never spoken of as work in silver struck in an Tìr Thall rather than the coin of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, and none of it was spent where a clerk of A' Chompanaidh might see. Known for the eastern silver.

**Doire uaine** (Muileann chiar). Founded 13 an Gearran, FE 2,879. After A' Chompanaidh's surveyors were lost on the high ground in the fifty-sixth year the people of the village at the foot of the hills left salt and coal for the sìth, as their grandparents had after any death there. A' Chompanaidh forbade coal to be left lying and had the offerings gathered up. The search party that went up after the surveyors came back with nothing but the tale of the Marbh-bheò. Known for the offerings gathered up.

**Dùn chiar** (Achadh àrsaidh). Founded 2 an Cèitean, FE 862. The weaving town of the north took a contract of A' Chompanaidh for canvas for the camp tents and sacks for the coal in the sixty-eighth year, by a vote of twenty-six to nine against its eldest weaver, Ealasaid Bhuidhe, who signed the roll of dissent and then wove canvas with the rest. The town throve on it. Its custodians noted that never before had it made anything for a use it did not approve. Known for the camp canvas.

**Dùn chrom** (Dùn chrom). Founded 7 am Faoilleach, GE 2,801. The fortified city on the crooked hill commands the roads south of the capital. Its rope-walks, which had spun cable for the fishing boats, turned wholly to winding-rope for the pit-heads in the thirty-first year, and the town grew by half on A' Chompanaidh's pay. A barracks was built there in the years of the constables. When Ashdown's column fell back through it after the ford at Àth chiar, the town shut its gates on the soldiers in the barracks and kept the column's wounded to nurse or to bury. Its citadel commands the roads south of the capital, and the barracks it housed were empty at the close of the age. Known for winding-rope, and the gates shut on Ashdown.

**Dùn dhearg** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 9 an Gearran, GE 4,274. The red hill-fort of the east sent Fionnghal nic Artair to Cathair dhearg in the early years, and hers is the only defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig that survives from the time it went out; the council filed her letter. The city kept its own counsel through the age. In the war its custodians sent grain south and read their declaration from the steps of the hall, quoting her sentence a hundred and twenty-seven years after she wrote it. The mills of Muileann dhomhain ground its bread and its custodians sent grain west to the camps in the hunger years by the old custom, asking nothing for it. Known for Fionnghal's letter, read again in the war.

**Dùn fhiadhaich** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 20 an Giblean, FE 1,384. The city under Cnoc naomh was where the tithe-gatherers began in the fifty-eighth year to weigh grain as well as coal, saying the town's farms fed the pits and shared in their gain. Griogair Fada, the largest farmer under the hill, asked the young gatherer who had set the new weight and got no answer he could carry home. The custodians entered the weighing in their roll under a name of their own coining, the tithe on the tithe. Known for the tithe on the tithe.

**Dùn ìseal** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1. The low fort-city of the east, an hour's walk from the silver town, kept a small constable post from the years of the constables. Cut off by the rising, it yielded to Comann an Airgid's riflemen after a single exchange of fire, and the whole east of the island stood clear of human arms. The old walls of Talla na Lasrach stand at it, where the keeper of the flame once settled the silver quarrel of the guild by giving each side half. Known for the post that yielded.

**Dùn thais** (Dùn thais). Founded 28 am Màrt, GE 2,473. The great hill city of the north-east kept the last hall of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, and Samuel Wren spent a winter there learning what the masters would teach a stranger. Its master Aonghas mac Coinnich put to his students the question why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal that every Dia-thìreach child sees, and did not answer it; a generation later George Tolley shut the hall over a lecture on whether that blindness was a kind of sickness, and Seònaid nic Dhùghaill was the last of its masters to teach openly. Am Fiabhras Glas came to it at the dark of a later year, and killed the physician Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had sent. The school's last masters went on teaching under the trees of Flidais after the hall was shut, and their pupils carried the disputations to Inis bhàn. Known for the shut hall of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean.

#### I

**Inis bhàn** (Inis bhàn). Founded 16 an Giblean, GE 3,916. The river port of the north-west opened a school of its own in the fifty-second year in answer to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's, and taught the old reckoning, the rolls and the names of the hills; the next year Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise complained in writing that the children who came to its school from Inis bhàn already knew how to argue, and the custodians kept the complaint as a testimonial. In the season of the hawk sermons its priests of the hawk sat down for the first time with the last teachers of the druid disputations. Its barges run down to Ros gheal on the coast, and its roll kept the names of the children who went to the custodians' school beside the names of those who went to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's. Known for its school, and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's complaint.

**Inis bheag** (Inis bheag). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,435. The river town took the eastern coal, carted over the rebuilt bridge at Ros fhionn and down to its quays, and sent it by barge to Caol chrom at the river mouth for shipping. A' Chompanaidh deepened the river at the quays in the fifty-third year, and the town's old fish market was moved to make room. Known for the moved fish market.

**Inis chrom** (Inis chrom). Founded 25 an Giblean, FE 1,601. The town a day's sail east of Baile dhìreach took in the human boatbuilders when they moved their yard there in the forty-seventh year for the timber A' Chompanaidh had promised them, and it made no joint council and no compact with them. Iain Hale refused the yard and stayed at Baile dhìreach. Within a generation the boatbuilders faded from the town's rolls. Known for the boatyard.

**Inis mhin** (Inis mhin). Founded 5 an Lùnastal, FE 2,644. The Tuathaich harbour town of the north coast ate its seed corn in the second winter of Gorta Baile chrom, and was fed through that season by the kitchen of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise at the harbour, three hundred a day on fish broth and biscuit brought by sea from Cathair gheal. Its landing was walled by the humans. In the last year of the age the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lay twelve hours in a boat-shed there, heard that Strake's constables rode the western roads daily, and hired a carter of the town with a covered cart and a mule who asked nothing of what he carried. Known for the harbour kitchen of the hunger.

**Inis mhòr** (Inis mhòr). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, GE 4,328. The river port of the north-east grew in the age from a fishing town into a city on the trade of the strangers. Its shipwrights learned to build in the humans' fashion for A' Chompanaidh's coasting trade, and its fishwives kept the old market on the steps where cloth was still bartered for fish long after the mark was law. In the war the townsfolk burned A' Chompanaidh's coal where it lay stacked on the quays, sooner than let it fuel one more ship like the one that shelled Seann Toll. Its barges run down the Abhainn ghorm to the sea, and in the years of An Togail its carpenters were among the men Riaghaltas nan Coigreach took for the building of the beacon towers. Known for its shipwrights, and the coal burned on its quays.

**Inis mhòr** (Seann Vell). Founded 12 an t-Sultain, LE 730. The river port just east of the capital stacked on its quays the coal that the barges carried down the Abhainn fhionn to A' Chompanaidh's steamships at Cathair dhomhain. In the last year of the age its townsfolk set the stacks alight rather than let a ship carry them off to burn against another Seann Toll, and the ships put in at Ros dhomhain and burned their own stores. The word reached the muster of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe at Seann Skell. Known for the coal it burned itself.

**Inis thais** (Inis thais). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 2,408. The walled temple city of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west declined in the first years to join the joint council of Baile dhìreach, a few miles off, its custodian writing that one town may be a trial but two would be a rule. In the war its priests heard Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe's letter and would send no men, since that was not what Òrd na Cloiche was for, but shut the harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships and opened an Fhianna's roads to the hawk-faithful. Its temple of Lia Fàil, the stone that cries out, is the chief house of Òrd na Cloiche, and its priests keep a driftwood fire that burns blue-white with the salt. Known for the harbour shut in the war.

**Inis uaine** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 3 an t-Ògmhios, LE 980. Pilgrims of Na Seann Spioradan bound for the spring of Allt an Àigh, which never failed through the three dry years, gathered at the town, and its folk fed them freely, as Na Seann Spioradan require, and opened their own granary to them rather than see them go hungry on the road home. Its wells were low, and it gave away more water than it kept. Known for the pilgrims fed.

#### M

**Muileann àrsaidh** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 10 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,444. The Tuathaich town of the concession blocked its road with carts in Cogadh nam Beann and kept a watch on it against both sides. No one attacked it, and the watch was kept to the end of the war. Known for the watch against both sides.

**Muileann bhàn** (Muileann bhàn). Founded 24 an Dàmhair, GE 2,378. Where Rathad na Mèinne from the eastern diggings met the mills, silversmiths settled in the eighties and worked the guild's bar into brooches, clasps and buckles for the humans' own market. Theirs was the one craft of the island sold across the sea under its own name. It stands at the meeting of Rathad na Mèinne and the mills with a citadel above it, and its smiths' marks were known in the humans' shops across the sea. Known for its silversmiths.

**Muileann bheag** (Muileann bheag). Founded 23 an Giblean, FE 1,789. The workings of the north-eastern town among the druid villages stopped with the rest on Là Stad nan Sloc, the day of the fire. Its custodian wrote that it was the first thing the town had done with the hills in a hundred years. Known for the first thing done with the hills.

**Muileann bheag** (Muileann leathan). Founded 14 an Giblean, LE 1,530. The small mill town on the north coast stands beside Taigh-solais Muileann bheag, the only one of the five lights to burn coal. Its keeper Ailig mac Griogair asked three winters running to go back to the old lamp, and its fishermen complained that the colour the coal flame cast on the water drove the herring off. Lowe came to see the flame and the keeper's son answered him on the point. Within a season the herring came back, and the complaint was withdrawn. In the stoppage of the hundred and forty-third year its pits stopped with the rest. The coal flame's colour on the water was still remarked by every stranger who passed the cape at night. Known for the coal-burning light.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 12 am Màrt, FE 2,570. The small northern town shares its name with the town of the cellar, and in the hundred and twenty-fifth year three years of copies bound for the cellar came to it by mistake. Its old custodian kept them whole and dry, and when Cailean mac Eachainn walked north to fetch them he said only that a roll is a roll, and that he had kept it well until someone came to say it was theirs. Known for the mis-sent rolls, kept well.

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 3,218. The narrow mill town in the eastern hills held, in the cellar under its mill house, the copies of the custodians' rolls that Na Trì Teaghlaichean of the town made fair winter after winter, the fullest record of the eastern hills and the one no stranger's eye was meant to read. Gormshuil nic Fhearchair was called back from it to the council in the first years, and the rubbing of the first mark went to its loft. Seònag Bhàn kept the copying until her eyes failed, and Cailean mac Eachainn took up the hand at four-and-twenty; it was there he found Sloinneadh Aisling and there, in the last days of the hundred and fiftieth year, that the four chests of the age's rolls came down to him by cart. The copying was done at a long table under a single window, and every copy was made twice, so that no one fire or flood could take the only record of a town. Known for the cellar of copied rolls.

**Muileann chiar** (Muileann chiar). Founded 23 an t-Iuchar, LE 365. The coal-breakers' mill town west of the silver country grew so crowded with the guild's refiners and carters in the eighty-second year that it was called by the silver town's name from then on, and the rolls speak of the old town and the new without always saying which. It lived on the carrying trade between the two. It began as a coal-breaking mill for the diggings in the hills east of the capital, and the carters of both towns shared one inn and one quarrel for the rest of the age. Known for the silver town's second name.

**Muileann chiar** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 10 an Lùnastal, FE 7. The silver town lies in the far east of the hills on a shelf of the valley under the moor, an hour's walk from the old walls at Dùn ìseal. Its guild, Comann an Airgid, held its seam under a compact that Ùna locked in the guild chest in the first half-century, and the surveyors who came for its ledgers were turned back at the adit. The guild sent its bar to the sea by Seann Bhral rather than A' Chompanaidh's quays, paid for the mark in silver, refused Martha Gale's partnership in the sixty-seventh year by a count of hands in its hall, and in the years before the war bought rifles from the raiders of the eastern waters and entered them in its ledger as refining tools. In the rising its riflemen took Dùn ìseal and cleared the east of human arms. The seam is silver near the great vein but not of it. Catrìona nic Eachainn, a refiner of the guild, died there an old woman in the hundred and fourth year, and Ùna nic Choinnich headed the guild into her eightieth winter. Known for the guild compact and its riflemen.

**Muileann chrom** (Muileann chrom). Founded 11 an Gearran, FE 1,556. The mill on the bend of the river is the heart of the coal country. Six sacks of its hill's coal went down to the strangers in the first years, and the first contract was read aloud at the mill. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill took A' Chompanaidh's staff here and a house with a slate roof, and his son Dòmhnall, his grandson Iain and his great-granddaughter Mòrag held it after him, until Mòrag broke it across her knee on A' Chompanaidh's step in the hundred and forty-eighth year. Seven men drowned in its flooded gallery, and the inquiry struck her testimony out. On the twenty-eighth of an Gearran in the hundred and forty-ninth year its people took the walled store at first light, and the war began here. Its mill still ground grain for the central country through all the years of the coal, and the steelyard ledgers of its weigh-house, in which the hill's coal had been set down by the ton since the first contract, burned green in the ledger fires of the hundred and fiftieth year. Known for the overseer's staff, and the first morning of the war.

**Muileann dhearg** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 30 an t-Sultain, LE 2. The mill town a short way from Cill ghlas was where Griogair mac Aonghais told Fearchar Bard to sing the song that went round every pit of the hills without his name on it. In the three years before the rising the smith Uilleam Gobha turned A' Chompanaidh's blasting-powder, bought a keg at a time on a chit of A' Chompanaidh, into bombs packed in tin from the coal sheds' scrap, and forged pike-heads by day out of rail-iron; the rebels' council wrote that without his forge the rising could not have been fought past its first weeks. Taigh na Fèithe above the town kept Leabhar a' Chùraim of the hill through the long centuries, and its keepers set down A' Chompanaidh's coming in the same hand as everything before it. Known for Uilleam Gobha's forge.

**Muileann dhomhain** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 8 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,747. The mill on the deep race grew rich carrying grain to the camps. When the crews brought to break the strike at Cnoc chaol were marched through it, its townsfolk turned them from every door, and they slept in A' Chompanaidh's barns; several went home the next season. After Scàineadh Cill ghlas its custodians met the people of the closed district on the moor road and lent them common ground, on which they built Achadh chaol. It is the seat of its province, and its custodians had long kept the right of the old roads to shelter any traveller who asked; they held that right did not reach men sent to take other men's work. Known for the doors shut on the strikebreakers.

**Muileann fhionn** (Caol mhòr). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, AE 23. The Tuathaich mill town of the north-west shut its roads against Am Fiabhras Glas in the hundred and forty-first year and kept them shut a season, turning the concession's human carters back at the town's edge with their loads still on the carts. No custodian there ordered it, and every custodian there defended it. Known for the roads shut against the fever.

**Muileann gheal** (Muileann chiar). Founded 20 an Lùnastal, FE 2,347. The herders' village under Binnean a' Chlachair, the highest ground of the island, refused James Fenn a night fire on the summit in the sixth year, keeping the custom of the hills. Torcall Clachair laid one stone on the herders' cairn there, and Fenn took his fire to the headlands instead. Known for the summit left dark.

**Muileann mhin** (Muileann mhin). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,458. The river port just east of the capital argued three days over the war, as much on trade as on loyalty, and then sent its boats to the council at Cathair dhearg. Through that winter and the next the boats carried food down the Abhainn fhionn to the capital by night. Known for the boats sent to the council.

**Muileann naomh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 4 an t-Ògmhios, FE 599. The custodians of the town offered the officers of An Togail silver in the eighty-ninth year to halve its tally. The officers weighed the purse, kept it as an offering to A' Chompanaidh's granary, and read the whole list uncut. The complaint was lodged at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and filed, and no other town on record offered a bribe after it. Known for the bribe that bought nothing.

**Muileann òg** (Dùn chrom). Founded 10 am Faoilleach, FE 905. The old barter market at the ford, where hill and coast had met to trade since An Aois Naomh, closed after a poor last season in the hundred and thirtieth year, when barter was struck down, and the green shoulder of ground above the ford stood empty from then on. Known for the empty market ground.

**Muileann shean** (Muileann shean). Founded 1 an t-Samhain, FE 1,093. The old mill of the north, whose wheel Clàr nan Rìghrean already calls ancient, took Merriman's first constable post in the hundred and thirty-second year, a stone house with a yard for horses on the northern coal road. The townsfolk called it the humans' second Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and did not mean it kindly. In the first week of the rising the post was taken at first light and its constables sent south on foot. Its walls went up in the years of the constables, around the post and the mill together, and its miller ground for the post and for the town at the same price. Known for the first constable post.

#### R

**Ros àrsaidh** (Ros bheag). Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,221. Strake posted constables at the town north of Ros bheag in the last year of the age to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh. The townsfolk brought them food and news, and the news was always a day old. Known for the day-old news.

**Ros bheag** (Ros bheag). Founded 2 an Dàmhair, GE 1,274. The citadel harbour of the western coast was the humans' western port from the earliest years, and in the autumn of the hundred and fiftieth year it became the last seat of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, when Strake came down the Abhainn gheal with his officers and clerks and the human families of the west and south came in behind its walls. It ran short of food within weeks, and Strake ordered A' Chompanaidh's store opened to humans and townsfolk alike at one measure, with no ledger kept. The last ship from an Tìr Thall anchored off it at Samhain. Its Dia-thìrich townsfolk kept their own houses and their own market cross through three generations of A' Chompanaidh's officers at the quay, and found themselves strangers in their own gates in the last autumn. Known for the last seat, and the last ship.

**Ros dhìreach** (Cnoc mhòr). Founded 22 an t-Ògmhios, LE 76. The harbour on the straight headland of the gulf became A' Chompanaidh's second coal port in the seventieth year, to carry off the yield of the southern workings without the long haul round to Ros dhomhain. Edward Vane laid an iron tram-road drawn by mules from the pits down to its quay; it halved the cost of shipping coal and ended the carting trade of the villages on the old road. A' Phlàigh Uaine fell on it among the first of the coast towns. It is the harbour of Cnoc mhòr's cattle trade, and the drovers kept their own quay beside A' Chompanaidh's coal stage for the whole of the age. Known for the tram-road and the second coal stage.

**Ros dhomhain** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,694. Ros dhomhain lies a short walk below the capital on the lake shore, and it grew in the age into a second town of sawn timber and dressed stone beside the first. Pike's trading post stood on its quay, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on the rise above it, and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chapel below. The mark and its hundred pence were first paid across its counter, its dockers struck beside the humans' own dockers, and the inquiry into the flood at Muileann chrom sat in Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's panelled room. In the war the harbour quarter held itself apart from both sides for a year, until its own men burned the tithe books of the counting-house by night and opened the lower gates to Buidhnean na Comhairle. Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir was found stripped at the end of an t-Sultain, its letter-books left whole on the shelves. Its quays took the coal of the hill from the barges for more than a century, and its steelyard and counting-house scales weighed every load. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chaplains kept their register of the dead in the chapel below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and Hannah Webb's brother Daniel was shipped from its quay with the human dockers after the strike. Known for the counting-house fire and the letter-books.

**Ros fhionn** (Caol shean). Founded 10 am Màrt, FE 1,262. The city of the eastern workings stood by the rebuilt bridge on the eastern coal road. In Cogadh nam Beann its crews stopped the pumps and walked out, and the lower galleries flooded; A' Chompanaidh's engineers went down the Abhainn chaol and took ship at Seann Mhorn for Ros dhomhain, and the bridge fell silent. Known for the flooded galleries.

**Ros gharbh** (Ros gharbh). Founded 3 am Faoilleach, LE 255. The fishermen of the southern harbour town carried salt fish up to the camps by night in the years of Sìol-lann na Companaidh, past its ration and its rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of that decade that ran the right way. Known for fish carried by night.

**Ros gheal** (Ros gheal). Founded 29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,009. The largest of the three towns of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig has been a hawk town since the second house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig was founded there. When Lisle opened a customs house in a hired loft by its fish-steps in the forty-second year, its fishwives chased the officer out twice in his first year, and the roll says only that he went away by water. In the fever years its hawk-faithful raised a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall itself, in open sight of the customs house. It shares its bay with Seann Skell and Ros leathan and has quarrelled with them over moorings for as long as the rolls run. Known for the customs officer who went away by water.

#### S

**Seann Bhral** (Seann Bhral). Founded 30 an Lùnastal, VE 1,005. The greatest harbour of the south-eastern coast, where the oyster-beds lie in the shallows, loaded the silver town's bar for the coasting boats as it had since An Aois Naomh. From the forty-fourth year the guild sent all its silver south by this road, eighteen miles down the valley, and paid the custodians of the port in silver by the Muileann chiar weight on every bar. When a collier burned off the coast A' Chompanaidh's agents said at its quays that the guild had paid the raiders to do it; the charge was never proved. Torcall's crews built its new quay in the first years of the strangers. Its harbour is the largest of that coast, and in the war its custodians turned A' Chompanaidh's coasters away without a shot fired. Known for the silver road to the sea.

**Seann Bhrenn** (Seann Bhrenn). Founded 12 an Giblean, VE 321. Gorta Baile chrom reached as far east as the village in the ninety-sixth year. Its custodians levered open the sealed grain-pits of An Aois Naomh on the chalk hill above the town, unopened in living memory and kept against a need no one thought would come, and found in them only dust. Known for the grain-pits of dust.

**Seann Chwen** (Seann Dunn). Founded 1 am Faoilleach, VE 1,236. The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, further west on the south coast, joined the raids along the shore in the last year of the age. The rolls tell the two towns apart by the names of their boats. Known for the other Seann Chwen.

**Seann Chwen** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an Giblean, VE 32. Fishing boats of the southern town and of Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast in the last year of the age, boarded a coaster of A' Chompanaidh at anchor and burned her, and A' Chompanaidh drew its coastal shipping back to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag. Known for the coaster burned.

**Seann Dunn** (Baile chaol). Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd, VE 320. The eastern port got a customs house of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach in the ninety-eighth year and a store of A' Chompanaidh with it, opened as help against a bad year. The store sold the east its seed and its tools, and within a few years its ledgers held the debts of half the district, entered against named households; Coinneach Òg told the custodians so at the fire inside the wall of Ceann àrsaidh when they met to draft the petition. Baile ruadh borrowed its seed corn there in the drought. Known for the store's ledgers.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, VE 1,833. The walled harbour of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig heard Murchadh Seabhag preach the hawk's old freedom against the strangers' tithe, and a century later Ìomhar Seabhag's sermons went out from it in copies to the camps and the burial clubs. The hawk-shrines opened again along its bay in the season the fever returned. Its fishing families were proud to the end of the age of having chased A' Chompanaidh's first customs men off their harbour. Murchadh Seabhag preached from the steps of its temple, and copies of his sermons were carried inland to the camps by fishermen. Its harbour was shut to A' Chompanaidh's shipping in the war. Known for the hawk sermons.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 6 an Gearran, VE 173. The great river port of the west, a short march north-east of Ros bheag, was where the company of the hawk-faithful mustered under Ìomhar Seabhag's eye in the early summer of the hundred and fiftieth year, and where the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe were told they were one company with one name. The company held the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war. It is the largest place on the island after the capital, and its barges run down the Abhainn naomh to Ros àrsaidh. Known for the hawk company's muster.

**Seann Toll** (Muileann chrom). Founded 8 an Gearran, VE 92. The old river port in the hollow of the rock was made a coal landing early in the age, and its barge-stage took the hill's coal down the Abhainn uaine for more than a century. In the first winter of the war a ship of A' Chompanaidh came up the river and shelled the stage to keep it from the rebels; three-and-twenty of the fishing town behind it died, and the ship burned island coal to do it. Its walls follow Macha. Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe passed the burned stage on the first day of their walk north and found a woman sorting stone from ash with her bare hands at what had been her hearth. Known for the shelling of the coal stage.

**Seann Vell** (Seann Vell). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, VE 1,197. The harbour town on Eilean ruadh became in the hundred and twenty-third year the seat of the district of the outer coasts, ruled from its harbour office, where the revenue cutters of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach lay. Its surveyors walked the edge of the great moss beyond the town, found no way across, and left the rest of the district's map blank; the custodians of those coasts were no readier to be counted than the moss. Known for the blank map.

**Seann Vell** (Seann Vell). Founded 1 an t-Ògmhios, VE 3,673. The river port east of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn took An Scàird Fhuilteach from the coal barges in the sixtieth year, after a sick bargeman was put ashore there. Its custodians, led by Mairead nic Amhlaidh, shut the only barge landing the town had for a whole season, though it cost every fee the landing had ever earned; A' Chompanaidh fined the town for the lost fees, and Mairead read the letter to the council on the landing steps within sight of that season's graves. Known for the shut landing.

**Seann Vell** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, GE 3,560. The harbour on the capital shore, eighteen miles down the river from Ros dhomhain, shut the only quay it had for the coal traffic in the season of the flux and let no barge tie up; it paid A' Chompanaidh's fine from the purse that had buried its dead. Anne Colby walked there to help lay out the last of them. In Stad-oibre a' Chalaidh of the hundred and thirty-fourth year its dockers, with no human among them, refused to load the coal sent round to them; they were not shipped over the sea, but neither were they hired again for two years. It stands on the old quay stones of the Seann-Dhaoine, still seen at low water, and its harbour-master's rolls show its dockers unhired two years running. Known for the quay shut against the flux.

**Seann Warr** (Àth chiar). Founded 15 an Gearran, VE 2,245. The farming town of the south-east, not the salt port of that name in the west, sent grain to the hills by the eastern roads from the first winter of Cogadh nam Beann, and the council's roll lists the carts; Dùghall of the harbour quarter counted them at Ros dhomhain. Known for the grain carts.

**Seann Warr** (Seann Warr). Founded 27 am Màrt, VE 725. Seann Warr on the capital's western shore boils salt from the brine springs in the reed marsh behind the town, and it was the first place on the island to sell to Pike's counter, in the third year of the strangers, putting up its price when it heard what he would pay. Its carters took the salt round the lake to the capital for a century on their own roads. In the siege year it sent grain to the hills and the capital every month, by carts that went the long way round to avoid Strake's patrols. A' Chompanaidh tried twice to buy the pans outright and was twice refused, the salt-boilers holding that brine rising from the ground was no more theirs to sell than the rain. Known for brine salt, and the grain trains of the siege.

#### T

**Tobar dhearg** (Tobar dhearg). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, GE 2,947. The large village of the red well gave its name to Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, the last of the five lights as the ring is counted round the coast from Baile chrom. Its first keeper was chosen by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach on the custodians' word. In the first spring of the war its keeper Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill put the light out with her own hand, before any order reached her, rather than guide A' Chompanaidh's ships along a coast the council held; when the truce was signed the council had it lit again. The keeper's daybook there ends its entries for the war with a line of Raonaid's own, and takes them up again without comment at the relighting. Known for the light put out in the war.

**Tobar dhìreach** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, VE 42. The eldest of the three wells that claim the mason's crack is the home of Clann na Ceiste, who keep lines longer than any roll. Cailean mac Eachainn walked the hill road there in the hundred and twenty-sixth year with seven names copied on a scrap of paper inside his coat, to ask whether a line so old could truly be Donnchadh's own, and came back with Sloinneadh Aisling. Its water runs along a straight stone channel through the village, and the keepers of the lines there asked Cailean nothing in return but that the line be copied fair. Known for the keepers of the long lines.

**Tobar dhomhain** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 17 am Màrt, AE 32. The village of the grasslands in the western hills lay off every road but the one from Ros bheag to the northern concession. In the last year of the age the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lay eleven hours in the long grass above that road and counted every rider who passed, Gillebrìde keeping the tally on a strip of bark: forty-one constables' riders in a day, all going south and none north. Known for the count in the grass.

**Tobar fhiadhaich** (Tobar fhiadhaich). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, GE 1,879. Am Fiabhras Glas took one household in three at the northern village in the hundred and forty-first year. Its custodians burned no huts; they had heard of Àth ghlas in their grandparents' time, but judged it too late. Known for the huts not burned.

**Tobar ghorm** (Tobar ghorm). Founded 31 am Faoilleach, FE 950. The village of the blue spring holds the greatest wool fairs of the north, older than the strangers' coming. A second constable post was raised there in the hundred and thirty-third year near the northern workings; its custodian was paid rent for the ground, and with it bought the village out of its debts to A' Chompanaidh's store. The post fell with Muileann shean's in the first week of the rising. The humans' wool-buyers came to its fairs every year of the age, and paid in marks once the coin was struck. Known for the wool fairs, and the rent that paid the store.

# Appendix A — The Council, Na h-Àrd-mhaoir and the Overseers

For a hundred and fifty years Dia-thìr had two heads and would own to neither of them. Comhairle a' Chùraim, sat at Cathair dhearg as it had since An Aois Naomh, with a Ceann a' Chùraim, at the end of its table; and from the eighth year Riaghaltas nan Coigreach of the strangers, Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, sat in Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir above Ros dhomhain under An t-Àrd-mhaor, sent from over the sea. Between them stood A' Chompanaidh, which held the pits, and the overseers it set over the crews of the hill. This appendix gives each office as the rolls and the letter-books give it at the close of the age, with the years and ages of those who held it. Years are counted from the coming of the ships; ages are given as the rolls give them, at the taking of the office and at its end.

## The high custodians

Ceann a' Chùraim was chosen by the council from among its own members, for life or until he laid the seat down, and signed for the council in all its dealings with the strangers. The seat carried no crown and no guard. Its holder read letters aloud to the sitting, kept the order of speaking, and put his name to what the council agreed.

**Tormod mac Ailein**, Ceann a' Chùraim from the second year to the twentieth. He was forty-six when the rolls first name him in the seat and sixty-four when he died at Cathair dhearg. He signed Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg for the custodians in the council hall in the eighth year, across the table from Josiah Pell, and could not read the tongue it was written in. Six custodians carried him to the ground behind the hall with the bells of the capital ringing.

**Coinneach Glas** of Ceann àrsaidh, from the twentieth year to the forty-fourth. He was chosen on the second night of Tormod's waking, at forty-five, a broad, slow-spoken man from twenty miles up the east road, and died in the seat at sixty-nine. It was in his years that the coin was struck, Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig went out, and the first pits were sunk at Muileann chrom.

**Alasdair Liath**, from the forty-fourth year to the seventy-first. He was forty-nine when he was chosen, a custodian who had sat on the council since before Puingean a' Chalaidh and had voted to sign them; the roll gives his choosing in a single line with his age and the number of voices. He held the seat twenty-seven years, through A' Phlàigh Uaine, and died at seventy-six.

**The empty seat**, from the seventy-first year to the eighty-first. The council could not agree on a head, and said among itself, in the hearing of no clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, that an empty seat answered no letters and signed no papers. Àrd-mhaoir who wished to address the council in those years stood before the whole table.

**Artair mac Iain** of the eastern shires, from the eighty-first year to the hundred and fifth. He was six-and-fifty when he was seated, a quiet man who had kept his own town's rolls without a blot for thirty years and had never once been summoned to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir. Fearghas mac Mhuirich said the order's blessing over him, both horses named. He died at Cathair dhearg at eighty, Ceann a' Chùraim twenty-four years.

**The empty seat**, from the hundred and fifth year to the close of the age. After Artair the council chose no head again. The old chair stood where it had always stood, since no one thought to move it and no one had the right to sit in it, and Edward Vane addressed the council in his good coat with his hat in his two hands before a table with no one at its end. In the first winter of his rule Lionel Strake had the council hall locked and its keys lodged at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and the custodians sat on the floor of Macha's temple for two years, until the townsfolk broke the locks in the spring of the hundred and forty-ninth year.

## Comhairle na Coille

In the late summer of the hundred and forty-eighth year the custodians of the mining country, the crew-leaders of the pits and the priests of Macha who had left the capital's temple met by night in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag near Cnoc bheag and made one council of the whole mining country, of which no human writing kept a line. It chose **Eilidh nic Raghnaill** of Baile thais to speak for it. She was forty-three, crew-leader of Baile thais and a member of Faire nan Lòchran, and had drafted the sentence of An Dàrna Athchuinge that Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir had underlined. Strake ordered her taken with the council's members in am Faoilleach of the hundred and forty-ninth year; she had gone two days before, and the council sat on through the war. Its clerk in the war years was a woman named Fionnuala, who kept its roll and read the names of its dead aloud. Comhairle na Coille's envoys signed the truce at Àth àrsaidh, and at the close of the age it held the hills, the east and the capital.

## A' Chompanaidh

**Edmund Harrow**, captain of Na Trì Longan that lay off Cuan shean in the first year, founded A' Chompanaidh with Thomas Pike under licence of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach. Once Pell had built Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir Harrow went back to the sea trade. He sailed north-about on a second voyage with three hulls and was lost at sea in the twenty-first year, at fifty-six.

**Thomas Pike**, trader of the post at Ros dhomhain, kept A' Chompanaidh's counter on the quay from the first years and was master of A' Chompanaidh after Harrow. He chose the ground for the warehouse at Cathair dhomhain and wrote home of the island's coal before anyone on the island called it a trade. A' Chompanaidh's later masters sat over the sea and are known on Dia-thìr only by their seals.

## Na h-Àrd-mhaoir

An t-Àrd-mhaor was appointed over the sea and answered to Riaghaltas nan Coigreach there. His commission, read aloud at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on his landing, named his powers and, until the last, the leave and counsel of Comhairle a' Chùraim.

| Àrd-mhaor | Years | Age at taking office | Age at its end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Josiah Pell | 8–24 | 48 | 64 |
| Henry Maddox | 24–41 | 29 | 46 |
| Arthur Lisle | 41–61 | 41 | 61, died in office |
| Walter Crane | 61–75 | 46 | 60, died in office |
| Martha Gale, holding the seal | 75–76 | 45 | 46 |
| George Tolley | 76–98 | 46 | 68 |
| Robert Haskins | 98–114 | 53 | 69 |
| Edward Vane | 114–132 | 44 | 62, died in office |
| Charles Merriman | 132–146 | 47 | 61 |
| Lionel Strake | 146–150 | 46 | 50 |

**Josiah Pell** built Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain, signed Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, and sailed home at the end of his term and did not return. **Henry Maddox** barred the hawk-priests from the camps, for their preaching slowed the work. **Arthur Lisle** opened the customs house at Ros gheal, sent his surveyors to the adit at Muileann chiar, raised the tithe from one part in five to one part in three, and died at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir of a fever of the heart. **Walter Crane**, who had been A' Chompanaidh's chief agent at the pits, walked the camps in the worst of A' Phlàigh Uaine and died of it at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir. **Martha Gale**, A' Chompanaidh's agent at Ros dhomhain, held the seal for the months between Crane's death and Tolley's landing; eight years before, Comann an Airgid had refused her partnership by every hand in its hall save one. **George Tolley** set the quarantine at Caol mhin, asked Macha's priests to bless the new coin, issued An Togail, and retired with honours. **Robert Haskins** ordered that the council be consulted on the tithe and set the tithe before the council met; in the drought he answered each custodian's petition alone. **Edward Vane**, the only Àrd-mhaor born on the island, at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir itself, laid the tram-road to Ros dhìreach and died in the bed he was born in. **Charles Merriman** brought the first armed constables, built the posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, tripled the constables after the fight at Muileann chrom, and went home in poor health. **Lionel Strake**, a soldier, had the council hall locked, sent the iron bird over the coal country, issued Àithne a' Ghlacaidh and the order to take Comhairle na Coille, held Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir through the first year of the war, went down the Abhainn gheal to Ros bheag in the autumn of the hundred and fiftieth year, and sailed from Cuan shean in the last ship able to make the crossing. Of his landing over the sea nothing is known.

## The overseers of Muileann chrom

In the thirty-sixth year A' Chompanaidh set a man of the island over the Dia-thìreach crews of the hill, gave him a staff and a house with a slate roof, and called him its overseer; the hill called him the Maor. The custodians hoped the office would die with the first man to hold it. It passed instead from father to son for four generations, and the staff with it, brass-capped and iron-shod.

**Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill, Raghnall Maor**, from the thirty-sixth year to the sixty-second. He was forty-six when he took the staff from the agent's hand, having led the first crew of thirty under the first contract, and seventy-two when he died. His mother's neighbours gave him his byname the week he moved into the slate-roofed house.

**Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor**, from the sixty-second year to the eighty-seventh. He took the staff at forty-two and died with it at sixty-seven. He signed the granary order after Stad-oibre Baile thais.

**Iain Maor**, from the eighty-seventh year to the hundred and thirty-first. He took the staff at thirty-seven, the first overseer schooled at Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, and held it until his death at eighty-one. He wrote letters to Riaghaltas nan Coigreach for which he was dismissed, and was taken back because no one else would be trusted by the camps.

**Mòrag nic Iain Maor**, from the hundred and thirty-first year to the hundred and forty-eighth. She took the staff at thirty-six, the first woman to hold it, and A' Chompanaidh approved her in a letter as a safe pair of hands. At the inquiry into the flood at Muileann chrom she bore witness that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order, and her words were struck out. In the summer of the hundred and forty-eighth year, at fifty-three, she refused the order to clear eleven households and broke the staff across her knee on A' Chompanaidh's step. On the twenty-eighth of an Gearran in the hundred and forty-ninth year she led the crews that took the walled store at Muileann chrom, and the war began.

The overseers of the other pits held their staffs under the same terms. Griogar Camshron of the north pit at Muileann chrom, the overseer of Cnoc chaol, and a third at the edge of the silver country laid theirs down in the same season as Mòrag, and A' Chompanaidh set humans in their places.

## Comann an Airgid

Comann an Airgid of Muileann chiar governed its own seam under a compact older than any contract of A' Chompanaidh, and chose its heads by a count of hands in its hall. **Ùna nic Choinnich** stood with the ledgers at the adit when Lisle's surveyors came, locked the compact in the guild chest, and headed the guild into her eightieth winter; she refused Martha Gale's partnership at about eighty-two and died at eighty-five, in the seventieth year. After her the guild's roll gives its heads by name and year and nothing else. In the war its riflemen took their orders from the guild hall.

## The keepers of the five lights

Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh of the coast were built at the humans' asking on the headlands of the old driftwood fires, and kept by the households that had kept the fires, on the custodians' word.

- **Taigh-solais Àth dhearg**, on the north-eastern cape: Tormod mac Pheadair, a mason, keeper from its lighting until his death at eighty-eight, who began the first daybook.
- **Taigh-solais Baile ìseal**, on the eastern cape: kept by the households who had kept the fire, and by no one else, which was the first thing they asked for.
- **Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg**, in the south: Anna nic Dhòmhnaill, a fisherman's widow, its first keeper; at the close of the age Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill, who put the light out in the war.
- **Taigh-solais Muileann bheag**, on the north shore: Ailig mac Griogair, who kept the coal-burning lamp and asked three winters running to go back to oil.
- **Taigh-solais Baile chrom**, on the north-western headland, the last built: Uisdean mac Lachlainn, keeper from the ninety-first year, who was thirty when he took it and died at sixty-five; and his son Lachlann mac Uisdein, forty at the close of the age, who watched the last Àrd-mhaor's ship stand out north.

# Appendix B — The Faiths under the Strangers

The strangers brought one faith with them and found a great many. The orders of Dia-thìr were old when the ships came: Òrd Mhacha at the capital and in the south, Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west, the hawk along the north-central coast, Manannan in the harbours, Scoiltean nan Draoidhean of the north-east, and the old keeping of the vein by the custodians, which was less an order than a habit of the whole island. None of them was put down in the age. Some were barred, some were bought, and one was shut by order, and each of them in its own way outlived Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that tried it. This appendix gives each as it stood at the close of the age.

## An Eaglais and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise

The humans' faith came ashore at Cuan shean in the first year. Its people prayed in a sail-loft of the town that first winter, and their clerics sat down with the custodians at Cathair dhearg in the season of speech-making. They worshipped one god and a son of his, and the Dia-thìrich wrote the son's name *Crìosd* as the clerics said it; the whole company of their believers the priests called by a word the island made into *an Eaglais*. On the island An Eaglais worked through its house, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, which answered to its masters over the sea and not to An t-Àrd-mhaor, though the two were seldom far apart.

Samuel Wren, the thin, coughing cleric who made the word-lists with Gormshuil nic Fhearchair, finished a grammar of Dia-thìris for Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, careful and true in most things, which gave the word for the vein's custodians as "keepers of the coal." He copied Carragh Cnoc bheag and sent it over the sea, and no answer came; he spent a winter in disputation with the druid masters at Dùn thais. He died in the thirty-third year.

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise raised the first church on the island, a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain, with the first iron bell on Dia-thìr; the custodians asked that it not be rung before the fishing fleet was out, and the bell was rung once before the fleet was out all the same. Thereafter Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise kept a chapel in every camp and a chaplain to write the dead. It counted four hundred and six dead of A' Bhreac Bhallach, and the custodians counted more and wrote the difference in the margin of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's list. Its nurse Anne Colby made a sick-house of the chapel in the flux, kept a canvas sick-house at Achadh dhomhain through A' Phlàigh Uaine, and came back to the island for the famine kitchens at Baile chrom and Cathair gheal. It sank the deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom in the drought. Its school at Ros dhomhain took thirty pupils in its first year, most of them overseers' children; Iain Maor was schooled there. Its cleric Edwin Lowe dug at Làrach an Teampaill and copied Colbh Cnoc chiar and Calbh Cnoc ghorm, seeking an older faith, and left with his notebooks. Its minister Matthew Dunne preached from the chapel pulpit against the night shift, saying the Dia-thìrich were right that even the ground must rest, and was called home. Its hospital at Cathair gheal took in Dia-thìrich and human sick side by side in Am Fiabhras Glas. In the last autumn Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's clergy went down the Abhainn gheal with Strake, and its chapels stood empty.

Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise counted its first Dia-thìreach converts among its first pupils. Neither Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's register nor the custodians' rolls give many more.

## The rite of the rock face

Every hewer's son on the hill learned the old words said at the rock face before a man puts his pick in before he learned to swing. The custodians had kept the vein since An Aois Naomh by the handful and the measure, eleven baskets and not twelve, and the crews of A' Chompanaidh's pits went on keeping what they could of that under the ton. Two pit-mouth shrines held the rite in the strangers' years. At Cill dhìreach, a temple village of Macha at the edge of the workings, the crews left the first piece of coal from every new gallery, and A' Chompanaidh suffered it since it cost a stone a gallery. At Cill ghlas the custodians kept the old rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting while A' Chompanaidh's pits deepened round them; it was the last shrine in the district the crews still visited on the old feasts, and there the custodians met to agree the word *fuil-ghuail* for the physicians' book. Scàineadh Cill ghlas swallowed the cutting and the shrine together. The custodians' roll set the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead.

When Tolley's letter-book blamed A' Phlàigh Uaine on the dust, the Dia-thìreach custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order, the camps heard of it, and the coal set on the breast of the dead for the going-down went on being set.

## The hawk

Òrd an t-Seabhaig keeps Mòd, An Seabhag Acrach of Acaill, who starves those that eat faster than the land can feed them. Its houses lie along Bàgh an t-Seabhaig at Seann Skell, Ros gheal and Ros leathan, and inland at Cnoc bheag, whose priests asked Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise for Wren's grammar to read what the humans wrote of them and filled its margins.

Murchadh Seabhag preached Mòd's hunger at Seann Skell in the first decades of the strangers, and his sermon, copied and carried to the camps, was the first writing of the Dia-thìrich A' Chompanaidh ever seized. Henry Maddox barred the hawk-priests from the camps because their preaching slowed the work, and the overseers enforced it, though several of them were hawk-faithful. The camps carried the sermons in themselves instead, and in A' Phlàigh Uaine the overseers' reports list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a matter for punishment; they went back up as fast as they were taken down. The fishing families of Ros gheal twice chased A' Chompanaidh's customs officer off their harbour.

In the years of Am Fiabhras Glas Ìomhar Seabhag preached at Seann Skell that Mòd's hunger had turned on those who had eaten the hill. The hawk-shrines of the west became meeting-houses for Faire nan Lòchran, and the shrine to Mòd that Ros gheal raised on its harbour wall was built again three times in a season after the constables ordered it down. At Inis bhàn the hawk-priests sat down in disputation with the last keepers of the druid questions, the first time in living memory, and settled nothing. In the war Ìomhar declared from the shrine at Seann Skell that the war was Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it; the hawk-shrines became mustering houses, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe carried the council's letters to them, and the company of the hawk-faithful held the road north of Ros bheag.

## Scoiltean nan Draoidhean

The masters of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean taught by question and disputation, and their hall at Dùn thais was the last of the old schools to teach in the open. They received Samuel Wren for a winter: he asked them why the vein should be holy, and they asked him why his fuel should be burned, and neither telling of that winter names a winner. About the fiftieth year the master Aonghas mac Coinnich put to his students a question the school's register calls new, why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal that every Dia-thìreach child sees, and did not answer it; his students carried it to the hall of disputation at Baile Mòr uaine, whose record of the argument runs to four hundred leaves. A generation later George Tolley shut the hall at Dùn thais over a lecture on whether that blindness was a kind of sickness. The masters taught in their own houses and under the trees of the sacred forest of Flidais near Muileann chiar, and held their last open disputation on the threshing-floor at Doire chiar on the eve of Bealltainn, on whether a question may be forbidden. Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, the last master to teach openly, died at Dùn thais, and the school's register ends with her death. In Am Fiabhras Glas the old houses of the masters at Dùn thais were opened as sick-rooms.

## Macha and the blessing of the coin

Òrd Mhacha, the order of the capital and the crown, keeps the rite of Macha's two horses, Dubh Sainglenn the black and Liath Macha the grey, each of which, the order teaches, has its due. At Tolley's asking its priests at Cathair dhearg blessed Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's new coin. Fearghas mac Mhuirich would not stand for the blessing, and he and the priests who refused with him left the capital's temple and settled in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag near Cnoc bheag. There they kept the older reading of the two horses, lit their fire of hazel under the oaks with both halves of the words said in the old order, and took in custodians who had lost their seats. Fearghas said the blessing over Artair mac Iain with both horses named.

The priests who stayed in the capital's temple and had blessed the coin opened their floor to Comhairle a' Chùraim when Strake locked the council hall, and sheltered there the custodians who had petitioned against the coin they had blessed. The dissenters in the forest took in Comhairle na Coille of the mining country and sat at its fires. At the close of the age the order stood in two halves under one goddess, and neither half had unsaid anything.

## Òrd na Cloiche, Manannan and the old rites

Òrd na Cloiche keeps the stone Lia Fàil at Inis thais, which cries out under the rightful king, and the oldest shrines of the order at Cnoc àrsaidh on Imrich nam Pantar. It declined the joint council of Baile dhìreach, took no part in the strikes, and would send no men to the war, since that was not what Òrd na Cloiche was for; but it shut Inis thais's harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships and opened an Fhianna's roads to the hawk-faithful.

Òrd Mhanannain keeps the harbours. The traders of the order founded Baile dhìreach, the whale-boats of Àth fhionn thanked Manannan for each whale, and at Ceann mhòr the priests of the order kept Oidhche Glaise with the human fishing families of the concession. When Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise reported that human labourers near Baile chrom kept vigil by night in the fields under the sign of a grey goose, which they called an Gèadh Fiadhaich, the priests of Manannan at Ceann mhòr answered that the practice owed something to the Dia-thìrich, but to their own harbours and not to Baile chrom. Hannah Webb, who first kept it alone behind a byre, said only that they kept the sky.

The ancestor rite of the old roads is kept at Àth fhionn and along the coast at Caol ìseal; Na Seann Spioradan, the oldest folk rite of the island, at Baile ghorm. The strangers left all of them alone, having never learned where they were kept.

## The keeper and nighean an rìgh

In the camps of the hill the washing-women of Achadh dhomhain said of a girl of the spoil-houses that she did not grow, and called her *nighean an rìgh*, meaning Ailean Mòr, whom the gods crowned in the grove; most who said it did not believe a word of the thousands of years, or said they did not. The custodians met at the shrine of Cill ghlas and agreed a plain word for the change for the physicians' book, *fuil-ghuail*, coal-blood, and wrote it in their columns against four names by the close of the age, and reported none of them to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir. The camps said a person who kept their youth past its season had *Aisling-aois*. Cailean mac Eachainn found the girl's line in the roll of the camp at Àth ìseal, written seven names back, and Clann na Ceiste at Tobar dhìreach told him whose son the last of them was. The camps told the rest as the camps tell things, and the rolls kept only the names.

# Appendix C — Strikes, Sicknesses and Cogadh nam Beann

An Aois Choigreach was not an age of armies until its last two years. For a hundred and forty-seven years Riaghaltas nan Coigreach kept no standing force of its own until Merriman brought his constables, and the Dia-thìrich kept none at all. What killed people in those years was sickness, hunger and the pits, and what the crews had to answer with was the stopping of work. This appendix sets down, as the custodians' rolls and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's registers give them, the sicknesses and hungers of the age, the strikes and the stoppage, the constables and their posts, and the fighting of Cogadh nam Beann, with the dead where the rolls count them. Where Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's count and the custodians' differ, both are given.

## The sicknesses

| Sickness | Years | Where | Dead, as counted |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fiabhras nan Coigreach | 9 | Cuan shean and the west coast | 91 Dia-thìrich, 11 humans |
| An Casad Tioram | 26 | the camps at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich | 38, most of them boys at the breaking |
| A' Bhreac Bhallach | 39 | Ros dhomhain, Rathad na Mèinne and the camps; Baile chiar | 406 by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's count; more by the custodians' |
| An Scàird Fhuilteach | 59 | the quays of Ros dhomhain; Seann Vell | under 200 at Ros dhomhain |
| A' Phlàigh Uaine | 73–76 | 26 settlements of the mining country | uncounted whole; 40 in the first month at Achadh dhomhain |
| The drought-fever | 109 | Baile Mòr ruadh; Cnoc shean | 17 at Baile Mòr ruadh |
| Grodadh nan Scamhan | from 119 | the night crews at Cnoc chaol and Baile thais | slow, and never counted as one sickness |
| Am Fiabhras Glas | 138–140 | the whole island; returning in the north-west | the camps worst; one household in three at Tobar fhiadhaich |

**Fiabhras nan Coigreach** came ashore with a crowded ship at Cuan shean and ran down the west coast. It killed the custodian of Baile àrsaidh and both her sons, in a town where no human lived at all, and the custodians of the west took note of it. Cuan shean shut itself to ships for a season, and Pell protested in writing. At Cnoc àrsaidh the townsfolk blocked the road with carts and turned back every traveller, and the fever never reached them; Riaghaltas nan Coigreach fined them for hindering trade, and they paid in wool.

**An Casad Tioram**, the coughing sickness, was a dry cough among the boys who broke coal at the pit-mouth. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's surgeon called it a winter complaint, and it lasted through the summer. Cill thais took in the orphans at its own custodians' cost; A' Chompanaidh, asked to give toward the house, sent a crate of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's primers.

**A' Bhreac Bhallach** came ashore at Ros dhomhain on a ship of A' Chompanaidh and climbed Rathad na Mèinne into the camps, worst in the huts at Àth ìseal and at Achadh dhomhain. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise counted four hundred and six dead, and the custodians wrote the difference between their count and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's in the margin of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's list. At Baile chiar in the south the custodians cut the names of their dead into the stone lintel of the shrine.

**An Scàird Fhuilteach** broke out in the crowded quarters by the Ros dhomhain quays. Anne Colby made a sick-house of the chapel. The coal barges carried it to Seann Vell, whose custodians shut the only quay the town had for the coal traffic and paid A' Chompanaidh's fine from the purse that had buried their dead.

**A' Phlàigh Uaine** began at Achadh dhomhain: a greenish pallor, then a cough that brought up dark dust, then weakness. It spread from the camp to Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and wider along the coal roads. At Cnoc naomh the dead filled the old shrine's burial ground and then a field that was never ploughed again; at Àth ghlas Sìne Ruadh had every hut where a death had been burned with its bedding, and the sickness stopped sooner there than anywhere. Nathaniel Bright began to weigh the dust in the lungs of the dead at Muileann chrom and never finished his table. Àrd-mhaor Crane, who walked the sick-rows, died of it. Tolley blamed the dust, the custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines.

**The drought-fever** followed Tiormachd Achadh shean into the towns. At Baile Mòr ruadh the wells had been deepened into the old middens, and Coll of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise named the cause rightly. Cnoc shean closed its one well and drank from carts for a year.

**Grodadh nan Scamhan** was a wasting of the lungs among the night crews, slower than A' Phlàigh Uaine. A' Chompanaidh paid the families of the dead a fixed sum and entered it under the cost of the working. The old women of the camps called the cough that the kin of the coal-blood lived through Casad Dhonnchaidh, after Aisling's father.
