**Am Fiabhras Glas** was a fever of the chest that came in on the ships and killed the young and strong more than the old. It shut the market at Cathair mhòr for the first time in the town's memory, took Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's physician at Dùn thais and two of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's nurses, and came back to settle in the north-west, where it killed humans as readily as Dia-thìrich; at Cathair gheal the two peoples' sick lay in one ward. Muileann fhionn shut its roads for a season; Tobar fhiadhaich lost one household in three and burned no huts.

## The hungers

**The short hunger** in the hills came in the thirtieth year, when the men were drawn from the farms into the pits and the oats of the hill villages rotted in the rain with none at home to cut ahead of it. The meal-carts came from Doire fhiadhaich by the custom of An Aois Naomh.

**Gorta Baile chrom** followed a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements of the north-west from the ninety-fourth year, made worse because An Togail had taken one in five of the grown folk to the pits. It was worst at Baile chrom, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields. Doire ghlas sent its young folk to the camps for the ration; Inis mhin ate its seed corn in the second winter and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise fed three hundred a day at the harbour; at Seann Bhrenn the custodians opened the grain-pits of An Aois Naomh. A relief ship from an Tìr Thall lay a month at Ros dhomhain while Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and A' Chompanaidh disputed who should pay for its unloading.

**Tiormachd Achadh shean** lay on the east three dry seasons together from the hundred and sixth year to the hundred and tenth: ten districts of drought country, cattle driven west in a column a day long, the herds of Baile chaol slaughtered, and the coal tally not lowered.

## The strikes and the stoppage

**Stad-oibre Baile thais**, the eleven days of the seventy-seventh year and the first stoppage of the age: Catrìona nic Eachainn called the halt when A' Chompanaidh would not close the gallery A' Phlàigh Uaine had come out of, and it ended when the food ran out. After it A' Chompanaidh built its own granary at Muileann chrom and forbade the camps to keep grain beyond a week's ration.

**Stad-oibre Cnoc chaol** at Cnoc chaol, in the hundred and seventeenth year: the crews refused the night shift, and within the week were replaced by crews brought from the coast through Muileann dhomhain, whose townsfolk turned them from every door. Faire nan Lòchran's purse ran dry keeping the strikers fed.

**Stad-oibre a' Chalaidh** at Ros dhomhain, in the hundred and thirty-fourth year: Dia-thìrich and human dockers refused to load coal for nine days over the new berth charges, the only strike of the age in which the two peoples stood together. Merriman broke it and shipped the human dockers over the sea. The dockers of Seann Vell refused the coal sent round to them and were not hired again for two years.

**Là Stad nan Sloc**, in the hundred and forty-third year: on one day, at a beacon lit on the hill above Doire mhòr, every working of the Muileann chrom district halted, and with them Baile thais, Cnoc chaol, the silver town, the north-eastern pits at Muileann bheag and the quarrymen of Cnoc gheal, unasked. It ended when the constables shut A' Chompanaidh's stores in every district at once. Forty crew-leaders were taken; thirty-two were let go without charge.

## The constables

Charles Merriman landed with a small company of armed constables in the hundred and thirty-second year, the first standing force Riaghaltas nan Coigreach kept on the island. His first posts were at Muileann shean on the northern coal road and Tobar ghorm near the northern workings. After the fight at Muileann chrom he tripled the constables and posted companies at Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, each with a walled store, paid from the tithe, and built a barracks at Dùn chrom for two hundred men. Lionel Strake, a soldier, added patrols on the western roads out of Ros bheag.

## Cogadh nam Beann

**The companies of the council** were the crews of the pits under their own crew-leaders, armed at first with pikes and felling-axes and the rifles of the stores they took, and later with the pike-heads and tin-cased powder of Uilleam Gobha's forge at Muileann dhearg. **Comann an Airgid's riflemen**, armed through the raiders of the eastern waters, held the east with the riflemen raised at Cnoc leathan. **The company of the hawk-faithful** mustered at Seann Skell under Ìomhar Seabhag's eye and held the road between Ros bheag and the north-west; **Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe**, seven men of the river towns under the lead hawk cast from the cartridges of Muileann chrom, carried the council's letters to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig and stood in that company's first rank. Against them Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had its constables, A' Chompanaidh's guards, a few ships, and what came from over the sea, which was one ship with dispatches and some crates of cartridges.

The rolls give the war's course thus:

- **28 an Gearran, AE 149.** The store at Muileann chrom taken at first light by Mòrag nic Iain Maor's crews; eleven constables yield without a shot. The coal quay at Ceann fhada taken, and two loaded barges sunk across its mouth.
- **The same spring.** Sèist Baile thais: the constables of Baile thais hold the walled pithead eleven days and yield on the twelfth when the well fails; thirty-one are marched to the coast unharmed on Eilidh nic Raghnaill's word. The northern pits rise with the posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm. The capital rises: the council hall retaken, the bridge held three days with carts, the warehouse at Cathair dhomhain emptied. Muileann mhin argues three days and sends its boats to the council. Strake fortifies Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and A' Chompanaidh's quarter of the harbour. The road cut at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr.
- **Blàr Àth chiar.** At the ford, Major Peter Ashdown's column meets the crews of Baile thais on the far bank and falls back with forty lost and its baggage taken; the rebels lose nineteen. Dùn chrom shuts its gates on the barracks as the column passes.
- **The east cleared.** Comann an Airgid declares for the council; the post at Dùn ìseal yields after one exchange of fire; Cnoc leathan's riflemen hold the eastern road; Dùn dhearg reads its declaration; Ros fhionn stops its pumps.
- **Winter, AE 149–150.** Loscadh Seann Toll: a steamship of A' Chompanaidh shells the coal stage at Seann Toll, and twenty-three die. Inis mhòr burns A' Chompanaidh's coal on its quays; the fishing boats of both Seann Chwen burn a coaster at anchor. The southern beacons go dark, Tobar dhearg first by Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill's own hand, then Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal; two ships of A' Chompanaidh are lost on the reefs.
- **Spring and summer, AE 150.** Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe walks to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig in six days. The hawk-shrines open and the hawk company musters at Seann Skell. Cathair gheal shuts its gates and asks to be left alone. The lines hold: the council has the hills, the east and the capital; Strake Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, the harbour quarter and the western ports.
- **An t-Iuchar to an t-Sultain, AE 150.** The burning of the tithe-books, in three raids: the counting-house at Ros dhomhain, the tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, the weigh-house at Muileann chrom. Blàr Cnoc ghorm: the sally from the harbour driven back, the last Riaghaltas nan Coigreach made. The harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain opens its lower gates to the council; A' Chompanaidh's flying machine is burned in its shed; Cuan uaine opens its quays. Strake leaves Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir by water on the twenty-first of an t-Sultain, and Buidhnean na Comhairle find it stripped next morning, its letter-books whole.
- **An Dàmhair to an Dùbhlachd, AE 150.** Ros bheag the last seat, with outposts at Ros àrsaidh; hunger, and the stores opened to both peoples. Fosadh Àth àrsaidh. The columns go north under the council's guard; no column is attacked on the road.
- **1 am Faoilleach, AE 151.** The war ends, and An t-Aiseag is shut.

# Appendix D — Two Dates on Every Page: Reckoning, Coin and Measure

The strangers changed how the island counted three things: time, value and coal. They changed none of them by proclamation. Each change came in on paper, in a treaty or a contract or a schedule written in the humans' tongue, and each was taken up first by the clerks who had to settle the paper and only afterwards by anyone else. By the close of the age every page the custodians wrote carried two dates, most of the island's trade went by a coin it had not struck, and the hill that had once been measured by the handful was weighed by the ton. This appendix sets down those three reckonings as they stood when the rolls came down to Muileann chaol.

## The two dates

Before the ships the custodians dated their rolls by their year of An Diosal, counted from An Diosal of Cabhlach an Scaraidh, and by the moon. They reckoned time by nights and not by days: the night went before its day, a feast began at dusk on its eve, and a debt of ten nights fell due at the tenth dusk. The year began at Samhain with the dark half of the year and held twelve moons of thirty nights and twenty-nine in turn, each begun on the night of the full and turning at the dark: Samhnas, Dubhlas, Faolach, Gearras, Sìolach the seed-time, Bearnach the gap, Bealltach, Ògach, Teasach, Lùghnas, Pailteach and Damhrach the stags' moon. About every thirtieth moon the keepers of the reckoning put in a thirteenth, Eadrach, the between-moon, at the year's end, so that Samhain should not come round before the summer was over.

The humans' calendar was fixed to the sun and paid no heed to the moon. Its year began in the dead of winter and had twelve months of set lengths; they counted by days from midnight, divided the month into weeks of seven days, and numbered their years from an epoch in their own land that no scribe of the island set down. In the season of speech-making Samuel Wren drew his year for Gormshuil nic Fhearchair as a wheel cut into twelve, and she set her moons against his months one by one, as near as they would go. When she drew the thirteenth moon he could find nowhere on the wheel to put it, and wrote it in the margin with the humans' sign for a question after it. That wheel, which survives in Wren's list in Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's letter-books, is the first writing on Dia-thìr in which the two reckonings meet.

Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg, in the eighth year, was dated by the humans' day, month and year alone. The custodians entered it in their roll under its year of An Diosal and the moon in which it was signed, and left the day to Riaghaltas nan Coigreach. So it went with Puingean a' Chalaidh, Cairt na Companaidh and every contract for the pits. From those years the custodians' clerks wrote the humans' year at the head of each page and its year of An Diosal beneath it, and kept the moon in the margin where the roll needed it; the copyists of Seilear Muileann chaol, making their fair copies, set the two years side by side and it is from them that the practice takes its name, *the two dates*. A contract that fell due on a day of the humans' month could not be settled by the moon, and the clerks who settled such contracts went over to the humans' months first and to the humans' new year after. By the third change of coin, in the hundred and twenty-ninth year, every contract on the island ran from am Faoilleach, and the civil year of the Dia-thìrich had moved to the humans' beginning without any decree.

The humans' months took Dia-thìris names in the clerks' mouths, most of them from the moon Wren's wheel set beside each: am Faoilleach from Faolach the wolf-moon, an Gearran from Gearras the short moon, an Cèitean for the first of summer as Bealltach was, an t-Ògmhios the young month, an t-Iuchar the hot month, an Lùnastal from Lùghnas, an Dàmhair from Damhrach, an t-Samhain from Samhnas and an Dùbhlachd from Dubhlas, the black month. Am Màrt and an t-Sultain the clerks took from the humans' own names for them; an Giblean no one could explain, and the old folk said it meant the gap, as Bearnach had. The old folk went on calling am Màrt the seed-time and an t-Sultain the month of plenty through all the age. An Gearran takes a twenty-ninth day every fourth year, as the humans' calendar has it; the moon-year had no such day and needed none, since the between-moon did its work.

The moon-year did not die. It kept the four fire-feasts, each on the first night of its moon, in the shrines and the hill villages; it was taught as the old reckoning in the custodians' school at Inis bhàn from the fifty-second year; and the hewers of the hill kept their rest on the nights of the full and the dark as they always had. Cunntas an Riaghaltais in the hundred and twenty-second year and its register in the hundred and twenty-seventh were dated by the humans' reckoning alone.

## The week

The week came to the island with A' Chompanaidh's contracts before it came with Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise. The first contracts paid their crews by the week and let them rest on the humans' day of rest, so that the Dia-thìrich who worked for A' Chompanaidh learned the week before any of them was christened. When Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise raised its chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain in the thirteenth year and opened its school in the fifty-first, it taught the week with its prayers, and its first converts named the days. Gormshuil had counted Wren's absent mornings on her fingers, one in seven, and written the seven names into her list with the thing she knew of each beside it, which for six of them was nothing.

The hewers made less of the difference than Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise did. Matthew Dunne, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's own minister at Ros dhomhain, told A' Chompanaidh against Àithne na h-Oidhche that the Dia-thìrich were right that even the ground must rest, and was recalled over the sea for it.

## The coin

**The mark and its hundred pence.** The humans' coin was brought in beside the old barter in the seventeenth year, for ease, it was said. The coins were struck at Ros dhomhain from silver and copper shipped from an Tìr Thall, and the first striking bore a ship on one face and nothing of Dia-thìr on either. Within ten years nothing that needed a tool from over the sea could be had for anything else. Cathair mhòr refused the mark for a whole year and gave way when the tool-sellers would not cross its bridge; at the market of Cathair dhearg the tool-sellers took only marks while cloth and fish still went by barter, and the custodians' clerks began to keep two sets of books and complained of it in both. The market's clerk Tadhg kept the dues by the old reckoning in his left-hand book, so many fleeces and so many creels, and by the mark in his right-hand book, ruled in the humans' manner.

**Silver for marks.** From the eighty-third year Comann an Airgid of Muileann chiar sold bar silver to A' Chompanaidh for marks at a price the guild set, the only ware on the island in the age priced by Dia-thìrich hands.

**The blessing and the second change.** In the eighty-fifth year, at George Tolley's asking, the priests of Macha at Cathair dhearg blessed Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's new coin, and in the eighty-sixth the barter goods of the Dia-thìrich were marked down against the coin a second time, on terms Riaghaltas nan Coigreach alone set.

**The third change.** In the hundred and twenty-ninth year the old barter was struck down as lawful payment altogether, and every bargain on the island went by the humans' coin. The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish had changed hands without coin since before An t-Aiseag, were shut by order, and a clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir wrote that the ledgers were now complete for the first time. The fishwives of Inis mhòr took no coin for a week and gave their fish away. The hill villages borrowed marks at interest from A' Chompanaidh's stores to buy seed, and within a few years most of the villages of Muileann chrom owed A' Chompanaidh more than a year's crop. The old barter market at Muileann òg closed after its last season. Barter went on regardless in quiet corners the clerks never reached, cloth for fish at the steps of Inis mhòr and a day's labour for a day's milk between crofts, and at the end of the age the wool merchants of Caol leathan were selling inland by barter again, against the law.

## The measure of coal

Before the strangers the coal of the hill was measured and counted, but never weighed. The custodians kept the vein by the handful and the basket: a hewer's measure in the season of the handful, eleven baskets to a cutting and not twelve. The first contract of the eleventh year paid the crew of thirty at Muileann chrom by the ton, in iron tools and lamp-oil, and from then on A' Chompanaidh's steelyard stood at every pit-head. The weigh-house at Muileann chrom kept the steelyard ledgers, in which the coal of the hill was entered by the ton from the first contract to the last, until they burned green in the hundred and fiftieth year. The ton was the humans' weight, and the island had no word of its own for so much coal in one place.

A' Chompanaidh measured its crews by the tally, the yield each working was bound to raise in a season. The tally was not lowered for A' Phlàigh Uaine, nor for the drought, nor for the night shift, and when the custodians of the east petitioned Robert Haskins against it in the drought each was told that the matter was under consideration.

Nathaniel Bright, Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's physician, kept one other weighing: from the seventy-fifth year he weighed the dust in the lungs of the dead at Muileann chrom, in a table he never finished. His book, with its broken-off row, was filed at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir and never taken up again.

## The tithe

Riaghaltas nan Coigreach took a share of all the coal mined on the island, the tithe, paid to it by A' Chompanaidh and entered against every settlement of the hills in the tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh. The first schedule set it at one part in five. In the fifty-seventh year Arthur Lisle's schedule raised it to one part in three, and what the Dia-thìrich received did not rise with it; the custodians had their copy in the humans' tongue with a rendering made by a pupil of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise. In the next year the tithe-gatherers at Dùn fhiadhaich began to weigh grain as well as coal, saying the farms fed the pits, and the custodians' roll called it the tithe on the tithe. Robert Haskins ordered the council consulted on the tithe and set it before the council met. From the hundred and fortieth year the constables were paid from it.

In the war the rebels burned the tithe ledgers in three raids, at the counting-house of Ros dhomhain, the tithe-house of Ceann àrsaidh and the weigh-house of Muileann chrom. The custodian of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared to keep the record entire, and his townsfolk refused him.

## The daybooks

The five lights kept a count of their own. Each keeper wrote a daybook every night of the year: the wind, the oil, the wick, the ships seen and their bearing. The first was begun at Àth dhearg by Tormod mac Pheadair, and A' Chompanaidh's clerk who read it called its keeper civil but of no assistance. Because the daybooks were kept every night by the same hand in the same plain words, the copyists of Muileann chaol leaned on them wherever the other witnesses quarrelled, and dated by them what the rolls left undated. It is from Lachlann mac Uisdein's daybook at Baile chrom that the day and the hour of the last Àrd-mhaor's leaving are known. On the nights when no ship passed, the keepers wrote three words, first at Baile chrom and then along the whole coast: *Cha tàinig long*, no ship came. In the last winter of the age they wrote them every night.

# Appendix E — Words of An Aois Choigreach

The age that began with a cup and a loaf held up across a table ended with two peoples who could each say the other's word for most things and still did not always mean the same by it. Gormshuil nic Fhearchair and Samuel Wren made some hundreds of words on each side in their first season, near enough even by the council clerk's count, and the island went on making words for the strangers' things, and for what the strangers did, through all the hundred and fifty years. This appendix gives the words of the age that the rolls and the camps kept, as they were used at its close. Words the island already had are given only where the age changed their meaning.

## The forty colours

On the morning of the basket Gormshuil laid broken coal on the table between herself and Wren and named its colours one by one, as any child of the hills could have done: the green that lies under the black like deep water under weed, *uaine*, and the word for that green and no other, which is not the green of grass nor of the sea; the red at a fresh break that deepens if you breathe on it; the grey-violet of the old cuttings that no dyer has matched; the brown that shows a piece came from near the surface; the blue that runs along a split edge like the light on a mackerel's back; colours like heather in Lùnastal, the dark of a blackberry and rust on a nail left out in the rain; the ember before it goes grey and the ember after; a hair-line like gold; and a sheen like a pigeon's neck, with a word for each of the two colours it shows and a third for the piece that shows both. She gave forty. There were more. She stopped because Wren had stopped writing. He tapped the whole heap with his pen and wrote one word for all of it.

The first leaf of Muireall's fair copy holds the forty words in the left-hand column and, in the right-hand column where Wren's words should stand, nothing but a note at the foot saying what happened. It is the most handled leaf in the cellar. Nine years later Raghnall, guiding the prospectors, named the colours at a fresh break for Hugh Mercer, *gual donn-ruadh* where the red ran into the brown and *gual airgid* for the sheen, and Mercer nodded the way a man nods at a child who has shown him a pebble. Aonghas mac Coinnich's question at Dùn thais, why the humans cannot see what every Dia-thìreach child sees, was never answered in the age.

## Words for the strangers and their things

**an Tìr Thall** · "the land beyond". The strangers named their homeland in their own tongue, but no scribe of the island wrote the word down. From the first season the scribes called it an Tìr Thall, and its people simply the humans.

**an Eaglais** · the humans' faith, from the word their priests used of the whole company of their believers. The son of their god the scribes wrote *Crìosd*, as the clerics said it.

**A' Chompanaidh** · the Company, the trading house that Edmund Harrow and Thomas Pike founded under licence, which held the pits.

**Riaghaltas nan Coigreach** · "the government of the strangers", the Administration.

**An t-Àrd-mhaor** · "the high steward", the Commissioner; his house above Ros dhomhain was **Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir**, the Residency.

**Puingean a' Chalaidh** · "the points of the harbour", the Harbour Articles of the nineteenth year, which fixed the dues and anchorages of Ros dhomhain in A' Chompanaidh's favour. Gormshuil refused them.

**maor** · "steward". Under A' Chompanaidh, a Dia-thìreach set over Dia-thìrich crews, with a staff and a slate roof. The byname Raghnall Maor was given at a mill door by a woman who said, loud enough to carry, "There goes Raghnall Maor to his castle," and the hill kept it for four generations.

**mòine** · peat. The island's old word, which Wren learned over a brazier; beside it Gormshuil wrote what he told her of *the black stone the humans dig in their own country and burn on their hearths*. It was one line among two hundred, and she thought nothing of it.

**seachdain** · the week, which came with A' Chompanaidh's contracts and the prayers of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise. The island had never before divided time by seven.

**Eadrach** · the between-moon. Wren could find no place for it on his wheel and wrote it in the margin with a question after it.

**eun-iarainn** · "the iron bird", A' Chompanaidh's flying machine, which went the length of the working districts in the winter of the hundred and forty-seventh year. By evening of the day it first flew over Muileann chrom every hearth had the word, borrowed from nowhere and understood at once. The old women said a bird that did not beat its wings had no soul in it and could carry none away.

## Words the age made for itself

**fuil-ghuail** · "coal-blood". The plain word the custodians agreed at the shrine of Cill ghlas, fit for the physicians' book, for the change that had come upon some children of the camps, so that they did not grow as others do. The humans rendered it *coal-touched*. The custodians wrote it in their columns against four names by the close of the age, and reported none of them to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir.

**nighean an rìgh** · "the king's daughter". What the washing-women of Achadh dhomhain called the girl of the spoil-houses who did not grow, meaning Ailean Mòr, whom the gods crowned in the grove; half in jest, and as the seasons went by, half not.

**Aisling-aois** · "Aisling-age". The camps' word for anyone who kept their youth past its season, the kind of word boys use for a thing they are half afraid of and wholly certain will never touch them.

**Tìodhlac a' Choimhdich** · "the Keeper's gift". What the camps called the change, holding that it was the gift of Coimhdeach na Fine woken in the first king's line. The rolls do not use the phrase. The copyists of Muileann chaol found that the line itself stood written, seven names back.

**A' Phlàigh Uaine** · "the green plague", the Green Death of the seventy-third year, named for the greenish pallor it gave its dead.

**Gorta Baile chrom** · the Great Hunger of the north-west, named for the town where it was worst, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields.

**Tiormachd Achadh shean** · the Long Drought, named for the town whose wells failed first.

**Scàineadh Cill ghlas** · "the Rending of Cill ghlas", the collapse of the hill under the old cutting in the hundred and thirty-seventh year.

**Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe** · "the company of the leaden hawk", the seven of Cuan dhearg who carried the council's letters to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig, each with a hawk cast in lead from the cartridges of Muileann chrom at his throat.

## Names the age gave

The rolls of the age named its places, papers and griefs in Dia-thìris, as the island names everything; the humans' own names for the same things are given here beside them, once.

**Dath a' Ghuail** · "the colour of the coal". What every Dia-thìreach child sees in broken coal and no human ever did; the name the copyists of Muileann chaol gave their fair copy of the age's rolls.

**Linn an Acair** · "the era of the anchor", the Anchor Era. The count of years the custodians kept from the first ship's anchor off Cuan shean; the rolls of the age are dated by it beside the year of An Diosal.

**Coinneachadh nan Long** · "the meeting of the ships". The two boats of Achadh àrsaidh meeting Na Trì Longan off the north-west cape, where the age begins.

**Clàr nan Dà Fhichead Dath** · "the list of the forty colours". Gormshuil nic Fhearchair's first leaf, the forty words for the colours of broken coal, with the humans' column left empty.

**Taigh nan Dìlleachdan** · "the house of the orphans". The house at Cill thais where the orphans of An Casad Tioram were kept at the custodians' own cost.

**Scoil na Teachdaireachd** · "the school of the Mission". The school of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise at Ros dhomhain, where Barabal nic Dhùghaill and Iain Maor learned the humans' letters.

**Cairt Chathair gheal** · "the charter of Cathair gheal". The market charter of the concession town, the only one of the age that names no custodian.

**Crann-tomhais a' Chalaidh** · "the weighing-beam of the harbour", the steelyard at Ros dhomhain. From its day a hewer's work was what the beam said it was.

**Sìol-lann na Companaidh** · "the Company's granary". The granary at Muileann chrom built against a stoppage after Stad-oibre Baile thais, with its rule of a week's ration and no more.

**Cùmhnant an Airgid** · "the covenant of the silver", the Silver Compact. The agreement Ùna nic Choinnich signed with Arthur Lisle in both tongues, which left the silver to the guild; it lay in the guild chest under three locks.

**Comann an Adhlacaidh** · "the fellowship of burial", the burial club. The society of Baile thais and Cnoc chaol that bought ground and a box for the dead of the pits, under whose cover Faire nan Lòchran met.

**Riaghailt Dunstan** · Dunstan's rule, a human's name kept as written. The ruling of the magistrate Oliver Dunstan in the case of Thomas Hale, that customary rights descend only through the line Riaghaltas nan Coigreach owns; under it eleven customary cuttings passed to A' Chompanaidh, and Mairead nic Aoidh stopped entering marriages in the roll.

**Lagh na h-Aon Loidhne** · "the law of one line". The humans' rule that land passes down a single line of heirs, against the island's way of holding by the whole kin.

**Slighe a' Ghuail** · "the way of the coal", the coal line. A' Chompanaidh's iron road from the pits at Muileann chrom by Cathair dhearg to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain; its engines burned the island's own coal, and the carters of Doire chaol lost the long haul.

**Na Trì Teaghlaichean** · "the three households". The three copying families of Muileann chaol who kept the cellar's rolls, winter on winter.

**Seilear Muileann chaol** · "the cellar at Muileann chaol". Where the copies of the custodians' rolls were kept from the reach of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and where Cailean mac Eachainn found the line.

**Sloinneadh Aisling** · "the line of Aisling". The seven names of Aisling's father's line found written in the roll of Àth ìseal, as the custodians write a marriage.

**An Acair Uaine** · "the green acre". The plague-field beyond the spoil-heaps of Achadh dhomhain, named by no one on purpose.

**An Dithis a Nigh Còmhla** · "the two who washed together". The camps' name for Anne Colby and Beitris Bhàn, who washed the dead of A' Phlàigh Uaine side by side.

**A' Chiad Athchuinge** · "the first petition". The first written grievance the custodians laid before Riaghaltas nan Coigreach acting together and not settlement by settlement, drafted over three days at Ceann àrsaidh; it was not answered, and An Dàrna Athchuinge followed it.

**Leabhar Baile thais** · "the book of Baile thais", the book of grievances. The book of complaints set down at Baile thais by many hands over some years: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. It went to Muileann chaol in the four chests at the close of the age.

**Coinneachadh an Fhearainn** and **Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh** · "the meeting of the land" and "the meeting of the moor". The standing stone on the moor road where the custodians of Muileann dhomhain lent the dispossessed their poorest common land, and the place above Cnoc naomh where the crew-leaders of the northern pits fixed the week of their rising and left a cairn of spoil-stones.

**Cnoc an Rabhaidh** · "the hill of the warning". The hill above Doire mhòr where the beacon of Là Stad nan Sloc was lit.

**an Spiorad Naomh** and **am Bìoball** · "the Holy Spirit" and "the Bible". Words of An Eaglais the scribes took as they heard them; the priests of Manannan found the wild goose of an Spiorad Naomh in their own harbours.

**An Dealachadh** · "the parting", the Severance. The closing of An t-Aiseag at the end of the war, when the last ship went north and the humans' way over the sea was shut; the rolls also call it a' Scaradh.

## Sayings

*Cha tàinig long.* "No ship came." The line a keeper wrote in the daybook on a night with no ship to note, first at Baile chrom and then along the whole coast. By the last winter of the age it was habit more than grief; the sentence had outlived the asking it once answered.

*Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc.* "They burned the book, but they did not burn the hill." The verse the camp folk of Muileann chrom made while the steelyard ledgers were still burning green, sung by the market women of Ros dhomhain within the week without knowing where it came from.

*Further than a man can walk in one day.* Abel Stone's words for the black seam, the only words of the prospectors' walk the humans kept.

*Put what happened.* Gormshuil's answer to Muireall, asking what to write in the empty column beside the forty colours. The copyists of the cellar took it for their rule.

*I never told you a man lived four thousand years. I told you whose son he was.* Said by an old woman of Clann na Ceiste at Tobar dhìreach, of a line kept by people who had stopped expecting anyone would come asking for it; carried to Muileann chrom by a copyist.

*A debt kept on paper can always be raised again by whoever next holds the paper.* Said by a woman of Ceann àrsaidh whom the telling would not name, as the last ledger went on the fire.

*Write down that they were gentle about it.* Said by an old man lifted from his own doorstone at Doire mhòr under Àithne a' Ghlacaidh.

*We keep the sky.* Hannah Webb's answer when Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise asked what she kept in the fields at night.

*One town may be a trial, but two would be a rule.* The custodian of Inis thais, declining the joint council of Baile dhìreach.

*An empty seat answers no letters and signs no papers.* Said in the council, in the hearing of no clerk of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, in the years it chose no head.
